data.summary: Node for UAE Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 (establishment of the Insurance Authority and organisation of insurance operations, as amended), the primary statute cited as the legal basis for Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 25 of 2014 (Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies) and referenced in related CBUAE instruments. It is the enabling law defining the regulator, licensing of insurers, and the scope for executive regulations and board decisions. It binds insurance companies incorporated in the UAE and licensed foreign branches, together with agents and brokers operating in the State; supervisory functions have since transferred to the CBUAE.
lookup_terms: Executive Regulation Board Decision No. 2 of 2009

data.summary: Section 6 of the Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies sets the principles for organising accounting books and records of insurance companies, agents and brokers, and the data those books must contain. It prescribes minimum book types (ledgers, journals, technical accounting books), separation of books between Insurance of Persons/Fund Accumulation and Property and Liability operations, backup storage in a separate location, auditing of books, and the regulator's inspection and information-request powers. It binds licensed insurers (including foreign branches) and their agents and brokers.
lookup_terms: separate books life and general insurance

data.summary: Section 7 of the Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies governs the accounting policies to be adopted and the forms used to prepare and present reports and financial statements. It requires preparation under IFRS plus the Authority's policies and prescribed forms, separate plus consolidated statements where a company writes both Insurance of Persons/Fund Accumulation and Property and Liability business, bilingual annual submissions (Arabic and English) and Arabic quarterly submissions, and preserves the regulator's right to amend the prescribed forms. It binds licensed insurance companies, including UAE operations of foreign branches and related companies.

Concept node on External Auditor obligations under the Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies. It covers additional duties the regulator may impose (expanded audit scope, notification of financial violations, reservations on accounts or reserves, control and financial-statement deficiencies), protection of the auditor from breach-of-duty claims when performing those duties, strict independence criteria (no board, management, agency, kinship or competing interest), mandatory replacement if independence lapses, and signing/review requirements for quarterly (limited review, 45 days) and audited annual statements. It binds the insurance company and, through it, its appointed external auditor.

Concept node on internal audit and internal control expectations for insurance companies under the Financial Regulations, particularly around investment activities. It requires documented investment procedures under effective oversight, segregation of duties between execution, recording, authorisation, reconciliation and assurance, and audit procedures giving full coverage of investment activity; where performed internally, the audit function must be independent and report to the Audit Committee or its equivalent in a foreign insurance company's governance structure. It binds the insurance company's board and management.

Concept node on the Audit Committee in the insurance governance framework, as referenced across the Financial Regulations and related CBUAE instruments. It is the board-level body to which an internal audit function must report independently, and which works with the board-level Investment Committee to determine the scope of audit procedures covering investment activities and identifying internal control and system deficiencies. It binds the boards of licensed insurance companies, with an equivalent body required in the governance structure of foreign insurance company branches.

Concept node for the use of International Financial Reporting Standards as the mandatory accounting basis under the Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies. It fixes IFRS (with IASB/IFRIC interpretations) plus the Authority's own accounting policies and prescribed forms as the basis for preparing and disclosing financial statements, and sets out the required content of notes to the accounts. It binds licensed insurance companies, including those writing both persons/funds accumulation and property/liability business (which must produce separate and consolidated statements).

Node covering the prescribed financial statement forms in Appendix (1) of the Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies and the reporting articles that invoke them. It governs the format, signing, audit/limited review and submission deadlines for quarterly (45 days after quarter end) and annual reporting packs, including the board, actuary, auditor and management reports. Binding on insurance companies and branches of foreign insurers filing with the Authority; the appendix and addendums are an integral part of the regulations.

The Insurance Authority Board of Directors' Decision No. (41) of 2019 adopting the FinTech regulatory framework (supervisory rules for the experimental environment / sandbox) for the insurance sector. It adopts the annexed rules as integral, and empowers the Director General to amend them and to waive mandatory legislative requirements for participants within the scope and period of an acceptance letter. It binds insurance-sector licensees and FinTech firms seeking to test innovative solutions in the State.

Concept node for the FinTech experimental environment (sandbox) itself: eligible applicant categories, entry conditions and the safeguards applied during testing. Eligibility covers licensed Innovative Solutions Owners (whether or not the solution falls within their licence) and free-zone, national or foreign-branch FinTech companies, the latter only via partnership with an accountable licensed entity plus an acceptance letter. Testing conditions include customer disclosure of test status, AML/CTF controls, customer data protection and risk reporting.

Concept node for the acceptance letter that authorises entry into the insurance FinTech sandbox. It specifies the letter's mandatory content (approved solution summary, test period, approved tools, customer-protection measures), the Authority's right to suspend testing and withdraw the letter for breach of its conditions, and its evidentiary use with other financial services firms. Critically, the letter is not a licence to conduct the underlying business outside the sandbox and cannot be used to evade obligations.

Defined-party node for the Innovative Solution Owner, the participant admitted to the insurance FinTech experimental environment. It sets out that party's obligations: identifying and controlling risks from the solution, readiness and testing methodology, an exit plan protecting insureds and beneficiaries, periodic risk reporting, and compliance with Authority-imposed restrictions on customer numbers, transaction type and size, holding client funds and customer consents/disclosures.

Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 18 of 2020 (UAE), the Electronic Insurance Regulations, which govern insurance business conducted through websites, smart applications and other electronic/smart systems. It sets definitions (Company, Insurance-Related Professions, Insurance Proposer, Insurance Agent, Insurance Broker, Electronic Insurance Operations), the prior-approval regime including a board-approved action plan with volume projections and risk analysis (cyber, adverse selection, ML/TF, strategic risk), and defers to the federal electronic commerce and confidentiality laws for matters not specifically addressed. It binds licensed insurance companies (including branches of foreign insurers and Takaful companies), insurance-related professions, and bancassurance distribution to the extent relevant.

Chapter Four of the Electronic Insurance Regulations, governing insurers' and intermediaries' dealings with Price Comparison Websites. It prohibits companies and insurance-related professions from dealing with such websites except through Insurance Brokers, binds the insurer to the prices and coverage displayed, and imposes registration, corporate-purpose, activity-restriction and agreement-filing conditions on comparison sites (referral fee as lump sum only, no commission, no policy issuance or marketing, customer contact reserved to the broker), with escalating sanctions up to site blocking. It binds insurance companies, insurance brokers and the operators of registered comparison websites.

The defined term and scope concept of "Electronic Insurance Operations" – business carried out by an insurance company through electronic and smart systems – together with the related definitions and the Article (2) scope and Article (3) approval conditions. It determines which activities trigger the regulations and the prior Authority approval with a board-approved action plan covering projected volumes and risk mitigation. It binds licensed insurance companies and insurance-related professions conducting business electronically.

The website/smart-application obligations of the Electronic Insurance Regulations (Chapter Three, including Articles 7 and 10), covering governance and operational duties for the insurer's electronic channel. Requirements include establishing an IT department responsible for the official website, prior Authority approval before outsourcing website management, appointing a communication officer, scalability, 24/7 availability with limited maintenance windows and notification of outages, prohibited-content and legality checks, secure handling of sensitive user data, and security auditing. It binds insurance companies and insurance-related professions, and indirectly the outsourced website operator.

Article (16) of the Electronic Insurance Regulations on identifying the customer before selling or issuing a policy electronically, plus the adjacent selling rules in Article (17). It requires verification of customer identity and supporting documents, application of AML/CTF and counter-proliferation of illegal organisations legislation with reporting of suspicious activity through the electronic channel, retention of customer identity records for at least ten years, and creation of a protected electronic customer account (periodic password change, session re-authentication, email verification, board-approved two-factor login policy). It binds insurance companies and insurance agents, and insurance brokers when issuing insurance certificates.

Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 on the Establishment of the Insurance Authority and Organisation of Insurance Operations (as amended), the primary UAE insurance statute cited as the legal basis for insurance regulations and resolutions, including the Electronic Insurance Regulations. Functions of the former Insurance Authority under this law were subsequently assumed by the Central Bank under Federal Law No. 14 of 2018. It binds insurance companies, reinsurers, insurance agents, brokers and other insurance-related professions operating in the State.

Sets the valuation rules an insurance company must apply when determining which assets count as Admissible Assets backing accrued insurance liabilities, including the prudent person principle, mark-to-model governance (senior management/Investment Committee awareness, model change control, periodic model review, risk function understanding of model weaknesses) and independent real estate revaluation thresholds. It also addresses assets held for life contracts where investment risk is borne by policyholders (unit-linked and index-linked benefits). Binds licensed insurance companies and branches of Foreign Insurance Companies in the UAE, with solvency-related consequences for asset admissibility.

Governs the records an insurance company must organise, maintain and make available to the supervisory Authority: complete transaction records kept in original form, UAE-booked business held locally and accessible, segregated records where both persons/fund accumulation and property/liability licences are held, off-site backups, and validity of electronic records. It prescribes an enumerated list of record types (underwriting, claims, complaints, technical provisions, solvency, reinsurance, investments, related-party transactions, policyholder and shareholder funds, policies and procedures, actuarial reports) and a retention period of at least ten years, plus the Authority's examination and inspection powers and the waiver of actuary confidentiality.
lookup_terms: separate records persons and property liability

data.summary: Sets quantitative concentration and asset allocation limits for insurance company investments, with carve-outs for Statutory Deposits and unit-linked funds, application to UAE-policy insurance fund assets for branches of Foreign Insurance Companies, and a rating benchmark for what counts as strong/very strong. It also fixes transitional compliance periods (three years for real estate limits, two years for other limits) and frames Investment Risk (market, credit quality, concentration, liquidity, derivatives) as a Board responsibility.
lookup_terms: real estate investment limit three years
Foreign Insurance Company branch insurance fund

data.summary: Describes the required investment governance architecture: Board-approved investment and risk management policies reviewed annually, an overall investment strategy policy covering objectives, risk/liability profile, strategic asset allocation, restricted asset types and derivatives/structured products use, and a Board-level Investment Committee with its own charter and mandate. The Committee's minimum remit includes proposing strategy and policy, setting guidelines, monitoring investments, and working with the Audit Committee on audit scope; related duties cover limit monitoring, counterparty creditworthiness assessment, and at least annual stress testing (demonstrated at head-office level for foreign branches).

Sets out appointment, duties and professional obligations of the Actuary in relation to Technical Provisions and Mathematical Reserves: Board appointment of an Authority-registered actuary, notification of changes, review and approval of gross and net technical provisions, data quality assessment (accuracy remaining management's responsibility), professional liability, and an annual report to the Authority on current and future risks. It also constrains valuation methodology — consistent, non-arbitrary methods, discounting on AAA-rated sovereign securities (US$ proxy where AED long-term yields are unavailable), and treatment of unit-linked reserves for solvency.

Defines Risk Management for insurance companies and sets expectations for integrating it into organisational structure and decision-making: Board-set risk appetite, entity-wide assessment across all risk types including emerging risks, timely and accurate management information, proportionality of systems and controls to nature/size/complexity, and regular review. It links to the solvency assessment framework by mapping main risk areas — life and non-life underwriting risk, market and liquidity (investment) risk and its sub-modules (interest rate, equity, and related sensitivities) — to Solvency Capital Requirement modules.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk equity risk sub-module

data.summary: A cross-reference node for UAE Federal Law No. 1 of 2006 on Electronic Commerce and Transactions as it is invoked in the Insurance Authority's Electronic Insurance Regulations (Board Resolution No. 18 of 2020). It is cited both as a legal basis for that resolution and as the residual legal framework governing electronic conclusion of insurance contracts and other e-insurance matters not specifically addressed by the regulations. Practically, it binds licensed insurance companies, insurance-related professions and banks marketing policies electronically, whose e-contracting validity rests on the electronic transactions law.

Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 9 of 2011 issuing the Instructions for Licensing Health Insurance Third Party Administrators and regulating and supervising their business, made under the Federal Law No. 6 of 2007. It sets the definitions, licensing and registration regime, conduct obligations, supervisory inspection powers, joint liability with insurers, fees, and transitional rectification period for existing operators. It binds entities administering health insurance claims in the UAE and, in parts, the insurance companies contracting with them.
lookup_terms: Register of Health Insurance Third Party Administrators

data.summary: Defined-role node for the Health Insurance Third Party Administrator, the licensed entity that administers and settles health insurance claims on behalf of insurers and contracts with medical service providers on their behalf. The instructions circumscribe the role: no selling or marketing of health policies, no ownership or management stake in medical facilities or health insurers, segregated accounts for claims funds, and no service agreements with insurers not licensed in the UAE. Obligations attach to the TPA itself, with knock-on contractual duties for insurers and providers.

Node covering the entry and maintenance conditions for a TPA licence: qualification and experience thresholds for the director and a specialist key officer, employment of a licensed and professionally independent physician to verify treatment cases, plus annual registration, renewal filings and audited financial statements. It also permits a TPA to serve multiple insurers and providers subject to separate records and bank accounts per insurer contract, and imposes identification and claim-payment conduct duties. Binds licence applicants and licensed TPAs vis-à-vis the Insurance Authority.

Node on the mandatory content and discipline of the agreement between the TPA and the insurance company, including insurer access to books and records, claim settlement and payment periods, authority to contract with medical service providers on the insurer's behalf, controls over contractual funds, and prescribed statistical reporting and record-keeping. It is paired with financial-conduct duties: separate accounts per insurer, no underwriting or reinsurance, no extra charges to insureds or beneficiaries, return of unused balances and of any unagreed commission or interest, and notification to the Authority of insurer payment delays beyond 15 days. Binds TPAs and, reciprocally, contracting insurers.

Node on the TPA's relationship with Medical Service Providers: the tripartite/parallel agreements setting out rights, obligations, tariffs and settlement periods, evidenced by an insurer document confirming the TPA contracted on the insurer's behalf. It also carries the TPA's conduct duties toward providers and insureds — notifying the insurer of any new, amended or terminated provider contract, impartiality in claim settlement, confidentiality of data obtained, restrictions on advertising without insurer consent, and investigation rights such as reviewing a patient's file. Binds TPAs, with cooperation duties on providers, beneficiaries and insurers toward the TPA's physician.

Consolidated licensing instructions for Health Insurance Third Party Administrators (IA Board Resolution 9/2011, now within the CBUAE insurance supervisory perimeter), covering permitted TPA activities, licensing conditions, conduct and record-keeping duties, and the supervisory sanctions ladder. It binds licensed TPA companies and shapes the contractual allocation of duties between them and the insurance companies they act for, including joint responsibility toward third parties and liability for associates' fraud, forgery or abuse. Relevant to anyone assessing whether an outsourced claims administrator is properly licensed, what records it must keep (minimum five years), and what happens on suspension, cancellation or termination of the TPA agreement.

Sub-node within the TPA Licensing Instructions dealing with the financial entry conditions for health insurance third party administration, including corporate form, minimum paid-up capital of AED 5 million, exclusivity of business purpose, and the associated security/guarantee arrangements required of applicants. It binds companies seeking or holding a TPA licence, and failure to continue satisfying these conditions is an express ground for licence cancellation. Useful when checking ongoing eligibility rather than one-off authorisation.

Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 25 of 2014 issuing the Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies: a consolidated prudential rulebook with a binding glossary plus seven sections on policyholder-rights investment, solvency margin and minimum guarantee fund, technical provisions, admissible assets, mandatory records and data to be made available to the supervisor, accounting books for companies/agents/brokers, and reporting formats. It binds insurance companies incorporated in the State and licensed foreign branches, with defined terms applying throughout unless context requires otherwise. Start here to locate which section governs a given prudential or reporting question.

Section 1 of the Financial Regulations, setting the basis for investing the rights of policyholders: general investment requirements and investment policy, asset distribution and concentration limits with transitional compliance periods, investment risk management, domiciling of investments, derivatives, outsourced investment activity, borrowed funds and supervisory reporting, plus addendums forming an integral part. It binds licensed insurance companies and feeds directly into solvency work, since admissible asset values are capped by these limits. Consult it for any question on asset eligibility, concentration breaches or investment outsourcing.

Section 2 of the Financial Regulations, governing the Solvency Margin regime: Minimum Capital Requirement, Minimum Guarantee Fund, Solvency Capital Requirement, group capital adequacy, risk assessment and risk management systems, composition of Basic and Ancillary Own Funds, continuous maintenance duties and the limits on assets admissible for solvency. It binds insurance companies at all times, not only at reporting dates, and requires supervisory approval for certain Own Funds items such as subordinated liabilities and ancillary elements. Go here for capital adequacy, own-funds eligibility and solvency disclosure questions.

Section 3 of the Financial Regulations, prescribing the types and calculation basis of technical provisions: unearned premium and unexpired risk reserves, outstanding loss and IBNR reserves, allocated and unallocated loss adjustment expense reserves, and mathematical reserves, together with rules on reinsurance credit and on holding matching investments inside the UAE gross or net of reinsurance. It binds insurance companies and imposes duties on the Board to appoint a registered Actuary who reviews and approves provisions, assesses data quality, is professionally liable for advice, and reports annually to the supervisor. Relevant to reserving adequacy, actuarial sign-off and localisation of assets backing liabilities.

Concept node for the Liquidity Coverage Ratio as applied in the CBUAE liquidity guidance: a 30-day stress metric covering bank-specific and market-wide stress, calibrated on the Basel III LCR standard with national discretions noted. It sits alongside ELAR, ASRR and NSFR as one of the quantitative liquidity ratios, with a phased compliance path rising from 70% to 100%. It binds banks that are approved to be assessed under the Basel III liquidity framework rather than the ELAR regime.

Concept node for the Net Stable Funding Ratio: a structural ratio of available stable funding to required stable funding, to be maintained at 100% or more on an ongoing basis over a one-year horizon. It complements the LCR by limiting maturity cliff effects, and the underlying BCBS October 2014 standard prevails over the guidance manual where there is ambiguity. It applies to banks approved under the Basel III liquidity framework, with reporting preceding the compliance date.

Defines the eligible stock of High Quality Liquid Assets for the LCR, split into Level 1 (0% risk-weighted, no haircut, no cap, with a sub-limit on unrated 0% risk-weighted assets) and Level 2A/2B (capped at 40% and 15% respectively, subject to haircuts). It also sets expectations on unencumbered status, currency matching, diversification and sole use for liquidity management, and records national discretion for unrated UAE GRE/PSE issuers. Binding on banks computing the LCR.

Orientation node for the Basel III liquidity framework as incorporated by reference into the CBUAE liquidity regulation and guidance, covering the BCBS LCR (January 2013) and NSFR (October 2014) standards. It explains the two-track approach: banks either remain under ELAR/ASRR or apply for approval to be assessed under Basel III, after which reversion is not permitted and both LCR and NSFR must be met. Also relevant to proportionality: qualitative requirements are not relaxed for Basel III-aspiring banks.

Sets out the expected characteristics of a bank's Contingency Funding Plan: proportionate to complexity and role in the system, with diversified contingency measures, identified funding sources and amounts, escalation and activation procedures, lead times, defined roles including authority to invoke, and a crisis team. The CFP must be integrated with ongoing liquidity risk analysis and with stress-test scenarios covering firm-specific and market-wide stress. Applies to banks as part of the qualitative liquidity risk management requirements.

Concept node covering the qualitative liquidity risk management expectations derived from the BCBS 2008 sound liquidity principles, including stress-sensitive identification and measurement of liquidity risk across all jurisdictions and on/off-balance-sheet positions, and pricing of liquidity costs, benefits and risks into products and the new product approval process. It also anchors board responsibility for setting liquidity risk tolerance and senior management's role in implementation. Binding on banks' liquidity risk management and governance frameworks.

Defined-term and obligation node for the "Risk Governance Framework" under the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation 153/2018 — the board- and management-level structure for setting strategy and risk approach, articulating and monitoring risk appetite and risk limits, and identifying, measuring, managing and controlling risk. It also carries the group dimension: where CBUAE is not the primary regulator and group entities control or influence risk management, the bank's framework must address group-relationship risks, linkages and differences with the group framework, dependence on group risk functions, and group monitoring/reporting lines. It binds banks licensed to take deposits in the UAE, with an associated public disclosure duty (annual report and website) on the framework and the nature and extent of risk exposures.

Defined-term and Article 3 node for the "Risk Management Function" under Risk Management Regulation 153/2018: the aggregate of systems, structures, policies, procedures and people that measure, monitor and report risk bank-wide and, where relevant, group-wide. It requires documented roles and responsibilities, policies ensuring all material risks are identified, measured, managed, mitigated and reported, contingency arrangements (business continuity, contingency funding), and adequately resourced compliance and internal audit functions providing independent assurance. Senior Management implements the board-approved framework; the Board remains ultimately accountable notwithstanding delegation.

Definitional node capturing the enabling statute referenced by Risk Management Regulation 153/2018 — Union Law No. 10 of 1980 on the Central Bank, the Monetary System and Organization of Banking, as amended or replaced — alongside related defined terms (Bank, Board, Central Bank, Central Bank regulations, Group, Parent, Affiliate, Islamic Financial Services). It matters mainly for scope and hierarchy: it identifies the legal basis on which CBUAE resolutions, regulations, circulars, rules, standards and notices bind licensed banks. Note that the 1980 law has been superseded in UAE practice, so the "as amended or replaced" wording is the operative link.

Node on the Board's role under Risk Management Regulation 153/2018: the Board approves the risk appetite statement and risk limits, must have sufficient expertise to understand and oversee risk measurement systems including models, and remains ultimately accountable even where model approval or other responsibilities are delegated to management. It also carries escalation duties — exceptions to risk policies, procedures or limits must be addressed immediately by the appropriate management level or the Board, and the bank must notify the Central Bank immediately of significant deviations from the approved risk appetite or policies, or of a material risk not adequately addressed. Binds banks' boards of directors as defined in the Regulation.

Node on stress testing and internal risk reporting under Risk Management Regulation 153/2018: banks must run a stress-testing programme proportionate to their risk exposures and feed results on an ongoing basis into risk management, contingency planning and internal capital and liquidity assessment. Internal capital/liquidity adequacy processes must reflect the nature and level of risks taken, covering all material risks beyond those specified in the Capital Adequacy and Liquidity Regulations and Standards. It also requires information systems capable of measuring and reporting exposures bank-wide and group-wide across risk types, products and counterparties, with timely reporting to Board and Senior Management in usable formats.

The instrument itself: CBUAE Risk Management Regulation, Circular No. 153/2018 dated 27 May 2018, addressed to all banks. It sets an overarching prudential framework for risk management — Board and Senior Management oversight, the risk management function alongside internal audit and compliance as independent control functions, risk appetite and limits, measurement and models, stress testing, information systems and disclosure — with accompanying Standards. Risks-specific standards and supervisory expectations sit in other CBUAE regulations; this is the umbrella governance instrument aligned to leading international practice.

Article 4 of the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation (153/2018) requires each Bank to maintain risk measurement and monitoring systems proportionate to its risk profile, nature, size, structure and complexity, and requires the Board to have enough expertise to understand and oversee those systems, including any models used. Where models are used to measure risk components, the Bank must have internal development and approval processes and carry out regular independent validation and testing, with the Board remaining ultimately accountable even if model approval is delegated to management. The surrounding text also imposes immediate escalation of breaches of risk policies/limits and immediate notification to the Central Bank of significant deviations from the board-approved risk appetite statement or unaddressed material risks. Binds banks licensed by the CBUAE (and their boards/senior management).

Article 5 of the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation (153/2018) requires a Bank to run a stress-testing programme for material risks commensurate with the size of its risk exposures, and to feed the results on an ongoing basis into risk management, contingency planning and its internal capital and liquidity assessment. The internal capital and liquidity adequacy process must reflect the nature and level of risks taken and cover all material risks beyond those specified in the Central Bank's Capital Adequacy and Liquidity Regulations and Standards. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: Capital Adequacy and Liquidity Regulations and Standards

data.summary: Article 6 of the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation (153/2018) requires a Bank to maintain information systems capable of measuring, assessing and reporting the size, composition and quality of risk exposures bank-wide and, where applicable, group-wide, across all risk types, products and counterparties. Reports must reach the Board and Senior Management on a timely basis and in formats they can use and understand. This is a reporting/MI obligation on banks, linked to the wider risk governance framework and its compliance and internal audit components.

Article 7 of the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation (153/2018) is the provision on strategic and operational decisions, sitting between the internal reporting requirements (Article 6) and group risk management (Article 8) in the regulation's structure. It addresses how risk considerations must inform a Bank's strategic and operational decision-making within the board-approved risk governance framework. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks; the substantive text should be read in the source, as only the table of contents and adjacent articles appear in the extracted context.

Article 8 of the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation (153/2018) deals with group risk management, including local or regional application of group policies and procedures and the assessment of local/regional risks. Where the Central Bank is not the primary regulator of a bank belonging to a Group and elements of its risk management approach are controlled or influenced by another group entity, the bank's own risk governance framework must address risks arising from the group relationship and clearly identify linkages and material differences from the Group framework, whether its risk management function is wholly or partly derived from the Group, and the monitoring/reporting process to the Group. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks that form part of a wider group, including subsidiaries and branches of foreign groups.

Article 9 of the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation (153/2018) requires a Bank to make publicly available — including in its annual report and on its website — information on its Risk Governance Framework and on the nature and extent of its risk exposures. It is a public disclosure/transparency obligation binding CBUAE-licensed banks, complementing the internal reporting duties in Article 6.
lookup_terms: nature and extent of risk exposures

data.summary: UAE Cabinet Resolution No. (7) of 2019 setting the framework for administrative fines imposed by the Insurance Authority under Federal Law No. (6) of 2007. It defines key terms (Company, Person, Insurance-Related Professions), sets the scope of application, empowers the Authority to levy the fines listed in the annexed schedule, doubles fines for repeat violations within one year up to a two million dirham cap, and provides a 15-day grievance route to the Board with a 60-day decision deadline. It binds insurance companies, licensed insurance-related professionals and any person committing a listed violation.

The schedule annexed to Cabinet Resolution No. (7) of 2019, forming an integral part of it, listing each insurance-sector violation against a fixed dirham fine amount. Entries cover company-level breaches such as failure to pay contractual compensation on an insured event, non-compliance with investment rules, solvency margin and minimum guarantee fund, technical provisions, asset-liability matching and reinsurance criteria. Amounts are subject to doubling on repetition within a year and may be amended by the Cabinet.

Concept node for the Financial Regulations applicable to insurance companies, referenced as the benchmark for many violations in the fines schedule (investment basics, solvency margin and minimum guarantee fund, technical provisions calculation, assets matching insurance liabilities). The surrounding schedule text also enumerates penalties for insurance brokers, insurance agents and health insurance TPAs for breaches of their respective licensing, conduct, segregation-of-funds and registration obligations. Relevant to insurers and licensed intermediaries supervised by the Insurance Authority.

Guidance manual accompanying the UAE liquidity regulations (Circular 33/2015), setting out qualitative liquidity risk management expectations drawn from the Basel Committee's 2008 Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management, plus the quantitative ratio framework. It assigns ultimate responsibility for liquidity risk and risk tolerance to the board, requires pricing of liquidity costs, benefits and risks into products and new product approval, and requires identification, measurement, monitoring and control of liquidity risk across all jurisdictions and on/off-balance-sheet positions. Binds banks operating in the UAE.
lookup_terms: Basel Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management

data.summary: Concept node on eligible liquid assets and the ELAR, the simpler liquidity ratio available to banks not applying the Basel III LCR. The surrounding guidance defines Level 1 assets (0% risk-weighted under the Basel II standardised approach, no haircut, with a 25% sub-cap on unrated 0% risk-weighted assets), Level 2A and 2B assets with haircuts and caps (40% overall, 15% for Level 2B), the unencumbrance requirement, currency matching and diversification expectations, and national discretion for unrated UAE GRE/PSE issuers. Applies to banks in the UAE.

Concept node on the Advances to Stable Resources Ratio, the structural funding measure applied to banks that captures actual and likely uses of funds against the contractual maturity and behavioural profile of funding sources, to limit maturity mismatches and cliff effects, with requirements detailed in Central Bank BRF 7 reporting. It sits alongside the LCR and the NSFR (available stable funding over required stable funding, minimum 100%) in the liquidity ratio suite. Binds banks in the UAE.

Article 6 of the CBUAE Risk Management Standards (issued under Notice 153/2018) sets requirements for risk data aggregation, management information systems and internal risk reporting supporting a bank's comprehensive approach to risk management. It sits alongside the surrounding provisions on stress testing, bank-wide/group-wide consistency of risk identification and the feed of stress results into ICAAP and contingency funding. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE and is mandatory and enforceable in the same manner as the Risk Management Regulation, with the board ultimately accountable.

Article 7 of the CBUAE Risk Management Standards requires banks to have approval procedures for new products, material product modifications and strategic or major operational initiatives (systems, business model changes, acquisitions), with board or board-committee approval and possible delegation of product approvals to management while the board remains ultimately responsible. It prescribes minimum content: scenario-based risk assessment including pessimistic cases, an assessment of whether control and support functions have the expertise and tools to manage the risks (with power to withhold approval), and ongoing performance-versus-projection review. It also flags special risk challenges from mergers, acquisitions, disposals and group restructuring. Binds all CBUAE-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: due diligence on group structure change

data.summary: Node for Article 8 of the CBUAE Risk Management Standards, addressing risk management on a group basis; the supplied context covers adjacent material on Article 7 approval procedures for new products and strategic initiatives and on the roles of the risk management, compliance, internal audit and business line functions within the risk governance framework. Relevant where a bank has subsidiaries or affiliates and must apply consistent bank-wide and group-wide risk identification, measurement and control. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks and their boards.

Defines the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process requirement in the CBUAE Risk Management Standards: a bank must maintain a formal documented process for assessing overall capital adequacy against its risk profile, plus a strategy to hold capital above regulatory minima, documented and submitted annually to the Central Bank as the ICAAP Report. It lists the elements the ICAAP must demonstrate — board and senior management oversight, a sound capital assessment process, comprehensive assessment of credit, market, operational, interest rate, concentration, liquidity and other risks, monitoring and reporting of exposures and capital needs, and internal control review. The ICAAP must explicitly incorporate all material risks identified through the bank's risk management approach, with stress test results feeding capital and liquidity planning.

Concept node for the three lines of defence model as reflected in CBUAE risk governance requirements: business line management owning and operationalising risk limits, an independent risk management function headed by the CRO plus a compliance function, and internal audit providing independent assurance reporting to the board audit committee. It describes the mandatory minimum elements of a bank's risk governance framework, which must be documented and board-approved and may be scaled to the bank's risk profile, nature, size and complexity. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks and their boards.

Concept node for the risk appetite statement under the CBUAE Risk Management Standards: the board must approve, maintain and oversee the risk governance framework including the risk appetite statement and risk limits allocated by legal entity, business line or management unit consistent with that statement. The risk management function must develop metrics tied to the risk appetite statement, monitor and report on them and escalate breaches, while business lines operationalise the limits. Capital and liquidity implications must be reflected in the risks the bank is prepared to assume and in the associated limits.

Node for the Islamic banking article of the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation 153/2018, sitting alongside the Regulation's defined terms (Bank, Board, Group, Parent, Subsidiary, Islamic Financial Services) and the Article 9 public disclosure duty on the risk governance framework and risk exposures. It addresses how the risk governance requirements apply to Shari'a-compliant activity, including conventional banks operating Islamic Windows. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE; note this is a UAE instrument, not a SAMA rule, and the captured context is mainly definitions plus the adjacent disclosure article rather than the full Islamic banking text.

Parent node for the CBUAE Risk Management Standards 153/2018, the detailed companion to the Risk Management Regulation. It sets out expectations for the risk governance framework, the three-lines roles (board, senior management, risk management function/CRO, compliance, internal audit, business lines), risk identification and impact assessment, risk appetite and limit metrics, board-approved risk management policy, risk measurement and models, stress testing, and internal reporting. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE, on a bank-wide and where relevant group-wide basis.

Article 2 of the CBUAE Risk Management Standards requires each bank to establish, document and maintain a board-approved risk governance framework of policies, processes, procedures, systems and controls, proportionate to its risk profile, nature, size, complexity and structure. It allocates minimum roles to the board, senior management, the risk management function, compliance, internal audit and business line management, requires probability-and-impact assessment of risks, and lists the material risk categories the framework must at least cover. It binds CBUAE-licensed banks, with deviations from the listed elements only if the bank can demonstrate a comprehensive approach to the Central Bank.
lookup_terms: roles of compliance and internal audit

data.summary: Article 3 of the CBUAE Risk Management Standards governs the independent risk management function and the CRO: independence safeguards (no risk-taking-based remuneration, not the CEO or head of finance, compliance or internal audit), direct reporting to the board or board risk committee, and unfettered access including meetings without other executives. It lists the function's key activities, including identifying material and emerging risks, measuring exposures, monitoring against approved risk appetite and limits, operating early-warning and breach escalation, challenging material risk decisions and reporting to the board. It binds CBUAE-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: CRO reporting line board risk committee

data.summary: Article 4 of the CBUAE Risk Management Standards requires banks to use risk measurement methodologies proportionate to their risk profile, nature, size, complexity and structure, such as VaR, scenario analysis and stress testing, with outcomes analysis and back-testing. It requires explicit treatment of known model weaknesses and model error, and mandates that model-based approaches be supplemented by qualitative assessment, particularly for hard-to-quantify risks such as operational, compliance and reputational risk. It binds CBUAE-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: hard to quantify operational compliance reputational risk

data.summary: Article 5 of the CBUAE Risk Management Standards requires a forward-looking stress testing programme covering credit, market and operational risk plus any other risk material to the bank's business (e.g. concentration, IRRBB, liquidity, currency, reputation and compliance, contagion, country and transfer, legal and strategic risk). It assigns the risk management function responsibility for recommending actions from results, requires communication to business lines and functional heads, and links results into contingency planning, liquidity and contingency funding, capital planning and the ICAAP on a bank-wide and where applicable group-wide basis. It binds CBUAE-licensed banks.

CBUAE Standard on Liquidity at Islamic Banks, issued under the Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018) and forming part of, and read together with, the Regulation re Liquidity at Banks. It sets legally binding qualitative liquidity risk management and governance expectations, quantitative ratios (ELAR, ASRR, LCR, NSFR) and reporting duties, calibrated for Shari'ah-compliant business. It binds licensed banks conducting all their activities per Islamic Shari'ah (Islamic Banks); banks with an Islamic Window remain under the conventional liquidity regime but must report stand-alone measures for monitoring only.
lookup_terms: Standard re Liquidity at Islamic Banks

data.summary: Article 5 sets the qualitative liquidity requirements for Islamic Banks: a board-approved strategy and policies covering normal and stressed scenarios, a framework to identify, mitigate and manage liquidity risk across on- and off-balance sheet items, impact analysis for new products, internal controls, limits and internal audit. It also layers Shari'ah governance onto liquidity risk, requiring ISSC involvement in approving Shari'ah-compliant liquidity and hedging instruments, verifying non-commingling of funds with conventional parents, and vetting placements. It addresses contract-specific liquidity risks (Murabaha, Ijarah, Salam, Mudarabah, Musharakah, Sukuk) and the interaction of funding and market liquidity.
lookup_terms: Ijarah Salam Mudarabah Musharakah liquidity risk

data.summary: Article 6 covers the quantitative liquidity requirements applicable to Islamic Banks, i.e. the Shari'ah-adapted calibration of the Eligible Liquid Asset Ratio, Advances to Stable Resources Ratio, Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio referred to in the Standard's structure. It determines how Shari'ah-compliant liquid assets and funding sources are recognised for ratio purposes. It binds Islamic Banks; Islamic Windows report these measures on a stand-alone basis for monitoring only.

Defined-term node for the Internal Shari'ah Supervisory Committee: a committee of Islamic finance scholars appointed by an Islamic Bank that independently supervises its transactions, activities and products for Shari'ah compliance and issues binding resolutions and fatwas, subject to not contradicting HSA resolutions. It is supported by the Internal Shari'ah Control Division/Section and the Shari'ah Audit function, all of which must be free from undue influence. In the liquidity context the ISSC must approve Shari'ah-compliant liquidity and hedging instruments and oversee non-commingling of funds and placements.

Defined-term node for the Higher Shari'ah Authority, the CBUAE's central authority for Islamic banking and financial activities. Its resolutions, fatwas, regulations and standards are the top tier of the Shari'ah compliance hierarchy; an institution's ISSC resolutions are valid only where they do not contradict HSA resolutions. The concept recurs across multiple CBUAE Islamic-finance instruments and binds all licensed institutions carrying on Shari'ah-compliant activities.

Cross-reference node for the CBUAE Regulation re Liquidity at Banks, the parent instrument of which the Islamic Banks liquidity Standard forms part and with which it must be read. It sets the baseline qualitative, quantitative and reporting liquidity obligations for licensed banks, including banks housing an Islamic Window, which comply with this Regulation rather than the Islamic ratios. Useful for identifying the general liquidity requirements that the Islamic Standard supplements or adapts.

This node covers the market risk governance framework requirement — the policies, processes, procedures, systems and controls a Bank must establish, implement and maintain to identify, assess, monitor, mitigate and control market risk — together with the defining terms that frame it (marking-to-market, marking-to-model, parent/subsidiary, residual risk, risk appetite, risk governance framework, risk limits, trading book). It fixes Board ownership: the framework must be documented, approved, maintained and overseen by the Board, integrated with the Bank's overall risk management, and supported by active Board and Senior Management involvement in market risk control. It binds Banks; institutions holding trading books carry an additional obligation to maintain separate trading book policy statements and risk frameworks.

This node sets prudent valuation expectations for market risk positions: sourcing and periodic review of market inputs, use of generally accepted valuation methodologies, independent development, approval, testing and periodic review of valuation models, formal change control and secure model copies, and awareness of model weaknesses by an independent risk management function. It also requires procedures for valuation adjustments — including where third-party valuations are used or positions are marked to model — with credit valuation adjustments, unearned credit spreads, close-out costs and operational risk among the minimum items to be considered. Related internal audit provisions require annual independent review of pricing model and valuation system approval processes used by front- and back-office staff. It binds Banks.

This node aggregates stress testing obligations across several instruments, centred on market risk: a Bank must run supervisory scenarios (both those requiring no simulation, such as reporting largest losses against internal capital measures, and those requiring simulated stress scenarios), plus internally developed scenarios reflecting its own portfolio characteristics, and submit results to the regulator. Scenario design must cover past periods of significant market disturbance and sensitivity to shifts in volatility and correlation assumptions, including extreme historical values. It binds Banks and interacts with back-testing, internal model validation and capital adequacy assessment.

This node governs a Bank's back-testing programme for internal market risk measurement models: formal quarterly evaluation of exceptions (trading outcomes not covered by the risk measures) using the most recent twelve months of modelled results and profit data, documentation and explanation of every exception, and capacity to back-test at both whole-portfolio and material sub-portfolio/book level. Back-tests must use both actual (cleaned of fees, commissions, brokerage and non-market-risk reserve movements) and hypothetical trading outcomes. It binds Banks using internal models and feeds into model validation and trading book capital charge provisions.

This node sets the independence and validation requirements around internal market risk models: initial and ongoing validation by a risk management function independent of risk-taking, with more frequent validation after significant structural market changes, portfolio composition changes or material model changes; validation must go beyond profit-and-loss attribution and back-testing to test the model's assumptions. It also requires daily independent risk reporting to Senior Management, integration of model output into day-to-day risk management and trading limits, relevant pricing risk factors with proxies that track actual positions, and at least annual independent internal audit review of the market risk measurement system. It binds Banks using internal models.
lookup_terms: internal audit review of market risk

data.summary: This node carries the definition of the trading book — positions in financial instruments and commodities held with trading intent or to hedge other trading book elements — and the mandatory assignment criteria (short-term resale, profiting from short-term price movements, arbitrage, hedging such positions, and any further instruments determined by the regulator). It links that boundary to consequences: separate trading book policy statements and risk frameworks, and capital charges for interest rate, options and equity positions in the trading book, with equity exposure, foreign exchange, commodity and options risk calculated on entire positions and banking book interest rate risk addressed through the internal capital adequacy process. It binds Banks.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: Section 7 of the CBUAE Corporate Governance Standards for Banks (83/2019), setting out group-level governance duties owed by the Board of a Bank acting as Controlling Shareholder — a group corporate governance framework, group management and internal control structure, intragroup conflict-of-interest controls, approval policies for new legal entities, and information exchange across entities. It also allocates responsibility to subsidiary/branch boards for assessing compatibility of group policy with local legal and regulatory requirements, and requires the Board and Senior Management to avoid or mitigate risks from complex or non-transparent structures lacking economic substance. It binds banks licensed by the Central Bank that head or sit within a banking group, including foreign branches through equivalent local structures.

Section 12 of the CBUAE Corporate Governance Standards for Banks (83/2019), governing the bank-wide compensation system: the mandate and independence of the compensation committee, its annual review of compensation plans and outcomes, and an external independent assessment at least every five years. It requires Board oversight of remuneration for all staff (not only Senior Management), alignment with strategy and Risk Appetite, contraction of Board compensation and staff bonus pools on negative performance or net loss, and compensation of Control Function staff on terms independent of the business lines they monitor. It binds bank boards, compensation committees and Senior Management.

Section 13 of the CBUAE Corporate Governance Standards for Banks (83/2019), specifying the minimum content of a bank's annual corporate governance statement, including governance structures, major shareholdings and voting rights, Related Party Transactions, Board recruitment and diversity (including female representation), Board and Senior Management qualifications and individual compensation, committee composition and meeting frequency, risk exposures and strategies, and Shari'ah reporting for Islamic banking. The node also carries the associated defined terms (Related Parties, Related Party Transactions, Pillar 3, Material Risk Takers, Risk Appetite). It binds all banks subject to the Corporate Governance Regulation and Standards.

Concept node for the defined term "Material Risk Takers" — staff whose work is deemed to have a significant impact on the overall risk profile of the bank or group — as used across CBUAE governance and risk standards. It matters mainly for compensation design, risk-culture and Board oversight obligations, and for determining which staff fall within enhanced remuneration and accountability controls. Relevant to banks and their boards, compensation and risk committees.
lookup_terms: risk culture and tone from the top

data.summary: Concept node for "Control Functions" under CBUAE governance standards — risk management, compliance and internal audit, plus Shari'ah compliance and audit for banks offering Islamic financial services. It anchors requirements on independence (including compensation set independently of the business lines monitored), fit-and-proper selection via the nomination committee, and the obligation on branches of foreign banks to maintain robust local Control Functions reporting to local management while accountable to group heads. Binds banks, their boards, nomination and compensation committees, and foreign bank branches in the UAE.

CBUAE Market Risk Standards addressing internal models for market risk measurement: required risk factor coverage for equity, commodity and options exposures (including market-wide equity factors, directional, forward gap/interest rate and basis risk for commodities, and volatility/Vega risk for options), with proportionality to the size and complexity of positions. It also mandates Board-approved policies providing for at least annual independent internal audit review of the market risk measurement system, covering model scope, data accuracy and independence, valuation and pricing model approval, and integration of risk measures into daily risk management. Binds banks using internal models for market risk capital and their boards, risk functions and internal audit.
lookup_terms: independent internal audit review of risk models

data.summary: This node is the UAE Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities), cited here as the enabling authority under which the Central Bank issues binding regulations and standards — in this context the Standard on Liquidity at Islamic Banks forming part of the Regulations re Liquidity at Banks. It supplies the legal basis for supervisory expectations to be legally enforceable, and also underpins defined terms such as Bank and Confidential Information (disclosure restrictions under Article 120). It binds licensed financial institutions generally, including licensed banks conducting all or part of their activities in accordance with Islamic Shari'ah.
lookup_terms: Islamic banks liquidity standard legal basis

data.summary: This node is the Corporate Governance Standards for Banks (Circular 83/2019), which expand on the Corporate Governance Regulation and are mandatory and enforceable in the same manner as the Regulation. It sets out definitions (Affiliate, Board, Control Functions, Controlling Shareholder, Related Parties, Material Risk Takers, Risk Appetite) and detailed requirements on board composition and assessment, senior management, risk governance, related party transactions, group structure, code of conduct, whistleblowing and disclosure. It binds all licensed banks, including branches of foreign banks and banks offering Islamic financial services.

This node is the Corporate Governance Regulation (Circular No. 83/2019), the parent instrument that the Corporate Governance Standards elaborate on article by article. It frames obligations on board and senior management accountability, the Risk Governance Framework (including the three lines of defence and, for Islamic financial services, internal Shari'ah audit), group-level governance and internal control, code of conduct prohibiting fraud, sanctions breaches, money laundering, bribery and consumer rights violations, and related party controls. It binds all banks licensed by the Central Bank, with group-wide duties on a bank acting as Controlling Shareholder.

This node covers the board responsibilities article of the Corporate Governance Standards: board composition, size and use of committees, annual self-assessment of the board, its committees and individual members (with an external independent assessment at least every five years), fit and proper suitability review, and chairman duties on agenda, participation and shareholder communication. It also addresses quorum and voting, coordination between audit and risk committees, and independent Shari'ah compliance oversight for banks offering Islamic financial services. It binds the boards of all licensed banks, with local governance structures required for branches of foreign banks.
lookup_terms: audit committee and risk committee coordination

data.summary: This node covers the risk management article of the Corporate Governance Standards, including senior management's accountability to the board for day-to-day prudent management, implementation of risk management systems, risk culture and internal controls, and non-interference with the independence of risk, compliance, internal audit and Shari'ah control functions. It also addresses group-wide risk management by a bank acting as Controlling Shareholder, local entity boards' assessment of compatibility with local law, and mitigation of risks from complex or non-transparent structures. It binds boards and senior management of licensed banks and their group entities, including foreign branches.

This node concerns Pillar 3 disclosure requirements as defined and applied in the corporate governance framework — the Basel Committee's consolidated and enhanced disclosure framework (March 2017 and subsequent revisions) — together with the annual corporate governance statement disclosures. It requires published qualitative and quantitative remuneration disclosures for Senior Management and Material Risk Takers (system design, fixed and variable pay, guaranteed bonuses, sign-on and severance payments, deferred remuneration), plus disclosure of ownership, related party transactions, board composition and risk exposures. It binds licensed banks, including additional Shari'ah reporting for banks offering Islamic financial services.

Defines settlement finality for Retail Payment Systems as the discharge of an obligation by a transfer of funds that is irrevocable and unconditional, extinguishing legal rights that would otherwise allow reversal of a Transfer Order processed in an RPS. It ties finality and netting certainty to the Central Bank Law provisions on Financial Infrastructure Systems, including treatment of netting where a participant is insolvent or bankrupt, preservation of rights in underlying transactions, and notification of insolvency. It binds System Operators and Settlement Institutions of licensed/designated RPS, and affects participants' insolvency-related rights.

Defines the System Operator (SO) as the person responsible for operating a Financial Infrastructure System, including comprehensive risk management across the system and ensuring operation complies with the RPS Regulation and other central bank regulations. The SO is a primary addressee of the retail payment systems licensing, designation and ongoing oversight regime, alongside Settlement Institutions. Relevant to determining who bears compliance and oversight obligations for a designated RPS.

Defines the Settlement Institution (SI) as an institution providing settlement services and settlement accounts (single- or multi-currency) to a Financial Infrastructure System, and in some cases granting participants access to intraday liquidity. The SI sits alongside the System Operator as an addressee of the RPS licensing, designation and ongoing requirements regime. Useful for allocating settlement-layer obligations and identifying who must comply with finality and oversight rules.

Explains how a payment system supporting a Stored Value Facility business and scheme is treated under the RPS designation framework: although such a system normally falls within the RPS definition, the regulator does not intend to designate a payment system run by an SVF licensee purely to support its own SVF business, since the SVF Regulation already governs its safety and soundness. Sits within the guidance on categories of RPS (including bank-owned systems and payment card systems) and the scope of designation. Relevant to SVF licensees assessing dual-regime exposure.
lookup_terms: Clearing and Settlement System for SVF

data.summary: The Stored Value Facilities Regulation is the licensing and supervisory framework for SVF issuance, replacing the earlier stored value and electronic payment systems framework and grounded in the Central Bank Law provisions on licensed financial activities and supervisory powers. It sets definitions (including Money's Worth, device-based and non-device-based SVF, single-purpose SVF, Operating Rules, Senior Management) and licensing plus ongoing conduct, governance and AML-related obligations. It binds providers/issuers of stored value facilities in the State, excluding Financial Free Zones.

Defines a Stored Value Facility as a non-cash facility into which a customer (or someone on their behalf) pays money or Money's Worth in exchange for storage of that value and the issuer's Relevant Undertaking to supply goods/services or make payment to a merchant or third party. The definition covers device-based and non-device-based (network account, e-wallet) facilities and distinguishes single-purpose/closed-loop facilities; Money's Worth extends to reward points, crypto-assets and virtual assets. It determines who falls within the SVF licensing perimeter and, by cross-reference, the retail payment systems framework.

This node covers the market risk requirements applicable to banks offering Islamic financial services, sitting alongside the quarterly Report on Market Risk Exposures and back-testing exception reporting obligation, and the specification of equity and commodity risk factors for internal models. It requires such banks to maintain a market risk management and reporting framework covering all assets (especially illiquid or highly volatile ones), to set and annually review a market risk strategy and risk appetite reflecting contractual arrangements with fund providers and restricted investment account portfolios, to disclose that strategy to fund providers, and to support tradable-asset risk appetite with capital. It binds banks as supervised entities, with the Islamic-specific provisions applying to those offering Islamic financial services.

This is the Retail Payment Systems Regulation (Circular 10/2020), which sets the framework for licensing, designating and overseeing systemically important retail payment systems under the Central Bank Law. It covers which types of RPS fall in scope (including payment card systems and clearing and settlement systems), the designation criteria and process, ongoing obligations of designated systems, and the appeal mechanism for licensing/designation decisions. It binds System Operators and Settlement Institutions of licensed and/or designated RPS; it excludes Financial Free Zones unless expressly stated, and generally does not target bank-owned in-house systems serving only their own customers, or a Payment System run by an SVF Licensee for its own scheme.

This node is the defined concept of a Retail Payment System under the Retail Payment Systems Regulation — a system providing transfer, clearing or settlement of retail payment obligations, operated in the State or capable of handling obligations in the Currency, any currency or a Regulated Medium of Exchange. The definition determines which arrangements can be licensed and designated as systemically important, and expressly captures payment card systems and clearing and settlement systems supporting SVF schemes. Scope carve-outs matter: bank-operated systems serving only the bank's own customers are generally not designated, but may be if the bank provides RPS services to other payment service providers or financial institutions.

This node covers the designation process for a Retail Payment System, initiated by the Central Bank under the Central Bank Law where an RPS meets or is likely to meet the systemic importance criteria (monetary/financial stability, public interest or public order). It describes the Central Bank's power to require information and documents from any Person holding them, including the System Operator, Settlement Institution or a Participant Person, and the procedures for suspension/revocation of a licence or designation, including written representations, notification, and objection to the Grievances & Appeals Committee. Designation implies oversight, not endorsement, and revocation does not affect transactions already cleared and settled.

This node is the defined concept of the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures — the CPMI-IOSCO international standards for payment systems, central securities depositories, securities settlement systems, central counterparties and trade repositories. Under the Retail Payment Systems Regulation, designated RPS must observe and comply with the relevant PFMI principles on an ongoing basis, in addition to the Regulation's own ongoing requirements, and the Central Bank may impose requirements higher than the PFMI on risk-specific or general policy grounds. It binds System Operators and Settlement Institutions of designated systems in their ongoing operations and reviews.

This node is the Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities, as amended), the enabling statute relied on across multiple CBUAE regulations, here surfaced through the definitions and scope provisions of the Retail Payment Systems Regulation. It supplies the Central Bank's powers to license, designate and oversee Financial Infrastructure Systems, and underpins defined terms such as Clearing, Clearing and Settlement System, Designated System, Currency, Default Arrangements, Financial Free Zones and the Grievances & Appeals Committee. It binds licensed financial institutions and infrastructure operators in the State and is the source of appeal rights against Central Bank decisions.

Part I of the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities Regulation setting the scope of application and the requirement for prior Central Bank licensing before issuing or operating an SVF in the State. It covers the carve-out for Single-purpose Stored Value Facilities, a discretionary risk-based exemption route (subject to value and customer-number thresholds and possible FinTech sandbox testing, with the Central Bank able to demand information or revoke the exemption), and a prohibition on unlicensed overseas SVF schemes advertising or soliciting the UAE public. Binds any issuer or operator of an SVF, including foreign schemes targeting UAE customers.

Concept node covering the safeguarding and management of the Float (customer funds/Money's Worth held against stored value) under the CBUAE SVF Regulation. Requires accurate and timely customer ledger reconciliation against total Float, segregation of Float assets from the Licensee's own funds and other business funds, internal controls against theft, fraud and misappropriation, and liquidity-focused Float management ensuring funds are always available for redemption; it also bars business models relying on investment returns from the Float. Binds SVF Licensees.

Concept node on the AML/CFT obligations applicable to SVF Licensees under the CBUAE SVF Regulation. Requires customer due diligence models calibrated to the customer profile and SVF product features, compliance management arrangements including Senior Management oversight and appointment of a Compliance Officer and Money Laundering Reporting Officer, comprehensive AML/CFT policies aligned with UAE AML/CFT law, an independent audit function, and risk assessment before launching new products, services or technology. Binds licensed SVF issuers/operators.

Definitional node anchoring "Money's Worth" and related defined terms in the CBUAE SVF Regulation, including Float, Licence/Licensee, Operating Rules, Senior Management, Single-purpose Stored Value Facility, State and Stored Value Facility. Money's Worth extends the value paid into an SVF beyond cash to items such as values, points, Crypto-Assets and Virtual Assets, which determines whether a scheme falls within the SVF perimeter. Relevant to anyone testing whether a product is a licensable SVF.

Article (8) of the CBUAE SVF Regulation setting corporate governance and risk management expectations for SVF Licensees, including risk policies proportionate to the scale and complexity of the scheme and board-level governance responsibilities. It expressly disapplies these requirements to licensed banks conducting SVF business, which instead follow the Central Bank's bank corporate governance regulation and standards. Adjacent text also covers Central Bank discretion to impose higher financial resource requirements and an unconditional irrevocable bank guarantee for paid-up capital.
lookup_terms: banks exempt from SVF governance article

data.summary: Capital/financial resources node under the CBUAE SVF Regulation requiring a Licensee to hold Aggregate Capital Funds of at least 5% of total Float received from Customers, alongside a minimum capital amount in approved currency. It defines the composition of Aggregate Capital Funds (paid-up capital, reserves excluding revaluation reserves, retained earnings) and the deductions (accumulated losses, goodwill), and requires demonstration of sufficient resources for sustainable operation, disclosure of source of funds, and capacity for an orderly wind-down. Binds SVF applicants and Licensees.

A technology and payment-security risk component of the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities Regulation, requiring Licensees to maintain a risk management framework covering computer and payment systems and the safety and efficiency of SVF scheme operations, proportionate to the nature, size, complexity and technology of the business. It also imposes an incident management framework with senior oversight, including timely notification to the Central Bank of confirmed technology-related fraud, major security breaches and cyber-attacks, prolonged service disruption and systemic incidents causing customer monetary loss or data leakage, plus a stakeholder communication strategy. Binds SVF Licensees (and, for the general risk/internal control provisions, licensed banks conducting SVF business in the UAE).

The business continuity management component of the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities Regulation, addressing vendor support obligations, reliance on external shared computing (e.g. cloud) for disaster recovery, senior management ownership of the continuity function, and an annual chief-executive statement to the board on the validity of recovery strategies and testing of the plan. It expects at least annual testing with participation of senior management and primary/alternate personnel, documented test plans and results, and a post-mortem review signed off by senior management. Binds SVF Licensees.
lookup_terms: chief executive annual statement to board

data.summary: Sets out reputation risk management duties within the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities Regulation, sitting alongside the general risk management and internal control requirements (board-approved risk framework, liquidity risk process). Licensees must operate a reputation risk process proportionate to size and complexity, embed due diligence to assess reputational implications of plans and activities, act proactively to avoid or contain risks, conduct surveillance to detect emerging reputational threats, and provide early warning and assurance to management. Binds SVF Licensees; the general risk and internal control provisions also apply to licensed banks conducting SVF business.
lookup_terms: general risk management and internal control systems

data.summary: Article 13 of the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities Regulation governs business conduct and Customer protection: SVF schemes must be operated prudently and competently without adversely affecting the interests of Customers or potential Customers, and Licensees must also comply with the Central Bank's existing consumer protection regulatory requirements. It requires responsible, honest and professional conduct and equitable, honest and fair treatment of both Customers and merchants at all stages of the relationship, and conduct that does not undermine the stability of any payment system in the State. Binds SVF Licensees and licensed banks carrying out SVF business.
lookup_terms: fair treatment of customers and merchants

data.summary: Article 14 of the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities Regulation sets the AML/CFT expectations for SVF Licensees, including due diligence models calibrated to the Customer profile and SVF product features, compliance management arrangements enabling AML/CFT system implementation, senior management oversight, and appointment of a Compliance Officer and a Money Laundering Reporting Officer. Licensees must maintain comprehensive AML/CFT policies and procedures under the applicable AML/CFT law and regulations, and must risk-assess and mitigate risks before launching new products, services or technology; FATF risk-based guidance on virtual assets and VASPs is referenced. Binds SVF Licensees (and licensed banks conducting SVF business).

Article 15 of the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities Regulation makes any breach of the Regulation subject to supervisory action and administrative and financial sanctions as the Central Bank sees fit, including replacing or restricting the powers of senior management or the board, interim management of the Licensee, fines, or barring individuals from the UAE financial sector. The surrounding articles cover interpretation (Regulatory Development Division), repeal of the 2016 Regulatory Framework for Stored Value and Electronic Payment Systems, publication/application, and the one-year transition period requiring existing Licensees to complete implementation and submit an independent assessment report. Binds SVF Licensees and their senior individuals.
lookup_terms: repeal of 2016 Stored Value and Electronic Payment Systems framework

data.summary: Node covering the outsourcing provisions of the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities (SVF) Regulation, permitting a Licensee to outsource activities and processes to third parties or intra-group companies only with Central Bank approval.
