It fixes the Licensee as ultimately accountable for the adequacy, service levels, quality, security and continuity of outsourced activities and for the integrity and protection of information held by providers, and requires a comprehensive independent risk assessment plus due diligence on the provider's financial soundness, reputation, management, technical/operational capacity and regulatory capability before outsourcing. It binds SVF Licensees (and is relevant to controlling shareholder / fit-and-proper assessment sitting alongside it in the same chapter).

Node for Article 9 of the CBUAE SVF Regulation on general risk management and internal control systems, requiring a Licensee to maintain risk management policies and procedures proportionate to the scale and complexity of its SVF scheme, a board-approved risk management framework, and dedicated staff with sufficient expertise to oversee risk and internal control. It also addresses liquidity risk management processes. Unlike the information/accounting article, these general requirements expressly extend to licensed banks conducting SVF business in the State.
lookup_terms: licensed banks carrying out SVF business

data.summary: Node for Article 10 of the CBUAE SVF Regulation, setting requirements for robust information and accounting systems: timely and accurate recording of business activities, quality management information, an appropriate audit trail, proper books and accounts, and financial statements/returns meeting applicable reporting and accounting standards, plus record-keeping policies. Scope limit: this Article does not apply to licensed banks carrying out SVF business, which instead follow the Central Bank's banking regulations in these areas. Related material addresses information ownership, classification, storage, transmission, processing and retention of customer data collected through SVF registration and payment transactions.

Node for Article 11 of the CBUAE SVF Regulation on management, protection and safekeeping of the Float. It requires accurate and timely maintenance of the customer ledger so aggregate balances always reflect the Float, segregation of Float assets (cash and bank deposits) from the Licensee's own funds and funds of other business lines, internal controls against theft, fraud and misappropriation, liquidity-focused management of the Float to ensure funds are always available for redemption, and a prohibition on business models relying on investment returns from the Float. Material non-compliance or unresolved reconciliation discrepancies must be reported immediately to the Central Bank with rectification measures.
lookup_terms: reporting material non-compliance to Central Bank

data.summary: Node for Article 12 of the CBUAE SVF Regulation on technology and specific risk management, requiring a Licensee to design and operate technology and risk management systems in line with international best practice and to establish an effective technology and cyber security risk management framework covering IT control adequacy, cyber resilience, and the quality, reliability, robustness, stability, availability and security of its systems. These requirements apply to SVF Licensees and expressly also to licensed banks carrying out SVF business in the State.

Node covering the cyber resilience provisions within the technology risk part of the CBUAE SVF Regulation: managing cyber security risk through the Licensee's technology risk management process, committing adequate resources to identify risk, protect critical services, contain incidents and restore services. It also addresses cyber threat intelligence (including subscribing to relevant services and industry information sharing), periodic assessment of the need for penetration and cyber-attack simulation testing scoped to the cyber risk profile and covering networks, applications, social engineering and emerging threats, timely remediation based on impact and risk exposure, and risks from internet-connected devices. Binds SVF Licensees (and banks conducting SVF business under Article 12).

Concept node for the Financial Action Task Force, cited in CBUAE instruments (notably the Stored Value Facilities Regulation) as the inter-governmental standard-setter for anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist-financing standards. It functions as a definitional and interpretive reference rather than a directly binding instrument: licensees are pointed to FATF outputs, including risk-based approach guidance for virtual assets and virtual asset service providers, when calibrating AML/CTF controls. Relevant to any licensee whose CBUAE obligations are framed by reference to international AML/CTF standards.
lookup_terms: money laundering and terrorist financing standards

data.summary: Institutional node for the Central Bank of the UAE, the licensing, regulatory, supervisory and enforcement authority across the instruments in this corpus. Its powers derive from Decretal Federal Law No. (14) of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities, including licensing of activities such as stored value facilities and the imposition of supervisory action and administrative and financial sanctions. Binds all licensees and entities subject to CBUAE regulation; also the reference point for interpretation of its regulations.

Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 3 of 2010, issuing instructions on the code of conduct and ethics for insurance companies operating in the UAE. It sets market-conduct duties including utmost good faith, disclosure and transparency, accurate and clear information to clients, non-discrimination in rates and terms except on technical or actuarial grounds, and rules on application forms, policy drafting and renewal. It binds companies registered with the Insurance Authority and operating in the State, including foreign insurers' branches, whether marketing directly or through agents or brokers.
lookup_terms: Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 3 of 2010

data.summary: Institutional node for the Insurance Authority, established under Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 concerning the Establishment of the Insurance Authority and the Regulation of Insurance Business, and the issuing body for the insurance conduct and prudential instruments in this corpus (functions later assumed by the Central Bank). Its Board, Chairman and Director General are the decision-making organs referenced in the resolutions. Relevant to determining the issuing authority, scope of registration, and supervisory reach over insurers, agents and brokers.

Sub-node of the 2010 insurance code of conduct dealing with pricing and related conduct duties owed to clients. The surrounding provisions require clear, accurate and truthful information on products, cover terms and limits, and prohibit refusal of proposals, refusal to renew, or discrimination between insured persons on rates, terms and benefits unless justified on technical or actuarial grounds or the company's experience with the client. Binds insurance companies registered with the Insurance Authority and operating in the State.

Article 7 of the 2010 insurance code of conduct, governing how the insurance policy document must be arranged and presented. It requires clear legal and technical language, legible printing with nullification or forfeiture clauses and the arbitration clause set out conspicuously or separately, inclusion of all governing terms, secure binding and page numbering, accurate description of the subject matter and sum insured, a conspicuous non-payment termination clause, investment-reporting statements for life and unit-linked policies, prompt delivery of the policy and endorsements to the insured, an internal issuance mechanism, and that amendments are valid only by agreement of the parties. Binds insurance companies in scope of the instructions; read with Article 8 on renewal and disclosure of material facts.

Article 3 of the CBUAE Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities Regulation (Circular 7/2020) sets the licensing gateway for crowdfunding companies wishing to conduct LCAs in the UAE (outside the Financial Free Zones), including application form and language/currency requirements, selection and justification of Category 1 or Category 2 status, upgrade/downgrade conditions, Central Bank powers to require further information or inspections, and a bank guarantee in favour of the Central Bank equal to required paid-up capital. It binds companies applying for or holding an LCA licence, including those whose platforms are hosted abroad but which serve UAE-resident clients or use a UAE correspondence address. Note this is a CBUAE instrument, not SAMA, so it is comparative rather than directly applicable to KSA-licensed entities.

Article 4 of the CBUAE Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities Regulation sets the prudential floor for crowdfunding companies: minimum capital of AED 1,000,000 (Category 1) or AED 300,000 (Category 2), with an obligation to hold the higher of that amount or capital equal to 5% of outstanding lending volume. It binds licensed LCA crowdfunding companies on an ongoing basis and underpins the bank guarantee requirement in the licensing article. Comparative UAE material; not a SAMA requirement.

Article 5 of the CBUAE Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities Regulation covers corporate governance of licensed crowdfunding companies, including fitness and propriety bars (e.g. confiscation of property, court receivership absent rehabilitation or pardon) and compliance with Emiratisation requirements and subsequent Central Bank requirements. The surrounding definitions article fixes key defined terms such as Borrower, Client, Client money, Pricing Platform, Commitment period and Controlling interest. It binds companies licensed or seeking licence for LCAs in the UAE outside the Financial Free Zones.

Article 6 of the CBUAE Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities Regulation requires a proportionate risk governance framework identifying all material risks, with policies, processes, systems and controls to identify, measure, monitor and mitigate them, plus mitigating action plans. It expressly lists operational, conduct, employee fraud, cybercrime, money laundering, default management, mis-selling and terrorist financing risks; the board is ultimately accountable, the CRO reports directly to the board, and a detailed exit/wind-down plan protecting lender funds and loan administration is required. Binds licensed crowdfunding companies and their boards.
lookup_terms: material risks money laundering terrorist financing

data.summary: Article 7 of the CBUAE Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities Regulation requires adequate internal controls, segregation of duties within the organisational structure, and documented policies, authorities and procedures. It also subjects material outsourcing arrangements to prior Central Bank approval and defines materiality by reference to disruption, insolvency or detrimental impact on the ability to serve clients. Binds licensed crowdfunding companies conducting LCAs in the UAE.

Article 8 of the CBUAE Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities Regulation governs how licensed crowdfunding companies deal with clients; the accompanying definitions and categories articles supply the operative concepts — pricing-model-only business, cooling-off period of at least two business days after the commitment period, funding goal, on-boarding, personal loan, and the Retail Lender versus Market Counterparty client classification (net assets above AED 2,000,000 outside primary residence, with self-attestation verified by the platform). Category thresholds turn on cumulative loans facilitated in a calendar year (AED 5,000,000 and above for Category 1). Binds crowdfunding companies intermediating between lenders and borrowers in the UAE outside the Financial Free Zones.

Article 9 of the IA Code of Conduct and Ethics (original 2010 text) sets the conduct obligations an insurance Company owes when handling a claim from a Client: a documented claims mechanism, free clear claim forms, defined required documents, a stated settlement timeframe, progress updates on request, a decision notification within 15 days of receiving complete documents (extendable with reasons notified), prompt payment against a discharge/subrogation document, and written reasons for any full or partial rejection. It binds insurers registered and operating in the UAE (and, as appropriate, insurance-related professions) in favour of the Insured and Beneficiary. Useful as the baseline fair-treatment standard for claims turnaround and rejection transparency.

Reference node for Ministerial Resolution No. 296 of 2004 (Rules for Insurance Companies' Transactions in the UAE Insurance Market), issued by the Minister of Economy. It is identified in Article 15 of IA Board Resolution No. 3 of 2010 as the instrument expressly replaced by the Code of Conduct and Ethics Instructions, which took effect three months after publication in the Official Gazette. Relevant only for legacy/transitional analysis or when tracing the predecessor rule applicable to insurer market conduct before 2010.

The consolidated (as at 16/09/2019) version of IA Board Resolution No. 3 of 2010, the Instructions on the Code of Conduct and Ethics for insurance companies and insurance-related professions in the UAE. It sets market-conduct duties covering utmost good faith, disclosure and transparency, accurate information to Clients, policy issuance and renewal, advertising standards, claims handling, dealings with the regulator, and settlement of inter-company balances and disputes. It binds insurers registered by the Insurance Authority and operating in the State (including via agents or brokers) and, proportionately, licensed insurance-related professions.
lookup_terms: scope of application insurers and insurance-related professions

data.summary: Node for Insurance Authority Board of Directors Decision No. (40) of 2019, the amending instrument that produced the consolidated 16/09/2019 text of the Code of Conduct and Ethics (Resolution No. 3 of 2010). Its principal effect visible in the consolidated text is extension of the Code to insurance-related professions alongside insurance companies, with defined terms (Company, Client, Insured, Insurance Agent, Policy) retained. Consult it for version control and to establish which conduct obligations applied before versus after September 2019.

CBUAE Circular No. 7/2020, the Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities (LCA) Regulation, establishing the licensing, regulatory and monitoring framework and minimum standards for loan-based crowdfunding in the UAE. It defines the Loan-based Crowdfunding Company and platform model (lenders select opportunities, the platform prices the loan), on-boarding, personal loan and regulated activity, and tiers firms into Category 1 (large) and Category 2 (small) by annual cumulative lending volume against an AED 5,000,000 threshold. It binds crowdfunding companies engaging in LCAs in the UAE wherever their platform is hosted, excluding the Financial Free Zones, with stated aims of financial-system protection and consumer protection.

Decretal Federal Law No. (14) of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities is the primary enabling statute for CBUAE rulemaking, licensing and supervision. It is cited across CBUAE regulations (including the loan-based crowdfunding, payments and related instruments in this set) as the source of the Central Bank's power to issue and enforce those regulations. Open it to verify the legal basis, licensing perimeter and enforcement powers underpinning a specific CBUAE regulation.
lookup_terms: Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities

data.summary: Concept node for the Client Agreement that a crowdfunding company must conclude with its Clients (Lenders and Borrowers) under the CBUAE crowdfunding regulation, including the mandatory terms set out in the appendices. It anchors conduct obligations such as disclosure of terms and conditions and subsequent updates, inclusion of dispute-handling and grievance-redress details, loan administration and default arrangements, applicable lending limits for Market Counterparties, and contingency/platform-failure arrangements. It binds licensed crowdfunding companies in their contractual dealings with Clients.

Concept node covering the disclosure and transparency duties imposed on crowdfunding companies, including disclosing business terms and conditions and updates, written warnings of material risks, conflict-of-interest situations that must be identified and managed, publication of default rates, and the further disclosure items listed in the regulation's appendix. It sits alongside related conduct prohibitions (no advice to Clients, no direct marketing of offers/Borrowers, no borrowing by shareholders, directors or employees) and information-sharing with Al Etihad Credit Bureau. It binds licensed crowdfunding companies toward their Clients and the Central Bank.
lookup_terms: Al Etihad Credit Bureau information sharing

data.summary: Defined-party node for the Lender on a crowdfunding platform, i.e. the Client providing funds to Borrowers through the CFP. It governs the crowdfunding company's duties toward Lenders: onboarding care, suitability assessment and risk understanding, identity and address verification (in addition to AML checks), communication of Borrower due diligence and risk scoring, and the Lender-specific Client Agreement terms on loan administration, default steps, applicable lending limits for Market Counterparties and contingency arrangements. It binds the licensed crowdfunding company; it also frames the Lender's own compliance with lending limits.

Defined-party node for the Borrower raising funds through a crowdfunding platform. It governs the crowdfunding company's Borrower-side obligations: due diligence and risk assessment, credit-bureau based information gathering and risk scoring/pricing, AML checks and identification of the ultimate beneficial owner, measures preventing borrowing for personal use, at least annual review of the Borrower's financial situation, escalation and action plans where risk increases, use of the Central Bank's default definition and methodology, and Borrower declarations of current and intended borrowing from other platforms and sources. It binds the licensed crowdfunding company and imposes disclosure duties on Borrowers via the Client Agreement.

The CBUAE Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation (Circular 15/2021), which sets the licensing rules and ongoing requirements for providing the nine categories of Retail Payment Services (payment account and payment instrument issuance, merchant acquiring, payment aggregation, domestic and cross-border fund transfers, payment token, payment initiation and payment account information services) and for operating Card Schemes. It also requires contractual arrangements between account-issuing PSPs and initiation/account-information providers, addresses Card Scheme fees reporting and regulation, and sets conditions for PSPs participating in wages distribution and accessing the Wages Protection System. It binds licensed Payment Service Providers, applicants and Card Schemes in the UAE.

Defined-term node for the Central Bank Law, Decretal Federal Law No. (14) of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Services, as amended or substituted. It is the enabling statute underpinning CBUAE licensing and supervision, including the licensing regime for money transfer, electronic retail payments and digital money services and the incorporation requirements referenced for licence applicants. It is cross-referenced across multiple CBUAE regulations and binds all entities carrying on licensed financial activities in the UAE.
lookup_terms: Organization of Financial Institutions and Services

data.summary: Article 9 of the CBUAE Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities Regulation setting periodic reporting duties to the Central Bank (quarterly for Category 1, semi-annual for Category 2, within 30 days of period end, plus annual audited financial statements) and the minimum content of those reports, including financial position, client money held, complaints and resolution status, loans arranged and defaults/near-defaults. It also imposes record-keeping obligations: adequate books and records at all times, availability for Central Bank inspection, a ten-year retention period for client money and completed transaction records, and a prescribed list of record categories (marketing and online content, internal policies, corporate/financial ledgers, client and regulator reports, client communications and classification confirmations, suitability assessments). Binds licensed loan-based crowdfunding companies operating in the UAE outside the Financial Free Zones; the surrounding text also places ultimate board responsibility for contingency loan-portfolio administration arrangements.

The client money and disclosure provisions of the CBUAE loan-based crowdfunding framework: a crowdfunding company may not take full ownership of client funds, must hold funds received or disbursed on a client's behalf in segregated/escrow accounts in the client's name, must have those accounts externally audited monthly (Category 1) or quarterly (Category 2), and may only place client funds with Central Bank-licensed local retail banks. Adjacent requirements cover disclosure of terms and conditions and material risk warnings, information sharing with Al Etihad Credit Bureau, conflict-of-interest situations, the prohibition on shareholders/directors/employees borrowing on the platform, the bar on giving advice or directly marketing offers, and dispute handling, grievance redress and collections policies. Binds crowdfunding companies conducting loan-based crowdfunding activities in the UAE.

Concept node for Al Etihad Credit Bureau (AECB) as used in the CBUAE loan-based crowdfunding regime: AECB reports are a required input to borrower due diligence, risk scoring and loan pricing, and regular AECB checks are the expected means of monitoring whether borrowers are drawing loans from other platforms or sources. The same context sets borrower/lender due diligence duties (including AML checks and identifying the ultimate beneficial owner), annual review of borrower financial position, lending ceilings per retail client and market counterparty, a borrower ceiling of AED 10,000,000 per calendar year, single-platform listing per project, all-or-nothing loan release, and client information confidentiality. Binds crowdfunding companies; relevant to credit information sharing obligations elsewhere in the regulation.

Cross-reference node to CBUAE Regulations No. 29/2011 on Bank Loans and Other Services Offered to Individual Customers, invoked in the loan-based crowdfunding regulation as the source of the defined term "personal loan" (a loan to an individual borrower repaid from verifiable regular income from a well-defined source), as amended or superseded. It matters because crowdfunding borrowers must be UAE-registered companies or sole proprietors and platforms must prevent borrowing for personal use. Relevant to anyone mapping the boundary between retail consumer lending rules and crowdfunding activity.

Cross-reference node to UAE Federal Law No. 2 of 2015 on Commercial Companies, cited as the corporate-form requirement for a loan-based crowdfunding company (partnerships and limited partnerships excluded) whose objects include e-finance or similar activities. Appears in the CBUAE Loan-based Crowdfunding Activities Regulation (Circular 7/2020), which is issued under Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018 and applies to crowdfunding companies engaging in loan-based crowdfunding activities in the UAE except the Financial Free Zones. Useful for eligibility and licensing-scope questions rather than conduct obligations.

Definitions article of the CBUAE loan-based crowdfunding regulation, anchoring the term Crowdfunding Platform (CFP) as a web-based platform, social networking site or similar means used for crowdfunding, together with linked defined terms: Borrower (UAE-registered company or sole proprietor), Client (borrower or lender), Client Money, Pricing Platform, commitment period, cooling-off period of at least two full business days, funding goal, Loan, and Lender split into Retail Lender and Market Counterparty (net assets over AED 2,000,000 excluding primary residence, self-attested and verified by the CFP). It also sets the territorial trigger for being treated as conducting these activities in the UAE (incorporation, hosting, UAE correspondence address, or serving UAE-resident clients). Determines who falls within the licensing perimeter and how client categories drive downstream conduct duties.

CBUAE Circular 9/2020 (effective January 2021) issuing the Large Value Payment Systems Regulation, addressed to all System Operators and Settlement Institutions of licensed and/or designated large-value payment systems in the UAE. It sets the licensing requirements for operating an LVPS in the State and the ongoing obligations applying to a designated LVPS, including compliance with the PFMI and provisions of the Central Bank Law on netting, insolvency and preservation of rights. Note this is a UAE (CBUAE) instrument, not a SAMA rule, and is relevant for cross-border or comparative analysis only.

Defined term in the CBUAE Large-value Payment Systems Regulation: a clearing and settlement system designed mainly to process large-value and/or wholesale payments among financial market participants, or involving money market, foreign exchange or commercial transactions. Bilateral clearing and settlement arrangements that do not amount to a "system" are expressly excluded. The definition sets the perimeter for who needs a CBUAE licence and which arrangements can be designated and supervised.

Defined term and related operative provisions: netting means converting the various obligations owed to or by a Participant Person towards all other participants in a clearing and settlement system into a single net obligation. Where netting is effected in an LVPS meeting the designation conditions of the Central Bank Law, the System Operator and/or Settlement Institution must take account of the statutory netting treatment of insolvent or bankrupt parties' obligations. The Regulation does not limit the Central Bank Law provisions on preservation of rights in underlying transactions or a participant's duty to notify insolvency.

Concept node covering the ongoing prudential and governance requirements applying to an LVPS that is systemically important or designated, expressed as the PFMI principles restated in the Regulation. These include a sound legal basis, transparent governance, comprehensive risk management framework, credit and liquidity risk controls, settlement finality by end of value date, and settlement in central bank money where practicable. The obligations bind the System Operator and/or Settlement Institution of the designated system.

Reference concept: the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures, which with IOSCO issued the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures. The Regulation defines PFMI by reference to these bodies and requires designated LVPS to comply with PFMI requirements, making the international standards operative through the CBUAE instrument rather than as standalone soft law.
lookup_terms: Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures

data.summary: Reference concept: the International Organization of Securities Commissions, whose Technical Committee jointly with CPMI issued the Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures. Within the Regulation, IOSCO appears only as a source of the PFMI standards that designated LVPS are required to comply with; the Regulation also identifies the Securities & Commodities Authority alongside the Central Bank as the domestic Regulatory Authorities.

A defined-term node in the CBUAE Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation (Circular 15/2021) that fixes what "AML Law" means for licensed payment actors — the UAE federal AML/CTF decree-law and its implementing Cabinet decision, together with related Central Bank instructions and guidance, as amended. It anchors the Regulation's substantive AML/CFT article, which obliges Payment Service Providers to apply risk-based preventive measures, maintain internal AML/CFT policies and controls, conduct enterprise-wide and relationship-level ML/FT risk assessments, periodically risk-profile Retail Payment Service Users, and report suspicious transactions to the Central Bank's Financial Intelligence unit without hiding behind banking or contractual secrecy. It binds all licensed Payment Service Providers (and, through the incorporation clause, tracks amendments to the underlying AML framework).
lookup_terms: banking secrecy no bar to reporting

data.summary: Core regulated-entity concept of the CBUAE Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation: the licensed person providing one or more of the nine categories of Retail Payment Services (payment account and payment instrument issuance, merchant acquiring, aggregation, fund transfer, payment token and payment information/initiation services). The node's context covers the conduct side — liability and refund duties for Unauthorized Payment Transactions, timing of refunds and value-dating, the fraud-suspicion carve-out with written notification to the Central Bank, and allocation of loss between account-issuing PSPs and Payment Initiation Service Providers. Binds all licensed PSPs and, indirectly, their Agents.

Defines Card Scheme as the rule-set, practices and standards enabling card-based payment transactions in the UAE, distinct from the underlying payment system infrastructure, and includes the Card Scheme Governing Body accountable for its operation; it may be publicly or privately operated. Related definitions distinguish Card Issuer, Cardholder, Card-based Payment Transactions, and Three- versus Four-Party Card Schemes (a three-party scheme converts to four-party once it licenses other PSPs, co-brands or uses agents). Card Schemes must hold a Card Scheme Licence and are subject to ongoing obligations and Central Bank oversight of fees and charges.

The scoping concept of the Regulation: Retail Payment Services are the digital payment activities in the UAE that trigger a Central Bank licensing requirement, grouped into nine categories and split across licence Categories I to IV. The node's context includes the covering circular, which explains the licensing rules, the obligation on Card Schemes to be licensed, mandatory contractual arrangements between account-issuing PSPs and initiation/account-information providers, and additional ongoing requirements for PSPs seeking Wages Protection System access. Determines who falls inside the perimeter and must be licensed.
lookup_terms: nine categories of retail payment services
Category I II III IV licence

data.summary: Annex II is the Regulation's guidance on best practices for technology risk and information security, referenced from the binding technology-risk article. That article requires each Payment Service Provider to maintain a proportionate technology and cyber-security risk management framework covering IT controls, cyber resilience and the reliability, security and availability of its systems, with the Annex itself framed as guidance to consult rather than a standalone mandate. Additional security and cyber obligations attach to PSPs providing Payment Token Services, including per-token security risk assessment and periodic consideration of penetration and cyber-attack simulation testing above a monthly transaction-value threshold.

Annex I lists the Retail Payment Services that a licensed Payment Service Provider may provide, subject to the Regulation's requirements; it is the operative catalogue behind the licensing categories. Read with the definitions and the covering circular, it delimits activities such as payment account and payment instrument issuance, merchant acquiring, payment aggregation, domestic and cross-border fund transfers, payment token services and payment initiation/account information services. Consult it to confirm whether a specific business model falls within a licensable activity and under which permission.
lookup_terms: Annex I list of retail payment services
domestic and cross-border fund transfer service

data.summary: Concept node for the Wages Protection System (WPS), the central bank-hosted reconciliation mechanism for timely and secure payment of wages, and for the related defined terms WPS Payment Account and WPS Payment Account Holder. It governs eligibility of Payment Service Providers to apply for and be granted access to the WPS, the requirement for prior central bank approval, the ability to use an SVF scheme or Bank to hold credited wages, and the demonstration of stringent security measures; once admitted, PSPs may open WPS Payment Accounts. Binds licensed Payment Service Providers seeking or holding WPS access, and is relevant to employers/wage payers as end users of the system.

Concept node for the License requirement under the retail payment services regime, covering the four License categories (I–IV) mapped to specific Retail Payment Services, and the separate licensing of Card Schemes. It sets out that a Person intending to provide Retail Payment Services must apply for the appropriate category, that Card Schemes must be licensed before commencing operations in the State, the 90-day decision timeframe, the central bank's discretion to impose conditions or refuse, and its exclusive right to issue BINs. Binds Applicants, licensed Payment Service Providers and Card Schemes; exemptions may be granted and withdrawn by the central bank.
lookup_terms: Category I II III IV License

data.summary: Definitional node situating Crypto-Asset alongside related defined terms — Virtual Assets, Virtual Asset Service Providers, Virtual Asset Token — and its use within the Money's Worth definition for stored value facilities. It matters for scope: a Virtual Asset Token is a type of Crypto-Asset, and Crypto-Assets or Virtual Assets can constitute value topped up, held or redeemed on an SVF account. Relevant to Payment Service Providers, SVF issuers and any person assessing whether crypto-linked value falls inside the retail payments perimeter or the VASP/FATF perimeter.

Definitional and obligations node for the Retail Payment Service User, the person on whose behalf Payment Accounts, Payment Instruments and payment initiation or aggregation services are provided. It anchors the transparency duties owed to users: pre-contractual disclosure of terms in clear language in Arabic and English, disclosure to existing users on request, at least 30 calendar days' advance notice of changes, and a right to terminate free of charge if revised terms are not accepted. Binds Payment Service Providers in their dealings with each new and existing user.
lookup_terms: right to terminate free of charge

data.summary: Concept node for the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard as a mandatory minimum information security baseline. It requires Card Schemes to apply and meet at least PCI DSS together with the UAE Information Assurance Standards as amended, to report compliance to the Board at least annually and to transmit that report to the central bank, and to notify the central bank of any Data Breach without undue delay and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware. Binds licensed Card Schemes and their Boards.
lookup_terms: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard

data.summary: Concept node for the UAE Information Assurance Standards as the minimum technology and information security benchmark under the retail payments regime. Payment Service Providers must apply and meet at least these standards as amended, within a broader technology risk management framework covering IT governance, an independent technology audit function and Board-level responsibility; Card Schemes must meet these standards together with PCI DSS and report compliance. Binds Payment Service Providers, Card Schemes and their Boards or designated committees.

A node drawn from the CBUAE Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation covering the Card Scheme strand: the defined terms that scope the regime (Card-based Payment Transactions, Card Issuer, Cardholder, Card Scheme, Card Scheme Governing Body, Card Scheme Licence, Category I and II Licences) together with ongoing conduct obligations on licensed Card Schemes. The obligations shown are governance-facing — a Board-approved compliance policy, conflicts-of-interest and code-of-conduct requirements, internal escalation of suspicious transactions to the AML/CTF compliance officer and reporting to the competent authority, and an independent, permanent internal audit function operating under a Board-audit-committee-approved charter. It binds Card Schemes licensed by CBUAE and their Boards and Management; note this is a UAE instrument, relevant to SAMA work only as a comparator, not as KSA law.

Definitional node for "Payment Token" under the CBUAE Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation: a fiat-backed Crypto-Asset that is digitally tradable and functions as a medium of exchange, unit of account and/or store of value, without legal tender status and without representing any equity or debt claim. The definition is the gateway to the Payment Token regime — issuance requires a Category I Licence, a White Paper and prior CBUAE approval before any offer to the public — and it sits alongside neighbouring definitions (Payment Service Provider, Payment Instrument, Payment Account, Payment Initiation Service). Relevant to entities seeking to classify a stablecoin-type product, and to distinguish it from Virtual Asset Tokens, Security Tokens and Commodity Tokens.

Defines "Payment Token Services" as the Retail Payment Services comprising Payment Token Issuing, Buying, Selling, Facilitating the Exchange of Payment Tokens and related activities, placing them inside the CBUAE licensing perimeter for Retail Payment Services. The node also carries the perimeter exclusions: Security Tokens and Commodity Tokens fall to the Securities and Commodities Authority, and Virtual Asset Token services sit outside the Regulation; it further treats Payment Token Services as inherently high ML/TF risk requiring risk assessment, mitigation and adherence to FATF virtual-asset guidance. Binds Payment Service Providers licensed or seeking licence to carry on these activities.
lookup_terms: Facilitating the Exchange of Payment Tokens

data.summary: Covers the Reserve of Assets backing Payment Tokens under the CBUAE regime: a documented stabilisation mechanism policy (asset type, allocation and composition; credit, counterparty, market and liquidity risk assessment; creation and destruction procedures; investment policy; redemption procedure and eligible redeemers). It imposes matching of token creation/destruction against the reserve, segregation from the issuer's own assets, a no-encumbrance/no-pledge rule, custody with a Bank or a Payment Token Custody provider within a short post-issuance window, prompt access for redemption, and independent bi-annual audit from White Paper approval. Binds Payment Service Providers issuing Payment Tokens.

Defines the White Paper as the mandatory pre-offer disclosure document for Payment Tokens under the CBUAE regime, specifying required content: descriptions of the holding, storage and transfer arrangements, risks of the issuer, the token, the public offer and the project, governance arrangements including third parties responsible for operation, investment and custody of the Reserve of Assets, the reserve and its custody and segregation, investment policy, and the nature and enforceability of holders' rights including direct redemption and treatment in insolvency. It also sets form requirements — plain, non-misleading language, dated, endorsed by Management, published on the issuer's website only after CBUAE approval. Binds Payment Service Providers issuing Payment Tokens; no public offering may proceed without it.

Concept node for the Financial Action Task Force standards as incorporated by reference across CBUAE instruments, including the FATF-derived definitions of Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers (exchange between virtual assets and fiat or between virtual assets, transfer, safekeeping/administration, and participation in an issuer's offer or sale). It anchors the requirement that providers of Payment Token Services — treated as high ML/TF risk because of speed, anonymity and cross-border reach — conduct risk assessment and apply mitigation consistent with the FATF risk-based approach guidance for virtual assets and VASPs. Useful for tracing where international AML/CTF standards become operative obligations on licensed providers.

Concept node for the Grievances & Appeals Committee, the statutory review body established under the Central Bank Law to which any person aggrieved by specified Central Bank decisions (such as licensing, suspension or revocation decisions concerning large-value payment system operators and settlement institutions) may refer the decision. Referral must be made in writing to the Central Bank stating the grounds for review, in accordance with the committee's charter. It binds/serves any Person affected by the listed decisions and frames the administrative appeal route within the LVPS regulation.

Concept node for the CPMI strategy on reducing the risk of wholesale payments fraud (seven elements covering prevention, detection, response and communication), which the regulation incorporates as a mandatory reference point. System Operators and Settlement Institutions of designated large-value payment systems must take the strategy and its amendments into account when implementing security measures. It sits alongside the PFMI principles applied to systemically important LVPS and is backed by administrative and financial sanctions for non-compliance.

The Leverage Ratio Standard sets a non-risk-based capital constraint: Tier 1 capital over a total exposure measure covering on-balance-sheet items, derivatives, securities financing transactions and off-balance-sheet commitments (with specified credit conversion factors). It fixes quarter-end calculation (more frequent averaging only with Central Bank approval), applies the same regulatory consolidation scope as the risk-based capital framework, generally bars recognition of collateral or other credit risk mitigation, and requires independent review and challenge of the calculations. It binds licensed banks, which must meet the minimum leverage ratio at all times.

Concept node for the Basel III framework as the international benchmark the Central Bank's capital standards are calibrated to, alongside Basel II's standardised approach implemented in 2009. It underpins capital adequacy, capital supply/instruments and leverage standards, with local adjustments such as a minimum total capital requirement of 10.5% excluding buffers and grandfathering arrangements for pre-2017 AT1 and Tier 2 instruments. Relevant to all licensed banks subject to the capital adequacy regulation and standards.

Concept node for Common Equity Tier 1, the highest-quality component of regulatory capital and the base for the leverage ratio's Tier 1 capital measure, buffer requirements and MDA restrictions. The context covers recognition of minority interest from common shares issued by fully consolidated subsidiaries (only where the instrument would qualify as common shares if issued by the bank and the issuing subsidiary is itself a bank), and the exclusion of profit-sharing investment accounts, investment risk reserves and profit equalisation reserves from Islamic banks' regulatory capital. Binds banks, including Islamic banks, calculating regulatory capital.

Concept node for Additional Tier 1 capital: the eligibility criteria for AT1 instruments (including no features hindering recapitalisation, no bank-funded purchase, SPV proceeds availability for Islamic banks, and loss absorbency at the point of non-viability), treatment of related share premium, and recognition limits for Tier 1 issued by consolidated subsidiaries to third parties. It interacts with CET1 recognition rules and feeds the Tier 1 capital measure used in the leverage ratio. Binds banks issuing or classifying capital instruments.

A concept node on the use of external credit assessments (ECAI ratings) within CBUAE capital standards, covering when an external or inferred rating may drive risk weights for securitisation and other exposures. It sets recognition conditions — inferred ratings must reflect subordination and maturity of the reference exposure and be kept current — and bars reliance on assessments that rest on the bank's own unfunded support or that already embed credit risk mitigation, to prevent double counting. Binds banks subject to CBUAE capital adequacy standards when assigning risk weights.

Defines Point of Non-Viability (PONV) and the related "Non-Viable" trigger for Tier capital instruments: the Central Bank's determination that a bank has or will become non-viable absent a write-down of principal or a public capital injection. It also frames the eligibility/grandfathering process for existing AT1 and Tier 2 instruments, including when a Central Bank letter activating a conditional PONV clause is required and the need for external legal certification. Binds banks issuing or grandfathering regulatory capital instruments under CBUAE capital standards.

Node for the CBUAE Capital Adequacy Regulation (Circular 52/2017) as referenced in the capital standards: it fixes the minimum ratios (including total capital of at least 10.5% of RWA) and the buffer architecture — capital conservation buffer, countercyclical buffer, D-SIB buffer and any individual Supervisory Capital Guidance add-on from the SREP. It also underpins recognition limits for Tier 1 and total capital issued by consolidated subsidiaries to third-party investors, including surplus-capital deductions. Binds all banks licensed by the CBUAE.

Concept node for the comprehensive approach to collateral under the credit risk mitigation framework, under which collateral value is adjusted by haircuts rather than substituting the collateral's risk weight. It is the only approach permitted in the trading book, cannot be combined with the simple approach in the banking book, requires prior Central Bank approval, and is also used for counterparty risk charges on OTC derivatives and repo-style transactions. Binds banks calculating risk-weighted assets under CBUAE credit risk standards.

Concept node for the simple approach to collateral under the credit risk mitigation framework, available only in the banking book and mutually exclusive with the comprehensive approach. Capital relief requires the same minimum conditions as the comprehensive approach: legal certainty and enforceable right to liquidate or take possession on default or insolvency, no material positive correlation between collateral value and counterparty credit quality, and robust liquidation procedures. Binds banks recognising collateral for regulatory capital purposes under CBUAE credit risk standards.

Node drawn from the CBUAE retail payment services and card schemes instrument; despite the label, the supplied material is the definitions article setting out core payment terms — Payment Account, Payment Aggregation Service, Payment Data, Payment Initiation Service, Payment Instrument and its issuance, and Payment Service Provider. It also defines the Payment Token regime (issuing, buying, selling and exchange facilitation), including the Category I licence, white paper and prior Central Bank approval conditions for offering tokens to the public. Binds entities licensed or seeking a licence to provide retail payment services, including merchant aggregators and token service providers.

A CBUAE capital adequacy standard setting out how banks must calculate risk-weighted assets for counterparty credit risk arising from derivatives and long-settlement transactions, replacing earlier CCR measurement approaches for regulatory capital purposes. It follows the Basel standardised approach for CCR, but is applied against the UAE's higher minimum capital requirement, which caps the effective charge on a single exposure. It binds all banks licensed in the UAE and applies on a consolidated basis, sitting alongside the credit risk, securitisation, equity-investments-in-funds and CVA standards.
lookup_terms: standardised approach for counterparty credit risk

data.summary: Defines the netting set as the unit of account for counterparty credit risk exposure measurement: exposure at default is computed separately for each netting set as replacement cost plus potential future exposure, scaled by a fixed alpha factor. It distinguishes margined from un-margined netting sets (with the margined result capped at the un-margined result), sets minimum margin periods of risk including a doubling where repeated unresolved margin disputes occurred, and requires each transaction to be allocated to a hedging set by asset class. Relevant to banks calculating regulatory capital for derivatives portfolios.

Defines replacement cost as the netting-set-level component of counterparty credit risk exposure, derived from the current market value of in-scope derivative contracts net of eligible collateral after haircuts, producing the net current value. Different calculation methods apply to margined and un-margined transactions, and RC is floored at zero for un-margined netting sets. A related fallback applies when valuing fund derivative exposures: where replacement cost cannot be determined, the derivative's notional amount is used instead.

Exposure at default is the exposure amount recognised for counterparty credit risk, computed per netting set as replacement cost plus potential future exposure multiplied by a fixed scaling factor, and then risk weighted. The concept also appears in the treatment of exposures to qualifying central counterparties, where the QCCP's aggregate exposure to clearing members feeds the default fund capital calculation subject to a floor, and in securitisation and fund look-through contexts. Applies to banks computing regulatory capital for derivatives and cleared transactions.

Potential future exposure is the add-on component of counterparty credit risk exposure, calculated per netting set from asset-class add-ons and combined with replacement cost to derive exposure at default. It is also referenced where derivative exposures arise inside securitisations and funds, with a prescribed proportion of notional used as a substitute where PFE cannot be determined. Binds banks measuring regulatory capital for derivative and long-settlement exposures.

The PFE multiplier is the netting-set-level scaling factor applied to the aggregate asset-class add-on to recognise the risk-reducing effect of over-collateralisation and negative mark-to-market, computed from net current value and the aggregate add-on subject to a prescribed floor. Where the formula yields a value above one, the multiplier is set to one. It sits within the supervisory factor, correlation and volatility parameter table used by banks in the standardised CCR calculation.

Concept node for Tier 2 capital as defined within the CBUAE capital adequacy standards, setting out which elements count as the supplementary (going/gone-concern) layer of the regulatory capital base — notably general provisions or general loan loss reserves capped by reference to credit risk-weighted assets, qualifying Tier 2 instruments not already counted in Tier 1, and related share premium. It also ties into the treatment of Tier 1 and Tier 2 instruments issued to third-party investors by fully consolidated subsidiaries, including the surplus-capital deduction mechanics. Binds banks licensed in the UAE when computing eligible capital and capital adequacy ratios on a solo and consolidated basis.
lookup_terms: surplus Tier 1 attributable to third party investors

data.summary: The anchor instrument node: CBUAE's capital adequacy framework and the supporting standards that elaborate supervisory expectations on minimum capital, capital components and buffers, issued under the Central Bank Law and aligned to Basel II standardised and Basel III calibrations. It fixes the UAE-specific minimum total capital requirement above the Basel 8% baseline (excluding buffers) and permits the Central Bank to impose requirements beyond the minimum lists in individual articles. Binds all CBUAE-licensed banks and shapes consolidated-group capital treatment.

Concept node covering credit risk under the standardised approach in the CBUAE capital adequacy standards, including risk weighting of exposures, specific risk charges on credit derivatives (including first-to-default baskets and hedging offsets), and the supervisory review expectation that banks assess credit risk at borrower and portfolio level. Sets out the minimum coverage of the internal credit review for capital adequacy purposes: rating systems, portfolio aggregation, securitisation and complex credit derivatives, and large exposures/concentrations. Binds banks calculating credit risk-weighted assets and their ICAAP-type internal capital assessments.

Concept node on credit risk mitigation — the conditions under which collateral, guarantees and credit derivatives reduce regulatory capital requirements, including treatment of currency, maturity and asset mismatches between protection and the underlying exposure, and the option to apply only the higher of the two capital charges where conditions are met. Recognition of CRM techniques for regulatory capital is conditional on meeting risk management and disclosure requirements subject to Central Bank supervisory review. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks claiming capital relief from credit protection or eligible collateral.

Concept node for credit conversion factors, the mechanism converting off-balance sheet items into on-balance sheet credit exposure equivalents for risk weighting. Identifies the categories attracting a 100% CCF (direct credit substitutes, sale and repurchase agreements and asset sales with recourse, forward asset purchases and certain commitments, securities lending or posting of securities as collateral, and other unclassified credit substitutes) alongside lower CCF bands, and interacts with CRM rules where the converted exposure is collateralised. Binds banks computing credit risk-weighted assets and, separately, exposure measures for leverage purposes.

Concept node for domestic systemically important banks within the CBUAE capital framework — the designation-driven layer of additional capital expectations sitting above the general minimum ratio and buffers. The surrounding material situates it in the supervisory review process, where the Central Bank calibrates capital to an individual bank's risk profile, control environment, stress testing and governance quality, and may set requirements above the stated minimums. Binds banks designated as D-SIBs by the Central Bank, and informs supervisory dialogue for all licensed banks.

Node covering the recognition of guarantees (and, alongside them, credit derivatives) as eligible credit risk mitigation under the CBUAE capital adequacy standard, including the operational conditions protection must satisfy and the effect of residual-maturity shortfalls on recognition. It sits within the broader CRM chapter that also sets out eligible financial collateral and the simple versus comprehensive approaches. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE when computing risk-weighted assets and regulatory capital.

Node on the regulatory treatment of credit derivatives in the CBUAE capital framework, spanning their recognition as unfunded credit protection, the meaning of a written credit derivative and offsetting of purchased protection for leverage ratio purposes, and the counterparty credit risk add-on calculation for credit derivative hedging sets. It addresses conditions such as reference-name identity, pool versus single-name protection, and supervisory factors by rating. Applies to CBUAE-licensed banks measuring capital, leverage and counterparty exposure.

Node dealing with maturity mismatches between a hedge and the underlying exposure for risk-weighted asset purposes, including the conservative definition of maturity on both legs, treatment of embedded call options, and the non-recognition rule where the protection has a short original maturity. Adjacent material covers sovereign guarantees and counter-guarantees and the separate maturity conventions used for securitisation tranches. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks applying credit risk mitigation and securitisation capital rules.

Node associated with currency mismatch adjustments and haircut mechanics in the CBUAE capital standard, drawing on the comprehensive-approach haircut rules (including scaling for re-margining/revaluation frequency and holding-period conversion) and on the foreign exchange risk capital requirements for net open positions. It explains how currency differences between exposure and collateral or protection are penalised through haircuts. Applies to CBUAE-licensed banks calculating credit risk mitigation benefit and market risk capital.

Node on first-to-default credit derivatives, covering how specific risk capital is charged on basket protection (capped by the maximum possible credit event payment) and when a bank may offset the charge against a hedged reference credit instrument, including the rule limiting offset where multiple underlying positions are held. Related material addresses partial allowance where currency, maturity or asset mismatches exist between protection and the underlying. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks measuring market risk and credit protection recognition.

Node on second-to-default (and by extension nth-to-default) credit derivatives within the CBUAE capital framework, treated alongside first-to-default baskets for specific risk capital and credit protection recognition, including the conditions for allowance and offset where mismatches exist. It sits in the same pool-of-mitigants and basket-derivative material as first-to-default treatment. Applies to CBUAE-licensed banks calculating capital for basket credit protection.

Concept node for the hedging set, the grouping level within a netting set used to aggregate derivative trade-level inputs when computing the potential future exposure add-on under the standardised counterparty credit risk approach. It sets the allocation rules per asset class (e.g. one hedging set per currency for interest rate derivatives, with maturity-category subdivision and offset rules), and requires basis transactions and volatility transactions to sit in their own distinct hedging sets. It binds banks calculating counterparty credit risk exposure amounts under the CBUAE capital standards.

Concept node for the adjusted notional amount, the trade-level input used in the add-on calculation for counterparty credit risk. For interest rate and credit derivatives it is the trade notional scaled by a supervisory duration based on the start and end dates of the referenced period, and it includes specific rules for determining trade notionals for state-contingent payoffs, formula-based notionals, variable-notional and leveraged swaps, and multiple principal exchanges. It applies to banks computing exposure at default for derivative transactions.

Concept node for the supervisory delta adjustment, the prescribed directional/optionality multiplier applied to each derivative's adjusted notional and maturity factor to produce the effective notional amount for a hedging set or reference entity. It is used consistently across interest rate, foreign exchange, credit, equity and commodity asset classes in the counterparty credit risk add-on formulas. It binds banks calculating derivative exposure amounts under the CBUAE capital framework.

Concept node for the maturity factor, the time-scaling input in the counterparty credit risk add-on formulas. For margined transactions it is derived from the margin period of risk, with prescribed minimum MPOR floors (including for non-centrally cleared and centrally cleared daily-margined trades and large netting sets) and a doubling requirement where repeated unresolved margin call disputes have occurred. It binds banks computing derivative exposure at default, and interacts with maturity-category and maturity-mismatch concepts elsewhere in the capital standards.

Concept node for the table of supervisory factors and supervisory correlation parameters used to convert effective notional amounts into asset-class and hedging-set add-ons for counterparty credit risk. Supervisory factors are differentiated by asset class and, for credit and equity, by rating or single-name versus index status; supervisory correlations drive the aggregation formulas for credit, equity and commodity hedging sets (energy, metals, agriculture, other). It binds banks applying the standardised counterparty credit risk approach.

Concept node for the credit derivative add-on in the counterparty credit risk calculation: effective notional amounts are computed per reference entity or index from adjusted notional, maturity factor and supervisory delta, then scaled by the rating-dependent supervisory factor, with unrated single names treated at the BBB factor. Related context addresses the treatment of written credit derivatives and offsetting purchased protection for leverage ratio exposure purposes, including when pool-level protection may offset single-name protection sold. It binds banks measuring derivative exposures and leverage ratio exposure.
lookup_terms: single name and index credit derivatives

data.summary: A component of the CBUAE counterparty credit risk standard setting out how the potential future exposure add-on is built for interest rate derivatives: contracts are sorted into three remaining-maturity buckets, and effective notional amounts are derived per currency hedging set from adjusted notional, supervisory delta and maturity factor. It also frames the general rule that basis and volatility transactions sit in their own hedging sets within each asset class. It binds banks calculating regulatory capital for derivative exposures.

Covers the add-on calculation for foreign exchange derivatives under the CBUAE counterparty credit risk standard, where each currency pair forms a hedging set and the absolute effective notional is scaled by the FX supervisory factor and aggregated across hedging sets. Adjacent context also touches market risk treatment of net open FX positions (including gold, AED/USD relationship and the 8% charge). Applies to banks computing derivative exposure and FX capital requirements.

Sets out the equity derivatives add-on: entity-level effective notionals (single name or index) are scaled by supervisory factors, then combined at hedging-set level using supervisory correlations, with basis and volatility trades placed in separate hedging sets. Related context also addresses the separate market risk specific/general charges for equity positions and derivatives. Binds banks calculating counterparty credit and market risk capital.

Describes the commodity derivatives add-on: effective notionals are computed per commodity type, scaled by supervisory factors, then aggregated into four hedging sets (energy, metals, agriculture, other) using a supervisory correlation, with basis and volatility trades in separate hedging sets. It notes the hedging sets ignore location and quality differences, so basis risk within a set is not captured. Applies to banks computing derivative exposure for capital purposes.

Defines the preferential capital treatment for bank exposures to qualifying central counterparties, covering trade exposures as clearing member or client, posted collateral and default fund contributions, including the 2% risk weight and a 10-day minimum margin period of risk for OTC derivatives. It also permits a bank to fall back to non-qualifying CCP treatment where that produces lower combined RWA. Binds banks with cleared derivative exposures.

Explains the CBUAE rationale and framework for capitalising bank exposures to central counterparties, distinguishing qualifying from non-qualifying CCPs and assigning lower risk weights where qualification standards are met. Surrounding context also covers combined replacement cost and PFE treatment where one margin agreement spans multiple netting sets. Applies to banks clearing or providing client clearing for OTC derivatives.

Concept node for the Standardised Approach to securitisation exposures (SEC-SA) under the CBUAE securitisation capital standard, covering how a bank determines the exposure amount (including a 100% credit conversion factor for non-mitigant off-balance-sheet facilities) and then derives a risk weight, with the outcome driven by the parameters A, D and KA and a weighted-average formula where the attachment point falls below KA. It also carries the associated floors and constraints, notably the 15% risk-weight floor and the rule that an unrated junior exposure cannot attract a lower risk weight than the next more senior rated exposure. It binds CBUAE-licensed banks computing risk-weighted assets for securitisation positions held in the banking book.

Concept node for the attachment point (A) and detachment point (D) of a tranche, the inputs that define where a securitisation or CDO tranche sits in the loss waterfall. In the CBUAE standard these parameters drive SEC-SA risk weighting, the tranche-thickness adjustment under SEC-ERBA, the decomposition of tranched credit protection into sub-tranches, and the supervisory delta adjustment for CDO tranche derivatives under the counterparty credit risk calculation. Relevant to banks calculating capital for securitisation positions and for securitisation-related derivatives.

Concept node for tranche maturity (MT), a tranche's remaining effective maturity in years used as an input to securitisation risk weighting. Under the external ratings-based approach (SEC-ERBA) the risk weight is obtained by linear interpolation between the published one-year and five-year risk weights for the relevant rating, subject to a floor and to a separate thickness adjustment for non-senior tranches. Applies to banks using SEC-ERBA for rated securitisation exposures, including inferred-rating cases for lower-priority sub-tranches.

Concept node for resecuritisation exposures, defined as securitisation exposures where the risk of an underlying pool is tranched and at least one underlying exposure is itself a securitisation exposure. The node sits alongside the standard's other definitions (early amortisation, excess spread, implicit support, originating bank, pool) and is significant because resecuritisations are excluded from STC-compliant treatment and attract more conservative capital treatment. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks holding, originating or sponsoring such positions.

Concept node for Simple, Transparent and Comparable (STC) securitisation, the qualifying category that permits alternative (more favourable) regulatory capital treatment where the criteria in the standard's appendices are met. It sets out scope exclusions (synthetic securitisations, securitisations of revolving credit facilities and resecuritisations are not STC-compliant), the originator/sponsor disclosure duty, the investor's own obligation to assess STC status, and the requirement that the criteria be satisfied on a continuing basis. Binds originators, sponsors and investing banks under CBUAE supervision.

Concept node for asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) conduits and programmes: a special purpose vehicle issuing commercial paper against claims on underlying assets, and the programme of paper it issues. Under the CBUAE standard, short-term STC status for an ABCP conduit requires the appendix criteria to be met at both conduit and transaction level, with sponsor duties on transaction documentation and independent legal review, retention of a material net economic exposure to align interests, and limits on maturity transformation. Relevant to banks acting as sponsor, liquidity/credit support provider or investor, and to the originating-bank definition where sponsoring makes a bank an originator.

Concept node within the CBUAE capital standards covering non-contractual (implicit) support to securitisation structures, distinguished from contractual credit enhancement provided at inception (e.g. overcollateralisation, subordinated notes, spread accounts, clean-up calls above the 10% threshold). It is framed as a risk-management and capital-integrity issue: banks must recognise the likelihood that they would support their own securitisations under stress, measure that potential support as part of reputational-risk assessment and stress testing, and reflect it in the ICAAP and Pillar 2 capital. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE, in particular originators and sponsors relying on securitisation as a funding tool.

Concept node on clean-up calls and related early amortisation features in securitisation transactions under the CBUAE capital standards, including the operational conditions determining whether an originating bank may exclude underlying exposures from risk-weighted assets. It sets out early amortisation triggers that subordinate or otherwise increase the originator's exposure, and lists structures (replenishment, term-mimicking, certain revolving structures) that may still qualify while capital is held against retained securitisation exposures. Binds originating banks structuring traditional or synthetic securitisations; the surrounding context also touches Additional Tier 1 call conditions requiring prior Central Bank approval.
lookup_terms: call option prior Central Bank approval

data.summary: Node covering the market risk elements of the CBUAE capital standards, including the separate specific-risk and general-market-risk capital charges for equity positions (8% of gross equity positions and 8% of the overall net position respectively), market-by-market netting, and the treatment of equity derivatives, stock indices and index arbitrage. It also sits alongside the Pillar 2 requirement that market risk be addressed in the bank's comprehensive risk assessment. Binds banks licensed in the UAE holding trading-book and equity-price-sensitive positions.

Node covering operational risk under the CBUAE capital standards: qualifying criteria for the operational risk management framework (use in risk and management reporting, regular reporting of exposures and material losses to business units, senior management and the board, documented policies and treatment of non-compliance, independent validation and review by external auditors or the Central Bank) and additional conditions for the Alternative Standardised Approach (ASA), which is closed to large diversified banks and requires retail/commercial banking to represent at least 90% of income. Binds banks licensed by the CBUAE seeking or using these approaches.

Node for the CBUAE Pillar 2 / Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process standard, setting the principles of supervisory review across interest rate risk in the banking book, credit risk (stress testing, residual and concentration risk), operational risk, securitisation and cross-border supervisory cooperation. Key scope constraints: only a Pillar 1 Plus approach is permitted, internal models may not be used to estimate ICAAP capital requirements (reported figures must follow the Standardised Approach), buffers are additive with no offsetting against Pillar 1, and the Central Bank alone determines the capital quality (CET1, AT1, Tier 2) required for Pillar 2 risks. Binds all banks required to submit an ICAAP to the CBUAE.
lookup_terms: IRRBB interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: Node for the CBUAE Pillar 3 market disclosure standard, which supersedes the 2009 Pillar 3 requirements and prescribes the disclosure tables, their quarterly, semi-annual or annual frequency, and publication as a stand-alone report on the bank's UAE-specific website (or as a discrete section of financial reporting with the tables still disclosed separately). It applies to all UAE banks at consolidated level and to all branches of foreign banks, effective from Q2 2020, and extends to banks offering Islamic financial services for Shari'ah-compliant activities parallel to those described.
lookup_terms: branches of foreign banks consolidated disclosure

data.summary: Defines the look-through approach, the first and most granular of the three permitted methods for risk weighting banks' banking-book equity investments in funds under the CBUAE capital adequacy standard. It requires the bank to risk weight the fund's underlying exposures (including derivative-related counterparty credit risk) as if held directly, and is mandatory where the fund reports with sufficient frequency and granularity and the underlying exposures are verified by an independent third party such as a custodian, depository or fund management company. Binds all UAE banks on a consolidated basis holding in-scope equity positions in funds.

Defines the mandate-based approach, the second tier in the hierarchy for risk weighting banks' banking-book equity investments in funds where the conditions for the look-through approach are not met. It risk weights the fund's assets on the conservative assumption that the mandate is used to the maximum extent in the highest risk-weighted assets, with prescribed fallbacks for derivative replacement cost and potential future exposure, a 1.5 multiplier for CVA risk, and calculation of the fund's average risk weight. Binds all UAE banks on a consolidated basis.

Node for the fall-back approach, the third and most conservative method in the CBUAE hierarchy for risk weighting banking-book equity investments in funds, applied where neither the look-through nor the mandate-based approach conditions can be satisfied. The supplied context frames it only by its position after the MBA calculation of the fund's average risk weight; the detailed treatment sits in the underlying standard. Applies to all UAE banks on a consolidated basis.

Sets out the leverage adjustment applied to the average risk weight of a fund when determining the risk weight for a bank's equity investment in that fund. Leverage is the ratio of total unweighted fund assets to fund equity, derived from actual holdings under the look-through approach or from the maximum leverage permitted by the mandate or governing regulations under the mandate-based approach; the resulting risk weight (average risk weight multiplied by leverage) is capped at 1250 percent. Binds all UAE banks holding in-scope equity positions in funds on a consolidated basis.
lookup_terms: RWA for equity investments in funds

data.summary: The CBUAE securitisation standard, based on the Basel revised securitisation framework, setting risk-based capital requirements for banking-book securitisation and resecuritisation exposures, including retained tranches, asset-backed investments, liquidity facilities, credit enhancements and credit risk mitigants. It includes key defined terms (originating bank, pool, implicit support, excess spread, early amortisation, resecuritisation), a prohibition on implicit support with punitive capital and public disclosure consequences, and specific resecuritisation parameters with a 100 percent risk weight floor. Applies to all UAE banks on a consolidated basis.

Node covering the external ratings-based approach within the CBUAE securitisation capital framework, one of the hierarchy of methods for assigning risk weights to securitisation exposures. The surrounding provisions address how the exposure amount is determined (100 percent credit conversion factor for non-mitigant off-balance-sheet facilities, counterparty credit risk treatment for securitisation-related derivatives), the multiplication of exposure amount by the applicable risk weight, risk-weight caps, overlapping exposures, and deduction from CET1 of equity increases arising from securitisation. Binds UAE banks on a consolidated basis.

Node covering the leverage ratio component of the CBUAE capital standards: a non-risk-based Tier 1 capital measure (CET1 and/or AT1) over a total exposure measure, calculated at least quarter-end and required to meet or exceed the minimum ratio set in UAE regulations at all times. It sets the scope of regulatory consolidation (aligned to the risk-based framework), treatment of capital investments in entities outside consolidation, gross-accounting exposure measurement with limited recognition of collateral or credit risk mitigation, credit conversion factors for off-balance-sheet commitments, and independent review/audit of the calculation. Binds banks licensed and supervised by the CBUAE (UAE regime, not SAMA).

Node for the Basic Indicator Approach, the simplest gross-income-based method for calculating the operational risk capital charge under the CBUAE capital standards. The surrounding standard text also addresses credit risk mitigation (simple vs comprehensive collateral approaches, minimum legal-certainty and liquidation conditions) and the look-through, mandate-based and fall-back approaches for equity investments in funds. Applies to banks in the UAE under CBUAE supervision; use of certain approaches requires prior Central Bank approval.

Node for the Standardised Approach to operational risk capital within the CBUAE capital standards, including the qualifying criteria a bank must meet — board and senior management oversight, integration of operational risk data into risk and management reporting, documented policies and controls, independent validation, and external audit or Central Bank review. Related context covers the comprehensive assessment of all material risks (credit, concentration, securitisation, large exposures) in the internal capital adequacy process. Binds UAE-licensed banks on a consolidated basis.

Node for the Alternative Standardised Approach (ASA) to operational risk capital under the CBUAE capital standards, an optional variant of the Standardised Approach subject to Central Bank permission. Eligibility is restricted: large diversified banks may not use it, and an applicant must show that retail or commercial banking accounts for at least 90% of income and that gross income is not a reliable exposure indicator. Sits within the operational risk standard defining operational risk (including legal and compliance risk, excluding strategic and reputational risk) and gross income, applicable to UAE banks on a consolidated basis.
lookup_terms: Central Bank approval operational risk approach

data.summary: Node covering interest rate risk in the trading book under the CBUAE market risk capital standard, including the banking book/trading book boundary and the conditions for a position to receive trading book capital treatment. Requirements include a documented and senior-management-approved trading strategy, active management on a trading desk with monitored position limits, at least daily mark-to-market or model parameter assessment, senior management reporting, and policies governing transfers between books. Binds UAE banks holding trading positions.
