Node setting out the equity position risk capital charge in the CBUAE trading book/market risk standard: a specific risk charge of 8% of gross equity positions (long plus short, absolute values) and a general market risk charge of 8% of the overall net position, computed market by market. It also covers equity derivatives, stock indices and index arbitrage, position calculation, and related specific risk rules for correlation trading and securitisation exposures, including the cap at maximum possible loss. Applies to banks in the UAE holding equity and equity-derivative trading positions.

Capital treatment of a bank's pre-funded contributions to a qualifying central counterparty's (QCCP) default fund, setting out the RWA formula and its inputs (the 20% risk weight subject to Central Bank uplift, the bank's contribution DFM, the total default fund DF, and the QCCP's aggregate clearing-member EAD). It imposes a floor requiring RWA of at least 2% of the bank's pre-funded contributions and specifies that member exposures are measured as bilateral counterparty credit risk trade exposure using a 10-day margin period of risk, net of collateral the QCCP can legally claim on default. Binds UAE banks that are clearing members of, or contribute to the default fund of, a CCP, on a consolidated basis.

The CBUAE Standard governing calculation of risk-weighted assets for credit valuation adjustment (CVA) risk, based on the Basel III standardised CVA approach. It scopes in all derivative transactions other than those faced directly with a central counterparty, plus fair-valued securities financing transactions unless the Central Bank deems the CVA loss exposure immaterial, and defines the CVA portfolio as all covered transactions together with eligible CVA hedges. Applies to all UAE banks on a consolidated basis.

Sets the eligibility conditions for hedges to be recognised in the CVA capital calculation: the instrument must be an index CDS, single-name CDS, single-name contingent CDS or equivalent directly referencing the hedged counterparty, and it must form part of the bank's CVA risk management programme and be managed with the intent of mitigating the counterparty credit spread component of CVA risk. Recognised CVA hedges are carved out of the bank's market risk capital calculation, while non-eligible transactions are treated as ordinary instruments for regulatory capital. Binds UAE banks applying the CVA Standard.

The mechanics of computing CVA capital: discounting each counterparty's total EAD by a supervisory discount factor reflecting the notional weighted-average maturity of the netting set, summing across netting sets where multiple exist, and computing discounted values of eligible single-name hedges by hedge maturity. It sits within the wider capital adequacy framework (minimum total capital of 10.5% of RWA plus CCB, CCyB, D-SIB and any SREP-based supervisory capital guidance add-on). Binds UAE banks on a consolidated basis.

A cross-cutting concept node for single-name exposure as used in CBUAE capital standards — most directly in the CVA framework (single-name hedges and counterparty-specific exposure) and in exposure-level risk weighting under the securitisation standard. The supplied context is drawn from the securitisation chapter (SEC-SA risk weights, floors, look-through and capital caps) and securitisation definitions, so the node is a weak anchor for the term itself. Open the underlying standards rather than relying on this node for a definition; relevant to UAE banks calculating RWA on a consolidated basis.

The CBUAE Standard on capital requirements for banks' banking-book equity investments in funds, aligned to BCBS 266, requiring RWA to be computed as if the bank held the fund's underlying exposures directly, via a hierarchy of look-through, mandate-based and fall-back approaches. It covers off-balance-sheet exposures such as unfunded commitments to future capital calls, excludes exposures deducted from capital, and requires a leverage adjustment (assets to equity) applied to the fund's average risk weight, with an overall 1250% risk weight cap. Applies to all UAE banks on a consolidated basis.

Node covering the foreign exchange component of the market risk capital framework: how a bank identifies net open positions in each foreign currency and in gold, converts them at spot into local currency, and derives an overall net open position (greater of aggregate net long or net short positions, excluding US dollar, plus the absolute gold position) to which an 8% capital charge applies. It also addresses consolidated measurement, including use of internal currency position limits as a proxy for marginal foreign branches/subsidiaries subject to ex-post monitoring. It binds banks subject to the central bank's capital adequacy/market risk standard, and links into the broader ICAAP-style comprehensive risk assessment expectations.

Node on commodities risk within the market risk capital framework, covering the maturity ladder treatment (gross-position charges per time band plus cumulative net-position charges and a final spread charge across all bands) and the alternative simplified approach for commodity positions. The surrounding context ties commodity exposures into the requirement that all material risks be captured in the bank's internal capital assessment, with board and senior management review of new products and firm-wide risk limits. Binds banks holding commodity or commodity-derivative positions.

Node setting out how options are captured in market risk capital: two alternative methods, a simplified approach available to banks holding only purchased options and a delta-plus approach for more complex option books. It also explains how to identify the underlying where this is ambiguous (e.g. FX) and the use of nominal value where the underlying's market value may be zero. Binds banks with option or option-like positions (including caps, floors and swaptions) in the trading book.

Node describing the delta-plus method for options, under which options enter each market risk category as a delta-weighted position (market value of the underlying times delta), with equity options fed into the equity charge, FX and gold options into the foreign exchange charge, commodity options into the simplified or maturity ladder approach, and interest rate/debt options slotted into time bands on a two-legged basis. Applies to banks that write options or otherwise cannot use the simplified option approach.
lookup_terms: options on foreign exchange and gold

data.summary: Node on the simplified option treatment, available to banks whose option books consist only of purchased options, presented alongside the simplified approach for commodities (a 15% charge on the net position plus 3% of the gross position per commodity, valued at current spot prices). It marks the boundary between banks eligible for simplified carve-outs and those required to use delta-plus. Binds banks calculating market risk capital for option and commodity positions.

Node on the specific risk capital charge for trading book positions, including the correlation trading portfolio (larger of aggregate net long or net short specific risk charges), securitisation exposures (banking book risk weight multiplied by 8%, with 1250%-weighted positions excludable from general market risk), the cap at maximum possible loss, hedged positions with currency, maturity or asset mismatches, and first-to-default credit derivatives. Binds banks holding credit derivatives, securitisation or correlation trading exposures in the trading book.

Concept node covering the general market risk capital charge under the CBUAE market risk standard, i.e. the charge on a bank's overall net position in a given market (for equities, the net of longs and shorts, charged at 8%), as distinct from the specific risk charge on gross positions. It also frames how the charge is applied market-by-market and extended in modified form to equity derivatives, stock indices and index arbitrage. It binds banks calculating trading book capital requirements under the standardised approach.

Concept node for the maturity-based approach to measuring interest rate risk in the trading book, in which positions are slotted into time bands and zones with vertical and horizontal disallowance factors, and for related maturity definitions used elsewhere in the capital framework (maturity mismatch of hedges, and weighted-average versus legal maturity for securitisation tranches). It sets the conservative conventions banks must use when defining effective maturity of exposures and credit protection. Applies to banks computing risk-weighted assets and market risk capital under CBUAE standards.

Concept node for the alternative duration-based method of calculating the general market risk charge for interest rate positions, under which banks with adequate capability may, with Central Bank consent, measure price sensitivity of each position to specified rate shocks and slot the results into time bands subject to a vertical disallowance and zone-based horizontal disallowances. Use of the method requires continuous application unless a change is approved, and separate maturity ladders and capital charges per currency. Binds banks electing this approach for trading book interest rate risk.

Appendix-level guidance setting minimum expectations for prudent valuation of trading book positions, covering governance systems and controls (documented valuation policies, independent reporting lines up to a board executive director) and valuation methodologies beginning with at-least-daily marking to market at independently sourced close-out prices. It underpins supervisory assessment of fair value practices, including for complex or illiquid instruments. Binds banks holding fair-valued positions.

Concept node defining risk concentration as a single exposure or group of correlated exposures (same counterparty, geography, industry or risk factor) large enough to threaten a bank's creditworthiness, core operations or risk profile, and requiring analysis at both legal entity and consolidated level. It sits within the Pillar 2 / ICAAP comprehensive assessment of risks, requiring aggregation of similar exposures across entities, asset types and risk areas, and routine reporting of concentrated positions to senior management. Binds banks in their internal capital adequacy assessment.

Concept node on interest rate risk in the banking book as a material risk that must be captured in the bank's internal capital adequacy assessment, requiring a measurement process covering all material interest rate positions with full repricing and maturity data, behavioural and maturity assumptions, and documented techniques. It sits alongside related Pillar 2 expectations on market risk stress testing and concentration management. Binds banks assessing and holding internal capital for IRRBB.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book
rate index repricing caps and floors

data.summary: Node covering counterparty credit risk within the CBUAE capital standards (Doc 1691 v2), spanning specific-risk capital treatment of credit derivatives (including currency, maturity and asset mismatches, and first-to-default basket products) and the supervisory expectation that credit risk be comprehensively assessed in the ICAAP. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE, requiring methodologies for borrower- and portfolio-level credit risk, internal rating systems, and treatment of concentrations and complex credit derivatives. Relevant only as comparative material for a SAMA analyst; it is UAE, not KSA, law.

Node on reputational risk and implicit (non-contractual) support to securitisations under the CBUAE capital standards, including the duty to identify reputational risk sources when entering new markets or products, to reflect it in stress testing, and to quantify the support a bank might feel compelled to provide. It also sets out the consequence of providing implicit support and the distinction between contractual credit enhancement and implicit support. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks and their boards/senior management through Pillar 2 and ICAAP.

Node addressing liquidity and firm-wide risk management expectations within the CBUAE ICAAP framework, framed around the seven features of a rigorous capital assessment process, board and senior management oversight, risk appetite setting, MIS, and internal controls. It also confirms that Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 requirements are separate and cannot be netted. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks, with primary accountability on the board and senior management.

Node labelled Herfindahl-Hirschman Index but drawn from CBUAE capital standard material on CVA capital calculation (index hedges, single-name decomposition, CVA RWA multiplier of 12.5, and the simple alternative approach) and on specific/general market risk charges for equity derivatives and index arbitrage strategies. Useful for concentration-metric and CVA/market risk questions; binds CBUAE-licensed banks. Check the source before relying on any HHI-specific formula, as the context is concentration/index-weighting rather than a defined HHI test.

Node on the CBUAE securitisation framework and supervisory review, including defined terms (early amortisation provision, excess spread, implicit support, originating bank, pool, resecuritisation exposure) and the capital treatment of resecuritisation exposures with a 100% risk-weight floor. It prohibits originators from providing implicit support and imposes capital, gain-on-sale and public disclosure consequences where support is given. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks acting as originators, sponsors or investors.

Node setting out the CBUAE leverage ratio: Tier 1 capital as the capital measure, quarter-end calculation, the regulatory scope of consolidation, and the composition of the total exposure measure (on-balance-sheet, derivative, SFT and off-balance-sheet exposures). It restricts recognition of collateral, guarantees and other credit risk mitigation in the exposure measure and addresses possible temporary exemption of central bank reserves with offsetting recalibration and disclosure. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks on an ongoing basis.

A sub-part of the CBUAE capital adequacy Standards dealing with how derivative positions enter the leverage ratio exposure measure, including client-clearing arrangements. It sets when a bank acting as clearing member may exclude client trade exposures (conditions on portability/segregation and non-reimbursement of client losses), requires guarantees of client performance to the CCP to be measured as if the bank had transacted directly, and treats trades with consolidated affiliates as proprietary exposures. It binds banks licensed in the UAE calculating leverage ratio exposure at the relevant level of consolidation.

Concept node for the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision as the source of the international minimum standards that the CBUAE capital adequacy Standards implement (Basel II standardised approach, adopted in the UAE in 2009, and Basel III). The introduction explains that the Standards are issued under the Central Bank Law, follow Basel calibration (1250% maximum risk weight on an 8% total capital base) but impose a higher UAE minimum of 10.5% excluding buffers, and that the Central Bank may add requirements beyond those listed. Binds all banks licensed in the UAE.

Defines and sets the leverage ratio treatment of written credit derivatives, i.e. contracts through which a bank effectively sells credit protection, which generate notional credit exposure in addition to counterparty credit risk on fair value. It specifies the conditions for offsetting with purchased protection (symmetrical fair-value adjustments to effective notional, exclusion where the offsetting protection relates to client-cleared trades), states that reference names match only if the same legal entity, and permits pool protection to offset single-name protection where economically equivalent. Binds banks computing the leverage ratio exposure measure.

Covers the treatment of securities financing transactions (SFTs) in the exposure measure, including when cash payables and receivables with the same counterparty may be netted — same explicit final settlement date, legally enforceable set-off including on default/insolvency, and intent/mechanism for net or functionally net settlement, with failed securities legs split out and treated gross. It also requires a counterparty credit risk add-on to the adjusted gross SFT amount, and sits alongside credit conversion factor and failed-trade/non-DvP provisions. Binds banks measuring SFT and off-balance sheet exposures.

Sets the risk-weighted asset treatment of exposures to qualifying central counterparties, distinguishing the bank's role as clearing member from its role as a client of a clearing member. Key rules include a 2% risk weight for trade exposures to a QCCP, a minimum 10-day margin period of risk for OTC derivative trade exposures to QCCPs, treatment of clearing member exposures to clients as bilateral trades (minimum 5-day MPOR), recognition of collateral passed on to the QCCP, coverage of multi-level client structures, and the option to treat exposures as if the CCP were non-qualifying where that produces lower RWA. Binds UAE-licensed banks with cleared derivative activity.

CBUAE Regulations No. 29/2011 (23/02/2011) on bank loans and other services offered to individual (retail) customers, issued under the 1980 Union Law on the Central Bank and addressed to all banks and finance companies. It defines retail lending terms and imposes conduct and affordability limits — e.g. a 50% gross salary deduction cap on instalments, scheduling so that only 30% of income or pension is deducted where repayment extends past retirement age, a cap on security cheques at 120% of loan value, and special rules for armed forces staff including a prohibition on taking or copying military ID cards. Binds conventional and Islamic banks and finance companies in their dealings with individual customers.

Consolidated (version 2) text of the CBUAE regulation on bank loans and other services offered to individual (retail) customers, issued under Notice 29/2011 pursuant to the Union Law on the Central Bank, monetary system and banking organisation. It sets the conduct and product terms governing the relationship between banks (conventional and Islamic) and finance companies and their individual customers, covering loan definitions, instalment/salary-deduction caps (including a special regime for Armed Forces staff), bank account types, account closure timelines, and commissions, fees and charges. It binds all licensed banks and finance companies lending to individuals in the UAE.
lookup_terms: Bank Loans and Other Services Offered to Individual Customers
armed forces staff loans salary deduction

data.summary: Article 2 of the original (version 1) regulation defining the Personal Loan as a loan to individual customers repaid from salary, end-of-service benefits or other verifiable regular income from a defined source. It fixes the maximum exposure at twenty times the borrower's salary or total income, limits the repayment tenor, ties monthly deductions to the salary-deduction ceiling in Article 7, extends the same treatment to loans to sole proprietorships and companies secured by owner/partner salaries, and requires use of the prescribed application/agreement form. Binds banks and finance companies granting personal loans.
lookup_terms: sole proprietorship loan secured by salary

data.summary: Article 3 of the original regulation defining the Car Loan as financing extended by a bank or finance company for the purchase of a private vehicle, treated separately from the personal consumer loan. It caps financing at eighty percent of the financed vehicle's value, limits repayment to sixty months, requires security by mortgage over the car, and applies the same terms to car loans to sole proprietorships and companies secured by owner/partner salaries. Binds banks and finance companies offering vehicle finance to individuals.

Article 5 of the original regulation defining Credit Cards as cards linked to an electronic network with a set credit limit, where the issuer settles purchases and cash withdrawals on the holder's behalf for repayment in the following month or by instalment. It sets issuer obligations: minimum annual income eligibility (or issuance against a pledged deposit of a specified minimum), separate statistical recording for non-customer/resident status, monthly expense statements, immediate investigation of disputed items, and use of the prescribed agreement form. Binds card-issuing banks and finance companies.

Article 6 (with Appendix 1) of the original regulation prescribing how interest or profit is calculated on personal loans, car loans, overdrafts and unpaid credit card balances. It mandates a stated computation method, prohibits deducting interest up front from the loan amount by requiring reducing-balance calculation on the outstanding monthly balance, limits credit card interest to balances outstanding after the full-payment due date, and requires prepayment/top-up penalty rates and applicable interest rates to be declared in the published rate table. Binds banks and finance companies pricing retail credit.
lookup_terms: credit card interest on unpaid balance

data.summary: Node covering the regulation's ceiling on repayment instalments, i.e. the limit on deductions from a borrower's salary or regular income for all loans extended by banks and finance companies, set out in Article 7 and cross-referenced by the personal, car, overdraft and credit card articles. The consolidated text applies a fifty percent of gross salary ceiling to all instalments and facilities for Armed Forces personnel. Binds all banks and finance companies assessing borrower affordability for individual customers.

This node is the pre-2018 UAE federal banking statute (Union Law No. 10 of 1980 on the Central Bank, the Monetary System and Organization of Banking) as invoked in the CBUAE Regulations No. 29/2011 on bank loans and services offered to individual customers. It functions as the enabling authority for those retail lending/consumer regulations (cited articles 5, 18, 94 and 96) and as the sanctioning basis, with Article 107 supplying the fine imposed per violation and accrued daily once a breach is established. It binds banks and finance companies dealing with individual customers, with violations referred to the Central Bank's Legal Development Unit.
lookup_terms: Central Bank, Monetary System and Organization of Banking
legal basis for retail lending regulations

data.summary: This is the CBUAE Specialized Banks with Low Risk Regulation (Circular 21/2022, effective 10/01/2022), issued under the Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018), creating a dedicated licensing and supervisory framework for a restricted-scope bank category. It sets out licensing, permitted activities, deposit-taking and funding caps, capital, liquidity, credit exposure, governance/AML/consumer-protection compliance and credit-reporting duties, aimed at protecting depositors and consumers and preserving financial stability. It binds all Specialized Banks, with all UAE branches treated as a single bank and single legal entity.

This node is the defined-term node for "Specialized Bank" (formally 'Specialized Bank with Low Risk'), the licensed entity category created by the CBUAE Circular 21/2022 regime. It identifies an institution licensed to conduct only a narrow set of Licensed Financial Activities in UAE Dirham for UAE Residents, subject to deposit caps (e.g. natural-person aggregate limit and juridical-person concentration limit), Dirham-only deposit accounts, and constrained wholesale lending and funding ratios. The term determines who falls within the whole regulation; all UAE branches of one Specialized Bank count as a single entity, and the commercial name may use "specialized bank" but not "bank" alone.

This node covers Article 3 (and the adjacent Article 2 licensing provisions) of the Specialized Banks with Low Risk Regulation, which exhaustively lists the Licensed Financial Activities a Specialized Bank may perform: retail finance, mortgage finance, wholesale finance, issuance of debit/credit/prepaid cards under UAE-licensed schemes, stored value and electronic retail payment/digital money services, and agency distribution of third-party products with the relevant authority's approval. Activities are confined to UAE Residents and to UAE Dirham, and any activity beyond the list requires prior Central Bank approval. It binds licensed Specialized Banks; Islamic windows in conventional Specialized Banks are prohibited.

This node covers Article 4 (Minimum Capital Requirements) of the Specialized Banks with Low Risk Regulation, together with the surrounding Article 3 balance-sheet limits. It defines Aggregate Capital Funds (paid-up capital, reserves excluding revaluation reserve, retained earnings, less accumulated losses and goodwill), cross-refers minimum paid-up capital to the Minimum Capital for Banks Regulation, and imposes a 60% UAE national ownership floor, alongside caps on participations in other companies, interbank deposit placements, immovable property holdings, total consolidated assets and off-balance-sheet exposures. It binds Specialized Banks and their shareholders.

This node covers Article 6 (Credit Exposure Restrictions) of the Specialized Banks with Low Risk Regulation, defining a Large Credit Exposure as exposure to a single borrower or group of Related Entities at or above 5% of Aggregate Capital Funds, with specified deductible items. The surrounding provisions set capital ratio floors (12.5% of total assets, 17% in the first three years), prior Central Bank approval for profit distributions and capital changes, a 20% single-shareholding cap, application of the Banks' liquidity Regulation, and Article 7-8 duties on corporate governance, AML/CFT (including STR filing to the Central Bank's FIU), consumer protection and mandatory Al Etihad Credit Bureau reporting and enquiry. It binds Specialized Banks.

A historical UAE Ministry of Economy resolution setting the conditions and procedures for registration in the register of actuaries, cited as a predecessor instrument in the Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 9 of 2017 on licensing and registration of actuaries. The 2017 Decision expressly repeals it together with its amendments, so it is relevant mainly for legacy status, transitional regularisation of previously registered actuaries and interpreting rights accrued before the new regulations. It bound persons seeking registration as actuaries and the ministry/authority administering that register.

CBUAE Capital Adequacy Regulations issued under Circular 52/2017, aligning the regulatory capital framework for UAE banks with the Basel III standards on capital quality, minimum ratios, buffers, disclosure and transitional arrangements. It sets out the composition of regulatory capital (CET1, Additional Tier 1, Tier 2), regulatory adjustments and deductions, minimum ratio requirements, the capital conservation and countercyclical buffers, the D-SIB surcharge, supervisory capital guidance add-ons, reporting and interpretation. It binds all banks licensed in the UAE.

Defined component of regulatory capital under the CBUAE capital adequacy framework, comprising Common Equity Tier 1 (ordinary shares and qualifying reserves, net of regulatory adjustments) plus Additional Tier 1 instruments. It carries its own minimum ratio requirement separate from CET1 and total capital, and non-qualifying legacy instruments are phased out over a defined horizon. Relevant to all banks calculating and reporting capital ratios to the Central Bank.

Defined supplementary layer of regulatory capital under the CBUAE capital adequacy framework, added to Tier 1 to produce Total Capital for the total capital adequacy ratio. Instruments that cease to qualify as Tier 2 (or as non-common equity Tier 1) are phased out gradually under the transitional rules, with eligibility criteria detailed in the accompanying Standards. Applies to all banks determining regulatory capital and ratio compliance.

A CET1 buffer required on top of the minimum CET1 ratio, phased in to its full level under the transitional table in the capital adequacy framework. Where a bank operates within the buffer range, constraints on distributions apply on a sliding scale by earnings, and the bank must have a plan to rebuild the buffer through its internal capital adequacy assessment process, restore it within a timeframe agreed with the Central Bank, and accept closer supervisory monitoring. Binds all banks subject to the Capital Adequacy Regulations.

A macroprudential CET1 buffer that the Central Bank may activate within a defined range to address system-wide risk from excess credit growth, sitting alongside the capital conservation buffer in the transitional phase-in table. Breach consequences track the buffer regime generally, including restrictions on distributions and a requirement to restore the buffer. Applies to banks in the UAE, with the applicable rate set by the Central Bank.

Node for the UAE Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities, as amended), the enabling statute under which CBUAE issues licensing and supervisory regulations. In the cited context it supplies the legal basis and defined terms (e.g. "Bank" as a juridical person licensed primarily to take deposits and carry on other Licensed Financial Activities) for the Specialized Banks with Low Risk framework. It binds all persons carrying on licensed financial activities in the UAE and grounds CBUAE's powers to license, supervise and sanction.
lookup_terms: Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities

data.summary: Node covering CBUAE Circular No. 13/2021, the earlier Specialized Banks with Low Risk Regulation, which is expressly cancelled and replaced by the later Specialized Banks regulation (Circular 2/2022). Useful for version control: it marks the repeal point and sits alongside the successor's articles on regulatory reporting (financial year, outsourcing reporting), Islamic Specialized Banks standards and enforcement. Relevant to Specialized Banks and to anyone tracing which instrument applied on a given date.
lookup_terms: Specialized Banks with Low Risk Regulation

data.summary: Node on the credit reporting obligations imposed on Specialized Banks: submitting borrower credit information to Al Etihad Credit Bureau (and any future UAE credit information agencies) at least monthly, and obtaining credit information before extending credit to an individual or corporate borrower. It sits in the same part of the regulation as cross-references to CBUAE corporate governance, AML/CFT (including STR reporting to the FIU) and consumer protection requirements. Binds licensed Specialized Banks.

Node for Insurance Authority Board of Directors Decision No. 9 of 2017 on licensing and registration of Actuaries and regulation of their operations (functions now under CBUAE). It sets entry conditions, the Register, duties, supervisory and disciplinary measures (warning, suspension, cancellation, two-year bar on re-application, appeal within 30 days), transitional regularisation within one year, and repeals Ministry of Economy Resolution No. 22 of 1985. Binds actuaries and insurance/Takaful companies engaging them.

Defined-term node for "Actuary" as a licensed and registered natural or corporate person performing actuarial functions for insurance companies. It captures scope and conflict rules: support staff are exempt from licensing but cannot sign actuarial reports or give actuarial advice; combining the actuary role with insurance agent, broker, consultant or surveyor/loss adjuster roles or other company positions is prohibited; caps apply on the number of insurance companies an actuary may serve (resident vs non-resident, natural vs corporate); appointment, contracting and dismissal require a board resolution and notification to the Authority. Binds actuaries and the insurance companies that engage them.

Node on the professional liability (professional indemnity) insurance requirement for licensed actuaries under the 2017 actuaries regulations. It specifies that the policy be issued by an Authority-licensed insurer in the actuary's name, be non-revocable and valid for the licence term, carry a minimum sum insured of AED 1,000,000 with deductible not exceeding AED 30,000 per accident, require a replacement policy at least seven days before expiry if not renewed, and that amendments need the Authority's written approval. Binds actuaries seeking or holding a licence.

Node for the Domestic Systemically Important Banks concept as it sits within the CBUAE Capital Adequacy Regulations (Circular 52/2017), the UAE's Basel III implementation. The surrounding text governs the capital buffer framework — capital conservation buffer with graduated earnings-retention/dividend-restriction tiers keyed to CET1 ratios, remediation planning tied to the internal capital adequacy assessment process, a Central Bank-agreed timeline to restore the buffer, and the countercyclical buffer. It binds banks licensed and supervised by the CBUAE (with heightened buffer expectations for banks designated as systemically important domestically).

CBUAE Board of Directors' Decision No. 59/4/2019 setting the supervisory and enforcement framework for anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and financing of illegal organisations. It obliges Financial Institutions and their concerned persons to comply with Decree Federal Law No. 20 of 2018, Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019 (Executive Regulation) and CBUAE instructions/guidance; it grants the Central Bank powers of periodic and unannounced inspection, information requests, administrative sanctions, appeal rights and publication of sanctions. It binds all persons licensed or registered by the CBUAE that carry out the financial activities listed in Article 2 of the Executive Regulation.

Node for Decree Federal Law No. (20) of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organizations — the UAE primary AML/CTF statute, referenced here as the legal basis of CBUAE Board Decision 59/4/2019. It supplies the substantive AML/CTF obligations and the catalogue of administrative sanctions the Central Bank may impose. It binds Financial Institutions licensed or registered by the CBUAE and their concerned persons.

Node for Cabinet Decision No. (10) of 2019, the Executive Regulation implementing Decree Federal Law No. 20 of 2018 on AML/CTF. It is the instrument whose Article 2 defines the financial activities and operations that determine whether a licensed or registered entity falls within the definition of "Financial Institution" for AML purposes, and it carries the detailed implementing obligations. It binds Financial Institutions and their concerned persons, alongside CBUAE instructions and guidance.

Node for CBUAE Circular No. 24/2000 (Regulation concerning Procedures for Anti-Money Laundering) and its amendments — the predecessor AML procedures regime. It is expressly cancelled by Article 7 of Board Decision 59/4/2019, so it is relevant only for historical or transitional analysis of obligations arising before that repeal.

Defined-term node: "Financial Institution" under CBUAE Board Decision 59/4/2019 means anyone licensed or registered by the Central Bank who conducts one or more of the financial activities or operations specified in Article 2 of the Executive Regulation, for or on behalf of a customer. This definition sets the perimeter of the AML/CTF compliance duty and of the Central Bank's inspection, information-gathering and sanctioning powers over the entity and its employees. Note the "for or on behalf of a customer" limb, which matters when assessing whether a given activity or counterparty relationship falls in scope.
lookup_terms: licensed or registered by the Central Bank

data.summary: Version 1 of the UAE Insurance Authority's regulation establishing standing committees to settle and resolve insurance disputes (IA Board resolution). It sets out definitions (Company, Insured, Beneficiary, Insurance Dispute, Complainant, Defendant), the committees' formation, reporting to the Authority, procedural powers outside ordinary civil procedure rules, jurisdictional scope over disputes of any value against licensed insurers, and express carve-outs (interim/summary matters and attachment, disputes already pending in court before entry into force, and arbitration-clause disputes). It binds insurance companies licensed in the State, including branches, agents and Takaful operators, and governs the rights of insureds and beneficiaries bringing complaints.
lookup_terms: settlement and resolution of insurance disputes

data.summary: Consolidated version 2 of the same regulation on committees for the settlement and resolution of insurance disputes, carrying the resolution reference IA-BOD-RES 33/2019. It restates definitions, general provisions (Arabic as the language of proceedings, interpreters, neutral hearing, evidentiary latitude), committee formation and membership terms, and competence/non-competence, and adds an exclusion for insurer subrogation claims against third parties causing loss. Relevant where a researcher needs the current consolidated text binding insurers and shaping complainants' procedural routes.

Concept node for the Committee for the Settlement and Resolution of Insurance Disputes as defined and constituted under the regulation. It covers the committees' administrative and financial reporting line to the Authority, seat locations and ability to sit elsewhere, composition (chairman, members, alternates, possible delegated judge), one-year renewable membership with hold-over until reappointment, judge-equivalent conduct obligations, quorum and majority decision-making, and freedom from ordinary civil procedure constraints. Directly relevant to assessing forum, standing and procedural fairness in insurance complaints against licensed companies.

Concept node on the defined term Remote Communication Technology and its use across the dispute process. It establishes that registration, notification, filing, appearance, publicity, pleading, witness and expert hearings, deliberation, decision-issuance and enforcement steps are valid whether performed wholly or partly by audiovisual remote means, while parties may request in-person hearings at any stage. It also covers notification of decisions (including by registered mail, licensed delivery office, email or remote means), the executory effect of decisions, and the 30-day window to challenge before the competent court of first instance.
lookup_terms: 30 days challenge court of first instance

data.summary: Concept node distinguishing Dispute Settlement (reconciliatory resolution between the parties) from Dispute Resolution (binding decision of the committee), and mapping the two-stage process. It covers the reconciliation phase, its fifteen-working-day deadline extendable by consent or by the committee chairman, attestation of a deed of reconciliation, escalation to resolution where reconciliation fails, and session procedures including consequences of a party's unexcused absence (deletion of the dispute, re-registration within thirty days, or decision in absentia).

CBUAE Country and Transfer Risk Regulation issued by Circular 154/2018, addressed to all banks and made under the Central Bank Law, with accompanying Standards. It sets minimum acceptable requirements for banks' management of country risk and transfer risk (the risk a borrower cannot convert local currency to foreign exchange to service foreign-currency debt), requiring a risk governance framework with policies and procedures to identify, measure, monitor and report such risks across international funding, lending and investment, on a bank-wide or group-wide basis including intra-group exposures. Banks with material exposure must additionally have board-approved risk appetite limits, documented roles and responsibilities, and a definition of materiality reflecting cross-border exposures relative to total business; the Central Bank may impose requirements beyond the listed minimums.

Concept node for "country risk" as used in the CBUAE country and transfer risk requirements for banks, covering exposures arising from international funding, lending and investment activity. It anchors obligations to identify, measure, monitor and report such risk through the risk governance framework, set board-approved limits in the risk appetite statement, define materiality by reference to cross-border exposure size and nature, monitor developments and apply countermeasures, and ensure prudent provisioning. Binds banks supervised by the Central Bank, on a bank-wide and, where relevant, group-wide basis including intra-group exposures.

Defined-term node for "transfer risk": the risk that a borrower cannot convert local currency into foreign exchange and therefore cannot service debt in foreign currency. It is treated jointly with country risk in the bank's risk governance framework, risk management function, limit-setting, provisioning and stress testing (including scenarios such as imposition of capital or exchange controls in relevant foreign jurisdictions). Applies to banks with exposures to such risks, at bank and group level.

Instrument node for CBUAE Circular 161/2018, the Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Regulation, issued to all banks. It requires a sound internal control framework and permanent, independent and effective compliance and internal audit functions, and addresses compensation of staff in those functions and group-wide consistency. It is read together with the accompanying Standards and with the Central Bank's corporate governance regulation, which supplies the overarching prudential framework.

Concept node for the compliance function as a mandated, independent and permanent control function in banks. The board must ensure it exists and monitors and reports on observance of applicable laws, regulations and standards and on staff and board adherence to legal requirements, codes of conduct and conflict-of-interest policy; a board-approved compliance policy, adequate and competent staffing, primary reporting to the CEO with direct access to the board or its audit/risk committees, and a risk-based compliance programme subject to internal audit review are required. Binds banks and, where applicable, groups, including consistency of compliance policy across the group.

Concept node for the internal audit function, which banks must maintain as independent, permanent and effective, proportionate to size, nature of operations and organisational complexity. It provides independent assurance to the board and senior management on internal controls, risk management, compliance and governance; reports to the board or its audit committee; requires unrestricted access to staff, records and data; must follow the IIA international professional standards; and operates under a board-committee-approved internal audit charter and risk-based annual plan. Binds banks and, where relevant, group entities, subsidiaries, affiliates and international branches.

Concept node for the internal control framework banks must establish, with the board and senior management responsible for ensuring it is adequate for a properly controlled operating environment reflecting the bank's risk profile. Senior management must design controls that identify, measure, monitor and control all risks, covering organisational structure, accounting and financial reporting, checks and balances, safeguarding of assets and investments, and measures against unauthorised trading and system intrusion; organisational structures should reflect a three-lines-of-defence approach with balanced skills and authority in back-office and control functions. Binds banks and, where applicable, groups.

A concept node for the Institute of Internal Auditors' International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing, incorporated by reference in the CBUAE Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Regulation (Circular 161/2018). Under that Regulation the head of internal audit must ensure the function operates in conformity with these external professional standards, alongside a board-audit-committee-approved internal audit charter, a risk-based annual audit plan, and group-wide consistency where the bank has subsidiaries, affiliates or international branches. It binds banks supervised by the CBUAE (and, where relevant, their groups), operating through the head of internal audit and senior management.

CBUAE Guidance Note on the Charter of the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee, issued to complement the Shari'ah Governance Standard and to clarify supervisory expectations for the Charter. It sets a minimum-content template covering the ISSC's definition, member qualifications, independence, appointment, membership term, dismissal/resignation, and responsibilities, which institutions may supplement but not contradict. It applies to all licensed Islamic Financial Institutions, which were to align their Charters with the template from 21 April 2021.

Concept node for the CBUAE Shari'ah Governance Standard, the primary standard for licensed financial institutions conducting all or part of their business in accordance with Islamic Shari'ah. It sets the governance framework the Guidance Note on the ISSC Charter supplements, including eligibility, competency and independence requirements for ISSC members and rules on their appointment, term, dismissal and resignation. It binds Islamic Financial Institutions and must be read together with standards and resolutions of the Higher Shari'ah Authority.

CBUAE Financial Reporting and External Audit Regulation (Circular 162/2018), issued under the Central Bank Law and to be read with the Corporate Governance Regulation and Standards for banks. It governs record-keeping, preparation of financial statements under IFRS and CBUAE instructions, publication of audited annual statements, and the appointment, rotation, independence and supervision of the External Auditor. It binds all banks licensed by the CBUAE, with duties also falling on boards, board audit committees and external auditors.
lookup_terms: Financial Reporting and External Audit Regulation

data.summary: The external audit component of CBUAE Regulation 162/2018: banks must annually appoint one or more CBUAE-approved External Auditors, with the board audit committee recommending appointment, reappointment, dismissal and remuneration. It mandates rotation of the audit firm at least every six years and of the engagement partner every three, prohibits non-audit services that could impair objectivity, and requires audits under the International Standards on Auditing. The CBUAE may meet the auditor, access working papers, require rescission of an appointment, commission special-purpose reports at the bank's expense, and act against auditors who breach independence or duties.

The financial reporting component of CBUAE Regulation 162/2018: banks must keep appropriate records and prepare financial statements in line with IFRS and CBUAE instructions, with board responsibility for governance and control over fair-value measurement and valuation/estimation processes. Audited statements with the independent External Auditor's opinion must be submitted to the CBUAE at least three weeks before the general assembly and within three months of year-end, published on the bank's website within four months, and made available on request. Distribution or repatriation of profits, retained earnings, reserves or other regulatory capital components, and any public release or presentation of audited statements, require the CBUAE's prior written no-objection.

Concept node for the UAE's primary AML/CTF statute, Federal Decree-Law 20/2018 (as amended, including by Federal Decree-Law 26/2021), on combating money laundering, terrorist financing and financing of illegal organisations. It is the enabling law underpinning customer due diligence, suspicious transaction reporting and the prompt application of UN Security Council-based targeted financial sanctions directives (Article 16.1). It binds all licensed financial institutions and DNFBPs in the UAE, including licensed exchange houses supervised by CBUAE.

Concept node for Cabinet Decision 10/2019, the Implementing Regulation of Federal Decree-Law 20/2018, which converts the AML/CTF statute into operational obligations. It is the source of detailed requirements on CDD and beneficial ownership, the risk-based approach, appointment and independence of the compliance officer (Article 21), and application of targeted financial sanctions directives (Article 60). It binds licensed financial institutions and DNFBPs, and is cross-referenced throughout CBUAE sectoral guidance and Standards.

Defined-entity node for the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit, the national body that receives suspicious transaction/activity reports and issues typologies and risk publications used by institutions. In the sourced guidance it appears both as the mandatory reporting destination for STRs/SARs and as a credible source input to country and customer risk assessments. Relevant to every licensed financial institution subject to AML/CTF reporting duties.

Concept node for Chapter 16 (AML/CFT Compliance) of the CBUAE Standards accompanying the Regulations Regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business, Version 1.20 (November 2021), amending Version 1.10 (February 2018). It sets sector-specific AML/CTF expectations for exchange houses, including compliance officer and alternate compliance officer appointment, compliance committee and corporate governance (Chapter 6), and sanctions obligations. It binds licensed exchange houses (LEH) supervised by CBUAE, applied with proportionality for smaller firms.
lookup_terms: Regulations Regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business

data.summary: CBUAE Regulation 165/2018 (with accompanying Standards) on Interest Rate and Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book, issued under the Central Bank Law. It requires banks to maintain policies, processes, systems and controls to identify, measure, monitor, report, control and mitigate IRRBB, and defines related terms such as the trading book. It binds all banks licensed in the UAE; the Central Bank may impose requirements beyond the minimum items listed.
lookup_terms: Interest Rate and Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book

data.summary: Node covering Article 2 (risk governance framework) and Article 3 (risk management function) of the IRRBB Regulation 165/2018. It requires a bank-wide and, where relevant, group-wide IRRBB strategy and governance framework aligned with the risk appetite statement, risk profile and systemic importance, with Board approval and at least annual review, Board- and Senior Management-approved limits, model validation, exception tracking and reporting MIS. Obligations fall on the Bank, with allocated duties for the Board, Senior Management and the risk management function.

A concept node for the International Standards on Auditing as incorporated by reference into the CBUAE Financial Reporting and External Audit Regulation (Circular 162/2018) applicable to banks. It fixes the methodology the external auditor must follow — a risk- and materiality-based approach to planning and performing the audit — alongside related duties on auditor appointment, rotation (firm and engagement partner), audit committee oversight, and prohibition of objectivity-impairing non-audit services. It binds banks in their engagement of external auditors and, indirectly, the approved auditors themselves.
lookup_terms: Financial Reporting and External Audit Regulation

data.summary: CBUAE guidance setting out supervisory expectations for Licensed Exchange Houses on their AML/CFT statutory obligations, issued under the Article 44.11 mandate of Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019 (implementing Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018). It covers sector ML/FT risks, enterprise risk assessment, governance and compliance officer, CDD/EDD, transaction monitoring, sanctions, training, independent audit and record keeping, cross-referring to Chapter 16 of the Standards for the Regulations Regarding Licensing and Monitoring for Exchange Business. It is guidance, not new legislation: it does not override the legal framework, but LEH are expected to demonstrate compliance against it, subject to proportionality.

A concept node describing the required AML/CFT Program for Licensed Exchange Houses: documented policies and procedures communicated to staff, plus the governance architecture of a dedicated Compliance Officer (Article 21 of the AML-CFT Decision; Paragraph 16.4 of the Standards), an Alternate Compliance Officer and a Compliance Committee. The Compliance Officer role must be ring-fenced to AML/CFT tasks to avoid conflicts of interest, and must have adequate resources and autonomy. Binds LEH management and boards; the program's content is driven by the entity's risk assessment findings.

A concept node on the enterprise-wide ML/FT risk assessment obligation for Licensed Exchange Houses under Article 4 of the AML-CFT Decision and Paragraph 16.2 of the Standards. It requires a documented methodology, documented findings (inherent risk, controls evaluation, residual risk, mitigation), a written risk appetite statement, and mechanisms to supply the assessment to the CBUAE on request; senior management/board must review and approve at least annually. The assessment must be proportionate to the LEH's nature, size and complexity, updated on material change, and must feed the AML/CFT program's policies, controls and training.

A cross-cutting concept node on Customer Due Diligence as applied across CBUAE-licensed financial institutions, with detailed treatment for Exchange Houses. It covers customer identification (CID), CDD and EDD triggers by customer type, activity and value (including high-risk natural persons, high-risk circumstances and third-party transactions), beneficial ownership, PEPs, and customer-base risk segmentation. It also anchors ongoing monitoring under Article 7 of the AML-CFT Decision: profiles must be reviewed and refreshed at least annually or on expiry of ID/trade licence/authorised-signatory ID, whichever is earlier.

A cross-cutting concept node on the continuous transaction monitoring duty of licensed financial institutions, grounded for Exchange Houses in Article 7 of the AML-CFT Decision and Paragraph 16.24 of the Standards. It addresses monitoring transactions against the customer/counterparty profile, re-rating risk on profile change, triggering EDD or relationship termination (notably after an STR/SAR filing), and maintaining an auditable record of alert generation, investigation and disposition. It also lists indicative transaction red flags (structuring below CDD thresholds, unexplained complexity, activity inconsistent with financial standing, attempts to dissuade reporting).

CBUAE Circular 12/2021 (Minimum Capital for Banks Regulation), issued under Article 75 of the UAE Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law 14/2018), setting the minimum paid-up capital that licensed Banks must hold at all times as a licensing prerequisite. It fixes thresholds for UAE-incorporated Banks, Specialized Banks and branches of foreign banks, requires the requirement be met solely with fully paid-up capital, and states it operates independently of risk-based capital rules. It binds all Banks operating in the UAE, including foreign bank branches — note this is a UAE (CBUAE) instrument, not a SAMA rule.

Concept node for the minimum capital requirement as defined in CBUAE's Minimum Capital for Banks Regulation: an ongoing, licensing-condition floor of fully paid-up capital (AED 2bn for UAE-incorporated Banks, AED 300m for Specialized Banks, AED 100m at branch level plus AED 2bn eligible capital at entity level for foreign bank branches). It also specifies quality criteria for branch allocated funds (irrevocable, unconditional, non-interest-bearing, in AED, with head-office shortfall undertaking) and confirms non-interaction with other capital regimes. Binds Banks and, at entity level, their foreign head offices.

Concept node for the Basel framework as referenced in CBUAE rules, used to define "eligible capital" (regulatory capital) at entity level for branches of foreign banks, as implemented in the bank's home jurisdiction. It functions as an external reference standard rather than a standalone CBUAE obligation, and is relevant where UAE capital tests defer to home-state regulatory capital definitions.

CBUAE Circular 83/2019 (Corporate Governance Regulation for Banks) and its accompanying Standards, issued under the Central Bank Law, establishing the overarching prudential framework and minimum acceptable standards for bank corporate governance. It covers board structure and committees, fit-and-proper and Central Bank no-objection for board appointments/removals, compensation caps for Senior Management and Material Risk Takers, and disclosure/transparency, while leaving risk management, internal control, compliance, audit and outsourcing to separate instruments. It binds all Banks and Groups operating in the UAE, with ultimate responsibility on the Board; this is a CBUAE, not SAMA, instrument.

Concept node for corporate governance as regulated by CBUAE for Banks: the required comprehensive approach covering strategy, organizational structure, control environment, risk management responsibilities and Board/Staff compensation. It includes bonus limits (individual bonuses capped relative to fixed pay with escalating Board and General Assembly approvals; aggregate staff bonus capped against net profit) and mandatory annual corporate governance disclosure in the annual report. The onus is on each Bank's Board to demonstrate compliance; banks may exceed the minimums.

Concept node on Board of Directors composition, structure and responsibilities under the CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation for Banks. It covers chair accountability, minimum six meetings a year, a non-member board secretary, minute-keeping, delegation of authority but not responsibility to committees, UAE-national chair and majority requirement, twelve-year cap on Independent Member tenure, multiple-directorship limits, government shareholder representation, a rigorous candidate selection and Fit and Proper Process with a 20% female candidate requirement, and Central Bank no-objection before appointment, renewal or removal. It binds Banks and individual Board Members.

This node covers the compensation (remuneration) requirements within the CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation for Banks, sitting alongside articles on financial reporting/external audit and outsourcing. It requires compensation outcomes to be symmetric with risk outcomes, with deferral, malus and clawback mechanisms, fixed-only pay for Board members, predominantly fixed and independently determined pay for risk, compliance and internal audit staff, and performance-based components with reduction/reversal triggers for Senior Management and Material Risk Takers. It binds licensed banks, their Boards and Senior Management, with detailed control-function governance set out in separate CBUAE regulations and standards.

This is the CBUAE Small to Medium Sized Enterprises (SME) Market Conduct Regulation (Circular 1/2021, dated 26/01/2021), issued under the Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018) and addressed to all Banks and Finance Companies. It sets market conduct, governance and oversight obligations for Licensed Financial Institutions when designing, promoting and selling Financial Products or Services to SME Customers, with the aim of improving SME access to finance. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions, including Islamic Financial Institutions, and defines key terms such as Authorised Agent, SME size tiers, HSA and ISSC.
lookup_terms: market conduct banks and finance companies

data.summary: Article 2 of the SME Market Conduct Regulation sets disclosure and transparency duties owed to SME Customers, including proactive and timely information, plain language, warnings on key characteristics, risks, costs, fees, rates, penalties and lock-in terms, and effective disclosure at all stages of the relationship including changes to terms. It also requires reasons for application rejection to be given (subject to Financial Crime risk or legal prohibition), bans partial or biased disclosure to entice customers, mandates English and Arabic availability, accuracy of disclosures, and ongoing monitoring of disclosure effectiveness using complaint analysis and satisfaction surveys. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions dealing with SME Customers.

This node represents Article 3 (Responsible Conduct) of the SME Market Conduct Regulation, which sits between the disclosure requirements (Article 2) and responsible financing practice (Article 4) in the instrument's structure. It addresses how Licensed Financial Institutions and their Staff and Authorised Agents must conduct themselves towards SME Customers in promoting, selling and servicing Financial Products and Services. Note that the surrounding extract largely reproduces the table of contents and neighbouring articles, so the operative Article 3 text should be checked in the source.

Article 5 of the SME Market Conduct Regulation requires Licensed Financial Institutions to operate a fair, accessible, free-of-charge complaint handling process, supported by an independent complaints management function reporting directly to Senior Management, documented policies and a complaint management system. It also requires customer awareness of rights, staff and Authorised Agent training, institutional responsibility for complaints about Authorised Agents' activities, root cause and trend analysis, quarterly SME Complaints Data reporting to Senior Management, and participation in any external complaints resolution or ombudsman mechanism. It binds banks and finance companies in their dealings with SME Customers.

Article 6 of the SME Market Conduct Regulation requires Islamic Financial Institutions (IFIs) to embed and uphold Shari'ah principles across reporting, business conduct, risk management and oversight, and to ensure staff dealing with SME Customers have sufficient knowledge of the Shari'ah aspects of the products and services offered. The node also carries the definitional framework for Shari'ah compliance, the Higher Shari'ah Authority (HSA) and the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee (ISSC), whose fatwas and resolutions are binding. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions conducting all or part of their business in accordance with Islamic Shari'ah.

Defined-term node for the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee: an independent committee that each Licensed Financial Institution conducting all or part of its business in line with Islamic Shari'ah must establish, staffed by specialists in Islamic finance jurisprudence. It supervises and approves the institution's businesses, products, services, contracts and documentation and sets their Shari'ah requirements, operating within the rules, principles and standards of the Higher Shari'ah Authority; its fatwas and resolutions bind the institution and must not contradict HSA resolutions. It sits alongside related definitions (HSA, Islamic Financial Institution, Licensed Financial Activities/Institutions) used across multiple CBUAE instruments.

Defines "Credit Information Agency" as Al Etihad Credit Bureau and any other credit information agency established for credit reporting purposes, within a regulation whose "Customer" is limited to SMEs obtaining or prospectively obtaining financial products/services. The operative consequence is that Licensed Financial Institutions should obtain the relevant credit bureau details before extending credit, alongside monitoring of credit-granting and sales representatives and complaint-handling duties. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions (banks and finance companies) in their SME dealings.

The CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation for Banks, setting the framework for outsourcing arrangements: defined terms (Outsourcing, Confidential Data, Master System of Record, Material Business Activity, Group/Parent/Subsidiary), governance and risk requirements, an outsourcing register, data protection duties, mandatory contractual clauses and conditions for outsourcing outside the UAE. Key constraints include retained bank and customer ownership of data, CBUAE access and on-site inspection rights over service providers, in-country maintenance of the Master System of Record (with a limited exception for foreign bank branches), and prior CBUAE approval plus customer consent before sharing Confidential Data abroad. Binds banks licensed in the UAE, including on a group basis.

Article 2 of the Outsourcing Regulation places full responsibility for outsourcing risk on the bank and requires a documented process for assessing materiality of outsourced activities. The Risk Governance Framework must cover assessment, identification, measurement, monitoring and reporting of outsourcing risk on a bank-wide and, where applicable, group-wide basis, with a Board-approved policy, Board (or Board committee) approval of material arrangements, conflict-of-interest management, clear allocation of roles, and inclusion of outsourced critical functions in disaster recovery and business continuity plans. Banks remain accountable for the service provider's information security and for compliance with all laws applicable to outsourced activities.

Article 3 of the Outsourcing Regulation requires banks to maintain a comprehensive, up-to-date register of all outsourcing arrangements — material and non-material — on both a solo and group-wide basis. Minimum content includes service provider details, start and end dates, a service description, whether Confidential Data is involved, and whether the arrangement is material. Binds banks and supports supervisory oversight of the outsourcing portfolio.

Article 4 of the Outsourcing Regulation requires banks to comply with applicable UAE data legislation when managing and processing data under outsourcing, to retain ownership of all data given to a service provider while preserving customers' ownership of their own data (including Confidential Data), and to ensure customers can exercise related rights. Where subcontracting involves Confidential Data, the bank must ensure the subcontractor meets the same legal and regulatory requirements, and data must be secured against unauthorised access including by the provider's own staff. Read with the definition of Confidential Data and the contractual requirements in Article 5.

Article 5 of the CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation for Banks sets the mandatory contractual content of any outsourcing arrangement: retention of bank and customer data ownership, unfettered bank access to data during and after the contract, confidentiality and data-destruction terms, data-protection standards, limits and conditions on subcontracting, prohibition on onward disclosure of Confidential Data without bank or customer authorisation, Central Bank (and its agents') access and on-site inspection rights at the service provider, and prompt breach notification. It binds Banks licensed in the UAE, which must ensure all outsourcing is governed by a formal written contract; it operates indirectly on outsourcing service providers and their subcontractors through those terms.
lookup_terms: Central Bank on-site access to service provider

data.summary: Article 6 of the CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation governs cross-border outsourcing by Banks: the Master System of Record including all Confidential Data must be maintained and stored in the UAE (with a Central Bank–approved exception allowing foreign bank branches to hold a daily-updated copy locally), and customer Confidential Data may not leave the UAE without Central Bank approval plus prior written customer consent and acknowledgement of possible foreign legal access. It also requires compliance with applicable personal data protection law, dedicated policies, controls, monitoring, staff training, defined security requirements, subcontractor compliance, and contemplates Central Bank cooperation with foreign authorities. Binds Banks operating in the UAE.
lookup_terms: data localisation Master System of Record
customer consent to share data abroad

data.summary: Defined term in the CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation for Banks: the full collection of data, including Confidential Data, needed to run all of a Bank's core activities — serving clients, managing risks, and meeting legal and regulatory obligations. Its significance is operative: the Master System of Record must be continuously maintained and stored inside the UAE, with a limited, approval-based copy alternative for foreign bank branches.

Defined term in the CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation for Banks: account or other data relating to an identified or identifiable bank customer, including where identification is possible by combining that data with other information available to a person granted access. The definition sets the perimeter for the Regulation's strongest controls — ownership retention, access restrictions, authorisation before onward disclosure, breach notification, and the prohibition on sharing outside the UAE without approval and customer consent.

Cross-reference node: the CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation and Standards must be read together with the Risk Management Regulation and Standards (which set banks' overarching risk approach and define the Risk Governance Framework) and the Operational Risk Management Regulation and Standards (business continuity and disaster recovery). It frames the scope rule that the outsourcing requirements apply to all Banks in the UAE on a solo and Group-wide basis, and the core principle that outsourcing must not weaken obligations to customers or impede Central Bank supervision, with Banks remaining fully responsible for outsourced risks.

The Outsourcing Standards for Banks (Circular 14/2021) are the enforceable elaboration of the CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation, mirroring its article structure. They require an outsourcing-inclusive risk governance framework addressing operational and compliance risk from service providers, confirm the Board's ultimate responsibility for outsourced activities, keep outsourced activities within internal audit and compliance scope (including power to extend third-party audit scope), require management of cross-border provider and subcontractor risk, and set the minimum submission pack for obtaining Central Bank non-objection before outsourcing a Material Business Activity. Binds all Banks operating in the UAE.
lookup_terms: Central Bank non-objection material business activity

data.summary: The IRRBB Standards are the detailed, mandatory elaboration of the CBUAE Interest Rate and Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book Regulation, enforceable on the same footing as the Regulation itself. They set expectations on risk governance, staff competence, risk appetite and self-imposed exposure limits, and on measurement systems that capture repricing, yield curve, basis and option risk across both earnings and economic value, including embedded optionality. They bind all Banks licensed by the CBUAE, with banks offering Islamic financial services required to apply the same principles to rate of return risk; the article on definitions fixes terms such as IRR, IRRBB, option risk, Group, Parent and Subsidiary.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: The IRRBB Regulation is the CBUAE instrument requiring each Bank's Board to establish and oversee an interest rate and rate of return risk governance framework proportionate to the Bank's risk profile, nature, size, structure and complexity. It prescribes the framework's mandatory components — Board oversight, policies, ALCO or equivalent for larger/complex banks, measurement, monitoring and enforcement of limits, stress testing feeding decision-making, risk function oversight, internal audit assurance and reporting to Senior Management and Board — plus a Board-approved risk appetite statement and separation of duties between risk control and position-taking functions. It binds all Banks, with the Board bearing the onus of demonstrating an adequate approach; the accompanying Standards are enforceable in the same manner.
lookup_terms: Board oversight of interest rate risk

data.summary: Article 5 of the IRRBB Regulation is the stress testing component of the interest rate and rate of return risk framework, sitting between the articles on measurement/models (Article 4) and information systems and internal reporting (Article 6). The governance framework requires stress testing of IRRBB and the use of its results in decision-making, alongside monitoring and enforcement of IRRBB limits. It applies to all Banks, including Islamic banks and windows applying the same principles to rate of return risk.

Rate of return risk is the Islamic-finance analogue of interest rate risk addressed by the IRRBB Regulation and Standards: Banks offering Islamic financial services must apply the same governance, measurement, limit-setting, stress testing and reporting principles to it, and the Regulation contains a dedicated Islamic banking article. Related defined concepts include Islamic Financial Services (covering Islamic Banks and Islamic Windows of conventional banks), displaced commercial risk, risk limits, risk governance framework and Senior Management. It binds Islamic Banks and conventional Banks with Islamic Windows.

Displaced commercial risk is a defined term in the IRRBB Regulation: the market pressure on a Bank offering Islamic financial services to pay investment account holders a return exceeding the rate actually earned on the assets financing them, in order to attract or retain those funds. It is relevant to how Islamic Banks and Islamic Windows identify and manage rate of return risk within the IRRBB governance and measurement framework. The concept is definitional rather than a standalone obligation; the operative duties sit in the Regulation's governance, measurement and Islamic banking articles.
lookup_terms: rate of return risk Islamic banks

data.summary: The CBUAE Financial Reporting and External Audit Standards (162/2018) govern the appointment, rotation, independence and oversight of a Bank's External Auditor and the Board audit committee's supervisory duties. They require re-tendering and firm rotation at least every six years with a three-year cooling-off period, audit partner rotation every three years, annual assessment of auditor quality, committee review of the audit plan, representation letter and significant audit matters, and an approved policy on permitted and prohibited non-audit services (read together with the UAE auditing profession law and the IESBA Code of Ethics). They bind Banks, their Boards and audit committees, and shape the terms on which External Auditors may be engaged.
lookup_terms: Financial Reporting and External Audit Standards 162/2018

data.summary: Article 4 of the CBUAE Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Standards (161/2018) sets the mandate, independence, staffing and scope requirements for a bank's internal audit function. It requires a written internal audit policy (covering standing, authority, reporting line to the Board, use for advisory work, adherence to IIA professional standards and Code of Ethics, and coordination with the external auditor), conflict-of-interest safeguards including cooling-off after rotation, collective competence and ongoing training, and confidentiality. Scope must extend to the whole bank including subsidiaries, branches, outsourced activities and matters of regulatory interest. It binds licensed banks, their boards/audit committees and the head of internal audit.
lookup_terms: IIA International Standards Code of Ethics
audit scope subsidiaries and outsourced activities
Internal Controls Compliance and Internal Audit Standards 161/2018

data.summary: This node covers the internal control framework in Article 2 of the CBUAE Standards 161/2018 and its three lines of defence model: business/client-facing units (first line, transaction-based), risk, compliance, legal and other control/support functions (second line, risk-based), and internal audit (third line, risk-based periodic assurance). It fixes minimum internal control content (organisational structure and delegation, accounting and reconciliation, four-eyes/segregation of duties, safeguarding assets and fraud prevention) and requires at least annual board or audit committee review of control effectiveness. Responsibility for internal control does not shift between lines; it binds licensed banks' boards, senior management and control functions.
lookup_terms: first line second line third line

data.summary: A concept node for "internal control" as used across the CBUAE Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Standards 161/2018 — the system of policies, checks, reporting and oversight that internal audit must evaluate alongside risk management, compliance and governance processes. It anchors the requirement that internal audit coverage extend to the entire bank, its subsidiaries, branches, outsourced activities and matters of regulatory interest. Relevant to banks' boards, senior management and control functions.

The CBUAE Standard on risk management requirements for Islamic banks forms part of the Risk Management Regulation (Circular 153/2018) and is mandatory and enforceable in the same way. It applies to Islamic banks and banks housing an Islamic Window (for their Shari'ah-compliant business, integrated into the existing risk framework) and addresses risks specific to Islamic finance — Shari'ah non-compliance, displaced commercial, rate of return and equity investment risk — plus governance roles for the Board, Risk Committee, ISSC, internal Shari'ah compliance and internal Shari'ah audit. It supplements rather than replaces the other CBUAE risk management standards.

The CBUAE Risk Management Regulation (Circular 153/2018) and its accompanying Standards are the baseline framework for risk governance in licensed banks: board-approved risk governance framework and risk appetite statement, three lines of defence, coverage of credit, market, liquidity and operational risk, ICAAP and internal control review, risk reporting and disclosures, and the role of the risk management function/CRO. Sector-specific standards (including the Islamic banks standard) are issued under it and are enforceable in the same manner. It binds licensed banks' boards, risk committees and senior management.

Article 11 of the CBUAE Islamic banks risk management Standard sets credit risk requirements for Islamic banks and Islamic Windows: a credit strategy including pricing and risk tolerance, oversight structure, credit policies, criteria, review processes, accepted risk mitigation and limits, measurement and analysis of exposures, and systems to monitor individual financings, handle remedial action and ensure adequate provisions.
