It requires a credit risk management and reporting framework covering all assets across the stages of Shari'ah-compliant products, investments and securitisation. It binds Islamic banks and banks housing an Islamic Window in addition to general CBUAE credit risk requirements.

Orientation node for the CBUAE Financial Reporting and External Audit Regulation and its accompanying Standards (162/2018), covering how banks prepare and report financial information and how the external audit relationship is governed. It sets requirements on audit firm procurement and rotation, partner rotation and cooling-off, annual board audit committee assessment of auditor quality, communication of significant audit matters, and a board-approved policy on permitted and prohibited non-audit services. It binds banks (their boards, board audit committees and senior management) and, through engagement terms, their external auditors.
lookup_terms: Financial Reporting and External Audit Regulation

data.summary: Article-level node on the external audit requirements within the CBUAE Financial Reporting and External Audit framework (162/2018). It addresses selection of the audit firm via procurement at least every six years with firm rotation and a three-year cooling-off, three-yearly audit partner rotation, annual audit committee assessment of auditor quality and the auditor's internal quality control reporting, review of the representation letter and audit plan adherence, and approval of a non-audit services policy listing prohibited services. It binds the bank's board audit committee and senior management, with corresponding duties on the external auditor.

Concept node for the defined role of the External Auditor across several CBUAE instruments, anchored in the Financial Reporting and External Audit Standards (162/2018). It sets the auditor's eligibility and independence obligations (including professional indemnity insurance in the UAE, annual independence reporting to the board audit committee, securities dealing restrictions during blackout, and a two-year bar on joining the bank's board or senior management), and mandates engagement terms allowing supervisory meetings with the Central Bank, disapplying confidentiality toward the Central Bank, and granting access to working papers. It binds the external auditor and the bank contracting it.
lookup_terms: duty of confidentiality to Central Bank

data.summary: Node for the CBUAE Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Standards (161/2018), which set out detailed expectations for the internal audit function: a written policy with conflict-of-interest and rotation cooling-off safeguards, staffing competence and training, confidentiality, the content of the internal audit charter, and the scope of audit coverage. Scope must extend to the whole bank including subsidiaries, branches, outsourced activities and matters of regulatory interest, and must evaluate internal control, risk management, compliance and governance. It binds banks, their boards and board audit committees, and heads of internal audit.
lookup_terms: Internal Controls Compliance and Internal Audit Standards

data.summary: Orientation node for the CBUAE Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Regulation and its Standards (161/2018), the framework governing a bank's internal control system and its second- and third-line functions. It covers the mandate, independence, competence and reporting lines of the internal audit function, the required charter content, coordination with the external auditor, and group-wide coverage of all activities and controlled entities. It binds banks operating in the UAE, their boards, board audit committees and senior management.
lookup_terms: Internal Controls Compliance and Internal Audit Regulation

data.summary: Article-level node on the compliance function under the CBUAE Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Standards (161/2018). It sets the function's AML/CTF duties (examining suspicious transactions and reporting to the Central Bank's Financial Intelligence Department, bi-annual AML/CTF framework assessments sent to FID with senior management comments, ongoing ML/TF training), staff knowledge and training expectations, unrestricted access to staff, records and data, group-level organisation options, at least annual board-level performance assessment with an independent external quality assurance review every five years, and limits on outsourcing compliance tasks. It binds banks, their boards and board committees, and heads of compliance.

Node for the market risk article of the CBUAE Standard on risk management for Islamic banks, which supplements the Risk Management Regulation (Circular 153/2018). Market risk is one of the material risk categories that an Islamic bank's Shari'ah-compliant risk governance framework must address, alongside credit, liquidity, operational, displaced commercial, equity investment and rate of return risk. It binds licensed Islamic banks and conventional banks housing an Islamic Window (the latter in respect of their Shari'ah-compliant business), with board and Risk Committee accountability for the framework.

Node for the equity investment risk article of the CBUAE Islamic banks risk management Standard, dealing with risks from profit-sharing and partnership-based investments (Mudaraba, Musharaka, Wakala). It requires Shari'ah-compliant risk mitigation, consistent and mutually agreed valuation methodologies, controls against misstated partnership earnings, and documented exit/extension/redemption strategies approved by the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee, while recognising capital-impairment risk that resembles but is not conventional credit risk. Binds Islamic banks and banks with Islamic Windows; equity investment risk must also feature in the risk appetite statement and management reporting.

Node for the rate of return risk article of the CBUAE Islamic banks risk management Standard, to be read together with the Interest Rate and Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book Regulation and Standards (Circular 165/2018). It requires Islamic banks to maintain a comprehensive risk management and reporting process assessing how market factors affect returns on assets relative to returns expected by Investment Account Holders. Applies to Islamic banks and Islamic Windows; the risk must be covered in the risk appetite statement and reported to the Board and Senior Management.

Node for the displaced commercial risk article of the CBUAE Islamic banks risk management Standard — the risk arising where an Islamic bank foregoes part of its own returns to sustain payouts to Investment Account Holders. It is a mandatory component of the risk governance framework, must be expressly covered in the risk appetite statement, and must be measurable and reportable through the bank's risk information systems under Risk Committee oversight. Binds Islamic banks and banks housing an Islamic Window.

Node for the Shari'ah non-compliance risk article of the CBUAE Islamic banks risk management Standard. The Standard treats this as a material risk to be managed within the risk governance framework and the three-lines-of-defence model, requires zero tolerance in the risk appetite statement, and assigns Risk Committee supervision and control-setting in consultation with the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee via the internal Shari'ah control function, with Internal Shari'ah Audit reflected in the ICAAP internal control review. Binds Islamic banks and Islamic Windows.

Cross-reference node to the CBUAE Interest Rate and Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book Regulation and accompanying Standards (Circular 165/2018), cited by the Islamic banks risk management Standard as the instrument to be read alongside its rate of return risk requirements. It sets the baseline banking-book rate risk regime that Islamic banks must satisfy in addition to the Islamic-specific requirements. Relevant to licensed banks generally, including Islamic banks and banks housing an Islamic Window.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book
rate of return risk in the banking book

data.summary: A cross-reference node for the CBUAE Market Risk Regulation and accompanying Standards (Circular 164/2018), invoked within the Islamic banking risk governance framework as the baseline market risk regime that Islamic Banks must read together with their Shari'ah-specific requirements. In that setting it sits alongside the Risk Management Standards (153/2018) and frames board-level risk appetite, the three-lines-of-defence model, and market risk identification, pricing, valuation, income recognition, limits and MIS reporting, including for restricted investment account portfolios. It binds licensed banks, and in this context Islamic Banks and Islamic windows, with additional coverage of Shari'ah non-compliance, displaced commercial, rate of return and equity investment risk.

Defines the Solvency Margin regime under the Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies: the obligation to hold Own Funds at all times against the largest of the Minimum Capital Requirement, Minimum Guarantee Fund and Solvency Capital Requirement, with prescribed composition (Basic vs Ancillary Own Funds) and disclosure tables. It also sets immediate reporting to the Authority on breach plus a recovery plan within thirty days and restoration within six months. Binds Takaful insurance companies incorporated in the State and licensed foreign Takaful branches.

Sets out the types and calculation basis of Technical Provisions for Takaful companies — unearned contribution, unexpired risk, outstanding loss, IBNR, loss adjustment expense reserves and mathematical reserve — computed both gross and net of Re-Takaful. It also imposes localisation rules requiring investments matching specified provision categories to be held in the State, and actuarial requirements including appointment of an Authority-registered Actuary, actuarial review and approval of provisions, data quality assessment and annual reporting to the Authority. Binds Takaful insurance companies and, professionally, their appointed Actuaries.

The parent instrument: the Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies, issued by Insurance Authority Board Decision and now administered by CBUAE, covering investment of participants' rights, solvency margin and own funds, technical provisions, asset valuation, accounting policies and prescribed financial-statement and disclosure formats. Includes templates for gross and net contributions and claims, Re-Takaful cessions and accepted business. Applies to Takaful insurance companies incorporated in the State and foreign Takaful insurers licensed to operate there.
lookup_terms: Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies

data.summary: The defined-terms section of the Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies, fixing the meaning of terms such as Mathematical Reserve, Insurance or Underwriting Surplus, Beneficiary, Insurance Agent, External Auditor, Authority Examiners and Unit Linked Insurance Policies. The glossary is expressly stated to apply across both Parts of the regulations, and a separate article fixes the scope of application to domestic and licensed foreign Takaful insurers. Use it to confirm how a term is defined before relying on any substantive article.

Defines the Solvency Capital Requirement for Takaful companies as risk-based capital covering underwriting, market and liquidity (investment), credit and operational risk, calculated across all Participants' Risk Funds and the Shareholders' Funds consistently with their risk profiles. It requires the SCR and Minimum Guarantee Fund to be met by Basic Own Funds plus only 50% of Ancillary Own Funds, with the entire Shareholders' Funds available for Qard Hasan to cover any PRF deficit and Qard Hasan assets accounted for and valued separately. Binds Takaful insurance companies, with immediate notification and recovery-plan duties to the Authority on breach.

Defined solvency floor under the CBUAE Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies: the Minimum Guarantee Fund must be at least one-third of the Solvency Capital Requirement and is also built up from per-line-of-business minimum amounts (an absolute minimum or a percentage of net earned contributions, whichever is higher, as set by the Authority). It is one of the three benchmarks (with Minimum Capital Requirement and Solvency Capital Requirement) whose largest value the Company must cover with Own Funds at all times, and it must be fully met by Own Funds (Basic plus only 50% of Ancillary). Binds licensed Takaful and Re-Takaful operators, with immediate notification to the Authority and a recovery plan on breach.

Defines the capital resources eligible to cover Takaful solvency requirements: Own Funds equal Basic Own Funds (excess of admissible assets over liabilities, less treasury shares, plus approved subordinated liabilities) plus Ancillary Own Funds (loss-absorbing items callable with prior Authority approval, e.g. rights to call supplementary contribution). Sets eligibility limits: the Minimum Capital Requirement must be met 100% by Basic Own Funds, while the Solvency Capital Requirement and Minimum Guarantee Fund are met by Basic Own Funds plus only 50% of Ancillary Own Funds. Binds Takaful and Re-Takaful companies; breaches trigger immediate reporting and an Authority-approved recovery plan.

Technical-provision concept in the Takaful financial regulations: the Unearned Contribution Reserve is calculated pro rata from risk inception, with a larger reserve required where the risk pattern over the policy period is non-uniform, and a 25% minimum of annual contributions for marine cargo (individual shipment) unless the Actuary justifies a lower figure with Authority approval. UPR is mandatory for each line of business and requires at least annual actuarial certification; where inadequate, an Unexpired Risk Reserve must be added. Binds Takaful/Re-Takaful companies and their appointed Actuary.

Supplementary technical provision required where the Unearned Contribution Reserve is judged inadequate to cover future liabilities: the Unexpired Risk Reserve is created at line-of-business level to cover the shortfall, with its calculation including cost of capital or other profit loadings. Unlike UPR it is created only as needed, but is subject to at least annual actuarial certification. Binds Takaful and Re-Takaful companies determining technical provisions for solvency and reporting purposes.

One of the mandatory technical provisions listed in the Takaful financial regulations: the Outstanding Loss Reserve (case reserves) is calculated for each claim reported but still outstanding at the reporting date. It sits alongside UPR, URR, IBNR, loss adjustment expense reserves and mathematical reserves, and investments equivalent to OSLR (net of Re-Takaful) must be held inside the UAE. Binds Takaful and Re-Takaful companies in provisioning, asset localisation and solvency reporting.

Technical provision for claims incurred but not reported, covering both claims not yet reported (IBNYR) and incomplete provisions for reported claims. The regulations require sufficient data (with management certifying completeness, appropriateness and accuracy), actuarial methods proportionate to size, scale and complexity, consistency of method year to year, and explanation to the Authority of any material methodology change; specialised portfolios (treaty/excess-of-loss accepted, credit guarantee) may need other methods. Binds Takaful and Re-Takaful companies, their management and appointed Actuary.

A technical-provisions concept within the CBUAE Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies, covering reserves for loss adjustment expenses alongside the unearned contribution, unexpired risk and outstanding loss reserves. It sets how takaful operators must quantify liabilities for claims handling costs and unexpired exposure, including actuarial certification and minimum percentage floors for certain lines. Binds licensed takaful companies (and branches of foreign takaful operators) and their appointed actuaries when valuing liabilities and reporting to the Authority.

Defines the mathematical reserve for family takaful / insurance of persons and fund accumulation business under the CBUAE takaful financial regulations, including prudent assumption setting, margins for adverse deviation, treatment of negative reserves, guaranteed surrender values, unit-linked business, bonuses and expense allowances. It constrains the actuary's discretion, e.g. barring lapse or surrender allowances that would reduce liabilities. Applies to takaful companies writing life/persons business and to their appointed actuaries.

Covers the Shari'ah-based interest-free loan from shareholders' funds used to remedy a deficit in the Participants' Risk Fund under the CBUAE takaful financial regulations. It requires the entire shareholders' funds to be available for this purpose, and assets earmarked for qard hasan to be separately accounted for and valued under the asset-valuation rules for solvency. Relevant to takaful operators, their boards and actuaries assessing solvency capital adequacy.

Addresses the fee models by which takaful operators are remunerated — wakala fees as a share of contributions and mudaraba fees as a share of investment income, or a wakala-only model — and their presentation in the prescribed financial statement forms. Sits in the accounting and reporting section of the CBUAE takaful financial regulations, affecting how operator income and participant-fund charges are disclosed. Binds licensed takaful companies preparing statutory financial reports for the Authority.

Defines the Participants' Risk Fund (PRF) as the segregated pool of contributions from which takaful claims are met, and its role in the solvency architecture of the CBUAE takaful financial regulations. Solvency capital requirements are assessed across all PRFs and shareholders' funds, covering underwriting, market/liquidity, credit and operational risk, with shareholders required to backstop PRF deficiencies. Binds takaful companies, their boards and actuaries in fund segregation, solvency calculation and reporting.

Defines admissible assets as total assets after applying the constraints and limits used in calculating the solvency margin, and sits within the CBUAE takaful rules on assets meeting accrued insurance liabilities. It ties to the prudent person principle, Shari'ah compliance, asset security/quality/liquidity/localisation requirements, and special treatment where investment risk is borne by participants (e.g. unit-linked). Binds takaful companies and branches of foreign takaful operators in asset valuation and solvency reporting.

Defines Application Programming Interface (API) and related terms (API Lifecycle, API Provider) within the joint CBUAE/SCA/DFSA/FSRA Guidelines for Financial Institutions adopting Enabling Technologies, and sets expectations for API design, architecture, security and governance. It distinguishes Private, Partner, Open and Composite APIs and lists design attributes such as accessibility, interoperability, privacy by design and stability. Addressed to Institutions in scope of the Guidelines as supervisory expectations (largely 'should'-level guidance), including where API use is outsourced.

Covers the Cloud Computing chapter of the Enabling Technologies Guidelines: materiality assessment, governance framework, auditability, outsourcing to Outsourcing Service Providers, design and business continuity. It sets the test for when a cloud arrangement is 'material' (impact on operations, risk management, regulatory compliance, or confidentiality/integrity of Personal Data) and expects early engagement with the relevant Supervisory Authority before implementing material arrangements. Binds Institutions subject to the Guidelines and interacts with existing outsourcing requirements of each Supervisory Authority.

Defines Biometrics as automated recognition of individuals via biophysical, biomechanical and behavioural attributes, and flags its uses including customer identification and verification at onboarding, ongoing authentication, and ongoing due diligence and transaction scrutiny. Sits within the Enabling Technologies Guidelines' definitions and dedicated Biometrics section of key principles and detailed guidance. Relevant to Institutions relying on biometric authentication, with a direct read-across to CDD/identity verification obligations and personal data protection.

Sets out the Big Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence chapter of the Enabling Technologies Guidelines: materiality assessment of each AI/analytics Application, governance framework, explainability to avoid 'black-box' outcomes, data governance and representativeness of training data, independent validation and testing before deployment, and the ability to suspend material Applications. Expectations scale with the Application's purpose, criticality and impact on decision-making. Addressed to Institutions using such models in financial services.

Covers the Distributed Ledger Technology chapter of the Enabling Technologies Guidelines: governance of the ledger (ownership model, participant and validator rules, access approvals, key management, consensus protocol, off-chain procedures), roles and responsibilities of core groups, qualified users, participants and third parties, plus security, data standardisation/interoperability, retention and business continuity. Notably expects Personal Data to be kept off-chain and ledger pruning/key destruction to support retention and erasure. Applies to Institutions deploying DLT Applications, including via Outsourcing Service Providers.

The umbrella node for the joint Guidelines issued by CBUAE, SCA, DFSA and FSRA on adopting Enabling Technologies (APIs, cloud, biometrics, big data/AI, DLT) in financial services, including their legal basis, objectives, scope and cross-cutting key principles. Those principles cover data protection compliance, effective audit/compliance/risk control functions, periodic independent review or audit, and adequate skills, knowledge and expertise, with responsibility retained even where activities are outsourced. Applies across the four Supervisory Authorities' regulated populations and is principles-based rather than prescriptive.

A concept node covering the role of the Shari'a Committee within the CBUAE Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies. It identifies the matters that require Shari'a Committee sign-off alongside Authority approval — notably the Takaful operating model (Wakala/Mudaraba) and its limits, subsequent model changes, and the use of a capped share of the annual insurance/underwriting surplus for participants' funds (including the higher exceptional percentage supported by actuarial justification). It binds licensed Takaful insurance companies and their boards; approval is dual (internal Shari'a governance plus supervisory consent), so Shari'a clearance alone is not sufficient.

A concept node on the accounting and disclosure framework referenced in the CBUAE Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies, where AAOIFI standards operate alongside IFRS/IASB pronouncements and Authority-prescribed reporting templates. It frames the required content of financial statement notes (Takaful contract liabilities, Re-Takaful assets, accounting policies, related party and segment disclosures) and connects to actuarial reserving requirements for mathematical reserves. It binds Takaful insurance companies, their appointed actuaries and auditors for financial reporting purposes.

CBUAE Country and Transfer Risk Standards (154/2018), a prudential instrument setting requirements for identifying, measuring, governing and provisioning for cross-border exposures. It requires a board-approved risk appetite statement addressing sovereign, contagion, currency, indirect country, liquidity and macroeconomic risk, a risk management function proportionate to exposure, stress-testing, information systems and internal and supervisory reporting. It binds banks supervised by CBUAE, with obligations scaled by materiality of country and transfer risk exposure.

A concept node for the stress-testing article within the CBUAE Country and Transfer Risk Standards (154/2018), which sits between the risk management function requirements and the information systems/reporting articles. It concerns the requirement for banks to test the resilience of cross-border and country exposures under adverse scenarios and to feed results into governance, limits and provisioning decisions. It binds banks with country and transfer risk exposure, with intensity proportionate to risk profile, nature, size and complexity.

A concept node on the internal country risk assessment and rating approach expected under the CBUAE Country and Transfer Risk Standards (154/2018). It covers quantitative and qualitative ongoing assessment of each country of exposure, formal analysis at least annually with interim monitoring, the risk categories to be captured in the board-approved risk appetite statement, and the setting and monitoring of individual and aggregate country limits. It binds banks with material country and transfer risk exposure, whose boards and senior management must receive bank-wide (and where relevant group-wide) exposure reporting.

Joint Guidelines for Financial Institutions adopting Enabling Technologies, issued by CBUAE with SCA, DFSA and FSRA under their respective statutes. They set cross-authority key principles for firms using Enabling Technologies in Innovative Activities, covering data protection, control functions (audit, compliance, risk), periodic independent review, and adequacy of skills, knowledge and expertise, including expectations where technology audit is outsourced to an outsourced service provider. They apply to institutions licensed or authorised by any of the four Supervisory Authorities, including new entrants.

Node covering the outsourcing limb of the CBUAE Guidelines for Financial Institutions adopting Enabling Technologies, focused on outsourcing of cloud computing services. It sets supervisory expectations for a pre-engagement outsourcing risk assessment (materiality of the outsourced service, due diligence on the provider, benefits weighed against risks), a documented governance framework allocating roles between the institution and the provider, senior management accountability for reliance on providers for material services, and retention of documentation (strategy, materiality and risk assessments, due diligence, contracts) for review, audit and supervision. Addressed to licensed Institutions adopting these technologies; it is guidance-level expectation rather than a self-standing rulebook, and it operates alongside the outsourcing requirements of the relevant Supervisory Authority.

Node on the API governance expectations in the CBUAE Guidelines for Financial Institutions adopting Enabling Technologies. It expects a documented governance framework covering roles and division of duties between the Institution, API Provider and API developer, policies and controls across the API Lifecycle, change management and performance monitoring, pre-publication and ongoing testing (load, stress, conformance monitoring), and a framework to assess, monitor, report and mitigate API-related risks. Binds Institutions using or publishing APIs; expressed as supervisory expectations rather than prescriptive rules.

Node capturing the API design and development expectations in the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines, including design elements such as accessibility, interoperability, reuse, independence, extensibility, stability, privacy by design and transparency. It also addresses documented technical specifications, encryption of Personal Data in transit and at rest, access management, secure credential storage, and multi-factor authentication for customer access to API-enabled online services. Applies to Institutions and, where relevant, API Providers developing APIs.

Node on ongoing management and monitoring of APIs under the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines, drawn from the same governance provisions: tools for communication, change management and performance monitoring across the API Lifecycle, testing strategies (load, stress, crash-point) and a monitoring framework verifying conformance of critical interfaces, plus production monitoring, coding controls and post-deployment support. It also expects secure architecture that can evolve without disrupting existing applications. Directed at Institutions operating APIs, at guidance level.
lookup_terms: load testing and stress testing APIs

data.summary: Node defining when a cloud computing arrangement is material under the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines: where service disruption or a breach of security or confidentiality could materially affect business operations, risk management capability, regulatory compliance, or the confidentiality/integrity of the Institution's or Customer's Personal Data. It sets out the factors for the materiality and risk assessment (criticality, likelihood and impact of failure or data breach, cost) and expects early engagement with the relevant Supervisory Authority before implementing a material arrangement, consistent with existing outsourcing requirements. The materiality conclusion drives the depth of due diligence and the strength of mitigating controls.

Node on the Outsourcing Service Provider (OSP) as an actor under the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines, principally in cloud arrangements. It covers the due diligence expected before engagement — verifying the provider's maturity, adequacy and appropriateness against the intended use, with depth proportionate to the materiality of the arrangement and the degree of reliance — the clear allocation of roles and responsibilities between Institution and OSP, contract management and review, and record-keeping of due diligence and contractual documentation. The obligations rest on the Institution, not the OSP; the provider is the object of assessment and contractual control.

Defined collective term used in the CBUAE-led Guidelines for Financial Institutions adopting Enabling Technologies, covering the Central Bank of the UAE, the Securities and Commodities Authority, the DFSA (DIFC) and the FSRA (ADGM), each acting under its own enabling law. It identifies which regulator's expectations apply to an institution using enabling technologies (APIs, cloud computing, outsourcing) and to whom notification, access-to-information and materiality assessments are owed. It binds licensed institutions in each authority's jurisdiction, with the applicable authority determined by the institution's licensing regime rather than by the Guidelines themselves.

Refers to the Tier Capital Supply component of the CBUAE Standards for Capital Adequacy, which sets out eligible capital instruments and the composition of CET1, Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2, including the treatment of capital issued by subsidiaries to third parties (minority interest surplus) in consolidated capital and the deductions from regulatory capital. It is cross-referenced from the credit risk standardised approach, where exposures deducted under these standards receive specified risk-weight treatment. It binds banks subject to CBUAE capital adequacy requirements at solo and consolidated levels.

The highest-quality regulatory capital tier under the CBUAE capital adequacy framework, used both to meet minimum capital ratios and, in the portion not already consumed by Tier 1 and total capital minimums, to satisfy buffer requirements. The material illustrates how freely available CET1 is calculated against the effective combined buffer (capital conservation buffer, countercyclical buffer, D-SIB surcharge) and the consequent earnings-retention and distribution restrictions. Relevant to all banks subject to CBUAE capital adequacy and buffer rules.

The CBUAE treatment under which significant investments in the common shares of unconsolidated banking, financial and insurance entities and deferred tax assets arising from temporary differences are deducted from CET1 only above specified limits, with amounts below the limits aggregated and risk-weighted at 250% up to a further aggregate cap. The appendix explains the individual and aggregate limit calculations and the hypothetical CET1 base used for the aggregate test. Applies to banks computing regulatory capital under the CBUAE capital adequacy standards.

The set of deductions and adjustments applied to regulatory capital under the CBUAE capital adequacy standards, including full deduction of goodwill and other intangibles (net of associated deferred tax liabilities) and of DTAs from carried-forward losses, with deducted items excluded from credit risk RWA. Related Pillar 3 disclosure templates require banks to publish the composition of regulatory capital and its reconciliation to the balance sheet. Binds banks reporting regulatory capital to the CBUAE, with disclosure obligations extending to local banks and, on a scaled basis, branches of foreign banks.

Explains the regulatory capital treatment of deferred tax assets: those arising from net losses carried forward are deducted in full from CET1, while DTAs that rely on future profitability and arise from temporary timing differences fall under the threshold deduction regime rather than full deduction. Deductions are taken net of associated deferred tax liabilities where permitted. Applies to banks calculating regulatory capital and RWA under the CBUAE capital adequacy standards.

Supervisory guidance provisions on the lifecycle control of material Big Data Analytics and AI models, covering explainability, data governance and representativeness of training data, independent pre-deployment validation and testing, and the ability to suspend an application at will. It also sets expectations for a documented post-deployment review framework (monitoring, re-training, calibration, bias and fairness review, contingency/human intervention), error detection, remediation and escalation, and disciplined model versioning with records. Addressed to financial institutions adopting these enabling technologies, framed as 'should' expectations rather than prescriptive rules.
lookup_terms: Big Data Analytics and AI Application

data.summary: Guidance setting out the governance framework institutions are expected to approve and document before relying on Distributed Ledger Technology, covering platform and node ownership, the operating model (e.g. consortium vs single institution), participant and validator rules, access approval for ledger data, key management, consensus protocol and off-chain procedures. It also allocates roles and responsibilities across the core design/operation group, qualified users, participants and third parties including outsourcing service providers, and requires audit-ready evidence, logs, off-chain/on-chain linkage records and retention of DLT code and updates. Binds financial institutions deploying DLT applications.

Guidance on how DLT applications should be designed and secured, including optimisation to the intended use, and design principles for applications managing financial assets such as flexibility and traceability (with anonymity to be avoided). It extends to network integrity controls (node throughput limits, blocking abusive nodes/IPs, permissioned designs), selection of consensus methodology against performance, scalability, governance and resilience criteria, avoidance of clear-text personal data on-chain, and cryptographic key controls. Applies to financial institutions handling customer assets, personal data or restricted-participant arrangements on DLT.

Guidance addressing anonymity and pseudonymity risk in permissionless DLT: institutions building such applications are expected to ensure users are neither anonymous nor pseudonymous, given the exposure to tax evasion, bribery, money laundering and terrorist financing, and to consider chain analytics to trace transactions on pseudonymous chains. It sits alongside ongoing management and monitoring expectations (periodic review, code review and validation, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, privacy and data protection impact assessments) and code confidentiality/integrity controls. Relevant where a financial institution's DLT use intersects with AML/CTF customer identification duties.
lookup_terms: money laundering terrorism financing DLT risk

data.summary: Guidance on cryptographic key management for DLT and related environments: controls over key generation, secure storage and transmission of private keys, treatment of offline root keys (split among multiple owners) and online root keys (in hardware security modules), and issuance/revocation of keys to staff on leaving or changing roles. It links to physical and environmental security, prohibition on keeping personal data on-ledger, and data retention approaches including purging ledger records and destroying encryption keys to render data inaccessible, plus business continuity planning and testing for DLT services. Directed at financial institutions operating DLT applications.

Guidance on protecting data across storage, transmission and use, principally in cloud computing arrangements: recoverability within pre-defined timeframes, secure backups, segregation in multi-tenancy or co-mingled environments, controls against unauthorised access and network attacks, cryptographic key management, encryption or tokenisation of personal data, identity and access management with multi-factor authentication, and logging of user access and activity. It connects to the data governance expectations for AI and analytics models (accuracy, completeness, consistency, security, timeliness and documented quality gaps). Binds financial institutions and shapes what they must require of outsourcing service providers.
lookup_terms: data in transit and at rest

data.summary: Guidance node within the CBUAE Guidelines for Financial Institutions adopting Enabling Technologies dealing with the cloud-computing lifecycle at its end stage: stressed exit scenarios and documented exit plans for outsourced cloud arrangements, sitting alongside materiality assessment, governance, auditability and business continuity expectations. It frames expectations (expressed as 'should') on institutions to anticipate disruption that continuity measures cannot absorb and to maintain the ability to withdraw from or transition away from an Outsourcing Service Provider. Binds CBUAE-licensed Institutions using cloud arrangements, with knock-on contractual obligations on the OSP and access rights for the relevant Supervisory Authority.

Concept node collecting the business continuity expectations in the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines, applied both to material cloud computing arrangements (BCP ownership, key risk indicators and triggers, dependency on a single provider, roles, recovery objectives, at-least-annual testing) and to DLT applications (loss of data/processing capability, cyber-crime, periodic testing). Where the arrangement is outsourced, the institution must be satisfied with the Outsourcing Service Provider's own continuity plan and test jointly. Binds CBUAE-licensed Institutions' business continuity and crisis management functions.

Concept node on biometric identity management in the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines: identity proofing and enrolment (validation of documentary evidence, verification that the identity belongs to the person), ongoing authentication, credential protection, multi-factor and risk-based/adaptive authentication, and monitoring across the whole Identity Lifecycle. It also carries data-protection compliance and controlled/auditable access where biometric functions are outsourced. Binds CBUAE-licensed Institutions deploying Biometric Applications; relevant where identity proofing intersects with customer due diligence and onboarding.

Node labelled for the credential service provider role, but the underlying text is the outsourcing strand of the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines: pre-engagement outsourcing risk assessment, due diligence on prospective Outsourcing Service Providers proportionate to materiality, IT asset classification and logging, contractual management and review, documentation retained for audit and supervision, and Senior Management responsibility for reliance on OSPs for material cloud services. Binds CBUAE-licensed Institutions engaging third-party technology providers; check the source before relying on the label, as the extracted context does not define 'Credential Service Provider'.

Concept node on fairness, reliability and post-deployment control of Big Data Analytics and AI applications under the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines: a documented framework for pre- and post-deployment review of algorithms, models and data; triggers for re-training, recalibration, redevelopment or discontinuation; review of outcomes for unintentional bias (e.g. false positive/negative rates); contingency measures including human intervention; error detection, rectification, escalation and model versioning records. Binds CBUAE-licensed Institutions using material AI/analytics applications, with accountability retained by the Governing Body and Senior Management.

Concept node setting the governance architecture for Big Data Analytics and AI in the CBUAE enabling-technologies guidelines: materiality assessment of each application (use case, criticality, disruption impact), an approved and documented governance framework with policies covering design, development, monitoring and use, pre-launch validation, explainability to avoid 'black-box' models, a data governance framework addressing quality gaps and representativeness of training data, independent validation and testing, and the ability to suspend an application promptly. Binds CBUAE-licensed Institutions, with the Governing Body and Senior Management accountable for outcomes and automated decisions.
lookup_terms: Big Data Analytics and AI governance
board and senior management accountability AI

data.summary: A concept node within CBUAE capital adequacy material dealing with how minority interest and capital issued by subsidiaries to third parties is recognised in consolidated regulatory capital, illustrated by a worked parent/subsidiary example. The surrounding context also covers Pillar 2 items such as interest rate risk in the banking book, indicating the node sits inside broader capital adequacy/ICAAP guidance. It binds banks (conventional and Islamic) operating in the UAE that consolidate subsidiaries for capital reporting.
lookup_terms: surplus capital attributable to third parties

data.summary: A concept node covering the composition and calculation of the tiers of regulatory capital (CET1, AT1, Tier 1, Tier 2, Total Capital), including how amounts issued by a parent and by subsidiaries to third parties are aggregated into consolidated capital. It also touches capital planning and stress-testing expectations, including management actions and Central Bank engagement before counting planned capital increases. Applies to banks in the UAE for capital adequacy and ICAAP purposes.

A concept node on Additional Tier 1 capital, including its derivation as the difference between Tier 1 and CET1 and how AT1 issued by a subsidiary to third parties is partially included in consolidated group capital. The illustrative example shows parent holdings of a subsidiary's CET1, AT1 and Tier 2 and the resulting eligible amounts. Relevant to UAE banks computing consolidated capital ratios.

A concept node labelled Maximum Distributable Amount, but the attached context concerns the mandate-based approach (MBA) and look-through approach for risk-weighting bank investments in funds, applying conservative maximum-leverage and maximum-notional assumptions. Read it as capital-calculation material on conservative 'maximum permitted' assumptions rather than buffer-based distribution restrictions; distribution restriction material appears elsewhere in the same instrument. Binds UAE banks calculating RWA for fund exposures.

A concept node on transitional recognition and amortisation of legacy capital instruments, appearing alongside guidance on gross-up clauses for AT1 and Tier 2, point of non-viability (PONV) share issuance sequencing, and distribution restrictions tied to CET1 levels and distributable earnings. Also includes FAQ material on significant investments in commercial entities and eligibility of minority interest from non-bank regulated subsidiaries. Binds UAE banks issuing or holding capital instruments.

A concept node on credit risk in the Pillar 2/ICAAP context, with emphasis on credit concentration risk (name and sectoral concentration) as a material risk the Central Bank expects all UAE banks to assess and capitalise. It links to the Large Exposures regime (the 10% of capital threshold) and to real estate exposure standards, while noting that Pillar 2 measurement should use a broader concentration concept than the regulatory large-exposure test. Binds banks in their risk identification, measurement and capital planning processes, with Board and Senior Management approval expectations.

Node covering the sovereign exposure class under the CBUAE standardised approach to credit risk, including the condition for preferential (including 0%) risk weighting where a GCC sovereign exposure is both denominated and funded in that sovereign's domestic currency, and the default rule that all other sovereign exposures follow the sovereign's external rating. It also addresses the rating regime: only solicited ratings from eligible ECAIs may be used, with unsolicited ratings permitted only for the UAE federal government. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE when computing risk-weighted assets and may extend to collateral and guarantee treatment under credit risk mitigation.

Node on the public sector entity exposure class, distinguishing non-commercial PSEs (administrative bodies and non-commercial undertakings of the UAE federal, emirate or local governments) from commercial government-related entities. Non-commercial PSEs do not automatically get sovereign treatment; preferential treatment is limited to UAE entities, requires satisfaction of all seven classification criteria and CBUAE approval, with exceptional sovereign-equivalent treatment only where formal arrangements remove the distinction from sovereign risk. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks classifying and risk-weighting PSE counterparties, with internal audit/compliance expected to review classification periodically.

Node on the CBUAE Government Related Entities list and the definition of GREs as commercial undertakings wholly owned or majority-owned by the federal or emirate governments. Such exposures must be classified as GRE and risk-weighted as corporate claims according to the entity's credit rating; banks must apply the latest published GRE list and notify the CBUAE of information supporting additions or removals. Internal audit/compliance functions of CBUAE-licensed banks must periodically verify PSE and GRE classification against the list.

Node on exposures to multilateral development banks, which are generally treated like claims on banks but without the preferential short-term treatment, save for highly rated MDBs meeting specified criteria that qualify for a 0% risk weight. Eligibility follows the BCBS list of qualifying MDBs, which banks must consult and apply; the CBUAE takes no role in assessing individual MDB eligibility. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks in assigning risk weights to MDB exposures.

Node defining the bank exposure class, covering interbank claims, nostro accounts, certificates of deposit issued by banks and repurchase agreements. Unrated bank claims attract 50% (long term) and 20% (short term) risk weights, subject to a floor that no unrated bank claim may be weighted below the claim on its sovereign of incorporation; intragroup exposures follow the external rating of the counterparty entity. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks calculating risk-weighted assets on bank counterparties.

Node on the corporate exposure class under the CBUAE standardised approach, which is the treatment applied to commercial counterparties including government related entities that operate competitively, risk-weighted by reference to the entity's external credit rating from an eligible ECAI. Only solicited ratings may be used for corporate exposures. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks when classifying and risk-weighting corporate and GRE counterparties.

A capital-adequacy asset-class concept defining which exposures qualify for the regulatory retail portfolio under the standardised approach, by reference to the Credit Risk Standard's four tests (orientation, product, granularity and value criteria), with non-qualifying retail claims risk weighted at 100%. It explains how aggregated exposure to one counterparty is measured on a gross basis (after credit conversion factors for off-balance-sheet items) and how connected small businesses are treated as a single beneficiary. Claims secured by residential property and past-due retail loans are carved out and handled in separate asset classes; it binds banks calculating regulatory capital.

Defines the standardised-approach asset class for loans secured by residential property (self-occupied or rented) where the property is fully mortgaged in favour of the bank, and sets out the loan-to-value measure and the rule that valuation is held at origination value unless the Central Bank requires a downward revision or an extraordinary idiosyncratic event permanently reduces value. Supervisory Q&A clarifies that customers holding more than four properties are reported as commercial property at 100% risk weight and that the 35% preferential risk weight applies only to completed, not under-construction, properties. It binds banks in capital adequacy reporting and risk weighting.

Covers the counterparty credit risk framework (SA-CCR) and related capital topics, including exposure measurement for written and purchased credit derivatives, capping effective notional at maximum potential loss, and offsetting conditions requiring protection on a pari passu or junior reference obligation with same-or-more-conservative terms. The surrounding material links this to capital planning, leverage ratio and ICAAP material-risk identification, including credit concentration risk and IRRBB. It binds banks calculating derivative exposures and setting capital demand.

Explains the supervisory duration input used in the SA-CCR add-on calculation for interest rate derivatives, where adjusted notional equals trade notional multiplied by a prescribed duration formula based on the start and end dates of the referenced period. It sits within worked guidance and FAQs on trade classification, hedging sets, maturity buckets, supervisory delta, supervisory factors and correlations. It binds banks computing counterparty credit risk exposure on derivative portfolios.

Sets out when netting sets may be recognised for counterparty credit risk purposes: banks must run an internal process assessing legal enforceability with review and challenge, and the Central Bank reviews netting-set identification supervisorily rather than pre-approving jurisdictions or counterparties. A standard ISDA agreement alone does not establish valid netting, and where recognition conditions fail each transaction forms its own single-trade netting set. It also covers replacement cost aggregation across netting sets under a margin agreement, including variation margin and NICA.

A concept node for the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision as the international standard-setter whose frameworks underpin the local capital rules discussed here, notably the leverage ratio as a non-risk-based backstop to risk-based capital and the CVA capital charge introduced to close the Basel II gap on derivative fair-value credit losses. It provides background rationale rather than direct obligations, but frames how Central Bank capital requirements are to be read as a mutually reinforcing package binding banks.

A market-risk concept node within CBUAE capital adequacy guidance covering how commodity exposures are identified and capitalised, including restrictions on offsetting between positions and the two standardised computation routes (simplified and maturity ladder). It also sits within the wider Pillar 1/Pillar 2 market risk framework, where banks must calibrate analysis to portfolios, asset classes, risk factors, geographies, products and tenors. It binds banks licensed in the UAE for capital calculation and ICAAP purposes; supervisory approval is required for correlation-based offsetting.

One of the two standardised alternatives for computing the commodity capital charge under CBUAE capital adequacy guidance, contrasted with the simplified approach and structured as a multi-step calculation across maturity time bands. Relevant where a bank wants a more granular treatment of basis, interest rate and forward gap risk than the flat simplified percentages. Applies to UAE-licensed banks calculating market risk capital.

An options treatment under the intermediate approach to market risk in CBUAE capital adequacy guidance: options enter the standardised calculation as delta-weighted positions (market value of the underlying times delta), with separate additional charges for gamma and vega risk. It is distinguished from the simplified approach for hedged and outright option positions, and specific risk is charged on the delta-equivalent. Binds UAE-licensed banks holding option exposures for capital purposes.

Defines operational risk as loss from inadequate or failed internal processes, people or systems, or from external events, expressly including legal and compliance risk but excluding strategic and reputational risk. Covers the operational risk capital charge (converted to risk-weighted assets by a 12.5 multiplier) and the expectation that banks assess whether Pillar 1 gross-income-based approaches understate their exposure, addressing any shortfall in Pillar 2 / ICAAP. Binds UAE-licensed banks, including those operating on a Shari'ah-compliant basis.

One of the Basel-based methods referenced in CBUAE guidance for calculating the Pillar 1 operational risk capital charge, alongside the Standardised and Alternative Standardised Approaches. The guidance flags that gross-income-based measures such as this are risk-insensitive and may understate exposure, so banks are expected to test adequacy under Pillar 2. Applies to UAE-licensed banks determining operational risk capital under the Capital Adequacy Standards.

The business-line-based method for the operational risk capital charge, using gross income and prescribed beta factors per business line, with Alternative Standardised Approach options substituting loans and advances for commercial and retail banking and applying different beta combinations. The guidance notes gross income is a risk-insensitive proxy, so banks must consider a Pillar 2 add-on. Binds UAE-licensed banks, with a Shari'ah-compliant equivalent calculation expected where applicable.

Orientation node for the CBUAE securitisation capital framework, which sets out how banks in the UAE determine regulatory capital for banking-book securitisation exposures, closely tracking the Basel Committee's revised 2014/2016 standard. It defines what counts as a securitisation (tranching with differentiated loss absorption, payments driven by underlying pool performance rather than the originator's obligation), excludes simple pass-through structures, and identifies borderline cases such as real-estate cash-flow deals that may instead be specialised lending. It binds banks holding or originating securitisation exposures and requires consultation with the Central Bank where classification is uncertain; note this is UAE (CBUAE), not SAMA, material.

Concept node for the Standardised Approach to securitisation exposures (SEC-SA) within the CBUAE capital hierarchy. It sits below the External Ratings-Based Approach (SEC-ERBA) for ordinary securitisations and is the starting point for resecuritisations, with a 1250% risk weight applying where neither approach can be used; internal ratings-based approaches are not permitted for UAE banks. Relevant to banks calculating banking-book securitisation capital; CBUAE instrument, not SAMA.

Concept node explaining tranche thickness, the size of a securitisation tranche relative to the whole transaction, measured as the gap between attachment and detachment points. It is an input to risk-weight calculations under both SEC-ERBA and SEC-SA, with thinner tranches generally riskier at a given attachment point and non-senior tranches subject to a thickness adjustment subject to a floor. Applies to banks computing capital on securitisation positions under the CBUAE framework.

Node covering market risk as treated in the CBUAE ICAAP/Pillar 2 guidance, including expectations that banks calibrate market-risk analysis around key drivers (portfolios, asset classes, risk factors, geographies, products, tenors) and include stressed periods, and that amortised-cost portfolios be assessed for market-versus-book value differences under Pillar 2. It sits within the broader material-risk identification, measurement, monitoring and capital-planning duties owned by Senior Management and the Board. Binds banks in the UAE preparing ICAAP submissions.

Node on interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB), and its Islamic-banking analogue profit rate risk in the banking book (PRRBB), which the CBUAE treats as a material Pillar 2 risk (trading-book interest rate risk being covered under Pillar 1 market risk). It requires a Board-approved IRRBB risk appetite, supporting policies and a full identification-measurement-reporting-monitoring-mitigation process, with measurement drawing on CBUAE ICAAP standards, the 2018 interest rate/rate of return risk rules, model management standards and the Basel SRP 31 framework, and covering basis risk, repricing gaps, commercial margins, currency optionality and non-maturing deposits. Binds UAE banks and their boards.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: Node grouping equity risk within the CBUAE ICAAP material-risk taxonomy, where banks must identify, measure, report, monitor and mitigate all risks material to their business model and risk profile across the group, including branches and subsidiaries, and feed that assessment into Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 capital demand. The surrounding context addresses market and operational risk treatment under Pillar 2 and the Board/Senior Management approval of the risk-estimation framework; the document contains limited equity-specific text, so open it mainly for the general material-risk and Pillar 2 expectations. Binds UAE banks preparing ICAAP.

Concept node covering the Alternative Standardised Approach, one of the Pillar 1 methods for computing operational risk capital, in which an average volume of outstanding loans and advances scaled by a fixed factor replaces gross income as the exposure indicator for the retail and commercial banking lines. It sets out which credit portfolios feed the commercial loans and advances measure and the rationale of avoiding distortions from differing income margins. It binds banks subject to the Central Bank's capital adequacy framework, and use of the approach — as well as any reversion to the Standardised Approach — is conditional on supervisory satisfaction and approval.

Concept node explaining gross income as the exposure indicator for operational risk capital under the Basic Indicator Approach and the Standardised Approach, including its composition (net interest plus net non-interest income), the gross-of-provisions and gross-of-operating-expenses conventions, treatment of outsourcing fees, and exclusion of items such as securities sale gains and extraordinary income. It also covers how years of negative gross income are dropped from both numerator and denominator and the resulting potential distortions warranting supervisory attention under Pillar 2. Applies to banks calculating regulatory operational risk capital.

Concept node on the IOSCO Code of Conduct Fundamentals for Credit Rating Agencies as a benchmark in the Central Bank's eligibility criteria for External Credit Assessment Institutions. It requires an ECAI to adopt and follow a code of conduct consistent with the IOSCO CRA Code and to be supervised on an ongoing basis by a competent authority with a consistent regime and a registration system, alongside criteria on transparency, disclosure, no abuse of unsolicited ratings and cooperation with the supervisor. It binds ECAIs seeking or holding recognition, and indirectly banks relying on their ratings.
lookup_terms: Code of Conduct Fundamentals for Credit Rating Agencies

data.summary: Concept node on how external ratings map to risk weights and how banks must apply them: mappings are expressed on a scale closest to one major agency's notation for consistency with the Basel framework without endorsing any agency, and banks may choose among eligible ECAIs. It sets the operational rules for consistent use, no cherry-picking, exclusion of unsolicited ratings, treatment where two or three or more ratings diverge, and the bar on using a group entity's rating for affiliates. Binds banks applying the standardised credit risk and securitisation capital rules.

Concept node linking risk weighting to the capital adequacy and ICAAP material-risk framework: banks must meet minimum capital plus buffers under business-as-usual and minimum capital under stress, plan capital including the leverage ratio, and identify, measure and cover both Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 risks across the group. It notes that credit concentration risk and IRRBB are treated as material, and that the gross-income-based Pillar 1 operational risk approaches may understate risk, so Pillar 2 capital must compensate. Binds banks, with framework approval sitting with Senior Management and the Board.
lookup_terms: operational risk approaches BIA SA ASA

data.summary: Concept node on risk-weighted assets as the denominator of risk-based capital ratios within the capital planning and ICAAP expectations, including the requirement to look beyond risk-based ratios to the leverage ratio and to anticipate regulatory changes such as revised standardised approaches for credit, market and operational risk. It ties RWA-based Pillar 1 outcomes to the bank's own assessment of material risks and Pillar 2 add-ons. Binds banks subject to the Central Bank's capital adequacy and ICAAP framework.

Guidance node explaining which instruments may be recognised as eligible hedges when computing the credit valuation adjustment (CVA) capital charge, and the exclusions that apply. It confines eligibility to index CDS, single-name CDS or contingent CDS and equivalent instruments directly referencing the hedged counterparty (including swaptions without knock-out on a credit event), excludes tranched and nth-to-default products, requires the hedge to have been entered into expressly to hedge the counterparty credit spread component of CVA risk, and removes recognised hedges from market risk capital. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE calculating counterparty credit risk and CVA capital.

Worked-example node showing how an eligible index CDS is recognised as a hedge of systematic CVA risk in the CVA capital formula. It illustrates derivation of the supervisory discount factor from the index maturity, the weighted-average risk weight across the index constituents' ratings, and the resulting reduction in CVA capital and RWA. Relevant to CBUAE-licensed banks applying the standardised CVA capital calculation.

Node covering the simplified/alternative route to CVA capital within the CBUAE framework, set against the background of why a CVA charge exists (crisis-era mark-to-market losses on counterparty credit risk rather than outright defaults). It situates regulatory CVA as distinct from accounting CVA, notably excluding own-credit effects (DVA), and frames hedging recognition. Applies to banks determining CVA capital requirements for derivatives and in-scope SFT exposures.

FAQ-style node on maturity and supervisory duration inputs used in the standardised counterparty credit risk and CVA calculations, alongside related clarifications on supervisory deltas and hedging sets. It confirms mandatory use of the standardised formulas for all options, treatment of hedging sets with or without a netting set, and CVA-specific points such as QCCP exclusions, non-netting of DVA, and hedge instruments creating new counterparty exposure. Directed at banks computing SA-CCR and CVA capital.

Node explaining the capital treatment of banks' equity investments in funds held in the banking book, based on the Basel hierarchy of the look-through approach, the mandate-based approach and the fall-back approach. It sets out scope (banking book only; trading book equity sits in market risk), confirms the CBUAE declined national discretions to exempt zero-risk-weight-debt entities and official programme investments, and describes how the fund's average asset risk weight is scaled by leverage subject to a 1250% cap. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks holding fund equity exposures.

Node on the non-risk-based leverage ratio as a backstop complementing risk-based capital requirements, including how the exposure measure is built up and adjusted. It confirms that total balance-sheet assets are the starting point, that derivative and SFT-related on-balance-sheet items move into their respective exposure components, that on-balance-sheet collateral remains in the exposure measure, and that unconditionally cancellable commitments to issue direct credit substitutes attract a 10% rather than 100% conversion factor. Applies to CBUAE-licensed banks calculating the leverage ratio.

A node within CBUAE prudential guidance keyed to Potential Future Exposure, but the surrounding material addresses conversion of off-balance-sheet items into exposure amounts: a mandatory 100% credit conversion factor for securitisation-related off-balance-sheet exposures (including undrawn servicer cash advances, where the Central Bank declined the Basel national discretion), the risk-weight treatment of overlapping exposures, and leverage ratio exposure-measure FAQs. It binds banks licensed by the UAE Central Bank when computing risk-weighted assets and the leverage ratio exposure measure. Useful for confirming how add-on/exposure components and CCFs are applied rather than for a definition of PFE itself.

Covers how exposure amounts are built up for capital and leverage purposes under CBUAE prudential standards: total balance-sheet assets as the starting point for the leverage ratio, exclusion of derivative and SFT-related balance-sheet items from the on-balance-sheet component, gross treatment of collateral, and credit conversion factors for commitments (including the 10% CCF for unconditionally cancellable commitments to issue direct credit substitutes versus 100% for securitisation-related items). Applies to banks calculating risk-weighted assets and the leverage ratio. Consult it to resolve which bucket an exposure falls into and which CCF applies.

A node labelled for the standardised approach to counterparty credit risk, but the surrounding text sits in CBUAE ICAAP/Pillar 2 guidance: banks must assess whether standardised credit risk weights reflect inherent risk, benchmark capital consumption under the Standardised Approach against a foundation IRB estimation (using IFRS one-year PDs where F-IRB PDs are not calibrated), and integrate material risk identification, capital planning and the leverage ratio into the ICAAP. Binds banks and their Boards/Senior Management, which must approve the capital-demand estimation framework. Open it for supervisory expectations on internal capital adequacy rather than for SA-CCR mechanics alone.

Explains the regulatory credit valuation adjustment capital charge under CBUAE standards, including how regulatory CVA differs from accounting CVA (no debit valuation adjustment / own-credit effect) and which instruments qualify as eligible CVA hedges — index CDS, single-name and contingent CDS, equivalent instruments directly referencing the hedged counterparty, and CDS swaptions without knock-out clauses — with tranched and nth-to-default CDS excluded. Also touches the treatment of written and purchased credit derivatives in the leverage ratio exposure measure. Binds banks with derivative counterparty exposure calculating CVA and market risk capital.

Sets out the conceptual basis and formula for the standardised CVA capital charge under CBUAE standards: a value-at-risk construct at a one-year, 99% confidence level, giving the 2.33 multiplier applied to the standard deviation of changes in CVA, with the Central Bank using simpler notation than the BCBS formula while producing the same result. Also confirms the exclusion of own-credit/DVA effects and the limited set of eligible hedges. Relevant to banks computing CVA capital and to reviewers validating the calculation's inputs and confidence-level assumptions.

Worked-example material from CBUAE guidance showing how derivative exposure add-ons are built: supervisory duration and adjusted notional, supervisory delta (+1 long / -1 short for linear trades), maturity factor scaling for sub-one-year un-margined trades, effective notional aggregation, and supervisory factors by asset class (e.g. rating-based factors for single-name credit, investment-grade treatment for CDS indices) with hedging sets and offsetting rules for commodities. Binds banks calculating counterparty credit risk exposure on derivatives. Open it for numerical illustration of the parameters rather than for the underlying rule text.

Supervisory guidance elaborating CBUAE expectations for the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process, covering how the ICAAP is run, approved and reported, and what the ICAAP report must contain (including executive summary, capital composition, forward-looking and stressed capital positions). It binds all banks licensed by the CBUAE, with proportionality in supervisory evaluation but no exemption from full scope for smaller or less complex banks; for foreign bank branches, board-level references map to the Managing Director or the highest UAE committee. It also addresses methodological questions such as optional use of a foundation IRB comparison (PD floor of 0.03%, fixed 45% LGD, no own LGD estimates) and quantification of climate-related financial risk.

Node covering the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process as the supervisory counterpart to the bank-run ICAAP: the CBUAE analyses banks' capitalisation levels and the ICAAP's internal view of capital adequacy. Where capital levels are judged unsatisfactory, the Central Bank may impose an adjusted Minimum Capital Adequacy ratio on the individual bank. Applies to all CBUAE-licensed banks.

Defines Pillar 2 capital as the additional capital each bank must determine and hold for risks not covered, or insufficiently covered, by Pillar 1 (credit, market, operational) capital under the CBUAE capital adequacy framework. Pillar 2 operates as both an internal process reported through the ICAAP and a supervisory evaluation, and requires banks to maintain capital consistent with risk profile and strategy, including stressed positions and Board-approved management actions. Binds all CBUAE-licensed banks.
lookup_terms: Standards and Guidance re Capital Adequacy

data.summary: Sets the governance requirements around the ICAAP: the Board of Directors owns the ICAAP, must approve it annually, and must approve the ICAAP governance framework with clear assignment of responsibilities, with assumptions and conclusions challenged at expert-committee, Senior Management and Board levels. Also frames the required ICAAP report elements (capital composition against minimum requirements, three-year forward-looking capital plan including dividends, stress scenario analysis with mitigation, assessment of risk management processes and a concluding capital adequacy opinion). Binds CBUAE-licensed banks; for foreign bank operations, Board references map to the local senior governance body.

Articulates the use test for stress testing: stress tests must not be a standalone ICAAP exercise but must be embedded in business decision-making and risk management across the organisation, with Senior Management and the Board leading and approving assumptions, methodology and use of results. Requires that risk mitigations be considered in light of severity and likelihood, with documented justification where no action is taken, and sits alongside requirements for reverse stress testing to identify scenarios rendering the business model non-viable or breaching minimum capital requirements. Applies to all CBUAE-licensed banks.

Covers capital planning within the ICAAP: banks must project capital under baseline and stress scenarios and identify credible, quantifiable management actions with trigger points tied to the internal risk appetite, reporting stressed results both with and without Board-approved actions. Planned capital increases may only be counted where they have Senior Management approval, form part of the official capital plan and have been discussed with the Central Bank; reputational consequences of management actions must also be weighed. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks.

Concept node for Pillar 1 minimum capital requirements (credit, market and operational risk) as the baseline against which Pillar 2 add-ons are assessed in the CBUAE capital adequacy framework. The surrounding guidance explains that banks must cover Pillar 1 risks with capital under the Capital Adequacy Regulations and Standards, and then quantify residual risks not adequately captured by Pillar 1 as Pillar 2 capital, feeding capital planning, stress testing and management actions. Binds all banks licensed by the UAE Central Bank, at group and entity level.

Concept node for Pillar 2 risks: those material risks not covered, or not sufficiently covered, by Pillar 1 capital, which each bank must identify, measure, monitor and capitalise through its ICAAP. Sets expectations on material risk identification across the whole group (branches and subsidiaries), Board and Senior Management approval of the capital-estimation framework, continuous review of the applicable risk universe, and treatment of direct versus indirect risks; credit concentration risk and IRRBB are designated material. Applies to banks licensed by the UAE Central Bank and is assessed by the supervisor through SREP.

Concept node for Pillar 3 regulatory market disclosure requirements, aimed at market discipline through comparable public reporting of capital, RWAs and risk exposures. Covers scope (all UAE banks at top consolidated level and foreign bank branches, including Islamic financial services providers), publication as a standalone report on the bank's website with a five-year archive, disclosure frequency and signposting, periodic external audit of annual reports, a Board-approved disclosure policy with senior officer attestation, and the process for seeking Central Bank approval to withhold proprietary or confidential items.

Concept node defining credit concentration risk as incremental credit loss caused by high correlation between the credit risk drivers of exposures, arising from name concentration, sectoral concentration or correlated obligor drivers even in apparently granular portfolios. Treated by the Central Bank as a key material Pillar 2 risk for all UAE banks, measured for ICAAP purposes on a broader basis than the regulatory large-exposure threshold, with a specific requirement to analyse real estate exposures. Binds banks in their ICAAP risk identification and Pillar 2 capital calibration.

Concept node for interest rate risk in the banking book (and its Islamic-banking analogue, profit rate risk in the banking book), defined as the risk of loss in the banking book from interest rate changes and addressed under Pillar 2 rather than the Pillar 1 market risk framework. Requires a Board-approved IRRBB risk appetite, supporting policies and a full identification-measurement-reporting-monitoring-mitigation process, with measurement referencing the ICAAP Standards, the dedicated interest rate and rate of return risk regulation, model management standards and the Basel SRP 31 framework, and covering basis risk, repricing gaps, commercial margins, optionality and non-maturing deposits.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: Concept node for model risk as a Pillar 2 / material risk topic, sitting between the ICAAP guidance's treatment of non-Pillar 1 risks and the Central Bank's model management standards and guidance. Relevant where banks rely on internal models to quantify credit, market, operational and other risks and must therefore govern model development, validation and use, with the risk-estimation framework approved by Senior Management and the Board. Binds banks licensed by the UAE Central Bank; consult the model management source for the operative requirements.

Section of the CBUAE ICAAP guidance dealing with business model analysis (BMA) and strategic risk as a Pillar 2 material risk. It frames BMA as the risk that the bank's organisation, expertise, systems and processes fail to deliver its business and strategic objectives, and strategic risk as the business model or strategy ceasing to be adequate for Board-set objectives. It binds banks subject to the ICAAP regime, with responsibility sitting with the Board and Senior Management for risk identification, measurement and capital calibration.

Node covering the treatment of financial risks from climate change within the ICAAP, largely through supervisory Q&A. It indicates that no specific capital charge methodology is prescribed, but banks are expected to understand climate-related impacts on sustainability and business strategy, develop quantification methodologies proportionate to size and business model, and explore stress testing and scenario analysis (including green asset ratio assessment). It applies to banks preparing ICAAP submissions.

Part of the ICAAP guidance's material-risk taxonomy addressing liquidity risk and funding cost alongside market and operational risk under Pillar 2. It sits within the expectation that banks identify, measure and hold capital or take mitigating action for risks not fully captured by Pillar 1, including amortised cost portfolio analysis and operational risk shortfalls. It binds banks conducting the ICAAP and their Boards.

Section requiring each bank to implement a stress testing framework serving both the ICAAP and wider risk management, covering enterprise-wide, internal portfolio-level and regulatory (supervisor-prescribed) stress tests. Tests must be integrated, forward-looking and at least annual, with more frequent execution where circumstances require, and the Central Bank may challenge key assumptions. The Board is accountable for implementation, with delegation to Senior Management and subject-matter experts under Board-approved policies.
