Sub-section setting the expectation that banks conduct reverse stress tests in addition to normal stress testing, starting from a predefined non-viability or breach-of-minimum-requirements outcome and working back to the scenarios and shocks that would produce it. It requires assessment of whether such outcomes are realistic and whether mitigating actions (including hedging viability under stressed market conditions) are warranted, and links to the use test requiring stress results to drive decision-making. It applies to banks within the ICAAP framework, with Board and Senior Management ownership of assumptions and methodology.

Node labelled for the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index methodology, used in the ICAAP guidance context for measuring credit concentration risk, a risk the Central Bank treats as material. The supplied context consists of technical annex-style capital calculation material (equity position risk charges and CVA capital with index hedges), so the document should be opened to confirm the precise HHI formula, inputs and application. It is relevant to banks quantifying concentration and Pillar 2 capital add-ons.

Article 8 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation, setting the framework for Complaint management and resolution by Licensed Financial Institutions. It requires an independent complaint function reporting to Senior Management, a free and accessible complaint system, adherence to Central Bank-prescribed turnaround times and written responses, staff and Authorized Agent training, and consumer awareness of rights. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions in the UAE, including for complaints arising from products or services sold by their Authorized Agents.

Article 11 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation, addressing Shari'ah compliance in the delivery of financial services, together with related definitions (Higher Shari'ah Authority, Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee). It obliges Islamic Financial Institutions to uphold Shari'ah principles, comply with their ISSC, and have the Board and Senior Management embed Shari'ah compliance in culture, processes, operations and code of conduct. Also notes that the Regulation supplements other regulators' requirements and does not alter financial crime compliance obligations.

The CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation (Circular No. 8/2020, dated 25/11/2020), issued under Article 121 of Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018, is the overarching principles-based conduct framework for protecting consumers of financial products and services in the UAE. It sets institutional obligations on business and market conduct, governance over product design and sale, responsible financing and over-indebtedness, disclosure and transparency, complaint redress and financial literacy, supplemented by detailed Standards. It binds all Licensed Financial Institutions in the State and must be read with other CBUAE regulations, including Shari'ah governance rules.

Section 3.2 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation on governance of Retail Operations, plus supporting defined terms (Retail Operations, Senior Management, Person, Reducing Balance Method, Permissible, Regulation). It requires Licensed Financial Institutions to maintain strong governance and management oversight over design, development, promotion, sale, distribution and ongoing review of financial products and services, to assess consumer needs, suitability and affordability, and to protect consumer assets, information and data. Institutions offering Shari'ah-compliant products must also meet separate Shari'ah governance requirements.

Article 4 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation, setting responsible Market conduct duties for Licensed Financial Institutions. It requires upholding high ethical practices, prohibiting abusive sales, marketing and pricing practices, promoting disclosure, transparency and non-discriminatory competition, avoiding unreasonable barriers to consumer access, and ensuring independent control functions are competent in market conduct principles. Also carries adjacent business-conduct duties on staff ethics, competence, remuneration and institutional responsibility for staff actions.

Article 5 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation on responsible Business conduct, covering internal culture and behaviour across product design, promotion, sales, distribution and lending/financing. It requires Licensed Financial Institutions to act with due skill, care, diligence, fairness and honesty, to manage and disclose Conflicts of Interest, to maintain a staff code of conduct with training and complaint monitoring, to ensure customer-facing staff are competent and qualified, and to set remuneration and appraisal policies that do not incentivise mis-selling or unreasonable risk-taking. Institutions remain responsible for the acts of their staff.

CBUAE standard on Shari'ah governance for Islamic financial institutions and Islamic windows, setting the mandate, supervision duties and reporting obligations of the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee (ISSC) within the framework set by the Higher Shari'ah Authority. It covers ISSC responsibility for Shari'ah supervision of all activities, products, contracts, profit allocation between investment account holders and shareholders, internal/external Shari'ah audit oversight, and includes the template for the annual Shari'ah report to shareholders. Binds licensed Islamic financial institutions, their boards and senior management (who remain responsible for actual Shari'ah compliance) and their ISSCs.

Concept node for the AAOIFI Shari'ah Standards as the reference standards used within the CBUAE Shari'ah governance framework for assessing Shari'ah compliance of products, contracts and operations. It is relevant where the ISSC and Higher Shari'ah Authority determine Shari'ah parameters and issue resolutions on institutional activities. Applies indirectly to Islamic financial institutions and Islamic windows through the Shari'ah governance regime rather than as a standalone binding instrument.

The CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation (Circular 8/2020), issued under Article 121 of Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018, establishing the principles-based conduct framework for the protection of Consumers of financial products and services, supported by detailed Standards. It covers disclosure and transparency, institutional oversight, market and business conduct, protection of consumer data and assets, responsible financing, complaints handling, consumer education, financial inclusion, and Shari'ah compliance of financial services. Binds all Licensed Financial Institutions, including those operating wholly or partly in compliance with Islamic Shari'ah, and their boards and senior management.

Article 3 of the Consumer Protection Regulation, setting the institutional oversight requirement: Licensed Financial Institutions must have robust management oversight and responsibility structures across product design, development, promotion, sales and distribution, plus compliance, risk and audit controls, current policies, procedures and training, and qualified staff. It places an explicit duty on the board and senior management to instil a consumer-focused culture and to actively monitor, identify and address misconduct and market conduct risk. Binds all Licensed Financial Institutions and their governing bodies.

Defined-term node for the Key Facts Statement: a concise, plain-language summary of the key features and risks of a financial product or service provided to a Consumer. It is the anchor for pre-contractual disclosure obligations under the Consumer Protection Regulation and related standards, and sits alongside defined terms such as Lender/Financier, Credit Products, Credit Information Agency and Personal Data. Relevant to all Licensed Financial Institutions marketing or selling products to Consumers.

Article 7 of the Consumer Protection Regulation on responsible financing practice, requiring institutions to obtain credible and independent information on a Consumer's financial situation, assess obligations, dependants, capacity and needs before granting credit, and ensure the credit does not cause over-indebtedness or undue financial burden. It also prohibits unreasonable fees and the provision of excessive credit beyond what the Consumer requires. Applies across the whole credit granting process and ongoing management by Licensed Financial Institutions; the adjacent Article 4 sets responsible market conduct duties.

A concept node for the Foundation Internal Ratings Based approach as it appears in the CBUAE capital adequacy standards and guidance. Its practical significance here is negative: internal ratings-based approaches are not accepted for UAE bank capital calculations, so the securitisation hierarchy starts with the external ratings-based approach (SEC-ERBA), then the standardised approach (SEC-SA), with a 1250% risk weight where neither applies. Relevant to all CBUAE-licensed banks computing risk-weighted assets, including ECAI selection, multiple-rating and unsolicited-rating rules.

Node covering the internal adequacy assessment processes under Pillar 2 of the CBUAE capital framework, framed principally around the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) and its liquidity counterpart. It requires each licensed bank to identify and quantify risks not fully captured by Pillar 1 (credit, market, operational), determine additional Pillar 2 capital, and evidence governance, risk appetite, MIS, stress testing and capital planning. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks and feeds the supervisory review and evaluation process, which may result in an adjusted minimum capital ratio.

Node on the CBUAE leverage ratio, a simple, transparent, non-risk-based backstop that caps total exposure relative to capital and complements risk-based capital adequacy requirements. It sets out the exposure measure starting from total on-balance-sheet assets with prescribed adjustments, separate treatment of derivatives and securities financing transaction exposures, credit conversion factors for off-balance-sheet items, and gross treatment of collateral. Applies to banks licensed by the CBUAE.

Concept node for the Central Bank Model Management Standards and Guidance as cross-referenced in the Pillar 2 framework, notably as the prescribed methodology for calculating and reporting interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB). It also anchors model risk treatment in ICAAP: banks must categorise models by risk, estimate potential model-driven losses through validation, benchmarking, sensitivity analysis and stress tests, and assess the quality of their model risk management. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks using models for risk, business or accounting purposes.

A CBUAE guidance note setting supervisory expectations for the Annual Shari'ah Report issued by the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee (ISSC), complementing the federal central bank law and the Shari'ah Governance Standard. It fixes responsibility for preparing the report on the ISSC, requires prior review and approval by the Higher Shari'ah Authority, submission to the HSA within two months of financial year end, and presentation to the general assembly; a report template is annexed. Applies to all Islamic financial institutions, including Islamic windows.

Defined-term node for Islamic Financial Institution (IFI) as used in CBUAE Shari'ah governance instruments, covering full-fledged Islamic institutions and, where indicated, institutions operating Islamic windows. Being an IFI triggers obligations to maintain Shari'ah governance policies, an ISSC with supervisory authority over all activities, products, contracts, policies, financial statements and profit allocation, and internal (and where applicable external) Shari'ah audit, within the parameters set by the Higher Shari'ah Authority. Senior management remains responsible for the institution's actual compliance with Islamic Shari'ah.

Node covering the fair-treatment limb of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation and its supporting Standards (Article 5, section 5.2, read with the responsible-financing duties at 5.1.2). It requires Licensed Financial Institutions to treat all Consumers equitably, honestly and fairly at every stage of the relationship, embedding fair treatment in governance, business conduct and corporate culture, and it bars abusive contract terms, misleading or aggressive sales practices, tied selling and bundling, profiting from Errors, and coercive debt-collection pressure; it also requires monitoring of Borrowers/Financees in difficulty and provision of credit counselling. Binds all Licensed Financial Institutions (including Islamic Financial Institutions) in their dealings with Consumers.

Article 6 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation, covering Consumer Data protection (6.1) and protection of Consumer assets, information and Data against financial crime, misappropriation and misuse (6.2). It builds on the confidentiality duty in Article 120 of Decretal Federal Law No. (14) of 2018, requiring data minimisation, informed and express Consumer consent to collection, use and sharing (internally and with third parties), prevention of misuse, compensation for actual harm from breaches, and sound first-line security management. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions handling Consumer data and assets.
lookup_terms: financial crime first line of defence

data.summary: Article 9 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation on Consumer education and awareness, grounded in Article 121/2 of the Decretal Law requiring the Central Bank and Licensed Financial Institutions to jointly raise public awareness of banking services, financial products and their inherent risks. It places responsibility on institutions to improve Consumers' financial literacy and ability to assess products, as a risk-mitigation element of the consumer protection framework. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions; also frames a shared Central Bank role.

Article 10 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation on financial inclusion (10.1) and gender and racial equality (10.2). It requires Licensed Financial Institutions to design products and services with vulnerable groups and People of Determination in mind, offer basic low-cost products, train staff to identify and assist such Consumers, ensure accessible branches and ATMs, demonstrate compliance with Federal Law No. 29 of 2006, adopt an anti-discrimination code of conduct, and (as good practice) track disaggregated Consumer data on access and usage. Binds all Licensed Financial Institutions.

Reference node for UAE Federal Law No. 29 of 2006 on the rights of People of Determination (persons with special needs), as incorporated by the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation. Within this Regulation it operates as an external compliance benchmark: Licensed Financial Institutions must be able to demonstrate their compliance with that Law in relation to People of Determination, alongside the accessibility, product-design and staff-training duties in Article 10. Relevant to institutions serving Consumers with disabilities.

CBUAE Regulations re Liquidity at Banks (Circular No. 33/2015, issued 27/05/2015), setting the prudential framework for controlling and monitoring bank liquidity in line with Basel Committee recommendations and international practice, supplemented by a later Guidance Manual. It imposes qualitative requirements for a liquidity risk management framework — including prudent management of liquidity risk and ultimate Board responsibility — alongside quantitative requirements, with supervisory review applied proportionately to bank size, scope of operations, interconnectedness and systemic impact. Binds all banks operating in the UAE at all times.

Article 3 of the CBUAE Major Acquisitions Regulation (Circular 02/2020), setting the board's duty to adopt policies and procedures identifying, understanding and mitigating risks inherent in Major Acquisitions, including mandatory board approval and ongoing risk reporting to the board and senior management. It specifies the minimum content of the board's review, covering capital, income, liquidity, financial position and group-structure impacts. Binds the boards of all banks (and banking groups) licensed by the CBUAE; it sits alongside the separate 10% of Total Regulatory Capital cap on holdings in commercial companies and the prior-approval regime in Article 2.

Definition node from the CBUAE Major Acquisitions Regulation: Total Regulatory Capital is the sum of a bank's CET1, Additional Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital, and functions as the denominator for the regulation's thresholds — over 5% for a Major Acquisition, over 1% (but below the Major threshold) for a Notification Acquisition, and the 10% cap on commercial company holdings. The surrounding context also defines Major Acquisition, Notification Acquisition, Purchase Price, Senior Management and Subsidiary, and sets out Article 2's prior written approval requirement and minimum application content. Relevant to any bank calculating whether a transaction triggers approval or notification.

The CBUAE Transfer of Significant Shareholding Regulation (Circular 05/2020), issued under the Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018, Art. 95), sets minimum standards for changes in bank ownership. It requires prior written CBUAE approval for acquiring, increasing or divesting shareholdings at or above 5% of issued ordinary shares and convertible instruments, and for Significant or Controlling Shareholdings and equivalent voting rights, with suspension of voting rights and dividends on excess shareholdings held without approval. It binds banks (including foreign bank branches via parent-level changes), their boards, and any person acquiring or disposing of such interests.

Concept node on the Significant Shareholder under the CBUAE Transfer of Significant Shareholding Regulation, read with Article 8 (duty to report). Banks must immediately notify the CBUAE of any change or proposed change in a Significant or Controlling Shareholder/Shareholding and of material information affecting their suitability, collect required information from such shareholders annually, and look through nominees to beneficial shareholders; fit-and-proper status is a continuing requirement and approval may be revoked. Non-compliant shareholders must divest excess shareholding above 5% and lose related voting rights and dividends.
lookup_terms: duty to report Central Bank shareholding
suitability fit and proper continuing requirement
foreign bank branch parent shareholding change

data.summary: Definition node for Control, Controlling Shareholder and Controlling Shareholding in the CBUAE Transfer of Significant Shareholding Regulation: ownership or control of more than 50% of issued ordinary shares and convertible instruments or of related votes, control over election of a majority of directors or board decisions, or controlling influence over policy, strategy, governance, management or financial affairs as determined by the CBUAE. It also defines Group and treats direct, indirect, sole and acting-in-concert holdings alike. Determines when prior approval, notification and ongoing reporting duties are triggered for banks and shareholders.

Article 2 of the CBUAE Transfer of Significant Shareholding Regulation makes the board responsible for establishing and maintaining an up-to-date shareholder register and written records of all shareholders and their shareholdings, supported by policies and procedures to identify and record Significant and Controlling Shareholders. It is paired here with Article 3's prior written approval requirements for obtaining, increasing or divesting shareholdings at or above 5%, and Article 8's reporting and divestment consequences. Binds bank boards and, indirectly, shareholders seeking to transfer interests.

Provision within a CBUAE bank ownership/shareholding regulation setting the prior-written-approval gateway for acquiring or increasing a Significant or Controlling Shareholding (or equivalent voting rights) in a bank, directly or indirectly. It also deals with breaches: a holding above five percent acquired without approval triggers an immediate approval application, suspension of voting rights and dividends on the excess portion, and a bar on disposal without Central Bank direction, with the Board responsible for enforcing these restrictions. Related articles let the Central Bank deem persons acting in concert to be significant/controlling shareholders and specify the content of the approval application (fit-and-proper questionnaire, direct/indirect and nominee holdings, three years of financial information). Binds shareholders and prospective acquirers of bank shares and the bank's Board.

CBUAE standard setting minimum Shari'ah governance requirements for Islamic Financial Institutions, covering objectives, defined terms (Shari'ah supervision, internal/external Shari'ah audit, compliance with Islamic Shari'ah) and the institutional architecture for ensuring Shari'ah compliance. It applies to all IFIs on both a solo and group-wide basis, including subsidiaries, affiliates and international branches, and must be read together with Higher Shari'ah Authority standards and resolutions. The Central Bank may impose requirements additional to the stated minimums.

Node covering the Internal Shari'ah Control Division or Section required in each IFI: a support function for the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee, resourced in proportion to the institution's size and activities, technically supervised by the ISSC, headed by a person appointed to report to the Board. It must be organisationally separate from business divisions and kept distinct in reporting lines and staffing from the internal Shari'ah audit function, consistent with the three lines of defence. Binds IFIs, their boards and the heads of these functions.

Node on the Internal Shari'ah Audit Division or Section, which performs Shari'ah audit and monitors IFI compliance with Islamic Shari'ah under an annual plan approved by the ISSC in coordination with the audit committee. It sets independence safeguards (promotion, bonus, appraisal and removal decisions escalate to the Board via the audit committee, not to audited management), a prohibition on executive powers over audited activities, qualification and minimum five-year experience requirements for internal Shari'ah auditors, and duties such as maintaining an internal Shari'ah audit manual. The audit committee must assess the function's independence, scope and effectiveness and meet its head at least twice yearly.

Node addressing External Shari'ah Audit: an annual assessment by an external body of the IFI's compliance with Islamic Shari'ah and of the adequacy and effectiveness of its Shari'ah supervision governance systems. It also sets the audit committee's related duties — reviewing the scope, results and adequacy of the external Shari'ah audit, facilitating the external auditor's work, reviewing its reports to confirm senior management has acted on them, and meeting the external Shari'ah auditor at least once per financial year.

Concept node applying the three lines of defence model to Shari'ah governance in IFIs: business lines, the internal Shari'ah control function supporting the ISSC, and the internal Shari'ah audit function, which must remain separate in reporting and human resources, with external Shari'ah audit providing annual independent assessment. It frames the definitions of Shari'ah supervision, internal and external Shari'ah audit, and compliance with Islamic Shari'ah (HSA resolutions plus non-conflicting ISSC resolutions). Binds IFIs and their boards in structuring Shari'ah control and audit functions.
lookup_terms: segregation of Shari'ah control and audit

data.summary: Article 2 of the CBUAE liquidity regulations setting the qualitative (non-ratio) limb of the Liquidity Risk Management Framework that every bank must maintain alongside the quantitative ratios. It allocates ultimate responsibility to the board (including articulating liquidity risk tolerance and having at least one board member with detailed liquidity risk understanding), requires senior management to implement strategies, policies and practices within the approved tolerance, continuous review with regular board reporting, embedding liquidity costs/benefits/risks in product pricing and approval for significant business activities, and sound identification, measurement, monitoring and control processes. Binds all banks, with supervisory review applied proportionately to size, scope of operations, interconnectedness and systemic impact; effective from 1 July 2015.

Concept node capturing how the CBUAE liquidity regulations incorporate Basel Committee (BCBS) standards by reference: qualitative terminology follows the 2008 Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision, while LCR and NSFR definitions follow the January 2013 LCR and October 2014 NSFR Basel III texts. It also covers the Level 1 / Level 2 HQLA classification and run-off rates for cash outflows, which take their definitions and conditions from the Basel III LCR document, with full detail deferred to the Guidance Manual. Relevant to banks determining the substantive content of ratio definitions and to the ELAR definition (eligible liquid assets to total liabilities).
lookup_terms: high quality liquid assets Level 1 Level 2
Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision 2008

data.summary: Concept node for the Guidance Manual that the Central Bank undertakes (under Article 10) to issue on compliance with ELAR, LCR and NSFR, including the definitions and assumptions for LCR/NSFR calculation aligned to Basel III and the detailed HQLA and cash-outflow treatment. Article 7 makes the Manual the source of reporting frequency and scope and requires banks to use its liquidity reporting templates; reports must be based on contractual data without behavioural assumptions, with the Central Bank applying homogeneous assumptions for micro- and macro-prudential analysis. Practically, it means the regulation cannot be read in isolation for calculation or reporting detail.

Node recording the repeal provision (Article 9): Circular No. 30/2012 of 12 July 2012 on liquidity regulations at banks is withdrawn from the effective date of the current liquidity regulations. It sits alongside the commencement and transition timeline — ELAR and the qualitative requirements from 1 July 2015, LCR and NSFR transition from 1 January 2016 for approved banks, with NSFR compliance required from 1 January 2018. Useful for dating obligations and checking which instrument governed a given period.

CBUAE Major Acquisitions Regulation (Circular 02/2020, dated 24 March 2020), issued under the Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018) and addressed to all banks. It establishes a prudential framework governing how banks and banking groups propose and undertake major acquisitions, aiming at bank soundness, financial stability and retail customer protection, and places the onus on the board to demonstrate a comprehensive approach. Listed requirements are minimums — the Central Bank may impose additional requirements — and the regulation defines key terms including Major Acquisition, Notification Acquisition, Purchase Price, Senior Management and Subsidiary.

Defined term in the Major Acquisitions Regulation: an acquisition or investment by a bank in assets, including shares but excluding debt other than convertible debt, whose aggregate amount in a single juridical person exceeds 5% of Total Regulatory Capital, or which the Central Bank deems in advance to be a Major Acquisition. It is the threshold that triggers the regulation's prudential approval and governance obligations, and is distinguished from a Notification Acquisition (above 1% but below the Major Acquisition criteria). Purchase Price is measured gross, and the definition binds all banks subject to the regulation.

Concept node covering the Shari'ah governance architecture for Islamic Financial Institutions: defined terms (internal and external Shari'ah audit, Shari'ah supervision, compliance with Islamic Shari'ah) and the organisational requirements for the internal Shari'ah audit division, including board appointment of a Shari'ah controller and his eligibility criteria. It establishes a hierarchy of authority in which the Higher Shari'ah Authority's resolutions and fatwas prevail over those of an institution's Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee. It binds licensed Islamic financial institutions (and Islamic windows) and their boards, internal audit functions and external Shari'ah auditors.

Original 2009 UAE Cabinet Resolution setting the minimum capital regime for insurance and reinsurance undertakings, issued under the Insurance Authority law (Federal Law No. 6 of 2007). It fixes paid-up capital floors, imposes a national/GCC ownership threshold, and subjects capital increases and reductions to Insurance Authority approval, with a three-year transition for existing companies. Binds insurance companies incorporated in the UAE and licensed foreign insurers operating through a branch or agent, including cooperative/Takaful and reinsurance companies, excluding free-zone companies.

Concept node isolating the substantive capital requirement in Cabinet Resolution No. 42 of 2009: the subscribed and paid-up capital floors for insurers and reinsurers, the ownership condition requiring a majority stake held by UAE/GCC nationals or wholly national-owned juridical persons, and the Authority-approval gateway for increasing or reducing capital. Scope covers all licensed companies except those in free zones. Relevant to licensing, shareholder changes and capital restructuring decisions.

Reference node for the UAE Commercial Companies Law (Federal Law No. 8 of 1984, as amended or replaced), cited as a legal basis and defined term in the insurance minimum capital resolution. It matters here because capital increases and reductions of insurance companies remain subject to general company-law requirements in addition to Insurance Authority approval. Not itself a sectoral instrument; consult for corporate-law overlay on capital actions.

Consolidated version (as of 15/05/2017) of Cabinet Resolution No. 42 of 2009 on insurance company minimum capital, incorporating the amendments made by Cabinet Resolution No. 16 of 2017. It retains the capital-increase/reduction approval regime, the transitional rectification period and the Board's power to issue implementing instructions, while the shareholder-eligibility provision is now framed as a matter for a Board resolution. This is the operative text to cite for the post-2017 position applicable to insurers, Takaful operators and reinsurers.

Amending instrument node: Cabinet Resolution No. 16 of 2017, which amended the 2009 insurance minimum capital regulations and produced the consolidated text effective 15/05/2017. Its visible effect in the consolidated version is on the shareholder/ownership provision, which is delegated to a Board of Directors resolution setting the conditions for natural and juridical persons to hold shares in an insurance company. Use it to establish the date and scope of change when comparing pre- and post-2017 obligations.

data.label: Regulations Regarding Mortgage Loans (VER1)
data.summary: Original (Version 1) text of CBUAE Circular No. 31/2013 setting minimum standards for granting mortgage loans in the UAE, issued under the Central Bank's powers in Union Law No. 10 of 1980. It covers definitions, risk-management and lending-policy requirements, key ratios (including debt burden and loan-to-value), disclosure and transparency, housing programmes, Shari'ah-compliant finance, reporting and supervision, and cancels an earlier notice. It binds banks, finance companies and other financial institutions providing mortgage loans, collectively 'mortgage loan providers', whether lending to nationals, GCC nationals or expatriates.

data.label: Regulations Regarding Mortgage Loans (Consolidated VER2)
data.summary: Consolidated bilingual (Arabic/English) version of CBUAE Circular No. 31/2013 on mortgage loans, containing the same framework as Version 1 in cleaner, readable form: purpose, application, Article 1 definitions (mortgage loan, LTV, property appraisal, mortgage loan providers, tenor) and Article 2 risk-management requirements including a board-approved, standalone mortgage lending policy with limits on property-lending exposure and the overall loan book. It applies to banks, finance companies and other financial institutions offering mortgage loans, sets only a floor, and permits more conservative internal limits. This is the preferred reading copy where the Version 1 scan is degraded.

data.label: Regulations No. 29/2011 (Real-Estate Lending Transparency)
data.summary: Node for a related/predecessor real-estate lending instrument referenced alongside the mortgage loans regulations; the available text is drawn from the Circular 31/2013 consolidated version, principally Article 4 (disclosure and transparency) and the definitions/risk-management provisions. The substantive obligations shown require lenders to give borrowers sufficient, transparent information on costs and risks, to publish fees, charges and interest/profit rates with the calculation method, and to document property, borrower contribution, loan amount, repayment period, instalments, rate, insurance, disbursement and prepayment terms, with fees in a separate schedule annexed to the loan contract. It binds mortgage loan providers dealing with individual borrowers; verify the exact instrument number against the source before citing.

data.label: Regulations Regarding Bank Loans and Other Services to Individual Customers
data.summary: Cross-referenced CBUAE instrument governing bank loans and other services offered to individual customers, invoked by the mortgage loans regulations as the source of the maximum debt burden ratio (stated there as 50 per cent of gross salary and any regular income from a defined and specific source at any time). The mortgage rules direct that this ceiling is a cap, not a default: lenders must still assess the individual borrower's repayment capacity and exposure. Relevant to banks and finance companies lending to retail/individual customers.

data.label: Union Law No. (10) of 1980 concerning Central Bank
data.summary: Enabling statute cited as the legal basis for the mortgage loans regulations: Union Law No. (10) of 1980 concerning the Central Bank, the Monetary System and Organization of Banking, specifically Articles 5, 18, 94 and 96. It confers the CBUAE's rule-making and supervisory powers over banks, finance companies and other financial institutions. Open this node to confirm the source of authority for CBUAE circulars rather than for operative lending requirements.
lookup_terms: monetary system and organization of banking

data.label: Notice No. 3871/2012
data.summary: Earlier CBUAE notice on mortgage/real-estate lending that is expressly withdrawn by Article 10 of the mortgage loans regulations as from the date those regulations take effect (one month after publication in the Official Gazette). It has no continuing force; relevant only for historical or transitional analysis of obligations before Circular 31/2013. Interpretation of the superseding regulations rests with the Central Bank's Legal Development Unit.

An amending instrument of the CBUAE Board of Directors that modifies the Regulations Regarding Mortgage Loans (C 31/2013); it is referenced as one of two amendments folded into the consolidated text dated 8 April 2020. It is not a free-standing regime but changes provisions on mortgage lending, and binds mortgage loan providers (banks, finance companies and other financial institutions offering mortgage loans). Open it to confirm which articles (e.g. risk management, LTV, income verification) were altered and the effective date of the change.

A CBUAE Board of Directors resolution amending the Regulations Regarding Mortgage Loans (C 31/2013) and reflected in the consolidated version as of 8 April 2020, following the earlier amendment by Resolution 96/2019. It operates on the mortgage lending framework rather than creating one, and binds all mortgage loan providers, including banks and finance companies. Consult it to date the current wording and identify which mortgage requirements were revised.

Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 08 of 2011 sets the instructions governing the business of insurance agents: registration in the Agents Register, agency contract requirements, professional indemnity cover, handling of premiums through a dedicated bank account, and a code of conduct and ethics. It applies to all insurance agents in the UAE other than those in free zones (unless free-zone rules provide otherwise), and constrains insurance companies from contracting with unregistered agents. Relevant where questions concern agent licensing, single-principal restriction, non-assignment of the agency, or client-money handling.

The federal statute establishing the Insurance Authority and regulating insurance business in the UAE; it is the enabling law cited as the legal basis for the insurance agents instructions and supplies core defined terms (Company, IA, Law). It binds insurers, intermediaries and related insurance-sector persons operating in the State. Open it for statutory authority, licensing perimeter and definitions rather than for detailed agent conduct rules.

The Insurance Authority Board resolution issuing the Implementing Regulations of Federal Law No. 6 of 2007; it is cited as a legal basis for the 2011 insurance agents instructions and fills out the statutory framework for insurance business in the UAE. It binds licensed insurance companies and related regulated persons. Consult it for the executive-level rules underlying registration, appeals against rejection, and ongoing supervisory requirements.

Cabinet Resolution No. 13 of 2013 prescribes the schedule of fees payable to the Insurance Authority by third party health insurance administrators (licence examination, registration and renewal of companies and branches, data amendments, grievances, official extracts) and sets administrative fines for late renewal or late annotation of register data. It binds TPAs licensed by the IA to administer health insurance claims. Use it for fee amounts, penalty calculation (per month of delay with annual caps) and effective-date questions.
lookup_terms: third party health insurance administrator fees

data.summary: UAE Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 37 of 2017 setting the licensing, registration and operating rules for Points of Sale established by insurance companies in the UAE. It limits permitted Point of Sale functions (issuing motor, health and travel policies, assessing vehicle damage, receiving claim documents), bars payment of compensation, and prescribes the initial-approval documentation and registration in the Authority's register. It binds insurance companies incorporated in the UAE and licensed foreign insurers operating through a branch or insurance agent, including Takaful companies.
lookup_terms: motor health travel insurance policy issuance

data.summary: Definitional and scope node for "Points of Sale" as used in Insurance Authority Board Decision 37/2017: a body established by an insurance company under those instructions, together with the related defined terms (Company, Register, Insurance Policy, Authority). It fixes which functions a Point of Sale may perform, where it may be located, and the prohibition on operating without Authority authorisation and registration. Relevant to insurers determining whether a distribution outlet falls inside the Point of Sale regime.
lookup_terms: permitted insurance lines Point of Sale

data.summary: Insurance Authority Administrative Decision No. 122 of 2018 fixing the minimum qualification conditions for the Designated Officer under the bancassurance instructions (BoD Decision 13/2018). It requires thirty accredited training hours at an insurance company, three specified or Maharati-equivalent training courses with success within two years, submission of course content to the Authority, and enrolment in a continuous training plan on new products. It binds banks and insurance companies appointing Designated Officers for marketing insurance policies through banks.

Node for Insurance Authority Board of Directors Decision No. 13 of 2018, the instructions governing the marketing of insurance policies through banks (bancassurance), which is the parent instrument for the Designated Officer role. The available context reaches it only through Administrative Decision 122/2018, which supplies the Designated Officer's minimum qualification conditions. Relevant to banks distributing insurance and to the insurers whose products they market.

Insurance Authority Board of Directors Resolution No. 10 of 2016 regulating existing licensed composite insurance companies, i.e. those writing both insurance of persons and fund accumulation and property and liability insurance. It mandates complete operational separation of the two insurance types (technical, financial, technological, administrative, legal, systems and staff, except the general manager), separate investment strategies, books and records, and both consolidated and separate financial reporting. It binds composite insurers already licensed in the UAE.
lookup_terms: insurance of persons and fund accumulation
consolidated and separate financial statements insurer

data.summary: Concept node for the separation requirement imposed on existing licensed composite insurers: full segregation between insurance of persons and fund accumulation operations and property and liability operations across procedures, systems, records and personnel, with the general manager as the only shared function. It also covers the class definitions cross-referenced to the Implementing Regulations and the separate investment strategy, bookkeeping and dual (consolidated plus per-type) reporting obligations. Useful when assessing whether a composite insurer's ring-fencing arrangements meet the standard.
lookup_terms: separate books and records insurance type
insurance of persons and fund accumulation classes
Article 4 and 5 Implementing Regulations insurance classes

data.summary: A referenced UAE Cabinet instrument on fees for insurance supervision, control and insurance transactions; it appears here only as a cited authority in the surrounding text, which is Cabinet Resolution No. 13 of 2013 setting licence/registration fees and administrative fines for third party health insurance administrators. The operative fee schedule and delay penalties in the provided context bind TPAs licensed by the Insurance Authority and are collected in the manner set by the Ministry of Finance. Useful only for fee/penalty quantum and the legal basis chain, not for conduct or prudential obligations.

Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 13 of 2018 setting the instructions for bancassurance: insurance and Takaful companies may market policies through banks (including finance companies licensed by the Central Bank) only with prior IA approval, and only for an exhaustive list of product classes. It caps the bank relationship to a marketing channel (no agency, brokerage or consultancy), limits marketing to the bank's own customers, and imposes quarterly/annual reporting of premiums, expenses and claims per bank and per line. Binds insurance companies operating in the State (free-zone companies excluded unless the Law says otherwise), with warnings, suspension or cancellation of approval as sanctions.

Consolidated version (as at 15/09/2019) of IA Board Decision No. 13 of 2018 on marketing insurance policies through banks, reflecting amendments made by IA Board Decision No. 42 of 2019. It covers the approval application file (including the bank–insurer agreement subject to IA approval and a continuing training plan), Designated Officer qualification conditions, IA decision timelines and appeal rights, grounds for cancelling approval, and a six-month rectification period for existing arrangements. Binds insurance and Takaful companies distributing through banks; the Arabic text prevails over this translation.

UAE Federal Law No. 1 of 2006 on electronic transactions and commerce, cited as one of the legal bases for the bancassurance instructions. Its relevance in this context is enabling the use of the Authority's adopted Electronic Means for applications such as temporary or full suspension of marketing, resumption, and notification of agreement termination. It is a referenced enabling statute rather than the substantive source of insurance-distribution obligations.

UAE Federal Law No. 10 of 1980 on the Central Bank, monetary system and organisation of banking, cited in the bancassurance instructions as the statute establishing the Central Bank. It matters here because the defined term "Bank" in those instructions means a bank or finance company licensed by the Central Bank to operate in the State. Referenced as an institutional/definitional anchor; this node is not the source of the marketing conduct rules.
lookup_terms: finance company licensed by Central Bank

data.summary: UAE Federal Law No. 6 of 1985 on banks, financial institutions and Islamic investment companies, listed among the legal bases for IA Board Decision No. 13 of 2018 on marketing insurance policies through banks. It supports the licensing framework for the bank counterparties in bancassurance arrangements, including Islamic institutions. Cited authority only; the enforceable marketing, reporting and penalty provisions sit in the IA instructions themselves.
lookup_terms: banks and financial institutions law UAE

data.summary: Founding UAE Insurance Authority decision issuing the Regulation of Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policies, under which the standard Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Loss and Damage is set. It fixes the mandatory contract terms between insurer and insured — general conditions, total-loss and depreciation-based compensation, salvage/towing and repair-quality obligations on the company, dispute handling over damage value, and an exhaustive list of exclusions (unlicensed drivers, racing, overloading, use outside the declared purpose, intentional traffic offences). Binds insurers writing motor own-damage cover in the UAE and defines the rights of insured vehicle owners.

Amending Insurance Authority Board decision that modifies the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Loss and Damage originally issued under Decision 25/2016; its changes are carried into the consolidated policy text (as at 18/01/2021). Relevant mainly for tracing which policy conditions, definitions (e.g. Rider, Premium, Basic and Ancillary Deductible, Natural Disaster, Insurance Period) and coverage terms were altered and from when. Binds insurers issuing motor own-damage cover and affects insureds' contractual entitlements.

Second amending instrument to the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Loss and Damage (issued under Decision 25/2016), reflected in the consolidated version dated 18/01/2021. Used to establish the current in-force wording and the effective date of later changes to the standard motor own-damage policy. Binds UAE-licensed insurers and shapes policyholder rights under the unified wording.
lookup_terms: motor vehicle loss and damage policy

data.summary: Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 27 of 2020 issuing the Instructions for Licensing Insurance Producers, applying to all Insurance Producers operating in the UAE. It prohibits unlicensed/unregistered producer activity, bars companies from dealing with unlicensed producers, confines the producer role to marketing and lead referral (including via electronic links to the company or agent), restricts nationals/non-nationals by product class, prohibits combining the role with agent or broker activity or serving more than one company, and sets fitness, qualification, training and assessment conditions for licensing and registration.
lookup_terms: insurance agent vs broker vs producer

data.summary: Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 18 of 2020 on the Electronic Insurance Regulations, cited as a legal basis for the Insurance Producer licensing instructions. It governs the conduct of insurance business through electronic channels, websites and smart applications, and is the reference regime for producers whose activity is limited to routing electronic insurance applicants to the company's or agent's website. Binds insurance companies, agents and related professions distributing insurance electronically in the UAE.

Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 3 of 2010 issuing the Instructions on the Code of Conduct and Ethics to be observed by insurance companies operating in the UAE, as amended. It is cross-referenced as the conduct standard that Insurance Producers must follow when advertising, promoting and marketing insurance (electronic or ordinary). Binds insurance companies and, by incorporation, those marketing on their behalf.
lookup_terms: Code of Conduct and Ethics insurance

data.summary: Amending instrument (Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 42 of 2019) that modifies Board Decision No. 13 of 2018 on marketing insurance policies through banks, producing the consolidated bancassurance instructions as of 15/09/2019. The underlying regime conditions insurer–bank distribution arrangements: prior Authority approval of the marketing application and of the insurer–bank agreement, qualification and training conditions for the bank's Designated Officer, continuing training plans, and decision/appeal timelines and approval renewal. It binds licensed insurance companies (including Takaful) using banks as a distribution channel, and indirectly the participating banks and their designated staff.

Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 22 of 2017 setting out how insurers apply the investment (asset distribution and allocation) limits contained in the Financial Regulations, and is read as complementary to those Regulations. It prescribes treatment of breaches and new investments outside the limits, distinguishing cases with and without a shortfall in Minimum Capital Requirement, Solvency Capital Requirement or Minimum Guarantee Fund, and requires portfolio analysis reporting or a detailed corrective plan as applicable. It binds insurance companies incorporated in the UAE and branches/agents of foreign insurers, including Takaful companies.

Referenced instrument: Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 25 of 2014 containing the Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies, the source of the asset distribution and allocation (investment) limits, capital adequacy requirements and the periodic investment reporting obligations applied by Decision No. 22 of 2017. It sets the prudential baseline for conventional insurers operating in the UAE. Relevant where a question turns on the substantive limit, solvency measure or reporting article rather than its application mechanics.

Referenced instrument: Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 26 of 2014 containing the Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies, the Shari'a-compliant counterpart to Decision No. 25 of 2014. It supplies the investment limits, capital and solvency requirements applied to Takaful operators, including through Decision No. 22 of 2017 on applying investment limits. It binds Takaful insurance companies licensed in the UAE.

data.summary: The Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Loss and Damage (own-damage motor cover), setting mandatory standard policy terms: the insurer's compensation obligations, total-loss and depreciation treatment, salvage/recovery and repair-quality duties, and the exclusions for which no compensation is payable (e.g. indirect loss, overloading, unlicensed or improperly licensed drivers, racing, prohibited use). It standardises the contractual bargain between insurer and insured, binding insurers writing motor loss-and-damage cover in the UAE and defining policyholder entitlements.

Consolidated version of the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Loss and Damage (IA-BOD-RES 25/2016), containing the insurer's obligations chapter: repair, cash settlement or replacement on total loss, depreciation on new original parts, optional riders for additional cover, limits on refusing claims for late notification with acceptable excuse, and a prohibition on side agreements (including under fleet policies) that reduce cover or restrict the right to claim. It binds insurers issuing motor loss-and-damage policies and protects insureds and beneficiaries against contractual derogation.

data.summary: UAE Insurance Authority Administrative Decision No. 140 of 2019, issued under the Arabic-language requirement of Federal Law No. 6 of 2007, listing the classes of insurance policies exempt from being written in Arabic (marine and aviation hull, satellites/balloons/spaceships, oil insurance, and policies of an international nature requiring English). It also sets out the electronic product-licensing submission package insurers must file with the Authority for life/funds accumulation and property and liability products, including bilingual policy wordings, specification tables, application and claim forms, actuarial material and reinsurance arrangements. Binding on insurance companies operating in the State; notably it requires a certificate from the company's AML/CFT compliance officer assessing product-related money laundering risks and the internal controls managing them, plus an undertaking of legal compliance.

data.summary: Insurance Authority Board of Directors' Decision No. 14 of 2018 applying the financial solvency requirements of Chapter Two of the Financial Regulations to branches of foreign insurance companies operating in the UAE, including Takaful and reinsurance branches. It prescribes how a branch calculates and discloses the parent company's net assets available to cover UAE risk exposures, with mandatory deductions (parent capital, additional paid-up capital, intangibles, reserves earmarked elsewhere, capital or guarantees pledged for solvency in other jurisdictions, and other unallocated obligations). It also requires annual filing of the parent's home-country solvency margin calculations, audited financial statements and supervisory capital adequacy documents, and a deficit report analysing the impact of any parent solvency shortfall on the branch.

data.summary: Defined-term node for the "Financial Regulations", meaning Insurance Authority Board Decisions No. 25 of 2014 (Financial Regulations for Insurance Companies) and No. 26 of 2014 (Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies), as applicable. It is the baseline prudential framework whose Chapter Two solvency requirements Decision 14 of 2018 extends to branches of foreign insurers, and it sits alongside the related definitions of Branch of the foreign company, Parent company and Home country. Relevant to insurers, Takaful operators, reinsurers and their UAE branches.

Insurance Authority Board of Directors' Decision No. 12 of 2018, the regulation on licensing and registration of insurance consultants and the organisation of their operations, replacing the earlier 1985 ministerial framework. It prohibits practising insurance consultancy in the State without an IA licence and registration in the Register, bars insurance companies from dealing with unlicensed consultants, and sets the consultant's professional duties, permitted legal forms and fit-and-proper, qualification and experience conditions. Binds natural persons, sole proprietorships and corporate consultants, and indirectly insurance companies that engage them.

data.summary: Defined-term node for "Consultant" (Insurance Consultant) under BoD Decision 12 of 2018: a natural or corporate person who studies clients' insurance requirements, advises on suitable coverage, assists with claims preparation and is paid fees by the client (as distinct from commission-based intermediaries). The node also carries the licensing conditions and scope rules: consultants may be natural persons, sole proprietorships or companies, may be licensed for all or specific classes, and may not combine consultancy with any other insurance-associated profession. Sets the eligibility gate (capacity, good repute, no disqualifying convictions or disciplinary cancellations, and minimum academic and professional experience thresholds differing for Nationals and non-Nationals).

Reference node for Ministerial Resolution No. 23 of 1985 on the Regulation of Insurance Consultancy and its amendments, cited in the recitals of BoD Decision 12 of 2018 as part of the legal basis for the current insurance consultant regime. Useful only for tracing the historical/predecessor framework for consultancy licensing; the operative requirements are those in the 2018 regulation.

Insurance Authority (now CBUAE) Board of Directors Decision No. 23 of 2019 setting the regulatory framework for reinsurance operations, including defined terms (cession, retrocession, retention, facultative, treaty and facultative-obligatory reinsurance) and the conditions under which a reinsurance company may write both persons/fund-accumulation and property/liability reinsurance, or add Takaful reinsurance. It binds reinsurance companies established in the State, branches of foreign reinsurers, and licensed insurers in respect of ceded and accepted reinsurance business, as well as pools and underwriting syndicates; P&I Clubs are addressed separately. Conditions include authorisation in the Articles of Association, Shariah compliance for Takaful reinsurance, and full technical and financial separation between conventional and Takaful reinsurance books.

Concept node for "reinsurance" as defined and regulated under the 2019 reinsurance decision, covering the definitional vocabulary of the risk-transfer chain: cession, retrocession, retention, reinsurance ceded versus accepted by an insurance company, and the facultative, treaty and facultative-obligatory placement types. It also carries the permission for reinsurers to combine persons/fund-accumulation and property/liability lines, and for Takaful reinsurers to write family and general Takaful reinsurance, subject to constitutional-document and separation conditions. Relevant to insurers, reinsurers and Takaful reinsurers licensed or registered in the State.

Cross-reference node for the Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 4 of 2010 (Takaful Insurance Regulations) as applied through the reinsurance decision. It supplies the defined terms for Takaful and Takaful reinsurance business and is made applicable to reinsurers to the extent consistent with Takaful reinsurance, alongside Shariah compliance and full technical and financial separation between conventional and Takaful reinsurance operations. Binds Takaful insurance and Takaful reinsurance companies and conventional reinsurers that add a Takaful reinsurance window.

Insurance Authority Board of Directors Decision No. 25 of 2016 issuing the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policies — the mandatory standard forms for third party liability cover and for loss and damage cover, which insurers may not amend except in favour of the insured or beneficiary. It defines key terms (including Motor Vehicle Driver), obliges insurers to issue third party liability cover for licensed vehicles on request, restricts refusal to insure or renew loss-and-damage cover, and requires compliance with the Orange Card treaty for cross-border Arab cover. Binds all insurance companies, including Takaful insurers subject to Takaful terminology.

The unified standard-form motor third party liability policy: the compulsory cover protecting injured third parties, setting the scope of bodily injury and property damage cover, the treatment of passengers and excluded persons (insured, driver, certain employees), judicially awarded amounts including third-party legal costs but excluding fines, and the AED caps for death/disability per injured person and for property damage per accident. It also fixes repair obligations toward the injured third party, including agency repair in the vehicle's first year, parts quality and depreciation rules. Binds insurers writing compulsory motor cover in the State and determines third-party claimants' entitlements.

The unified standard-form motor loss and damage (own damage) policy, covering the insurer's obligations to the insured and the circumstances in which the insurer has recourse against the driver or insured — including driving under the influence, intentional causation of the accident, uncovered trailers, off-road use without additional cover, and theft (recourse against the thief). It also governs policy termination: neither party may cancel while the vehicle licence is valid, with limited exceptions (licence cancellation, replacement policy, transfer of title) and pro-rata premium refund under the short rate schedule where no claims are paid or outstanding. Binds insurers issuing own-damage motor cover and defines insured and driver exposure.

Node for the UAE Ministerial Resolution No. 54 of 1987 on Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policies, the predecessor instrument for standard-form motor cover. It is expressly repealed by the Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 25 of 2016 (together with any contrary decisions), so it is relevant mainly for legacy policies, historical comparison and transitional questions. It bound insurance companies underwriting motor business in the State; the surrounding context here concerns insurer obligations on repair, original parts and depreciation for injured third parties.

Node for the Insurance Authority Board of Directors' Decision No. 3 of 2010 on the Code of Conduct and Ethics for insurance companies operating in the State, as amended. It is incorporated by reference into the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policies Regulation, which requires insurers to observe it alongside the insurance principles of utmost good faith, disclosure and transparency when issuing policies and dealing with customers. It binds licensed insurance companies (including branches of foreign insurers and Takaful companies) in their market conduct toward applicants, insured persons and beneficiaries.

data.summary: Consolidated version (as of 18/01/2021) of Insurance Authority Board of Directors' Decision No. 25 of 2016 regulating the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policies, incorporating amendments made by Decisions 42/2017 and 26/2020. It sets the mandatory framework for issuing third party liability and loss-and-damage motor cover: duty to issue TPL cover on request, limits on refusal or discrimination in loss-and-damage cover, conduct and disclosure duties, claims handling timelines (written acknowledgement, missing-document notice, settlement within fifteen days, reasoned rejection), total loss and market value compensation, and tariff compliance. It binds insurance companies licensed to write motor business in the State and repeals Ministerial Resolution 54/1987.
lookup_terms: Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policies Regulation

data.summary: Node for the standard-form Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Third Party Liability issued under the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policies Regulation (version 1). It sets the mandatory policy wording: insurer obligations on repair and parts replacement, depreciation treatment, grounds for insurer recourse against the insured or driver (including intentional accidents, prohibited driving, undeclared trailers, off-road use, theft), termination and premium refund rules, and general conditions. It governs the contractual relationship between the insurer, the insured/driver and injured third parties for motor vehicles licensed in the State.
lookup_terms: third party liability motor policy wording

data.summary: Node for UAE Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 on the Establishment of the Insurance Authority and the Organization of its Operations, as amended, the enabling statute for insurance supervision in the State (supervisory functions later transferred to the CBUAE). It is the legal basis relied on for subordinate instruments such as the Executive Regulation (Decision 2/2009), the AML/CTF procedures for insurance activities (Decision 13/2015 and Administrative Decision 79/2015) and the Points of Sale licensing instructions (Decision 37/2017). It binds insurance companies, branches of foreign insurers, Takaful operators and related insurance intermediaries operating in the State.

Node for the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Third Party Liability as annexed to IA-BOD-RES 25/2016 (later version). It fixes the compulsory cover terms and monetary limits: AED 200,000 per deceased person for a spouse, parent or child with disability compensation scaled to the disability percentage, payment of all treatment expenses and a letter of commitment to treatment providers, judicially awarded amounts and costs excluding fines, and AED 2,000,000 per accident for property damage. It also sets insurer duties on accident occurrence — repair to pre-accident condition, market value payment where damage exceeds 50% of market value, replacement vehicle or cash settlement at the injured party's option, and original-parts/depreciation rules. It binds insurers writing compulsory motor TPL in the State vis-à-vis insureds and injured third parties.
lookup_terms: Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Third Party Liability

data.summary: An inspection/verification checklist node describing the role, appointment and supervision of the AML/CTF Compliance Officer in UAE insurance companies and insurance-related professions. It covers evidence of appointment notified to the Insurance Authority, qualifications and ongoing training, suspicious transaction handling and freezing, exclusive reporting of STRs/SARs to the UAE FIU via goAML, tipping-off prohibitions, biannual reporting to senior management and the Authority, and independence of internal control. It binds licensed insurance companies and related professionals and their compliance function, and informs internal/external auditors reviewing them.

A concept node consolidating KYC, customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence obligations for UAE insurance companies and insurance-related professions, referenced to Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 and Cabinet Resolution No. 10 of 2019. It covers identification and verification for natural persons, legal persons and NGOs, third-party/agent transactions, beneficial owner and life/Family Takaful beneficiary identification, PEP screening with senior management approval and source of wealth checks, and record retention. It binds companies establishing or maintaining business relationships and is used as an audit/inspection benchmark.

Sets out the self-assessment and risk-assessment reporting framework for UAE insurance companies and insurance-related professions, including the governance self-assessment form, the annual governance report, and the periodic risk and compliance self-assessment covering insurance, credit, market, operational, regulatory, related-party, financial crime, fraud and cyber risks. It also describes the AML risk-based approach: assessing ML/TF risk by customer type, products/services and technology, applying mitigation procedures, and classifying business relationship risk across at least four risk factors, plus minimum content of AML policies and procedures. Binds insurance companies and insurance-related professionals reporting to the Authority.

data.summary: Specifies the internal audit, risk management and AML/CTF reporting forms that UAE insurance companies and insurance-related professionals must submit to the Authority alongside annual financial statements. It prescribes mandatory internal audit report content (executive summary, scope, methodology, findings, recommendations, challenges), the minimum internal controls to be reviewed (AML policies, risk-based approach, CDD/EDD/ongoing DD, STRs, record keeping, training), and the external auditor's report on AML control effectiveness. It binds internal audit staff, compliance functions and external auditors of licensed insurers and related professions.

Insurance Authority Board of Directors' Decision No. (49) of 2019 issuing instructions for life insurance and Family Takaful insurance in the UAE, including its recitals and defined terms (State, Company, Insurance Agent, Insurance Broker, Financial Regulations, etc.). It sits within a framework referencing the Insurance Law, AML/CTF Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 and terrorism-lists resolutions, and prior IA decisions on conduct, Takaful, agents, brokers, actuaries and bancassurance. It binds insurance companies (including Takaful), distribution channels and insurance-related professions licensed in the State.

data.summary: The commission-control provisions of IA Decision No. (49) of 2019, setting scope of application and caps on commissions payable to distribution channels for life and Family Takaful products. It fixes maximum commissions for pure protection and savings products (including single and ad-hoc premium), limits first-year indemnity commission to 50% with the remainder spread over the premium payment term, and imposes a minimum five-year commission claw-back; commission limits apply across all distribution channels as if there were only one. Binds companies, distribution channels and insurance-related professions for policies concluded after entry into force.

Node covering the third party liability limits and insurer obligations under the UAE Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Third Party Liability (IA-BOD-RES 25/2016). It fixes compensation ceilings (notably AED 200,000 per deceased/disabled person for specified family members and certain drivers, and AED 2,000,000 per accident for property damage), obliges the insurer to meet judicially awarded amounts excluding fines, and to settle medical treatment costs directly with providers including via a letter of commitment. It binds insurance companies issuing compulsory motor cover in the UAE and confers direct claim rights on injured third parties.

Node containing the annexed schedules to the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy Against Third Party Liability, setting depreciation percentages applied to replaced parts for private vehicles and for taxis, public transport and rental vehicles, the short-rate table of recoverable premium on early cancellation, and the list of safety-critical parts replaced new with no depreciation deduction. These schedules form an integral part of the policy contract and bind insurers when settling repair and refund claims.

data.summary: Node on the insurer's post-accident repair and settlement duties under the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy, including restoring the vehicle to pre-accident condition, paying market value where damage exceeds 50% of market value, replacing a total-loss vehicle or paying cash at the claimant's request, and using agency repair shops. It also covers the rule that parts of vehicles under one year old are replaced new without depreciation, and the framework for valuation/adjustment where damage assessment is disputed. Binds insurance companies settling motor claims in the UAE.

data.summary: Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 19 of 2020 adopting the Guidance Manual (and attached forms) for insurance companies and insurance-related professions on submitting data, information and supervisory reports. It applies to UAE-established insurers, branches and agents of foreign insurers, and related professions, requiring submission within periods set by the Director General; the manual and forms are an integral part of the decision. Its recitals tie the reporting framework to the federal AML/CTF decree-law and its executive regulations and to the terrorist-lists/UN sanctions regulations.

The Guide to Regulatory Information, Data and Reports issued under the Insurance Authority framework, setting out what insurers and insurance-related professions must keep updated in the Authority's registers and electronic systems and what periodic reports they must file. It covers updating company, board, principal officer and staff/Emiratisation data (some changes requiring prior Authority approval), and mandates compliance officer reports, internal audit and external auditor reports on AML/CTF internal controls, plus biannual and annual AML/CTF self-assessment filings by set deadlines. Binds licensed insurance companies and related professions.

data.summary: The AML/CFT component of the reporting guide, including the internal audit report form and the verification checklist used to test an insurer's AML/CFT systems and controls. It addresses independence of the internal control unit, group-wide application of UAE AML standards to foreign branches (with notification to the Authority where host-country rules are weaker or compliance is impossible), CDD/EDD and ongoing monitoring, record keeping, training, compliance officer appointment and notification, tipping-off prohibitions, and STR/SAR filing exclusively to the UAE FIU via goAML with freezing of the relevant transactions. Binds insurance companies and related professions and their compliance and audit functions.

data.summary: Concept node on the mandated role of the Actuary under the UAE life insurance and family takaful instructions (IA/CBUAE Decision No. 49 of 2019). It fixes the Actuary as the certifying party for the Protection Benefit Ratio calculation in product certification, as the person responsible for ensuring each savings product remains profitable across the policy term without front-loading cost onto the policyholder, for equitably allocating surrender charges, and for setting wakala fee levels on long-term products by reference to expense analysis and policyholder reasonable expectations. It binds licensed life/family takaful companies through their appointed actuary, and has consequences for product approval and pricing decisions.

Defined term and substantive rule: the Free Look Period is the window during which a life/family takaful policy may be cancelled or surrendered against refund of premium paid. The instructions set a minimum of 30 calendar days running from the earliest of policy issuance, commencement of cover, or client signature, bar the selling distribution channel from demanding an explanation for cancellation, permit only non-selling staff to seek reasons (pressure being a conduct breach), and require a policy for full premium refund on surrender within the period. Binds insurers and their distribution channels.

Defined metric used to test how much genuine protection a savings product delivers, calculated as the present value of protection benefit payouts divided by the present value of premiums over the policy term, and certified by the Actuary. Where the ratio falls below 10% for any age, gender, smoker status, premium payment term or policy term, the product may only be marketed with sufficient client warnings, including a bold red disclosure that protection benefit is limited or absent, signed by the client directly beneath it. Binds companies marketing savings products and their distribution channels.

Concept node on how the commission and cost rules apply across Distribution Channels (agents, brokers, banks) selling life and family takaful products. Commission caps and claw-back apply as if a single channel exists even where several channels are involved or the channel changes mid-term, costs of each channel must be allocated to clients within that channel, and separate treatment is set for credit life products, initial access fees and net-of-commission quoting. Binds insurers and every distribution channel in the sale chain.

Consolidated version (as of 20/03/2020) of Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 49 of 2019 issuing the Instructions for Life Insurance and Family Takaful Insurance, as amended by IA Board Resolution No. 15 of 2020; functions now sit with CBUAE. It governs product design, illustrations and disclosure, free look, commissions and claw-back, surrender values, wakala/mudaraba fees and actuarial certification for life and family takaful business, and contains the definitions chapter (Annualized Premium, Ad-hoc Premium, Actuarial Funding, Charges, Insurance Agent, Insurance Broker). Binds licensed life/takaful companies, agents, brokers and banks distributing these products; its preamble also invokes the federal AML/CTF decree and the terrorism-lists/UNSCR regime as part of its legal basis.

data.summary: Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 6 of 2010 setting the regulatory framework for Surveyors and Loss Adjusters in the UAE: definition of the activity (investigating causes of damage, assessing coverage, determining payable compensation), the mandatory Register maintained by the Authority, personal and non-transferable registration, registration requirements and grounds for cancellation. It binds natural and juridical persons practising surveying and loss adjustment, and also constrains insurance companies, which may not engage unregistered surveyors except in defined special-expertise cases notified to the Director General.

Provisions from the UAE regulation on Surveyors and Loss Adjusters covering the scope of licensable surveying/loss-adjustment work, the special Register maintained at the Insurance Authority, conditions and cancellation of registration (including that registration is personal and non-transferable), and ongoing obligations on books, records, annual audited submissions and supervisory audits. It also sets out the Director General's power to impose disciplinary sanctions for breaches of the Law or the Regulations. It binds natural and corporate surveyors and loss adjusters operating in the UAE, and is administered by the Insurance Authority/Director General (functions now under CBUAE).

Sets the minimum mandatory content of the settlement (loss adjustment) report prepared by a Surveyor and Loss Adjuster, including identification of insured/beneficiary, the requesting party, policy terms, causes and quantification of damage, use of outsourced specialists, and the technical opinion on coverage and payable compensation. Adjacent provisions impose record-keeping duties and general conduct obligations (acting within registration classification, integrity and transparency, informing affected parties, assessing insurer liability under the policy). Binds registered surveyors and loss adjusters when handling claims for insurers and claimants.
