data.summary: CBUAE Standard setting minimum regulatory and supervisory requirements for conventional financial institutions that house an Islamic Window, aimed at sound Shari'ah governance, financial stability and consumer protection. It covers scope (solo and group-wide, including subsidiaries, affiliates and international branches), Islamic Window organisation and the Head of Islamic Window (CBUAE approval and reporting lines), asset-liability segregation, separate liquidity reporting, treatment of non-Shari'ah-compliant income, separate branding, and separate regulatory reporting. It binds all Institutions housing an Islamic Window and must be read with HSA standards and resolutions.

Concept node for the Islamic Window itself: the dedicated channel through which all Shari'ah-compliant activities and businesses of a conventional institution must be offered. Requirements include appointing a dedicated Head of Islamic Window approved by CBUAE, reporting lines to the CEO/Executive Management Committee, prior notification of the organisational structure, and separate liquidity metrics (LCR/NSFR/ELAR) with a Shari'ah-compliant HQLA stock against 30-day net outflows plus documentation retention. Binds institutions housing an Islamic Window and their senior management.

data.summary: Requires an institution housing an Islamic Window to establish an Asset and Liability Management framework for Shari'ah-compliant assets and liabilities, including ring-fencing and demonstrable segregation from the institution's conventional book (separate product codes mapped to specific General Ledger accounts, with alternative methods only on CBUAE approval). Related provisions govern managing surpluses/deficits in a Shari'ah-compliant way, ISSC and CBUAE approval of the internal funding mechanism, treatment of non-Shari'ah-compliant income, a prohibition on converting or transferring Shari'ah-compliant assets to the conventional side, and separate branding of Islamic products.

data.summary: Reference node for the UAE federal AML/CFT decree-law on countering money laundering, terrorist financing and financing of illegal organisations, cited here as legal basis for an Insurance Authority decision on supervisory data, information and reporting by insurance companies and related professions. The surrounding context also cites the Cabinet resolutions containing the executive regulations and the terrorist-lists/UN sanctions implementation regime. It binds financial institutions and DNFBPs generally; in this instrument it anchors obligations on insurers, branches of foreign insurers, insurance agents and related professions operating in the State.

Referenced instrument: the Executive Regulations implementing the UAE federal AML/CTF decree-law, setting out the operative CDD, KYC, enhanced due diligence, beneficial ownership and record-keeping obligations. In this context it is invoked as the source standard that insurance/Takaful companies and their compliance officers must satisfy, including PEP identification, senior management approval, source of wealth enquiry and identification of life/Family Takaful policy beneficiaries. It binds financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses subject to the federal AML regime, with sector supervisors verifying compliance.

Referenced instrument: the UAE regulation on terrorism lists and domestic implementation of UN Security Council resolutions concerning terrorism, terrorist financing and proliferation financing. It is cited as a legal basis for sector instructions (here, life insurance and Family Takaful), meaning listed-person screening and freezing duties sit alongside the AML/CTF due diligence regime. It binds entities subject to targeted financial sanctions obligations under UAE law and their supervisors.

Referenced primary statute: the UAE Central Bank Law governing the Central Bank and the organisation of financial institutions and activities. It is the enabling authority under which CBUAE issues regulations and standards (e.g. the Islamic Window standard) and contains the confidentiality provision relied on for defining confidential information. It binds licensed financial institutions and frames the Central Bank's supervisory and rule-making powers.

data.summary: CBUAE Standards supplementing the 2014 Regulations on licensing and monitoring of Exchange Business, setting baseline requirements across licensing and continuing obligations, management and governance, risk management and security, AML compliance, and customer protection. Compliance is continuous, with non-compliance charges applied per the appendix schedule and ultimate responsibility placed on the board (or owner/partners) for adequate policies, systems and staffing. It binds all Exchange Houses (Licensed Persons) operating in the UAE, including new entrants.
lookup_terms: Regulations regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business

data.summary: Chapter of the Exchange Business Standards defining the permitted scope of an exchange licence and the activities a Licensed Person may carry out — foreign currency exchange, remittance operations and wage payment via WPS — and confirming that Exchange Business requires written licensing by the Governor or a delegate. It makes operating beyond licence scope a serious supervisory matter subject to non-compliance charges. It binds every Licensed Person conducting Exchange Business in the UAE.

Chapter of the Exchange Business Standards addressing permitted legal forms, licence categories (A, B and C, distinguished by permitted activities) and the related minimum paid-up capital and bank guarantee to be maintained in favour of the Central Bank, calculated by licence category, legal form and remittance volumes. The supplied extract also surfaces onboarding CDD/EDD requirements for legal persons and legal arrangements — beneficial owner identification, authorised signatories and representatives, expected activity and sanctions screening — so check which chapter the operative text sits in. It binds Licensed Persons and new licence applicants.

CDD for legal persons and legal arrangements

data.summary: Chapter 15 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business sets the minimum business continuity management obligations for Licensed Persons (exchange houses), requiring identification and impact assessment of disruption risks and implementation of a Business Continuity Plan. It prescribes the mandatory content of the BCP, including crisis assessment, protection of the entity and staff, minimising suspension of operations, sensitive-data storage and recovery, and notification of the Central Bank and correspondents. It binds all licensed exchange businesses as a continuing operational-resilience requirement.

Chapter 16 is the AML/CFT compliance core of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business, setting minimum requirements for the AML/CFT Program, enterprise-wide ML/FT risk assessment, written policies and procedures, and their approval, annual review, distribution and group-wide application to majority-held branches, subsidiaries and affiliates. It also governs appointment, seniority, independence, resourcing, qualifications and duties of the Compliance Officer, including transaction monitoring, STR/SAR filing with the FIU, training, board reporting, record retention, gap analysis and bi-annual compliance reporting. It binds Licensed Persons carrying on exchange business, with some requirements scaled by licence category.

The Regulations regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business (issued January 2014, as amended by Notice No. 269/2016) are the primary CBUAE instrument defining the scope of Exchange Business and the licensing framework that the Standards elaborate. They establish that exchange business may only be carried out under a written licence from the Governor, define permitted activities (foreign currency exchange, remittances, wage payments), and underpin the Central Bank's enforcement against activity outside licence scope. They bind all Licensed Persons and applicants for exchange business licences in the UAE.
lookup_terms: Regulations regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business 2014

data.summary: Federal Decree Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organisations is the UAE's primary AML/CFT statute, cited as the legal basis with which a Licensed Person's AML/CFT Program must align, together with its amendment by Federal Decree Law No. 26 of 2021. Within this node's context it functions as the governing law referenced by the Standards for Exchange Business rather than as text reproduced in them. It binds financial institutions and DNFBPs in the UAE, including licensed exchange houses supervised by the CBUAE.

money laundering and terrorist financing law

data.summary: Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019 is the Implementing Regulation of the UAE AML-CFT Law, referenced as the detailed rulebook with which exchange houses' AML/CFT policies, procedures, CDD, monitoring, reporting and record-keeping must comply. In this node it appears as the governing implementing instrument underpinning the CBUAE Standards' AML/CFT chapter rather than as reproduced text. It binds supervised financial institutions and DNFBPs, including Licensed Persons carrying on exchange business.

Category A License is a defined CBUAE licence class under the Standards for Exchange Business, permitting the Licensed Person to conduct foreign currency exchange only (no remittances or WPS wage payments). The category drives downstream requirements, including minimum paid-up capital and bank guarantee calculations and the minimum experience threshold for the Compliance Officer. It is relevant to applicants and existing Licensed Persons assessing permitted activity scope and scaled compliance obligations.

Chapter 9 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business sets the conditions under which a Licensed Person may have a third party perform a function, in whole or in part, on its behalf. It permits outsourcing generally but prohibits it outright for the AML compliance function (except document retention, with certain specific AML tasks allowed only after a Letter of No Objection from the Banking Supervision Department) and for the Licensed Person's Permitted Activities such as currency exchange and money transfer execution. Accountability for outsourced functions stays with the Licensed Person and its Board (or Owner/Partners), which must continue to meet all regulatory obligations and maintain internal ownership of the arrangement.

Chapter 10 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business requires each Licensed Person to operate a risk management framework covering identification, measurement, recording, mitigation and monitoring of business risks. Ultimate responsibility rests with the Board (or Owner/Partners), which must approve a Risk Management Policy reviewed at least annually, and a designated Risk Officer must hold overall responsibility, with role combination allowed only subject to conditions cross-referenced to the audit, AML and compliance chapters. It also mandates maintaining a risk register logging risk analysis results, mitigating measures and risk ownership.

Chapter 11 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business sets minimum requirements for an Anti-Fraud Framework that every Licensed Person must implement to prevent, detect, investigate and respond to fraud incidents. It classifies fraud as internal (by employees) or external (by outside parties) and gives a non-exhaustive list of conduct treated as fraud, including misappropriation, misrepresentation of financial and non-financial statements, corruption (bribery, illegal gratuities) and misconduct such as breaches of internal policy or of applicable laws, regulations, notices and the Standards.

Chapter 12 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business obliges each Licensed Person to maintain procedures, equipment and training to detect counterfeit currency and to report incidents. Procedures must be approved by the Manager in Charge and reviewed annually; every licensed premises needs counterfeit detection machines programmed for at least five major currencies including the local currency, plus UV lamps and regular software updates, with counterfeit-detection training twice in an employee's first year and annually thereafter. Reporting duties run to the police of the relevant Emirate, to the FID as a fraud case via the STR system, and to the Banking Supervision Department on the Counterfeit Incident Reporting (CIR) Form — immediately for all local currency cases regardless of value, and for foreign currency cases at or above AED 36,000 per person (single or multiple transactions); a counterfeit register must be kept and reviewed annually.

Chapter 13 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business is the general (physical/premises) security chapter of the Risk Management and Security Standards part, addressing the baseline protective measures a Licensed Person must maintain. The supplied extract contains only the table of contents and unrelated Chapter 2 material on license categories, legal forms, capital and bank guarantees, so the chapter's operative requirements are not reproduced here. Open the source document for the actual Chapter 13 provisions before relying on it.

Chapter 14 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business sets minimum information security measures for Licensed Persons, framed as illustrative rather than exhaustive, with additional controls expected in line with business size and complexity and the findings of penetration tests and external IT audits. It mandates independent corporate email systems (public webmail is prohibited), a dedicated CBUAE-facing email address notified in writing to the Banking Supervision Department by an authorized signatory — the Central Bank will correspond only through it — and a ban on employees using office systems for personal email, social media or non-business sites. It also requires an Information Security Policy governing the protection of customer information and transaction data.

Chapter 3 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business sets out the licensing requirements and application process for parties seeking authorisation to conduct Exchange Business in the UAE, including the content of a new licence application (e.g. details of the proposed legal form, cross-referenced from the capital/legal form chapter). It sits within Part A (Licensing and Continuing Obligations Standards) and operates together with the three licence categories (A, B, C) that delimit permitted activities: foreign currency exchange, remittance operations and wage payment via WPS. It binds applicants for, and holders of, a CBUAE Exchange Business licence (Licensed Persons).

Chapter 4 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business sets the ongoing conditions a Licensed Person must satisfy after authorisation, as the counterpart to the initial licensing standards in Chapter 3. It forms part of Part A of the Standards and underpins the supervisory regime applied through Central Bank examinations and the reporting forms listed in the appendices. It binds all holders of a CBUAE Exchange Business licence across Category A, B and C activities.

Chapter 5 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business addresses Central Bank examinations of Licensed Persons — the supervisory inspection process through which compliance with the Standards is verified. It connects to obligations elsewhere in the Standards to keep files and records available or accessible at the Head Office for examiners, and to the supervisory powers and non-compliance charges set out in the appendices. It binds Licensed Persons conducting Exchange Business in the UAE.

Chapter 6 sets management and corporate governance standards for Licensed Persons conducting Exchange Business, covering how powers and responsibilities are distributed within the management structure. It includes concrete requirements on the Head Office (must be in the UAE, staffed by the Manager in Charge and functional heads, not in a free zone or access-restricted location, records available or accessible for examination, relocation only with a Letter of No Objection from the Banking Supervision Department) and on opening a separate Management Office subject to a Letter of No Objection. It binds Licensed Persons, their Boards of Directors (or Owners/Partners where no Board exists) and senior management.
lookup_terms: Letter of No Objection Banking Supervision Department

data.summary: Chapter 7 sets standards on accounts and audit for Licensed Persons, including the internal audit function: adherence to internal audit professional standards and ethics, breadth of audit coverage (all business activities, core and non-core functions, branches, Head Office and Management Office, reconciliation and unreconciled items, unclaimed funds, liquidity, capital adequacy, plus AML and regulatory compliance), access to staff, data and records, and the Annual Internal Audit Plan approved by the Board (or Owner/Partners). It also requires timely remediation of audit findings and annual review of the Internal Audit Charter and Plan by the Audit Committee with a summary to the Board. It binds Licensed Persons, their Boards/Owners, Audit Committees and internal auditors.

Chapter 8 sets minimum human resources standards for Licensed Persons, requiring a Board-approved (or Owner/Partner-approved) Human Resource Policy covering recruitment and Know Your Employee (KYE), induction and training, job descriptions and KPIs, segregation of duties, staff rotation, working hours and overtime, leave, performance evaluation, employee rights and responsibilities and the disciplinary process, consistent with UAE law and reviewed periodically. It prescribes a minimum KYE process including CV screening, verification of academic qualifications, testing and interview, and employment history verification with previous employers. It binds Licensed Persons and interacts with function-combination limits referenced in the audit and AML/CFT chapters.

Defines the Manager in Charge role for a Licensed Person under the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business: the senior individual accountable for the effective management of all the firm's activities. It sets prior-approval (no-objection) and fit-and-proper conditions for appointment, minimum qualification and experience thresholds by licence category, full-time/exclusivity and UAE-residency requirements, and notification plus replacement timelines when the post falls vacant. It binds the Licensed Person (and its board or owners/partners) rather than the individual directly.

Covers the Compliance Officer function of a Licensed Person carrying on exchange business, principally as the head of the AML/CFT compliance function. It addresses prior CBUAE no-objection for appointment, consequences of rejection, notification of commencement and resignation to both the Banking Supervision and AML/CFT Supervision Departments, replacement deadlines, and independence/reporting lines to the board or owners. Obligations fall on the Licensed Person, with the officer's authority protected from interference by management.

Establishes the mandatory Alternate Compliance Officer role supporting the AML/CFT compliance function of a Licensed Person and ensuring continuity when the Compliance Officer is absent or the post is vacant. It sets employment, residency, reporting-line and independence conditions, limits on combining the role with other functions depending on licence category, prior no-objection for appointment, and notification and replacement timelines. Duties bind the Licensed Person; CBUAE retains removal powers.

Sets out the internal audit function for a Licensed Person: scope covering all business activities, branches, core and non-core functions, reconciliation, liquidity and capital adequacy alongside AML and regulatory compliance. It requires adherence to professional auditing standards, access to staff and records, a board-approved annual audit plan developed with the audit committee, timely remediation of findings, and a dedicated, non-combined role with escalation of independence or conflict concerns. Adjacent provisions govern external auditor appointment subject to CBUAE no-objection and the regulator's power to appoint auditors itself.

Identifies the CBUAE Banking Supervision Department as the supervisory channel through which Licensed Persons obtain letters of no objection and file notifications — covering senior appointments (Manager in Charge, Compliance Officer, Alternate Compliance Officer), external auditor appointment, foreign and hedge account openings, and special products or services. It also receives resignation and vacancy notifications, often in parallel with the AML/CFT Supervision Department. Relevant for identifying the correct regulatory counterparty and filing deadlines.

Sets the KYC framework for Licensed Persons in exchange business: a risk-based obligation to identify customers and satisfy themselves that funds have legitimate sources and uses, understand the purpose of the relationship and the customer's ownership and control structure. It distinguishes three tiers — Customer Identification, Customer Due Diligence and Enhanced Due Diligence — applied according to ML/FT risk and specified transaction value thresholds, and requires refusal or termination plus consideration of suspicious reporting to the FIU where KYC cannot be completed. Additional provisions address repeat low-value exchanges, acceptable identification such as seafarer documents within capped weekly limits, and demonstrating adequacy to CBUAE examiners.

Defines the Customer Identification (CID) Process as the lightest of the three KYC tiers that a Licensed Person (exchange house) must apply under the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business, based on ML/FT risk and transaction value. It sets out the identification steps and the value bands (notably lower-value foreign currency exchange by natural persons) at which CID alone suffices, with CDD/EDD layered on above the thresholds. Binds Licensed Persons; failure to complete CID/CDD/EDD triggers a prohibition on onboarding or transacting and consideration of an STR/SAR to the FIU.

Sets the Customer Due Diligence tier of the KYC framework for Licensed Persons under the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business, covering identification and verification, source of funds and purpose of transaction capture, PEP screening, and periodic profile review and ongoing monitoring (at least annually or on ID expiry, and on any profile change). Also specifies minimum customer data to be recorded at point of sale and printed on transaction receipts. Binds Licensed Persons; CDD is mandatory for all legal persons/arrangements and for natural persons above the CID band.

Describes Enhanced Due Diligence as the highest KYC tier under the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business: additional information on source of funds, nature of business and purpose of transaction, plus more intensive monitoring and acceptance controls, applied in addition to CDD. Triggered by value thresholds for natural persons (e.g. foreign exchange or outward transfers at or above AED 55,000, aggregated over defined day windows) and automatically for legal persons/arrangements, counterparties, PEPs, DNFBPs/DPMS, high-risk customers or circumstances, and third-party transactions. Binds Licensed Persons.

Covers the Politically Exposed Person concept and the mandatory PEP check under the CBUAE exchange business framework: all PEPs, whether natural-person customers or beneficial owners of legal persons/arrangements, must undergo EDD regardless of transaction type or value, and CID/CDD alone is insufficient. Adjacent provisions address related higher-risk categories such as non-profit organisations, shell banks/companies, and PEP screening of all parties in trade-related and third-party remittances. Binds Licensed Persons and their compliance function.

Addresses the beneficial owner concept in the exchange business context, including the 'beneficial owner of funds' in third-party transactions where a representative transacts for another natural or legal person. Sets conditions for accepting such transactions (power of attorney or verified letter of authority with validity limits, identification of both parties, EDD on remitter and beneficial owner, common shareholding or a valid agreement for cross-border legal entities, capture of all party names at point of sale, and PEP and sanctions screening of every party). Binds Licensed Persons; unresolved doubt requires the beneficial owner to attend in person, failing which the relationship is terminated and the case reported to the FIU.

Prudential/safeguarding rule requiring Licensed Persons holding a Category B or C licence to maintain a Designated Remittance Intermediate Account with a CBUAE-licensed bank, deposit customer remittance funds into it by end of banking hours on the next business day, and use those funds solely to settle remittances with foreign correspondents. Also prescribes the General Ledger accounting treatment (separate control account, optional sub-accounts, transfer to correspondent ledgers on payment order transmission) and is subject to external auditor agreed-upon procedures verifying ring-fencing and funding. Binds Licensed Persons conducting remittance business and their external auditors.

Capital-adequacy-style security requirement in Chapter 2 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business: every Licensed Person must maintain a bank guarantee issued by a UAE-licensed bank in favour of the Central Bank, valued at the higher of 100% of the minimum paid-up capital for its licence category or 5% of the prior financial year's monthly remittance average value (capped at AED 75 million). It also sets the annual Certificate of Remittance Value filing, the duty to top up on Central Bank demand, transitional instalment deadlines, and the consequence of failure — capping monthly remittance volume at twenty times the existing guarantee or downgrading/surrendering the licence. Binds exchange houses (Category A/B/C Licensed Persons) and ties directly to the minimum paid-up capital thresholds.

Defines the Transmittal Letter as the Central Bank's formal written communication of examination findings and areas of non-compliance to a Licensed Person, issued after full-scope or fast-track examinations and structured by severity (major issues, violations, other observations). It creates enforceable response obligations: a written reply per finding with a detailed remediation action plan within the stated period or, absent one, thirty calendar days, signed by the authorised signatory and filed in hard copy with the Supervision & Examination Division. Also covers follow-up examinations and mandatory exit/follow-up meetings involving the Manager in Charge, Compliance Officer and Board/owners.

Recurring prior-approval mechanism under the Standards for Exchange Business: a Licensed Person must obtain a written Letter of No Objection from the Banking Supervision Department before certain acts, including opening hedge or foreign accounts (via the Foreign Account Application form), offering any product or service outside the standard permitted activities (drawn from the Special Product Matrix), and appointing or re-appointing an External Auditor within the rotation limits. Functions as a regulatory gate on scope expansion and key appointments; binds all exchange houses licensed by the CBUAE.

Covers Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions as a defined AML/CFT customer category (per the AML-CFT Decision) and as reporting entities to the UAE FIU. Under the Standards, a Licensed Person must be able to identify when a customer is a DNFBP and must apply enhanced due diligence before entering a business relationship or processing transactions, including verifying that the customer is supervised by the appropriate DNFBP supervisor and that it complies with applicable AML/CFT preventive measures. Relevant to KYB/customer-classification decisions for exchange houses.

Deals with dealers in precious metals and stones as a high-risk DNFBP category and with the related cross-border declaration controls. It links the AML/CFT enhanced due diligence duties for DNFBP customers (including PEP-linked beneficial owners and legal persons/arrangements) to the Customs Declaration Form regime for travellers carrying currency, precious metals or stones, or bearer negotiable instruments above AED 60,000, requiring the Licensed Person to collect and retain the original CDF and to reconcile partial exchanges against the declared value.
lookup_terms: dealers in precious metals and stones

data.summary: The CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business (Version 1.20, November 2021), issued under the Regulations regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business, setting baseline compliance requirements for all exchange houses operating in the UAE, including new entrants. Organised into licensing and continuing obligations, management and governance, risk management and security, AML compliance, customer protection and appendices, with permitted activities limited to currency exchange, remittance, WPS wage payments and Central Bank-approved special products. Binds every Licensed Person continuously; the Board (or Owner/Partners) is accountable, and breaches attract non-compliance charges under Appendix 4.
lookup_terms: Regulations regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business

data.summary: Sets the travel-rule style obligations for Licensed Persons (exchange houses) acting as ordering, intermediary and beneficiary institutions in cross-border and domestic money transfers, specifying the originator and beneficiary data that must accompany every transfer, verification of that data, and the fallback use of a unique transaction reference number where no account exists. It prohibits execution of transfers that fail these conditions, requires intermediaries to preserve accompanying information through the chain (or record it where technical limits intervene) and to detect transfers with missing information using straight-through-processing-compatible measures, with a three-business-day window for the ordering institution to make information available on request. Binds Licensed Persons under the CBUAE AML/CFT standards; record-keeping cross-refers to the retention paragraph.

Defines a third party transaction as one executed by a representative on behalf of a beneficial owner of funds, and establishes a general prohibition subject to narrowly listed exceptions. For natural-person representatives the exception requires a duly executed power of attorney or an in-person signed letter of authority (validity capped at two years) that specifies the transaction type, identification details of both parties and, for transfers, the beneficiary; signatures must be verified against passport or Emirates ID. Binds Licensed Persons; interacts with beneficial ownership identification, CDD/EDD and transaction monitoring rules that require special attention to third party activity.

Covers targeted financial sanctions screening duties for Licensed Persons: written escalation and clearing procedures for potential matches, five-year retention of clearing logs from transaction receipt, and immediate (preferably automated) updating of the UN Consolidated List and the UAE Local Terrorist List in point-of-sale and core systems, with registration on the Executive Office portal for listing/de-listing alerts. On a confirmed match the Licensed Person must freeze funds immediately, without delay and without prior notice. Sits alongside transaction monitoring obligations and feeds reporting duties to the FIU, Central Bank and Executive Office.

Describes use of the goAML portal as the single reporting channel for both suspicious activity and targeted financial sanctions matters. Confirmed sanctions matches must be reported as a Fund Freeze Report within two business days and potential matches as a Partial Name Match Report, with suspension maintained until goAML instructions are received; these reports reach the Central Bank and Executive Office simultaneously. Separately, STRs/SARs and other report types must be filed without delay regardless of amount, using information from both ordering and beneficiary sides, with terrorism-financing suspicions reported within 24 hours; binds Licensed Persons and their Compliance Officers.

Sets the minimum five-year retention baseline for Licensed Persons across transaction records, KYC/CDD/EDD files, ongoing monitoring, correspondence and ID copies, measured from transaction completion, end of the business relationship or account closure. Extends the same period to AML training records and materials, transaction monitoring and investigation files, and STR/SAR documentation (running from the report date), with an extended trigger where litigation or an enforcement investigation is pending. Records include electronic and hard-copy material and must be sufficient to reconstruct individual transactions.

Covers the Compliance Officer's bi-annual AML/CFT compliance report and its place in the Licensed Person's regulatory reporting calendar. The report must cover gap analysis against AML laws and standards, breaches raised in Central Bank examinations and audit reports, statistics on internal disclosures and STRs, policy changes, training coverage and gaps, resource requests, recommendations to the Manager in Charge and Board (or owner/partners), and a forward six-month action plan. Also situates related annual submissions such as audited financial statements and external auditor findings on AML/CFT under agreed-upon procedures, with specified filing channels and deadlines.

Chapter 17 of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business sets the minimum complaint-handling requirements binding on a Licensed Person (exchange house): documented resolution procedures, a dedicated complaints phone number and email displayed on receipts and in premises, and a designated head-office complaints officer who records, resolves and periodically reports complaints to the Manager in Charge. It allows the complaints role to be combined with another suitable function subject to conditions elsewhere in the Standards, creating a link to compliance-function segregation rules. The surrounding context also carries the KYC chapter's structure (CID, CDD, EDD tiers and the duty not to onboard or transact where due diligence cannot be completed).

This node captures the AML/CFT chapter of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business and its anchoring legislation — the UAE AML/CFT Decree Law of 2018 as amended in 2021, together with its implementing Cabinet Decision. It sets out what a Licensed Person's AML/CFT programme must contain: enterprise-wide ML/FT risk assessment, board- and senior-management-approved policies reviewed at least annually, group-wide application to majority-owned branches, subsidiaries and affiliates, and appointment of a senior, board-reporting and adequately resourced Compliance Officer.

A cross-reference node identifying the legal instruments that the AML/CFT chapter of the CBUAE Standards for Exchange Business must be read alongside: the 2018 AML/CFT Decree Law and its 2021 amendment, Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019 (the implementing regulation), and CBUAE AML procedures, guidelines and exchange-house-specific guidance issued by notice. The surrounding extract also contains licensing provisions on grounds for withdrawal, suspension or revocation of a licence, notification timelines, branch openings and relocation of licensed premises.

Original text of CBUAE Circular 25/2005, addressed to banks, finance companies and investment companies, setting lending limits for loans used to purchase company shares against pledge of those shares. It caps advances by reference to nominal, book or market value depending on whether the borrower is a founder, an IPO subscriber or a holder of shares in an established company, extends a lower cap to GCC-incorporated company shares, requires collateral prioritisation by quality and liquidity, and penalises book-lending to share subscribers by forfeiture of the resulting interest.

Consolidated version of CBUAE Circular 25/2005 as amended by Notice No. 2418/2006, effective 28 May 2006, binding on banks, finance companies and investment companies. It reproduces the share-purchase lending caps of the original circular with the key amendment raising the limit on loans secured by shares of companies operating for more than five years from 70% to 80% of market value; other caps, the GCC-company limit, collateral prioritisation rule and book-lending sanction remain unchanged.

Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 11 of 2016 requires insurers writing property and liability business to have their pricing policy reviewed and assessed twice per financial year by an Actuary licensed and registered with the Authority. It prescribes the minimum content of the actuarial report (risk factors, expense and reinsurance ratios, profit margin, claims history and IBNR provisioning, pricing controls, product-level adequacy, impact on financial position and on policyholder protection), sets submission and management-response deadlines, and empowers the Director General to order corrective measures.

A UAE Insurance Authority Board resolution (No. 12 of 2016) setting the periods after which the effect of a disciplinary sanction imposed on a person practising an insurance-related profession, or on their employee, lapses: 60 days after conditions are rectified for a warning, and 180 days from the decision lifting a suspension. It binds licensed insurance-related professionals (brokers, agents, loss adjusters and similar) and their employees, and is stated to operate without prejudice to penalties under other legislation. Useful only for the rehabilitation/expiry of disciplinary records, not for the grounds or process of imposing sanctions.

UAE Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 15 of 2019 issuing instructions on ownership ratios in the capital of insurance companies, including the regime for applications to acquire control. The excerpted articles cover the Authority's 30-day decision period on a control application, grounds for rejection (unmet conditions, harm to policyholders/company/sector, conflict of interest, competition and anti-monopoly concerns), and a 20-working-day grievance route to the Board. Binds prospective and existing shareholders seeking control in insurance companies, and the companies themselves.

UAE Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 20 of 2020 granting a 45-day extension (ending 30/06/2020) to the reporting deadlines in the 2014 Financial Regulations for insurance and takaful companies for quarterly financial statements and other required periodic reports. It also delegates standing authority to the Director General to extend submission deadlines for financial statements and other required reports from insurance companies and insurance-related professions. Relevant mainly as a time-limited relief measure and as the source of the DG's delegated extension power.

UAE Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 25 of 2020 setting the procedure for challenging administrative fines imposed by the Authority: an interested party may file a reasoned, fully documented grievance with the Board within 15 days of notification, and the Board must decide (reject, amend the fine, or cancel it) within 60 days. It binds any party fined by the Authority, including fines arising under the AML/CTF framework referenced in its preamble. Procedural only; it does not set the fine amounts, which sit in Cabinet Resolution No. 7 of 2019.

UAE Central Bank Circular No. 468 of 1987 supplementing Circular 444/1987 for public subscriptions to the capital of companies established abroad. Banks operating in the UAE must additionally file an authenticated Arabic translation of the home-country regulator's approval permitting the company to offer shares abroad, and report the number of shares allocated to UAE subscribers versus those applied for; all approval applications must reach the Central Bank at least two weeks before the issue opens. Binds all banks acting as underwriters or intermediaries for foreign share offerings.
lookup_terms: Central Bank prior approval share issue

data.summary: UAE Central Bank Circular No. 444 of 1987, consolidating earlier circulars, requiring all licensed banks and representative offices to obtain prior Central Bank (Banking Supervision) approval before accepting public subscriptions to the capital of new or existing companies, whether UAE or foreign. It defines when a bank acts as an underwriter or intermediary (advertising the issue or collecting application forms, as opposed to mere fund transfers), sets the content of approval applications, and imposes subscriber-protection duties on disclosure, acknowledgements, refunds, share certificate delivery, verification of founders' paid-up shares, and use of segregated subscription accounts subject to reserve requirements.
lookup_terms: prior Central Bank approval share issue

data.summary: Sets the AML/CFT training obligations in the exchange-business Standards, covering who must be trained (all employees plus the Manager in Charge, functional heads, board directors and owners/partners/shareholders), timing (within 30 calendar days for new joiners, who cannot serve customers unaided before completion), risk-based refresher frequency with an annual minimum for customer/product-facing staff, and event-driven retraining when laws, regulations, notices, the Standards or internal policy change. It also requires periodic awareness assessment, training registers and retention of training evidence for supervisory inspection, and periodic review of training materials. Binds Licensed Persons (exchange houses) and, through them, all staff and governing persons; the surrounding context also covers AML/CFT policy approval and Compliance Officer appointment/seniority and reporting lines.

Node for a Licensed Person application/authorisation form under the exchange-business Standards; the attached material describes the authorisation process (formal signed application letter, minimum qualification and competency requirements for the requested position, full disclosure duty, required documents, possible candidate interview and a 60-day notification of approval, conditional approval or refusal). The same extract also carries targeted financial sanctions reporting duties: Fund Freeze Reports for confirmed matches within two business days and Partial Name Match Reports for potential matches via goAML, with suspension maintained pending instructions. Binds Licensed Persons dealing with the Central Bank on approvals and on TFS reporting to the Central Bank and the Executive Office.

Node labelled for the Authorised Person's Appointment (APA) form used to obtain Central Bank approval for designated positions at a Licensed Person. The extracted context, however, is substantive AML/CFT material: KYC on representatives and beneficial owners of funds (including insisting the beneficial owner attend in person and terminating/reporting if refused), enhanced due diligence and conditions for trade-related remittances by legal persons (commercial rationale, invoices in the entity's name, sanctions screening of all parties), and wire transfer duties for ordering and intermediary institutions. Useful mainly if you are tracing appointment approvals or the adjacent EDD/wire-transfer rules; verify which of the two you need before opening.

Covers the Foreign Account Application (FAA) Form (Appendix 5), the prescribed application through which a Licensed Person seeks a Letter of No Objection from Banking Supervision before opening a hedge account with a financial institution inside or outside the country; hedge accounts may be used only to mitigate FX rate risk, never for speculation, with hedge accounting per IFRS and fully automated. The surrounding context sets out permitted remittance operations by licence category and the Designated Remittance Intermediate Account requirements. Binds Licensed Persons conducting FX and remittance business.

Chapter 18 of the exchange-business Standards defines when money-transfer funds become unclaimed (e.g. outward transfers to accounts not repaid to the remitter within seven calendar days of cancellation or return; cash payouts not collected within ninety calendar days; expired demand drafts) and requires the Licensed Person to recover funds already settled with the bank or transfer provider. It then imposes management duties: board-approved policies and procedures, defined roles, segregation of the funds in local currency cash or a local bank account with no use in day-to-day business, ongoing customer contact to refund, monthly assessment and disclosure as a separate current liability in the monthly return, and internal audit review reporting to the board. Binds Licensed Persons as a customer-protection obligation.

Appendix 6 sets the minimum agreed-upon procedures an External Auditor must perform on the Remittance Intermediate Account and report on, as required by the exchange business regulations and Chapter 4 of the Standards. Procedures include confirming a Designated Remittance Intermediate Account is held with a locally licensed bank, that customer remittance funds are deposited by the end of banking hours on the next business day, that the balances are ring-fenced against any use other than prefunding or settling foreign correspondent accounts, and risk-based sampling of ledger recording, transfers to correspondent accounts on payment-order transmission, and adequacy of correspondent prefunding. Binds External Auditors in their reporting duty and, indirectly, Licensed Persons holding a Category B or C licence.

CBUAE's 2011 Personal Loans Manual (issued Abu Dhabi, 28 April 2011) setting retail lending conduct and prudential-style caps for banks: debt-burden limits, maximum tenor, interest calculation method, fee and early-settlement charge rules, and restrictions on security. It binds banks lending to individuals in the UAE, distinguishing loans outstanding before 1 May 2011 from new or rescheduled facilities after that date. Note it is a UAE (CBUAE) instrument, not a SAMA rule, and is relevant mainly for cross-border comparison with KSA consumer finance/responsible lending requirements.
lookup_terms: flat rate vs effective rate disclosure

data.summary: CBUAE Circular 04/2020 regulation creating a five-year 'prudential filter' that lets banks and finance companies add back part of the increase in IFRS 9 Stage 1 and Stage 2 ECL provisions to regulatory capital, applied retroactively from 1 January 2020 and fully unwound by 1 January 2025. It defines scope, the add-back calculation, offsetting adjustments to exposure values and Tier 2, use of adjusted capital in all capital metrics, and mandatory disclosure of both filtered and unfiltered ratios. Binds all banks (including foreign bank branches) and finance companies operating in the UAE; interpretation is reserved to CBUAE and breaches attract supervisory sanctions.

Concept node for the Targeted Economic Support Scheme, established by CBUAE Board Decision No. 49/3/2020 (5 April 2020) as the COVID-19 relief framework from which the accounting-provisions/capital transitional arrangements regulation flowed. Here it functions as the enabling policy context and effective-date anchor for the IFRS 9 prudential filter notified to banks and finance companies (Notice CBUAE/BSD/N/2020/2016, 22 April 2020). Relevant to anyone tracing why the 2020-2024 add-back phase-down exists and which entities it covered.

Concept node for IFRS 9 expected credit loss provisions as treated under the CBUAE transitional-arrangements regulation: only Stage 1 and Stage 2 IFRS 9 provisions qualify for the phase-in, measured as the excess over the 31 December 2019 baseline. It expressly does not cover the separate CBUAE provisioning requirements under the loan classification rules (Circular 28/2010), and it supersedes the transitional guidance in the March 2018 IFRS 9 implementation guidance note. Useful for confirming which provisions are in or out of scope of capital add-back for banks and finance companies.

CBUAE's July 2023 AML/CFT and illegal-organisations guidelines for financial institutions, summarising and elaborating the minimum statutory duties under the UAE AML-CFT Law and its implementing Decision: risk identification and assessment, CDD scope, appointment of a qualified compliance officer, internal controls and MIS, suspicious-transaction indicators, STR filing and cooperation with competent authorities. It is guidance addressed to CBUAE-supervised FIs, which remain solely responsible for compliance with the underlying law, Decision and all notices and circulars. Comparable in function to SAMA AML/CTF rules and guidance for KSA institutions.
lookup_terms: CBUAE AML guidelines for financial institutions

data.summary: Concept node for the risk-based approach as required of financial institutions under the UAE AML-CFT Law and Decision: FIs must identify, assess, document and continuously update their ML/FT risk assessment and make it available to the supervisory authority on request. It covers the business-wide (enterprise) risk assessment methodology — inherent risk across customers, products/services/transactions, delivery channels and geography, then controls and residual risk — as the basis for calibrating mitigation, risk appetite and resource allocation. Binds CBUAE-supervised FIs; conceptually parallel to the enterprise-wide ML/TF risk assessment expected under SAMA's AML/CTF regime.
lookup_terms: risk factors customers products channels geography

data.summary: Concept node for Enhanced Due Diligence as treated in the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions, sitting inside the wider CDD programme (identification, profiling, acceptance, risk rating, monitoring, investigation, documentation). It explains the risk-based approach under the AML-CFT Law and Cabinet Decision, requiring intensified measures (e.g. source of funds, adverse-media and sanctions screening of customers, beneficial owners, beneficiaries and controlling persons) where higher ML/FT risk is identified, and contrasts this with SDD for low-risk, non-suspicious cases. It binds supervised financial institutions in the UAE, including those in financial and commercial free zones.

Concept node covering Suspicious Transaction Reporting under the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions: internal escalation to the compliance officer, the officer's decision to file, and immediate reporting to the UAE FIU through its goAML system or other FIU-approved means. It also flags confidentiality/tipping-off controls, post-filing handling of the business relationship, and the criminal liability (fines and/or imprisonment) for failure to report, with no exemptions available to FIs. Binds all supervised FIs and their managers and employees, whether onshore or in free zones.

Instrument node for Cabinet Decision No. (10) of 2019, the Implementing Regulation of Federal Decree-Law No. (20) of 2018, as summarised in the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines. It operationalises the statutory AML/CFT obligations — risk identification and assessment, scope of due diligence, appointment of a qualified compliance officer, internal controls and MIS, suspicious-transaction indicators, and reporting/cooperation with Competent Authorities. It binds supervised institutions (financial institutions and DNFBPs) across the UAE, including free zones.

Instrument node for Federal Decree-Law No. (20) of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Financing of Illegal Organisations — the primary AML/CFT statute referenced throughout the CBUAE Guidelines, together with its defined terms (e.g. "Customer", "Decree-Law", "Decision"). It sets the minimum statutory duties on supervised institutions and underpins the criminal offences of ML, TF and financing of illegal organisations. Applies federally across the UAE, including financial and commercial free zones.

Alias/concept node for the AML-CFT Law (Federal Decree-Law 20/2018) as applied in the CBUAE Guidelines, focusing on its core obligations: continuous identification, assessment, documentation and updating of ML/FT risk; defining the scope of due diligence measures; internal controls and policies; suspicious-transaction indicators; and reporting to Competent Authorities. It anchors the risk-based approach that must be proportionate to each institution's exposure. Binds supervised financial institutions and their senior management and employees.

Node for the Cabinet UBO Resolution No. (58) of 2020 as a companion instrument within the UAE AML/CFT framework described in the CBUAE Guidelines for Financial Institutions; the surrounding context here is the framework overview (legal hierarchy, Supervisory Authorities, free-zone coverage) rather than the resolution's own text. Open it for beneficial-ownership registry and disclosure matters; note the Guidelines also cross-refer to the separate TFS regime under Cabinet Decision No. (74) of 2020. Relevance is to supervised institutions and to legal persons subject to UBO disclosure.

This is the CBUAE's AML/CFT and counter-financing-of-illegal-organisations Guidelines for Financial Institutions, a joint supervisory-authority document explaining how licensed FIs should meet their statutory duties under the UAE AML-CFT Law and its implementing Cabinet Decision. It sets out minimum expectations on the risk-based approach, business-wide ML/FT risk identification, assessment, documentation and updating, plus core obligations such as customer due diligence, appointment of a qualified compliance officer, internal controls and policies, suspicious-transaction indicators, STR filing and cooperation with competent authorities. It binds supervised financial institutions (and informs their senior management and staff), while expressly leaving the FI solely responsible for compliance with the underlying law, decision, notices and circulars; UN targeted financial sanctions guidance sits in a separate instrument.

A defined-term/background node identifying MENAFATF as the FATF-Style Regional Body for the Middle East and North Africa, referenced in the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines' glossary and its overview of the international AML/CFT architecture alongside the UN, FATF and other FSRBs. It is contextual rather than obligation-creating: it explains the standard-setting and mutual-evaluation environment that shapes national AML/CFT requirements. It binds no institution directly, but informs how FIs should read the origin and intent of UAE AML/CFT rules.
lookup_terms: Middle East and North Africa Financial Action Task Force

data.summary: A glossary/context node defining the Egmont Group as the intergovernmental network of Financial Intelligence Units that enables secure exchange of financial intelligence and expertise to counter ML/FT. It appears in the definitions section of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines together with FATF, FSRBs, Financial Group and Financial Institution, and supports the Guidelines' discussion of FIU information sharing with foreign counterparts. It imposes no direct duty on FIs but frames how STR-derived intelligence may travel internationally.

A contextual node covering the United Nations' role in the international AML/CFT framework as described in the CBUAE Guidelines, including the UNODC Global Programme against Money Laundering and the UN-derived targeted financial sanctions regime. It also appears in the Guidelines' useful-links annex. It creates no standalone obligation here; UN TFS listing obligations for UAE institutions are addressed under the separate Cabinet Decision No. (74) of 2020 framework referenced by the Guidelines.

This node describes goAML, the UAE FIU's reporting platform through which financial institutions file suspicious transaction reports and receive FIU feedback and trend analysis. The Guidelines treat registration as an enforceable step: FIs must register on goAML, keep registration active, and newly licensed FIs must register immediately after obtaining their financial services licence so they are ready to report from the outset; the compliance officer is the designated system user. It binds all supervised FIs and is the operational channel for the STR and related reporting duties.

This node covers the enterprise-level ML/FT risk assessment expectations in the CBUAE Guidelines: identifying inherent risks across customers, products and services, transactions, delivery channels and geographies, calibrating mitigating controls, and determining residual risk and control gaps. It requires the assessment methodology and rationale to be documented, kept current and made available to the supervisory authority on request, with proportionality to the size and complexity of the business. It binds supervised financial institutions and underpins risk appetite, resource allocation and CDD intensity decisions.
lookup_terms: documentation and updating of risk assessment

data.summary: A concept node within the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions covering the UAE's national AML/CFT strategy framework and the resulting minimum statutory obligations placed on supervised institutions. It orients the reader to the federal legislative architecture (the AML-CFT Law and its implementing Cabinet Decision) and to core duties such as risk identification and assessment, CDD scoping, appointment of a compliance officer, internal controls, suspicious transaction indicators and STR reporting. It binds licensed financial institutions supervised by CBUAE, and their senior management and staff; note this is a UAE instrument, not a SAMA rule.

A concept node describing the UAE's national institutional AML/CFT coordination framework, including the National Committee for Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organisations, situated in the overview chapter of the CBUAE Guidelines for Financial Institutions. It explains how federal criminal and AML/CFT legislation applies across the State including the Financial and Commercial Free Zones, and how Competent and Supervisory Authorities divide implementation and enforcement. It is contextual rather than directly obligation-creating, but frames which authority binds a given institution.
lookup_terms: National Committee for Combating Money Laundering

data.summary: A concept node on the enterprise-wide ML/FT business risk assessment required as the first step of a risk-based approach under the AML-CFT Law and implementing Decision. It covers identification of inherent risks across customers, products, services and transactions, delivery channels and geographies, the mapping of mitigating controls, and the determination of residual risk and control gaps to inform risk appetite and resource allocation. It binds supervised financial institutions, which must document, maintain and update the assessment and produce it to the Supervisory Authority on request.
lookup_terms: risk factors customers products channels geography

data.summary: A concept node on simplified due diligence as the lower-intensity end of risk-based CDD, available only where low risk has been identified and there is no suspicion of ML/FT. It sits within the CDD chapter alongside enhanced due diligence, and stresses that customer risk profiles are dynamic so institutions must be ready to escalate the type and level of due diligence. It binds financial institutions applying CDD measures under the AML-CFT Law and Decision.

A concept node on assessing and classifying customer or business-relationship risk, which drives the intensity of CDD applied. It sets out relevant risk factors — customer type and base, maturity and nature of the relationship, ownership and control complexity, transparency of beneficial ownership, regulated versus unregulated activity, PEP and higher-risk sector links, and non-resident status — and requires the classification to reflect the NRA, Topical Risk Assessments and the institution's own business risk assessment, with input from the AML/CFT compliance officer. It binds financial institutions; methodology may scale with size and complexity.

A defined-term node for Beneficial Owner as used across multiple CBUAE AML/CFT guidance documents, covering the duty to identify and verify customers together with beneficial owners, beneficiaries and controlling persons — whether natural persons, legal persons or legal arrangements — using reliable and independent sources. Timing, extent and method of verification vary with customer type and risk level, and enhanced measures (sanctions and adverse-media screening, more rigorous verification) apply to high-risk customers or beneficial owners. It binds supervised financial institutions and references the UAE beneficial-owner procedures resolution.

Concept node for money laundering as defined and criminalised under the UAE AML-CFT Law, as explained in the CBUAE AML/CFT and Illegal Organisations Guidelines for Financial Institutions. It covers the constituent acts (transferring/concealing/acquiring proceeds, assisting a perpetrator to escape punishment), the deliberately broad definition of "funds" (including virtual assets, securities, contracts, IP and physical property), and the international standard-setting architecture (UN/GPML, FATF Recommendations, FSRBs) that frames national obligations. It binds supervised financial institutions in the UAE and is relevant to KSA teams only as comparative/cross-border material.
lookup_terms: CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions

data.summary: Concept node for financing of terrorism (FT) under the UAE AML-CFT Law as presented in the CBUAE Guidelines for Financial Institutions, including its status as a criminal offence not subject to the statute of limitations and its treatment alongside financing of illegal organisations. It also situates FT within the Guidelines' scope statement (minimum supervisory expectations for identifying, assessing and mitigating ML/FT risk) and cross-refers the separate UN Targeted Financial Sanctions regime under Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020. Binds UAE supervised financial institutions; sanctions/TFS obligations sit in a distinct instrument.

Concept node explaining predicate offences in the UAE ML framework: ML prosecution is independent of the predicate offence, and suspicion does not require proof that a predicate offence occurred or that proceeds are illicit. It also records that any felony or misdemeanour can serve as a predicate, and lists absolute prohibitions on FIs (anonymous/fictitious accounts, relationships where CDD cannot be completed, dealings with shell banks, invoking secrecy to avoid reporting, bearer shares). Directed at UAE supervised financial institutions and their STR/CDD decision-making.

Concept node describing the three phases of money laundering — placement, layering and integration — as used in the CBUAE Guidelines to help FIs map where their products, channels or institution can be misused. It frames phase analysis as an input to enterprise-wide and relationship-level inherent ML/FT risk assessment, with examples such as commingling, structuring/breaking up amounts and foreign exchange purchases. Guidance-level material addressed to UAE supervised financial institutions.

Concept node cataloguing ML/FT typologies and red flags in the CBUAE Guidelines, spanning layering and integration techniques (cross-border transfers, shell companies to hide beneficial owners, real estate and securities investment, stored-value products) and sector-specific abuse such as life and general insurance premium overpayment or early cancellation. It also points FIs to FATF guidance on virtual assets and VASPs and to UAE FIU trends and typologies reports. Used by UAE supervised FIs to calibrate risk assessment and transaction monitoring expectations.

Concept node on the risk-based approach and enhanced due diligence obligations, including the specific duty to apply CDD measures and countermeasures toward High Risk Countries designated by the UAE National Committee, reflecting UN Security Council Chapter VII decisions, the Terrorist Financing Suppression Convention, the NPT, and FATF/FSRB calls. It links business-wide ML/FT risk assessment (inherent versus residual risk, control gaps, risk appetite) to EDD triggers such as foreign PEPs, source of funds enquiry and intensified ongoing monitoring. Binds UAE supervised financial institutions, which must maintain internal policies and controls proportionate to size and risk.

A section of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions dealing with correspondent banking and similar relationships (including securities and funds-transfer arrangements), read against Article 25 of the AML-CFT Decision. It sets out the due diligence expected before and during such relationships: assessing the respondent's home regulatory and supervisory framework, ownership and management (including PEP exposure), the nature and scale of its business, and whether it offers downstream or nested correspondent services. It binds licensed financial institutions maintaining correspondent relationships with foreign or domestic institutions, and reiterates the prohibition on dealing with shell banks or institutions that permit shell-bank use of their accounts.

Guidance section on financial institutions' relationships with Money or Value Transfer Services, referencing Articles 26 and 30 of the AML-CFT Decision, plus the associated originator/beneficiary information requirements for wire transfers. It requires risk-based CDD on MVTS counterparties: confirming licensing or registration (including physical inspection of the original Hawala Provider registration certificate issued by the Central Bank), assessing the MVTS's AML/CFT controls, agent network, ownership and customer base. It binds FIs that open accounts for or maintain business relationships with MVTS providers and Hawala Providers.

A node drawn from the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines that, in the extracted context, mainly surfaces the glossary of defined terms (High Risk Customer, Illegal Organisations, Intermediary Account, Intermediary Financial Institution, Legal Arrangement, Law Enforcement Authorities, MENAFATF) together with the MVTS due diligence section. It is useful chiefly for establishing defined-term meanings used throughout the Guidelines rather than for a self-contained NPO obligation set; the label suggests non-profit organisation risk treatment, which should be verified in the source before relying on it.

Extracted material covering identity verification and documentation standards (powers of attorney, board resolutions, official registry extracts, court orders, certification of copies, Apostille, four-eyes review) alongside the third-party reliance section under Article 19 of the AML-CFT Decision. Despite the wire-transfer label, the context here is about how customer identity is verified and authenticated and how reliance on third parties for CDD must be controlled. It binds FIs conducting CDD on customers and authorised representatives.

Guidance addressing virtual assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers within the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines, pointing FIs to the FATF Recommendations and risk-based guidance on VAs/VASPs, and extending originator/beneficiary information (travel rule) expectations to virtual asset transfers between originating and beneficiary VASPs. The same extract covers intermediary FI obligations to detect transfers lacking required originator or beneficiary data and to decide whether to execute, reject or suspend them, plus insurance-sector laundering typologies. It binds FIs dealing with VA/VASP exposure and intermediary institutions in payment chains.

Consolidated guidance (across two CBUAE AML/CFT guidance instruments) on reliance on a third party for all or part of the CDD process, including introduced business, under Article 19 of the AML-CFT Decision. Reliance is permitted only where the third party is regulated and supervised and applies compliant CDD and record-keeping, and where identification data and documentation can be obtained from it without delay; the relying FI retains ultimate responsibility for CDD outcomes, customer risk classification and ongoing monitoring. It binds FIs that outsource or rely on introducers, group entities or other regulated parties for customer identification and beneficial ownership verification.

Section 8.2 of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions, sitting under the governance/internal-controls chapter and keyed to the AML-CFT Decision provisions on employee screening and ongoing training. It sets the supervisory expectation that FIs screen employment candidates to high standards and deliver risk-calibrated, regularly refreshed AML/CFT training so staff understand the institution's ML/FT exposure and can identify suspicious transactions; training design should reflect the NRA and topical risk assessments, business/customer risk profile, and delivery, frequency and effectiveness-testing considerations. It binds financial institutions supervised by CBUAE, with practical responsibility on the Compliance Officer and senior management.

Section 8.3 of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines addresses group-wide AML/CFT programmes, keyed to AML-CFT Decision Articles 20, 31 and 32. It requires an FI that forms part of a financial group to implement and apply group-wide AML/CFT policies across all branches and majority-owned subsidiaries, including those abroad, at standards mirroring those applicable in the UAE. It binds FIs that are members of a Financial Group (as defined in the Guidelines) and is the entry point for host/home country conflict and foreign-branch standards questions.

Section 8.4 of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines, tied to AML-CFT Decision Article 20.6, covering the mandatory independent audit function that tests the adequacy and effectiveness of an FI's AML/CFT internal policies, controls and procedures. It addresses staffing, competence and proportionality to the FI's ML/FT risk, nature and size, and permits smaller FIs to source capability from qualified, regulated external providers while retaining internal oversight; it also sets out the expected audit scope (CDD policies, training adequacy, outsourced compliance functions, case management and STR processes). It binds all CBUAE-supervised financial institutions.

Section 8.5 of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines sets out senior management involvement and accountability for AML/CFT compliance, cross-referenced to multiple AML-CFT Decision articles (including those on risk assessment, CDD approval, compliance officer appointment and reporting). It requires senior management to approve internal AML/CFT policies, controls and procedures, ensure they are reviewed, updated and applied across branches and majority-owned entities, and that they reflect NRA and topical risk assessment outcomes and be proportionate to the FI's own ML/FT business risk assessment. It binds boards and senior management of CBUAE-supervised FIs.

Section 8.6 of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines addresses governance where an FI is small or mid-sized and cannot maintain full separation of duties. It confirms that small size gives no exemption from AML-CFT Law and Decision obligations, and expects that a compliance officer holding dual roles should not have day-to-day sales or customer relationship responsibility, with compensating measures for CDD, STR identification and reporting, high-risk country measures and sanctions/local list monitoring. It binds smaller CBUAE-supervised financial institutions, including exchange houses and other non-bank FIs.

Chapter 9 of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines covers record-keeping obligations and required record types, referencing AML-CFT Law Article 16.1 and AML-CFT Decision Articles 7.2, 24, 36 and 37.3. It sets the minimum five-year retention period running from the latest of relationship termination, completion of an occasional transaction, completion of a supervisory inspection or the date of a final judgment, requires records to be organised so transactions can be reconstructed, and to be made available to Competent Authorities immediately on request; it also categorises transaction records and CDD records and addresses data protection, archiving, destruction of expired records and audit/quality assurance over record-keeping. It binds all CBUAE-supervised financial institutions.

A concept node within the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions describing the three-lines-of-defence structure that an AML/CFT programme must cover: internal policies, procedures, controls and employee training (first line); a designated compliance function headed by a compliance officer/MLRO (second line); and independent audit testing programme effectiveness (third line). It is framed as guidance interpreting the UAE AML-CFT Law and Cabinet Decision, so the underlying statutory articles, not the guidance, carry the enforceable obligation. It binds licensed financial institutions in the UAE (banks, finance companies, exchange houses and MSBs, insurers and intermediaries, securities firms, VASPs), with calibration permitted for business nature, size and complexity.
lookup_terms: CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions

data.summary: A concept node covering the requirement that financial institutions maintain documented internal AML/CFT policies, controls and procedures that mitigate the risks identified in their business-wide ML/TF risk assessment and reflect the National Risk Assessment and topical risk assessments. It sets expectations on senior management approval, periodic effectiveness review and updating, proportionality to risk, communication within the organisation, and group-wide application to branches, subsidiaries and majority-owned affiliates; it also extends to STR-related procedures and confidentiality controls. Binds financial institutions supervised by CBUAE under the UAE AML-CFT Law and Decision.
lookup_terms: AML/CFT policy approval by senior management

data.summary: A concept node on the confidentiality duty attaching to suspicious transaction reporting — the prohibition on disclosing to a customer or third party that an STR has been or will be filed, or that an ML/FT investigation is underway. It sits alongside guidance on STR timing (report to the FIU without delay once suspicion is established) and on controls protecting STR data from unauthorised access. It binds financial institutions and their staff under the UAE AML-CFT Law and Decision, with breach exposure at both institutional and individual level.

A concept node on continuous scrutiny of business relationships and transactions to confirm consistency with the customer's profile, source of funds and risk classification, and to keep CDD information current. It links customer/business-relationship risk assessment methodologies to the intensity of monitoring, and addresses the post-STR position: a reported relationship is by definition high risk, and if retained the decision and rationale must be documented and enhanced due diligence plus additional controls (added information requirements, product restrictions, transaction limits or approval gates) applied. Binds CBUAE-supervised financial institutions.
lookup_terms: maintaining a relationship after an STR

data.summary: A reference/definition node identifying the Wolfsberg Group as an industry association of international banks that issues non-binding AML/CFT standards and guidance (e.g. correspondent banking questionnaires and due diligence principles), cited in the CBUAE Guidelines alongside FATF, FSRBs and the Egmont Group as an external benchmark. It creates no direct obligation; its relevance is interpretive and as a source of good-practice benchmarks for institutions and groups. Useful chiefly for definitional orientation and glossary look-ups.

A concept node setting out the risk-factor categories used in the business-wide ML/TF risk assessment — customers, products, services and transactions, delivery channels, geographic locations, and other relevant factors — and how inherent risk is identified, weighted (likelihood, timing, impact) and classified before controls are applied to derive residual risk. It stresses that risks typically arise from combinations of factors and that identified factors drive both risk categorisation and the calibration of mitigation measures and internal policies. Binds CBUAE-supervised financial institutions applying the risk-based approach.

Section of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions dealing with record keeping: the categories of records FIs must retain (transaction records; CDD records covering customer and company information, third-party reliance, ongoing monitoring; and suspicious transaction reporting records) together with the retention and availability obligations. It sets a minimum five-year retention period running from the latest relevant trigger event (end of the business relationship or account closure, completion of an occasional transaction, completion of a supervisory inspection, or a final judgment), and requires records to be organised so transactions can be reconstructed and produced to Competent Authorities immediately on request. It binds financial institutions supervised under the UAE AML-CFT Law and its implementing Cabinet Decision, and expects supporting internal policies on archiving, destruction, data protection and audit testing.
lookup_terms: availability of records to Competent Authorities

data.summary: Node covering the international dimension of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines: the intergovernmental and standard-setting bodies (UN and its anti-money-laundering programme, FATF and its Recommendations and Immediate Outcomes, FATF-style regional bodies such as MENAFATF, the Egmont Group of FIUs) whose standards the UAE transposes, and the guidelines' treatment of international financial sanctions. It explains the source and status of these standards rather than creating stand-alone obligations, but frames the sanctions-screening and targeted financial sanctions duties applicable to supervised financial institutions.
lookup_terms: UNODC Global Programme against Money Laundering

data.summary: The defined-terms appendix and interpretive conventions of the CBUAE AML/CFT Guidelines for Financial Institutions, giving the meanings of capitalised terms used throughout (for example Financial Institution, Financial Group, Financing of Terrorism, Financing of Illegal Organisations, FATF, FSRBs, Egmont Group). It also records the interpretive rule that references to financing of terrorism include financing of illegal organisations, and that where the guidelines' paraphrases conflict with the AML-CFT Law or Cabinet Decision, the primary instruments prevail. Useful as the entry point for scope and terminology questions affecting all supervised financial institutions.

Node situating Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020 on terrorism lists within the UAE's AML/CFT legal architecture, alongside Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 and Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019.
