It relates to the designation and listing mechanism underpinning targeted financial sanctions and the corresponding freezing and reporting duties, and to the overall matrix of federal criminal legislation applying throughout the State including the financial and commercial free zones. It binds supervised financial institutions through their screening, freezing and notification obligations, and the surrounding text also summarises the minimum statutory AML/CFT obligations (risk assessment, CDD, compliance officer, internal controls, suspicious transaction reporting).

CBUAE prudential regulation on market risk, setting the required market risk strategy and governance framework for banks at entity and, where relevant, group level. It allocates Board responsibility for approving and annually reviewing market risk strategy, policies and processes, requires clear roles, separation of duties and conflict-of-interest avoidance, and obliges Senior Management to implement them; it also mandates policy content such as management information systems, market risk limits aligned to risk appetite and capital strength, exception tracking, model controls, intra-day limit management and trading book allocation, including submission of a trading book policy statement to the Central Bank. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE.

The systems and controls component of the CBUAE market risk regulation, requiring banks' market risk measurement, monitoring and control systems to support continuous capital adequacy and adherence to intra-day and other limits. It mandates at least annual independent internal review of the measurement system and overall market risk management process by functionally independent and competent staff, timely capture of all transactions, internal validation of models by parties independent of model development, periodic and as-needed external validation, and a back-testing programme comparing model outputs with realised trading results. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE, with duties falling on the Board, Senior Management and internal audit.

Article 5 of the CBUAE Market Risk Regulation, sitting alongside the valuation provisions of Article 4. It requires banks to hold capital at all times against unexpected losses arising from market risk exposures and to meet market risk capital requirements continuously, with related duties on independent model validation, prudent valuation adjustments for illiquid, concentrated or stale positions, and trading book valuation methodology. Binds all banks licensed by the CBUAE, on a solo and group-wide basis.

Article 7 of the CBUAE Market Risk Regulation on reporting, read together with the systems-and-controls duties requiring information systems that identify, aggregate, monitor and report market risk exposure to the Board and Senior Management. Related obligations cover market risk limits aligned to risk appetite, exception tracking and escalation, controls over risk models, trading book allocation policies, intra-day exposure limits, and submission of a trading book policy statement (and material changes) for Central Bank review. Applies to all CBUAE-licensed banks.

Article 8 of the CBUAE Market Risk Regulation, addressing application of the market risk framework to Islamic banking activity, within an instrument whose core is the market risk governance framework (Article 2) and systems and controls (Article 3). Those articles require a Board-approved market risk strategy, policies and processes giving a bank-wide and group-wide view of market risk, clear roles, separation of duties and Senior Management implementation under Board oversight. Binds banks, including those conducting Islamic banking business, subject to Shari'ah-compliant adaptation.

The enabling-law and scope anchor of the CBUAE Market Risk Regulation, covering the objective, scope of application and Article 1 definitions (Affiliate, Bank, Board, Group, Subsidiary, Trading Book). It confirms that the Regulation and its accompanying Standards apply to all banks, on a solo and group-wide basis where significant group relationships exist, and must be read with the CBUAE Risk Management Regulation and Standards. Relevant to determining legal basis, addressees and defined-term scope before applying any substantive article.

UAE Insurance Authority regulations implementing the Common Reporting Standard for automatic exchange of financial account information. They set out general provisions, the persons bound (Reporting Financial Institutions under the Authority's supervision, Account Holders/policyholders of Reportable Accounts, and other covered persons), the Authority's inspection and information-gathering powers, and due diligence record-keeping with a five-year retention period after reporting. Binds insurance-sector Reporting Financial Institutions and, for information requests, their Account Holders.
lookup_terms: automatic exchange of financial account information

data.summary: The Common Reporting Standard itself as incorporated by the UAE regulations, including the OECD CRS commentary which is treated as an integral interpretive part of the Standard for purposes of automatic exchange under a scheduled Agreement. It also fixes that the English version aligned to the OECD model prevails over the Arabic translation in case of conflict. Relevant to any Reporting Financial Institution determining classification, due diligence and reporting obligations for Reportable Accounts.

Definitional node identifying the OECD as the body that develops, amends and publishes the Common Reporting Standard and its interpretive commentary, which the UAE Insurance Authority CRS Regulations incorporate as an integral part of the Standard. It also fixes that the English version following the OECD international model prevails over the Arabic translation in case of conflict. Relevant to insurance companies supervised as Reporting Financial Institutions and to account/policy holders within scope.
lookup_terms: Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development
automatic exchange of financial account information

data.summary: Defined term for the institution that carries the CRS due diligence and reporting obligations — in this instrument, insurance companies (including Takaful) issuing Cash Value Insurance or Annuity Contracts under Insurance Authority supervision. The node anchors who must identify Reportable Accounts, when reliance on self-certifications, documentary evidence or AML/KYC information is permitted, and the aggregation rules that apply to it.

Concept node covering the general and special CRS due diligence requirements (Sections II–VII): the duty to establish, maintain and document procedures to identify Reportable Accounts, timing and valuation rules, permitted elections to apply stricter procedures, and the special rules on reliance on self-certifications and documentary evidence. It confirms that use of a service provider does not transfer the obligation, which remains with the Reporting Financial Institution.

Defined term for an account identified, through the CRS due diligence procedures, as held by a Reportable Person (or a Passive NFE with Reportable Person controlling persons) resident in a Reportable Jurisdiction. The node covers indicia-based classification, thresholds (including the USD 250,000 review threshold for Pre-existing Entity Accounts), change-of-circumstances triggers, and the duty to report undocumented accounts to the UAE Competent Authority.

Cross-regime concept: CRS permits a Reporting Financial Institution to rely on information collected and maintained under its AML/KYC procedures for certain determinations, notably identifying Controlling Persons and (below stated thresholds) their residence. It illustrates the interaction between AML customer due diligence records and tax information-reporting classification, while leaving the CRS obligation itself with the institution.

Defined term for a Non-Financial Entity that is not an Active NFE, or certain managed Investment Entities in non-participating jurisdictions. Classification matters because a Passive NFE account becomes reportable where any Controlling Person is a Reportable Person; the node also sets out the Active NFE criteria and the evidence (self-certification, public information, AML/KYC data) used to establish status.

A defined term within the UAE Insurance Authority Board Decision No. 32 of 2017 on the Common Reporting Standard Regulations, identifying the Ministry of Finance (established under Federal Law No. 1 of 1972) as the UAE Competent Authority. It matters because the Competent Authority is the body that agrees common meanings under tax treaties or competent authority agreements and is the counterparty for automatic exchange of financial account information. It binds insurance and takaful companies in the UAE that issue or make payments under Cash Value Insurance Contracts or Annuity Contracts, which must report through this authority.
lookup_terms: automatic exchange of financial account information

data.summary: A 1986 UAE Central Bank circular (No. 394) amending the earlier 1977 advances-to-deposits ratio rule and re-anchoring it to liquidity measurement. It caps the ratio at 1:1 between loans, advances and interbank placements with over three months remaining life, on one side, and stable resources (free own funds, interbank deposits received with over six months remaining life, and stable customer deposits) on the other, with defined inclusions such as bank-issued CDs and certain refinancing. It binds all local and foreign banks for their UAE operations, with local banks having overseas branches also complying on a worldwide consolidated basis.

CBUAE Circular No. 18/2021 (15/11/2021) setting the regulation on national shareholding in banks, requiring that national shareholding never fall below sixty percent of the capital of banks incorporated in the UAE, with natural persons holding that share being UAE citizens and juridical-person ownership computed by look-through to citizen shareholding. It places duties on the board and shareholders to take all reasonable measures to maintain compliance, including scheduling general assembly items, amending articles of association, or issuing reasoned voting advice, and to ensure shareholder voting complies with the Central Bank Law. It binds all banks incorporated in the UAE.
lookup_terms: Central Bank Law Decretal Federal Law 14 of 2018

data.summary: A cross-referenced instrument — Transfer of Significant Shareholding Regulation 05/2020 of 15 April 2020 — defined within the National Shareholding in Banks Regulation as the rules governing transfers of significant shareholdings in banks. The national shareholding regulation obliges bank boards and shareholders to comply with its requirements alongside the sixty percent national ownership floor. Relevant to banks incorporated in the UAE and to parties acquiring or transferring significant stakes.

CBUAE Circular No. 23/2022 (17/2/2022) establishing the Restricted Licence Banks Regulation, which sets the specific requirements applying to banks whose licences restrict them from onboarding natural persons as customers or conducting licensed financial activities with or for natural persons, and which bars accounts or facilities below AED 1,000,000 or equivalent. It covers minimum paid-up capital (AED 1 billion, with foreign branches following the Minimum Capital for Banks Regulation), capital quality, standalone calculation, breach notification and remediation, and approval for profit distributions. It binds all banks, including foreign bank branches, licensed to operate as restricted licence banks in the UAE; all other CBUAE regulations addressed to "all banks" continue to apply.

A cross-referenced CBUAE instrument, the Minimum Capital for Banks Regulation issued via Central Bank Circular No. 12/2021 (14/2/2021), which prescribes the capital that foreign bank branches licensed as restricted licence banks must maintain instead of the AED 1 billion paid-up capital floor applied to locally incorporated restricted licence banks. It is the governing reference for branch-level minimum capital under the Restricted Licence Banks Regulation.

Reference node for the superseded CBUAE Wholesale Commercial Banking Regulation (Board Resolution No. 41/4/2007), which is expressly repealed and replaced by the Restricted Licence Banks Regulation (Circular 23/2022), together with Board Resolution 21/2/88 and Board Circulars 495, 282 and 276. Licences previously issued under the 2007 wholesale banking regime are deemed to continue under the new Regulation from its effective date, with non-compliant banks required to file a compliance plan with the Central Bank within 90 days. Relevant to legacy wholesale/investment banks in the UAE and to anyone tracing the legal lineage of current restricted-licence requirements.

Defined term in the CBUAE Restricted Licence Banks Regulation setting the threshold test for a High-Net-Worth Customer: a natural person with net worth above AED 4,000,000 (excluding primary residence and loans secured on it) and liquid financial assets of at least AED 1,000,000. The definition matters because Restricted Licence Banks are barred from retail banking with natural persons unless the Central Bank grants a discretionary, condition-bound approval, and then only for persons the bank assesses as meeting this definition. Binds Restricted Licence Banks, including branches of foreign banks, when scoping permitted client segments.

Instrument node for the CBUAE Restricted Licence Banks Regulation (Circular 23/2022), covering licensing, permitted activities, and the capital regime for Restricted Licence Banks. Core capital rules require continuous maintenance of a minimum paid-up capital as a licensing prerequisite, AED 1 billion fully paid-up for locally operating restricted banks (foreign branches follow the Minimum Capital for Banks Regulation), no capital reduction without prior Central Bank approval, and possible higher institution-specific minima at licensing. Binds all banks licensed by CBUAE to operate as Restricted Licence Banks in the UAE, including branches of foreign banks.

Provision specifying the quality of capital eligible to meet the minimum requirement: a Restricted Licence Bank's Article 5.1 minimum must be satisfied entirely with fully paid-up capital. Read together with Article 7, which requires the minimum to be calculated on a standalone basis, and with the Central Bank's power to set a higher minimum and define eligible capital quality at licensing. Binds Restricted Licence Banks operating in the UAE.

Provision governing actual or anticipated breaches of the minimum capital requirement by a Restricted Licence Bank: immediate notification to the Central Bank, submission of a remediation plan for Central Bank approval to restore capital, and Central Bank approval for any proposed profit distribution. Operates as the supervisory escalation and capital-preservation mechanism attached to Articles 4–7. Binds Restricted Licence Banks, including branches of foreign banks.

Provision on how the Restricted Licence Banks Regulation interacts with the wider CBUAE rulebook: the Regulation sets only the requirements specific to Restricted Licence Banks, while all other Central Bank regulations, standards, guidelines and instructions that apply to "All Banks" remain fully applicable and enforceable to them. It also flags that restricted banks conducting activities supervised by another regulator must obtain the relevant licences from that regulator. Binds all banks, including foreign bank branches, licensed to operate as Restricted Licence Banks in the UAE.

Article 10 of the CBUAE Restricted Licence Banks (minimum capital) Regulation sets the consequence side of that instrument: breaching any provision of the Regulation or its accompanying Standards exposes the institution to supervisory, administrative and financial measures at the Central Bank's discretion. It indicates the range of available measures, including curtailing or replacing Senior Management or Board powers, interim management of the bank, fines, and barring individuals from the sector. It binds Restricted Licence Banks and, in effect, their directors and senior officers; read together with Article 9, which applies the general Bank Regulations to these entities.

Article 12 of the CBUAE Restricted Licence Banks Regulation lists the earlier Board resolutions and Board circulars that the Regulation repeals and replaces, and sits alongside Article 11 (the Regulatory Development Division as interpretive authority) and Article 13 (publication in the Official Gazette and entry into force one month after publication). It is a transitional/repeal provision rather than a conduct obligation. Useful for confirming which legacy instruments ceased to apply to Restricted Licence Banks and from what date.
lookup_terms: cancellation of previous resolutions and circulars

data.summary: CBUAE guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions on reporting suspicious transactions and activity to the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit, covering why reports matter, report structure and narrative quality, submission via the FIU's reporting portal, report types, amendments, expedited filing, confidentiality and the tipping-off prohibition, responses to FIU information requests, and post-filing handling of the customer relationship. It binds LFIs supervised by the CBUAE and informs how compliance functions and senior management govern the filing process. Read with the AML-CFT Law and AML-CFT Decision, which are the enforceable source of the reporting duty.

The UAE federal AML/CFT statute (Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018, as amended by Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2021) establishing the offences and core obligations for anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and combating the financing of illegal organisations. Relevant provisions include the duty to report suspicions promptly to the FIU with no minimum threshold, criminal sanctions (imprisonment and/or fines) for failure to report intentionally or by gross negligence, and safe-harbour protection from administrative, civil and criminal liability for good-faith reporting by institutions, board members, employees and authorised representatives. It binds all persons and entities within scope, including Licensed Financial Institutions and their managers and staff.

Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019, the implementing regulation of the UAE AML-CFT Law, which operationalises the statutory duties — including the suspicious transaction reporting process, confidentiality and tipping-off controls, and the liability protection for good-faith reporters. It sits between the Law and CBUAE supervisory guidance and binds subject entities, notably Licensed Financial Institutions. Consult it for the detailed procedural requirements behind a reporting or CDD obligation stated in general terms in the Law.

Concept node for the Suspicious Activity Report, one of several report types LFIs may file with the UAE FIU alongside the STR and information-request report types. The guidance treats SARs as covering suspicious activity (not only executed transactions), expects a structured narrative addressing who, what, when, where, why and how, and discourages defensive filings — filings made to avoid non-filing penalties on activity the institution does not genuinely find suspicious — as a sign of weak transaction monitoring and internal controls that may attract supervisory measures. Relevant to LFIs' reporting, quality-assurance and escalation decisions.
lookup_terms: report types AIF AIFT RFI RFIT

data.summary: Concept node for the Compliance Officer acting as the licensed financial institution's Money Laundering Reporting Officer under CBUAE AML/CFT guidance. It sets out the role's ownership of detecting ML/TF and illegal-organisation financing activity, reviewing and filing STRs/SARs with the FIU, taking post-filing actions (watchlisting, risk-rating changes, relationship measures), delivering staff training, and serving as primary liaison with the supervisor, FIU and law enforcement. It binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions through the designated individual and their accountability for an effective risk-based programme.

Concept node describing the first line of defence — customer-facing and business-area employees — within an LFI's transaction monitoring and suspicious activity reporting framework. It explains that institutions must not rely on automated monitoring alone, and that trained staff are expected to recognise red flags relevant to their customers, products, channels and geographies and escalate promptly to management and the second line without displacing their own reporting duty. Relevant to all CBUAE-licensed and supervised financial institutions, including exchange houses, finance companies, PSPs, hawala providers and insurers.

Concept node covering the second line of defence (compliance function) in an LFI's AML/CFT control structure. It provides policy advice, guidance, assurance, oversight and challenge to the first line, oversees the investigations programme across automated and manual monitoring, and holds the exclusive authority for the actual filing of STRs/SARs through the Compliance Officer or MLRO — even where Financial Crime Operations units in the first line conduct the investigation. Applies to all CBUAE-licensed and supervised financial institutions.

Concept node for the third line of defence — independent internal audit — within the CBUAE AML/CFT governance model for licensed financial institutions. It sits alongside the first and second lines in the suspicious activity detection, investigation and reporting framework set out in CBUAE STR/SAR guidance, which rests on Federal Decree-Law No. (20) of 2018 and its implementing decisions. Binds all natural and legal persons licensed or supervised by CBUAE across banking, exchange, finance, payments, hawala and insurance categories.

Concept node on the confidentiality duty and tipping-off prohibition attaching to suspicious activity reporting. LFIs must keep both the reported information and the fact of reporting confidential, protect it from unauthorised access, respond precisely to FIU information requests, and follow any FIU instructions on the transaction and the business relationship after filing. Post-filing decisions (retain, exit or restrict the relationship) rest on the LFI's own policies and risk appetite but must weigh the tipping-off risk; also covers expedited 24-hour filing where circumstances require.

Concept node for the Financial Action Task Force as the international AML/CFT standard-setter referenced across several CBUAE guidance instruments. In the cited material it sits within guidance on suspicious transaction reporting practice — report typology (STR, SAR, AIF, AIFT via goAML), submission triggers and the content expected in a report narrative. Useful as a cross-reference point rather than a binding instrument in itself; the binding obligations sit in the UAE federal AML framework and CBUAE guidance.

An annex of red flag indicators and money laundering/terrorist financing typologies published by the UAE FIU (Biannual Financial Crime Trends and Typologies Report, Jan–Jun 2020) that Licensed Financial Institutions are expected to embed into their AML/CFT programmes, policies, detection scenarios and suspicion-identification criteria. The surrounding material also addresses STR/SAR filing timelines including expedited 24-hour filing, confidentiality and the prohibition on tipping off, responding to FIU information requests, and how to handle the customer relationship after filing. It binds LFIs supervised by the central bank and informs both detection and post-reporting conduct decisions.

The Regulation to Impose Financial Sanctions for Strict Liability Violations (Circular 22/2021) creates a regime under which fixed financial penalties are applied automatically to Licensed Financial Institutions for defined, largely routine regulatory breaches, without further enquiry, representations or appeal (force majeure aside). It rests on the sanctioning powers in the Central Bank Law and covers obligations such as currency handling, court order processing, data reporting and customer certificates. It binds all LFIs, including national banks, foreign bank branches, exchange houses, finance companies and other financial institutions.

Article 2 of the strict liability sanctions regulation restates the central bank's exclusive currency issuance right and the statutory prohibition on issuing or circulating counterfeit or forged notes, coins or bearer instruments resembling legal tender. It makes LFIs strictly liable for circulating counterfeit or forged notes at collection, at transaction, or on delivery to their central bank account, whether deliberate, reckless or negligent, with a fixed fine per item plus the face value; lawfully withdrawn or replaced currency is not treated as counterfeit.

Article 3 addresses the Court Cases Management System, the automated channel through which court orders issued against Licensed Financial Institutions by the participating courts and prosecution bodies are transmitted and monitored. It confirms the obligation to process such court orders within the prescribed time limits and sets a fixed fine per violation plus a daily accrual for each working day of continued delay, subject to a cap.

Article 4 imposes strict liability reporting duties on Licensed Financial Institutions for cross-border SWIFT payment transactions, supporting the central bank's balance of payments and international investment position statistics. LFIs must make the full published list of purpose-of-payment codes available to customers without merging or amending it and must capture purpose codes when initiating cross-border transfers; non-compliance attracts a fixed fine per violation.

Article 5 sets strict liability data reporting requirements for card transactions, supported by definitions covering cashless payment modes (virtual wallets, digital cards, debit, credit, store and prepaid cards), ATMs, cash/cheque deposit machines, card BINs and the Integrated Regulatory Reporting System. Licensed Financial Institutions that fail to meet these card transaction reporting requirements face a fixed fine per violation.

Article of the CBUAE strict-liability financial sanctions regulation requiring banks to issue certificates — including liability statements and clearance letters — to retail customers within seven working days of the customer's application. It ties this duty to the account-closure and certificate provisions of Regulation No. 29/2011 and to a Central Bank circular on normal banking practice, and expressly excludes corporate customers from scope. Binds banks as Licensed Financial Institutions, with a fixed fine per violation plus an escalating daily rate up to a stated cap.

Core reporting article of the CBUAE financial sanctions regulation, setting the obligation of all Licensed Financial Institutions to file regulatory returns through the Integrated Regulatory Reporting System at the required frequency and format, with differentiated monthly/quarterly deadlines for banks, exchange houses and other licensed institutions. It also fixes per-violation fines for late filing, daily escalation rates with caps, and separate penalties for submitting erroneous data. Binds every category of Licensed Financial Institution; the penalty grid is summarised in the regulation's appendix.

Article requiring Licensed Financial Institutions that conduct all or part of their business under Islamic Shari'ah to file an annual Shari'ah report prepared by their Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee with the Higher Shari'ah Authority, by end-February and within two months of financial year end, so the Authority can comment before the general assembly. Grounded in Article 80 of the Central Bank Law. Non-filing triggers a fixed fine with a daily escalation up to a cap, and a separate penalty for erroneous regulatory returns.

Concept node for the CBUAE's Integrated Regulatory Reporting System, the mandated channel through which Licensed Financial Institutions submit regulatory returns at the prescribed frequency and format, and through which the Central Bank publishes changes to reporting obligations via system alerts. Institutions must monitor those alerts during the working day and maintain a formal internal process to meet filing duties. Relevant to all Licensed Financial Institutions; failure to file or filing incorrect data is a sanctionable violation.

Referenced instrument: the CBUAE regulation on bank loans and other services offered to individual customers, cited in the financial sanctions regulation as the source of the duty to close accounts without penalty after one year and to issue an appropriate certificate within seven days of application, alongside the standard account-opening agreement requirements. It applies to commercial banks dealing with individual (retail) customers. Here it functions as the underlying substantive rule that the strict-liability sanctions regime enforces.

CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards accompanying the Consumer Protection Regulation, covering Licensed Financial Institutions' duties on consumer data protection (collection, confidentiality, authorised use, profiling and data mining, disclosure by authorised agents) and on governance — board and senior management responsibility and resourcing of independent risk, compliance and audit control functions for retail operations. Obligations are framed as binding requirements on Licensed Financial Institutions, with confidentiality exceptions limited to lawful compulsion or express consumer consent.

Node covering the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation (Circular No. 8-2020) and its accompanying Standards, with the extracted material centred on Article 6 (protection of consumer data and assets) and parts of Article 5 on suitability/affordability assessment and acting in the consumer's best interest. It requires licensed financial institutions to hold board-approved policies and controls over collection, confidentiality and authorised use of consumer data, to inform consumers in writing how their personal data is processed, to extend confidentiality to authorised agents and new-technology/social-media profiling and marketing, and to retain sales-profiling assessments for at least five years. Binds all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions (including licensed foreign bank branches) in their dealings with Consumers; confidentiality yields only to lawful disclosure orders or express consumer consent.

Article 2 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards sets the disclosure and transparency baseline for all financial products and services across every channel (branch, phone, mobile, internet). It mandates bilingual Arabic/English disclosure, accessibility for People of Determination, and clear, plain, readable presentation; the extract also shows cross-references from Article 5 for credit products, structured products (prior CBUAE approval before sale/marketing) and remittances/transfers/FX (fixed-amount, pre-disclosed fees, including correspondent bank fees). Binds licensed financial institutions towards Consumers.

Node labelled as the Shari'ah governance standard for Islamic financial institutions; the extracted text is in fact Article 11 (Shari'ah compliance for financial services) of the Consumer Protection Standards plus Article 3 provisions on product data requests, "No Objection Letter" applications and enforcement for late filings. It requires IFI boards and senior management to ensure Shari'ah compliance, places responsibility on the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee, mandates fair profit distribution with investment accountholders, embedding Shari'ah compliance in culture and conduct, independent oversight, and consumer education on conventional versus Islamic products; detailed Shari'ah governance rules sit in a separate CBUAE regulation. Binds Islamic financial institutions and Islamic windows; the Higher Shari'ah Authority may add guidance.

Article 3 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards establishes the institutional oversight and governance framework for consumer protection and conduct risk: organisational structure, corporate culture, qualified staff, documented policies and monitoring/control frameworks under board oversight. It requires the regulation's principles to be embedded in management, board governance of conduct and compliance risk (with an equivalent designated representative or committee for licensed foreign bank branches under the Corporate Governance Regulation), and supports the annual Consumer Protection & Conduct Risk Management report and product approval framework. Binds boards and senior management of all licensed financial institutions.
lookup_terms: Consumer Protection & Conduct Risk Management annual report

data.summary: Article 4 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards governs responsible market conduct: institutions must act with integrity, fairness, honesty, competence and transparency, meet consumers only in premises ensuring confidentiality and transaction security, screen and verify retail staff (no fraud/financial-crime record or misconduct dismissal, fit and proper at all times) and require staff to identify themselves and their employer. The extract also shows compliance-culture duties including mystery shopping, thematic reviews, complaint data analysis, non-financial performance metrics and escalation of material code-of-conduct breaches. Binds licensed financial institutions and their staff and agents in dealings with consumers.

Node for Article 5 (business conduct) of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards; the extracted text is drawn largely from adjacent Article 3/4 provisions on compliance-culture monitoring, conduct risk mitigation and product oversight. It covers approved conduct risk frameworks with documented risk appetite and limits, mitigation strategies, independent assessment of retail business and control functions, annual reporting of conduct risk to the board, and a board-approved product approval framework. Binds licensed financial institutions' boards, senior management, control functions and retail business lines.

General product-level conduct and disclosure provisions applying across all Financial Products and/or Services under the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards, and the baseline section that the product-specific sections (deposits, credit, structured products, remittances) each incorporate by reference. It covers unsolicited marketing and promotional contact consent, the rule that silence or inaction is never affirmative consent to a new or optional product, fee or option, tying/bundling limits including the prohibition on Undue Pressure, and accountability and fit-and-proper due diligence for Authorized Agents; it also restricts Exchange Houses from soliciting credit products or assisting account opening. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions dealing with Consumers.

Product-specific disclosure and conduct requirements for Deposit Products, layered on top of the general provisions of Section 2.1.1. It addresses pre-contract disclosure of low-cost savings/current accounts, minimum balance and initial deposit conditions and consequences, expected annual interest/profit rate and payment frequency, all standard and optional fees, and account closure with 60 calendar days' advance written notice and reasons, subject to an exception permitting immediate closure or blocking where there are reasonable grounds of financial crime or fraud risk. Additional Shari'ah disclosure duties apply to IFIs offering compliant deposit products (mudarabah profit-sharing ratio, weights, distribution method, eligibility thresholds).

Provisions governing Credit/Financing Products offered to Consumers, building on Section 2.1.1 and read with the responsible financing requirements. It restricts issuing or bundling a credit card with a Credit Product and automatic credit limit increases without expressed consent, requires a fresh Al Etihad Credit Bureau check plus consent before any limit increase, requires notice and reasons for limit decreases or card closure, and regulates bundling so the Consumer may refuse bundled products while retaining the original credit offer — with a carve-out where credit insurance/takaful is a condition. The related fee schedule caps charges on credit cards and home loans/financing (late payment, early and partial settlement, letters and certificates).

Disclosure regime for structured investment products and Shari'ah compliant structured products, applying in addition to the general provisions of Section 2.1.1 and subject to prior Central Bank approval before marketing or selling. It requires pre-contract disclosure of the issuing bank or entity and its contact details, allocation of responsibilities between the Consumer's institution and the issuer for sales, performance and management, identification of the product's regulator and any Third Party developer and whether it is UAE-regulated, plus quarterly statement content on net interest/profit and loss, itemised and cumulative fees, and complaint channels. IFIs must additionally explain the applicable Shari'ah concepts and investment account rights and obligations in plain language.

Requirements for remittance, transfer and foreign exchange products and services, applying alongside the general provisions of Section 2.1.1 and the corresponding advertising rules in Section 2.3.5. It mandates clear disclosure of all applicable fees and buy/sell exchange rates, best-efforts disclosure (or an estimate plus disclaimer) of correspondent bank or disbursing provider charges, prominent in-branch display of "we buy"/"we sell" rates and remittance buy rates against AED, and prescribed warning statements in advertising about correspondent charges, FX rate exposure and penalties arising from customer error or incomplete information. Read with the business conduct rule that outward transfer fees must be a fixed amount, not a percentage.
lookup_terms: buy and sell exchange rates display

data.summary: Part of Article 2 (Disclosure & Transparency), covering advertising and marketing standards for Financial Products and/or Services and the product-specific advertisement rules that follow. It requires that forecasts of potential returns be labelled illustrative and non-indicative, be accompanied by a prominently displayed loss-risk warning and not be misleading when made; it exempts purely name-only or invitation-to-discuss material from the warning statements and obliges institutions to devise their own warnings where the prescribed ones do not fit their products. Deposit Product advertising quoting an interest/profit rate carries additional prescribed content; binds Licensed Financial Institutions.

Concept node for the annual Consumer Protection & Conduct Risk Management report that Licensed Financial Institutions must produce for the Board under the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards. It is the reporting vehicle through which compliance-culture assessment, code-of-conduct adherence monitoring (including mystery shopping, thematic reviews and complaint data analysis), and the type and level of conduct risk versus risk appetite are evaluated and escalated. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions, their Control functions, Senior Management and the Board.
lookup_terms: Consumer Protection & Conduct Risk Management annual report

data.summary: Concept node for the CBUAE "No Objection Letter" application requirement: Licensed Financial Institutions must apply for a No Objection Letter for new or revised Financial Products and/or Services where the Central Bank prescribes it, with content and turn-around times set by the Central Bank. Related material covers the Central Bank's power to demand detailed product data, additional guidance from the Higher Shari'ah Authority for Islamic Financial Institutions, enforcement exposure for undue delays in filing, and the annexed caps on retail fees and commissions.

Concept node labelled Consumer Mobility but whose extracted content covers the Licensed Financial Institution's duty to act in the Consumer's best interest — documented suitability, appropriateness and affordability assessments (retained five years, confidentiality-bound) — and the rules on blocking Consumer accounts or funds. The blocking rules set permitted grounds (Central Bank instruction, recovery of amounts owed, dishonesty/fraud/conviction, death), a 24-hour written notice duty with a financial-crime carve-out, and prohibitions on overdraft-generating fees, over-blocking, and blocking end-of-service payments for mortgage repayment.

Concept node for the handling of Unauthorized Transactions: Licensed Financial Institutions must offer 24/7 digital and phone reporting channels for loss, theft, fraud or misuse of accounts, cards and digital instruments, with performance standards, call monitoring and one-year record retention. It sets the evidential rule that transactions are treated as authorized where proper secure validation was applied unless the Consumer shows prima facie reasonable doubt, and grants Consumers at least 30 business days to report after being properly informed. Adjacent provisions cover debit card daily limits (with 60 calendar days' written notice of reductions) and ATM/POS investigation, merchant surcharging monitoring and tampering reviews.

Concept node for the Board-approved product approval framework and the associated product-level disclosure duties, with the extracted content focused on structured investment products and Shari'ah compliant structured products. It requires pre-sale disclosure of the issuing entity and its regulator, allocation of responsibilities between the Consumer's Licensed Financial Institution and the issuer, disclosure of Third Party involvement, suitability assessment of the target Consumer segment before advertising, and prescribed capital-loss warning wording in advertising. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions, including Islamic Financial Institutions offering such products.

Concept node on accountability for Authorized Agents: Licensed Financial Institutions must authorize agent access to Consumer Personal Data in writing, monitor it regularly and restrict it to the purpose of access, and include confidentiality and non-disclosure provisions in all outsourcing contracts. Authorized Agents must report significant Personal Data breaches to the institution's Data Management and protection function, and the institution's duty to protect Consumer Data extends to the acts of all Authorized Agents. Agents also act as a receiving point for Unauthorized Transaction reports, which triggers the institution's handling obligations.

Section 2.3 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards (Article 2: Disclosure & Transparency) sets the responsible advertising regime for Licensed Financial Institutions, applying to every promotional channel — branches, websites, apps, ATMs, telephone banking, statements, social and public media in audio, visual or print form. It requires balanced presentation of potential returns (illustrative-only forecasts plus prominent loss-risk warnings), permits omission of warnings in name-only or invitation-to-discuss material, and obliges institutions to craft their own warnings where prescribed ones do not fit their products. Sub-sections add specific content requirements for advertising Deposit Products and Credit Products, and the section must be read with Article 5 (Business Conduct).

Cross-cutting concept in the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards giving Consumers a Cooling-off Period of 5 complete business days after signing a contract for credit, insurance/takaful, structured or other Central Bank-regulated products, with the longer period prevailing where other law or regulation prescribes one. Licensed Financial Institutions must inform the Consumer of the right at signing, hand over all related documentation and disclosures, and may accept a signed written waiver containing a warning about immediate commitment. Anchored in Article 2 (Disclosure & Transparency, clauses on documentation and waiver) and Article 5 (Business Conduct), with price-sensitivity warnings for investment and structured products and a Shari'ah-contract clause requirement for Islamic products.

Concept node covering Article 11 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards, which binds Islamic Financial Institutions (IFIs) offering Islamic Financial Products and/or Services to ensure Board and Senior Management oversight of Shari'ah compliance, with the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee responsible for Shari'ah compliance and fairness under the separate Shari'ah Governance Standard. It also requires fair profit-distribution mechanisms between shareholders and investment accountholders, embedding Shari'ah compliance in culture and operations, independent oversight, and Consumer education on the differences between conventional and Islamic products. Detailed Shari'ah governance rules sit in a separate CBUAE regulation.

Concept node on rate disclosure under the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards, spanning both advertising (Section 2.3.3) and pre-contract disclosure (Article 2.1). Advertising of an Annual Percentage Rate for term lending/financing must be accompanied by a worked example showing total interest/profit and Fees over the term and any qualifying conditions, with an express carve-out for residential mortgages; deposit advertising must state whether the Annual Interest/Profit Rate is fixed or variable, per-term rates in equal prominence, minimum tenor/amount, payment frequency, calculation basis and conditions. Separately, institutions must prominently disclose to Consumers whether a Credit Product rate is fixed, variable or a combination, and the method of calculation.

Concept node on the Base Lending / base financing Rate under the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards: where such a rate forms part of the final interest/profit rate offered, the Licensed Financial Institution must disclose the rate's separate components (base rate plus a stated number of basis points), explain the concept with a clear example, state how often the rate may be revised, and say where rates are publicly posted. It sits alongside the obligations to disclose whether a Credit Product rate is fixed, variable or combined and to disclose all applicable Fees. Related material in Article 7 covers staff training, remuneration and suitability/affordability assessment for lending/financing.

Concept node drawn from Article 3 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards, requiring Licensed Financial Institutions to maintain a Board-approved conduct risk framework to identify, assess, monitor, mitigate and control conduct risk, with documented risk appetite and limits, mitigation strategies, and annual reporting to the Board through the Consumer Protection & Conduct Risk Management report. It also mandates a governance structure covering all retail products, services and Retail Operations including Third Parties, a Board-approved control framework, appropriate mandates for Compliance, Risk and Audit, staff competence in the Consumer Protection Regulation and Standards, and remuneration structures that deter mis-selling and irresponsible risk-taking. A linked requirement obliges a comprehensive Board-approved product approval framework.
lookup_terms: Consumer Protection & Conduct Risk Management annual report
three lines of defence / Compliance Risk Audit mandate

data.summary: Article 6 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation/Standards sets the core duties of Licensed Financial Institutions on collection, protection, confidentiality and authorised use of Consumer Data and Personal Data, anchored in Article 120 of Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018. It requires documented policies, procedures and control frameworks, written disclosure to Consumers on how their data is processed, a secure and confidential environment across all delivery channels, and confidentiality that survives outsourcing to Authorized Agents, subject only to legally compelled disclosure or the Consumer's expressed consent. It binds all CBUAE Licensed Financial Institutions and extends to profiling, data mining, marketing and sale of services via new technologies and social media.
lookup_terms: Protection of Consumer Data and Assets

data.summary: Governance provision requiring the Board of a Licensed Financial Institution to assign responsibility and accountability for the Data Management and Protection function to a senior manager reporting directly to Senior Management, with oversight of the Data Management Control Framework and UAE/CBUAE data protection and privacy requirements. The function must maintain monitoring and preventive controls against unauthorised or accidental loss, misuse, modification, access, disclosure or destruction of Personal Data, verify legitimacy of collection and data integrity, keep monitoring records for five years, review the Framework annually, and investigate and report material data incidents to Senior Management.
lookup_terms: data breach reporting to Senior Management

data.summary: Sets the consent standard for use and sharing of Consumer Personal Data: prior written disclosure of the intent to use/share and of the recipients, consent given freely and explicitly in clear and plain language, with notice of the right to refuse. Informed expressed consent is mandatory before use or transfer of Personal Data for direct marketing (including to Authorized Agents), the consent record must be kept five years after the relationship ends, and Consumers may withdraw consent at any time except where processing is needed for business operations on their own products and services. Related marketing conduct rules treat Consumers as opted out absent opt-in consent and bar telephone marketing of loans/financing to individuals.

Governs disclosure of Consumer Personal Data to Authorized Agents and Third Parties under outsourcing arrangements. Licensed Financial Institutions must apply a fit and proper standard to agents' data management, authorise access in writing, monitor it regularly and restrict it to the stated purpose; outsourcing contracts must contain confidentiality safeguards and prohibit unauthorised disclosure, with agents obliged to report significant Personal Data breaches to the institution's Data Management and Protection function. Liability is non-delegable: the institution's duty to protect Consumer Data covers the acts of all Authorized Agents, and on contract termination data must be retrieved or destroyed, with onward sharing by Third Parties contractually barred unless required by UAE law.
lookup_terms: contract termination data retrieval or destruction

data.summary: Addresses mandatory reporting of Consumer Data to government-authorised Credit Information Agencies (e.g. Al Etihad Credit Bureau) and the duty to inform Consumers of this reporting and of the possible impact on future access to Financial Products and/or Services. Where reported information contains errors, omissions or inaccuracies, the Licensed Financial Institution must correct it within seven complete business days of becoming aware, and must request deletion of Personal Data that was unlawfully collected and reported.

Sets retention and destruction standards for Consumer records: all Personal Data, documents, records and files must be securely retained for at least five years, running from the later of termination of the Business Relationship/account closure or completion of a casual transaction. Confidentiality and security standards continue after the relationship ends until destruction; data must not be processed or kept longer than necessary for its purpose, and after the mandatory period institutions must take reasonable steps to destroy or permanently delete it. Also covers the seven-business-day deadline to report Consumer-requested updates or corrections to Credit Information Agencies.

Conduct-of-business provisions in the CBUAE Consumer Protection instrument governing debit card usage limits, ATM and POS service quality, and terminal security. It requires Licensed Financial Institutions to obtain Consumer consent to daily ATM/POS transaction limits at issuance or reissuance, give 60 calendar days' written notice before reducing limits or changing card terms, investigate Consumer complaints about incorrect or failed ATM/POS transactions, monitor merchant clients for unauthorised surcharging, and monitor and document evidence of ATM/POS fraud and tampering (including reversing previously authorised transactions). It also imposes physical and technical security duties on ATMs (PIN pad shields, anti-skimming devices, sensors, cameras, progressive upgrades). Binds Licensed Financial Institutions in the UAE; note this is a CBUAE instrument, not SAMA.

General disclosure and conduct requirements for Credit/Financing Products under the CBUAE consumer protection framework, applied on top of the baseline provisions of the general section. Covers pre-contract disclosure of the expected Annual Percentage Rate, security/guarantor/collateral requirements and disposal rights, disclosure of how interest/profit is calculated at contracting, and rules on credit cards: no issuance, bundling or automatic limit increases without express Consumer consent, a fresh Al Etihad Credit Bureau check plus express consent before any limit increase, and notice with reasons for limit decreases or closures. Also regulates bundling (right to refuse bundled products, written explanation of benefits, Shari'ah compliance, and the credit insurance/takaful exception). Binds Licensed Financial Institutions offering credit or financing to Consumers in the UAE.
lookup_terms: credit card limit increase express consent

data.summary: Consumer protection provisions specific to remittance, transfer and foreign exchange products and services, layered on the general requirements of the relevant section. Requires clear disclosure of all fees and applicable buy/sell exchange rates (including best efforts to disclose or estimate correspondent bank and disbursing provider fees), prominent in-branch display of buy/sell rates for major currencies and remittance buy rates, and prescribed warning statements in advertising about correspondent-side fees, penalties for customer error or incomplete information, and FX-rate exposure. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions, including exchange houses and money transfer providers, in the UAE.
lookup_terms: buy and sell exchange rate display

data.summary: Requires every Licensed Financial Institution to maintain and operate a written Conflict of Interest policy proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of its Licensed Financial Activities, identifying circumstances that could harm Consumers and specifying mitigation procedures and non-compliance handling. Where conflicts are unavoidable, the institution must disclose their nature/source and obtain the Consumer's written acknowledgement before proceeding, and implement controls. Also covers commission-based distribution through Authorized Agents (disclosure, agent duty to act in Consumers' best interests, monitoring for abusive sales practices), information barriers between business lines and connected parties regarding Personal Data, gifts and inducements rules, and Board-level control over outsourcing/insourcing conflicts.
lookup_terms: fair treatment of consumers board framework

data.summary: Sets the Board-level control framework for fair treatment of Consumers (ethics in selling, complaint handling, assisting People of Determination, equal treatment, confidentiality, conflicts, service standards, prompt correction of Errors) together with a Code of Fair Treatment of Consumers that must be distributed to Staff, trained on, annually reminded by Senior Management and used in performance appraisal. It then sets specific duties towards financially distressed Consumers: providing qualified debt/credit counselling, giving reasonable consideration to alternative repayment arrangements, proactively assisting at the first signs of payment irregularity, and ensuring counselling Staff are trained and treat Consumers with respect. Binds the Board, Senior Management and Staff of Licensed Financial Institutions.

Governs how Licensed Financial Institutions and their authorised collection agents may pursue debts owed by Consumers. Requires written collection policies and procedures, documented discussion of financial difficulties before collection, enforcement of collateral/guarantees or litigation, engagement with the Consumer once an account is in Arrears and mandatory contact where Arrears persist 30 calendar days. Contact is restricted to 9 AM–8 PM with no unreasonable or excessive attempts, each communication must identify the institution/agent, department, contact number, working hours and caller, all communications must be recorded and retained for 5 years after settlement or write-off, and the Consumer must be told if a Third Party collector is appointed, what it may collect and the scope of its authority including receipt of payments.

Sub-section 6.2.1 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards setting conduct-based safeguarding duties over consumer assets, records and collateral, with accountability assigned to Senior Management and an internal control structure covering segregation of duties, operational risk mitigation, logical and physical access security, and documentation aligned with UAE AML/CTF guidance. It extends specific protections to unclaimed assets, Stored Value Facilities, digital money and dormant accounts, and requires collateral to be held and managed honestly, fairly and in the consumer's best interest. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions in the UAE and, indirectly, their staff, authorised agents and third parties with access to consumer assets.

Sub-sections 6.2.2–6.2.3 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards covering fraud detection systems proportionate to product risk, consumer notification of theft/loss/fraud reporting procedures, a dedicated fraud investigation and reporting function for financial crime compliance, and consumer alerts where fraud patterns emerge. It sets a reporting cascade to the Central Bank: immediate notification of significant fraud events, quarterly reporting of fraud-related consumer complaints and security vulnerabilities, and an annual summary report by 31 January. Adjacent provisions impose due diligence on third parties, authorised agents and staff, ATM maintenance records retained one year, and potential liability of the institution for direct losses from its own control breaches.

Article 7 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards, which governs responsible lending/financing and Credit Products offered to Consumers through any distribution channel, and must be read with Article 2 (Disclosure and Transparency) and Article 5 (Business Conduct). It subjects credit granting to the institution's credit risk policies, requires assessment of the consumer's ability to meet obligations and compliance with Central Bank Debt Burden Ratio limits, and imposes pre-contract consumer education including the offer document and Key Facts Statement. The source extract also carries the annexure of maximum fee and commission caps for retail customer services. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions dealing with Consumers.

Combines the business-conduct duty (5.1.1.13–5.1.1.16) to maintain policies, procedures, controls and training for consistently assessing consumers' needs, objectives and product appropriateness/suitability/affordability, with the Article 7 credit-specific suitability framework (7.1.3.3–7.1.3.5). It requires a free summary copy of any suitability/affordability assessment to the consumer, documented methods and clear approval authorities with independently reviewed exceptions, plus verification of income, purpose of credit and creditworthiness via the Credit Information Agency, and provision of General Advice. Profiling assessments must be documented, kept confidential and retained at least five years. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions and their sales and credit staff.

Affordability limb of the CBUAE consumer assessment duties, linking the Article 5 conduct requirement to assess affordability with Article 7 provisions (7.1.4.4–7.1.4.7) on interest/profit-rate stress testing, examination of the consumer's credit record and past credit behaviour, and determination of affordability from information supplied by the consumer and the Credit Information Agency. It requires a written stress-test summary acknowledged in writing by the consumer and a dated, signed affordability assessment summary given to the consumer, and ties the outcome to prudent observance of the Central Bank's Debt Burden Ratio. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions granting credit to Consumers.

Provisions on the Debt Burden Ratio and assessment of a consumer's total debt repayment obligations (7.1.4.7–7.1.4.9), requiring compliance with the Central Bank-prescribed DBR, comprehensive due diligence on overall secured and unsecured indebtedness, and verification with the Credit Information Agency. It prescribes how the approvable credit amount is calculated, including treatment of interest/profit-only construction-phase mortgages and discounted introductory rates (use the highest applicable rate; refuse the financing if the DBR is breached), and prohibits balloon structures used to circumvent DBR, personal financing limits or loan-to-value ratios. It also bars granting excessive credit beyond what the consumer needs or requested. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions.

An annexure schedule setting maximum permitted fees and commissions (in AED) that licensed institutions may charge retail customers across personal accounts, debit and credit cards, consumer, car and home loans/financing, remittances and term deposits. It caps items such as account closure, liability/no-liability letters, card replacement, late payment penalties, early/partial settlement (typically 1% subject to an absolute ceiling) and statement or certificate issuance. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions dealing with Consumers and operates as a hard pricing ceiling rather than guidance.

Provisions governing how Annual Interest/Profit Rate and Annual Percentage Rate must be disclosed in advertising of deposit and Credit Products, including fixed vs variable status, tenor and minimum amount conditions, payment frequency, calculation/compounding basis, and a worked example of total interest/profit and Fees (residential mortgages excepted). It also governs rate-change notification: where an increase applies to the margin over the variable Base Lending/Financing Rate, the institution must give 30 calendar days' notice with specified content, and must notify Consumers in Writing of missed payments and Arrears consequences. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions offering Credit Products to Consumers.

Article 8 establishes the end-to-end Complaint handling regime: a UAE-situated Consumer Complaint Management function independent of Retail Operations, Senior Management–approved policies, acknowledgment and turnaround-time standards, staff quality monitoring, and a free-of-charge Complaint Resolution Mechanism supervised by the Central Bank. It also requires ongoing monitoring and analysis of Complaint Data (received/closed/pending, substantiated, overdue, outside target time, before courts, escalated) for regulatory reporting. Binds all Licensed Financial Institutions in their dealings with Consumers.

Defines the required Complaint Management function: located in the UAE, capable of being combined with another suitable function based on business nature, size, Conflict of Interests potential and complexity, but independent of Retail Operations and able to review escalated Complaints and recommend redress. It lists the function's responsibilities (handling principles, channel monitoring, roles across Retail Operations/Risk/Compliance/Audit, service standards, governance, oversight and regulatory reporting) and the supporting process requirements, including written acknowledgment within 2 business days, a dedicated phone line and secure web portal, Senior Management–approved policies, Code of Fair Treatment of Consumers, and confidentiality of Complaint information. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions.
lookup_terms: Code of Fair Treatment of Consumers

data.summary: Article 9 requires Licensed Financial Institutions to establish a Consumer Education and Awareness (CEA) function delivering generic, minimally promotional educational programs for Consumers and the public, supporting the Central Bank law's financial literacy mandate. It mandates an annual summary report to the Central Bank by 31 January covering the prior year's activities and the coming year's proposed programme, permits collaboration with other organisations provided the institution's own consumer base has full access, and expects pre-release testing of initiatives. Adjacent material covers assessing Consumer needs, suitability and affordability, 5-year retention of profiling assessments, and the duty to act in the Consumer's best interest.

Labelled as the financial inclusion node, but the attached material addresses access-related conduct rules: account closure by the institution with 60 calendar days' written notice and written reasons (subject to a financial crime compliance exception), and strict limits on blocking accounts, transactions, funds or privileges except under Central Bank request, applicable UAE law, or a court order, with record-keeping for Central Bank review. It also covers marketing conduct — no unsolicited marketing calls without express consent, restrictions on Exchange Houses selling Credit Products or facilitating bank account opening, and the rule that silence or inaction is never consent to a new or optional Financial Product, Service or Fee. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions, including Exchange Houses.

This node is Table 2 annexed to the UAE Insurance Authority Board Decision No. (30) of 2016 on Motor Vehicle Insurance Tariffs, setting the premium rates for combined loss-and-damage plus third-party liability motor policies. It fixes, by vehicle category (saloon, 4WD, light and heavy trucks, buses by seating capacity and private/commercial use, equipment, motorcycles), a maximum rate percentage, a minimum premium, and fixed driver and passenger cover amounts for a 13-month insurance period. It binds insurance companies, agents and brokers writing motor cover in the UAE, which may not levy any additional charge without an Insurance Authority decision; note this is a UAE (not KSA) instrument and applies from 1 January 2017.
lookup_terms: own damage and third party liability premium

data.summary: This node is the operative preventive-measures part of the CBUAE AML/CFT guidance on payment-sector risks, explaining how licensed financial institutions (LFIs), including non-bank payment service providers, should apply risk-based controls across payment products, services and systems. It covers segmented expectations for LFIs serving payment customers directly (consumers and merchants, payers and payees) versus those serving other payment-sector participants, and addresses transaction monitoring and suspicious transaction/activity reporting to the UAE FIU. It is guidance rather than new law, but sets supervisory expectations for demonstrating compliance with the AML-CFT Law and AML-CFT Decision; relevant where payment chains are intermediated and each LFI retains its own monitoring responsibility.

This node is the referenced UAE primary AML/CFT statute — Decree Federal Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organisations, as amended by Decree Federal Law No. (26) of 2021 — as cited in the CBUAE payments guidance. Within this context it is invoked for the suspicious transaction reporting duty and for the obligation to apply targeted financial sanctions directives. It binds financial institutions and other reporting entities in the UAE; the node itself is a cross-reference within CBUAE guidance rather than the full statutory text.

This node covers UAE Cabinet Decision No. (74) of 2020 on the Terrorism Lists Regulation and implementation of UN Security Council resolutions on terrorism, terrorist financing and proliferation financing, as cited in the CBUAE payments guidance. It supplies the legal framework for targeted financial sanctions in the UAE, including the Local Terrorist List and the UN Consolidated List, alongside the duty to apply competent-authority directives promptly. It binds licensed financial institutions, which are expected to maintain a sanctions compliance programme covering customer and transaction screening.

This node captures the FATF standards and guidance relied on as an interpretive source in CBUAE AML/CFT guidance materials, including FATF-derived definitions (for example nesting in correspondent banking) and risk-based approach expectations. It is not binding law in itself; it informs how supervisory expectations and national requirements are framed and applied by licensed financial institutions. Useful when tracing the origin of a defined term or a risk typology cited by the supervisor.

This node is the concept of New Payment Products and Services within the CBUAE payments AML/CFT guidance: internet- and smartphone-based payment applications, prepaid cards and devices, and similar innovative channels offered by both banks and non-traditional participants. It matters because such participants may be regulated as financial institutions in some jurisdictions and not others, creating direct and indirect exposure for UAE LFIs. It shapes risk assessment and customer due diligence expectations for LFIs dealing with these providers or their underlying users, including crowdfunding platforms and charities.

Article 11 of the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards sets the conduct-side Shari'ah compliance obligations that apply when Islamic Financial Institutions offer Islamic Financial Products and/or Services, cross-referring to the separate Shari'ah Governance framework. It places duties on the Board, Senior Management and the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee covering Shari'ah compliance culture and independent oversight, fair profit distribution between shareholders and investment accountholders, consumer education on conventional versus Islamic products, disclosure of the legal consequences of contracts and consumer choices, access to internal Shari'ah functions, and limits on charity/late-payment obligations where a consumer is insolvent or bankrupt (not Mumatil). It also requires adherence to the Central Bank's Early Settlement Fee requirements and to permissible debt-retention limits under relevant HSA resolutions.
lookup_terms: Islamic Financial Products and Services disclosure

data.summary: This is the Annexure to the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation/Standards listing maximum caps (in AED) on fees and commissions that Licensed Financial Institutions may charge on retail customer services, covering personal accounts, debit cards, consumer loans/financing, car finance and remittances. It operationalises the Standards' fee provisions, under which institutions must not exceed Central Bank-prescribed caps, must obtain prior Central Bank approval for fees and fee increases, and must give consumers the applicable fee schedule. It binds all Licensed Financial Institutions dealing with retail consumers.
lookup_terms: maximum limits for fees and commissions
account closure fee / liability letter fee

data.summary: A cross-reference node to Higher Shari'ah Authority Resolution No. 76/3/2019 on early settlement, as applied through the CBUAE Consumer Protection Standards. The effect is that Licensed Financial Institutions may impose Early Settlement Fees only to the extent of actual costs incurred from the early settlement process, consistent with the HSA resolution, and must reflect this in product disclosure statements; related provisions address waiver of part of outstanding debt and permissible limits of debt/liability that IFIs may retain. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions, with specific relevance to Islamic financing.

Insurance Authority Board of Directors' Decision No. 30 of 2016 issuing the Regulation for Motor Vehicle Insurance Tariffs (now within CBUAE's insurance mandate), effective 1 January 2017. It fixes minimum and maximum premium tariffs for third-party liability policies (Table 1) and for combined loss/damage and third-party liability policies (Table 2), sets a 13-month insurance period with pro-rata premium, requires tariffs to be inclusive of coverages, administrative charges, commissions and ambulance/medical transport loading, and prohibits insurers, agents or brokers from taking any additional amount without Authority approval. It binds insurance companies, agents and brokers writing motor insurance in the UAE.
lookup_terms: third party liability motor premium cap

data.summary: A referenced instrument: Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 25 of 2016 issuing the Regulation of the Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policies, which supplies the standard policy wordings and coverages that the motor tariff Regulation prices. Within the tariff Regulation it functions as the baseline: any coverage agreed beyond the Resolution No. 25 policies requires a separately stated additional premium, set out in clear wording in a different colour or by addendum. It binds insurance companies issuing motor policies in the UAE.

Table 1 attached to the Motor Vehicle Insurance Tariffs Regulation, forming an integral part of it, setting the minimum and maximum AED premiums for Third Party Liability motor policies over a 13-month insurance period. Rates are banded by vehicle type and use (saloon private/commercial, four-wheel drive, etc.) and by engine cylinder count. It binds insurers pricing third-party liability motor cover, which must compete only within the stated floor and ceiling.
lookup_terms: saloon private commercial four wheel drive rates

data.summary: Concept node within the CBUAE payment-sector AML/CFT guidance describing nesting: where a payment-sector participant obtains indirect access to banking or correspondent services through another institution's relationship, so the account bank has no visibility of the ultimate underlying customers or merchants. It explains why long, multi-party payment chains (merchant acquiring, payment aggregation, gateways, card scheme operators) raise the likelihood of nested relationships and of layered reliance on someone else's merchant due diligence. Relevant to licensed financial institutions that bank or serve other payment-sector participants, and instructive for KSA analysts assessing analogous downstream-access and KYB/reliance risk.

Concept node in the CBUAE payment-sector guidance covering intermediation as an ML/FT risk driver: the insertion of multiple intermediaries (gateways, processors, aggregators, agents) between payer and payee that obscures who the underlying customer or merchant actually is. It is grouped with nesting and use of agents/affiliates as factors that degrade an institution's understanding of its merchant base, with heightened concern in cross-border chains and where CDD on merchants is outsourced to third parties. Directed at licensed financial institutions participating in or servicing the payment sector.

Instrument reference to the CBUAE Stored Value Facilities Regulation (Circular No. 6/2020, Notice 4834/2020), cited in the payment-sector AML/CFT guidance as the licensing framework for SVF providers. Its Article 14 is flagged as requiring all SVF licensees to meet CBUAE AML/CFT legal and regulatory obligations and to mitigate ML/FT risk through preventive measures. Binds SVF licensees (prepaid card and e-wallet issuers) as a subset of licensed financial institutions.

Concept node on Correspondent Banking Relationships as defined and applied in CBUAE guidance, anchored on Article 25 of the AML-CFT Decision: prohibition on dealing with shell banks, information gathering on the respondent, assessment of its AML/CFT controls, senior management approval, and clarity on each party's responsibilities. The guidance extends these duties to correspondent-type relationships with payment-sector participants (SVF providers, retail payment services, card schemes) and stresses that each institution remains responsible for monitoring transactions passing through it, including detecting nesting. Binds licensed financial institutions providing account or clearing access to other institutions.

CBUAE guidance setting out ML/FT risk understanding and expected preventive measures for the payment sector, including non-bank payment service providers, SVF providers, card schemes and banks acting as issuers or acquirers. It analyses risk drivers (transaction speed, limits, open vs closed loop, funding and cash access, cross-border movement, regulatory gaps, intermediation, nesting, agents) and then prescribes control expectations split between institutions serving customers/merchants directly and those servicing other payment-sector participants, plus targeted financial sanctions obligations. Non-binding in form but states supervisory expectations for demonstrating compliance with the AML-CFT Law, AML-CFT Decision and Cabinet Decision 74.

CBUAE guidance on ML/FT risks relating to Politically Exposed Persons, issued under the supervisory-guidance mandate in Article 44.11 of the AML-CFT Decision and read alongside the CBUAE AML/CFT Procedures and Guidelines. It sets definitions for PEPs, heads of international organisations and international organisations, and articulates supervisory expectations for identifying and managing PEP relationships. Addressed to CBUAE-licensed financial institutions; it states expectations rather than creating new legal obligations, with the underlying law prevailing on conflict.

CBUAE guidance applying the UAE AML/CFT framework to the insurance sector, mapping sector participants (conventional and Takaful insurers, reinsurers, tied agents, brokers, health insurance third-party administrators) and the product split between life/investment-related insurance and general insurance. It states that only life and other investment-related insurance products fall within the AML/CFT obligations under the AML-CFT Decision, making product classification the gateway to scope. It binds CBUAE-licensed insurers, reinsurers, agents and brokers, which must each assess their own ML/FT risks.

CBUAE guidance on when and how licensed financial institutions may rely on digital identity systems to perform customer identification and verification under the CDD obligation, which is treated as technology-neutral and open to non-documentary evidence. It requires LFIs to assess a digital ID system's assurance levels (self-assessed or via a credible expert body) and its appropriateness for the institution's business and risk profile, and to document and periodically refresh both assessments. Scope is limited to identity proofing/enrollment and authentication for natural-person customers; it does not cover legal-person representatives or beneficial owners, nor portability/interoperability.
