Section of the CBUAE payment-sector AML/CFT guidance dealing with CDD, EDD and ongoing monitoring where onboarding is digital rather than face-to-face (e-KYC). It confirms that payment-sector participants (stored value facilities, retail payment services, card schemes) generally form business relationships rather than occasional-customer dealings, so the full CDD set applies to every customer type, with added emphasis on confirming the person using the service is the identified customer and on ID-document verification. It binds LFIs offering or exposed to payment products and services.
lookup_terms: new payment products and services NPPS

data.summary: Section of the CBUAE payment-sector AML/CFT guidance setting out correspondent banking due diligence duties: no relationships with shell banks, information gathering on the respondent's business and reputation, evaluation of its AML/CFT controls, senior management approval before onboarding, and clarity on each party's AML/CFT responsibilities. It applies these duties to relationships with payment-sector participants and stresses that in intermediated transaction chains each LFI remains responsible for monitoring transactions passing through it, with attention to nesting and indirect access risk. Binds LFIs providing correspondent or account services to payment firms.
lookup_terms: payment service provider bank account access

data.summary: The sanctions/risk-understanding component of the CBUAE payment-sector AML/CFT guidance, framing how LFIs are exposed to payment participants that may be regulated financial institutions in some jurisdictions and unregulated in others, directly or indirectly. It walks through the roles in a card-based e-commerce transaction (payment gateway, scheme operator, payment processor, issuing and acquiring banks, payment account information services) to show where screening visibility and regulatory gaps arise. Relevant to LFIs assessing sanctions and ML/FT exposure across cross-border and intermediated payment flows.

Section of the CBUAE payment-sector AML/CFT guidance on ongoing transaction monitoring and suspicious transaction reporting. LFIs must monitor all customer activity using information gathered through CDD, calibrated to customer, product, channel and geographic risk, and must report to the UAE FIU whenever there are reasonable grounds to suspect proceeds of crime or a crime-related transaction or attempted transaction, regardless of amount. It stresses that in intermediated payment chains each LFI remains responsible for monitoring the transactions it processes, using the information available to it.

Node within CBUAE guidance on politically exposed persons dealing with the concept of a Related Customer, i.e. a PEP's direct family members (spouse, children, children's spouses, parents) and close associates (joint ownership or other close business ties, or persons holding interests on the PEP's behalf), who must be treated as if they were PEPs themselves. It explains that the listed relationships are a mandatory minimum rather than an exhaustive list, and that risk rating should reflect the underlying PEP's risk plus the nature, strength and persistence of the connection, including where multiple PEP links exist (higher rating applies). Binds licensed financial institutions supervised by the CBUAE under the AML-CFT Decision.

Node covering the enhanced due diligence regime for PEPs under the AML-CFT Decision as explained in CBUAE guidance: senior management approval before establishing or continuing the relationship, reasonable measures to establish source of funds and wealth, and enhanced ongoing monitoring, on top of standard CDD. It distinguishes the automatic application of these measures to foreign PEPs and their Related Customers from the risk-triggered application to domestic PEPs and heads of international organisations and their Related Customers (only where the relationship is high risk). Binds licensed financial institutions; the guidance stresses that PEP status is not a basis for blanket de-risking.

Node on identifying and classifying customers and beneficial owners as PEPs or Related Customers, which the guidance expects to occur at the CDD stage before the relationship begins, with ongoing screening thereafter. It notes the differing legal standards (risk management systems for foreign PEPs; sufficient measures for domestic PEPs and HIOs) but recommends screening all customers in practice, including nationals who may qualify as foreign PEPs, and touches on looking beyond the 25% beneficial ownership threshold where PEP families hold fragmented stakes. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Node addressing the requirement to take reasonable measures to establish the source of funds and source of wealth of PEPs, Related Customers and their beneficial owners as part of PEP enhanced due diligence. It explains the expected analysis: collecting declared net worth and principal income sources, corroborating with public or third-party information such as asset declarations or published salaries, and testing consistency of declared wealth against both declared income and actual financial behaviour, with deeper verification where risk is higher. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Node within CBUAE AML/CFT guidance for the insurance sector describing the sector's participants (insurers, reinsurers, tied agents, brokers, third-party administrators) and the general customer due diligence expectations applicable to them. It is important for scope: only life insurance and other investment-related (funds accumulation) products fall within the AML/CFT framework, while general property and liability insurance does not. Binds CBUAE-licensed insurance companies, reinsurers, agents and brokers conducting in-scope business.

Node covering enhanced due diligence expectations for the insurance sector under CBUAE AML/CFT guidance, applied to higher-risk customers, products and distribution arrangements within in-scope insurance business. It sits on the same scope basis as the sector's general CDD: life and investment-related insurance products are within the AML/CFT framework, general insurance is not, and each licensed insurer, reinsurer, agent and broker must assess its own ML/FT risk. Binds CBUAE-licensed insurance operators and intermediaries.

A node within CBUAE's AML/CFT guidance for the insurance sector (UAE instrument, persuasive comparator only for KSA work) dealing with simplified due diligence in insurance. The surrounding material scopes the sector — conventional and Takaful insurers, reinsurers, tied agents, brokers and third-party administrators — and limits AML/CFT application to life and other investment-related insurance products, general insurance falling outside the UAE AML-CFT Decision. Any SDD relief must therefore be read against that product scope and against the operator's own ML/FT risk assessment; the extract supplied here is sector definition, so the SDD conditions themselves must be checked in the source.

A node within CBUAE's insurance-sector AML/CFT guidance addressing reliance on third parties and outsourcing of CDD functions. It is relevant because the insurance distribution chain involves tied agents, independent brokers and health insurance third-party administrators, each of which may touch customer onboarding on the insurer's behalf. The key regulatory consequence is allocation of responsibility: reliance on an intermediary does not displace the licensed insurer's own CDD and record-keeping obligations — confirm the specific conditions in the source text, as the excerpt supplied is the sector participant definitions.

Covers identification and verification of beneficial owners under the UAE AML-CFT Decision as applied to insurance operators: for legal-person customers, all natural persons with a controlling ownership interest of 25 percent or more, falling back to senior managing officials only as a last resort where no such person is identified; for legal arrangements, the settlor, trustee(s) and equivalent positions. It also links BO uncertainty to enhanced due diligence — corroborating source of wealth, external intelligence reports, screening benefactors, and scrutinising customers holding multiple policies with a common beneficial owner. Binds licensed insurers, reinsurers, agents and brokers conducting CDD.

Node on the enterprise-wide ML/FT risk assessment expected of insurance operators under CBUAE guidance. Its analytical anchor is that only life and other investment-related insurance (long-term savings/investment-type cover) falls within the UAE AML/CFT perimeter, while general property and liability insurance does not — so the risk assessment must be product-scoped, and cover customers, distribution channels (tied agents versus independent brokers), and geography. Binds each licensed insurer, reinsurer, agent and broker individually.

CBUAE guidance on the use of digital identity systems for CDD by licensed financial institutions. It requires an LFI to assess both the system's assurance levels (performed itself with due diligence on the IDSP, or via audit/certification from a competent expert body applying publicly disclosed assurance frameworks) and its appropriateness for the institution's business and risk profile, with both assessments documented and updated periodically and on trigger events. It also flags the interaction with official identity infrastructure (Emirates ID online validation gateway) and with data protection and privacy law.

Section of the CBUAE digital ID guidance dealing with the identity proofing and enrollment stage: presence, resolution, evidence, validation and verification factors, illustrated against no/high/very high assurance tiers adapted from NIST digital ID guidelines. No specific assurance level is mandated; the LFI must assess and justify what level is appropriate given its ML, TF, fraud and other illicit financing risks. It also identifies the threat landscape — stolen or counterfeit identity evidence, impersonation and synthetic identities — that the proofing stage must withstand.

A referenced external technical standard (NIST Digital Identity Guidelines) that the CBUAE digital ID guidance adapts, for illustration only, into a table of reliability factors — presence, resolution, evidence, validation, verification — mapped across no/high/very high assurance tiers for the identity proofing and enrollment stage. It is not itself binding: the guidance neither mandates nor recommends a particular assurance level, leaving licensed financial institutions to judge appropriate levels against their ML/TF, fraud and illicit finance risk. Relevant to UAE LFIs assessing whether a digital ID system is reliable and independent for CDD; it is persuasive reference material only for KSA-regulated entities.

Sets out the first limb of the CBUAE digital ID expectation: before adopting a digital ID system for CDD, an LFI must establish the system's assurance levels — its reliability and independence — either by performing the assessment itself or by relying on audit/certification from an expert body. Self-assessment triggers due diligence on the ID service provider, including its governance; reliance on an expert body (including a group entity or independent third party) requires a reasonable basis that the body correctly applies publicly disclosed assurance frameworks. The assessment must be documented and refreshed periodically and on trigger events; no specific internal function is prescribed to own it.

The second limb of the CBUAE digital ID expectation: having established a system's assurance levels, an LFI must separately determine whether that system is appropriate for CDD given its own business and risk profile, including financial-inclusion considerations where biometric authentication may fail for certain vulnerable groups. Like the assurance assessment, the appropriateness determination must be documented (within or outside the enterprise risk assessment) and updated periodically and on event triggers. Binds UAE LFIs adopting digital ID for customer identification and verification.

Node covering the CBUAE guidance's use of the NIST 800-63 Digital Identity Guidelines as an illustrative benchmark for grading the identity proofing and enrollment stage across assurance tiers, alongside the two-route assurance assessment (self-assessment with IDSP due diligence, or expert-body audit/certification). Useful for understanding what evidence quality, validation and verification expectations look like in practice when judging a digital ID system's reliability. Non-mandatory reference; the operative obligation is the documented assurance and appropriateness assessment by the LFI.

Addresses the UAE government-supported validation channels — the online validation gateway of the Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs & Port Security, UAE Pass, or equivalent — that LFIs are expected to use to confirm identity information presented during digital onboarding matches reliable government sources. Sits within the proofing sequence of collection, validation, verification (including biometric/liveness checks), and enrollment/binding of credentials and authenticators. Binds UAE LFIs performing remote identity verification; the KSA analogue would be locally mandated national identity verification sources.
lookup_terms: Federal Authority for Identity Citizenship Customs & Port Security

data.summary: A concept node within CBUAE guidance on digital ID for AML/CFT purposes, flagging that digital identity systems collect and process personal data (including biometrics) and therefore sit under UAE data protection and privacy requirements alongside identity-proofing rules. It points to the relevant UAE federal instruments (cybercrime/rumours decree-law, electronic transactions and trust services decree-law), internet access management policy and Emirate-level rules, and to reliance on official identity infrastructure such as Emirates ID, the Federal Authority for Identity and Citizenship validation gateway, UAE Pass and Emirates facial recognition. Relevant to licensed financial institutions deciding whether and how to use digital ID for CDD, and to how they retain copies and verification records.
lookup_terms: Federal Authority for Identity and Citizenship validation gateway
Federal Decree-Law No. 46 of 2021 electronic transactions and trust services

data.summary: A concept node from CBUAE digital ID guidance covering the authentication stage of a digital ID system: confirming that the claimant is the same person who was identity-proofed, enrolled and credentialed. It distinguishes knowledge, possession and inherence (biometric) authentication factors, addresses multi-factor authentication for high-risk customer activities such as personal-data changes, third-party payee registration and high-value transfers, and discusses phishing-resistant authenticators and continuous/behavioural biometric authentication. It informs how licensed financial institutions calibrate authentication controls for ongoing account access and fraud/ML risk.

UAE Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020 on the Terrorism Lists Regulation and implementation of UN Security Council resolutions on terrorism, terrorist financing and proliferation financing, abrogating Cabinet Decision No. 20 of 2019. It sets the procedures for listing, de-listing and re-listing persons on Local Lists and for proposing designations to the UN Security Council or a Sanctions Committee, and for publication, freezing and other measures, including grievance routes before the Competent Court. It binds the Supreme Council for National Security, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Executive Office, supervisory and law enforcement authorities, and, through freezing obligations, financial institutions and DNFBPs.

Defined-term node for "the Council" under Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020, meaning the UAE Supreme Council for National Security. It is the body that assesses designation criteria, proposes listings and de-listings on Local Lists via the Ministry of Presidential Affairs to the Cabinet, proposes designations to the UN Security Council or Sanctions Committees, and decides on requests to lift freezing or other measures within set time limits. Understanding this role matters for identifying who makes designation decisions versus who merely publishes or implements them.

Defined-term node for "the Office", the Executive Office of the Committee for Goods Subjected to Import and Export Control, under Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020. It publishes and circulates the Sanctions List and Local Lists to supervisory authorities, financial institutions and DNFBPs without delay and without prior notice to the listed person, receives and routes de-listing and unfreezing requests to the Council, collects implementation outcomes and statistics, and conducts outreach, training and guidance on compliance. It is the operational interface between the designation authorities and regulated entities implementing freezing measures.
lookup_terms: Committee for Goods Subjected to Import and Export Control

data.summary: Defined-term node for "Sanctions Committee" under Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020: any UN Security Council committee established under its resolutions, including the 1267/1989 (ISIL and Al-Qaida), 1988 (Afghanistan) and 1718 (DPRK proliferation) committees. The node sits alongside related defined terms such as Listed Person, Ombudsperson and Focal Point, and is referenced in the procedure by which the Council proposes designations to the UN. It matters for distinguishing UN-level designations from Cabinet-issued Local Lists and for identifying the correct de-listing channel.

A conceptual section of CBUAE digital ID guidance explaining the second stage of a digital ID system: authentication (confirming the claimant is the same person who was identity-proofed and onboarded) and ongoing identity lifecycle management, including binding and re-binding of authenticators. It classifies authentication factors (knowledge, possession, inherence), addresses assurance levels, step-up controls for high-risk account activities such as personal data changes, payee registration and high-value transfers, and describes continuous/behavioural authentication as a supplement to point-in-time login checks. It informs CBUAE licensed financial institutions (LFIs) applying CDD and ongoing monitoring obligations, and is expectation-setting guidance rather than standalone binding rules.

Node covering UAE Pass, the UAE national digital identity and digital signature solution, as referenced in CBUAE digital ID and AML/CFT guidance. It is presented as a national-level identification system LFIs should understand and may use for remote identification, e-KYC verification of identity evidence, and digital signing, alongside the Federal Authority validation gateway. Relevant to LFIs designing non-face-to-face onboarding and identity verification consistent with CDD requirements.

Node covering the Emirates ID, the mandatory government-issued identity card for UAE citizens and residents, as an identity evidence source in CBUAE digital ID and AML/CFT guidance. It addresses use of the card's digital certificates and biometrics, and the expectation that LFIs validate the card through the Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs & Port Security online gateway, UAE Pass or other government-supported solutions, and retain a copy plus the verification record. Applies to LFIs collecting and verifying the identity attributes required for CDD on natural persons.

Explains reliance on a third party for customer identification and verification at onboarding in a digital ID context, anchored in the AML-CFT Decision's reliance provision, including the condition that the relying institution immediately obtain the identification/verification information and applicable assurance levels. It distinguishes reliance (using another regulated entity's own CDD on its existing customer) from outsourcing (a provider performing control functions under the institution's own policies), and confirms that ultimate responsibility for CDD stays with the relying institution. Also links authentication data to ongoing due diligence and transaction monitoring. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Node on multifactor authentication within CBUAE digital ID guidance: combining factors from different categories (knowledge, possession, inherence) to raise authentication assurance, with stronger controls expected for higher-risk actions such as changes to customer contact data, adding third-party payees, high-value transfers and limit changes. It also flags the expectation that biometric-based MFA at login consider phishing-resistant, public-key-based factors. Directed at LFIs authenticating existing customers and protecting account integrity.

Node representing FATF standards and guidance as the international reference underpinning CBUAE AML/CFT guidance issued under the Implementing Regulation of the AML/CTF Decree-Law, which tasks supervisory authorities with providing guidance to financial institutions. The associated guidance sets CBUAE expectations for demonstrating compliance without creating new legal obligations, and expressly defers to the in-force legal and regulatory framework in case of conflict; it includes FATF-derived typologies such as PEP red flags and indicators of suspicion. Relevant to LFIs and their supervisors when interpreting national AML/CFT requirements.

Concept node for the UAE domestic (Local) terrorist designation lists issued by the Cabinet on proposal of the Executive Office/Council, covering listing, re-listing, updating and de-listing procedures and the effective date and publication of those decisions. It also drives the operational duties that flow to obliged entities: registration for notifications, screening of customers, counterparties, potential customers and beneficial owners, and immediate freezing on a match. It binds the Council, Ministry of Presidential Affairs, the Cabinet, the Office, supervisory authorities, and financial institutions and DNFBPs that must screen and freeze.

Concept node for the UN Sanctions List regime — the consolidated lists maintained under UN Security Council resolutions and their Sanctions Committees (including the 1267/1989/2253, 1988, 1718 and 2231 regimes) — and the national procedure for proposing persons or organisations for designation. It covers how the Council gathers identifying information, coordinates with the relevant state and submits proposals through the Office, as well as requests for listing addressed to other countries under UNSCR 1373. It binds the Council, the Ministry, the Office, and indirectly all entities that must screen against and apply the published list.

Concept node for the substance of targeted financial sanctions: freezing of funds owned or controlled directly or indirectly by a Listed Person or persons acting on their behalf, funds derived from them, the prohibition on making funds or services available, and the treatment of accrued interest and contractual payments on pre-existing obligations. It also covers lifting freezing — authorised exemptions notified to the UN Security Council, and the false-positive mechanism (written request to the Office, thirty-day decision, immediate execution by the holding entity, and recourse to the Competent Court). It binds any person holding or controlling funds, financial institutions and DNFBPs, the Office, law enforcement and supervisory authorities, with bona fide third-party rights preserved.

Concept node for UNSCR 1373 (2001) as the basis for domestic and foreign-requested designations, distinct from committee-based UN listing. It underpins the Council's power to list, re-list, de-list and periodically review Local Lists on reasonable grounds and irrespective of criminal proceedings, and to request designations by other states supported by identifying information meeting the 1373 criteria. It binds the Council, the Ministry of Justice in the review process, law enforcement and other state bodies supplying information, and feeds the freezing duties of obliged entities.

Concept node collecting the compliance duties placed on financial institutions and DNFBPs under the TFS decision: immediate notification of matches, frozen funds, attempted transactions, unfrozen funds and unresolved false positives; internal controls and procedures to ensure compliance; a tipping-off prohibition covering customers and third parties; and cooperation with the Office and supervisory authority. It sits alongside the parallel duties of supervisory authorities to collect and forward this information within set timeframes, supervise onsite and offsite, and impose administrative sanctions. It binds FIs, DNFBPs and their supervisors, with the Office as national coordination point.

Concept node for the de-listing channels available to designated persons — the UN Ombudsperson (for the ISIL/Al-Qaida regime) and the Focal Point for other regimes — and the national procedures supporting them. It covers the Office's role in responding to requests for additional information, coordinating with competent authorities, submitting de-listing requests for deceased persons or defunct organisations with supporting evidence, and ensuring frozen funds are not transferred to other listed persons or listed heirs. It binds the Office and cooperating authorities, and is the due-process route for Listed Persons and their representatives.

Concept node for the Higher Shari'ah Authority, the central Shari'ah body whose resolutions and requirements sit alongside the Central Bank's own rules for Islamic financial institutions and Takaful Companies. It appears in the corporate governance and disclosure context as the source of binding Shari'ah rulings, the reference point for annual Shari'ah reports, and a co-setter of requirements for a Takaful Company's internal Shari'ah governance framework. It binds boards of Takaful/Islamic institutions, which must demonstrate full Shari'ah compliance and disclose compliance with HSA resolutions.

Standards setting out the required systems of risk management and internal controls for insurance and Takaful companies, including the board-approved three lines of defence model, mandatory risk policy coverage (credit, market/ALM, reserving, insurance, reinsurance, operational, concentration and group risk), and the minimum content of the internal controls system. It also addresses control functions (risk management, compliance, actuarial, internal audit), model validation, stress testing and annual board or audit committee review of control effectiveness. Binds the board and senior management of licensed insurance companies, extending to subsidiaries, affiliates and international branches.

Node for the Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation (Circular 25/2022) as the instrument under which the insurance-sector risk management and internal control standards are issued. It establishes the obligation to establish, implement and maintain proportionate risk management and internal control systems and assigns ultimate responsibility for risk oversight to the board. Binds insurance and Takaful companies licensed by the Central Bank and their group entities.
lookup_terms: Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation

data.summary: Defined-term node for Risk Appetite, the board-determined level of risk a company accepts, set against the competitive and regulatory landscape, long-term interests and actual capacity to manage risk. It anchors risk limits, early warning indicators, capital needs beyond regulatory minimums, mitigation decisions (reduce, transfer or cease the activity) and reporting, with any deviation requiring board review and approval. Operative for boards, senior management and control functions of insurance/Takaful companies and at group level.

Concept node for the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment, the forward-looking internal assessment linking a company's risk profile, risk appetite and its own view of capital needs over and above regulatory capital requirements. ORSA results and related action plans must be reported to the board at least annually and interact with stress testing, model validation and solvency requirements. Applies to insurance and Takaful companies and, where relevant, at group level.

Concept node for the actuarial function as a second-line control function, whose authority and responsibilities must be documented in the company's governance framework and staffed by suitably qualified persons with unrestricted access to information. Its duties include the sufficiency, accuracy and quality of data, methods and assumptions for technical provisions, back-testing best estimates against experience, opining on reinsurance arrangements and product development, pricing and underwriting capital, and reporting a reasoned reliability and sensitivity analysis to the board and senior management. Binds insurance and Takaful companies and the head of the actuarial function.

CBUAE Corporate Governance Standards for Insurance Companies, issued as an extension of the Corporate Governance Regulation (Circular No. 24/2022) and mirroring its article structure. It sets binding governance requirements — definitions (Affiliate, Authorised Manager, Board, Company, Related Parties, Independent Member, Material Risk Takers), board and senior management duties, group-level governance and internal control frameworks. It binds all insurance companies incorporated in the UAE and UAE branches of foreign insurers, including Takaful companies, with local governance structures responsible for local implementation even within a group framework.

Node covering the duties of Senior Management and the Board's oversight of it under the CBUAE insurance corporate governance framework. Senior Management is accountable to the Board for compliance, fair treatment of policyholders, record keeping and prudent day-to-day management, and must implement strategy, risk systems and internal controls consistent with the Board-set Risk Appetite while respecting the independence of risk, compliance, internal audit and (for Islamic business) Shari'ah functions. The Board must hold Senior Management accountable, review governance annually, meet regularly, challenge information provided, and plan succession.

Node on the Board-elected risk management committee for insurance companies under the CBUAE governance standards, set in the context of board committee mandates (alongside the audit committee reporting obligations). The committee proposes risk management policies, risk tolerance and Risk Appetite for Board approval, follows up and updates them annually, ensures regular risk assessments, monitors the risk management process and obtains assurance from internal and external providers, including on the resources and expertise of the risk management function.
lookup_terms: risk tolerance and Risk Appetite approval

data.summary: Node on compensation governance for insurance companies: the compensation committee oversees management's implementation of the company-wide compensation system, monitors whether it creates the right incentives for managing risk, capital and liquidity, and works with the risk committee on incentive evaluation. It must have clear terms of reference, review compensation plans, processes and outcomes at least annually, and obtain an independent external assessment at least every five years; the Board retains oversight of the whole compensation structure, which must align with strategy and Risk Appetite and not incentivise excessive risk-taking.

Node covering Related Parties and Related Party Transactions in the CBUAE insurance governance framework, including the defined scope (Group, Controlling Shareholders, Board and Senior Management and their Relatives, and persons with control or significant influence) and the wide transaction perimeter (on- and off-balance sheet exposures, service contracts, asset sales, leases, derivatives, borrowings, write-offs). It requires arm's length terms, no more favourable terms than for non-related counterparties, policies to identify and aggregate exposures, independent review or audit, escalation of exceptions, and ongoing Senior Management monitoring with Board oversight; it connects to the conflict-of-interest policy including abstention from voting.

Node for the underlying CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation (Circular No. 24/2022), which the insurance Standards expand on and which is enforceable in the same manner. It frames Board responsibilities — setting Risk Appetite, approving key policies on liquidity, capital adequacy, technical provisions and solvency margin, overseeing the external auditor and Senior Management, approving annual financial statements — plus corporate culture and "tone from the top", group structure and intragroup conflict controls, and Shari'ah governance for Takaful companies.
lookup_terms: tone from the top corporate culture

data.summary: CBUAE Circular No. 24/2019 establishing the regulatory framework for hawala (money transfer) intermediaries operating in the UAE, issued under the Central Bank Law and the federal AML/CFT and counter-terrorism laws. It sets registration/certification conditions, undertakings, ongoing obligations (including agent due diligence, reporting to the Central Bank and AML/CFT compliance) and defines core terms such as Registered Hawala Provider and its agents. It binds registered hawala providers and their agents in the UAE; note this is a CBUAE instrument, not a SAMA rule, and is relevant only as comparative/cross-border material for KSA work.

Concept node for the Hawala Provider Certificate — the CBUAE authorisation instrument evidencing registration as a hawala provider. Article 3 material covers the Central Bank's discretion to grant or refuse, written notification with reasons on refusal, a one-year validity renewable for like periods, and the Central Bank's power to attach terms and conditions; grant is conditional on fit-and-proper style criteria (good conduct, no honour/honesty convictions, no unresolved insolvency, adequate education and managerial/professional experience) and on undertakings including electronic reporting of remitter and beneficiary data. Binds applicants for and holders of the certificate.

Defined-term node: a Registered Hawala Provider is a natural person holding a valid UAE residency visa, or a UAE juridical person, entered in the Central Bank's Hawala Providers Register under this Regulation, and the definition expressly extends to the provider's agent or agent network. A related definition captures the Registered Hawala Provider's Agent (any person acting for the provider by contract or under its direction). The term fixes the scope of who is bound by the Regulation's obligations, including responsibility flowing through to agents.

Concept node for the Central Bank's Remittance Reporting System — the reporting channel through which applicants must undertake to submit remitter and beneficiary data and information electronically, on Central Bank forms, as a precondition to obtaining a Hawala Provider Certificate. It is framed as a licensing/registration condition and an ongoing data-submission duty, sitting alongside other conditions such as security arrangements and use of authorised cash transit providers. Binds hawala provider applicants and registered providers.

Concept node grouping the Regulation's AML/CFT compliance expectations for hawala providers: undertakings to comply with all applicable UAE laws including the federal AML/CFT laws and Central Bank regulations, to guarantee customer transfers, to notify competent authorities of violations, to hold a settlement account with a UAE bank, to exercise due diligence when approving agents and maintain a current agent/country list, and to supply data and statistics to the Central Bank on a confidential basis. The supplied context states these as domestic obligations; it does not itself reproduce FATF Recommendation text, so treat the FATF label as an interpretive framing rather than cited standards.
lookup_terms: confidentiality of data provided to Central Bank

data.summary: Reference node for Decretal Federal Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism and Financing of Illegal Organisations and its Executive Regulations, cited as a legal basis for the Registered Hawala Providers Regulation alongside the Central Bank Law and the 2014 counter-terrorism law. Within this Regulation it operates as the primary AML/CFT statute that registered hawala providers, their customers and agents must comply with, including reporting violations to competent authorities. The underlying law binds UAE financial institutions and DNFBPs generally; here it is invoked as the enabling and compliance benchmark for hawala providers.

Node covering the overarching corporate governance framework requirement for insurance and takaful companies under the CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation and accompanying Standards, including the Article 10 communications/disclosure duties and the Article 9 financial reporting and external audit duties. It requires each company (and, where relevant, its group) to adopt board-approved governance policies and processes spanning strategy, organisational structure, control environment, risk responsibilities and compensation, and to publish an annual corporate governance statement plus audited financial statements. It binds licensed insurance/takaful companies supervised by the CBUAE, and sits alongside separate regulations on risk management, internal control, compliance and outsourcing.

Node on the composition, structure and governance duties of the Board of Directors of a CBUAE-licensed insurance/takaful company. It sets quantitative and qualitative requirements: board size and term limits, all-non-executive composition with a minimum proportion of Independent Members, female candidate quota, multiple-directorship caps, minimum meeting frequency, an independent board secretary, minutes, government shareholder representation, related-party exposure controls, and prior CBUAE non-objection for nomination, appointment, renewal and removal. It binds the company and its individual board members.

Defined-term and duty node for the Fit and Proper Process: the assessment of expertise and integrity of proposed and serving board members, Senior Management, key control function holders and any other persons designated by the CBUAE, with detailed criteria set in the accompanying Standards. It obliges the Board to establish the process for both initial selection and continued assessment, and to maintain succession plans, performance standards and training. Referenced across several CBUAE instruments, it binds the company's board and, indirectly, the individuals being assessed.
lookup_terms: duty of care duty of loyalty

data.summary: Node on the mandatory Board Audit Committee within the required committee structure (audit, risk, nomination, investment, compensation) of a CBUAE-licensed insurance/takaful company. It requires a written charter, access to resources and external expertise, a majority of Independent Members, an independent chair distinct from the board chair and other committee chairs, and collective experience in audit, financial reporting, accounting and risk; the audit committee may not be merged with the risk or any other committee. Internal audit and, with the risk committee, the actuarial function have reporting or direct access rights to it.

Node on the mandatory Board Risk Committee and the related Article 7 duties on risk management and internal controls. It requires a separate, non-merged committee chaired by an Independent Member with a majority of Independent Members experienced in risk management, and supports the company-wide (and group-wide) Risk Governance Framework, an independent risk management function with a direct reporting line to the Board or risk committee, and independent compliance and internal audit functions. It binds the Board, which owns design, approval and oversight of the framework and its alignment with Risk Appetite.
lookup_terms: Shari'ah compliance and internal Shari'ah audit

data.summary: Node on Article 8 remuneration duties for CBUAE-licensed insurance/takaful companies: a board-approved compensation system aligned with sound governance, prudent risk-taking and long-term financial soundness. It mandates risk-symmetric and deferred payouts with malus and clawback, fixed-only pay for board members (no performance bonuses), predominantly fixed pay for risk, compliance and internal audit staff, performance-based elements for Senior Management and Material Risk Takers, and caps on individual bonuses (with escalating board/general assembly approval) and on the aggregate staff bonus pool relative to net profit. It binds the Board, which approves Senior Management pay and oversees the policy.

A defined-term node for "Takaful Insurance" as used in the CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies (Circular 24/2022) and related insurance instruments: a collective cooperative contractual arrangement in which participants contribute to a participants' account from which compensation is paid, managed and invested by the takaful company for a defined fee. The definition determines which companies fall into the Shari'ah-governance overlay (Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee, Higher Shari'ah Authority oversight) on top of ordinary insurance corporate governance duties. It binds licensed insurance companies offering takaful products in the UAE, and their boards and senior management.
lookup_terms: Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies

data.summary: Article 12 of the CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies, together with the definition of "Takaful Regulation" (Insurance Authority Board Resolution No. 4 of 2010, as amended). It requires companies offering takaful products to align their corporate governance framework with the Takaful Regulation — internal Shari'ah control review and Shari'ah governance reporting, controls protecting participants' rights, establishment of the ISSC, transparent financial reporting on participants' rights — plus compliance with Higher Shari'ah Authority directions, immediate notification to the Central Bank of matters affecting an ISSC member's fit-and-proper status or independence, and publication of an annual Shari'ah report. It binds insurance companies offering takaful and their boards.

Article 13 of the CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies, governing the general assembly and shareholding. It sets the minimum national shareholding requirement (by reference to Cabinet Resolution No. 42 of 2009), obliges the board to ensure shareholder voting complies with the Central Bank Law and the Insurance Law, requires notification to the Central Bank when a proposed shareholding change is on the general assembly agenda, and preserves the Central Bank's powers to attend meetings (without voting) and to require a general assembly be convened. It binds insurance companies, their boards and shareholders.
lookup_terms: Cabinet Resolution No. 42 of 2009 minimum capital

data.summary: The CBUAE Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation for insurance companies, setting out the required risk governance system, risk appetite and limits, board approval and documentation of material changes to the risk management system, group-level risk linkages where CBUAE is not the primary regulator, the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA), stress testing of material risks, and the compliance function. It binds licensed insurance companies operating in the UAE, including their boards and senior management.
lookup_terms: Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation

data.summary: A concept node for enterprise-wide risk management as framed in CBUAE insurance risk instruments: the comprehensive, company-wide system for identifying, assessing, monitoring, mitigating and reporting all material risks, underpinned by risk governance, risk culture, risk appetite, risk limits and risk profile, and evidenced through ORSA and stress testing. It also addresses group dynamics where risk functions are partly derived from or monitored by a parent. Relevant to boards, senior management and risk/compliance functions of companies supervised by CBUAE.

A concept node on the board's role under the Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation: the board approves or delegates approval of models, oversees the forward-looking stress testing programme and internal capital and liquidity assessment, and is ultimately responsible for the compliance function and for a corporate culture of honesty, integrity and regulatory compliance. It also frames the board/senior management split in the risk governance system. It binds the boards of CBUAE-supervised insurance companies.

A thematic node gathering the CBUAE outsourcing requirements applicable to licensed insurance Companies: board and senior management responsibility for outsourcing risk, mandatory written contracts, due diligence on the service provider's capacity, authorisation, conflicts of interest and financial viability, and inclusion of outsourced critical functions in business continuity and disaster recovery planning. It also sets contractual minimums on Confidential Data — unfettered access to the Company's own data, non-disclosure, destruction or return on termination, limits and conditions on subcontracting, and an express right of access and on-site inspection for the Central Bank or its appointed agent. Material outsourcing requires prior non-objection, and core insurance activities plus key management and Control Functions (including senior management oversight and internal audit) are in principle not outsourceable.
lookup_terms: regulator right of access / on-site visit
core insurance activities and Control Functions

data.summary: Section of the CBUAE insurance standards requiring each Company to maintain policies, procedures and controls against internal and external insurance fraud across product development, client onboarding, staff hiring and dismissal, outsourcing, claims handling and dealings with Insurance Related Professions. It classifies fraud as internal, Insurance Related Professions' fraud and policyholder fraud, and mandates an independent audit of fraud controls, a whistleblowing policy, market fraud intelligence sharing, record-keeping and turnaround standards, board reporting, and staff/board training. Suspected or confirmed fraud must be reported immediately to law enforcement with notification to the Central Bank; the fraud strategy must be calibrated to the Company's Risk Profile.

CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies (Circular 24/2022) with accompanying Standards, issued under the Central Bank Law and supplementing Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 and related Insurance Authority decisions. It sets the overarching prudential governance framework — board composition and independence, organisational structure, control environment, risk management responsibilities, compensation, financial reporting/external audit and disclosure, including a published corporate governance statement. It binds all licensed insurance Companies on a solo and Group-wide basis, applies proportionately to smaller Companies, and applies to branches of foreign Companies (with an exception for Article 5 and an option for equivalent arrangements).
lookup_terms: Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies

data.summary: Reference node for UAE Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 on the Organization of Insurance Operations, its amendments and Executive Regulations — the primary insurance statute that the CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation and Standards supplement rather than replace. It is cited as part of the legal basis and hierarchy for insurance-sector rules, alongside the Central Bank Law and legacy Insurance Authority decisions. Relevant when tracing the statutory authority behind an insurance governance obligation or the scope of defined insurance activities and intermediaries.

Reference node for the Financial Regulations for insurance companies and for takaful companies (Insurance Authority Board Decisions No. 25 and No. 26 of 2014), used as the financial/prudential baseline that the Corporate Governance Regulation cross-refers to. It matters mainly for financial reporting and external audit obligations — preparing statements under applicable accounting frameworks, publishing audited annual financial statements with an opinion from a Central Bank-approved external auditor, and submitting supervisory data under the 2020 Guidance Manual decision. Binds licensed insurance and takaful Companies.
lookup_terms: external auditor approved by Central Bank

data.summary: Reference node for the SCA Public Joint Stock Companies' Governance Guide (Chairman of the Authority's Board Resolution No. 3/Chairman of 2020) and the Commercial Companies Law (Federal Law No. 32 of 2021), which continue to apply to listed insurance Companies. The CBUAE Corporate Governance Regulation and Standards are stated to be additional to those provisions, and an explicit conflict rule gives the Central Bank's requirements precedence where the SCA Regulation contradicts them. Useful for resolving dual-regulator governance questions for publicly listed insurers.
lookup_terms: Public Joint Stock Companies Governance Guide
Commercial Companies Law Federal Law No. 32 of 2021

data.summary: Concept node covering the role and accountability of Senior Management (alongside the Board) under the CBUAE Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation and Standards for Insurance Companies (Circular 25/2022). It sets out Board oversight of Senior Management, group-wide risk coordination duties where a Company has subsidiaries, affiliates or international branches, the elements of an effective risk management system, and joint Board/Senior Management ownership of fraud risk management. It binds insurance companies licensed by the CBUAE and, through group policies, their subsidiaries, affiliates and foreign branches.
lookup_terms: Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation

data.summary: Node for the countering-fraud obligations (Article 13) within the CBUAE Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation and Standards for Insurance Companies (Circular 25/2022, effective framework supplementing Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 and related Insurance Authority decisions). It requires companies to deter, prevent, detect, report and remedy internal and external fraud through a Board-approved fraud risk management strategy, structure, policies and procedures, with integrity standards for Board and staff. It binds all insurance companies in scope of the Regulation, with further fraud requirements reserved to future CBUAE decisions.

The CBUAE regulation establishing the Ombudsman Unit (Sanadak-type banking and insurance dispute resolution body), setting its governance structure, delegated powers from the CBUAE Board, funding mechanics (Annual Levy, Case Fee, Supplementary Levy) and oversight of performance. It creates institutional machinery for consumer complaint handling rather than direct conduct rules. It binds the Ombudsman Unit's board and staff, and indirectly Licensed Financial Institutions and Insurance Companies subject to its jurisdiction and levies.

Defined-entity node for the Ombudsman Unit, the CBUAE-established body responsible for receiving, handling and resolving consumer complaints against Licensed Financial Institutions and Insurance Companies. Its governance comprises a Board of the Ombudsman Unit with ultimate responsibility, a Chief Ombudsman for day-to-day operations, and staff subject to independence and conduct requirements. Relevant to consumer-protection teams assessing complaint escalation routes and levy obligations.

Node on the Board of the Ombudsman Unit: its composition, appointment by resolution of the CBUAE Board of Directors on the Governor's recommendation, three-year renewable terms capped at two terms, vacancy-filling within three months, and independence from Licensed Financial Institutions and Insurance Companies for at least two years before and throughout appointment. It also covers quorum, voting, five-year record retention of meetings and decisions, chairperson responsibilities and the power to make internal procedural rules subject to CBUAE direction. It binds Board members, the Chairperson and the Ombudsman Unit's internal governance.

Node on the Chief Ombudsman, the officer appointed by the CBUAE Board of Directors who runs day-to-day operations of the Ombudsman Unit under delegation from its Board. Duties include overseeing complaint acceptance, handling, review and resolution, ensuring staff, contractors, agents and consultants comply with the Unit's policies, terms of reference, code of conduct, conflict-of-interest rules, CBUAE regulations and the Decretal Law, and appointing and directing staff within delegated authority. Binds the Chief Ombudsman and, through supervision, Ombudsman Unit staff and engaged third parties.
lookup_terms: code of conduct conflict of interest

data.summary: Defines the Appeals Committee established under the CBUAE Ombudsman Unit (Sanadak) Regulation as the second-instance body reviewing Determinations issued by the Ombudsman Unit in Complaints against Licensed Financial Institutions. It sets out the Committee's composition, quorum and majority decision-making, its freedom from strict court rules of evidence, its duty to apply Central Bank laws, regulations and instructions, its evidence-gathering powers, and its authority to uphold, partially uphold or reject a Complaint or to refuse an appeal that fails the admissibility conditions. It binds the Committee itself, the Ombudsman Unit's secretariat, and indirectly the Licensed Financial Institutions and Complainants who are parties to an appeal.

Covers the Complaint resolution mechanism created by the CBUAE Ombudsman Unit Regulation, including its objectives, the end-to-end path from Consumer Complaint to Determination, and the 30-business-day window for either party to appeal before a Determination becomes final and enforceable. It also frames the standards the Unit follows and the referral routes to the Appeals Committee (banking) or the Insurance Dispute Resolution Committee (insurance). It binds the Ombudsman Unit, Licensed Financial Institutions and Insurance Companies, and sets the access rights of Consumers.

Explains how Insurance Companies fall within the scope of the CBUAE Ombudsman Unit Regulation, following the transfer of the Insurance Authority's competencies to the Central Bank, so that the Regulation covers both Insurance Companies under the Insurance Law and Licensed Financial Institutions under the Central Bank Law. It sets the scope of application, the prevalence of this Regulation over conflicting requirements of other regulators, and the Central Bank's power to impose additional requirements and issue guidance. It binds all Licensed Financial Institutions and Insurance Companies in their dealings with the Ombudsman Unit.

Addresses who qualifies as a Consumer or Complainant with free access to the Ombudsman Unit's Complaint resolution mechanism, and the admissibility conditions and exclusions for Complaints — including failure to raise the matter first with the institution, not allowing the institution 30 business days to give a final written response, time-barred matters, already-settled matters, and matters materially concerning the institution's risk management, internal pricing or anti-money laundering policies. It also covers multiple Complainants, filing format, and withdrawal with notification to the institution within 5 business days. It binds the Ombudsman Unit and, through the response obligation, Licensed Financial Institutions and Insurance Companies.

Defines the Insurance Dispute Resolution Committee as the appeal body for Complaints against Insurance Companies, mirroring the Appeals Committee's role for Licensed Financial Institutions, with the same 30-business-day appeal window and referral procedure. It sets out delivery of the Determination to both parties, the institution's duty to comply with any direction or recommendation within the specified or extended period and to notify compliance in writing within 14 business days, and the escalation of non-compliance to the Central Bank. It binds Insurance Companies, the Committee and the Ombudsman Unit.

Identifies the Central Bank's Regulatory Development Division as the authoritative interpreter of the Ombudsman Unit Regulation and related Central Bank Regulations, and provides that where the Ombudsman Unit refers an interpretive question to it, the Unit must not issue or proceed to a Determination inconsistent with, or while awaiting, that interpretation. Related provisions confirm that non-compliance with the Regulation by Licensed Financial Institutions or Insurance Companies is a regulatory violation exposing them to supervisory action, sanctions and penalties, and set publication and effective-date terms. It binds the Ombudsman Unit and the supervised institutions.

Defines the written outcome (upheld, partially upheld, or rejected) that the CBUAE Ombudsman Unit — and, on referral, the Appeals Committee or Insurance Dispute Resolution Committee — issues on a consumer Complaint, together with the grounds on which a Complaint may be upheld (breach of Central Bank regulations, deceptive/misleading/unfair conduct, improper motive or irrelevant grounds, inadequate explanation from the institution, prior unlawfulness finding, or breach of Consumer Protection Regulation principles). It also sets the appeal route: either party may refer a Determination for review within 30 complete business days, failing which the Determination becomes final and enforceable. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions, Insurance Companies and Complainants party to the dispute.

Sets out admissibility and handling rules for a Complaint before the CBUAE Ombudsman Unit: prerequisites (prior escalation to the Licensed Financial Institution or Insurance Company and a 30 complete business day response window), time-bar limits, standing of Complainants, filing format, withdrawal, and grounds for refusal or discontinuance (frivolous or bad-faith complaints, no vested interest, matters better suited to Courts, previously decided matters absent new material evidence, or a reasonable settlement offer). Notably excludes complaints materially relating to an institution's risk management, internal pricing policy, or Anti-Money Laundering policies and practices. Binds Complainants, Licensed Financial Institutions and Insurance Companies; the Ombudsman Unit's decision on jurisdiction and acceptance is final.

Establishes the funding mechanism of the CBUAE Ombudsman Unit: Licensed Financial Institutions and Insurance Companies must pay an Annual Levy, any Supplementary Levy and a Case Fee within 30 calendar days of assessment, with administrative late-payment charges and possible escalation to the Central Bank. It also covers Appeals Fees (potentially refundable and waivable by the Chief Ombudsman), pro-rata levies for entities entering or leaving the Unit's jurisdiction, and exemptions or reduced levies where an institution undertakes not to serve Consumers within the Regulation's scope.

A mandatory and enforceable CBUAE Standard, issued under the Central Bank Law, setting supervisory requirements for profit equalization in Islamic Banks; it supplements the Standards Re Risk Management Requirements for Islamic Banks and must be read with HSA Shari'ah requirements. It covers permitted equalization techniques (PER, IRR, Mudarib profit waiver, Hibah), governance and Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee approval, and disclosure duties toward Investment Account Holders. Applies to all Islamic Banks and banks with an Islamic Window in the UAE, on a solo and group-wide basis.

The baseline CBUAE Standards on risk management for Islamic Banks, referenced here as the framework that the Profit Equalization Standard supplements with additional requirements. Relevant mainly as the parent instrument governing identification, measurement and governance of Islamic banking risks, including the risk types addressed by profit equalization techniques. Binds Islamic Banks and banks operating an Islamic Window in the UAE.
lookup_terms: Standards Re Risk Management Requirements for Islamic Banks
Central Bank Law Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018

data.summary: Displaced Commercial Risk is the exposure arising where an Islamic Bank's return on assets financed by Investment Account Holders' funds underperforms competitors' returns, pressuring the bank to support payouts. The Standard requires Islamic Banks to develop, apply systematically and regularly review a sound methodology to identify, monitor, measure and report DCR impact and the mitigation amount, with changes justified and approved at the appropriate management level and by the Board where applicable; permitted mitigants include IRR, PER, forgoing Mudarib profit, and Hibah transfers, alone or combined.

IRR is a profit-equalization reserve defined in the CBUAE Standard on Profit Equalization for Islamic Banks: an amount appropriated out of Investment Account Holders' income after the Mudarib's profit share, held to absorb future investment losses of IAHs. Islamic Banks (including banks with Islamic Windows) must model its size and periodic build-up, obtain Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee approval for its establishment, maintenance, deployment and liquidation, disclose it in IA contracts and publicly, and dispose of outstanding balances on voluntary liquidation per agreed terms.

PER is a reserve created by setting aside amounts from profits before allocation between the Investment Account Holder and the Islamic Bank, usable in whole or part to lift IAH returns when the investment pool underperforms market expectations. The CBUAE Profit Equalization Standard binds Islamic Banks and Islamic Windows to Shari'ah approval of PER policies, contractual and website/branch disclosure of PER practices and ownership, Board-level oversight, and prescribed treatment on voluntary liquidation.

This node covers the Board's duties under the CBUAE Profit Equalization Standard for Islamic Banks: ensuring profit-equalization policies, procedures and controls exist, are periodically updated and are approved by the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee; approving investment and displaced-commercial-risk strategies including DCR limits and tolerance, profit-forgoing mechanisms and reserve appropriations; forming the independent reserves committee; and reporting periodically to Board committees, the ISSC and the Central Bank. It binds the boards of all Islamic Banks and banks housing Islamic Windows, on a solo and group-wide basis.

A Board-formed independent committee mandated to scrutinise the use of profit-equalization reserves (PER and IRR) and recommend to the Board, with the stated aim of protecting non-shareholder stakeholders in line with HSA and ISSC resolutions. Its minimum composition includes an independent non-executive director (preferably chairing) and a Board member; it sits within the Islamic Bank's governance framework for profit equalization and reserve utilisation.

IAHs are the holders of investment accounts whose funds Islamic Banks invest, typically on a Mudarabah basis, across one or more investment pools that must be accounted for separately. The CBUAE Profit Equalization Standard governs how IAH returns may be smoothed (PER, IRR, Mudarib forgoing profit, Hibah) and imposes contractual and public disclosure duties toward IAHs on rights, loss-bearing, early withdrawal, reserve appropriation and fees; it binds all Islamic Banks and Islamic Windows in the UAE.

CBUAE Regulation (Circular 20/2021) implementing Article 93(3) of the Central Bank Law on banks acquiring, buying back or dealing in their own shares. It prohibits such acquisition without prior written Central Bank approval (which may carry conditions), caps direct or indirect holdings of own shares at 10% of Paid Up Share Capital, and requires disposal of excess shares devolved in debt settlement within two years, extendable by the Central Bank. It applies to all Banks licensed under the Central Bank Law.
lookup_terms: shares devolved in settlement of debt

data.summary: This node captures the 10% ceiling on a bank's holdings of its own shares under the CBUAE Regulation on limits for banks' acquisition of their own shares (Circular 20/2021), issued under Article 93(3) of the UAE Central Bank Law. It sets the maximum direct or indirect purchase, buy-back, acquisition or holding of own shares at ten percent of Paid Up Share Capital, and sits alongside the prior written approval requirement and the two-year disposal window for shares devolved to the bank in settlement of a debt (extendable by the Central Bank). It binds all banks licensed by the CBUAE.
lookup_terms: shares devolved in settlement of debt

data.summary: Node for the CBUAE Model Management Standards, the binding standards governing how licensed institutions develop, validate, use and govern quantitative models across the model life-cycle. Scope covers all models supporting decision-making (credit risk rating/scorecards, pricing, valuation, stress testing and others), with defined terms such as Model, Model Risk, Materiality and Model Calibration, plus self-assessment, remediation-plan submission and ongoing reporting duties to the CBUAE. It binds UAE-incorporated institutions and their branches/subsidiaries, and UAE branches or subsidiaries of foreign institutions (applying the more stringent parent-regulator elements where relevant).

Node for the CBUAE Model Management Guidance, the companion document to the Model Management Standards that elaborates supervisory expectations on model governance, development, calibration, validation and documentation. It shares the MMS definitional framework (Model, Model Risk, Materiality, Model Calibration) and the same effective date and compliance timeline. It applies to the same population of CBUAE-licensed institutions, including UAE branches and subsidiaries of foreign institutions and UAE parent groups.

Defined-entity node for the Central Bank of the UAE as the issuing and supervisory authority under the Model Management Standards. It is the recipient of institutions' gap self-assessments, remediation plans and periodic progress and model-management reporting, and it approves compliance timeframes on a proportionate basis reflecting institution size and complexity. Relevant when tracing who exercises approval, review and reporting-recipient powers in the model risk regime.

Defines the Model Oversight Committee required by the CBUAE Model Management Standards: a dedicated committee, established separately from existing risk management committees, covering all models institution-wide and meeting at least quarterly. It is accountable for substantiated, documented decisions at each step of the model life-cycle, including strategic modelling choices, and must be accountable to Senior Management and the Board while remaining independent of business lines (majority of members not from business lines). It binds institutions subject to the MMS and frames the accountability of model owners, developers, validators, users and modelling data owners.
lookup_terms: Board and Senior Management accountability for models

data.summary: Node on the Chief Risk Officer's responsibilities under the CBUAE Model Management Standards. The CRO must ensure that model design and usage across the entire institution — not merely the risk function — is appropriate for decision-making, and that Model Risk is identified, measured, monitored, reported and mitigated. This sits within a wider accountability chain: the Model Oversight Committee reports to Senior Management and the Board, which under the Risk Management Regulation 153/2018 remains ultimately accountable for model usage and must set the institution's model risk appetite.

Concept node covering the allocation of model governance accountability under the CBUAE Model Management Standards, at Board, Senior Management, Model Oversight Committee and Chief Risk Officer level. It sets out that the Board is ultimately accountable for the appropriate use and management of models (linking to the Risk Management Regulation), must own materially significant modelling decisions and define model risk appetite, while the CRO must ensure institution-wide identification, measurement, monitoring, reporting and mitigation of Model Risk and that material decisions reach the Board or Board Risk Committee. Binds licensed UAE institutions subject to the MMS and their governing bodies and senior officers.

Defines the Data Management Framework required under the MMS for data used in model development and validation (expressly not routine risk analysis and reporting data). It requires a formal, resourced framework approved by Senior Management and the Board, documented with limitations and assumptions, covering the whole institution and all material risk types, independently validated, and comprising source identification, regular collection, quality control, secure storage/access and robust infrastructure, with named data owners and documented, largely automated collection across credit, market, concentration, liquidity, operational and fraud risk. Binds institutions subject to the MMS and the designated data owners within them.

Concept node for the model life-cycle as the organising structure of the MMS, spanning design, development, calibration, validation, monitoring and decommissioning, together with the defined terms that drive it (model, model calibration, model complexity, materiality, Model Risk). It also frames MMS scope: all model types used to support decision-making, including risk, pricing, valuation and stress-testing models, plus transitional remediation planning and ongoing reporting to the CBUAE. Binds institutions subject to the MMS across every stage at which models are built, used or relied on.
lookup_terms: reporting to CBUAE on model management

data.summary: Sets the requirement for independent validation of all models as a mandatory life-cycle step and the basis for assessing Model Risk, applying the three-lines model (model owner, independent validator, internal audit) and the Effective Challenge principle. Validation must follow a defined process with responsibilities, metrics, limits and reporting per model type, cover both qualitative and quantitative dimensions, run at minimum frequencies set in Part II, and use monitoring outputs as inputs; it may be outsourced to a third party, but the institution retains ownership of and responsibility for acting on validation reports, with internal oversight where both internal and external validators are used. Binds institutions subject to the MMS, including for internally developed and vendor-acquired models.
lookup_terms: three lines of defence model validation

data.summary: Concept node for the model development stage under the MMS, covering model design, specification, calibration and the documentation and data adequacy expectations attaching to it. It stresses suitability of calibration for statistical models using internal or external data, refuses lack of data as justification for shortfalls in material models (requiring interim mitigants instead), and warns against over-generalisation; it sits within the MMS scope covering risk, pricing, valuation and stress-testing models. Binds institutions subject to the MMS and their model development functions.

Concept node for ongoing model performance monitoring under the MMS, the recurring post-implementation check on whether a model still performs in line with its design objective. Monitoring is narrower in scope than independent validation but shares metrics with it and its results must feed the validation process; it operates within the MMS scope of all decision-support models and the associated CBUAE reporting expectations. Binds institutions subject to the MMS, with escalation of performance deterioration through the model governance chain.

Section 5 of the CBUAE Model Management Guidance (MMG), setting supervisory expectations for macroeconomic models — statistical constructions linking macro (independent) variables to risk or business metrics such as PD, Credit Index, LGD, cost of funds or revenues. It covers models used for Expected Credit Loss estimation and for internal and regulatory stress testing, and stresses that statistical performance must be balanced against business intuition, economic meaning and implementation constraints. Binds institutions within the MMS/MMG scope that choose to use such models, including UAE-incorporated groups' branches and subsidiaries.

Section 6 of the CBUAE Model Management Guidance on Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book models, treating conventional interest rate risk and Islamic profit rate risk alike. It supplements the CBUAE IRRBB Standards (notice 165/2018) and the 2016 Basel IRRBB Standards by setting modelling expectations for earnings and economic value metrics (NII, EVE), currency aggregation and offsetting for pegged currencies subject to basis risk capture, and treatment of non-performing assets. Governance, management, hedging and reporting for IRRBB sit in the separate CBUAE Standards, not here.
lookup_terms: interest rate risk in the banking book

data.summary: A model-type node covering net present value models, one of the six model families listed in the CBUAE Model Management Guidance alongside rating, PD, LGD, macro and IRRBB models. The MMG does not mandate use of these models; it sets minimum expected practices where an institution chooses to use them, so that model risk is managed appropriately. Scope of institutions follows the Model Management Standards, with branches/subsidiaries of foreign institutions applying the more conservative of MMG or home-regulator expectations.

Guidance on how institutions should compute observed default rates as the empirical basis for PD modelling and macro model construction. It requires estimation at portfolio level and, where feasible, at rating-grade level (with data-based justification if only pool-level estimation is used), using a 12-month observation window with performing obligors in the denominator and obligors defaulting at least once in the numerator. It also requires a consistent default definition across PD and LGD estimation, including for restructured facilities, with retroactive changes approved by the Model Oversight Committee and the risk management committee.

Covers the master rating scale and the use of rating models — how model scores map onto a single internal rating scale used across credit risk management, provisioning and capital assessment, and the principles for grade granularity, distribution of obligors across grades, and robust PD estimation per grade. It also sets re-rating expectations after a new or recalibrated model (70% of in-scope obligors within six months, 95% within nine months), batch rating by experts independent of business lines, and monitoring of rating archiving, frequency and correct model-to-obligor-type application.

Guidance on modelling point-in-time PD and the PD term structure, which directly affect provisioning outcomes. It describes the trade-offs between rating, time-step and segmentation granularity and sets minimum expected practices for three common methods — transition matrix, portfolio average/scaling, and the Vasicek credit framework — including adjusting a TTC transition matrix with forecast Credit Indices and pre-implementation coherence checks against long-term and current observed default rates. Methodology choices must be substantiated, documented and approved by the Model Oversight Committee, including where proposed by third-party consultants.

Node covering the independent model validation requirement under the CBUAE Model Management Standards, including its place in the three-lines-of-defence structure (model owner, independent validator, internal audit) and the Effective Challenge principle. It sets out that validation must be periodic, independent of development, cover both qualitative and quantitative dimensions, and be supported by defined responsibilities, metrics, limits and reporting; incomplete quantitative validation must be escalated to the Model Oversight Committee. Binds UAE-licensed institutions using models, including where validation is outsourced to third parties (the institution retains ownership of reports and responsibility for acting on them).

Node setting out the CBUAE Model Management Standards requirements for reporting model findings and remediating model defects, including severity-based and Tier-based maximum remediation periods, the use of temporary tactical solutions (overlays, adjustments, scaling) with expiry dates, and the twelve-month outer limit for high severity findings. It also addresses the fallback where an institution has no internal validation team, with internal audit reviewing the accuracy of findings reporting. Applies to institutions subject to the MMS and their model owners, validators and audit functions.

Appendix table consolidating all numerical thresholds in the CBUAE Model Management Standards with their source articles and their binding strength (mandatory versus strongly recommended). It covers the self-assessment deadline after the MMS effective date, quarterly Model Oversight Committee meetings, quarterly/annual reporting of model life-cycle and Model Risk to the Committee and Board, annual rating frequency, quarterly monitoring and validation reporting, maximum validation/monitoring intervals, and the twelve-month cap on remediating high severity findings. Useful as the quick reference for deadline and frequency obligations binding institutions under the MMS.

Section of the CBUAE Model Management Guidance addressing credit rating (score) models used to assess obligor or facility creditworthiness, including design and calibration expectations, replacement of persistently underperforming models, and the usage controls around rating assignment. It includes re-rating expectations after a new or recalibrated model (70% of in-scope obligors within six months, 95% within nine months), batch re-rating independent of business lines, archiving of ratings, and use of each model only on its documented obligor type. Guidance ('should') expectations for UAE institutions, read jointly with the MMS.

Node covering probability of default modelling in the CBUAE Model Management Guidance, positioned as the calibration layer downstream of rating models and linked to macroeconomic modelling for point-in-time estimates. The associated material frames PD alongside TTC/PIT distinctions, ECL and stress testing uses, and expects statistical rigour to be combined with causality analysis, economic meaning and documented judgement. Guidance-level expectations for UAE institutions developing or acquiring PD and related credit risk models.

Section of the CBUAE Model Management Guidance on Loss Given Default models, treating TTC LGD and PIT LGD as separate models each subject to the full MMS life-cycle (development, ownership, validation, documentation).
