It sets minimum development steps (data collection, realised LGD computation, driver and segmentation analysis, TTC then PIT modelling) and modelling constraints such as handling bimodal LGD distributions and testing logical features (collateral and recovery-period effects) during validation, plus analysis of the LGD–macro factor relationship. Guidance-level expectations for UAE institutions using LGD for provisioning, portfolio management and capital purposes.

A section of the CBUAE Model Management Guidance describing the portfolio-level scaling approach as an alternative to transition matrices for modelling the term structure of point-in-time PD, based on modelling average PD across rating grades rather than every rating-to-rating transition. It is presented as suitable for portfolios with smaller data sets, subject to the institution justifying its suitability against alternatives and following the design and estimation decision process set out in the Model Management Standards. It binds banks and other CBUAE-licensed institutions developing IFRS 9/ECL credit models.

A section of the CBUAE Model Management Guidance addressing use of the Vasicek one-factor credit model (and derivations) to build point-in-time PD term structures for ECL. It warns that the model was designed for portfolio-level economic capital and tail losses rather than obligor-level expected loss, that asset correlation to a non-observable systemic factor is hard to calibrate and highly influential, and that combining it with macroeconomic regressions raises further identification issues. Directed at institutions choosing and justifying ECL modelling methodologies.

Definitional node from the CBUAE Model Management Standards/Guidance glossary setting out the Credit Index (CI) as a synthetic quantity derived from observable default rates (e.g. via probit transformation) representing a systemic driver of creditworthiness. It is the pivot concept linking macroeconomic forecasts to through-the-cycle transition matrices and forward point-in-time PD estimates. Applies to institutions interpreting and applying the MMS/MMG credit modelling requirements.

Guidance on through-the-cycle LGD modelling in the CBUAE Model Management Guidance, covering the loss components framework, treatment of bimodal LGD distributions (cautioning against using an average between peaks at facility level) and logical consistency properties such as final LGD not exceeding unsecured LGD and decreasing with collateral. These logical features must be tested during model validation. Binds CBUAE-licensed institutions building credit loss models.

Section of the CBUAE Model Management Guidance requiring institutions to analyse the relationship between LGD and macroeconomic factors at an appropriate level of granularity and to let that analysis drive point-in-time LGD modelling strategy. It sets out four modelling options ranked by granularity (from macro-linked LGD parameters down to linking final LGD to obligor PD) and expectations on performance criteria, parameter justification, documentation and in-/out-of-sample evidence. Applies to institutions estimating IFRS 9 expected credit losses.

Glossary node from the CBUAE Model Management Standards/Guidance defining Expected Credit Loss as the probability-weighted expected loss metric supporting IFRS 9 provisions for credit risk on banking-book facilities and bonds. It anchors the PD, LGD and EAD modelling expectations used throughout the instrument. Relevant to CBUAE-licensed institutions and their model development, validation and oversight functions.

Section 5.11 of the CBUAE Model Management Guidance sets expected practice for macroeconomic scenario forecasting used in regular expected credit loss (ECL) estimation, requiring unbiased, probability-weighted, forward-looking forecasts extending to the longest portfolio maturity. It addresses governance of internally built versus third-party scenarios (review by the Model Oversight Committee and the ECL oversight committee, internal validation of vendor scenarios), consensus-based and economically coherent base/upside/downside narratives, use of the most recent PD and LGD models, and encouraged disclosure of scenario values and weights over three years. It also draws a boundary: ICAAP, recovery and resolution, and regulatory stress-testing scenarios (including CBUAE-supplied macro scenarios) may serve only as distant comparables, not as ECL inputs. Binds institutions supervised by the CBUAE that compute ECL.

Defines and sets modelling expectations for Economic Value of Equity (EVE) — present value of banking-book assets less liabilities — as an IRRBB metric under the CBUAE Model Management Guidance. It fixes the estimation principles (all interest-rate-sensitive banking book assets, liabilities and off-balance-sheet items; run-off assumption; exclusion of own equity), differentiates granularity expectations between LSIs (facility-level full revaluation) and non-LSIs (gap-based aggregation per Basel IRRBB), and requires all institutions to compute ∆EVE against the reporting-date baseline. Binds CBUAE-supervised institutions managing interest rate and profit rate risk in the banking book.

Defines Net Interest Income (NII) for the purposes of the Model Management Standards/Guidance, expressly covering both conventional net interest income and Islamic net profit income, as total interest (profit) income less expense over a horizon net of hedging; ∆NII (earnings at risk, EAR) is the change under stressed rate scenarios versus reporting-date rates. It sits alongside EVE as the earnings-based IRRBB metric and requires the underlying models to follow the model life-cycle, with assumptions escalated beyond ALM or market risk to a governance forum reporting to the Model Oversight Committee. Binds CBUAE-supervised institutions.

Covers optionality and related risk drivers in IRRBB modelling under the Model Management Guidance, including option risk and basis risk as granular inputs to EVE, and the treatment of currency aggregation of ∆EVE — no offsetting across currencies per Basel, with a conditional option to offset between pegged currencies (e.g. USD/AED) only where basis risk is demonstrably captured through dedicated stress scenarios. It also sets out the treatment of non-performing assets net of provisions: inclusion in EVE (via rate-sensitive discounting of recoveries and LGD, including rescheduled/forborne facilities), with NII treatment left to bank discretion. Binds CBUAE-supervised institutions computing IRRBB metrics.

Identifies the Basel Committee's April 2016 "Interest rate risk in the banking book" standards as the external reference the Model Management Guidance incorporates alongside the CBUAE's own IRRBB standards. Specific Basel articles are pulled in operationally — e.g. article 132 for gap-based EVE by non-LSIs, articles 120–124 for fixed rate loan prepayment risk (with Table 3 scalers), and articles 125–129 for term deposit early redemption risk — with institutions permitted to substitute documented internal scenario-specific behavioural rates. Relevant to CBUAE-supervised institutions building IRRBB and behavioural models.
lookup_terms: BCBS April 2016 interest rate risk banking book

data.summary: Refers to the CBUAE's "Interest rate and rate of return risk in the banking book Standards" (notice 165/2018) as the binding domestic IRRBB regime that institutions' models must be built to satisfy; the Model Management Guidance supplies modelling methodology only, while governance, management, hedging and reporting obligations remain in the separate CBUAE Standards. Under those Standards, interest rate risk (and, for Islamic products, profit rate risk) must be captured through both expected earnings and economic value of the balance sheet, driving the NII and EVE metric set and the identification of interest-sensitive positions. Binds CBUAE-supervised banks and financial institutions with banking book exposures.
lookup_terms: interest rate and rate of return risk in the banking book

data.summary: CBUAE supervisory guidance (issued under Article 44.11 of Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019) setting out expectations for licensed financial institutions dealing with hawala providers and, in a separate part, for Registered Hawala Providers themselves. It covers hawala risk factors (delivery channels, commingled non-hawala business lines, customer base), CDD/EDD on hawala-provider customers, registration-certificate verification, STR filing and permitted/non-permitted RHP services. It binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions and registered hawala providers; it is guidance that does not override the AML/CFT Law, AML-CFT Decision or CBUAE circulars.

Concept node covering targeted financial sanctions duties applicable to registered hawala providers and licensed financial institutions under UNSC and UAE listings. It explains freezing without delay (24 hours of the listing decision), acting without prior notice to the customer, suspending transactions on a potential match, record-keeping on match confirmation, and reporting listed persons and actions taken to the competent authorities. Binding on RHPs and LFIs as an absolute, risk-independent obligation distinct from CDD.

Concept node on customer identification and due diligence in the hawala context, spanning both LFIs identifying hawala-provider customers and RHPs identifying their own natural- and legal-person customers. It covers identity verification (including Emirates ID online validation), beneficial ownership at the 25% threshold and fallback to the senior managing official, understanding ownership/control structure and nature of business, sanctions screening of all related parties, document retention for five years, and the duty to refuse or exit a relationship that cannot be understood. Binds LFIs and RHPs.

Defined-term node for the Registered Hawala Provider: a natural or legal person holding a CBUAE-issued Hawala Provider Certificate and entered in the CBUAE Hawala Providers Register to carry on Hawala Activity (transfer and receipt of funds or equivalent value, settled through trade and cash). It fixes related defined terms (Originating/Beneficiary Hawala Provider, Hawala Activity, MVTS, beneficial owner, legal person) and the service perimeter distinguishing registered UAE providers from foreign hawala providers. Relevant to RHPs themselves and to LFIs assessing hawala-provider customers.

Defined-term node for CBUAE licensed financial institutions as the addressees of this guidance. It anchors their obligations when hawala providers are customers: identification and verification under Article 8 of the AML-CFT Decision, physical inspection of the original CBUAE hawala registration certificate, refusal to deal with unregistered hawala providers, and STR/SAR filing to the FIU under Article 15 of the AML-CFT Law and Article 17 of the AML-CFT Decision, including where a customer may be acting as an unregistered hawaladar.

Concept node on the reporting channel used to notify UAE authorities of suspicious activity and of sanctions matches and freezing actions. It sits at the intersection of STR/SAR filing to the FIU and TFS reporting on listed persons and measures taken, and applies to LFIs and registered hawala providers. Useful for confirming who must report, what is reported and to which authority, rather than platform mechanics.

A sub-section of the CBUAE hawala guidance setting expectations for Registered Hawala Providers (RHP) that use agents abroad to send or receive payment instructions on their behalf. It requires RHP to identify and assess the ML/TF risk arising from foreign agents and to know who those agents are, while confirming that agency arrangements inside the UAE are prohibited (no "nesting"), since an RHP must run its business personally. It binds RHP only; it sits alongside the customer EDD steps (management approval, source of funds/wealth, business information) described immediately before it.

Concept node for CBUAE Circular No. 24/2019, the registration framework for hawala providers in the UAE, as referenced throughout the hawala guidance. It underpins the Hawala Provider Certificate, the obligation to manage the business personally rather than through UAE-based intermediaries (anti-nesting), and the requirement to hold a settlement account with a UAE bank and notify the CBUAE of its details. It binds hawala providers operating in the UAE and indirectly shapes how licensed financial institutions treat them as customers.

Concept node for Cabinet Decision No. (10) of 2019 (the AML-CFT Decision), the implementing regulation cited as the legal source of the obligations in the hawala guidance. Articles referenced include the requirement to establish a risk-based AML/CFT programme (Arts. 4, 20, 26), the appointment and duties of a Compliance Officer (Art. 21), and the enterprise risk assessment (Art. 4.1). It binds hawala providers and licensed financial institutions as subject entities under the UAE AML/CFT framework.

Concept node for Decree Federal Law No. (20) of 2018, the primary UAE AML/CFT statute forming the legal basis of the CBUAE hawala guidance and of the AML-CFT Decision issued under it. In the surrounding text it anchors registration, FIU reporting (including goAML/IEMS enrolment), bank account and compliance programme obligations for Registered Hawala Providers. It binds all financial institutions and designated entities subject to the UAE AML/CFT regime.

Concept node for Cabinet Decision No. (74) of 2020, the UAE instrument governing targeted financial sanctions and the obligation to freeze without delay assets of UN- and UAE-listed persons. In this guidance it underpins the sanctions screening and immediate freezing duties imposed on Registered Hawala Providers, who may not process activity for listed persons absent authorisation. It binds RHP and, more broadly, UAE financial institutions and designated entities.

Cross-cutting concept node describing the risk-based approach as applied across several CBUAE AML/CFT guidance documents, including the hawala guidance for licensed financial institutions and for RHP. It covers the three components of an RBA — enterprise risk assessment (Art. 4.1 AML-CFT Decision), customer risk profiling and calibrated preventive measures — and requires higher-risk customer types such as hawala providers to be reflected in the assessment and documented. It binds LFIs and, in proportionate form, RHP, whose risk assessments must be documented and explainable to the CBUAE.

Article 18 of the CBUAE Large Exposures regulation, which layers additional aggregate and individual exposure caps on related parties over and above the general large exposure limits, including for shareholders holding 5% or more of a bank's capital together with their group of connected counterparties and related parties. The surrounding context also covers board notification and ex-post approval where an existing exposure becomes large without new lending, and enhanced monitoring/reporting of large exposures across credit, legal, compliance, market and interest rate risk. It binds banks licensed by the CBUAE (note: UAE instrument, not a SAMA rule).

Governance and risk-management provisions of the CBUAE Large Exposures regulation (Article 17 and related credit risk mitigation articles), requiring banks to identify and aggregate concentration risk, set risk-appetite thresholds, report material concentrations to the board, stress test concentrations and cover them in ICAAP and ILAAP. It also fixes senior management duties to monitor limits and escalate breaches immediately without board pre-approval, and sets out how eligible credit risk mitigation reduces the original exposure while creating a recognised exposure to the protection provider. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks and their boards and senior management.

Article 23 of the CBUAE Large Exposures regulation, setting the transitional grandfathering scheme for breaches arising solely from the move from Circular No. 32/2013 to the new framework. It fixes the grandfathered basis by reference to the position at 31 December 2022, ties it to a specific exposure and counterparty, and phases the relief down from 100% to 0% between 2023 and 31 December 2026, with full reporting plus supplementary disclosures and no relief for interbank exposures (full compliance by 31 December 2023). Binds banks relying on transitional relief.

Reference node for the predecessor CBUAE regime on monitoring large exposure limits (Circular No. 32/2013 and its guidelines), superseded by the current Large Exposures regulation and relevant mainly as the comparison baseline for grandfathering. The surrounding context sets out the current core definitions and thresholds: a large exposure at 10% of Tier 1 capital, the 25% single-counterparty limit, the 15% G-SIB-to-G-SIB limit, treatment of UAE local government exposures, and the measurement rules for exposure values. Relevant to CBUAE-licensed banks assessing legacy versus current limits.

Article 14 of the CBUAE Large Exposures regulation, governing how holdings of covered bonds are attributed to the issuing bank as counterparty: 100% of nominal value by default, or at least 20% where the instrument meets the covered bond definition and eligibility conditions on legal supervision and the cover pool. Related context covers exposure values for options and fund/securitisation structures and confirms that trading book covered bonds follow the same treatment. Binds CBUAE-licensed banks measuring counterparty exposure.

Defines "the Unknown Client" under the CBUAE Large Exposures regulation: where the counterparty behind an exposure cannot be identified, such as in structures that do not disclose holdings below a threshold, the exposure is assigned to a single notional client to which the large exposure limit applies. All such unidentified exposures are aggregated as one counterparty regardless of any actual relationship, and banks are barred from circumventing limits through multiple structures with identical underlying assets. Includes the look-through approach mechanics for structures and tranches; binds CBUAE-licensed banks.

CBUAE standard setting minimum Shari'ah governance requirements for incorporated Takaful insurance companies, covering the internal Shari'ah supervision committee, internal Shari'ah control and audit divisions, external Shari'ah audit and related fit-and-proper and reporting requirements. It is issued under the UAE insurance law and the central bank decretal law, and complements the Takaful Insurance Regulation and the Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies. It binds Takaful companies on a solo and group-wide basis (including subsidiaries, affiliates and international branches), and the regulator may impose requirements beyond the stated minima.
lookup_terms: Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies

data.summary: Node covering periodic Shari'ah reporting and the three-lines-of-defence reporting architecture within a Takaful company's Shari'ah governance framework. It addresses how the internal Shari'ah audit division reports to the board, routes Shari'ah matters through the ISSC for resolution and then to the audit committee, and submits reports at least semi-annually; it also insulates Shari'ah audit staff from the senior management they audit on promotion, bonus, appraisal and termination decisions. Binds the Takaful company, its board, audit committee and ISSC.
lookup_terms: Internal Shari'ah Audit Division reporting line

data.summary: Concept node for compliance with Islamic Shari'ah Provisions as the substantive benchmark against which a Takaful company's objectives, activities, operations and conduct are assessed. Context sets out the internal Shari'ah audit division's mandate to test that compliance through an annual plan and to assess the adequacy of internal procedures and the Shari'ah governance framework, plus fit-and-proper criteria (qualifications, professional certification, minimum experience, full-time and no-dual-role requirements, integrity) for the division head, whose appointment requires central bank approval.
lookup_terms: fit and proper head of Shari'ah audit

data.summary: Node for the 2022 Takaful Insurance Regulation as the defining instrument referenced by the Shari'ah governance standard, together with the standard's defined terms (Takaful Insurance Company, Higher Shari'ah Authority, Shari'ah Non-Compliance Risk, Confidential Information) and the general requirement of continuous Shari'ah compliance across all objectives, activities, operations and codes of conduct. The Regulation is the source of the HSA's mandate and of the incorporation and business conditions for Takaful companies; the standard supplements rather than replaces it.

Concept node for the External Shari'ah Auditor: an independent, central-bank-approved external Shari'ah audit firm a Takaful company may appoint to assess Shari'ah compliance against central bank regulations and standards and HSA/ISSC resolutions. The auditor must meet the ISSC before finalising its report and must report to the board and ISSC on compliance status, Shari'ah non-compliance risks, the quality of the risk management system for those risks, and other significant matters. The related article also repeals the prior 2019 Insurance Authority decision on the Shari'a controller's role.

Concept node describing the internal Shari'ah control division's functions in a Takaful company — Shari'ah consultation on contracts, products, marketing material and Shari'ah-related customer complaints; Shari'ah research and development; and the Shari'ah compliance function itself. The division cannot issue fatwas or resolutions and must refer matters to the ISSC, its staff cannot hold executive responsibility over activities they monitor, and Shari'ah compliance reports go to the ISSC before the CEO with a right of direct board access and only a dotted line to the company's general compliance head.
lookup_terms: dotted reporting line to head of compliance

data.summary: The CBUAE Large Exposures Regulation is the prudential instrument setting how banks identify, measure, limit, monitor and report concentrated credit exposures to single counterparties and connected groups, expressed as percentages of Tier 1 capital. It covers exposure measurement (on- and off-balance sheet, banking and trading book, counterparty credit risk), eligible credit risk mitigation, exemptions and special treatments (sovereigns, public sector entities, interbank), related-party limits, and board-level approval, monitoring and breach-notification duties. It binds banks licensed/operating in the UAE and is supervised by the Central Bank of the UAE; it is not a SAMA instrument, so it is relevant mainly as comparative GCC material.

This node captures the defining threshold and limits: an exposure is a "large exposure" when total exposure values to one counterparty or Group of Connected Counterparties reach or exceed 10% of Tier 1 capital, while the hard cap is 25% of Tier 1 capital at all times (15% for G-SIB-to-G-SIB exposures, with a 12-month transition after FSB listing). It also introduces the "unknown client" concept, aggregating undisclosed underlying counterparties into a single notional counterparty subject to the limit. Breaches must be reported immediately to the Central Bank and rectified, with Tier 1 capital reduced by the excess unless the Central Bank waives this.

Defines when two or more counterparties must be aggregated as a Group of Connected Counterparties — through a control relationship (direct or indirect) or economic interdependence (financial distress in one likely causing funding/repayment difficulty in the other) — and requires banks to assess relationships against prescribed criteria. The node also links to the stricter related-party regime, including individual and aggregate caps on exposures to 5%+ shareholders and their connected groups, plus board approval, immediate board notification where an exposure becomes large, and enhanced monitoring across credit, legal, compliance, market and interest rate risk.

Sets out which credit risk mitigation techniques may reduce exposure values in the large exposures framework — only unfunded credit protection and eligible financial collateral recognised under the standardised approach; IRB-only collateral is excluded and internally modelled haircuts are prohibited. It specifies the recognised amounts (protected portion, collateralised portion, CCR-recognised collateral, haircut-adjusted collateral) and requires substitution: any reduction against the original counterparty must be booked as a new exposure to the CRM provider. Treatment of maturity mismatches and enforceable loan/deposit netting follows the risk-based capital framework.

Specifies how exposure values are computed for large exposure purposes: exposures as defined under the risk-based capital framework, covering on- and off-balance sheet items in both banking and trading book and instruments carrying counterparty credit risk, valued at accounting value net of specific provisions. Counterparty credit risk instruments use exposure-at-default under the standardised approach; securities financing transactions use the comprehensive approach with standard supervisory haircuts; off-balance sheet items are converted via credit conversion factors with a 10% floor. Amounts already deducted from Tier 1 capital are excluded (except 1,250% risk-weighted exposures), and net short positions after offsetting need not be counted.

Sets the exemptions and special limits for sovereign and public sector counterparties: exposures to the UAE Federal Government, the CBUAE, and foreign sovereigns rated at least AA- (and their central banks) are exempt from the large exposure limit, and exposures guaranteed or secured by instruments issued by these counterparties are similarly treated. Emirates (local) government exposures carry a 150% aggregate Tier 1 cap including their non-commercial PSEs (25% individual for those PSEs), while commercial government entities face 25% individual / 100% aggregate caps. Self-sustainable commercial PSEs may, with Central Bank approval, be treated as separate counterparties subject only to the general limit; the annexed table summarises all limits, including interbank and intragroup branch exposures.

Defines the Sharia'a supervision committee as the internal organ of an Islamic Finance Company responsible for confirming that its conduct, transactions and application methodologies comply with Islamic Sharia'a, with its formation and working method set out in the company's articles of association. The committee is accountable for its own Sharia'a decisions, views and opinions while the board retains ultimate governance responsibility and is expected to be guided by the committee; disputes with management must be escalated to the Higher Sharia'a Authority. Management must implement the committee's rulings, appointment and termination of members and chairmen follow Fit and Proper criteria, and operations manuals must be committee-approved.
lookup_terms: Fit and Proper Sharia'a committee members

data.summary: Identifies the Higher Sharia'a Authority as the external supra-entity body whose directions and guidance on Sharia'a governance bind Islamic Finance Companies, and which decides disputes escalated by a Sharia'a supervision committee against company management. Islamic Finance Companies must also notify the Higher Sharia'a Authority, alongside the Central Bank, of material information affecting the fitness and probity of a Sharia'a supervision committee member.

Refers to Federal Decree Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies (as amended), one of the enabling statutes recited in the Finance Companies Regulation (Circular 3/2023) and a defined term in its glossary. It is the corporate-law baseline for finance companies, used in the Regulation for matters such as the number of founding shareholders.

Defined term covering Decree Federal Law No. 20 of 2018 on AML/CTF and illegal organisations together with Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019 (its Implementing Regulation), as amended, and all related instructions, guidelines and notices. It is cited as a legal basis of the Finance Companies Regulation, so finance companies and restricted licence finance companies are bound by the whole AML/CTF package through this compound definition.

Sets the composition, qualification and responsibility requirements for the board of directors of a Finance Company: minimum five members, at least 60% with finance/banking (or Islamic finance) experience, a UAE-national majority and chair, all members non-executive with no overlap with general management, and at least one third independent. Board members owe duties of care and loyalty, must ensure effective control and a robust corporate governance policy proportionate to risk, approve and oversee strategy, risk management, compliance and internal/external audit, and set the organisational structure and the authorities of the board and Senior Management.
lookup_terms: Duty of Care Duty of Loyalty

data.summary: Defines the Credit Information Agency as Al Etihad Credit Bureau or any credit information agency established for UAE credit reporting, and frames the credit reporting duties tied to it. Restricted Licence Finance Companies and their Agents must supply Borrower credit information to the Agency on its terms and must obtain a credit report before extending credit of AED 5,000 or more; sharing or accessing Borrower credit information, including from employers, requires the Borrower's express consent, with disclosure to the Borrower and full compliance with data protection law.

A node for Insurance Authority Decision No. 50 of 2019, surfaced in the context of the CBUAE Standard on Shari'ah Governance for Takaful Insurance Companies, which is issued under the insurance operations law and the CBUAE law and complements the Takaful Insurance Regulation and the Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies. The surrounding material sets out defined terms (Takaful Company, Shari'ah non-compliance risk, Confidential Information, Higher Shari'ah Authority) and the general requirement that a takaful company's objectives, activities, operations and codes of conduct comply with Islamic Shari'ah at all times. It binds licensed takaful insurance companies and their governance bodies; note this is a UAE (CBUAE/Insurance Authority) instrument, not a SAMA one.
lookup_terms: Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies

data.summary: The CBUAE Finance Companies Regulation, issued under the Central Bank Law, establishing the licensing, permitted-activity, prudential, governance and conduct framework for Finance Companies and Restricted Licence Finance Companies in the UAE. Its stated aims are customer protection, protection of the companies themselves, and financial-sector stability; the Central Bank may impose requirements additional to those listed in any article. It applies to Finance Companies and Restricted Licence Finance Companies and their branches, with carve-outs for certain non-business inter-corporate short-term credit, direct instalment payment to vendors, and factoring/finance lease activity.

Defined-term node for "Finance Company" under the CBUAE Finance Companies Regulation, covering the entity licensed to carry out the listed financing activities and subject to the Regulation's funding, licensing and audit obligations. Key constraints include taking deposits and issuing certificates of deposit only from/to Juridical Persons (with a strict prohibition on individual deposits and accounts other than loan accounts), foreign funding capped at 25% of aggregate funding plus deposits with hedging, licence updates for new activities and a Central Bank no-objection for new product lines within licensed activities. It also carries external audit duties, including Central Bank pre-approval of the auditor, firm rotation every six years and audit-partner rotation every three years.
lookup_terms: no objection letter new product line

data.summary: Defined-term node for "Restricted Licence Finance Company" under the CBUAE Finance Companies Regulation — a licensee permitted to offer only Short-Term Credit and barred from contracting with Agents. It sits within the same regulatory framework as Finance Companies (Article 3 application, including branches) and is subject to specific borrower-facing disclosure duties: key product features, total credit amount and expiry, repayment process, Fees in both amount and percentage terms, late-payment consequences and fees, enforceable signed contracts with a copy to the Borrower, and available hardship assistance. Binds the licensed entity toward its Borrowers and the Central Bank.

Defined-term node for "Agent" under the CBUAE Finance Companies Regulation: a party a Finance Company may, with Central Bank non-objection, contract with to offer Short-Term Credit to Borrowers — either distributing credit funded by the Finance Company or granting credit fully funded by the Agent itself. The Finance Company must ensure the Agent complies with the applicable Part II articles except licensing, licence restrictions and minimum capital; Restricted Licence Finance Companies may not use Agents, so an Agent must partner with a Finance Company or a Bank. Agents are directly subject to the borrower disclosure and fair-conduct obligations (product features, Fees, late payment consequences, signed documentation, hardship assistance).

Defined-term node for "Islamic Finance Company" under the CBUAE Finance Companies Regulation: a Finance Company whose permitted financing activities are conducted in compliance with Islamic Sharia'a provisions. It must have a Sharia'a supervision committee (with members experienced in Islamic finance) whose formation and functions are set in the articles of association, and which is accountable for its Sharia'a decisions and opinions; the board retains ultimate governance responsibility but is expected to be guided by the committee. Disputes between the committee and management must be referred to the Higher Sharia'a Authority, and the corporate governance framework must address Sharia'a compliance, the committee's role and protection of investment account holders' rights.

Concept node for climate-related financial risk as used in the CBUAE Principles for the Effective Management of Climate-related Financial Risks. It frames climate risk not as a standalone risk type but as a driver that materialises through physical and transition (and possibly liability) channels within traditional risk categories — credit, market, operational, underwriting, reputational and liquidity — over short, medium and long horizons. It binds licensed financial firms in the UAE (banks, insurers and other CBUAE-supervised entities within the stated scope), which are expected to maintain a sound climate risk management framework with a board-approved risk appetite.

Concept node for the roles of the board and senior management under the CBUAE climate risk Principles. It establishes that the board defines, approves and oversees climate risk appetite, remains ultimately accountable even where functions are delegated, and that both board and senior management must maintain sufficient knowledge, with training and capacity building for relevant staff. The Principles are structure-neutral: they do not mandate a particular board or management model, only clarity of roles and evidenced oversight.

Principle 3 of the CBUAE climate risk Principles requires the board of a financial firm to assign climate-related financial risk management responsibilities across the organisation, to board committees or appropriate senior management. Assignments must be formally documented, with clear functions, accountability, governance structure, escalation and reporting lines, including for any dedicated climate roles or departments. Responsibilities must be reviewed regularly against the firm's business model, complexity and evolving climate risk methodologies.

Principle 4 requires the board and senior management to oversee the embedding of climate-related financial risks into the firm's internal risk management framework, including policies and procedures to identify, assess, measure, mitigate, monitor and report exposures. It contains the materiality considerations referenced by Principle 2 and extends to group-wide coordination where a firm has significant relationships with subsidiaries, affiliates or international branches. It binds CBUAE-licensed financial firms.

Principle 5 requires financial firms to ensure internal reporting systems can monitor material climate-related financial risks and produce relevant, accurate and timely information for board and senior management decision-making, with reporting to relevant stakeholders where required. It also requires firms to collect, analyse and aggregate climate risk data, embed it in monitoring and escalation processes, and address identified information and data gaps. Extent, form and frequency of internal reporting should be proportionate to the nature and scale of exposures.

Principle 6 requires relevant financial firms to incorporate material climate-related financial risks into internal capital and liquidity adequacy assessment processes, evaluating liquidity, capital and solvency impacts over specified time horizons. Where a firm is required to perform an ICAAP, ILAAP, ORSA or similar process, climate risks must be integrated into those frameworks and any material impact recorded. Applies to CBUAE-supervised firms subject to such processes (banks and insurers in particular).

Article 4 of the CBUAE recovery planning regulation sets how recovery plans must be prepared at group level, requiring coverage of every Financial Institution in the group, intra-group financial support arrangements, material intra-group links, and any legal or practical impediments to cross-entity recovery options. It allocates approval to the parent's board and differentiates scope by structure: UAE-headquartered institutions must cover the whole group, UAE subsidiaries of foreign parents must have a plan covering the subsidiary that is consistent with the group plan, and UAE branches must tailor the plan to local operations. It also sets the minimum content a foreign group plan must contain for the Central Bank to accept it as sufficient for local operations, and preserves the Central Bank's power to require standalone plans for group entities.
lookup_terms: UAE branch of foreign institution recovery plan

data.summary: Article 5 requires Financial Institutions to have effective governance for producing, reviewing, approving, monitoring and implementing the recovery plan. Board approval is required before submission to the Central Bank; for branches of foreign institutions the branch Senior Management committee approves, with the Central Bank able to additionally require head office board approval, and the chief risk officer leads development alongside Senior Management. It also requires clear roles and responsibilities, governance for the communication plan, adequate information systems, consistency with a bank's liquidity contingency funding plan, and permits insurers to draw on ERM/ORSA tools.

Article 6 governs the recovery indicator and trigger framework: indicators must be calibrated to give early warning, and a trigger breach does not automatically require implementing recovery options but does start an escalation chain — immediate Senior Management notification and assessment, board notification within one business day, and Central Bank notification within two business days (or immediately on activation of the plan). It defines what activation means, requires integration into risk management and MIS, and mandates both quantitative indicators (capital, liquidity, profitability, asset quality, per the Annex) and qualitative indicators, with justification of the chosen calibration and described escalation governance.

Article 7 defines recovery options as capital, liquidity, restructuring and other measures a Financial Institution can deploy in response to actual or expected stress to restore or maintain viability. It requires the plan to set out a broad range of implementable options, an approach for selecting and sequencing them by stress circumstance, and processes for valuing and assessing marketability of Core Business Lines, operations and assets. Islamic Financial Institutions have an added ongoing obligation to monitor debt-based asset proportions in portfolios earmarked for sale so the sale remains permissible.

Article 8 requires recovery plans to be tested against at least an idiosyncratic stress scenario, a system-wide stress scenario and a combined scenario, so as to demonstrate the adequacy of indicators, governance and recovery options. Scenarios must reflect how other institutions' actions affect option feasibility (with scenario-adjusted impacts), align with capital and liquidity planning stress tests, and be severe enough to bring the institution to an identified point of near failure, with reverse stress testing encouraged as a design starting point. Each scenario must show indicator evolution and trigger breaches with and without recovery actions, use conservative point estimates, and explain option choice, sequencing and timing.

Article 9 defines recovery capacity as the maximum financial benefit achievable from the most effective and credible combination of recovery options across stress scenarios, distinguishing actual capacity (currently available options) from potential capacity (planned improvements or new options where concrete development steps exist). The plan must assess capacity in monetary terms and regulatory metrics, the contribution of each option, and implementation and benefit timelines, and must describe planned improvements. Minimum metrics are specified for Banks (CET1, leverage, LCR, NSFR, or eligible liquid asset and loans-to-stable-resources ratios) and for Insurance Companies (solvency, liquidity and earnings ratios).
lookup_terms: CET1 leverage LCR NSFR recovery metrics
loans and advances to stable resources

data.summary: Principle 7 of the CBUAE climate-related financial risk principles sets the supervisory expectation that relevant financial firms build and run climate scenario analysis and stress testing frameworks proportionate to their size, complexity, risk profile and activities. It covers objectives of the analysis, data inputs and metrics, coverage of physical, transition and liability risk pathways, use of short- and long-term horizons, and feeding results into risk management adequacy reviews and the internal capital and liquidity adequacy processes under Principle 6. It binds financial firms within the CBUAE's scope of application for this instrument, on a 'should' (supervisory expectation) basis, with acknowledgement that methodologies are still maturing.

This node covers the materiality assessment expectations under the risk management framework principle (Principle 4) of the CBUAE climate-related financial risk principles. It requires financial firms to assess how and to what extent climate risks affect their business, operations and portfolios across strategic, financial, operational and reputational dimensions, using defined materiality definitions and quantitative and/or qualitative thresholds covering both physical and transition risk exposure, and to update existing risk management frameworks on that basis. It also links to group-wide coordination and to the incorporation of material climate risks into capital and liquidity adequacy processes.

This node addresses Principle 6 of the CBUAE climate principles: the incorporation of material climate-related financial risks into internal capital and liquidity adequacy assessment processes. Relevant financial firms are expected to evaluate liquidity, capital and solvency impacts over specified time horizons, including via transmission through traditional risk categories, and firms already required to run ICAAP, ILAAP, ORSA or equivalent must embed climate risk into those frameworks and record any material capital or liquidity impact. Adjacent content covers monitoring, internal reporting to the board and senior management, and group-level coordination.

This node identifies the Basel Committee's Principles for the effective management and supervision of climate-related financial risks (June 2022) as a reference listed in the Annex to the CBUAE climate-related financial risk instrument. It is a non-binding international standard used as the conceptual source for the CBUAE principles rather than a directly enforceable UAE obligation; the binding expectations sit in the CBUAE principles themselves. Useful for tracing the provenance and intended interpretation of the local governance, risk management and scenario analysis principles.

This node refers to the NGFS Climate Scenarios (2022) and related NGFS/FSB materials listed in the Annex of the CBUAE climate-related financial risk instrument. These are external reference scenarios and supervisory guides, not binding rules; they are relevant because firms building scenario analysis capability may rely on existing or emerging global or regional climate scenarios while developing internal capabilities. Read alongside Principle 7 on scenario analysis and stress testing.
lookup_terms: Network for Greening the Financial System

data.summary: This node covers the CBUAE recovery planning requirements applying to Financial Institutions, including how a local recovery plan must align with and complement a group recovery plan, and the tailored treatment of UAE branches of foreign institutions where the Central Bank may accept, or require changes to, the group plan. It also sets minimum content for a group plan to be treated as covering local operations, governance and communication arrangements, information systems supporting the plan, consistency with a bank's liquidity contingency funding plan, insurers' use of ERM/ORSA inputs, and recovery indicators with calibrated triggers. Obligations here are mandatory in character and bind Financial Institutions, Banks and Insurance Companies within scope.

Node for the CBUAE Finance Companies Regulation (labelled here as the earlier Circular 112/2018, with the supplied text corresponding to the replacement Circular 3/2023 addressed to all Finance Companies and Restricted Licence Finance Companies). It sets the licensing and prudential-conduct framework for finance and restricted-licence finance activity, with stated objectives of customer protection, protection of the licensees themselves, and financial-sector stability. It binds finance companies, restricted-licence finance companies and all their branches, is issued under the UAE Central Bank Law, and expressly allows the Central Bank to impose requirements beyond the minimum lists in individual articles; note it also cross-references the AML/CTF decree law and its implementing regulation, the Credit Information Law and the Commercial Companies Law.

Defined product category within the Finance Companies Regulation governing small-ticket short-term lending by Restricted Licence Finance Companies and their Agents. Core obligations: no interest may be charged; total fees including late-payment fees are capped at 30% of the original credit (maximum recoverable 130%, including after restructuring, rescheduling or roll-over); repayment term capped at twelve months from the original agreement; the original term must be honoured with no early demand for full payment; and borrower movable or immovable assets may not be taken as security. The adjacent credit-reporting article requires reporting borrower data to the Credit Information Agency, mandatory credit enquiry before extending credit of AED 5,000 or more, and express borrower consent for sharing or accessing credit information, plus data-protection compliance.

A set of supervisory principles on the effective management of climate-related financial risks, addressed to financial firms and framed around board and senior management accountability. It covers board oversight and risk appetite, integration of material climate risk exposures into overall business strategy, documented assignment of roles and responsibilities, embedding climate risk into the internal risk management framework (identification, assessment, measurement, mitigation, monitoring, reporting), group-wide coordination, and internal reporting systems and data-gap remediation. Drafted as expectations ("should") issued in accordance with the relevant laws of each participating jurisdiction rather than as a single binding rulebook.
lookup_terms: Principles for effective management of climate-related financial risks

data.summary: Institutional node describing the UAE Sustainable Finance Working Group, established in 2019 as a cross-government and cross-regulator body (ministries, CBUAE, SCA, ADGM FSRA, DFSA and the UAE exchanges) to promote sustainable finance nationally. Its outputs include the 2020 Guiding Principles on Sustainable Finance and public statements setting three workstreams on ESG reporting, corporate governance and risk management, and taxonomy. It is a standard-setting/coordination forum, not a licensing authority; its principles take effect through each member regulator's own legal framework.

Reference node for the Network for Greening the Financial System, an international grouping of central banks and supervisors whose work is cited as a source standard behind the climate-related financial risk principles. It is relevant as interpretive background for supervisory expectations on climate risk governance, scenario analysis and risk management, not as a binding instrument. No direct obligations flow from this node itself.
lookup_terms: Network for Greening the Financial System

data.summary: Reference node for the Paris Agreement, the international climate treaty ratified by the UAE in 2016, cited as the policy anchor for the SFWG's creation and for domestic climate initiatives such as the UAE Green Agenda 2015-2030, the National Climate Change Plan 2017-2050 and the Net Zero by 2050 Strategic Initiative. It is contextual background rather than a source of direct financial-sector obligations; supervisory duties arise from the derived principles and each regulator's own instruments.

Article 10 of the CBUAE recovery planning regulation, requiring banks' recovery plans to contain an operational plan for accessing central bank standing liquidity facilities, including foreign central bank facilities where relevant. It specifies the minimum content of that plan (identification of facilities, eligibility assessment, eligible assets and drawing capacity, access processes and role allocation, and repayment-enabling recovery options), bars reliance on discretionary extraordinary central bank liquidity or public support in the plan, and mandates periodic operational testing with notification to the facility provider that transactions are tests. Binds licensed banks (Financial Institutions subject to the recovery planning regime) in the UAE.

Article 11 of the CBUAE recovery planning regulation, setting business continuity requirements inside the recovery plan: assessing additional crisis-time requirements for maintaining Financial Market Infrastructure membership (e.g. pre-funding or collateralising positions) and putting in place contingency arrangements covering infrastructure, IT systems, key suppliers and key staff. It also requires institutions to ensure key service level agreements survive recovery events and that contracts permit transfer to third parties. Binds Financial Institutions (banks and insurance companies) preparing recovery plans under the regulation.

Article 12 of the CBUAE recovery planning regulation, requiring Financial Institutions to develop an adequate communication strategy for the public, financial markets, staff and other stakeholders to be used if the recovery plan is deployed. Surrounding context links it to governance requirements that communication plan procedures be embedded in, and consistent with, the recovery plan's governance and escalation arrangements, and to group/branch consistency rules. Binds Financial Institutions subject to recovery planning, including UAE branches of foreign institutions.

Concept node for the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee (ISSC) as used in the CBUAE recovery planning regulation and related definitions of Islamic Shari'ah Provisions (HSA resolutions and ISSC resolutions that must not contradict them). In the recovery planning context, an Islamic Financial Institution must additionally obtain ISSC approval confirming the recovery plan complies with Islamic Shari'ah Provisions, on top of Senior Management involvement, internal audit self-assessment and board approval. Binds Islamic Financial Institutions and Takaful insurers within the recovery planning governance chain.

CBUAE Standard on the Annual Shari'ah Report of the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee, setting supervisory expectations and general requirements for issuing that report, together with a report template. It places responsibility for preparing the report on the ISSC, requires presentation to the general assembly, and requires prior submission to the Higher Shari'ah Authority for review and approval at least one month before the general assembly. Applies to all Takaful Insurance Companies licensed by the Central Bank and is read with HSA standards and resolutions.

Concept node for the CBUAE Standard Re Shari'ah Governance for Takaful Insurance Companies, referenced as the framework that the Annual Shari'ah Report standard complements alongside the Regulation Regarding Takaful Insurance. It underpins the requirement that Takaful companies maintain Shari'ah governance policies and mechanisms ensuring the ISSC's annual report meets applicable standards, with the Central Bank able to impose additional requirements beyond the stated minimums. Binds Takaful Insurance Companies licensed by the Central Bank and their ISSCs.

CBUAE standard setting the requirements for the charter (functional rules) of the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee in Takaful insurance companies, complementing the Shari'ah Governance Standard for such companies. It requires companies to have Shari'ah governance policies and mechanisms ensuring the adopted charter meets this standard plus Central Bank and Higher Shari'ah Authority regulations, standards and resolutions, and annexes a minimum-content charter template that may be expanded but not contradicted. It binds all Takaful insurance companies licensed by the Central Bank, with a one-year compliance window from issuance, and preserves the Central Bank's power to impose additional requirements.

The annexed template charter that a Takaful insurance company must adopt for its Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee, covering the committee's definition, member qualifications, meeting mechanics, decision-making and other procedural matters. It represents the minimum content; additional articles are permitted only if consistent with applicable regulations, standards and resolutions. It operates on the company's board/management in adopting the charter and on ISSC members through fit-and-proper eligibility requirements.

Concept node for the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee: a body appointed by an Islamic/Takaful institution, composed of scholars specialised in Islamic financial transactions, mandated to supervise independently the institution's transactions, activities and products and confirm Shari'ah compliance across objectives, activities, operations and codes of conduct. Members must satisfy the fit-and-proper eligibility requirements set in applicable regulations, standards and resolutions. Referenced across several CBUAE Shari'ah governance instruments.

Article 2 of a CBUAE instrument on financial reporting and external audit for (Takaful) insurance companies, placing responsibility on the Board and Senior Management for financial statements prepared under internationally accepted accounting policies, supported by record keeping, and published annually with an independent external auditor's opinion. It requires the Board audit committee to oversee financial reporting and significant accounting policies, mandates IFRS and Central Bank reporting instructions, and requires prior written no-objection from the Central Bank before distributing profits, reserves or other regulatory capital components. Binds licensed companies, their boards and senior management.

Article 4 sets special considerations for the external audit, obliging the Board audit committee to assess the external auditor's overall quality at least annually, obtain the audit firm's internal quality control report, review significant audit matters and the management representation letter, and evaluate adherence to the audit plan with documented reporting to the Board. It grants the committee the right to meet the external auditor without Senior Management present and requires discussion of matters affecting regulatory capital or disclosures. It also requires an approved policy on permitted and prohibited non-audit services, with restrictions on the audit firm and its affiliates providing such services.

Article 5 imposes a direct duty on external auditors to report promptly to the Central Bank any breaches of the Central Bank law, regulations or instructions and any Matters of Significance arising from the audit, with good-faith reporting protected from being treated as a breach of the auditor's obligations. Companies must notify the Central Bank of auditor resignation and reasons, and obtain non-objection before dismissing or changing the auditor; divergence of opinion is not valid grounds for dismissal. Material reservations must be reported before the audit is finalised, and a qualified opinion cannot be finalised without Central Bank non-objection; Article 6 permits appointment of an External Shari'ah Auditor for Takaful products.
lookup_terms: duty to report to Central Bank

data.summary: A CBUAE instrument section addressing external audit and Shari'ah audit arrangements for Takaful insurance companies, with the excerpted text setting out the Board audit committee's duties to appoint, monitor and annually assess the External Auditor. It binds the Board and its audit committee, Senior Management and the engaged audit firm (including affiliates and subsidiaries), covering audit quality review, private meetings without Senior Management, escalation of matters affecting regulatory capital or disclosures, and an approved policy restricting non-audit services. Relevant when assessing auditor independence, engagement scoping or audit-committee governance obligations of a Takaful/insurance company.

CBUAE Sandbox Conditions Regulation (Circular 6/2023, effective 31/12/2023), issued under the Central Bank Law powers to exempt specified activities from the licensing requirement and to set conditions for supervised testing. It establishes the Regulatory Sandbox framework: eligibility, application process, minimum safeguards during testing, and exit routes, applied case by case under Central Bank discretion. Addressed to all Licensed Financial Institutions and to any person seeking to test innovative models, products or services relating to Licensed Financial Activities.

Defines the Regulatory Sandbox as a supervisory tool allowing accepted Participants to test innovative financial products, services and business models within a defined space and time under Central Bank oversight, in lieu of holding a Licence. Sets scope limits: it is unavailable for deposit-taking of all types, insurance activities in the State, and acting as principal in financial products affecting the person's financial position (e.g. FX, derivatives, bonds and sukuk, equities, commodities). Licensed Financial Institutions may not participate; their out-of-scope innovation must instead be discussed with the Central Bank before market deployment.

Sets the eligibility criteria an Applicant must satisfy to enter, and continuously to remain in, the Regulatory Sandbox. The product, service, solution or business model must relate to financial products/services touching Central Bank objectives or constituting a Licensed Financial Activity, be genuinely innovative (new technology or novel use of existing technology), deliver benefit to Consumers or the financial services industry, show a real need for sandbox testing, and be intended for deployment in the State. Binds Applicants; assessment and admission remain at the Central Bank's discretion.

Cross-reference node for the CBUAE Consumer Protection Regulation (Circular 8/2020) as it interacts with the Regulatory Sandbox: sandbox Consumers may fall outside that Regulation's protections, so the Applicant must obtain express, informed written consent after clear, fair and not misleading disclosure of financial and other risks and a summary of the regulatory protections being foregone. Also anchors the sandbox safeguards on Consumer protection and financial-system protection, including complaints, compensation and dispute resolution, segregation of Consumer funds/assets in escrow with a Central Bank-licensed bank, data handling and protection, restrictions on which Consumers may be served, fitness and propriety of connected individuals, and AML/CTF measures. Binds Applicants and Participants.

Sets out the three-stage sandbox application process — preliminary (indicative suitability within 15 working days of a complete submission), evaluation (engagement on adjustments and required safeguards, up to 21 working days) and decision (final determination within 15 working days of resubmission, with reasons if rejected). Also lists the supporting information to accompany an application, including test scenarios and expected outcomes, operational readiness and testing plan, exit and transition strategy, reporting plan and metrics, client acquisition and communication strategy, wind-down plan, risk assessment with mitigations, and Consumer-facing disclosures. Binds Applicants; admission remains solely at the Central Bank's discretion and case by case.

Concept node drawn from the CBUAE Standard on the Shari'ah Compliance Function at Islamic Financial Institutions, addressing where responsibility for Shari'ah non-compliance risk sits: with the institution's risk management function rather than the Shari'ah Compliance Function, with an expectation of mutual information-sharing between the two. The surrounding articles frame the Standard as complementary to the Shari'ah Governance Standard and set out the stages the SCF's review process must cover. It binds licensed financial institutions conducting all or part of their business in accordance with Islamic Shari'ah, and the Central Bank reserves the ability to impose requirements beyond the stated minimums.

Instrument node for the CBUAE Guidance Note on the Shari'ah Compliance Function at Islamic Financial Institutions, issued to support implementation of the corresponding binding Standard. It applies to all IFIs, but on a comply-or-equivalent basis: institutions may follow the guidance or apply equivalent criteria to meet the Standard's requirements. It is to be read together with the Standard and with Higher Shari'ah Authority standards and resolutions notified to IFIs, and it elaborates the SCF review cycle from annual planning through field review, issues, reports and progress monitoring.

Concept node covering the sampling element of the SCF field review under the CBUAE Guidance Note. It expects the Shari'ah Compliance Function to adopt an objective, robust sampling methodology with a defined minimum sample proportion so that reviewed transactions fairly represent the review period, and to enlarge the sample where there is reasonable doubt whether an identified Shari'ah non-compliance incident is isolated or systemic. The trigger conditions for expanding samples must themselves be set out in the institution's methodology; generic guidance sits in an appendix.

Concept node for the appendix guidance on building a product review checklist for SCF reviews. It sets the coverage expected when checking a product for compliance with Islamic Shari'ah — the underlying structure, documentation templates, product manuals and workflows, accounting treatment, fees and charges, and the IT system's compatibility with the product's Shari'ah-compliant operation. It also indicates review frequency expectations for products, including a risk-based standard and a minimum review cycle.

Concept node covering how an IFI selects subjects for the SCF annual review plan. The Guidance Note expects the Board and senior management to approve the annual plan and secure cooperation from relevant department heads, and expects the institution to build a prioritization matrix based on review frequency, historical incidents, and product size and complexity. The appendix gives illustrative parameters, including review cycles for products, branches and distribution channels, early review of new products, and priority for areas with past systemic or major incidents.

Instrument node for the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation, which defines and regulates payment token activities — payment token issuing, custody and transfer, and conversion — and the persons performing them by way of business. It contains the core definitional architecture (Payment Token Issuer, Dirham vs Foreign Payment Token Issuer, Payment Token Conversion Provider, Payment Token Custodian and Transferor, Payment Token Data, Payment Token Transfer), including the rule that where a token is first passed to a distributor for onward sale, the distributor is treated as performing the issuing. It also prohibits interest-like benefits tied to holding periods and empowers the Central Bank to cap volumes, values or customer numbers, or to restrict further sales, transfers or onboarding.

Section 9 of the CBUAE Regulatory Sandbox Conditions, setting the minimum safeguards a Participant must maintain throughout testing, framed around two protective aims: consumer protection and protection of the financial system. Required measures include complaint/compensation and dispute-resolution mechanisms notified to participating Consumers, segregation of Consumer funds or assets in an escrow arrangement with a Central Bank–licensed bank, data handling and protection arrangements, limits on which Consumers may be served plus express informed written consent, ongoing fitness and propriety of connected individuals, and AML/CTF measures under applicable legislation. It binds accepted Sandbox Participants, with the Central Bank reviewing ongoing compliance ad hoc and through agreed reporting, and able to impose additional case-specific safeguards.

The exit-routes element of the CBUAE Regulatory Sandbox Conditions, which (per the Overview at section 4) is one of four matters the Conditions regulate alongside eligibility, the application process and minimum safeguards. It covers how participation ends and what a Participant must do on exit, including the route toward applying for a Licence for market-wide deployment. It binds Participants (applicants accepted in full by the Central Bank) and clarifies the Central Bank's role and powers over them; related definitions (Participant, Regulations, the State) sit in section 3.

Covers sections 10.3–12.1 of the CBUAE Regulatory Sandbox Conditions: grounds for discontinuing testing (purpose not achieved, risks outweighing benefits, breach of Central Bank requirements, voluntary exit, lapse of the period), the Central Bank's power to require immediate cessation and wind-down, the mandatory exit strategy (notifying Consumers, meeting Consumer obligations including compensation, reporting on implementation, secure disposal of Consumer information), the six-to-twelve-month testing duration with case-by-case extensions requested at least 30 calendar days before expiry, and the obligation to document and periodically report testing information. It binds Sandbox Participants and supports Central Bank supervision and review.

Article 5 of the CBUAE Shari'ah Compliance Function standard, requiring the Shari'ah Compliance Function (SCF) of an Islamic Financial Institution to review and evaluate Shari'ah non-compliance controls, report on them and monitor remedial actions. The IFI must adopt internal policies and procedures covering at least six review stages: annual plan, planning and scoping, field review, issues and actions, draft reports and progress monitoring. It also delimits responsibilities: managing Shari'ah Non-Compliance Risk sits with risk management, not the SCF, and the SCF reviews pre/at execution while Shari'ah audit reviews post-execution.

Article 6 of the CBUAE Shari'ah Compliance Function standard, making the SCF responsible for developing the annual review plan ("Annual Plan"). The plan requires approval by both the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee (ISSC) and the Board, establishing a dual governance sign-off. It binds Islamic Financial Institutions and their Shari'ah compliance functions, and sits as the first of the mandated review stages under Article 5.
lookup_terms: Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee ISSC approval

data.summary: Article 8 of the CBUAE Shari'ah Compliance Function standard, requiring the IFI's SCF to carry out a field review of the institution using procedures built on a robust methodological basis, with further detail available in the standard's guidance note. It follows the planning and scoping stage (Article 7) and precedes issues and actions (Article 9) in the mandated review cycle. It binds Islamic Financial Institutions through their Shari'ah Compliance Function.

A defined activity within the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation: Payment Token Conversion is one of the three licensable Payment Token Services (alongside Payment Token Issuing and Payment Token Custody and Transfer), performed by way of business by a Payment Token Conversion Provider. The node also carries the Central Bank's power to cap the volume or value of Payment Tokens a Conversion Provider may buy, sell or admit to trading on its platform, and to cap or freeze customer on-boarding. It binds licensed Payment Token Conversion Providers and Registered Payment Token Conversion Providers (including Virtual Assets Exchange Platform Operators, Banks and Exchange Houses holding a Non-Objection Registration).

Defines Payment Token Custody and Transfer as one of the three Payment Token Services under the CBUAE regulation, and links to the related defined terms Payment Token Transfer (an act initiated by Payer, Payee or the Payment Token Issuer to transfer a token or an interest in it) and Payment Token Data. Carries the Central Bank's power to limit the number of customers a Payment Token Custodian and Transferor may serve or to restrict new on-boarding. Binds Licensed Payment Token Custodians and Transferors and Registered Foreign Payment Token Custodians and Transferors.
lookup_terms: Registered Foreign Payment Token Custodian and Transferor

data.summary: The Dirham Payment Token is the token category referenced against AED and issued by a Dirham Payment Token Issuer under the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation; issuance requires a Central Bank licence. The Central Bank may cap the total volume or value of tokens such an issuer may sell or transfer, cap total customer numbers, or restrict new customer on-boarding. Means of Payment that are neither Dirham Payment Tokens nor Foreign Payment Tokens (including Algorithmic Stablecoins and Privacy Tokens) are subject to prohibitions on issuance, promotion and related services.

The Foreign Payment Token is the non-AED token category under the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation; its issuers may operate towards Persons in the UAE only via a Foreign Payment Token Issuer Registration. The regulation limits certain services and the promotion of services relating to Foreign Payment Tokens and restricts their acceptance as a Means of Payment, and the Central Bank may cap volume, value or UAE customer numbers. Binds Registered Foreign Payment Token Issuers, Registered Foreign Payment Token Custodians and Transferors, and persons promoting or accepting such tokens in the UAE.

Sets the regulatory capital regime for Payment Token Service Providers under Articles 13 to 15, comprising initial capital as a licensing precondition and ongoing capital thereafter. Payment Token Issuers hold a fixed minimum plus an add-on calculated on the fiat face value of outstanding tokens (a higher fixed amount and 2% add-on where the alternative Reserve of Assets treatment under Article 22(3) applies); custody/transfer and conversion providers hold a minimum scaled to monthly average transfer values. The Central Bank may impose additional or increased capital requirements as a condition of licensing. Binds applicants and Licensed Payment Token Service Providers.

Describes the Non-Objection Registration route under the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation, available to a Virtual Assets Exchange Platform Operator, Bank or Exchange House applying to the Central Bank, and the associated application process and conditions. Applicants must disclose their SCA or Local Licensing Authority licensing status and the nature and extent of that licensed business, and demonstrate they will meet the conditions and requirements the Central Bank imposes. It sits alongside the full Payment Token Service Licence and the Foreign Payment Token Issuer Registration as distinct authorisation types, and covers modifications to the scope of a granted registration.

Concept node covering the CBUAE registration route for Foreign Payment Token Issuers (and related Registrees such as Registered Foreign Payment Token Custodians and Transferors and Registered Payment Token Conversion Providers) under the Payment Token Services Regulation. It frames the Central Bank's licensing, registration, supervisory and ongoing reporting powers, and its power to cap the volume, value or number of UAE customers to which a Foreign Payment Token Issuer may sell or transfer tokens. It binds foreign issuers seeking to have their tokens used or promoted in the UAE, and constrains licensees dealing in such tokens.

Article 24 of the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation, imposing AML/CFT obligations on "AML Obligors" in addition to and without prejudice to the UAE AML Law and other AML/CFT rules. It treats Payment Token Services as inherently high ML/TF risk (speed, anonymity, cross-border), and requires enterprise and customer risk assessment, risk-rated CDD and ongoing due diligence, internal policies and controls, compliance management including a compliance officer and MLRO, and STR filing to the FIU, with secrecy unavailable as a defence to reporting.
lookup_terms: customer due diligence CDD risk rating

data.summary: Article 20 of the Payment Token Services Regulation, which applies the CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation for Banks (Circular No. 14/2021, as amended) to all Licensees as if each were a "Bank" under that regulation. The node also sits alongside the agency provisions, under which a Payment Token Service performed by an Agent is deemed performed by the principal Licensee, which remains responsible for agent training and qualifications.

Defined-term node for "Virtual Asset" as used in the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation, where a Payment Token is a Virtual Asset that purports to maintain a stable value by reference to a fiat currency (or another token in the same fiat currency). It marks the perimeter between CBUAE-supervised payment token activity and virtual asset activity licensed by SCA or a Local Licensing Authority, including information-sharing with those regulators and the post-Transition Period disapplication of the Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation and the Stored Value Facilities Regulation to crypto-asset/virtual asset activities.
lookup_terms: Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation

data.summary: Concept node for the CBUAE prohibition on Algorithmic Stablecoins: no Person, within the UAE or directing activity at Persons in the UAE, may issue them, perform services relating to them, or promote their issuance or related services. The ban is regulator-agnostic, applying to all Persons including those licensed or regulated by SCA or a Local Licensing Authority for virtual asset activities, and the Central Bank may demand evidence or periodic reporting of compliance.

Concept node for "Privacy Token" under the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation, which prohibits any Person in or targeting the UAE from issuing Privacy Tokens, performing services relating to them, or promoting them — including Persons licensed or regulated by SCA or a Local Licensing Authority. It connects to the traceability logic of the regime (identifiable transfer of disposal power between Wallets, white paper and customer agreement disclosure) and to the Central Bank's powers to limit volumes, values and customer numbers for token issuers and service providers.

Article 36 of the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation sets operational resilience duties for Payment Token Service Providers, requiring a business continuity management programme built on business impact analysis, documented and tested recovery strategies, and a business continuity plan covering recovery procedures, escalation and crisis management (including timely Central Bank reporting), customer and media communication, key-personnel contacts and primary/alternate recovery roles. It also mandates protection and timely restoration of business and Customer records, Customer access to their records, notification of record loss through operational failure or theft, at least annual testing with Senior Management participation, formal test documentation and a post-mortem signed off by Senior Management. Separately it requires a viable business exit plan for an orderly wind-down so failure or exit does not disrupt Customers or UAE payment systems.

Article 37 is the enforcement clause of the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation: breach of any provision of the Regulation, or commission of violations under the Central Bank Law, exposes a Licensee or Registree to administrative and financial sanctions and penalties at the Central Bank's discretion. It is the hook that makes the substantive obligations in the Regulation enforceable against licensed and registered payment token firms.

Article 38 gives the CBUAE additional information-gathering powers, allowing it to require information it considers necessary from Licensees and Registrees and from virtual asset service providers that are neither licensed/registered by the Central Bank nor licensed or regulated by SCA or a Local Licensing Authority. It also permits the Central Bank to enter information-sharing agreements or memoranda of understanding with, or request information from, SCA, Local Licensing Authorities and other regulators to exercise its powers or meet the Regulation's objectives.

Article 39 resolves the perimeter overlap between the Payment Token Services Regulation and the existing Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation and the Stored Value Facilities (SVF) Regulation.
