At the end of the Transition Period, persons licensed under those regulations for Crypto-Asset, Virtual Asset Token or Virtual Asset activities cease to be licensed for those activities, and both regulations stop applying to those defined crypto/virtual asset categories and their service providers.
lookup_terms: Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation

data.summary: Article 40 establishes a one calendar-year Transition Period from commencement of the Regulation during which Article 2 (the licensing/registration and prohibition provisions) does not apply, extendable at the Central Bank's discretion. Despite the grace period, the Central Bank may order cessation of any in-scope business of a service provider it judges unlikely to be able to comply with Article 2 after the Transition Period. The accompanying articles designate the Regulatory Development Department as the interpretive authority and set publication and entry into force one month after Official Gazette publication.

This node covers the defined term Payment Token Service Provider under the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation, the umbrella category for persons performing Payment Token Issuing, Payment Token Custody and Transfer, or Payment Token Conversion by way of business. It frames the Regulation's licensing and registration classes (Licensed Payment Token Service Providers, Registered Foreign Payment Token Issuers, Registered Foreign Payment Token Custodians and Transferors, Registered Payment Token Conversion Providers), the Central Bank's supervisory, reporting and quantitative limit-setting powers over volumes, values and customer onboarding, and the regime's objectives of safety and soundness, protection of the Reserve of Assets, risk-based licensing and consumer protection.

A cross-reference concept node for the UAE Securities & Commodities Authority (and Local Licensing Authorities) as it appears in the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation. It marks the points where the Regulation's prohibitions (e.g. on payment token transfers outside permitted dirham/foreign payment tokens, on algorithmic stablecoins and privacy tokens, and on related promotions) bite on all Persons regardless of being licensed or regulated by SCA or a local authority for virtual asset activities, and where CBUAE may demand evidence of compliance. It also flags the discretionary exemption where equivalent white-paper style documentation or obligations already exist under SCA or local licensing authority rules.

Article 25 of the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation sets the general conduct duties owed by Licensees and Registrees to Customers: prudent, competent, responsible, honest and professional operation that does not adversely affect Customer interests. It expressly layers the Central Bank's Consumer Protection Regulation and Standards on top, with the consumer protection provisions prevailing in case of conflict, and adds distributed ledger duties (keeping a copy of the relevant ledger and treating forked versions of a payment token as equivalent).

Article 26 governs the payment token White Paper: the mandatory disclosure document a Payment Token Issuer must publish, including due diligence on the underlying distributed ledger, the point at which lawful power of disposal passes between Tokenholders on a transfer, and risk warnings about failed, reversed or delayed transfers and redemption/compensation routes. The Central Bank may exempt an issuer from one or more of these requirements where equivalent documentation has been published or equivalent obligations complied with under SCA or Local Licensing Authority rules.

Article 27 requires every Payment Token Service Provider (defined here as a Licensee or Registree, excluding Registered Foreign Payment Token Issuers) to set out its contractual terms with each Customer in a Customer Agreement — a Framework Agreement or Single Payment Token Service Agreement — supplied far enough in advance for an informed decision, and to give Customers and Tokenholders a copy on request. It also covers advance notice of at least 30 calendar days for term changes, a free termination right where the Customer rejects revised terms, and extension of the agreement's rights and obligations to Tokenholders even where the issuer does not know their identity.

Article 28 lists the minimum terms and pre-contractual information that a Payment Token Service Provider (Licensee or Registree, excluding Registered Foreign Payment Token Issuers) must include in and provide with its Customer Agreement before any service is supplied. Content includes the fee, charge and commission schedule (redemption fees, conversion rates, withdrawal charges), provider and agent identification, consent and consent-withdrawal procedures for transfers, communication channels, safeguarding arrangements, notification timelines and liability allocation for unauthorised or incorrectly executed transfers, change-acceptance and termination terms, service levels and complaints procedures.

Article 29 of the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation addresses transactional information — the information a Payment Token Service Provider must give Customers in connection with individual payment token transactions, following on from the pre-contractual and Customer Agreement content required by Article 28. The provided context captures mainly the Article 28 list preceding it, so the operative text of Article 29 should be read in the source document.

Defined actor under the CBUAE Payment Token Services framework: the licensed (Dirham) or registered Foreign entity that performs Payment Token Issuing, i.e. sells or transfers payment tokens to Customers/Tokenholders. The node covers issuer-facing obligations including the prohibition on interest-like benefits tied to holding period, Central Bank powers to cap volume, value or Customer numbers (including on-boarding restrictions, and separately for Payment Token Conversion Providers and Custodian/Transferors), redemption duties and Customer Agreement/White Paper disclosure on transfer finality, forks and failed transfers. Binds licensed Dirham payment token issuers and foreign payment token issuers dealing with Persons in the UAE (CBUAE jurisdiction, not SAMA).

Concept node for the Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) on which payment tokens are issued and transferred, as treated in the CBUAE Payment Token Services regulation. It carries the issuer's duties to keep a copy of the ledger, provide a redemption route independent of normal DLT operation in case of failure or disruption, handle 'forks' by redeeming one version as the original, specify the DLT-specific point of transfer of lawful power of disposal, and warn Customers about failed, reversed or unwound transfers and settlement timing. Binds Licensed Payment Token Issuers under CBUAE (UAE) rules.

Institutional node describing the UAE Sustainable Finance Working Group, established 2019, comprising UAE ministries, financial regulators (CBUAE, SCA, ADGM FSRA, DFSA) and exchanges, which issued the Guiding Principles on Sustainable Finance and the Principles for Sustainability-Related Disclosures. It sets a common minimum expectation on ESG/sustainability disclosure for Reporting Entities, with implementation left to each member Authority's own framework. Not directly binding on firms; relevant as soft-law/comparative material for KSA analysts (UAE, not SAMA).

Principle 1 of the UAE SFWG Principles for Sustainability-Related Disclosures: Reporting Entities should have adequate policies, procedures and systems to report on sustainability matters, covering internal reporting systems for material sustainability risks and data-gap remediation within a data governance framework, timely internal reporting to the board and senior management, and timely public reporting. Expressed as expectations ('should'), binding only once translated into a member Authority's regulatory framework.

Principle 2 of the UAE SFWG Disclosure Principles sets the factors Reporting Entities should consider when disclosing sustainability-related risks and opportunities; the node also carries the Application section explaining that the Principles are a shared minimum expectation and that each Authority decides scope, entity thresholds, required disclosures, frequency, voluntary/'comply or explain'/mandatory status and implementation timeline. Useful mainly for understanding the non-self-executing legal status of the Principles. UAE instrument, not SAMA.

Principle 3 of the UAE SFWG Disclosure Principles sets the expected minimum content of sustainability disclosures along the governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets pillars, including board knowledge and oversight, senior management roles, transition plans, and short-, medium- and long-term effects on business model and financial results. Applies as an expectation to Reporting Entities under the member Authorities, subject to each Authority's implementation choices.
lookup_terms: governance strategy risk management metrics and targets

data.summary: Principle 4 of the CBUAE/Sustainable Finance Working Group ESG disclosure principles addresses product-level disclosure for sustainability-related products, covering naming, labelling and classification, and disclosure of sustainability objectives and strategies in offering documents. It is framed as an expectation on market participants offering such products, aimed at preventing misleading or inconsistent sustainability claims (greenwashing). As a principles document it is not directly binding; each Authority decides how and to whom it is translated into its own regulatory framework.

"Reporting Entities" is the addressee concept in the CBUAE-endorsed ESG Disclosure Principles: entities expected to maintain internal systems, policies and procedures to monitor, escalate to board and senior management, and publicly report sustainability-related risks and information. The Principles deliberately leave it to each Authority to determine which entities, size or profile thresholds, frequency, and whether reporting is voluntary, comply-or-explain, or mandatory. Useful for scoping who is captured before assessing substantive disclosure duties.

This node covers the substantive entity-level sustainability disclosure content set out in Principle 3: governance, strategy (including transition plans and short/medium/long-term effects), risk management integration with the overall risk framework including capital and liquidity, and metrics and targets. It states minimum expected disclosures for Reporting Entities, with additional requirements possible by entity type. Consult it for the TCFD-style four-pillar structure adopted in the UAE principles.
lookup_terms: governance strategy risk management metrics and targets

data.summary: A reference node explaining that the Disclosure Principles acknowledge existing voluntary frameworks (GRI, SASB, IIRC, TCFD, CDSB, ISSB) and the international move toward convergence, including ISSB standards and Basel Committee Pillar 3 climate disclosures. It provides context and objectives rather than obligations. Open it to understand which external standards the UAE principles are aligned to or expected to converge with.

The CBUAE Insurance Brokers' Regulation governs licensing, ongoing requirements, fit and proper assessment, brokerage agreements, premiums and claim settlement flows, financial soundness, corporate governance, risk governance and internal controls, conduct of business, financial and supervisory reporting, and record keeping. It binds all insurance brokers and insurance/reinsurance companies operating in the UAE, across primary insurance and (proportionately) reinsurance operations. Notably it prohibits brokers from collecting premiums, claim settlements or premium refunds in primary insurance, requiring direct client-company payment.

Article 1 sets the defined terms used throughout the Insurance Brokers' Regulation, including Applicant, Beneficiary, Central Bank, Central Bank Laws, Insurance Broker and its Representatives, Insurance Brokerage (solicit / negotiate / sell), Remuneration, and Internal Controls. These definitions determine the regulatory perimeter — notably what activity constitutes brokerage and therefore requires a licence. Read together with the Scope of Application and the proportionality principle.

Article 30 of the CBUAE Payment Token Services Regulation sets the data-protection obligations attaching to Personal Data handled in connection with payment token activity, including localisation of storage in the UAE absent Central Bank approval, a secure separate backup, and a five-year retention period. It requires licensed Payment Token Service Providers to meet applicable data protection law and the Consumer Protection Regulation, and to control, process and retain only Personal Data necessary for the service and only with the Customer's explicit consent. It binds licensed providers of payment token issuing, custody and transfer, and conversion services.

Article 31 allocates liability for Unauthorized Payment Token Transfers and sets the refund duty. A Payment Token Custodian and Transferor is fully liable for fraudulent or unauthorised transfers it initiates, facilitates, effects or directs, or otherwise made from a Wallet it maintains, whether before or after the Customer reports suspected fraud, unless the Customer acted fraudulently or with gross negligence in failing to keep the Wallet safe; where liability attaches, the amount must be refunded. It binds custody-and-transfer providers vis-à-vis Customers and Tokenholders, and links to Customer Agreement disclosure duties on notification timelines and liability.

Article 32 is the final business-conduct provision of the payment token conduct block (Articles 25–32) and addresses certainty and finality of payment token transfers, including the extent to which a provider is responsible for completion timing given execution on Distributed Ledger Technology, alongside a requirement that a comprehensive audit trail be available to the Customer. It bears on disclosure expectations to Customers about settlement on the ledger. It binds licensed payment token service providers dealing with Customers.

Article 33 (Part 9) requires effective, robust and well-documented corporate governance arrangements, including a clear organisational structure with defined and transparent lines of responsibility, proportionate to the nature, scale and complexity of the Payment Token Services provided. Minimum content includes an organisation chart with named responsible individuals and function descriptions, conflict-of-interest controls, integrity and transparency controls, and controls to ensure legal and regulatory compliance. For this Article, "Payment Token Service Provider" means a Licensee or Registree, excluding Registered Foreign Payment Token Issuers.

Article 34 sets the general risk management and internal control requirements for payment token businesses, sitting alongside Article 35 (technology risk) as the risk-policy limb assessed at licensing and covering matters such as record-keeping of Personal Data and Payment Data for five years. It is cross-referenced in the licensing chapter as one of the areas an applicant must demonstrate compliance with, together with capital, Reserve of Assets, conduct/customer protection and AML/CTF requirements. It binds Licensees and Registrees providing Payment Token Services.

Article 35 requires Payment Token Service Providers to establish an effective technology and cyber security risk management framework covering IT controls, cyber resilience, and the reliability, robustness, stability, availability and security of computer systems, proportionate to the nature, size, complexity and technologies of the business, and informed by recognised international standards. It mandates IT governance (IT function, technology risk management function, independent technology audit), Board-level responsibility for the risk framework, compliance with the UAE Information Assurance Standards, and specific policies on forking events, adverse ledger governance actions, redemption rights, and safeguarding self-held tokens. It applies to Licensees and Registrees, excluding Registered Foreign Payment Token Issuers.

Licensing article of the CBUAE Insurance Brokerage Regulation: it prohibits any person from carrying on Insurance Brokerage in the UAE without a Central Bank licence, and bars insurance/reinsurance companies from engaging unlicensed intermediaries. It sets the three licence categories (primary insurance, reinsurance, or both), incorporation and application conditions (including bank guarantee support), and a six-month window to obtain local licences and commence activity. Binds applicants and licensed Insurance Brokers, and indirectly the Companies that deal with them.

Enforcement article empowering the Central Bank to revoke, suspend, restrict or vary an Insurance Broker's licence at any time on stated grounds, including breach of licensing conditions, false or misleading information supplied by the broker or its Representatives, threats to the interests of Clients, and liquidation (ordered or voluntary). Binds licensed Insurance Brokers and their Representatives; relevant when assessing supervisory sanction exposure.

Sets continuing licence-maintenance obligations for Insurance Brokers: no combining brokerage with other Insurance-Related Professions, no partnership or agency with another broker, notification duties to the Central Bank on appointment, transfer, termination or vacancy of Specialised Employees (with replacement within 30 days), and adequate qualified staffing including at least one Specialised Employee per licensed line. Also requires prior written Central Bank approval before changing legal status, ownership, capital or premises.
lookup_terms: prior written approval change of ownership capital
staffing per licensed line of business

data.summary: Defines and operationalises the Fit and Proper Process for natural persons proposed as Insurance Broker's Representatives, Senior Management, Specialised Employees and others designated by the Central Bank. Criteria cover qualifications, knowledge and experience, integrity, competence and financial soundness, sufficient time, absence of Conflict of Interest, compliance with the insurance law's personal-suitability requirements, and passing the Central Bank's assessment (including good conduct, no unrehabilitated moral-turpitude conviction or bankruptcy).

Governs the written Insurance Brokerage agreements between brokers and Companies, and confirms the Central Bank may require amendment of specific terms case by case to protect the public interest. Read with the Article 1 definitions of Insurance Broker and Insurance Brokerage (solicit, negotiate, sell) that frame the independent intermediary role and remuneration by the Company.
lookup_terms: Central Bank amendment of contract terms

data.summary: Sets money-flow rules: Premiums for primary insurance must be paid by Clients directly to Companies, brokers must instruct Clients in writing before inception and keep evidence of acknowledgment, and brokers are prohibited from collecting Premiums, Claim Settlements or Premium refunds in primary business. Reinsurance flows are left to the reinsurance brokerage agreement; brokers earn Remuneration from the Company on conclusion of an Insurance Policy, and brokers and insurers must maintain the means to operate these flows.

Article 20 of the CBUAE Insurance Brokers' Regulation (Circular 1/2024) repeals the predecessor Insurance Authority instruments governing insurance brokerage, namely the 2013 Board resolution on the Insurance Brokerage Regulation as amended, the 2013 Director General implementing decision, and the Insurance Authority work guide for internal controllers at brokerage companies. It sits alongside the enforcement article making breaches of the Regulation subject to CBUAE supervisory action and sanctions. Relevant to anyone determining which instrument applies to an Insurance Broker from the Regulation's application date.

Defined-term node for "Insurance Broker" under the CBUAE Insurance Brokers' Regulation: a licensed person that independently intermediates between an insurance or reinsurance client and a Company, and is remunerated by the Company with which the cover is placed. The definition anchors related terms (Insurance Brokerage as soliciting/negotiating/selling, Insurance Broker's Representatives, Internal Controls) and drives the Regulation's conduct rules, including the prohibition on brokers collecting Premiums, Claim Settlements or Premium refunds in primary insurance. Binds all entities licensed or seeking licence for insurance brokerage in the UAE, and the Companies dealing with them.

Reference node for Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities, as amended, cited as one of the enabling powers for the CBUAE Insurance Brokers' Regulation. It is the statutory basis for CBUAE licensing, prudential and supervisory authority over insurance brokers alongside the 2023 insurance law. Useful when tracing the legal authority behind a CBUAE regulation or sanction.

Reference node for Decretal Federal Law No. 48 of 2023 Concerning the Organization of Insurance Operations, the sector statute under which (together with the 2018 Central Bank Law) the CBUAE issued the Insurance Brokers' Regulation. It underpins licensing, conduct and supervision of insurance and reinsurance intermediation in the UAE. Consult when identifying the primary insurance legislation behind broker obligations.

Reference node for Decretal Federal Law No. 32 of 2021 on Commercial Companies, cited in the Insurance Brokers' Regulation both as a recital and in the licensing article: applicants must be incorporated in the State under this law with insurance brokerage as their objective (or fall within the alternative licensing routes). Relevant to corporate form, incorporation and eligibility questions for broker licence applicants.

Reference node for Insurance Authority Board of Directors Resolution No. 15 of 2013 on the Insurance Brokerage Regulation, as amended — the predecessor regime for insurance brokers, cited in the recitals of CBUAE Circular 1/2024 and expressly cancelled by Article 20 of the new Regulation. Relevant only for historical or transitional analysis of broker obligations before the CBUAE Regulation took effect.

Article 14 of the CBUAE Insurance Brokerage Regulation sets the supervisory reporting obligations that licensed Insurance Brokers owe the Central Bank, sitting immediately after the financial reporting duties in Article 13 (IFRS-compliant statements, an annual signed activity report by the Broker's Representatives and audited annual accounts filed within ninety days of financial year-end). It binds Insurance Brokers licensed in the UAE and, indirectly, their Representatives who sign off on submissions. Note this is a UAE/CBUAE instrument, not a SAMA rule, so it is only relevant comparatively for KSA work.
lookup_terms: audited annual financial reports insurance broker

data.summary: Article 15 requires Insurance Brokers to retain all necessary records of Personal Data for ten years from receipt, unless other applicable law or the Central Bank requires otherwise, and to notify the Central Bank immediately of any material change affecting the accuracy or completeness of information given in a licensing application, with supporting information and documents. The notification duty falls on the Applicant or the Insurance Broker depending on the stage. UAE/CBUAE instrument; useful as a comparator to SAMA retention and change-notification duties.

Article 16 obliges Insurance Brokers to maintain policies and procedures to prevent and resolve data security breaches and protect Personal Data, to store and back up Personal Data inside the State for the ten-year retention period, to limit processing to data necessary for brokerage services, and sets an exhaustive list of permitted disclosures (client consent or law, the Central Bank, other regulators with prior Central Bank approval, courts, authorised government bodies, and insurance counterparties for underwriting or Claim Settlement). It also requires cyber risk to be managed through the risk governance process and a cyber incident response and management plan. Binds licensed Insurance Brokers; UAE/CBUAE regime, not SAMA.
lookup_terms: protection of Personal Data insurance broker

data.summary: Article 17 governs Outsourcing by Insurance Brokers: contracts must bind service providers to the Regulation, the Broker stays fully liable for the provider's acts and for provider training and qualifications, material business activity Outsourcing needs Central Bank non-objection supported by a defined minimum file (materiality and risk assessments, due diligence outcome, internal audit and compliance sign-off, related arrangements, Representatives' approval), and no activity may be outsourced outside the State. The Central Bank decides case by case within twenty business days. Binds licensed Insurance Brokers; UAE/CBUAE regime.

Article 18 lists the Central Bank's discretionary supervisory powers over Insurance Brokers: capping Remuneration for particular lines of business, liquidating bank guarantees where a Broker cannot meet liabilities, adjusting minimum capital and bank guarantee requirements case by case according to nature, scale and complexity, and raising the minimum UAE national shareholding percentage of paid-up capital. The node context also carries the Regulation's objectives and legal basis under the UAE central bank and insurance decretal laws. Binds Insurance Brokers indirectly by exposing them to these supervisory measures; UAE/CBUAE regime.
lookup_terms: powers of the Central Bank insurance broker
scope and objectives insurance brokerage regulation

data.summary: Article 19 covers corporate-event controls for Insurance Brokers: no merger, amalgamation or joint venture with any Person without prior written Central Bank approval, and a procedure for voluntary cancellation of licence supported by a closure rationale and plan, alongside treatment of liquidations, bankruptcies and financial restructuring. Binds licensed Insurance Brokers and their owners contemplating structural change or exit; UAE/CBUAE regime, comparator only for SAMA analysis.

Parent node for the CBUAE Credit Risk Management Regulation, which sets the enforceable framework for how licensed financial institutions govern, underwrite, classify, provision for and mitigate credit risk across the full credit lifecycle. It binds LFIs (including branches of foreign banks, with limited head-office accommodations) and allocates ultimate accountability to the Board, with a CCO-led credit review function, an independent CRO-led credit risk management function holding veto power over proposals, and active roles for internal audit, compliance and external audit. Articles 1-18 cover definitions, governance, framework, oversight roles, underwriting, default, SICR, restructuring, classification/provisioning, mitigation, portfolio management, non-performing assets and write-off, models, counterparty liability, enforcement and interpretation.

Article 6 sets the regulatory definition of Default for an Obligor, triggered by either non-payment or unlikeliness to pay. Non-payment arises where a material credit obligation is past due beyond 90 days, with a specific rule treating overdrafts as past due once a contractual or internal limit is breached or a lower limit is communicated; unlikeliness to pay arises where full repayment is improbable, and LFIs must document criteria and early warning signals using both financial and non-financial indicators. It binds all LFIs and feeds directly into SICR identification, classification and provisioning.

Article 7 requires LFIs to regularly assess and document whether credit risk on a financial instrument has increased significantly since initial recognition, aligning the assessment with accounting standards, their internal SICR policy and the regulation's accompanying standards. SICR findings must drive facility classification and associated provisioning, and the SICR methodology must apply to all Obligor types and be consistent with the unlikeliness-to-pay test in Article 6. It binds all LFIs.

Article 8 obliges LFIs to have documented processes to identify, execute and manage Restructured Credit Facilities, with correct classification under Article 9 continuing throughout and after restructuring, including provisioning consequences. The restructuring process must be subject to robust internal oversight and periodic internal audit review; branches of foreign banks may rely on equivalent head-office oversight arrangements, subject to Central Bank supervisory review and approval. It distinguishes distressed restructuring (terms amended amid Obligor financial difficulty) from non-distressed restructuring.
lookup_terms: branches of foreign banks head office oversight

data.summary: Article 9 requires each LFI to assess, monitor and classify every credit facility or portfolio by current and expected creditworthiness, using the Stages set in the accompanying standards or a system mapped to them, with the classification documented under a Board-approved (or head-office/branch senior management committee-approved) provisioning policy. It also requires a documented, resourced process to estimate provisions for all facilities across all Stages and portfolios, approved by Senior Management. Classification under this Article is the reference point for restructuring treatment under Article 8 and for SICR outcomes under Article 7.

Article 10 addresses Credit Risk Mitigation, defined in the regulation as cash flows from liquidation of collateral and other sources usable to reduce financial loss, as further specified in the accompanying standards. It operates alongside the underwriting requirements, which already require collateral and risk mitigation to be covered in credit policies and procedures. It binds LFIs and should be read with the Article 1 definitions of Credit Facility, Credit Risk and Country/transfer risk.

Article 13 of the CBUAE Credit Risk Management Regulation, requiring licensed financial institutions to hold methodologies and analytical approaches for measuring, analysing and categorising credit risk and computing provisions at facility, obligor, segment and portfolio level, including identification of concentration risk. Where models drive decision-making, LFIs must comply with separate CBUAE modelling standards and demonstrate that models are fit for purpose and adequately calibrated. Binds all LFIs in scope of the regulation; the surrounding context also carries the core definitions (Credit Facility, Credit Risk, CRM, CRO, DPD) and the Article 4–5 governance/underwriting duties.

A repealed CBUAE instrument on classification of loans and their provisions (together with its clarifications and guidelines manual), expressly cancelled by Article 17 of the Credit Risk Management Regulation. Its subject matter is now governed by the Regulation's Article 9 classification and provisioning duties and the accompanying Credit Risk Standards' stages. Relevant mainly for legacy/transition analysis and for tracing where an old classification requirement now sits.
lookup_terms: classification of loans and their provisions

data.summary: A repealed CBUAE notice on write-off of fully provisioned non-performing loans, cancelled by Article 17 of the Credit Risk Management Regulation. Write-off duties now sit in Article 12, which requires a Board-approved non-performing asset strategy, timely full or partial write-off where there is no reasonable recovery expectation, and realistic recovery assumptions. Useful for dating legacy write-off practice and locating the successor obligation.
lookup_terms: write-off of fully provisioned non-performing loans

data.summary: A repealed CBUAE notice containing final guidance on IFRS 9, cancelled along with related guidance and amendments by Article 17 of the Credit Risk Management Regulation. Expected credit loss and provisioning expectations are now carried by the Regulation and its mandatory accompanying Credit Risk Standards, which apply to all LFIs providing credit facilities, including on a consolidated basis for UAE-incorporated groups. Consult for legacy IFRS 9 interpretation history rather than current obligations.

The accompanying CBUAE Credit Risk Standards, mandatory and enforceable on the same footing as the Credit Risk Management Regulation. They set the scope of the credit risk management framework (group-wide view, all products, activities, geographies and instruments including off-balance-sheet and derivatives), its alignment with risk appetite and risk profile, climate-related credit risk, and the detailed powers and duties of the Credit Risk Management Function and the CRO. Binds LFIs and, operationally, their boards, senior management and risk functions.

Article 6 of the Credit Risk Standards defines default for all credit facilities and obligors, retail and wholesale, with Shari'ah-compliant facilities also meeting Shari'ah contract requirements. Default is triggered by non-payment (past due beyond 90 days on a material obligation, materiality set at more than 5% of the obligor's total funded exposure, with a consecutive DPD count across facilities for wholesale obligors) and/or unlikeliness to pay, for which indicative criteria are listed, including collateral deterioration, guarantee of a defaulted subsidiary, breach of facility terms, and for retail obligors loss of income sources or breach of the Debt Burden Ratio. Default must be assessed across all legal entities of a UAE banking group, including parent, branches and subsidiaries.

Node for the financial soundness (prudential) article of the CBUAE Insurance Brokers Regulation, issued under the UAE Central Bank Law and the 2023 insurance operations decree-law. It sits within the Regulation's prudential block covering financial soundness, risk management, internal controls, reporting and disclosure, and binds juridical persons licensed by the CBUAE as Insurance Brokers. Note that the supplied context is mainly the Regulation's preamble, objectives and definitions (including Fit and Proper Process and Insurance-Related Professions) rather than the operative soundness conditions, so the source should be opened for the actual requirements.

Sets the corporate governance obligation for licensed Insurance Brokers: effective, robust and documented governance arrangements with a clear organisational structure and defined lines of responsibility, proportionate to nature, scale and complexity. Prescribes minimum content, including an organisation chart, conflict-of-interest and integrity controls, controls for compliance with Central Bank Laws and Regulations, confidentiality, monitoring and audit of governance arrangements, a code of conduct for Representatives and Staff, and a whistleblowing policy protecting staff from reprisals. Also requires a three-lines-of-defence structure (business lines; risk and compliance; independent internal audit).
lookup_terms: code of conduct representatives and staff

data.summary: Requires Insurance Brokers to maintain a Risk Governance Framework (policies, processes, systems and controls) to identify, measure, monitor, report and mitigate material risks on a timely basis, expressly covering operational risk, conduct risk, insurance fraud, cyber attacks and money laundering/terrorist financing. Specifies internal audit's assessment duties and obliges the heads of risk management, compliance and internal audit to report violations of Central Bank Laws and Regulations and Matters of Significance directly to the Central Bank, with good-faith protection. Also restricts dismissal of Control Function heads without CBUAE non-objection, requires notification of their resignation, keeps outsourced activities within Control Function scope, and conditions combining positions on CBUAE approval.
lookup_terms: money laundering and terrorist financing risk

data.summary: Obliges Insurance Brokers to appoint a CBUAE-approved external auditor to audit annually both the financial statements (per accepted accounting standards) and the systems and controls of the brokerage operations. Empowers the Central Bank to require submission of the audit report in a prescribed form and timeframe, to request additional information, and to enlarge or extend the audit scope or require other examinations; the auditor must also verify positions with all Companies the broker deals with. Binds licensed Insurance Brokers and, indirectly, their appointed external auditors.

Conduct-of-business article binding Insurance Brokers, their Representatives and Staff: act honestly, fairly and transparently toward Clients, act in the Client's best interests when comparing products and selecting a Company, supply accurate underwriting information including Personal Data, and obtain written client authorisation on the CBUAE-approved form without restricting the Client's right to cancel. The supplied context also carries adjacent provisions on outsourcing (material outsourcing requires CBUAE non-objection, with the broker remaining fully liable for service providers) and on premiums, claim settlements and remuneration (direct payment between Clients and Companies; brokers prohibited from collecting premiums, claim settlements or refunds).

Requires Insurance Brokers to keep appropriate records and prepare financial statements under IFRS and Central Bank Regulations, and to file within 90 days of financial year-end a detailed activity report signed by the Insurance Broker's Representatives plus audited annual financial reports with the external auditor's report. Adjacent disclosure duties to Clients (remuneration basis, cancellation rights, brokerage agreements, conflicts of interest) and the quarterly reporting regime (reviewed interim statements, debt/credit accounts, company-by-company premiums and remuneration, complaints statistics, quarterly activity report within 30 days, and immediate notification of Matters of Significance) appear in the same context.

Article 7 of the CBUAE Credit Risk Standards sets the mandatory approach for identifying a Significant Increase in Credit Risk (SICR) since initial recognition, requiring documented, regular assessment aligned with accounting standards and internal policy. It fixes specific triggers — a deferral indicator (three or more deferrals in a rolling 24-month period on material Wholesale facilities above a 5% threshold), a rebuttable 30 days-past-due presumption, and forward-looking qualitative indicators — and requires assessment at facility, obligor and group level, with a watch list as a precursor. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs) and interacts with the cross-default rules preceding it and with Stage 2 classification under Article 9.

Article 8 of the CBUAE Credit Risk Standards governs the identification, approval and management of restructured credit facilities, splitting them into distressed restructuring (terms amended in a context of obligor financial difficulty, including post-90-day past due or unlikeliness to pay) and non-distressed restructuring (commercial or regulatory amendments absent distress). It requires separate retail and wholesale restructuring processes, a delegation-of-authority approval process mirroring new underwriting, eligibility and viability criteria, annual internal audit review, and treats a standstill exceeding 90 days as a default event. It binds LFIs, including those conducting Islamic financial services, which must also observe Shari'ah rules.

Article 9 of the CBUAE Credit Risk Standards sets the classification and provisioning regime: each LFI must operate a classification process covering facility, obligor and portfolio-level creditworthiness review, internal rating refresh at least every 12 months, early identification of deterioration and timely past-due recording. It links restructuring outcomes and SICR findings into staging and provisioning decisions, and is the article referenced by internal audit, compliance and external audit scope obligations in Article 2. It binds LFIs and their control functions.

Article 10 of the CBUAE Credit Risk Standards addresses credit risk mitigation — eligible collateral, haircuts and documented expected recovery cash flows — and is the reference point for deductions permitted when computing Stage 3 provisions. The surrounding context sets the credit risk management framework scope (group-wide view, all on- and off-balance-sheet exposures, concentration risk, climate-related credit risk) and the independent Credit Risk Management Function's powers over policy, measurement and defaulted facility review. It binds LFIs, their boards, CROs and credit risk functions.

This node sets out the mandatory three-stage classification system under Article 9, including the Stage 3 sub-categories (3.a–3.c) split by days-past-due with separate wholesale and retail bands for CBUAE reporting. It also fixes the cure and probation conditions for upward migration: Stage 3 to Stage 2 requires settlement of all arrears plus a minimum number of instalments funded from the obligor's own cash flows, and Stage 2 to Stage 1 requires SICR criteria to cease plus prescribed repayment frequencies over the probation period. LFIs may use more granular internal grading but must map it to these categories and justify their assessment.

This node covers the provisioning floor and capital interaction in Article 9 — where provisions fall short of the 1.50% of credit risk weighted assets floor, the shortfall may be held in a non-distributable 'impairment reserve-general' deducted from the capital base (Tier 1 for banks) — and the CBUAE's discretion to impose a higher floor where ECL model reliability or model management compliance is deficient. It also sets the dedicated methodology for Stage 3 wholesale provisions, computed net of eligible collateral after haircuts and documented recoveries, on a facility-specific basis rather than generic statistical LGD. The introduction confirms the standards are mandatory and enforceable alongside the Credit Risk Regulation for all LFIs, with board-level governance duties in Article 2.

CBUAE standards that sit alongside, and are enforceable to the same degree as, the Credit Risk Regulation, covering credit risk governance (board and senior management duties), write-off and memorandum account record-keeping, and the use, validation and override of credit risk models. The model-related articles require licensed financial institutions to hold analytical capability proportionate to portfolio complexity, to document why models are not used where that is the case, and to justify, document and report model output overrides. Binds all Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs) supervised by the CBUAE; note this is UAE rather than SAMA material.

CBUAE Standard setting the minimum requirements for the External Shari'ah Audit of Islamic Financial Institutions, including the Shari'ah reference hierarchy the external auditor must apply, referral to the institution's Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee where no provision exists, and fit-and-proper criteria for external Shari'ah audit firms (Central Bank approval, licensing, experience, resources, team composition and a formal methodology manual). It binds IFIs appointing external Shari'ah auditors and the audit firms themselves, which require Central Bank approval. UAE instrument, not SAMA.

A defined-term node for UAE Federal Decree Law No. 50 of 2022 (Commercial Transactions Law), referenced in the CBUAE External Shari'ah Audit Standard as part of the definition of compliance with Islamic Shari'ah Provisions. Section Six of Book Three of that Law, and its implementing bylaws, form the first tiers of the Shari'ah compliance reference hierarchy, ahead of Higher Shari'ah Authority and ISSC resolutions. Relevant to Islamic financial institutions and their Shari'ah auditors in the UAE.

CBUAE Standard applying External Shari'ah Audit requirements to Takaful Insurance Companies, covering the Shari'ah reference basis, referral of unresolved issues to the company's ISSC, and Central Bank approval and fit-and-proper criteria for external Shari'ah audit firms. It also addresses the case where a company has no head of Internal Shari'ah Audit, permitting an approved external firm to perform that role for a capped term while prohibiting the same firm from also conducting the external Shari'ah audit. Applies to incorporated Takaful Insurance Companies, whether the appointment is voluntary or regulatorily required.

A defined-term node for UAE Decretal Federal Law No. 48 of 2023 (Insurance Law), cited in the CBUAE Takaful External Shari'ah Audit Standard as the source of the Higher Shari'ah Authority's mandates and powers. It underpins the licensing and supervisory framework for insurance and Takaful business referenced by the Standard alongside the Executive Regulation and the Takaful Insurance Regulation. Relevant to insurers, Takaful companies and their Shari'ah governance functions in the UAE.

Defined-term node for the Takaful Insurance Company under the CBUAE External Shari'ah Audit Standard: an insurer incorporated and operating under the Insurance Law, its Executive Regulation and the Takaful Insurance Regulation, with all business and activities conducted in accordance with Islamic Shari'ah Provisions. The node also carries the Standard's scope provisions, applying to all incorporated Takaful companies, including those with group relationships, on voluntary or mandated appointment of an External Shari'ah Auditor. Useful for confirming which entities fall inside the Takaful Shari'ah audit perimeter.

A provision-level node within the CBUAE External Shari'ah Audit Standard for Takaful Insurance Companies dealing with the External Shari'ah Auditor's report: it must go to the general assembly only after Central Bank approval, with copies to the Board and the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee (ISSC) before the ISSC issues its annual Shari'ah report, and must be published in the annual financial statements including any reservations, subject to transaction confidentiality. Related articles cover the Shari'ah reference hierarchy the auditor must rely on, escalation of unresolved issues to the ISSC, fit-and-proper/licensing criteria for approved external Shari'ah audit firms, and a recommended minimum audit frequency of once every three years absent a regulatory requirement. It binds Takaful Insurance Companies and the external Shari'ah audit firms they engage.

Node covering the CBUAE External Shari'ah Audit Standard for Takaful Insurance Companies and its interface with the separate Shari'ah Governance Standard for Takaful Insurance Companies. It sets minimum requirements for appointing and using an external Shari'ah audit firm — applying both where appointment is voluntary and where a regulatory requirement exists — and addresses the fallback where a company has no head of Internal Shari'ah Audit, allowing an approved external firm to perform that role for up to five years (subject to Central Bank and HSA approval) while prohibiting the same firm from also performing the external Shari'ah audit. It binds all incorporated Takaful Insurance Companies, including those with group/subsidiary relationships established in the UAE.
lookup_terms: Shari'ah Governance Standard for Takaful Insurance Companies
head of Internal Shari'ah Audit Division

data.summary: CBUAE Fitness and Propriety Regulation (Circular No. 4 of 2024), which establishes the framework for assessing the fitness and propriety of Applicants, Authorized Individuals, Material Risk Takers and other persons designated by the Central Bank. It sets licensee responsibilities — including for branches of foreign licensees, staff suitability, collective board suitability, and notification of assessment outcomes to the Central Bank — and must be read with the corporate governance, finance companies, retail payment services and stored value facilities regulations. It binds all Licensed Financial Institutions, Insurance Companies, Takaful Insurance Companies and Insurance-Related Professions.

The Fitness and Propriety Standards that accompany and supplement the CBUAE Fitness and Propriety Regulation, elaborating the minimum criteria and the Fit and Proper Process for assessing persons before appointment and on an ongoing basis. They detail licensee responsibilities for assessment and reporting, and carry the list of positions subject to Central Bank Authorisation (Attachment 1). They apply to the same population as the Regulation: all Licensed Financial Institutions, Insurance Companies, Takaful Insurance Companies and Insurance-Related Professions.

Defined-term node for "Authorized Individual" under the Fitness and Propriety Regulation: any natural person authorised under the Central Bank Laws to carry on a Designated Function, extended to Senior Employees in the case of Insurance Companies and Insurance-Related Professionals. The surrounding provisions set the consequential obligations — prior Central Bank Authorisation for appointment, reappointment or contract amendments affecting tenure, no public announcement before Authorisation, removal from the Designated Function if assessed not fit and proper (replacement generally within 90 days), and Central Bank non-objection (plus HSA non-objection for ISSC members and heads of internal Shari'ah control/audit) before termination or dismissal. It binds Licensees and the individuals concerned.

Defined-scope node for "Licensee" under the Fitness and Propriety Regulation and Standards, covering collectively all Licensed Financial Institutions, Insurance Companies, Takaful Insurance Companies and Insurance-Related Professions. It frames the objective and reach of the fit-and-proper regime: requirements apply to the Licensee as a whole and to individuals involved in management, control or the exercise of significant power or responsibility, and UAE-established Licensees must extend compliance across subsidiaries, affiliates and international branches. Useful for resolving whether a particular entity or group structure falls within the regime.
lookup_terms: scope of application fit and proper

data.summary: Defines and imposes the Collective Suitability requirement: the Board as a whole must hold the combined experience, knowledge and skills to understand the Licensee's activities and risks, set strategy, exercise oversight and support constructive challenge, with diversity of skills, qualifications, background, age and gender factored into selection of Authorized Individuals. It binds Licensees (including insurance companies and insurance-related professions under the CBUAE fit-and-proper framework), which must support individual fit-and-proper assessments with a board-level suitability assessment and, where a deficiency is found, file a remediation action plan with the Central Bank. Related reporting duties require immediate notification of assessment results and of any circumstances that may adversely affect Collective Suitability.

A definitions node identifying the Insurance Law as UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 48 of 2023 regulating insurance activities, together with its Executive Regulations and amendments, as used in the CBUAE fitness and propriety instrument. It sits within a definitions article that also delimits related defined terms such as Insurance Company, Insurance Agent, Insurance Broker, Insurance Consultant, Insurance-Related Professions, Actuary, Health Insurance Claims Management Company, Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee and Higher Shari'ah Authority. It matters for scope: it determines which insurance-sector Licensees and individuals are captured by the fit-and-proper obligations.

Sets the Continuous Professional Development obligations attaching to Authorized Individuals and Material Risk Takers, who must maintain current and sufficient knowledge, skills and experience for their positions. Licensees must provide or facilitate CPD access, ensure a default minimum of ten hours per calendar year unless other Regulations specify otherwise, and keep detailed participation records with supporting evidence available to the Central Bank on request. The Central Bank may set function-specific competency, qualification and programme requirements.

The Fitness and Propriety Standards issued under CBUAE Circular No. 4/2024, which expand on the Fitness and Propriety Regulation and are mandatory and enforceable in the same way as the Regulation, article by article. It defines the core terms of the regime (Applicant, Authorisation, Authorized Individual, Affiliate, Actuary and others) and sets procedural duties on Licensees, including liaison with foreign regulators where a person was previously authorised abroad, notification of appointment within seven business days of Authorisation, filling a vacant Designated Function within thirty days subject to Authorisation, and submission of a training plan where remediable knowledge or skills gaps are identified.

Covers the concept of Designated Functions — the roles requiring Central Bank Authorisation, listed in Attachment 1 to the Standards and subject to amendment — and how Licensees must apply the regime by substance of the job description rather than job title. It sets selection requirements (assessment and verification of qualifications, experience, references and professional memberships, propriety checks, and contribution to Board Collective Suitability), and the rules on role changes, unexpected or temporary vacancies, interim appointments (normally up to six months, extendable with justification) and ongoing monitoring of fitness, propriety and suitability. Binds all Licensees and the individuals nominated for or holding such functions.

Sets out the Licensee's obligations to establish, implement and monitor a comprehensive fit-and-proper and suitability assessment framework, with the Board accountable for ensuring Board and Senior Management remain fit and proper on an ongoing basis. Prescribes the minimum content of policies and procedures: minimum criteria, process timing and accountabilities, triggers for reassessment (such as adverse press, risk-profile change, enforcement or supervisory action, performance deficiencies), remedial steps and Central Bank communication where a person is found not fit and proper, and required documentation. Also covers the Central Bank's Authorisation powers, including interviews, meetings with the Licensee, exit interviews, and discretionary bans on unsuccessful applicants.

Defined-term node for "AML Laws" as used in the CBUAE Exchange Business Regulation, pointing to the UAE federal AML/CTF decree-law and its implementing Cabinet decision, together with related instructions, guidelines and notices, as amended. It is the anchor for the Regulation's AML/CFT compliance obligation, which requires a Licensed Person conducting Exchange Business to comply with those laws and to maintain comprehensive internal AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls. Binds licensed exchange houses/money transfer providers supervised by the CBUAE.

Sets the minimum bank guarantee requirement for Exchange Business applicants and licensees: an unconditional, irrevocable, auto-renewing guarantee in favour of the CBUAE payable on first written demand, with a permitted alternative of an interest/profit-free cash deposit held at the Central Bank (supported by a notarised authorisation to use it for customer obligations). Source-of-funds evidence may be demanded, compliance is ongoing, and the guarantee sits on top of — and cannot be funded from — minimum Paid-up Capital. Binds applicants and Licensed Persons for exchange/remittance activity.
lookup_terms: cash deposit in lieu of bank guarantee

data.summary: Establishes minimum Paid-up Capital and related financial-ratio obligations for Exchange Business licensees, including the requirement of a CBUAE no-objection (LNO) before any increase or decrease, CBUAE discretion to impose additional capital based on risk, size and complexity, ongoing compliance after licensing, and evidence of source of funds for capital injections. It also fixes the Paid-up Capital to equity ratio and remediation where the ratio falls below the stipulated level. Binds applicants and Licensed Persons across licence categories.

Parent instrument: the CBUAE Exchange Business Regulation issued by Circular 7/2025 (16 June 2025) to exchange houses under the Central Bank Law, covering licensing, licence categories and permitted activities (currency exchange, remittances, WPS salary processing), ongoing supervision and enforcement. It also confirms that the accompanying Standards are legally binding and elaborate the detailed obligations. Binds any Person carrying on or engaging in Exchange Business in the UAE and applicants for such licences.
lookup_terms: Category I II III IV License

data.summary: Corporate-governance provision requiring an Exchange Business licensee to establish an internal audit function reporting directly to the Board of Directors (or the owner of a sole establishment), with a scope covering all business activities, core and non-core functions, branches and outlets, head and management offices, reconciliation and unreconciled items, Unclaimed Funds and financial ratios, in addition to AML/CFT and regulatory compliance. Sits alongside the mandatory appointment of natural persons to Designated Functions under the Fitness and Propriety Regulation. Binds Licensed Persons and their boards/owners.

Places responsibility on the Board of Directors (or sole-establishment owner) for establishing a risk management function to identify, mitigate, monitor and report business risks, supported by board-approved policies, procedures, systems and controls that are periodically reviewed and proportionate to the nature, size and complexity of the business, with risk exposures aligned to strategy and business plan. Related provisions address group-level management structures and system capabilities for AML/CFT, transaction processing, reconciliation and regulatory reporting. Binds Exchange Business licensees, their boards and group management.

Attachment 1 to the CBUAE Designated Functions framework, listing the senior roles (board members, CEO/deputy, CFO, CRO, chief internal auditor, CCO, AML compliance officer/MLRO, general counsel, CISO, Shari'ah committee and control/audit heads, and other executives reporting to the CEO/Board) that require prior CBUAE authorisation, presented separately for banks, insurance/reinsurance, finance companies, exchange houses, brokers/TPAs and other licensees. The list is indicative of substance rather than job title: licensees must map equivalent positions by duties and responsibilities, and are not required to maintain every listed function. It binds CBUAE licensees, which must run selection, qualification/experience verification, propriety checks and collective board suitability assessments, sign the prescribed forms, and track updates to the list.

The CBUAE Exchange Business Regulation issued by Circular No. 7/2025 (16 June 2025) to exchange houses, made under the Central Bank Law and covering Article 65 licensed financial activities of currency exchange and money transfer. It sets the licensing regime (Category I–IV licences and permitted activities), ongoing supervisory, prudential (paid-up capital, bank guarantee or cash deposit in lieu), corporate-change (LNO for acquisition, merger, joint venture, subsidiaries, divestment) and enforcement requirements. It binds any Person carrying on Exchange Business in the UAE, and is supplemented by the legally binding Standards; the Central Bank may impose requirements beyond the stated minimums.

data.summary: Defined term under the Exchange Business Regulation for the person holding a CBUAE licence to conduct Exchange Business; it is the primary obligation-bearer throughout the Regulation and Standards. Duties attaching to a Licensed Person include operating strictly within the scope of the licence and offering all licensed services continuously, maintaining the bank guarantee or substitute cash deposit on an ongoing basis, evidencing source of funds for that collateral, obtaining an LNO for acquisitions, mergers, joint ventures, subsidiaries, foreign offices and disposals, and the prohibition on lending money to any party (including customers, owners, directors, partners, shareholders) or holding current accounts for them.

data.summary: Defined activity term anchoring the scope of the Exchange Business Regulation: the licensed financial activities of currency exchange and money transfer/remittance services (and, under a Category I licence, salary processing through WPS subject to a separate LNO) referred to in Article 65 of the Central Bank Law. Carrying on or engaging in Exchange Business in the UAE triggers the obligation to apply for one of the four licence categories, unless the person already holds another Central Bank licence acceptable for that purpose. Relevant to any perimeter question about whether an activity or entity falls inside the exchange-house regime.

Defined term for the Standards for the Regulations Regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business, issued by CBUAE on 1 March 2018 via Notice No. 35/2018 and any later amendments. The Standards are expressly legally binding and supplement the Exchange Business Regulation with the detailed regulatory obligations and supervisory requirements. Any compliance assessment of a Licensed Person must read the Regulation together with these Standards, not the Regulation alone.
lookup_terms: Standards for Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business

data.summary: Defined term for providers of instant money transfer services that partner with exchange houses; such providers must first be registered with CBUAE, which maintains a register, and must accept CBUAE examination and regulatory reporting on their IMTS activities with Licensed Persons. IMTS Providers must comply with the AML laws and regulations and other CBUAE-directed regulations for their UAE activities, and are accountable for failures to report or for false, misleading or inaccurate reporting, with deregistration as a possible consequence. A Licensed Person must obtain an LNO before entering an IMTS arrangement and must embed CBUAE's on/off-site examination, information and reporting rights in the contract.

Article 15 of the CBUAE Exchange Business regulation sets a default prohibition on outsourcing by a Licensed Person, permitting it only where the Central Bank has issued a letter of no objection under the conditions and exceptions in the accompanying Standards. It further imposes an absolute bar on outsourcing the licensed exchange activities themselves (such as foreign currency dealing and money transfer acceptance or disbursement). It binds Licensed Persons carrying on Exchange Business, with the surrounding governance articles placing accountability on the board and senior management.

Article 16 requires a Licensed Person to maintain an anti-fraud framework covering prevention, detection, investigation and response to fraud incidents, in line with the Central Bank's Standards. Accountability is placed expressly on the Chief Executive Officer and the Board of Directors, or on the owner where the Licensed Person is a sole establishment. It applies to exchange houses licensed by the CBUAE and sits alongside the AML/CFT, internal audit and risk management obligations in the same regulation.

Article 17 obliges a Licensed Person to identify and analyse risks that could disrupt its business and to maintain a business continuity management framework including a business continuity plan ensuring continuation, timely recovery or orderly scale-down of critical operations. The BCP must be tested at least annually, with senior management and responsible staff participating. It binds CBUAE-licensed exchange businesses and complements the risk management function requirements under the corporate governance article.

Article 22 requires a Licensed Person to comply with the applicable AML/CFT laws and regulations as amended, and to maintain comprehensive and effective internal AML/CFT policies, procedures and controls. It operates as the gateway provision linking the exchange business regime to the federal AML/CFT framework defined in Article 1 (the AML decree-law and its implementing cabinet decision, plus related instructions and guidance). It binds all CBUAE-licensed exchange businesses.

Article 23 governs the books of accounts and external audit of a Licensed Person: records must be accurate, reflect financial position at all times and be available within the UAE. The external auditor may only be appointed after a Central Bank letter of no objection for each financial year, and draft audit reports and financial statements must be submitted for no objection before publication, with annual (and consolidated, where there are subsidiaries) reporting to the Central Bank. Related provisions require agreed-upon procedures by an external auditor over remittance intermediate accounts, reported monthly to the board or owner.

Article 20 requires a Licensed Person to comply with the Central Bank's Dormant Accounts and Unclaimed Funds Regulation and to have board-approved (or owner-approved) policies and procedures to assess, document, disclose and monitor unclaimed funds until paid to the customer or transferred to the Central Bank, with defined roles and responsibilities. Unclaimed Funds is a defined term covering money handed over for onward delivery to a beneficiary that stays undelivered where the rightful owner cannot be contacted for one year. It binds CBUAE-licensed exchange businesses and interacts with customer protection and internal audit scope.

This node covers the Open Finance Framework established by the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation (Circular 03/2025), comprising the Trust Framework, the API Hub and Common Infrastructural Services for cross-sectoral data sharing and transaction initiation on behalf of Users. It binds Licensees (mandated participation, phased onboarding beginning with banks including foreign branches and insurance companies), Open Finance Providers, Persons Deemed Licensed and the API Hub. It also confirms that technical service providers need no Open Finance Licence but that regulatory responsibility and liability cannot be outsourced to them, and that the Central Bank may levy fees to fund framework operation.

This node concerns the API Hub, the separately licensed operator at the centre of the UAE Open Finance Framework, which aggregates and standardises participant APIs and provides the participant integration layer. It sets licensing conditions and prudential-style obligations: a capital funding plan approved by the Central Bank, a minimum capital requirement the Central Bank may vary, prior approval for capital changes and no objection for profit or dividend distributions, plus immediate notification and a remediation plan on breach. It also restricts the API Hub to licensed activities, limits it to processing consented User Data only (no Personal or Confidential Data), and requires data protection controls and security incident/complaint procedures.

This node identifies the Trust Framework, one of the three components of the UAE Open Finance Framework alongside the API Hub and Common Infrastructural Services, with its minimum contents set out in Schedule 1 of the Open Finance Regulation. It must include a Participants Directory for validating participants and secure information exchange, identity and access management for enrolled market participants (enrolment, contact management, digital certificate and application registration/validation), and digital certificates for secure participant-to-participant communication. It is relevant to all Licensees, Open Finance Providers and the API Hub operating within the framework.

This node covers the Common Infrastructural Services component of the UAE Open Finance Framework, detailed in Schedule 1 of the Open Finance Regulation. Minimum contents include a Consent and Authorization Manager (a standalone User app or participant APIs supporting creation, management, enforcement and revocation of privacy/consent directives) and a sandbox for ongoing participant testing and official conformance certification. It matters to Licensees, Open Finance Providers and the API Hub for consent lifecycle and conformance obligations.

This node defines the Open Finance Provider, the holder of the new Open Finance Licence category created by the Regulation, permitting Data Sharing and/or Service Initiation (either or both). The licence is scope-limited: it does not authorise any other licensed activity, does not permit giving Advice, arranging or mediating Transactions in licensed activities, or holding customer funds, so separate licences must be obtained for those. It is distinguished from Persons Deemed Licensed (certain Licensee categories under Article 3) and from Technical Service Providers, who need no licence but cannot assume the provider's regulatory liability.

This node sets the conduct obligations of a Data Sharing Provider, a category of Open Finance Provider licensed to undertake Data Sharing. It may provide Data Sharing only on the User's explicit consent and instructions, must not Process User Data that is Sensitive Data even with explicit consent, must keep personalised security credentials (PINs, passwords) inaccessible to parties other than the issuer and transmitted through secure channels, must identify itself and communicate securely with the Data Holder and User, and must not use, access or store information for any purpose other than the User-requested service except where required by UAE law.

Defined term in the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation for a juridical person licensed by the UAE Central Bank to carry on Service Initiation activities, i.e. electronically initiating transactions on relevant Accounts or Products at the User's instruction. The node sets out its conduct duties (act only on explicit User consent and instructions, secure communication with the Service Owner) and its liability to the User for non-execution, late or defective execution, including failures of authorisation, authentication, accurate recording or secure communication, with the burden of proving correct processing resting on the provider in a dispute. It binds licensed Service Initiation Providers and interacts with Service Owner duties; note this is a UAE instrument, not a SAMA rule.

Defined term in the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation meaning a Licensee that holds User Data. The node covers the Data Holder's obligations when a User uses Data Sharing: to communicate the requested User Data, to treat the request as if made directly by the User, and to communicate securely with the Data Sharing Provider; it also frames the counterpart duties of Data Sharing Providers, including the prohibition on processing Sensitive Data. Binds UAE-licensed institutions holding User Data; scope is limited to User Data and does not displace other personal data protection laws.

Defined term in the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation for a Licensee that holds an Account or Product for a User. The node sets the Service Owner's duties where a User consents to initiation through a Service Initiation Provider — secure communication, immediate provision of information needed to initiate the transaction, status display until completion, and parity of treatment with instructions received directly from the User — plus authentication duties (at minimum two-factor, with stronger measures in higher-risk cases) shared with Data Holders, and liability to the User for non-execution or defective execution subject to carve-outs. Binds UAE Licensees holding customer accounts or products.

Defined activity under the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation: an online service providing a User with consolidated User Data relating to one or more Accounts. The node sets the governing conduct rules — provision only on the User's explicit consent and instructions, a prohibition on processing Sensitive Data even with consent, protection and secure transmission of personalised security credentials, self-identification to the Data Holder and User, and a purpose limitation on use, access or storage of information except where required by UAE law. It binds Data Sharing Providers and, correspondingly, Data Holders.

Defined activity under the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation: initiating, by electronic means, a Transaction relating to an Account or Product. The node covers the obligations attaching to the activity — it applies only to relevant Accounts and Products, requires the User's explicit consent and instructions, imposes information-provision, status-display and parity-of-treatment duties on the Service Owner, and allocates liability for non-execution, late or defective execution between the Service Initiation Provider and Service Owner. Relevant to licensed initiation providers and account/product-holding Licensees in the UAE.

Defined status under the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation for entities treated as licensed for Open Finance purposes without a separate Open Finance Licence. The node clarifies that Technical Service Providers supporting Open Finance Providers or Persons Deemed Licensed do not themselves need a licence provided they do not carry on regulated activities, that regulatory responsibility and liability cannot be outsourced to a Technical Service Provider or other third party, and that the Central Bank may levy licensing and other fees on Open Finance Providers including Persons Deemed Licensed. Relevant to perimeter and outsourcing/accountability analysis for UAE participants.

Node covering the remittances intermediate account requirement in Article 24 of the CBUAE Exchange Business Regulation (Circular 7/2025), read together with the Article 1 definitions of Remittances, Payer, Payee and Payment Account. The surrounding Article 24 provisions constrain how a Licensed Person may hold and move customer money — notably the prohibition on lending to any party (including customers, owner, directors, partners, shareholders) or maintaining current accounts on their behalf — and require a Letter of No Objection for acquisitions, mergers, joint ventures, subsidiaries and divestments. Binds Licensed Persons carrying on Exchange Business (currency exchange and/or remittances) in the UAE; the extracted context does not itself reproduce the text of Article 24.11, so open the source to confirm its exact wording.

Article 26 of the CBUAE Exchange Business Regulation sets the reporting duties owed to the Central Bank: timely submission of periodic compulsory returns (e.g. Exchange House Return Forms via the IRR system), pre-launch access to Central Bank reporting portals and to the FIU's suspicious transaction reporting channel, capacity to answer 'Search' and 'Search and Freeze' notices within the stated deadlines, and accurate provision of data and records on request. It also requires immediate notification of litigation or criminal investigations involving the Licensed Person, its owners/partners/shareholders (including holding and intermediate companies), directors, employees or subsidiaries, and obliges heads of regulatory compliance, financial crime compliance and internal audit to report concealed breaches directly, with protection against contractual confidentiality claims. Licensed Persons and their Senior Management are accountable for failures to report or for false, misleading or inaccurate submissions.

Defined-term node for the Letter of No Objection (LNO) under the CBUAE Exchange Business Regulation: a written (including electronic) no-objection letter issued by the Central Bank. The LNO operates as a prior-consent gate for specified corporate and business actions by a Licensed Person — including acquiring, merging with or entering a joint venture with another person (licensed or not), investing in or opening subsidiaries or offices inside or outside the UAE, selling/closing operations, and launching WPS payroll cards under a Category I licence. Relevant to any Licensed Person planning a structural, ownership or new-activity change.

data.summary: Node for the predecessor licensing framework for exchange business (Notice No. 1/2014 on licensing and monitoring of exchange business), now to be read against the CBUAE Exchange Business Regulation issued by Circular 7/2025 to Exchange Houses. The current Regulation rests on the Central Bank Law, which lists currency exchange and money transfer among Licensed Financial Activities, and covers licensing, ongoing supervision, examination and sanctions, with binding accompanying Standards. It establishes four licence categories (I–IV) mapping to permitted activities such as Currency Exchange, Remittances and WPS salary processing, and binds any person carrying on Exchange Business in the UAE.
