licence categories I II III IV

data.summary: Node linking the CBUAE Dormant Accounts and Unclaimed Funds Regulation with Article 20 of the Exchange Business Regulation, which requires Licensed Persons to comply with that Regulation and to maintain board-approved (or owner-approved, for sole establishments) policies to assess, document, disclose and monitor unclaimed funds until paid to the customer or transferred to the Central Bank. 'Unclaimed Funds' is defined as money handed to a Licensed Person for onward delivery to a specific beneficiary that remains undelivered and whose rightful owner cannot be contacted within one year. Relevant where remittance proceeds or customer balances go unclaimed and for allocating internal roles and responsibilities over them.
lookup_terms: Dormant Accounts and Unclaimed Funds Regulation

data.summary: The CBUAE Open Finance Regulation creates a dedicated Open Finance Licence for Data Sharing and/or Service Initiation, sets minimum requirements for Licensees mandated to provide Open Finance access, and identifies categories of Licensees treated as Persons Deemed Licensed. On-boarding of mandated Licensees is phased, starting with banks (including foreign bank branches) and insurance companies. Technical Service Providers supporting participants need no Open Finance Licence, but regulatory responsibility and liability cannot be transferred to them or any third party; the licence does not permit advice, arranging or mediating transactions, or holding customer funds, and the Central Bank may levy fees for the Open Finance Framework including the API Hub.

Article 22 of the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation sets the consent standard for processing Personal Data in Open Finance: explicit, purpose-specific, informed, unambiguous and freely given consent expressed through a clear affirmative act, with consent invalid where it extends beyond data necessary for the stated purpose. It also requires anonymisation or separate consent where User Data contains Personal Data of third-party natural persons, prescribes the transaction details consent must cover for Service Initiation, and preserves the prohibitions on Sensitive Data processing elsewhere in the Regulation. It binds Open Finance Providers (and Licensees generally) and is expressly without prejudice to other applicable data protection laws.

Article 18 of the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation requires Licensees acting as Data Holders and Service Owners to apply authentication whenever a User accesses Account or Product information via a Data Sharing Provider or initiates a Transaction via a Service Initiation Provider. The procedure must reliably verify identity and authority, use at least two factors drawn from knowledge, possession or inherence, be strengthened in higher-risk circumstances, and meet any further Central Bank requirements. Data Sharing and Service Initiation Providers may rely on the Data Holder's or Service Owner's authentication.

Article 19 of the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation requires all Open Finance participants to use common, secure open communication standards for identification, authentication, notification, information exchange and security measures. It covers interactions among Licensees that are Data Holders and/or Service Owners, Data Sharing Providers, Service Initiation Providers, Users, Payers, Payees and other relevant parties, and sits alongside obligations on protecting personalised security credentials and on Service Initiation Providers identifying themselves to the Service Owner for each Transaction.

Article 21 of the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation allocates liability to Users for unauthorised access to or loss of User Data, and for non-execution, late or defective execution of initiated Transactions. Open Finance Providers bear data-breach liability; Service Initiation Providers bear execution liability including failures of authorisation, authentication, accurate recording or secure communication, and carry the burden of proving correct processing in a dispute; Service Owners are liable for execution failures subject to carve-outs for acts or omissions of others. Related provisions expose Open Finance Providers to Central Bank administrative and financial sanctions for security breaches affecting Personal Data.
lookup_terms: burden of proof Service Initiation Provider

data.summary: This node is the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation issued under Circular No. 7/2023, which creates the Open Finance Licence for Data Sharing and Service Initiation, designates certain Licensees as Persons Deemed Licensed, and phases mandatory Open Finance access starting with banks (including foreign branches) and insurance companies. It clarifies that Technical Service Providers need no licence where limited to support services, that regulatory responsibility and liability cannot be outsourced to them or any third party, and that the Central Bank may levy fees to fund the Open Finance Framework and API Hub. It binds Licensees, Open Finance Providers, Persons Deemed Licensed and the API Hub.

This node captures the cross-reference in the CBUAE Open Finance Regulation requiring Open Finance Providers and the API Hub to remain at all times in full compliance with the CBUAE Fitness and Propriety Regulation and accompanying Standards issued by Circular No. 4/2024 (25/07/2024), as amended. It also reflects the requirement that persons holding or proposed for Authorized Individual positions obtain Central Bank authorisation, sits within the corporate governance provisions (confidentiality, data privacy compliance, governance monitoring and audit), and connects to Board composition rules including Central Bank representation and veto on the API Hub Board.

A defined-term/cross-reference node identifying the CBUAE Outsourcing Regulation for Banks and its accompanying Outsourcing Standards (Circular 14/2021, as amended) as used in the Open Finance framework, alongside the definition of "Outsourcing" (an arrangement, onshore or offshore, including with related parties, for another party to perform on a continuing basis an activity the provider could perform itself). Its operative consequence here is that the API Hub must comply with the Outsourcing Regulation as if it were a "Bank", subject to any Central Bank exemptions and any additional outsourcing requirements or minimum international standards the Central Bank imposes. It binds the API Hub and, by definition, Open Finance Providers relying on outsourced arrangements.

A defined-term node fixing the meaning of "AML Laws" for the CBUAE Open Finance framework: Federal Decree-Law 20/2018 on anti-money laundering, combating the financing of terrorism and financing of illegal organisations, Cabinet Decision 10/2019 (its implementing regulation), each as amended, plus related instructions, guidelines and notices. It does not itself create obligations but imports the whole AML/CTF regime into the Open Finance regulation by reference. Relevant to Applicants, Open Finance Providers, the API Hub and Licensed Financial Institutions subject to that regulation.

A defined-term node identifying the "Insurance Law" as Federal Decree-Law 48/2023 regulating insurance activities together with its Executive Regulations and amendments, as referenced in the CBUAE Open Finance definitions (which also define Insurance Company, Insurance Broker, Insurance Intermediation and Insurance Underwriting). It matters for determining which insurance-sector entities fall within the Open Finance perimeter as Licensees/Data Holders. Binds insurance companies and brokers licensed in the UAE where the Open Finance regulation cross-refers.

A concept/cross-reference node to the international Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (CPMI-IOSCO), which the CBUAE Open Finance regulation requires the API Hub to observe as to the relevant controls, alongside business continuity, data protection and data residency, and consent management duties. It functions as an imported external standard rather than a CBUAE instrument. Binds the licensed and supervised API Hub operator.

The full UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 6 of 2025 on the Central Bank, regulation of financial institutions and activities, and insurance business — the consolidated primary statute that replaces Decretal Federal Law 14/2018 and Federal Decree-Law 48/2023 (both expressly repealed), with a one-year transition for subject entities to reconcile their positions and continuity of existing regulations until replaced. It also addresses currency in digital form and confirms Virtual Assets are not Currency under the decree-law. Binds the Central Bank, all Licensed Financial Institutions and insurance-sector entities operating in the State.

The concept of "Licensed Financial Activities" under Article 61 of Federal Decree-Law 6/2025: the enumerated activities that may not be carried on or promoted without a Central Bank licence, including deposit-taking (incl. Shari'ah-compliant), credit and funding facilities, open finance services, exchange and money transfer, payment services using Virtual Assets, stored value/retail payment/digital money services, arranging and marketing of such activities, and principal dealing in financial products. Licensees must operate only within the scope of their licence, no person may hold themselves out as licensed, and the Board of Directors may grant exemptions; related provisions list grounds for suspension, withdrawal or revocation of a licence. Binds any person carrying on or promoting these activities in the State.
lookup_terms: stored value and retail payment services

data.summary: Node covering the office of the Governor of the CBUAE under Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025: the Governor is the Central Bank's legal representative, runs day-to-day management, signs instruments and contracts, and implements the decree-law, Central Bank regulations and Board decisions, subject to Board and Chairman powers. Related provisions cover delegation to deputies/assistants (appointed by federal decree on the Chairman's proposal), full-time dedication of service and conflict-of-interest bans on other positions, board seats at licensed financial institutions and public-sector contracts, plus Board meeting, quorum and remuneration rules. It binds the Governor, his deputies and assistants, and also prohibits any person in the State, including in financial and non-financial free zones, from using the misleading title "Governor".
lookup_terms: conflict of interest central bank officials

data.summary: Node for Decretal Federal Law No. (14) of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities, as amended — the predecessor statute expressly repealed by Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 (together with Federal Decree-Law No. (48) of 2023 on insurance activities). Relevant for legacy references: existing regulations, decisions and circulars retain their meaning until replaced, and entities subject to the new decree-law must reconcile their positions within one year of entry into force, extendable by the Board. Useful when tracing which instrument governed a past period or mapping old citations onto the 2025 law.

Node on the status of a Licensed Financial Institution under Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025, covering the grounds on which the Central Bank may suspend, revoke or withdraw a licence in whole or in part — including failure to take required measures, ceasing licensed activity or operations for over a year, inability to meet obligations, non-compliance with final judgments, liquidity/solvency or capital shortfalls, merger, bankruptcy, non-cooperation with Central Bank examiners, and revocation abroad for foreign institutions. It also covers external audit obligations: reading and publication of the auditors' and board reports, transmission to head office for foreign or Financial Free Zone incorporated entities, independence restrictions on auditors, a ban on extending credit facilities to auditors, and auditor liability with possible Central Bank action against them. Binds licensed financial institutions, their boards and their approved auditors.

Node defining and regulating the Insurance Company (Insurer) under Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 — a juridical person licensed to carry on insurance business in the State — alongside related defined terms (Reinsurance Company, Takaful Insurance and Takaful Insurance Company/Fund, Insured, Beneficiary, Insurance Policy). Provisions cover separation of property/liability insurance from persons and fund-accumulation insurance (with Board power to require adjustment or restrict new combined policies), prohibitions on chairmen, board members and Authorized Individuals (competing management, conflicting activity, acting as agent or broker, taking commissions, representing shareholders), and the requirement that insurance or brokerage of property in the State be undertaken only by licensed Insurance Companies, while reinsurance may be placed inside or outside the State or in a Financial Free Zone.

Node on the Takaful Insurance Fund under Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025: a Takaful, Re-Takaful or Insurance Company conducting Takaful business must establish a fund with independent legal personality and financial liability separate from the company, registered with and supervised by the Central Bank. Contributions (premiums) based on the concept of Tabaru' are deposited into the fund, which bears liability for compensation and benefits; Takaful business must comply with Islamic Shari'ah rules and the business models set by the Higher Shari'ah Authority, reflected in the company's constitutional documents. Related provisions address freeing up funds required to be maintained in the State when an insurer ceases a line of business.
lookup_terms: ceasing insurance business free-up of funds

data.summary: Node associated with the insurance-sector industry body referenced in Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025; the available context sets out the surrounding defined terms for the insurance market rather than the federation's own provisions. Those definitions include Premium (Contribution in Takaful), Insurance Broker as an independent licensed intermediary remunerated by commission, Insurance Agent acting on an insurer's behalf, Technical Provisions, Solvency Margin, and the scope of Insurance-Related Professions (agent, broker, surveyor and loss adjuster, consultant, Actuary, health insurance third-party administrators, and others determined by the Central Bank). Open the source to confirm the federation's mandate and membership obligations, which are not evidenced in this extract.

Reference node for the former UAE Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law No. 14 of 2018 on the Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities, as amended), which established CBUAE's mandate, licensing and supervision of financial institutions and activities. It is cited in the recitals of Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 and is expressly repealed by that decree-law, alongside the 2023 Insurance Law. Relevant to anyone tracing legacy obligations of licensed financial institutions, transitional continuity of regulations/decisions/circulars, and the one-year position-reconciliation period.
lookup_terms: UAE Central Bank and Organization of Financial Institutions and Activities

data.summary: Reference node for Federal Decree-Law No. (48) of 2023 Regulating Insurance Activities, the instrument that governed licensing and conduct of insurance and reinsurance business in the UAE and is the "Insurance Law" cross-referenced in CBUAE regulations. It is listed in the recitals of Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 and is repealed by that decree-law, which consolidates insurance business into the Central Bank law framework and carries over defined terms such as Insurance Company, Reinsurance Company, Takaful Insurance and Takaful Insurance Fund. Binds insurers, reinsurers, Takaful operators and related licensed persons.

The CBUAE Insurance Group Supervision Regulation, which sets out when and how the Central Bank supervises insurance groups on a group-wide basis, including scope of application, identification of Holding Companies, group reporting, coordination arrangements and enforcement. It defines key terms (Company, Group, Parent, Subsidiary, Affiliate, Holding Company, External Auditor) by reference to the Central Bank Law and the Insurance Law. Binds Insurance and Reinsurance Companies incorporated in the State, their parents and holding companies, and other group entities required to supply data to the Parent.

Concept node for "insurance Group supervision" as applied under the CBUAE regulation: supervision exercised at the level of a Company incorporated in the State that is a Parent of at least one Company or of a foreign (re)insurer, or at the level of a Holding Company. The Central Bank may apply it only at the ultimate domestic parent level, includes all group companies and branches in scope, and may exclude entities whose risks are negligible or whose inclusion would be misleading. Group entities incorporated in the State must supply the Parent with the data needed to meet group obligations.
lookup_terms: Parent of at least one Company

data.summary: Defined term and determination process for a "Holding Company": a juridical person incorporated in the State, other than a Company, identified by the Central Bank under the Insurance Law and Article (6) of the Insurance Group Supervision Regulation. Article (6) sets the criteria (including insurance revenue measured proportionally to capital held and audited consolidated revenue), the entity's duty to supply requested information, and the Central Bank's power to issue and revoke the determination, including where a criterion is met only temporarily. Determination brings the entity within group supervision and potential group-level reporting and sanctions.

Concept node for the Supervisory College as a coordination arrangement the Central Bank, acting as Group supervisor, may establish to cooperate with domestic and foreign supervisory authorities, including supervisors of foreign insurers, reinsurers, banks and other financial institutions in the Group. The Central Bank facilitates and leads the college and may conclude coordination agreements allocating additional tasks; as host supervisor it may instead join colleges run by other authorities. Related provisions cover group-level reporting designation and enforcement, including sanctions such as restricting senior management powers or interim management.

Parent node of a CBUAE regulation on insurance Group supervision, covering the scope provisions (Article 2) and the Parent's core duties (Article 3). It sets when the Central Bank supervises at Group level — a State-incorporated Company that is a Parent of at least one Company or foreign (re)insurer, or a Holding Company — permits supervision only at ultimate Parent level, allows case-by-case exclusion of negligible-risk entities, and obliges Group entities in the State to give the Parent the data it needs. It binds Parents, Holding Companies and Companies within an insurance Group under CBUAE jurisdiction (not a SAMA instrument).

Article 3 makes the Parent responsible for Group-wide adherence to Central Bank Laws and Regulations, expressly including corporate governance and risk management requirements. It gives the Central Bank power to direct the Parent to act or refrain from acting, and to ensure other Group entities do likewise, and to require remediation within a set timeframe in addition to measures on individual Companies. Binds the Parent (or ultimate Parent) of an insurance Group supervised by CBUAE.

Article 4 requires the Parent to report significant risk concentrations at Group level to the Central Bank at the frequency and deadlines it sets. It specifies the minimum exposures to be assessed — direct and indirect exposures to individual and interconnected counterparties, geographic areas or industry sectors, and natural disasters/catastrophes — and provides that the Central Bank sets reporting thresholds by reference to solvency capital requirements and/or technical provisions and may mandate risk types always reportable. Binds the Parent of a supervised insurance Group.

Article 5 obliges the Parent to report significant Intragroup Transactions to the Central Bank at the frequency and deadlines set by it. Transactions materially affecting the solvency or liquidity of the Group or of a participating Company are deemed significant, with a minimum list to be considered (investments, intercompany balances and cash-pooling, guarantees and letters of credit, derivatives, dividends and interest, reinsurance, service or cost-sharing arrangements, and asset purchase/sale/lease). The Central Bank sets thresholds based on solvency capital requirements and/or technical provisions and may designate always-reportable transaction types.

Article 6 sets the criteria and process by which the Central Bank identifies a Holding Company under the Insurance Law: control or acquisition of 15% of insurance activity volume in the State, or insurance activity and related services exceeding 50% of revenues, with calculation rules based on audited financial statements and proportional capital shares. The entity must supply requested data; the Central Bank issues and notifies a determination, may disregard temporarily met criteria, and may maintain Holding Company status where criteria lapse only temporarily.

Article 7 imposes notification and record-keeping duties on an identified Holding Company: immediate notice to the Central Bank of a 10% or greater increase or decrease in capital ownership or voting rights, changes or vacancies in board composition, planned mergers or acquisitions, and actual or likely insolvency, inability to meet obligations, or suspension of payments. Its board must keep minutes of meetings discussing insurance business and provide copies on request. Binds Holding Companies within a CBUAE-supervised insurance Group.

Node labelled "Resolution Authority" but the underlying text covers the establishment, composition, funding and powers of the Higher Shari'ah Authority attached to the UAE Central Bank under the 2025 Federal Decree-Law on the Central Bank and regulation of financial institutions. It sets Shari'ah rules, standards and governance requirements, supervises internal Shari'ah supervisory committees, opines on Central Bank and sovereign sukuk instruments, and may commission Shari'ah audits. Its resolutions and fatwas bind Islamic Financial Institutions, their internal Shari'ah committees and other entities seeking its opinion; those institutions also bear its costs.

Defines Financial Market Infrastructure as a multilateral system among Participant Persons (including its operator) used to clear, settle or record payments, securities, derivatives or other financial transactions, established or overseen by a Regulatory Authority in the State, together with related defined terms (Settlement Institution, Default Arrangements, Transfer Order). It also opens the Central Bank's chapter of powers over such infrastructures, including designation as systemically important. Binds FMI operators, settlement institutions and participants subject to Central Bank oversight.

Sets out how the Central Bank designates a Financial Market Infrastructure as systemically important ("Designated Infrastructure"), the qualifying conditions (operating in the State, Dirham clearing/settlement capacity, or retail/wholesale transfer capacity in any currency), and the notice, representation and decision timelines. It covers deemed designation for infrastructures established under Article 153, coordination where the FMI is licensed by another regulator, abroad or in a Financial Free Zone, and grievance rights before the Grievances and Appeals Committee. Binds FMI operators and their Settlement Institutions.

Sets out the Central Bank's enforcement toolkit: grounds for full or partial withdrawal, revocation or suspension of a licence (including failure to meet capital, liquidity or solvency requirements, non-cooperation with examiners, bankruptcy, cessation of activity), and the administrative and financial sanctions available for violations. Sanctions include restitution of customer funds, multiple-of-benefit fines, fines up to one billion Dirhams on institutions, fines and function bans on Authorized Individuals, delinking from Financial Market Infrastructures, licence conditions or revocation, and minimum fines for unlicensed activity or unlicensed infrastructure operation. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions, Authorized Individuals and any person carrying on or promoting financial activity without a licence.

Covers the currency regime: the State's exclusive issuance right exercised solely by the Central Bank, the prohibition on any person issuing or circulating currency or bearer-payable instruments resembling legal tender, legal tender status of notes, digital-form currency and coins (coins capped at fifty Dirhams per payment), and Board powers over denominations and specifications. It also governs withdrawal from circulation, exchange time limits, ten-year redemption at face value, destruction, non-liability for lost, stolen or counterfeit currency, and compensation for damaged notes and coins. Binds the Central Bank, Licensed Financial Institutions and any person handling or purporting to issue currency.

Covers the customer protection chapter: banking confidentiality of customer data and transactions (surviving the end of the relationship, binding directors, Authorized Individuals, employees, experts and consultants), and the listed carve-outs for judicial and Central Bank powers, auditors, cheque certificates, legal disputes, business transfers or mergers, and AML/CTF obligations. It also requires the Board to issue customer protection regulations proportionate to the activities and products of Licensed Financial Institutions, and mandates an independent unit with legal personality to hear and decide customer complaints with binding resolutions. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions and persons with access to customer data.

data.summary: Article 8 of the CBUAE Insurance Group Supervision Regulation sets out how the Central Bank, acting as group supervisor, cooperates with other domestic and foreign supervisory authorities to supervise an insurance Group. It allows the Central Bank to establish coordination mechanisms such as a Supervisory College and to invite supervisors of foreign insurance/reinsurance companies, banks and other financial institutions within the Group. It binds the Central Bank's own supervisory conduct rather than imposing direct duties on the Parent, though it frames the information exchange affecting Group entities; neighbouring provisions also address obstruction of inspections and designation of a Group reporting entity where the Parent is a Holding Company.

The CBUAE Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation is a prudential/governance instrument requiring Financial Institutions to identify, measure, manage and report Climate-related Financial Risks (Physical, Transition and Liability risk). It covers board and senior management responsibilities, risk appetite, strategy, integration into the risk management framework (credit, market, operational, liquidity), scenario analysis and stress testing, and capital/solvency assessment. It binds licensed FIs including banks and insurance companies, with enforcement and administrative/financial sanctions for breach.

Article 2 sets the governance and risk appetite requirements for Climate-related Financial Risks: the Board and Senior Management must have adequate knowledge and a holistic view of the FI's exposures, embed these risks in governance and Risk Appetite frameworks, and review the climate component of risk appetite at least annually. Delegation of operational functions to Board committees or Senior Management is permitted but must be documented with clear responsibility, authority and escalation/reporting lines, and assigned functions must be adequately resourced and trained. It also requires a governance framework for green/sustainable/ESG-labelled assets and liabilities, including labelling criteria and due diligence and ongoing monitoring of customers and use of funds for green products.

Article 3 requires Financial Institutions to assess and monitor how Climate-related Financial Risks affect their business environment, business model and activities across short, medium and long-term horizons. After accounting for existing resources and mitigants, the FI must develop measures or changes to its business strategy and cascade them internally for timely implementation. Strategic responses may touch products and services, processes and policies, market presence, customer engagement, organisational structure, IT infrastructure and resources.

Article 4 is the operative risk management article: FIs must embed Climate-related Financial Risks in their risk management framework (as a stand-alone category or within existing ones) through a structured process of identification, data gathering, measurement, reporting, control and mitigation. It addresses data management frameworks (without prejudice to UAE data protection law), metrics and indicators, and the treatment of climate drivers within credit/underwriting, market, operational (including business continuity and outsourcing), and liquidity risk. It also sets scenario analysis and stress testing requirements, including at least annual analysis, integration into ICAAP baseline and stress scenarios, documentation of scenarios and assumptions, and use of results in internal capital and liquidity planning.

Article 5 requires Financial Institutions to develop processes to evaluate the capital and solvency impact of Climate-related Financial Risks arising within relevant planning horizons. Such risks must be considered in the internal capital adequacy assessment, including through their effect on traditional risk categories, with banks incorporating them into ICAAP and insurance companies into their Own Risk and Solvency Assessment (ORSA). The adjacent Article 6 confirms that breaches may attract supervisory action and administrative and financial sanctions from the Central Bank.

Licensing gateway provision of the CBUAE Regulation on Representation Offices of Foreign Insurance and Reinsurance Companies, setting the cumulative eligibility conditions an applicant must meet before a licence is granted. It requires the applicant to be a foreign insurance or reinsurance company not otherwise writing business in the UAE, licensed and directly supervised in its home jurisdiction, with at least ten continuous years of supervised operation (reducible by Central Bank decision), and requires the Director and other designated individuals to pass the Fit and Proper Process; group financial position may also be weighed. The surrounding context also covers the approval/rejection notification window, one-year licence term with annual renewal, and prior notice for suspension of operations.

Article 14 of the CBUAE Representation Offices Regulation requires a Fit and Proper Process for the proposed Director and other persons designated by the Central Bank, assessed on qualifications, knowledge and experience, integrity, competence and financial soundness, with minimum experience thresholds (reduced for UAE nationals with higher qualifications) and accreditation of academic degrees. It binds the representation office of a foreign insurer or reinsurer as a condition of appointment and continued licensing, and links to the staffing requirements in Article 13 (notification of Director appointment, vacancy filling within thirty days, adequate qualified staff).

Article 15 of the CBUAE Representation Offices Regulation defines the Director's mandate and accountability: representing the office and its foreign insurer/reinsurer before the Central Bank, courts and official bodies, carrying out the permitted activities set out in Article 3 and signing related documents, and receiving notices, warnings and judicial papers. The Director is fully responsible for all procedures and actions of the representation office, making this the primary accountability anchor for supervisory and service-of-process purposes.
lookup_terms: foreign insurer representation in the State

data.summary: UAE primary legislation regulating insurance activities, cited as one of the two Central Bank Laws underpinning the CBUAE Representation Offices Regulation and referenced (with its Executive Regulations) as the "Insurance Law" in other CBUAE instruments. It provides the statutory basis for CBUAE licensing and supervision of insurance and reinsurance activity in the State, including the framework within which representation office rules operate. Binds insurers, reinsurers and related licensed entities operating in the UAE.

The UAE Central Bank Law, as amended, establishing the CBUAE and regulating financial institutions and activities; it is the enabling statute cited across CBUAE regulations, including the definition of a licensed Bank and the scope of licensed financial activities. Here it appears within a CBUAE regulation containing proportionality, definitions (Affiliate, Board, Group, Insurance Company, Climate-related Financial Risks, Critical Functions, Liability Risk) applying to banks and insurance companies. Binds all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.
lookup_terms: organisation of financial institutions and activities

data.summary: CBUAE AML/CFT guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions servicing the real estate and dealers in precious metals and stones (DPMS) sectors, explaining sector risk drivers and the regulatory perimeter. It clarifies when DPMS and real estate agents/brokers qualify as DNFBPs under Article 3 of the AML-CFT Decision (including the AED 55,000 transaction threshold for DPMS), who supervises them (Ministry of Economy in mainland/CFZs; FSRA and DFSA in financial free zones), and states that LFIs need not classify customers as DNFBPs but should establish that status through CDD. It also signals that CBUAE does not expect blanket de-risking of these sectors.
lookup_terms: dealers in precious metals and stones
real estate agents and brokers AML

data.summary: Concept node for Physical Risk as one of the three drivers of Climate-related Financial Risks in the CBUAE climate risk management standard/guidance for Financial Institutions. It matters mainly in measurement and in the traditional risk categories: geographic concentration metrics for assets, liabilities and collateral; operational risk and business continuity (including outsourcing and Critical Functions); and liquidity/funding effects such as withdrawal or credit-demand spikes after physical events. It binds licensed Financial Institutions (banks and insurance companies) as a supervisory expectation embedded in their existing risk management frameworks.

Concept node for Transition Risk — the financial effects on Financial Institutions of the shift to a low-carbon economy — within the CBUAE climate-related financial risk framework. It drives credit/underwriting assessment of customers' economic sectors, in-house or external rating and scoring of current and prospective customers, market valuation effects, and adverse liquidity impacts under normal and stressed conditions. Applies to Financial Institutions supervised by the CBUAE as part of their risk identification, measurement and mitigation obligations.

Concept node for Liability Risk, the third component of Climate-related Financial Risks alongside Physical and Transition Risk, covering exposure to claims and reputational consequences arising from climate-related events and conduct. It must be captured in market risk identification, operational risk and business continuity assessment, and — for insurance companies — in liquidity impact assessment via increased liability claims and counterparty defaults. Binds CBUAE-supervised Financial Institutions.

Concept node setting out the CBUAE requirement for climate scenario analysis as a core measurement and management tool for Climate-related Financial Risks. It requires at least annual analysis, integration into ICAAP baseline and stress scenarios where ICAAP applies, coverage of Physical, Transition and Liability risk drivers over short, medium and long horizons, qualitative and quantitative outputs showing impacts on provisions, capital and liquidity against a baseline, and use of results to test adequacy; institutions must build internal capability and may use existing external climate scenarios in the interim. Binds Financial Institutions supervised by the CBUAE, with ILAAP and stress-testing linkages.

CBUAE Circular No. 5 of 13 February 2025 issuing the Regulation on Representation Offices of Foreign Insurance Companies and Foreign Reinsurance Companies, setting licensing, regulatory and supervisory rules for such offices operating in the UAE. It must be read with the Central Bank Law (Decretal Federal Law 14/2018 as amended), the Insurance Activities Law (48/2023), the Commercial Companies Law (32/2021), the Financial Free Zones Law (8/2004) and the supervision fees Cabinet Resolution. It binds representation offices of foreign (re)insurers in the State and their staff — not a licence to carry on insurance business.

Article 3 of the Representation Offices Regulation defines the closed list of activities a representation office may carry out — market and economic research on the UAE insurance sector, gathering and supplying information and clarifications to the foreign (re)insurer, its clients and third parties, supporting local parties active in the foreign company's home markets, and maintaining relationships and following the parent's interests with clients outside the State. The permitted-activity boundary is enforced through the surrounding provisions on conduct of business, continuous commitments (approved premises, no other business at the premises, notification of status changes, data provision on request), naming requirements, and grounds for licence cancellation. Binds the representation office and its staff.

A concept node within CBUAE guidance for licensed financial institutions (LFIs) setting out how the risk-based approach and CDD/EDD components apply to customers from the dealers in precious metals and stones (DPMS) and real estate sectors. It covers customer identification and licensing checks, beneficial ownership identification at the 25% controlling-interest threshold with the senior managing official fallback, understanding the purpose of the account and nature of the business, and ongoing/transactional due diligence where a low-risk customer executes a high-risk sector transaction. It binds CBUAE-licensed LFIs (banks, exchange houses, finance companies, PSPs, hawala providers, insurers and brokers), not the DPMS/real estate firms themselves.

A concept node on the obligation of LFIs to file suspicious transaction reports with the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit where there are reasonable grounds to suspect that a transaction, attempted transaction or funds are linked to the proceeds of crime or to criminal use. It also flags non-exhaustive trigger scenarios (abandoned onboarding after CDD is explained, inability to evidence beneficial ownership or explain transactions) and, from the real-estate-focused source, indicator lists on payment means and transaction structure. Binding on CBUAE-licensed financial institutions; the reporting duty is statutory, not discretionary.

A concept node describing CBUAE's assessment of ML/TF risk arising from the real estate and DPMS sectors, including the sectors' economic significance, their attractiveness to illicit actors, their facilitation of cross-border value movement, and the FATF Mutual Evaluation findings that both sectors are highly important for risk and materiality in the UAE. It also covers licensing and supervision arrangements for real estate professionals across mainland, commercial and financial free zones. It informs risk assessment and customer risk rating obligations of CBUAE-licensed LFIs serving these sectors.

A concept node explaining when DPMS and real estate agents/brokers qualify as Designated Nonfinancial Businesses and Professions under Article 3 of the AML-CFT Decision — for DPMS, single or linked transactions exceeding AED 55,000; for agents/brokers, concluding property purchase and sale operations for customers — and the consequence that they become subject to preventive measures substantially equivalent to those on LFIs. Classification is made by the Ministry of Economy, which also supervises obliged DNFBPs; LFIs need not classify but must establish DNFBP status through CDD and must not treat non-DNFBP status as evidence of low risk.

Instrument node for the UAE's primary AML/CTF statute, Decree Federal Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organisations, which forms the legal basis for the CBUAE guidance referencing it. It establishes the core criminalisation and preventive-measures framework, including the suspicious transaction reporting duty relied on in the guidance. It binds financial institutions, DNFBPs and other obliged entities in the UAE; the guidance itself does not add to or override it.

Instrument node for Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019, the Implementing Regulation of Decree Federal Law No. 20 of 2018, which operationalises the UAE AML/CTF statute. It contains the DNFBP scoping rules (Article 3), the ongoing transaction-monitoring duty referenced in the guidance (Article 7.1), the STR requirement (Article 17), and the mandate for supervisory authorities to issue guidance and feedback (Article 44.11). It binds financial institutions and DNFBPs, and prevails over CBUAE guidance in the event of any discrepancy.

Concept node for the Supreme Committee for the Supervision of the National Strategy for AML/CFT/CPF, established under the UAE Federal Decree by Law No. (10) of 2025 and affiliated with the Presidential Court, with its formation and rules of procedure set by Cabinet resolution. It sits above the National Committee: it evaluates national AML/CFT/CPF strategies, sets requirements for the National Committee and Concerned Authorities, directs inter-agency support, supervises the Mutual Evaluation process, and proposes legislation. It binds public-sector bodies (the National Committee, Concerned Authorities), not licensed institutions directly, though its resolutions shape the supervisory expectations those institutions face.
lookup_terms: Federal Decree by Law No. 10 of 2025

data.summary: Concept node for the National Committee for AML/CFT/CPF under the UAE 2025 AML Decree Law, the operational coordination body that develops and implements national AML/CFT/CPF strategy, collects and analyses statistics to assess effectiveness, coordinates information exchange among represented entities, monitors the Mutual Evaluation process, and represents the State internationally. It is supported by a General Secretariat headed by a Secretary-General appointed by Cabinet, who also serves as Deputy Chairman and sits on the Supreme Committee. It binds government authorities and reports upward to the Supreme Committee; it is not a direct supervisor of financial institutions.

Definitional node for Targeted Financial Sanctions under the UAE AML/CFT framework: freezing funds and prohibiting their direct or indirect availability to persons or entities designated under Cabinet resolutions on Terrorist Lists or by UN Security Council Chapter VII resolutions on terrorism financing and proliferation financing. It sits alongside related definitions (Executive Office, Concerned Authorities, Law Enforcement Authorities, the Crime, Predicate Offence) and underpins the immediate-implementation duty placed on financial institutions, DNFBPs and VASPs. Useful for scoping who is designated, what conduct is prohibited, and which authority issues instructions.

Concept node for the Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation, defined as the authority responsible for implementing targeted financial sanctions within the UAE. Its instructions on TFS must be implemented without delay by subject entities, alongside their broader preventive duties (CDD, prohibition of anonymous/fictitious accounts, approved internal policies and controls, record retention). Relevant when identifying the issuing authority for freezing obligations and the interface between TFS instructions and AML programme requirements.
lookup_terms: Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation

data.summary: Node covering the repeal and transition position of UAE Federal Decree by Law No. (20) of 2018 on AML/CFT and financing of illegal organisations, which is repealed by Federal Decree by Law No. (10) of 2025 (in force two weeks after publication; issued 30 September 2025). Executive Regulations, resolutions and circulars issued under the 2018 law remain effective to the extent they do not conflict with the new Decree Law until superseded, and conflicting provisions generally are repealed. Essential for dating obligations, citing the correct instrument, and assessing whether legacy secondary instruments still apply.
lookup_terms: Federal Decree by Law No. 20 of 2018
Federal Decree by Law No. 10 of 2025

data.summary: CBUAE best-practices guidance on role-based AML/CFT/CPF training for licensed financial institutions, setting out how training should be tailored to the specific ML/TF/PF risks and responsibilities of particular roles rather than delivered as generic awareness training. It situates role-based training within a wider programme (new-hire, annual enterprise-wide, group-mandatory, localized, and board/senior-management training) and frames content by reference to UAE regulatory requirements and supervisory guidance, global financial-crime compliance standards, internal policies, and the institution's products, customers and geographies. Addressed to LFIs, including registered hawala providers, and expressed as expectations under a risk-based approach rather than hard rules.

A concept node within the CBUAE Best Practices on AML/CFT/CPF training covering role-based (including on-the-job) training tailored to the ML/TF/PF risk exposure of specific functions, alongside new-hire, annual enterprise-wide, group-mandatory, localised and board/senior-management training. It sets expectations that content, frequency and intensity be risk-based, that training be delivered to defined high-exposure groups across the three lines of defence, and that delivery, attendance, non-completion follow-up and corrective action be documented for audit and supervisory inspection. It is directed at CBUAE licensed financial institutions (banks, exchange houses, finance companies, PSPs, VASPs, hawala providers, insurers) and, through them, to employees and external staff performing AML/CFT/CPF functions.

A concept node describing the AML/CFT/CPF training expectations specific to an LFI's Board of Directors, owners/partners/shareholders and senior management, covering oversight of the compliance programme, enterprise-wide risk assessment findings, emerging ML/TF/PF typologies, audit follow-up, regulatory developments and tone-at-the-top culture. Training should be delivered as needed and at least annually, with attendance and materials recorded, supplemented by ongoing updates on regulatory issues and risk exposure. It binds the governing body and senior management of CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

A concept node on documenting and assessing the AML/CFT/CPF training programme: an annual, board- or senior-management-approved training plan specifying participants, topics, delivery methods, objectives, minimum standards by department and role, frequency and post-training assessment. It also covers mandatory record-keeping of delivered training, tracking of attendance and pass/fail outcomes, follow-up and consequences for non-completion (up to termination), and measurement of training effectiveness. It applies to CBUAE-licensed financial institutions, including support functions such as IT and external staff (vendors, contractors, third parties).

Reference node for Cabinet Decision No. (10) of 2019, the Implementing Regulation of Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 on AML/CFT and financing of illegal organisations, as amended by Cabinet Decision No. (24) of 2022 (the "AML-CFT Decision"). It is cited as part of the legal basis for the CBUAE best-practices guidance, alongside Cabinet Decision 74 of 2020 (terrorism lists/UNSC TFS) and Cabinet Decision 58 of 2020 (beneficial owner procedures). It binds all UAE financial institutions and designated entities within scope of the AML-CFT Law, including CBUAE licensees.

Reference node for Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organizations, as amended by Federal Decree-Law No. 26 of 2021 (the "AML-CFT Law"). It is the primary statutory foundation for the CBUAE best-practices documents on training and on risk-based institutional risk assessment, and training must make employees aware of these legal obligations and the consequences of non-compliance. It binds all UAE natural and legal persons subject to the AML/CFT regime, including CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

A CBUAE best-practices document on the risk-based approach and the institutional (enterprise-wide) AML/CFT/CPF risk assessment, setting expectations for how LFIs identify and rate inherent risk across customer, product/service, geographic, delivery-channel and other categories, and for consistency between the institutional assessment methodology and day-to-day risk rating. It addresses treatment of high-risk factors, granular risk factors, rationales for exclusions, and disclosure where system limitations (e.g. inability to capture exits for FCC reasons or STR/SAR volumes) elevate the inherent risk rating. It is guidance directed at CBUAE licensed financial institutions.

This node is the FATF Mutual Evaluation Report on the UAE (April 2020) as relied upon in CBUAE guidance on dealers in precious metals and stones (DPMS) and the real estate sector; the MER's finding that both sectors are highly important in terms of ML/TF risk and materiality is the evidentiary basis for that guidance. It is not itself a binding instrument, but it drives risk-based expectations for Licensed Financial Institutions banking DPMS and real estate customers. The guidance it underpins applies to CBUAE-licensed/supervised entities including banks, foreign bank branches, exchange houses, finance companies, payment service providers, registered hawala providers and insurance companies, agencies and brokers.
lookup_terms: DPMS dealers in precious metals and stones

data.summary: Federal Decree by Law No. (10) of 2025 is the UAE's primary AML/CFT/CPF statute, covering the money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing offences, provisional measures, the Financial Intelligence Unit, obligations on Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and Virtual Asset Service Providers, and penalties. It repeals Federal Decree Law No. (20) of 2018, while regulations, resolutions and circulars issued under the 2018 law remain in force so far as they do not conflict, pending replacement. It enters into force two weeks after publication in the Official Gazette; Executive Regulations and an administrative-penalties resolution are to be issued by the Cabinet.

This node captures the money laundering offence under the 2025 UAE AML law: intentionally converting, transferring or transacting in proceeds to conceal their illicit origin; concealing or disguising the nature, source, location, disposition, movement or ownership of proceeds; acquiring, possessing or using proceeds; or helping the predicate offender escape punishment. It confirms ML as an autonomous offence, excluded from concurrence rules under the Crimes and Penalties Law, with no requirement of a predicate conviction and knowledge inferable from objective circumstances. It binds any person, natural or legal, and shapes how reporting entities frame suspicion.

This node is the terrorism financing offence and related definitions in the 2025 UAE AML law: intentionally providing, collecting or making available funds by any means, directly or indirectly — including via digital systems, virtual assets or cryptographic technologies — knowing they will be used for terrorist acts, by a terrorist or terrorist organisation, or to finance travel of individuals for terrorist purposes. Supporting definitions cover targeted financial sanctions, suspicious transactions, freezing and seizure. It binds any person and is the predicate for TFS freezing obligations on reporting entities.
lookup_terms: Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation

data.summary: This node concerns proliferation financing under the 2025 UAE AML law, which treats it alongside money laundering and terrorism financing within the defined term "the Crime" and as a predicate offence. Related definitions capture funds used or allocated for proliferation financing, suspicious transactions referable to it, and targeted financial sanctions implemented by the Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation, including UNSC Chapter VII designations. Relevant to Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and Virtual Asset Service Providers for screening, reporting and freezing duties.
lookup_terms: Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation
UN Security Council Chapter VII designations

data.summary: This node covers the Financial Intelligence Unit established as an independent unit within the Central Bank, the exclusive recipient of Suspicious Transaction Reports from Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and Virtual Asset Service Providers, with powers to demand additional information, analyse and disseminate to Concerned Authorities, and exchange information with foreign counterpart units subject to use limitations. It also covers the Chief of the Unit's provisional powers to suspend a suspicious transaction for up to ten working days and to freeze suspected funds for up to thirty days without prior notice, extendable by the Attorney General. Reporting entities must lift freezes on cancellation or expiry unless extended.

temporary suspension of transaction 10 working days

data.summary: Guidance node on how a Licensed Financial Institution should build and document its institutional (enterprise-wide) ML/TF/PF risk assessment, covering the expected methodology for identifying and rating inherent risk across customers, products and services, geographies and other factors. It expects consistency between the institutional assessment and the risk segments and rating methodology used in the day-to-day AML/CFT/CPF programme, express rationales where high-risk factors are excluded, and explicit acknowledgement where data gaps inflate the inherent risk rating. Addressed to LFIs supervised by the CBUAE (note: UAE, not SAMA, instrument).
lookup_terms: customer risk / product risk / geographic risk

data.summary: Defines and elaborates the concept of inherent risk used in the institutional risk assessment: the ML/TF/PF exposure arising from an LFI's customer base, products and services, geographies and delivery channels before controls are applied. It sets expectations on granularity of risk factors within each category, standardised assessment approaches, and treatment of high-risk indicators such as exits for financial crime compliance reasons and STR/SAR volumes. Relevant to LFIs designing or defending the inherent-risk layer of their assessment.

Guidance on assessing and quantifying the effectiveness of an LFI's AML/CFT/CPF control environment, so that control strength can be applied against inherent risk. It sets out a stepwise approach: identify key controls, define effectiveness criteria, measure performance, score, aggregate (including weighting) and adjust for interdependencies among controls. Aimed at LFIs' compliance and internal audit functions preparing or validating the control-effectiveness component of the risk assessment.

Concept node for residual risk — the ML/TF/PF risk remaining after the effectiveness of the LFI's controls is applied to its inherent risk within the institutional risk assessment. It links the inherent-risk methodology (risk categories, granular factors, standardised segments) to control-effectiveness scoring, and is the output used to drive risk appetite and remediation decisions. Relevant to LFIs documenting the conclusions of their enterprise-wide assessment.

Treats CDD/KYC procedures as a key mitigating control to be identified, measured and scored when assessing control effectiveness in the institutional risk assessment. Effectiveness indicators referenced include rates of compliance with CDD/KYC requirements alongside monitoring, training and audit measures. Relevant where an LFI must evidence that its customer due diligence framework actually reduces inherent risk, rather than merely exists.

Sets expectations for AML/CFT/CPF training as a control: compulsory induction and periodic refresher training for all staff including the board and senior management, specialised role-based training (e.g. TBML and proliferation-financing awareness for trade finance teams), attendance and assessment record-keeping with follow-up on non-attendance or failures, and tailoring to the LFI's risk profile and local requirements. The same section introduces independent testing of the AML/CFT/CPF programme (suggested every 12–18 months or on significant change) and its autonomy. Binds LFIs and their governing bodies.

Guidance component of the CBUAE AML/CFT/CPF risk-based approach guidance describing Independent Testing as an objective, risk-based evaluation of the overall AML/CFT/CPF programme, covering policies, procedures, systems and controls and identifying remediation gaps. It indicates an expected testing cycle of roughly every 12–18 months or upon material change to risk profile, controls or compliance staffing, and allows internal audit, external auditors, consultants or other qualified independent parties to perform it. It addresses licensed financial institutions (LFIs) supervised by the CBUAE, with emphasis on preserving the autonomy/independence of the testing function; it sits alongside the training-controls expectations in the same section.

Node covering governance and control-effectiveness expectations within the CBUAE risk-based approach guidance, setting out how an LFI should identify key AML/CFT/CPF controls (CDD/KYC, transaction monitoring, training, compliance auditing), define effectiveness criteria, measure performance, score and aggregate results, and adjust for control interdependencies. It frames governance as the mechanism linking inherent risk assessment to residual risk. Directed at licensed financial institutions' boards, senior management and compliance functions.
lookup_terms: board and senior management AML oversight

data.summary: Cross-document node on internal controls within CBUAE AML/CFT/CPF expectations, drawing on both the risk-based approach guidance and a further CBUAE instrument. It concerns the design, measurement and scoring of AML/CFT/CPF control frameworks — CDD/KYC procedures, transaction monitoring, staff training and compliance auditing — and how their aggregate effectiveness is evidenced. It binds licensed financial institutions and informs supervisory assessment of programme adequacy.

Node for the Money Laundering Reporting Officer role as used in the CBUAE risk-based approach guidance, which is issued under the Supervisory Authority mandate in Article 44.11 of Cabinet Decision No. (10) of 2019 implementing Federal Decree-Law No. (20) of 2018. The context here is introductory and scope-setting rather than a standalone MLRO rulebook, so the node mainly locates the MLRO within the LFI's RBA and compliance programme. Relevant to licensed financial institutions and their appointed compliance officers.

Methodological section of the CBUAE risk-based approach guidance setting out a six-plus step approach for LFIs to quantify AML/CFT/CPF control effectiveness: identify key controls, define measurable effectiveness criteria, measure performance, apply a scoring scale, aggregate (optionally weighted) scores, and adjust for interdependencies between controls. It is expectation-setting guidance on how residual risk is derived from inherent risk, not a prescriptive rule. Applies to licensed financial institutions conducting enterprise-wide ML/TF/PF risk assessments.

Core definitional section explaining the Risk-Based Approach: LFIs must identify, assess and manage ML/TF/PF risks across customers, products and services, delivery channels, geographic locations/markets and operating structure, then apply AML/CFT/CPF measures proportionate to those risks — enhanced where risk is higher, simplified where lower, subject always to minimum UAE legal and regulatory requirements. Also contains the guidance's abbreviations (PEP, TFS, VASP, STR/SAR, TBML). Binds licensed financial institutions supervised by the CBUAE.
lookup_terms: risk factors customers products channels geography

data.summary: Section of CBUAE guidance explaining what correspondent banking is — a bilateral relationship in which a correspondent institution supplies services (cash management, cross-border wire transfers, cheque clearing, letters of credit, FX) to a respondent institution — and the ML/TF/PF exposure it creates. It sets supervisory expectations for risk-based due diligence on respondent and parent institutions, use of the Wolfsberg CBDDQ as the industry-standard due diligence questionnaire by both correspondents and respondents, and monitoring for correspondent banking red flags. It binds UAE Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs), not SAMA-supervised entities; useful as comparative/benchmark material for KSA correspondent banking analysis.

Guidance section defining cross-border payments (originator and beneficiary in different countries, wholesale and retail) and the obligations of every institution in the payment chain, including intermediaries with no direct customer relationship, to screen, monitor and pass on originator and beneficiary information. It cites the AML-CFT Decision wire transfer articles and the AED 3,500 threshold for qualifying cross-border wire transfers, listing the minimum originator and beneficiary data elements, and notes stricter screening duties for exchange houses. Applies to UAE LFIs; relevant to KSA analysis only as a comparator on travel-rule style requirements.

Explanatory background on the SWIFT messaging network as the infrastructure carrying most cross-border interbank payment instructions — a messaging layer only, with settlement occurring through correspondent accounts. It describes MT message series and how legacy formats (notably MT 103 and cover-payment practice) left intermediary institutions without full originator and beneficiary data, and notes the migration to ISO 20022 and retirement of the MT 1xx/2xx/9xx series from November 2025. Contextual/explanatory rather than obligation-creating; addressed to UAE LFIs.

Describes the ISO 20022 open, XML-based global messaging standard and its adoption by the SWIFT community for all cross-border payments, with a migration window from March 2023 and coexistence with MT messages until the MT 1xx/2xx/9xx series is retired in November 2025. Its compliance significance is richer structured originator and beneficiary data supporting screening and monitoring across the payment chain. Background context for UAE LFIs; not itself a rule text.

Addresses nested (downstream) correspondent activity, where indirect respondent institutions access a correspondent account through the direct respondent, adding a layer of intermediation that reduces the correspondent's visibility into the transacting parties. Sets expectations that correspondents require disclosure of nested relationships at onboarding and in ongoing reviews, review them at least annually, obtain lists of nested institutions and screen them (watchlist, adverse media, PEP, sanctions), assess the respondent's controls, and insist on transparent payment message formatting. Directed at UAE LFIs acting as correspondent institutions.

Defines payable-through (pass-through) accounts, where a respondent institution's own customers transact directly on the respondent's correspondent account — for example by writing cheques — so the correspondent faces customers on whom it has performed no due diligence. Grouped with nested relationships as a heightened ML/TF/PF risk requiring enhanced due diligence; the node also carries the guidance's glossary entries for correspondent banking, correspondent institution, nested activity and de-risking. Applies to UAE LFIs.
lookup_terms: direct customer access to correspondent account

data.summary: Concept node within CBUAE guidance on correspondent banking, covering the categories of ML/TF/PF risk factors that a correspondent institution must weigh when assessing a respondent institution (jurisdiction, ownership and management, products/services, customer base, nesting and payable-through arrangements). It frames correspondent banking as a bilateral relationship in which one licensed financial institution provides services such as cash management, cross-border wire transfers, cheque clearing, loans, letters of credit and FX to another. It binds LFIs supervised by the CBUAE and feeds the enterprise-wide risk assessment obligation under Article 4 of the AML-CFT Decision.

Concept node treating jurisdictional exposure as a driver of correspondent banking risk: where the respondent institution, its parent, branches and subsidiaries are located and operate, and whether those jurisdictions are high-risk. Presence in high-risk jurisdictions is listed as a trigger for enhanced due diligence on top of the baseline correspondent-specific measures. Applies to CBUAE-licensed financial institutions acting as correspondents.

Concept node on how a respondent institution's legal form, ownership transparency and executive management composition affect ML/TF/PF risk — state-owned, publicly listed versus privately held, opaque structures, UBOs or senior managers in high-risk jurisdictions, and PEPs in ownership or management. It directs correspondent institutions to document beneficial ownership and management structures before onboarding and throughout the relationship, and identifies PEP presence as an EDD trigger. Binds CBUAE-supervised LFIs providing correspondent services.

Concept node covering the preventive and mitigating controls expected across the correspondent banking lifecycle: enterprise-wide and relationship-level risk assessment, correspondent agreement terms (including termination/limitation causes and confirmation that the respondent does not serve shell banks or prohibited customer types), risk-based scaling of due diligence, and EDD for higher-risk respondents. Controls must sit inside the LFI's wider AML/CFT/CPF programme with governance, independent audit and training support, and be adjusted as the respondent's risk changes. Guidance is not exhaustive; LFIs remain bound by the UAE legal and regulatory framework in force.

Concept node setting out baseline CDD applied to a respondent institution at onboarding and on an ongoing basis: identification and verification via reliable independent sources (corporate and beneficial ownership registries, licensing authorities), identification and reasonable verification of UBOs, understanding the nature and purpose of the relationship for risk profiling, confirming the respondent is not a shell bank, and event-driven and periodic refresh. It also touches minimum due diligence for transactional non-customer RMA (SWIFT relationship management application) counterparties, including name screening against PEP and sanctions lists. Binds CBUAE-supervised LFIs; cross-refers to the CBUAE CDD/KYC and record-keeping guidance.

Concept node on the correspondent-specific due diligence layer that sits above standard CDD for cross-border respondent relationships, including understanding the respondent's business, reputation and AML/CFT controls, documenting responsibilities in the correspondent agreement, and applying enhanced scrutiny where listed risk indicators are present (nesting, payable-through activity, high-risk jurisdictions, adverse ownership/management, high-risk products or customer base). Explains the correspondent/respondent construct and the service range involved. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions acting as correspondents, on a risk-based, scaled basis.

Section of CBUAE guidance on correspondent banking setting out enhanced due diligence expectations where a respondent institution presents elevated ML/TF/PF risk, and listing the triggering risk factors (nesting and payable-through accounts, high-risk jurisdictions of the respondent or its group, PEP involvement in ownership/management, higher-risk products, and a high-risk downstream customer base). It frames EDD as a scaled, risk-based overlay on the baseline correspondent due diligence required of all such relationships, alongside enterprise-wide risk assessment duties anchored in Article 4 of the AML-CFT Decision. It binds licensed financial institutions acting as correspondent institutions.

Guidance section on post-onboarding obligations in correspondent banking: continuous transaction monitoring of activity to, from or through the correspondent account against the expected purpose and profile of the respondent, plus periodic relationship review to confirm the relationship stays within risk appetite. It sets an expectation of at least annual ongoing due diligence for high-risk correspondent relationships, refreshed CDD/KYC on a risk-sensitive basis, and risk-mitigation levers such as product restrictions, volume limits, real-time monitoring and elevated senior management approval. Applies to LFIs providing correspondent services.

Concept node on suspicious transaction and suspicious activity reporting in the correspondent banking context, covering when individual transactions or patterns become reportable and the escalation from monitoring alert to STR/SAR filing. It addresses the correspondent institution's use of targeted requests for information (RFIs) to the respondent, including information about the respondent's own customers, to assess reasonableness before deciding to report. Binds LFIs as reporting entities.

Guidance on governance arrangements for correspondent banking AML/CFT/CPF programmes, including senior management and Board oversight, the option of a dedicated governance body to approve high-risk relationships and act as escalation point for suspicious activity and termination decisions. It maps responsibilities across the three lines of defence (frontline/relationship management, compliance, and internal or external audit) and expects representation from all three in oversight. Applies to LFIs offering correspondent banking services.

Node on record-keeping duties attached to correspondent banking relationships, specifying a minimum five-year retention of due diligence records including the respondent's licence, the correspondent agreement, due diligence and AML/CFT/CPF assessments, a completed Wolfsberg CBDDQ, the anti-shell-bank statement, site visit and call reports, and the relationship risk assessment with CDD/KYC files, correspondence and STR/SAR material. It also requires secure storage and access controls consistent with data protection obligations. Binds LFIs; the surrounding context also covers tailored AML/CFT/CPF training expectations.

Explanatory and annex material describing how correspondent banking works (correspondent versus respondent institution, services provided under bilateral agreement, cross-border exposure) and setting out red flag indicators correspondent institutions should detect through continuous monitoring. It also sets best-practice expectations around the Wolfsberg Group 2023 Correspondent Banking Due Diligence Questionnaire as the industry standard for assessing a respondent's AML/CFT/CPF, sanctions, fraud and ABC controls. Directed at LFIs acting as correspondents, with expectations also articulated for respondent institutions.

An explanatory segment of CBUAE correspondent banking guidance dealing with SWIFT Relationship Management Application (RMA) links established with counterparties that are not customers of the institution, illustrating typical non-customer RMA use cases (corporate reporting, relaying payment instructions, sub-custodian/global custodian flows, trade finance messaging). It sets out the minimum due diligence expected before key exchange and periodically thereafter — name and address collection, screening against internal, PEP and sanctions lists, and a risk assessment against red flags — drawing on Wolfsberg Group standards, and notes RMA Plus as a means of restricting permitted message types. It is addressed to licensed financial institutions operating SWIFT connectivity; the surrounding material also covers the ISO 20022 migration and MT message retirement.

A descriptive section of CBUAE correspondent banking guidance explaining the Wolfsberg Group and its Correspondent Banking Due Diligence Questionnaire (CBDDQ, revised February 2023) as the industry tool for collecting information on a respondent institution's ownership, regulatory status, products, AML/CFT/CPF, sanctions, fraud and ABC programmes, and its CDD/KYC, EDD, monitoring and testing controls. It sits alongside guidance on assessing the respondent's licensing and home-jurisdiction AML/CFT/CPF regime, and stresses that the same risk factors apply to branches, affiliates and subsidiaries that are direct customers. It informs how licensed financial institutions structure correspondent due diligence; the Wolfsberg materials themselves are industry standards, not binding law.

An annex-level orientation to the global standards underpinning correspondent banking supervision, centred on FATF Recommendation 13, which sets enhanced due diligence expectations for institutions providing correspondent services to foreign respondent institutions and to similar cross-border relationships. It explains the rationale (limited visibility over the respondent's customers, non-equivalent supervision abroad) and lists the UAE legal instruments and acronyms/defined terms used throughout the guidance. Useful for tracing how international standards are mapped onto national obligations for licensed financial institutions.

Guidance on how licensed financial institutions should design and run a risk-based CDD/KYC programme, treating CDD and KYC as interchangeable terms for the ongoing process of identifying customers and assessing their ML/TF/PF and wider financial crime risk before onboarding and throughout the relationship. It addresses group-wide consistency — standardised global procedures, applying UAE standards in less stringent host jurisdictions to the extent permitted, standardised onboarding forms tailored by customer type — and record-keeping of the resulting CDD file. It also flags the expectation of sufficient CDD on customers with direct or indirect access to a correspondent bank account.

Guidance on the information licensed financial institutions should collect to identify customers and beneficial owners and to feed customer segmentation and risk rating, including purpose of account, source of funds and source of wealth, occupation or industry, channels, expected products, geographies and transaction volumes. It scales information demands to the assessed risk profile, with additional detail expected for higher-risk customers, and explains how the resulting baseline of expected activity supports ongoing monitoring and the SDD/EDD decision.

Guidance on constructing a customer risk profile using the same risk categories as the institution-level assessment — products and services, geography, and the customer's business, customers and counterparties — anchored in the obligation to understand the nature of the customer's business and the purpose of the relationship. It addresses UBO identification and verification timing (generally before the relationship starts, with a limited low-risk exception for completing verification afterwards) and the treatment of listed companies and their majority-owned subsidiaries where ownership data is available from reliable sources, while allowing institutions to prescribe higher-risk scenarios requiring full verification.
lookup_terms: nature and purpose of business relationship

data.summary: Node covering the ongoing monitoring element of CDD/KYC in the CBUAE's CDD/KYC guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions, anchored on Article 7 of the AML-CFT Decision. It treats monitoring as a continuous obligation across the whole business relationship — confirming activity matches the profile built at onboarding and feeding suspicious activity reporting — and sets risk-based expectations for periodic and event-driven customer reviews, review frequency by risk rating, alert-threshold calibration, and enhanced monitoring of high-risk or previously reported customers. It also addresses using digital identification systems to authenticate customers on an ongoing basis. Binds all LFIs supervised by CBUAE; automated transaction monitoring is expected of larger LFIs.

Node for Simplified Due Diligence (SDD) as treated in the CBUAE CDD/KYC guidance for LFIs — the reduced-intensity CDD option available for customers and relationships assessed as lower ML/TF/PF risk. Relevant to how an LFI justifies lighter information collection, less frequent review and higher monitoring thresholds, and how SDD sits against the EDD track within a risk-based programme. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions; SDD is a permitted calibration, not a waiver of CDD.

Node for Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) under the CBUAE CDD/KYC guidance and related CBUAE guidance, covering the additional measures applied to higher-risk customers and relationships (e.g. PEPs, opaque ownership, higher-risk jurisdictions, adverse media subjects). Touches the additional information sets expected — source of funds, source of wealth, business detail, expected counterparties and geographies — and the link to enhanced transaction monitoring and more frequent review. Binds LFIs licensed by CBUAE as part of their risk-based CDD/KYC programme.

Node on beneficial ownership identification and verification under Article 9 of the AML-CFT Decision and the AML-CFT Law definition of beneficial owner, as explained in CBUAE CDD/KYC guidance. It sets the cascade for legal-person customers: identify natural persons with a controlling ownership interest of 25 percent or more, and where none exists identify those exercising control by other means; it also links to Cabinet Decision 58 on Beneficial Owner Procedures and permits documentary, non-documentary or digital identification methods. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions onboarding and reviewing legal persons and legal arrangements.

The parent node for the CBUAE guidance on customer due diligence / know your customer for Licensed Financial Institutions, which treats CDD and KYC as interchangeable terms for the ongoing, risk-based process of identifying customers and assessing their ML/TF/PF risk before and throughout the relationship.
