It sets out the trigger events for CDD (notably establishing a business relationship), expectations for correspondent banking relationships, and group-wide consistency — including applying UAE standards in foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries where host-country rules are less stringent. Binds all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions, including their overseas branches and majority-owned subsidiaries.

Node on customer identification, verification and risk profiling under the CBUAE CDD/KYC guidance, reflecting Article 8 of the AML-CFT Decision's requirement to understand the nature and purpose of the customer relationship. It lists the baseline information expected at onboarding (purpose of account, source of funds and wealth, occupation or industry, expected channels, products, geographies and transaction volumes), scales additional information collection to the customer's assessed risk, and explains customer segmentation and initial risk rating as the basis for later monitoring thresholds, review cycles and SDD/EDD decisions. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

A sub-section of the CBUAE CDD/KYC and record-keeping guidance dealing with digital identity systems (electronic identity databases, digital credentials, biometrics, and identification APIs/platforms) as an alternative to documentary and non-documentary verification. It permits licensed financial institutions to identify and verify customers digitally provided the system is "reliable" and "independent" — meaning technology, governance and controls give adequate confidence in identity proofing, enrolment and authentication — while preserving the underlying principle that no relationship may be opened without a reasonable belief in the customer's true identity. It binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions (banks, exchange houses, finance companies, payment and payment token service providers, hawala providers, insurers) and cross-refers to the CBUAE's dedicated digital identification guidance; note this is UAE, not KSA, law.

Covers source of funds (SoF) and source of wealth (SoW) within the CBUAE CDD/KYC guidance, positioning them as additional information to be gathered as the customer's risk profile rises, alongside business description, expected turnover, counterparties and transacting countries. The purpose is to build a baseline of expected activity that supports risk-based ongoing monitoring, customer segmentation and risk rating, and decisions on simplified versus enhanced due diligence. Applies to CBUAE-licensed financial institutions; relevant as comparative material rather than binding KSA obligation.

Addresses name screening obligations under CBUAE AML guidance: screening customers, beneficial owners, natural persons acting for the customer and other related parties against ML/TF/PF information sources, negative media, PEP databases and internal watchlists before onboarding, with records of true matches kept in the KYC file. It also links screening to periodic and event-driven CDD refreshes, where re-screening is required and a true hit on a sanctions, PEP or adverse-media list is itself a trigger for review. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions; interacts with the separate TFS/sanctions screening regime.

Sets out when a CBUAE-licensed financial institution may rely on another financial institution or DNFBP to perform specified CDD elements — customer identification/verification, beneficial owner identification, and understanding the purpose and nature of the relationship — and the conditions attached, including immediate access to the information, a non-objection letter filed with the Central Bank, and retention of ultimate responsibility by the institution's Compliance Officer. It expressly excludes outsourcing, service provider, vendor and agency arrangements from the reliance concept, and adds expectations on written agreements, senior-official approval, ongoing review and termination for deficient third parties. Relevant when assessing analogous third-party CDD reliance questions in other jurisdictions.
lookup_terms: reliance on CDD by another institution

data.summary: Covers general CDD/KYC application expectations in the CBUAE guidance, including group-wide standardisation of CDD/KYC across branches and majority-owned subsidiaries, applying UAE standards where a host country's AML/CFT rules are less stringent, use of tailored onboarding forms by customer type, and heightened diligence in correspondent banking. It frames CDD/KYC as an ongoing, risk-based process performed at onboarding and at intervals thereafter, feeding risk rating and the identification of unusual or suspicious activity. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions and their foreign branches/subsidiaries.

Identifies the AML-CFT Decision (the implementing regulation to the UAE AML-CFT Law) as a core legal basis of the CBUAE CDD/KYC guidance, notably Article 15 on mandatory enhanced due diligence for foreign and domestic PEPs with high-risk factors, their family members and close associates, and for relationships with persons from high-risk countries. The node also records the guidance's status and scope: it supplements, and yields to, the binding legal framework, reflects FATF standards, takes effect on issuance with a one-month compliance window, and applies to all CBUAE-licensed/registered banks, exchange houses, finance companies, payment and payment token service providers, hawala providers, insurers, agents and brokers.

Defined term and obligation cluster within the CBUAE virtual asset transfer (travel rule) instrument: the Beneficiary is the intended recipient of a Virtual Asset Transfer, and the node carries the duties attaching to the Beneficiary's VASP and to Intermediary Providers. It covers verification of originator/beneficiary information, retention of collected information under the Implementing Regulation's record-keeping article, domestic-transfer simplification where verified data is otherwise available, and reporting systemic failures by counterparty VASPs to the Supervisory Authority. It binds licensed Virtual Asset Service Providers (originator-side, beneficiary-side) and Intermediary Providers handling virtual asset transfers.

Node for "the Decision" — Cabinet Decision No. 134/2025, the Implementing Regulation of Federal Decree-Law No. 10/2025 on combating money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing — which the virtual asset transfer rules repeatedly cross-refer to for risk assessment and record-keeping duties. Context also captures related definitions (Account, Beneficiary, Distributed Ledger Technology, Execute a Virtual Asset Transfer, Financial Free Zone) and the prohibition on executing transfers of Privacy Tokens. Relevant to any VASP or Intermediary Provider subject to the Decision, and to Supervisory Authorities issuing joint interpretive guidance.

Covers the enhanced due diligence and handling regime for Virtual Asset Transfers sent to or received from an Unhosted Wallet, excluding transaction (gas) fees. It requires obtaining missing originator/beneficiary information, considering delay or return of the asset, declining execution where requested originator information is not provided, and grounding decisions in the institution's ML/TF/PF risk assessment (purpose and nature of the relationship, transfer value, linked transfers). Binds Virtual Asset Service Providers acting for originators or beneficiaries, with parallel duties for Intermediary Providers including reporting systemic counterparty failures.

CBUAE Circular No. 6/2025 regulation setting administrative and financial penalties for Emiratization violations, issued under the Central Bank Law and the Insurance Law. It provides for collection of penalties (including deduction from funds held by the Central Bank if unpaid within ten working days), notification of NAFIS and judicial authorities, a fine range for fictitious Emiratization, and refund of incentives wrongly disbursed. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions, insurance companies and insurance-related professionals licensed in the UAE.

Defined-term and scope node for Emiratization — employment of UAE Nationals as a national initiative — as used in the CBUAE penalties regulation. It frames the regulation's objective of monitoring compliance with approved Emiratization targets and identifies the violation types targeted, including falsifying Emiratization percentages, submitting inaccurate information to obtain NAFIS benefits, and circumventing Emiratization requirements. Applies across the banking, financial and insurance sectors to Licensed Institutions in the UAE.

Definition node: NAFIS is the Emirati Talent Competitiveness Council, and "Beneficiary" means a UAE National benefiting from NAFIS, as defined in the CBUAE Emiratization penalties regulation alongside Central Bank, Central Bank Law, Insurance Law and Licensed Institutions. Useful for identifying which body receives notifications of violations and whose programme benefits are at issue in falsification or misrepresentation cases. Relevant to Licensed Financial Institutions, insurance companies and insurance-related professionals.

Concept node covering "fictitious Emiratization" under the CBUAE Administrative and Financial Penalties for Emiratization Violations Regulation (Circular 6/2025): the sham or artificial appointment of UAE Nationals to inflate Emiratization ratios or obtain NAFIS benefits. It sets out the consequences — penalties multiplied by the number of Nationals fictitiously appointed, CBUAE discretion to compel the institution to train and qualify the affected Nationals at its own cost, and a possible mandated salary increase of 10–30% after training. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions, insurance companies and insurance-related professionals, and bars them from recovering incentive amounts from the National; grievance against CBUAE penalty decisions lies only to the Central Bank within ten working days.

Defined-term node for the Tawteen System, the CBUAE platform used to facilitate and oversee recruitment and employment of UAE Nationals in the banking, financial and insurance sectors. It is the prescribed reporting channel under the Emiratization Violations Regulation, where Licensed Institutions must notify CBUAE of Beneficiaries who do not work full-time or cease employment after onboarding, and of changes to the terms of benefit. Failure to update the system attracts an administrative fine of AED 20,000 per National.

Scope and enforcement node identifying "Licensed Institutions" — licensed financial institutions under Decretal Federal Law 14/2018, insurance companies and insurance-related professionals — as the addressees of the CBUAE Emiratization penalties regime (Circular 6/2025). It sets CBUAE's power to impose cumulative financial and administrative penalties for violations listed in Schedule (1), to require refund of incentives received from government bodies, and to compel payment of incentives to Nationals, while prohibiting any recovery from the National. CBUAE retains discretion to reduce, waive, increase or allow instalment payment of penalties.

Instrument node for the CBUAE Enterprise Risk Management for Solvency Purposes Standards for insurance companies, which set requirements for an integrated ERM framework supporting risk identification, capital adequacy assessment, risk governance and the ORSA. They apply to all Companies on a solo and Group-wide basis where there are Subsidiaries, Affiliates or international branches, while branches of foreign companies must adapt the framework to local operations. Enforcement is proportionate, with CBUAE deciding the extent to which a smaller Company must meet the specifics.
lookup_terms: Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation for Insurance Companies

data.summary: Concept node on Enterprise Risk Management as required of insurance companies under the CBUAE ERM Standards, read together with the Relevant Regulations (risk management and internal controls, corporate governance, recovery planning, group supervision and the 2014 financial regulations for conventional and Takaful companies). It covers the Risk Management function's support to the Board, risk committee and Senior Management across solvency, capital and liquidity planning, product and business planning, reinsurance/re-takaful strategy, ALM and investments, plus risk identification, interdependencies and correlation under stress. Takaful operators must additionally address Shari'ah non-compliance risk, fund segregation and use of conventional reinsurance.

Concept node on the Own Risk and Solvency Assessment, the forward-looking self-assessment insurance companies must conduct at least annually as a core element of their ERM framework. The ORSA report must address current and projected financial soundness across scenarios, including year-end solvency and at least the following twelve quarters of projected solvency ratios, all material risks (underwriting, investment, credit, operational, liquidity), climate-related financial risks per the Climate-related Financial Risk Management Regulation, actual-versus-planned outcomes from the prior ORSA, risk policies and procedures, and quantitative analysis under normal and stress scenarios. It binds Companies on a solo and Group-wide basis.

This node is the UAE Virtual Assets Travel Rule issued under the CBUAE framework, setting the originator/beneficiary information requirements that must accompany virtual asset transfers and the definitions underpinning them (including Privacy Token, Unhosted Wallet, Virtual Asset, Receive, and STR). It imposes a risk-based regime covering collection and verification of transfer data, a daily aggregated AED 3,500 threshold for beneficiary identity verification, handling of transfers with missing information (reject, execute, delay, return, report, follow up), supervisory reporting of systemic failures, and record keeping aligned with the underlying AML Decision. It binds Virtual Asset Service Providers and Intermediary Providers operating within UAE federal, Emirate, Free Zone and Financial Free Zone territorial scope.

Defines and addresses the Virtual Asset Service Provider as the primary obligated entity under the UAE Travel Rule, acting either for the Originator (executing a transfer) or for the Beneficiary (receiving one). Obligations include collecting, verifying and transmitting prescribed transfer data, verifying beneficiary identity above the daily aggregated AED 3,500 threshold, applying enhanced due diligence in unhosted wallet scenarios, maintaining risk-based policies for incomplete transfers, and reporting systemic counterparty failures to the Supervisory Authority. Applies to VASPs in the UAE, including Free Zones and Financial Free Zones, and contemplates dealings with counterparty VASPs that may be unregulated in the UAE.

Covers the defined term Virtual Asset Transfer, the transaction trigger for the UAE Travel Rule, whether executed on behalf of an Originator, received on behalf of a Beneficiary, routed through an Intermediary Provider, or sent to/from an Unhosted Wallet. It governs what information must accompany the transfer, thresholds for verification, linked-transfer aggregation in risk assessment, and permissible responses where required data is absent; transaction (gas) fees are excluded from scope. Relevant to any VASP or Intermediary Provider determining whether a given movement of virtual assets falls within the rule.

Addresses the Intermediary Provider role in a virtual asset transfer chain, where an intermediary receives or forwards a virtual asset between the originator's and beneficiary's VASPs. Obligations include confirming and verifying the regulatory status of both counterparty VASPs before facilitating a transfer, logging all transfers including rejections for non-compliance, retaining and onward-transmitting all originator and beneficiary information, applying risk assessment to the transfer, and reporting systemic information failures by other providers to the Supervisory Authority. Binds intermediaries operating in the UAE transfer chain, including in relation to foreign or unregulated counterparties.

Defines the Unhosted Wallet (a wallet, address, smart contract or similar decentralised technology self-operated by an Originator or Beneficiary without third-party service provision beyond the technology itself) and sets the specific treatment of transfers to and from such wallets. A VASP must perform enhanced due diligence, request missing originator/beneficiary information and decline execution if it is not provided, and on inbound transfers consider obtaining missing data from the Beneficiary, delaying execution or returning the asset, guided by its risk assessment. Binds VASPs handling customer transfers involving self-hosted wallets; gas fees are out of scope.

Covers the Originator role and the originator-side information set required to accompany a qualifying virtual asset transfer, including full name, wallet or account number (or a unique traceability reference where none exists), and address, national identity or travel document number, customer identification number, and date and place of birth. The originator's VASP must not execute a transfer unless this data is collected, verified and transmitted immediately and securely, subject to the rule's threshold and exemption paragraphs; beneficiary-side VASPs and intermediaries must retain it and report systemic failures to supply it. Binds VASPs and Intermediary Providers within the UAE territorial scope.

A concept node within the CBUAE Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) standards for insurance companies, covering the self-imposed Risk Limits structure that a Company must establish as guardrails on its Risk Profile without jeopardising commitments to policyholders. Limits must be calibrated against strategic objectives, business plans, solvency position, Risk Appetite and projected outcomes of plausible but severe stress scenarios, and must interact with reinsurance arrangements and capital planning. It binds insurance and Takaful companies (Board, risk committee, Senior Management and the Risk Management function), with Takaful entities assessed both consolidated and per fund/account.

Concept node on Capital Adequacy and solvency within the CBUAE ERM/ORSA standards for insurance companies, linking risk quantification (stress testing, scenario analysis, models) to capital and solvency assessment. It sets expectations that the ORSA report present the year-end and at least twelve quarters of projected solvency positions, analyse material risks (underwriting, investment, credit, operational, liquidity), incorporate climate-related financial risks, and compare actual versus planned capital outcomes. Binds insurance and Takaful companies subject to the Relevant Regulations and their financial regulations on solvency.

Concept node covering asset-liability and liquidity risk management under the CBUAE ERM standards for insurance companies, requiring strategies, policies and processes so liabilities can be met as they fall due in normal and stressed conditions. Elements include liquidity stress testing, a portfolio of unencumbered liquid assets meeting stated quality criteria, a contingency funding plan, use of complaints data to ensure timely payment to Insureds and Beneficiaries, assessment of reinsurance programme effects on liquidity, and reporting to the Central Bank. Binds insurance and Takaful companies, with ALM support expected from the Risk Management function.

Concept node on recovery planning as an element of the CBUAE ERM standards for insurance companies, anchored in the Recovery Planning Regulation (Circular 4/2023) among the Relevant Regulations. It requires consistency between ORSA outcomes, stress testing results and the Recovery Plan, with the ORSA serving as a key input so that risk assessment and contingency planning are aligned. Binds insurance and Takaful companies and their Boards and Senior Management, which must develop plans and actions for periods of severe financial stress.

Defined-term node identifying the set of CBUAE instruments collectively called the "Relevant Regulations" in the ERM Standards: the Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation and Standards (Circular 25/2022), Corporate Governance Regulation and Standards (Circular 24/2022), Recovery Planning Regulation (Circular 4/2023), Insurance Group Supervision Regulation (Circular 4/2025), and Decisions No. 25 and 26 of 2014 on financial regulations for insurance and Takaful companies. These instruments impose the underlying obligations on risk identification and control, annual ORSA submission, forward-looking stress testing and recovery plans, and are the reference frame against which the ERM standards are read. Useful for tracing the legal basis of an ERM obligation to its source instrument.

Node on the CBUAE dormant accounts and unclaimed balances regime, setting the criteria by which a customer or account becomes dormant across banks, exchange businesses and insurance companies, including the three-year safe deposit box charge trigger, the one-year unclaimed funds rule for exchange businesses, and customer-level dormancy for insurance where no other active policy exists and the address is unknown. It also carries consumer protection duties: funds remain the property of the customer or heirs, interest continues to accrue per contract until transfer to the Central Bank, no debits or system-based charges may be applied, statement generation is suppressed but the customer is not excluded from routine communications. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs) and allocates certain responsibilities to customers on address updates and record-keeping.

Node covering the CBUAE Dormant Accounts and Unclaimed Balances/Funds Regulation's treatment of unclaimed balances and funds — including unclaimed bankers' cheques, bank drafts and cashier orders, safe deposit box contents, and unclaimed insurance and exchange-house funds. It sets out how licensed financial institutions must ring-fence such amounts in a dedicated internal ledger/unclaimed balances account after the customer-contact period expires, control access to dormant customer records, and disclose dormancy terms in account-opening, underwriting, exchange and safe-deposit terms and conditions; it also bars exchange businesses from booking unclaimed funds as income. Binds all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions, with sector-specific carve-outs for insurance companies and exchange businesses.
lookup_terms: bankers' cheque / bank draft / cashier order
exchange business unclaimed funds as income

data.summary: Node on Article 8 (and the linked Article 9 retention rules) of the CBUAE dormant accounts regime: the duty to transfer net dormant-account balances and unclaimed instrument proceeds to the designated Unclaimed Balances Accounts at the Central Bank after the prescribed dormancy period, subject to conditions such as the customer having no other active account and an unknown current address. It also covers reporting formats for movements in unclaimed insurance funds, the requirement to settle customer or heir claims only after receiving funds back from the Central Bank, and the cessation of interest accrual once funds are held centrally. Binds licensed financial institutions, with separate tracks for insurance companies and exchange businesses.
lookup_terms: Unclaimed Insurance Funds deposits and withdrawals
retention of funds by Central Bank

data.summary: Node on the claim and reclaim pathway under the CBUAE dormant accounts regime: how customers, legal heirs or beneficiaries claim dormant balances and other unclaimed funds from the institution (Article 4) and how institutions reclaim amounts already remitted to the Central Bank (Article 8). Covers reactivation and identity re-verification of dormant accounts, record-keeping of payments made, and the one-month settlement deadline for claims absent valid reasons for delay. Binds licensed financial institutions handling claims, including insurance companies for unclaimed insurance funds.
lookup_terms: claim of funds from dormant accounts

data.summary: Node on Article 7 of the CBUAE dormant accounts regime, which preserves the customer's (or heirs') ownership of dormant balances and unclaimed funds and constrains institution conduct: interest continues to accrue on interest-bearing accounts until transfer to the Central Bank, no fees beyond those already agreed may be charged, no debits or system-based charges may be applied, credits may still be received, and statements are suppressed without excluding the customer from other communications. It also requires dormancy terms to be disclosed in customer documentation, alongside customer-side expectations on updating contact details and retaining correspondence. Binds licensed financial institutions in their dealings with retail and other customers.
lookup_terms: fees and charges on dormant accounts

data.summary: Node linking the dormant accounts regime to the UAE AML/CFT/CPF framework: institutions must keep customer profiles current in line with the AML federal decree-law, its executive regulation and CBUAE AML notices, and must monitor reactivated or claimed dormant accounts closely to ensure they are not misused. It sits at the intersection of dormancy/reactivation controls (ID re-verification, payment records, one-month claim settlement) and ongoing CDD obligations. Binds licensed financial institutions, including insurance companies, subject to CBUAE AML supervision.

CBUAE guidance for licensed financial institutions on identifying, assessing and mitigating proliferation financing (PF) risk as part of the wider AML/CFT/CPF regime. It explains the UAE's counter-proliferation-financing framework — targeted financial sanctions implementation without delay, export controls and preventive/detective measures — and situates it against FATF standards and guidance on PF risk assessment and red-flag indicators. Issued under the supervisory authority's mandate to provide guidance; it binds CBUAE-supervised financial institutions as expectations for compliance with the underlying AML/CFT legislation.

CBUAE guidance addressed to licensed financial institutions (LFIs) on identifying, understanding and mitigating trade-based money laundering and illicit transshipment risk, set against the UAE's role as a trade and free-zone hub. It covers TBML typologies and red flags, preventive measures across CDD and trade-document review, suspicious activity reporting, and expects these controls to sit within a risk-appropriate AML/CFT programme organised on the three-lines-of-defence model with MLRO independence, resourcing and board/senior-management oversight, plus independent audit. Guidance-level expectations, but binding in practice on all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Concept node within CBUAE's counter-proliferation-financing guidance, framing proliferation financing (PF) as the funding of WMD development, acquisition or delivery systems and the role of financial institutions in detecting and disrupting it. It maps the applicable UAE framework — Federal Decree Law No. (20) of 2018 and its Implementing Regulation (Cabinet Decision No. (10) of 2019 as amended by No. (24) of 2022), targeted financial sanctions, export controls and dual-use goods lists — alongside relevant FATF guidance and PF red-flag indicators. Binds LFIs, and by reference DNFBPs and VASPs, to implement TFS without delay and embed CPF into the AML/CFT programme.

Concept node covering terrorist financing as one limb of the UAE AML/CFT/CPF regime as treated in CBUAE's proliferation-financing guidance, where TF sits alongside ML and PF in institutional risk identification, TFS implementation and reporting duties. The source material focuses mainly on PF and its sanctions framework, with TF appearing as the adjacent obligation set under Federal Decree Law No. (20) of 2018 and its Implementing Regulation. Relevant to LFIs (and DNFBPs/VASPs) determining the scope of their combined ML/TF/PF risk assessments and sanctions screening duties.

Concept node on how LFIs must identify, assess and understand proliferation-financing risk under Article 4 of the AML-CFT Decision and CBUAE Notice No. CBUAE/BIS/2023/5960, through a documented, regularly updated institutional risk assessment covering customers, products/services and transactions, delivery channels, geographies and operating structure. It requires LFIs to take account of the Proliferation Financing National Risk Assessment and other official sources, and to fold PF risk factors (customer attributes, transaction behaviour, red flags, external/geopolitical factors) into overall customer risk rating methodologies, without necessarily maintaining a separate PF-only methodology. Binds all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions and informs a risk-based approach.

Concept node explaining why trade finance and open-account trade are structurally vulnerable to proliferation financing and TBML — false or generic invoicing, over/under-valuation, misdescription of goods, and factoring arrangements that obscure the true nature of a transaction and the identity of counterparties. It notes that documentary instruments such as letters of credit give LFIs more visibility (goods, counterparties, routes, vessels) than open-account wire transfers, which carry little underlying detail, while still not reliably revealing dual-use or proliferation-sensitive content. Directs LFIs to assess which of their products and services carry elevated PF abuse risk.

Concept node on correspondent banking as a PF/ML exposure within CBUAE's counter-proliferation-financing guidance, where an LFI processes transactions for a respondent institution's underlying customers with limited direct visibility. The surrounding material sets the risk-factor framework LFIs must apply — customer attributes and ownership, jurisdictional exposure, transactional behaviour including dual-use goods flows, watchlist and control-list hits, and geopolitical developments — feeding into customer risk ratings and risk categories. Relevant to LFIs setting risk appetite and due diligence intensity for cross-border banking relationships.

A concept node within CBUAE proliferation-financing (PF) guidance explaining how trade-based money laundering techniques — mis-invoicing, over/under-valuation and misdescription of goods — can be exploited to fund or procure WMD-related and dual-use items. It contrasts documentary trade finance (richer data on goods, counterparties, routes, vessels) with open-account/wire-based trade, where message data is thin and PF risk is harder to assess. It is directed at Licensed Financial Institutions assessing PF threats and vulnerabilities across their own products and services.

Core concept node of CBUAE's TBML guidance: defines trade-based money laundering (following FATF) as manipulating domestic or international trade transactions to disguise criminal proceeds or the identity of trade participants, and situates it alongside financial-system and cash-movement laundering methods. It covers the UAE threat picture, the international trade and trade finance backdrop, and includes an annex of TBML and illicit transshipment red flags. Addressed to Licensed Financial Institutions for risk understanding, CDD and transaction monitoring purposes.

Concept node explaining transshipment — routing goods through intermediate destinations before the final country of destination — and how it is abused to evade sanctions, export controls and trade restrictions. It sets out typical illicit schemes (re-export from a sanctioned origin with falsified country-of-origin documents, imports by entities in low-restriction or corruption-prone jurisdictions, front companies established in third jurisdictions) and connects these to commodity typologies such as construction materials. Relevant to LFIs financing or processing trade flows and to sanctions/export-control risk assessment.

Defines documentary trade finance within the CBUAE TBML guidance: performance-based products such as letters of credit and documentary collections, and non-performance products such as guarantees and standby LCs, together with the document set (invoice, packing list, bill of lading, underlying contract, other transport documents) that LFIs collect and examine. The distinction matters because control expectations differ by product type, available information and the LFI's role in the transaction. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions calibrating trade-transaction controls.

Concept node on letters of credit as used in the CBUAE TBML guidance, focused mainly on LC-specific red flags: document discrepancies and mismatches between invoice, bill of lading and LC terms, repeated amendments or extensions, changes of beneficiary, payment location or country of origin, payment requests to third countries, willingness to waive discrepancies, and LCs routinely opened but left unutilised. Useful for LFIs reviewing presentations and deciding whether trade activity is consistent with the customer's profile.

Defines open account trade and non-documentary trade finance — where the exporter ships and payment falls due later, and the LFI finances or processes payment without collecting and inspecting underlying trade documents — and identifies these as among the highest-risk activities LFIs routinely engage in because of reduced visibility over parties and goods. Because document-based detection is unavailable, the guidance directs LFIs to rely on CDD/KYC, EDD and transaction monitoring for TBML indicators. Applies to Licensed Financial Institutions offering trade-related payment and financing services.

A section of CBUAE proliferation-financing guidance dealing with hawala and other non-traditional remittance channels, distinguishing Registered Hawala Providers (registered under the Registered Hawala Providers Regulation, Circular No. 24/2019) from unlicensed/unregistered providers, which may not operate in the UAE. It treats RHPs — like MVTS and exchange houses — as inherently high risk for PF and expects enhanced controls, and directs Licensed Financial Institutions to have policies and procedures addressing exposure to unlicensed providers. It binds LFIs servicing or exposed to hawala activity, and indirectly frames registration duties for hawala operators.

Guidance section defining shell companies (incorporated but without real operations, assets or staff) and front companies (operating businesses used to disguise illicit activity), and explaining how proliferators use opaque ownership structures and nominee shareholders to conceal beneficial ownership. It sets the expectation that LFIs apply risk-based CDD/KYC and EDD, including beneficial ownership identification and lowered ownership thresholds for higher-risk legal persons. Addressed to Licensed Financial Institutions onboarding or servicing legal-entity customers.

Section on PF vulnerabilities arising from trade, covering trade-based money laundering techniques (false, over- or under-valued invoices, misdescription of goods) and the contrast between documentary trade finance and open-account transactions, where wire messages carry little information about the underlying trade. It expects LFIs to assess which of their products and services could be misused to finance WMD programmes or the acquisition of dual-use or proliferation-sensitive goods. Applies to Licensed Financial Institutions offering trade finance and cross-border payment services.

Covers customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence expectations in the counter-proliferation-financing context, particularly for correspondent banking relationships where the correspondent lacks direct knowledge of the respondent's underlying customers. It also treats operational risk in CPF compliance (staffing, screening and risk-rating systems, monitoring and CDD refresh backlogs, training gaps) and the requirement to establish mitigating policies, procedures and processes. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions, especially those offering correspondent services.

Sets out ongoing monitoring and reporting expectations for PF risk, referencing the obligations under Articles 7 and 16 of the AML-CFT Decision to monitor all transactions for consistency with customer information and to identify activity warranting an STR or SAR. It describes risk-based measures such as PF-calibrated monitoring rules with lower alert thresholds, more frequent periodic reviews for high-risk files, pre-approval of atypical transactions, and lists transactional red-flag indicators. Binds Licensed Financial Institutions and their compliance functions.

Section explaining export control regimes as a distinct control layer from sanctions, administered by authorities such as the EOCN, MOD, FANR, ICP and SIRA, and covering controlled items, technology and services. It expects LFIs to be familiar with national and international export control frameworks because they finance and settle international trade and may be prohibited from financing controlled exports, and it supplies maritime and shipping red-flag indicators. Addressed to Licensed Financial Institutions handling trade finance and cross-border payments.
lookup_terms: Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation (EOCN)

data.summary: A concept node within CBUAE's trade-based money laundering guidance distinguishing non-documentary trade finance and open account trade from traditional documentary products (LCs, guarantees, documentary collections). It explains that here the LFI finances or settles trade without payment being tied to presentation of the full set of trade documents, so visibility into the underlying goods and counterparties is materially reduced. It informs the risk-based controls LFIs must calibrate to their role in the transaction and the information actually available to them.

Describes import and export factoring (international factoring) — purchase of an exporter's receivables by an Export Factor, with collection from the importer via an Import Factor — as a growing open-account financing channel. It sets out the specific ML vulnerabilities: factoring companies may apply weaker CDD/KYC and trade controls than banks, market themselves to de-banked clients, and receive far fewer trade documents, limiting understanding of the goods and parties. Relevant to LFIs and non-bank factoring companies assessing trade finance risk.

Defines forfaiting as the discounted, without-recourse purchase of an exporter's receivables by a bank or specialised finance firm, distinguishing it from factoring by the non-recourse feature, typical guarantee from the importer's bank, and conversion of receivables into tradable debt instruments. It notes typical use in capital goods and commodities trading. Relevant to LFIs assessing TBML exposure in non-documentary trade finance products.

Covers structured trade finance — lending across the production-to-sale cycle, including pre-export finance and warehouse (inventory) financing where goods serve as collateral in an approved or third-party managed warehouse. It sits within the guidance's taxonomy of non-documentary trade products and feeds the accompanying glossary of trade finance defined terms (bank guarantee, letter of credit, open account trade, dual-use items). Relevant to LFIs financing multi-stage trade flows.

Explains over- and under-invoicing of goods and services as a core TBML technique for transferring value across borders through collusive misstatement of price between supplier and buyer. It sets the expectation that LFIs identify such manipulation through independent market-value enquiry and external pricing sources (price validation), particularly for commodities. Sits within the guidance's framing of TBML as defined by FATF and binds LFIs supervised by CBUAE.

Addresses over- and under-shipment — misstating quantity, weight or type of goods relative to the invoice — as a TBML technique complementary to mis-invoicing, illustrated with commodity and construction-materials examples drawn from UAE FIU strategic analysis of SARs/STRs. It also links to transshipment manipulation used to evade sanctions and export controls. Relevant to LFIs conducting trade transaction review and red-flag analysis.

A concept node within the CBUAE proliferation-financing guidance covering dual-use and controlled goods — items with both civilian and WMD/military application that are subject to import/export control under Cabinet Resolution No. (50) of 2020 (the UAE Control List). It sets the supervisory expectation that licensed financial institutions screen trade-finance and international trade transactions against the Control List, consult the EOCN on whether commodities are controlled and whether valid permits exist, and use standardised product classification (Harmonized System codes) when recording and monitoring such transactions. It binds LFIs supervised by CBUAE offering trade finance or payment services connected to cross-border trade.

A concept node identifying the United Nations Security Council as the source of the global counter-proliferation framework — UNSCRs that impose targeted financial sanctions, activity-based and sectoral measures, which all Member States are obliged to implement domestically. The guidance notes uneven national implementation and enforcement, and that all UNSC sanctions regimes contain humanitarian exceptions whose jurisdictional requirements differ. Relevant to LFIs as the ultimate legal origin of the TFS obligations applied to them through UAE law and competent-authority directives.

A concept node on the Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation (EOCN), the UAE national body responsible for implementing export controls and issuing counter-proliferation-financing guidance for FIs, DNFBPs and VASPs, alongside MOD, FANR, ICP and SIRA. It publishes the lists of controlled chemical and non-chemical goods and is the authority LFIs are expected to consult on whether commodities are controlled and whether permits are valid. Directed at CBUAE-licensed financial institutions involved in financing or settling international trade.
lookup_terms: Executive Office for Control and Non-Proliferation

data.summary: An instrument node for Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020, cited among the legal bases on which the CBUAE proliferation-financing guidance is built (alongside Federal Decree-Law No. (20) of 2018 and the AML-CFT Decision). The surrounding guidance frames LFI duties to apply competent-authority directives implementing UN Security Council decisions without delay, to file STRs/SARs with the UAE FIU, and to face measures under Articles 13 and 14 of the AML-CFT Law for non-compliance. Binds all CBUAE-licensed and supervised entities, including banks, exchange houses, finance companies, payment and payment-token service providers, registered hawala providers and insurers.
lookup_terms: targeted financial sanctions UAE legal basis

data.summary: A concept node on FATF Recommendation 7, the standard requiring countries to implement targeted financial sanctions related to proliferation financing fully and without delay, with monitoring, inter-agency coordination and measures against sanctions evasion. The guidance situates it alongside Recommendations 1 and 2 (PF risk assessment; national cooperation) and related FATF guidance covering sanctions on North Korea and Iran, including activity-based and sectoral measures falling outside R.7. It is a supervisory benchmark informing CBUAE expectations of LFIs rather than a directly binding rule.

A concept node on UNSCR 1540 (2004), described as the overarching global obligation on proliferation financing: it is activity-focused rather than list-based, imposing no asset-freeze designations. It requires states to refrain from supporting non-state actors seeking to develop, acquire, possess, transport, transfer or use WMD and their delivery means, and to adopt and enforce corresponding domestic laws. It binds states directly; LFIs encounter it indirectly through UAE implementing legislation and CBUAE counter-proliferation expectations.
lookup_terms: weapons of mass destruction delivery means

data.summary: A TBML typology entry within CBUAE guidance on trade-based money laundering, sitting alongside over-/under-invoicing and over-/under-shipment in the typologies section. It describes how the same shipment of goods or services can be invoiced more than once to justify repeated payments and thereby move illicit value under the cover of a single underlying trade transaction. It is directed at licensed financial institutions (including trade finance providers) as risk-understanding material supporting their CDD, transaction monitoring and suspicious-activity detection duties; note this is UAE (CBUAE), not SAMA, guidance.

A TBML typology in CBUAE's trade-based money laundering guidance covering misdescription of the nature, type or quality of goods and services in trade and shipping documents, so that value is transferred while documents appear conforming. The guidance flags this as hard to detect and links it to proliferation financing where controlled items are substituted with non-controlled descriptions, and notes that documentary credit checks confirm document conformity rather than the true goods. Relevant to licensed financial institutions handling letters of credit, document examination and related trade payments; CBUAE, not SAMA, source.

A TBML typology entry distinguishing shell, front and shelf companies and explaining how each is used to conceal beneficial owners, obscure payment flows and defeat risk rating in trade transactions. It includes examples of front companies used to evade export controls and dormant shelf companies that acquire unwarranted longevity-based comfort from institutions. Aimed at licensed financial institutions' beneficial ownership identification, customer risk rating and ongoing monitoring; issued by CBUAE.

A typology and red-flag cluster in CBUAE's TBML guidance addressing the abuse of free trade zones and special economic zones, where separate company formation regimes, limited ownership transparency and reduced customs controls facilitate transshipment, repackaging and re-export schemes. It lists associated red flags such as unjustified FTZ involvement, circuitous routing, circular payment flows and trade patterns inconsistent with a jurisdiction's economy. Directed at licensed financial institutions assessing trade transaction risk; CBUAE-issued, of comparative rather than binding value in KSA.

A TBML typology describing how criminally derived cash is integrated into the financial system through trade, identified via three routes: use of non-bank financial institutions, offsetting or value-transfer arrangements, and infiltration of legitimate supply chains. It explains why cash characteristics (anonymity, fungibility, transportability) make it attractive in a trade context, and connects to adjacent material on sanctions and export-control evasion through re-export and origin disguise. Guidance for licensed financial institutions, including those with cash-intensive trade customers; CBUAE source.

The operative obligations section of CBUAE's TBML guidance, anchoring customer due diligence timing and minimum content (customer and beneficial owner identification and verification, understanding the nature of the business and purpose of the relationship, ongoing monitoring) in the UAE AML-CFT Decision, and applying it to trade. It stresses that the institution must identify which party to a trade transaction is its own customer — due diligence is not owed on every counterparty — and that open account trade warrants heightened attention and business-model enquiry, with EDD for higher-risk customers. Binds licensed financial institutions under UAE law; for KSA work it is persuasive comparison only, as SAMA/AML Law obligations govern.
lookup_terms: who is the customer in a trade transaction

data.summary: A TBML typology section within the CBUAE guidance on trade-based money laundering, describing how illicit actors fabricate or alter trade documents (invoices, shipping and customs papers, certificates of origin) because no uniform document standard exists. It sets the supervisory expectation that licensed financial institutions apply enhanced scrutiny where documents show clear discrepancies or visible alterations, and build familiarity with the document types their trade customers normally use. It binds LFIs handling documentary and open-account trade, including intermediary banks asked for supporting documentation.

A TBML typology in the CBUAE guidance covering accounts opened principally to obscure the audit trail, where funds are received and rapidly moved on so that value linked to trade transactions becomes difficult to trace. It frames the risk that account relationships with little apparent commercial substance are used as layering conduits in trade schemes. Relevant to LFIs conducting CDD, ongoing monitoring and suspicious transaction reporting on trade-linked accounts.

Section of the CBUAE TBML guidance addressing Registered Hawala Providers and other alternative remittance systems, which are vulnerable where they execute larger transfers for businesses conducting commercial or trade-related activity. It expects RHPs to establish the purpose and nature of transactions, to apply CDD/KYC to the underlying business where a customer acts on its behalf, and notes that such businesses must be UAE-registered and based to transact through the RHP. Binds RHPs and, by extension, LFIs servicing them.
lookup_terms: customer acting on behalf of a business

data.summary: Concept node on services-based money laundering within the CBUAE TBML guidance: the misuse of intangible services (for example consulting or advisory billing) rather than physical goods to move value, often between entities sharing a beneficial owner. Because no shipment exists to verify, pricing and volume misrepresentation is harder to detect, raising the importance of understanding customer profile and economic rationale. Directed at LFIs assessing trade and service-related payment flows.

Risk-assessment section of the CBUAE TBML guidance identifying economic sectors and products most exposed to trade-based laundering, including gold, precious metals and minerals, and construction materials, and explaining the shared traits of wide pricing margins, long supply chains and goods that are hard for customs to inspect. It supports risk rating of trade customers and products by LFIs. Informative for LFIs' business risk assessment and customer risk profiling rather than imposing a discrete obligation.

Section of the CBUAE guidance defining transshipment (goods routed through intermediate destinations before the final destination) and explaining how it is abused to disguise country of origin or end-user and to evade sanctions and export controls. It sets out recurring schemes such as re-export from non-sanctioned hubs, use of jurisdictions with weaker export restrictions, forged customs declarations, and third-jurisdiction front companies. Relevant to LFIs screening trade transactions for sanctions and export-control evasion risk.

A concept node within the CBUAE trade-based money laundering guidance covering targeted financial sanctions duties as they arise in trade finance. It explains that licensed financial institutions must promptly give effect to UAE competent-authority directives implementing UN Security Council Chapter VII decisions, with Cabinet Decision 74 of 2020 supplying the domestic framework, including the UAE Local Terrorist List and the UN Consolidated List, and requiring appropriate risk management arrangements. It binds LFIs supervised by the CBUAE and sits alongside the CDD, EDD and ongoing monitoring expectations set out in the same guidance.

A concept node referencing the UAE Financial Intelligence Unit as the recipient of suspicious activity reporting arising from trade-based financial crime detection. The surrounding guidance frames LFIs as uniquely placed to spot trade-based money laundering and illicit transshipment across fragmented trade transactions and to report them so law enforcement can connect the dots. Relevant to LFIs determining when and how trade-related suspicions must be escalated to the FIU.

A concept node citing the Wolfsberg Group, International Chamber of Commerce and BAFT trade finance principles as an external reference point in the CBUAE TBML guidance. It is used to establish that open account trade accounts for roughly 80 percent of international trade, framing the guidance's distinction between documentary and non-documentary trade finance and the differing controls expected by product type and LFI role. Persuasive industry standard material rather than a binding instrument, but informs supervisory expectations on LFIs.

A typology node in the CBUAE TBML guidance describing networks of surrogates or personal shoppers who buy goods on behalf of others to circumvent customs, export control or tariff restrictions, and who can be paid with criminal proceeds. The guidance highlights the decentralised and often anonymous character of these purchases, which obscures fund flows and true beneficiaries, and pairs it with an illustrative drug-proceeds/point-of-sale aggregation example. Relevant to LFIs calibrating customer risk ratings, transaction monitoring and suspicion assessment for card and merchant activity linked to trade.

A concept node covering the role of third-party intermediaries in trade transactions as a TBML and sanctions-evasion risk factor, set against the guidance's defined trade finance terms (buyer, bank guarantee, letter of credit, forfaiting, factoring, open account trade, dual-use items). The material illustrates how intermediaries and layered networks of import/export companies obscure true counterparties, origin of goods and beneficial ownership. Relevant to LFIs applying CDD, beneficial ownership identification and red-flag analysis to trade chains involving brokers, agents and re-exporters.

A typology node explaining back-to-back letters of credit: two linked LCs, one issued by the buyer's institution in favour of an intermediary and one by the intermediary's institution in favour of the supplier. The guidance recognises legitimate commercial uses (broker confidentiality on mark-up) but flags the structure's use to complicate financing arrangements, obscure the flow of funds and conceal sanctioned parties from detection. Directs LFIs handling such structures to heightened scrutiny of counterparties and underlying documentation.

A referenced UAE instrument (Cabinet Decision/Resolution No. 74 of 2020) that establishes the national framework for Targeted Financial Sanctions, covering the UN Consolidated List and the UAE Local Terrorist List and the prompt implementation of UNSC Chapter VII designations. In the surrounding CBUAE guidance it is cited as the source of licensed financial institutions' freezing and screening duties, including the Article 21 expectation that firms maintain suitable risk management arrangements. It binds CBUAE-supervised entities (banks and foreign bank branches, exchange houses, finance companies, payment service providers, registered hawala providers, and insurance/reinsurance firms, agents and brokers) alongside their AML/CFT statutory obligations.

Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025, the Executive Regulations implementing Federal Decree by Law No. 10 of 2025 on AML, CFT and proliferation financing; it replaces the 2019 executive regulations regime. It sets out definitions, the scope of Financial Institutions, DNFBPs, VASPs and NPOs, customer due diligence and suspicious transaction reporting duties, beneficial ownership and registrar obligations for companies, nominee arrangements, and supervisory authority powers. It binds regulated entities, companies and registrars, and supervisory authorities operating under the Decree by Law.

Federal Decree by Law No. 10 of 2025 is the primary UAE statute on anti-money laundering and combating the financing of terrorism and proliferation financing, and the parent law of Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025. Its definitions carry directly into the Executive Regulations, which elaborate the categories of Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and VASPs and their obligations. It binds all persons falling within those defined categories, together with supervisory authorities and the Financial Intelligence Unit.

A defined-scope concept: under Article 2 of the Executive Regulations, Financial Institutions are persons carrying out listed financial activities commercially for or on behalf of a Customer, including deposit-taking, lending and trade finance, financial leasing (excluding consumer-product leasing), money or value transfer services, issuance and management of means of payment including e-money, and guarantees and financial commitments. This classification determines who is subject to CDD, reporting, record-keeping and related AML/CFT duties, and is the trigger for risk-based supervision and inspection by the Supervisory Authority. Relevant for assessing whether financing, BNPL-type lending or payment-service activity falls inside the AML perimeter.

A defined category under the Executive Regulations covering Designated Non-Financial Businesses and Professions, which are subject to the same core AML/CFT obligations as Financial Institutions and VASPs. The Regulations require DNFBPs to apply customer due diligence to customers and pre-existing business relationships, prohibit establishing or continuing a relationship or executing a transaction where CDD cannot be applied, allow tipping-off-sensitive abstention with a suspicious transaction report, and bar dealings with shell banks. It binds non-financial designated sectors under the supervision of their respective Supervisory Authority.

A defined category under the Executive Regulations for Virtual Asset Service Providers, requiring any person conducting VASP activities, offering related products or services, or executing transactions from within the State to be licensed, registered or listed by the competent Supervisory Authority. VASPs must comply with specified AML/CFT obligations proportionate to their activities, and the Supervisory Authority is tasked with detecting and sanctioning unlicensed operators using public and non-public sources. Relevant for perimeter questions on virtual asset activity and for the overlap between VASP duties and those of Financial Institutions.

Node covering the enterprise-wide ML/TF risk assessment and risk-based approach expectations in the CBUAE trade-based money laundering (TBML) guidance, anchored to Article 4 of the UAE AML-CFT Decision. It requires licensed financial institutions to identify, document and periodically update their risk exposure across customer, intermediary, geographic, product/service, delivery-channel and operational categories, with explicit treatment of trade and trade finance risk (including an optional standalone trade finance risk assessment). Binds LFIs supervised by the CBUAE; note this is UAE, not SAMA, source material and does not apply to KSA-licensed entities.

Node setting out general customer due diligence expectations for trade-related business under Article 5 of the UAE AML-CFT Decision: identification and verification of the customer and beneficial owner, understanding the nature and purpose of the relationship, and ongoing monitoring, performed before or during onboarding or before an occasional transaction. It addresses the trade-specific question of which party to a trade transaction is the LFI's "customer" (due diligence is not owed on all trade parties), heightened attention to open account trade, record-keeping of onboarding and refreshed CDD, and pre-onboarding plus ongoing screening of customers, beneficial owners, authorised persons, directors/managers, executives of legal arrangements and known principal counterparties. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.
lookup_terms: who is the customer in a trade transaction
watchlist and sanctions screening at onboarding

data.summary: Node on enhanced due diligence for heightened trade-related risks within the CBUAE TBML guidance, situated against the FATF definition of TBML and the mechanics of documentary versus non-documentary trade finance. It frames when LFIs should go beyond general CDD, including where documentary evidence (invoices, packing lists, bills of lading, underlying contracts, other transport documents) is thin or where open account settlement dominates. Directed at CBUAE-licensed financial institutions handling trade finance.

Node describing expected sanctions screening practice for trade transactions: screening the data points carried in trade-specific financial messaging (originator, beneficiary, ultimate parties, country codes, intermediary banks, free-text high-risk terms) and screening names of individuals, entities and vessels irrespective of their role, plus the trade documents made available to the institution. It links sanctions/TFS obligations to the TBML and illicit transshipment typologies elsewhere in the guidance. Applies to CBUAE-licensed financial institutions; treat as supervisory expectation rather than KSA obligation.

Node combining AML/CFT governance, independent audit, training and record-keeping expectations across two CBUAE instruments. It sets the three-lines-of-defence model with senior management and board oversight, MLRO/compliance authority and independence, periodic and risk-calibrated TBML training with attendance records and knowledge testing, and record retention under Article 16 of the AML-CFT Law and Article 24 of the AML-CFT Decision covering risk assessments, transactions, CDD material, account files and SAR/STR analysis. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Node collecting TBML and illicit transshipment typologies and red flags in the CBUAE guidance, including transshipment through non-sanctioned intermediary countries, re-labelling of country of origin, diversion to prohibited end-users, exploitation of corruption-prone jurisdictions and use of third-jurisdiction front companies. It supports detection and suspicious activity reporting by licensed financial institutions, noting that no single typology is determinative and indicators should be used in combination. Introductory framing covers UAE free zone and trade-hub exposure to trade-based financial crime.

Node covering the customer due diligence and beneficial owner identification provisions (Division Three, Articles 6–15) of the UAE Cabinet Resolution issuing the Executive Regulations to the AML/CTF/PF Decree-Law. It sets when identity of the Customer and Beneficial Owner must be verified (before or during onboarding, with a limited low-risk deferral), the triggers for applying CDD (new business relationship, suspicion of a Crime, doubts about previously obtained data, occasional transactions), application of CDD to pre-existing relationships on a risk/materiality basis, the prohibition on establishing or continuing a relationship where CDD cannot be completed, the tipping-off carve-out with an STR to the Unit, and the bar on dealing with Shell Banks. It binds Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and Virtual Asset Service Providers.

Node grouping the additional/enhanced due diligence provisions (Articles 11–15) of the UAE AML/CTF Executive Regulations, including the exemption from identifying shareholders or beneficial owners of listed companies subject to adequate transparency-disclosure requirements and their controlled subsidiaries. It also sets due diligence and ongoing monitoring duties for beneficiaries of life and investment-linked insurance policies (naming, category/description, verification at payout, beneficiary as a risk factor), risk-based review of existing customers, and the prohibition on proceeding where due diligence cannot be applied. Binds Financial Institutions primarily for the insurance rules, and Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and VASPs for the general obligations.

Node covering the suspicious transaction reporting regime (Division Five, Articles 17–18) of the UAE AML/CTF Executive Regulations, plus the Financial Intelligence Unit's competences in handling such reports. It requires reporting entities to develop and continually update suspicion indicators and to report immediately to the Unit, without invoking banking or professional secrecy or contractual liability, any transaction, attempted transaction or funds suspected of being linked to a Crime, regardless of value, and to respond promptly to Unit requests. It binds Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and Virtual Asset Service Providers, with a narrow exemption for lawyers, notaries, other independent legal professionals and statutory auditors acting in defined legal-advisory or litigation contexts.

Node covering the politically exposed persons regime (Division Four, Article 16) of the UAE AML/CTF Executive Regulations together with the PEP definition. It requires risk management systems to detect PEP status, senior management approval to establish or continue the relationship, reasonable measures to establish source of funds and wealth, and enhanced ongoing monitoring for foreign PEPs, with a risk-triggered application of the same measures to domestic PEPs and persons holding prominent functions in international organisations; separate duties apply to life insurance beneficiaries before payout. Binds Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and Virtual Asset Service Providers; the definition extends to immediate family members and known close associates.

Node covering the wire transfer (travel rule) provisions (Division Three, Articles 28–29) of the UAE AML/CTF Executive Regulations. It sets the AED 3,500 threshold for verifying originator information on cross-border transfers, the originator and beneficiary data that must accompany transfers (including batch files and domestic transfers), a three working day response deadline for providing underlying data, the prohibition on executing non-compliant transfers, record retention, and the application of freezing and transaction-prohibition measures under Targeted Financial Sanctions; Article 29 sets intermediary institution duties where information is missing or lost in conversion. Binds originating, intermediary and beneficiary Financial Institutions.

Node anchoring the Shell Bank definition (a bank licensed in a jurisdiction where it has no physical presence and is not part of a regulated Financial Group) and its operative use in the correspondent banking rules (Article 26) of the UAE AML/CTF Executive Regulations, alongside record-keeping duties and the High-Risk Customers definition. Financial Institutions must not enter into or continue a correspondent banking or similar relationship with a Shell Bank or with any institution permitting its accounts to be used by Shell Banks, and must gather sufficient information on respondent institutions beforehand. Binds Financial Institutions; related record-retention and information-availability duties extend to DNFBPs and VASPs.

This node is the CBUAE/UAE Sustainable Finance Working Group's Principles for Climate Transition Planning, a bilingual guidance instrument setting out eight principles (objectives, governance, integration into strategy and risk management, metrics and targets, data and customer engagement, reporting and transparency, implementation, and review) for developing climate transition plans. It is expressed as expectations for 'financial firms' — UAE financial sector entities generally, whether new to transition planning or already producing plans — without distinguishing business models or licence categories. It is guidance rather than a binding rulebook, and is to be read alongside the SFWG Risk Management Principles and Disclosure Principles.

Refers to the SFWG's Principles for the Effective Management of Climate-related Financial Risks, issued November 2023, which address board and senior-management oversight and allocation of responsibility for climate-related financial risks, their integration into strategy-setting, risk management frameworks, capital and liquidity planning, and scenario analysis. It is the risk-management companion instrument that the Climate Transition Planning Principles must be read with. It applies to UAE financial firms as supervisory guidance on climate risk.

Refers to the SFWG's Principles for Sustainability-related Disclosures for Reporting Entities, issued June 2024, intended to prepare relevant UAE financial firms to produce high-quality, relevant sustainability disclosures. It sits alongside the Risk Management Principles and the Climate Transition Planning Principles as the reporting limb of the UAE sustainable finance framework, and is cross-referenced for the reporting and transparency expectations. Directed at UAE reporting entities in the financial sector.

Principle 1 of the Climate Transition Planning Principles deals with the objectives of a financial firm's climate transition planning — why the firm plans, what outcomes it targets, and alignment with UAE climate transition objectives. It frames the purpose-setting stage that the later principles on governance, strategy integration, metrics and reporting build on. Addressed to UAE financial firms as guidance-level expectations.

Principle 2 covers governance of climate transition planning, including board- and management-level oversight, allocation of responsibility, and embedding transition objectives into firm culture and practices; it contemplates that firms may align remuneration and incentives with climate transition objectives and run change management and internal communication programmes. These are discretionary or 'should' expectations rather than hard obligations. Applies to UAE financial firms.

Principle 3 requires climate transition planning to form part of, and be aligned with, the financial firm's activities on climate-related risks and opportunities and its business strategy: embedding it in short-, medium- and long-term business strategies and board-approved strategic plans, considering transition impacts on the business model, customer base, stakeholders, operations, policies and financial planning, and embedding transition considerations in the risk management framework including risk appetite and scenario analysis. Expressed as 'should' guidance for UAE financial firms, with overlap into prudential risk governance.

A defined-term node from the UAE Cabinet Resolution issuing the Executive Regulations of the AML/CTF/CPF Decree-Law, sitting among the definitions of Financial Institutions, DNFBPs, Senior Management, and the originating/intermediary/beneficiary institutions in a funds-transfer chain. It matters mainly for group-wide AML/CFT obligations: supervisory authorities calibrate inspection frequency and risk assessment by reference to the characteristics and internal controls of Financial Groups, apply consolidated group-level supervision, and require additional measures (up to closure of operations) where a host country prevents proper implementation at foreign branches and majority-owned subsidiaries. It binds licensed Financial Institutions and their group structures, and the Supervisory Authority exercising oversight.

Defines and sets the duties of the Registrar under the AML/CTF/CPF Executive Regulations regarding corporate transparency: obtaining, verifying, publishing and keeping up to date basic company information, nominee director/shareholder information, and beneficial owner information, and coordinating with the Supervisory Authority and National Committee on legal-person risk assessment. It also frames the corresponding company obligations (shareholder registers held in-State, 15-working-day updating of beneficial owner data, cooperation with FIs, DNFBPs and VASPs, and the prohibition on bearer shares). Binds the Registrar, registered companies, and indirectly the institutions that rely on such information for CDD.

Covers the treatment of Legal Arrangements (trusts and equivalent structures) under the AML/CTF/CPF Executive Regulations: trustees and persons in equivalent positions must obtain, retain, verify and update adequate, accurate and up-to-date beneficial owner and basic information, keep records on supervised intermediaries and service providers, and retain data for at least five years after their involvement ends. Trustees must disclose their status to Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and VASPs when opening a business relationship or conducting an occasional transaction above threshold, and cooperate with Concerned Authorities, Law Enforcement and the FIU on request. The rules reach both domestic and foreign legal arrangements connected to or doing business in the State.

Concerns the National Risk Assessment as the anchor of the risk-based approach in the AML/CTF/CPF Executive Regulations: Financial Institutions, DNFBPs and VASPs must identify, assess, document and mitigate their crime risks proportionate to nature and size, considering customer, geographic, product/service/transaction and delivery-channel factors, and taking account of NRA and sectoral assessment results. It also sets the National Committee's duties to update the NRA and national strategy at least every three years, disseminate it, and coordinate on legal-person and legal-arrangement risk. Binds supervised entities, the National Committee, the Registrar and Supervisory Authorities.
lookup_terms: risk factors customer geographic product channel

data.summary: Sets out the FIU's provisional powers under the AML/CTF/CPF Executive Regulations: the Chief of the Unit may, without prior notice, suspend or halt a suspected transaction for up to ten working days and freeze suspected funds held by Financial Institutions, DNFBPs or VASPs for thirty days, based on analysis of STRs and other domestic or foreign information. Institutions must implement freezing orders without notice; the Attorney General is notified and may amend, revoke, direct, or extend the freeze. Relevant to reporting entities' obligations on receipt of such orders and to tipping-off constraints.

Chapter of the AML/CTF/CPF Executive Regulations governing international cooperation and asset recovery: Concerned Authorities must provide the widest possible cooperation promptly and constructively, exchange information spontaneously and on request, prioritise incoming requests, conclude bilateral arrangements, join multilateral asset-recovery networks, and enable informal pre-request assistance. Application is subject to domestic legislation, treaties to which the State is a party, or reciprocity. Binds state Concerned Authorities rather than supervised entities directly, though it drives information demands on them.

A principle within the CBUAE Sustainable Finance Working Group's Principles for Climate Transition Planning (UAE, not KSA), dealing with metrics and targets. It expects financial firms to select quantitative and qualitative metrics and targets built on robust, science-aligned methodologies across defined time horizons, to disclose limitations and any data proxies used, and to monitor and review them regularly. Addressed to UAE financial sector entities collectively termed 'financial firms'; drafted as non-binding guiding principles rather than enforceable rules, and to be read with the SFWG Risk Management and Disclosure Principles.

Principle 5 of the CBUAE/SFWG Principles for Climate Transition Planning (UAE), covering data strategies and customer engagement. It expects financial firms to collect customer data regularly, set criteria for identifying and prioritising customers for engagement, tailor engagement goals and methods, and feed engagement outcomes back into transition objectives, product offerings and escalation arrangements. Applies to UAE 'financial firms' as guidance; note the 'customer' concept here is commercial/climate-related and distinct from AML/CTF customer due diligence obligations.

Principle 6 of the CBUAE/SFWG Principles for Climate Transition Planning (UAE), addressing reporting and transparency on climate transition plans. The retrieved context mainly carries the instrument's introduction and application section, which explains that the Principles complement the SFWG's earlier Risk Management Principles and the June 2024 Principles for Sustainability-related Disclosures, and support the UAE's Third Nationally Determined Contributions. Scope covers all UAE financial sector entities ('financial firms') regardless of business model, as guidance rather than binding rules.

Principle 7 of the CBUAE/SFWG Principles for Climate Transition Planning (UAE), on implementation strategy and actions to operationalise a climate transition plan. The retrieved context provides only the table of contents and the introduction/application sections rather than the principle text itself. Directed at UAE financial sector entities collectively defined as 'financial firms', on a guidance basis, to be read alongside the SFWG Risk Management and Disclosure Principles.

Principle 8 of the CBUAE/SFWG Principles for Climate Transition Planning (UAE), requiring regular review and, where needed, update of transition objectives, targets, assumptions, strategies and implementation actions in light of scenario analysis, customer feedback and local/international standards. Updates should go to the financial firm's board for approval and be embedded in governance, policies and frameworks, with material outcomes communicated to internal and external stakeholders. Applies to UAE 'financial firms' as guiding principles; relevant to board oversight duties.

CBUAE AML/CFT guidance for Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs) on customers that are legal persons and legal arrangements (UAE regime, not SAMA). It explains the risk that corporate and trust structures conceal controlling or benefiting natural persons, and sets out CDD information to be collected and verified under Article 8(b) of the AML-CFT Decision — name, legal form, memorandum and articles of association, head office/principal place of business, local legal representative for foreign entities, and senior management — plus verification and CDD on the natural person authorised to act for the customer under Article 8(a). Binds LFIs and must be integrated into the wider AML/CFT compliance programme with supporting governance and training; risk-based differentiation between entity types is expected.

A UAE federal instrument (Cabinet Resolution No. 56 of 2024) governing telemarketing activity generally, cited as a companion text that the CBUAE Telemarketing Regulation must be read alongside, together with its penalties resolution (No. 57 of 2024), the Consumer Protection Regulation and the Ombudsman Unit Regulation. It sets the baseline national telemarketing rules on which the Central Bank's minimum standards for Licensed Financial Institutions are layered. It binds persons conducting telemarketing in the State; for financial-sector firms it operates cumulatively with CBUAE requirements rather than in substitution.

Defines the Do Not Call Registry (DNCR) as the opt-out mechanism by which a Customer suspends receipt of telemarketing on a registered phone number.
