Licensed Financial Institutions are prohibited from telemarketing to any Customer who has opted out or rejected contact in any form, or whose number appears on the DNCR, and must publish an accessible guide on their official platforms explaining complaint and DNCR registration procedures. It also feeds disclosure duties during calls, where the Customer's DNCR right must be clearly stated.

Covers the substantive conduct rules for Telemarketing by Licensed Financial Institutions: prohibition on contacting opted-out or DNCR-listed Customers, mandatory telemarketing logs and records across all communication channels in the form and timeframe set by the Central Bank, a ban on untrue or fraudulent statements with full disclosure of Product/Service features, risks, charges and terms, immediate termination on Customer request, and restrictions on calling time (9:00 AM to 6:00 PM State time) and frequency. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions including where telemarketing is performed by Telemarketers on their behalf.

Sets the consent gateway for telemarketing: a Licensed Financial Institution must obtain the Customer's prior express consent before conducting Telemarketing, with the consent specifying preferred language, chosen channels, contact methods (including natural agents, AI-based agents or robocalls) and the Product/Service types covered. Terms and conditions for consent must be clear, unambiguous and in the Customer's preferred language, and robust age verification must be applied at the point of consent. Permitted consent methods include online sign-up with explicit written consent, signed physical forms, and Customer-initiated requests.

Circular No. 5/2026, the CBUAE Remuneration Regulation for Banks and Insurance Companies, establishing minimum requirements for responsible, risk-sensitive remuneration frameworks so that pay is commensurate with performance and risk outcomes. It applies to all Banks and Insurance Companies (including Reinsurance Companies), collectively termed Financial Institutions, and is read with the Central Bank Law and the Risk Management, Corporate Governance (banks and insurers) and Consumer Protection Regulations. It does not prescribe remuneration amounts for any Person, including Relevant Persons, but requires continuous demonstrable compliance to the Central Bank.

Covers the required remuneration framework and policy: Financial Institutions must develop, implement, monitor and regularly review a Board-approved remuneration policy that links pay to institutional performance, strategic objectives and risk-adjusted outcomes, and that does not incentivise inappropriate or excessive risk-taking, addressing the balance of fixed and variable components by role or Staff category. The Board must give final approval of total variable remuneration amounts and distribution on the remuneration committee's recommendation, ensure Control Functions Staff participate in designing and monitoring the policy, manage Conflicts of Interest (including for the ISSC on Shariah resolutions), and commission an annual independent remuneration review submitted to the Central Bank.

This node is the UAE federal AML/CFT primary statute (Decree Federal Law 20/2018 on Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organisations), cited as the legal basis for CBUAE guidance on legal persons and legal arrangements. It sits above the implementing Cabinet Decision 10/2019 (AML-CFT Decision) and Cabinet Decision 58/2020, and supplies the defined terms (beneficial owner, legal person, legal arrangement, settlor, trust) used in CDD obligations. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs) supervised by the CBUAE, whose CDD, beneficial ownership identification and risk-based controls must be embedded in their wider AML/CFT compliance programme with governance and training support.

This node covers Cabinet Decision 58/2020 on Beneficial Owner Procedures, which requires UAE-registered legal persons to identify, record in a Register, and report their beneficial owners (and nominee directors) to the relevant registrar, with limited exemptions for listed companies and their subsidiaries, and a fallback to a controlling individual where no 25% owner exists. In the CBUAE guidance context it frames what LFIs should expect from corporate customers: beneficial owners must be natural persons, ownership chains must be traced to individuals holding at least 25%, and customer statements alone cannot satisfy verification. It binds UAE legal persons directly and, indirectly, LFIs assessing customer credibility — a customer unaware of these obligations should be treated as at least high risk.

This node is the defined term "legal person" — any non-natural entity that can establish a customer relationship or own property (companies, bodies corporate, foundations, partnerships, associations) — and the CBUAE guidance on the ML/TF/PF risks such customers present through opaque ownership structures. It sets out the risk factors LFIs must weigh (legal form, formation controls, beneficial ownership reporting, recordkeeping, supervision) and the mandatory customer identification data set, plus identification of controlling owners and of the natural person authorised to act for the entity. It binds LFIs applying a risk-based approach and CDD to corporate customers.

This node is the defined term "legal arrangement" — a contractual relationship between two or more parties that creates no separate legal personality, such as a trust — together with the CBUAE guidance on its ML/TF/PF risk profile, where ownership, control and enjoyment of funds may be split between different persons. For such customers LFIs must identify and verify the settlor, trustee (or equivalent), beneficiaries or class of beneficiaries, and any other controlling individuals, and must apply the same risk-based assessment factors used for legal persons. It binds LFIs onboarding or servicing trusts and similar arrangements, including those formed in the Mainland, DIFC and ADGM.

This node is the CBUAE Telemarketing Regulation (Circular 3/2026), a consumer-protection instrument governing how Licensed Financial Institutions and their telemarketers may market financial products and services by phone and other communication channels. It imposes opt-out and Do Not Call Registry restrictions, a published telemarketing guide covering complaints and DNCR registration, mandatory telemarketing logs and record retention, disclosure standards prohibiting untrue or fraudulent statements, immediate termination on customer request, and limits on calling hours (9:00–18:00 State time) and contact frequency. It binds all Licensed Financial Institutions, including for conduct carried out through third-party telemarketers.

This node is the Central Bank Law — Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 on the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business — the enabling statute under which CBUAE regulations (including the Telemarketing Regulation) are issued. It underpins licensing of Banks and other Licensed Financial Institutions and supplies foundational defined terms used across CBUAE instruments (Affiliate, Bank, Board, Chief Executive Officer, Central Bank). It binds all entities carrying on Licensed Financial Activities and insurance business in the State, and establishes the Central Bank's rule-making and supervisory authority.

A provision in Chapter Eight (International Cooperation and Asset Recovery) of the UAE Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 issuing the Executive Regulations of Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 on AML/CFT and proliferation financing, addressing cooperation with foreign counterparts in relation to virtual-asset-related predicate and money laundering offences. It sits alongside the general cooperation duties (widest possible assistance, prioritisation, confidentiality, purpose limitation) that bind the Concerned Authorities rather than private sector entities. Note that the supplied context reproduces the surrounding general provisions rather than the full article text, so the operative wording should be read in the source.

Part of Chapter Eight of the UAE AML/CFT Executive Regulations (Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025) dealing with exchange of crime-related information involving law enforcement and other Concerned Authorities with foreign counterpart and non-counterpart authorities. It complements the supervisory-information-exchange duties (Article 63) and the general conditions on purpose limitation, consent and confidentiality. Obligations fall on state authorities, not on financial institutions, DNFBPs or VASPs.

Article 66 opens Part Three (International Judicial Cooperation) of Chapter Eight of the UAE AML/CFT Executive Regulations, requiring competent judicial authorities to provide prompt and effective mutual legal assistance to foreign judicial authorities under treaty or reciprocity in investigations, prosecutions and proceedings concerning the Crime. It authorises identification, tracing, valuation, seizure, freezing and confiscation of criminal funds or equivalent-value property (including where the accused is unknown or not criminally responsible), other investigative measures such as obtaining records from financial institutions, DNFBPs, VASPs and NPOs, searches, evidence gathering, covert techniques and controlled delivery, and surrender/recovery of persons and property. It binds judicial authorities but has direct consequences for reporting entities whose records may be compelled.
lookup_terms: records of financial institutions DNFBPs VASPs

data.summary: Within Part Three of Chapter Eight of the UAE AML/CFT Executive Regulations, this article permits execution in the State of foreign judgments or judicial orders imposing seizure, freezing, other provisional measures, or confiscation in any form over criminal property or funds of equivalent value. It signals a relaxed procedural route for recognising such foreign orders. Directed at competent judicial authorities, with downstream effects on holders of the targeted assets.

A Chapter Eight provision of the UAE AML/CFT Executive Regulations concerning the conditions and limits applicable to executing international cooperation requests, read together with Article 60 (no refusal on grounds of fiscal or customs matters, institutional secrecy, or differences in authority status; notification of reasons for refusal or deferral; dual criminality only for coercive measures). It governs when assistance may be granted, deferred or conditioned. It binds the Concerned Authorities; the supplied context does not reproduce the article's own wording, so verify the operative text.
lookup_terms: bank secrecy not a ground for refusal

data.summary: Final-provisions article of UAE Cabinet Resolution No. 134 of 2025 (Executive Regulations of Federal Decree-Law No. 10 of 2025 on AML/CFT and proliferation financing) repealing Cabinet Resolution No. 10 of 2019 and any conflicting provisions. Read with Article 71, which sets entry into force thirty days after publication in the Official Gazette. Relevant to anyone mapping legacy AML obligations and cross-references to the 2019 regulations.

Concept node covering the board-approved remuneration policy requirement under the CBUAE Remuneration Regulation for Banks and Insurance Companies. It requires the policy to link pay to institutional performance, strategic objectives and risk-adjusted outcomes, to avoid incentivising excessive or inappropriate risk-taking, to set the fixed/variable balance by role or staff category, to involve Control Function staff in design and monitoring, to address conflicts of interest (including for the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee), and to be subject to an annual independent review submitted to the Central Bank. It binds Banks and Insurance/Reinsurance Companies ("Financial Institutions"), with duties falling principally on the Board and its remuneration committee.

Concept node on variable (performance-based) remuneration under the CBUAE Remuneration Regulation, including deferral, performance adjustment, malus and clawback-style contractual provisions. It sets minimum deferral thresholds for Material Risk Takers (at least 40% deferred over at least three years) and Senior Material Risk Takers (at least 60% over at least five years), requires the variable proportion to rise with seniority and responsibility, and requires contract terms allowing reduction or reversal before vesting for poor performance, realised risk, misconduct or breaches of law, regulation or policy. It binds Banks and Insurance/Reinsurance Companies in respect of designated risk-taking staff.

Cross-reference node for CBUAE Circular No. 83/2019 (Corporate Governance Regulation for Banks and accompanying Standards), cited in the Remuneration Regulation as one of the instruments it must be read alongside. It matters here because the remuneration requirements are stated to be additional to compensation requirements in the Central Bank's corporate governance framework, while the Remuneration Regulation takes precedence in the event of conflict. Relevant to banks; parallel governance instruments exist for insurance companies (Circular 24/2022).

CBUAE Circular No. 5/2026 (13/03/2026), the Remuneration Regulation for Banks and Insurance Companies, setting minimum requirements for responsible, risk-sensitive remuneration frameworks so that pay is commensurate with performance and risk outcomes. It applies to all Banks and Insurance Companies (including Reinsurance Companies), does not prescribe pay amounts, and is read with the Central Bank Law and related regulations on risk management, corporate governance, consumer protection, fitness and propriety, and Shari'ah governance; it takes precedence where it conflicts with other regulations. Compliance must be demonstrable to the Central Bank on a continuous basis.
lookup_terms: Remuneration Regulation for Banks and Insurance Companies

data.summary: A second version/record of the same CBUAE Circular No. 5/2026 Remuneration Regulation for Banks and Insurance Companies, with identical introduction, objective and scope provisions. It sets minimum requirements for remuneration frameworks that incentivise prudent risk management and impose consequences for poor risk outcomes, binding all Banks and Insurance/Reinsurance Companies. Open only if version comparison with the 7031 record is needed.

Cabinet Decision No. 109 of 2023 on the Regulation of Beneficial Owner Procedures, governing how legal persons register, identify and update Beneficial Owner information. It sets out registration and licensing data to be filed with the Registrar, the criteria for identifying a Beneficial Owner, exemptions for listed companies subject to disclosure requirements and their majority-owned subsidiaries, and a notification/enquiry process with 15-day response windows before details are entered in the Beneficial Owners' Register. It binds legal persons and their registrars, and underpins AML/CTF beneficial ownership transparency and KYB/CDD verification by financial institutions.

CBUAE regulation setting the licensing and governance framework for Takaful insurance in the UAE, including definitions of the Takaful Insurance Fund, Participation Membership Policy and Takaful Insurance Policy. It permits an optional (and potentially Central Bank-mandated) Takaful Insurance Fund Board of Trustees to protect fund interests, and conditions conventional insurers' conduct of Takaful business through a Takaful Insurance Window on prior Central Bank approval, a Shari'ah governance framework and an Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee. It binds insurance companies and Takaful companies licensed by the Central Bank, operating alongside standards issued by the Higher Shari'ah Authority.

Article 4 of the CBUAE remuneration regulation, allocating ultimate responsibility to the board for approving and overseeing the financial institution's remuneration framework, including the remuneration policy and a standalone ISSC remuneration policy. It requires board approval of total variable remuneration on the remuneration committee's recommendation, involvement of Control Functions, conflict-of-interest safeguards, an annual independent remuneration review submitted to the Central Bank, and establishment of a remuneration committee. It binds boards of CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Article 5 of the CBUAE remuneration regulation, specifying the mandate, composition, expertise and documented terms of reference of the board's remuneration committee, including adequate independent non-executive representation. It sets the committee's duties: reviewing senior management remuneration levels and structures, aligning pay with long-term interests and risk appetite, setting performance and remuneration standards for Relevant Persons, periodic policy review, engagement with risk, compliance and audit committees, and access to Control Function information. It binds the boards and remuneration committees of CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Node covering Article 6 of the CBUAE remuneration regulation on the board risk committee's role in the remuneration framework, together with the Material Risk Taker identification provisions in Article 3. It requires annual review of the Material Risk Taker list by Control Functions and board approval on the remuneration committee's recommendation, formal notification of designated persons, and sets criteria for who must be designated (e.g. authority over material credit, underwriting, reinsurance or trading book exposures, or acceptance of large/non-standard risks). It binds boards, risk and remuneration committees of CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Article 8 of the CBUAE remuneration regulation, governing pay for staff in Control Functions (e.g. risk, compliance, audit). It requires direct board or board-committee oversight of their performance reviews and remuneration, a significant fixed proportion of total pay, performance assessment based on effectiveness and independence rather than financial or revenue contribution, and mitigation of conflicts of interest so variable pay does not compromise objectivity. It binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions and their boards.
lookup_terms: independence of compliance and risk staff
board oversight of control function pay

data.summary: Node covering the CBUAE remuneration regulation's variable remuneration rules (Article 11) and the related remuneration policy content requirements, including identification of awards subject to reduction or forfeiture. It requires alignment of performance incentives with long-term value creation and the risk time horizon, at least 50% of Material Risk Takers' variable remuneration in shares or equivalent non-cash instruments with gradual vesting of the deferred cash portion, and substantial reduction of variable pay on negative financial performance through Malus or Clawback. It also preserves ISSC independence in the ISSC remuneration review. It binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Node labelled as corporate governance but the underlying material is a CBUAE circular issuing a Remuneration Regulation for banks and insurance companies (collectively "Financial Institutions"), setting minimum requirements for remuneration frameworks aligned to performance and risk outcomes. It sits alongside and expressly supplements the existing corporate governance, risk management, fitness and propriety, consumer protection and Shari'ah governance instruments, and prevails over them in case of conflict. It binds all licensed banks and insurance companies and is the standard CBUAE applies when assessing their remuneration policies, procedures and practices.

Node keyed to the UAE AML/CFT Decree-Law; the material provided is Cabinet Decision No. 109 of 2023 on Regulating the Beneficial Owner Procedures, issued under that Decree-Law and replacing the earlier Cabinet Decision 58/2020 regime. It defines beneficial ownership concepts (nominee board member, senior management, trustor/trustee/trust fund, complex ownership structure) and requires legal persons to maintain a beneficial owner register and a register of partners or shareholders filed with the registrar. It binds legal persons registered in the UAE and the registrars and concerned entities supervising them, and underpins CDD/beneficial-owner identification duties of financial institutions and DNFBPs.

Defines the Wakala Contract as the agency arrangement under which the Takaful Insurance Fund (or the Participant) appoints the Company as agent to manage the Fund or the Participants' Investment Account for a Wakala Fee, and mandates Wakala as the operating model for licensed property/liability and persons/fund-accumulation takaful business. It requires segregation of the Takaful Fund account, the Participants' Investment Account and the Shareholders' Account, with revenues and expenses attributed to each. Binds takaful and re-takaful companies and insurers operating a Takaful Insurance Window under CBUAE supervision.

Concerns Insurance Surplus in takaful: amounts remaining in the Takaful Insurance Fund at financial year-end from contributions, investment returns and other revenues after settling all Fund obligations. Distribution must follow the approved surplus policy, be certified by the appointed actuary and receive prior CBUAE approval; a contingency provision may be retained, and up to 10% of surplus may be granted to the Company for sound management if provided in the Participation Membership Policy and decided when the surplus arises. Binds takaful/re-takaful companies and window operators, and shapes participants' entitlements.

Governs Qard Hasan: where Takaful Insurance Fund assets are insufficient to meet its liabilities, the Company must extend an interest-free loan to the Fund, capped at total shareholders' equity; the commitment is regulatory rather than contractual and must be disregarded by the ISSC when setting the Wakala fee. Recovery is only from future surplus, by general assembly decision with ISSC approval. Non-provision triggers notification to CBUAE, a fifteen-day cure period and possible suspension of business, so it is a solvency-support obligation on takaful companies.

Requires the Company, acting as agent of the Takaful Insurance Fund, to set a Shari'ah-compliant re-takaful policy for the Fund, approved by the Board, the Board of Trustees (where established) and the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee. Related provisions cover the optional (and potentially CBUAE-mandated) Board of Trustees protecting Fund interests and the licensing and Shari'ah governance conditions for operating a Takaful Insurance Window. Binds takaful and re-takaful companies and insurers with takaful windows.

This is the CBUAE Standard setting minimum controls and procedures for establishing and managing a Takaful Insurance Fund as a legal entity separate from the licensed Company, together with its core defined terms (Company, Fund, Wakala Contract, Fund Charter). It articulates the Central Bank's and Higher Shari'ah Authority's Shari'ah and supervisory expectations for Fund set-up and administration. It binds all insurance companies incorporated in the UAE to conduct Takaful business, foreign licensed Takaful companies operating in the UAE, and conventional insurers/reinsurers operating Takaful windows (for their Takaful activities only), and must be read with other CBUAE and HSA standards and resolutions.

This node is the enabling legislation — Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 on the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business — cited as the source of CBUAE's power to issue the Takaful Fund Standard. It establishes that licensed Takaful companies must comply with the Central Bank Law plus regulations, standards, resolutions and guidelines of the CBUAE and the HSA, and that CBUAE may impose requirements beyond the minimums stated in a standard. It binds all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions and insurance undertakings.
lookup_terms: regulation of financial institutions and activities

data.summary: This node covers the establishment requirements for the Takaful Insurance Fund together with the Standard's definitions article (Wakala Fee, Contribution, Re-takaful Insurance, Participants' Investment Account). It fixes the Shari'ah-based economics of the arrangement: Participants donate Contributions (tabarru') to the Fund, while the Company acts as agent for a Wakala Fee in managing and investing Fund assets. It binds the Company establishing and operating the Fund, including insurers with Takaful windows.
lookup_terms: family Takaful / insurance of persons and fund accumulation

data.summary: This node sets the mandatory contents of the Charter of the Takaful Insurance Fund: the Fund's purpose, its separation from the Company's articles of association, its ownership of assets and liability for its own obligations with an independent financial position disclosed in the Company's financial statements, Participant/Beneficiary status and criteria, the Fund's capacity to contract with the Company, liquidation distribution to Beneficiaries, and a 100-year automatically renewable term. It also limits the Company's benefit from the Fund to the agreed Wakala Fee. It binds the Company drafting and maintaining the Charter.

This node governs the Board of Trustees of a Takaful Insurance Fund: a separate Board per Fund, a five-member composition (two independent non-executive Board members, one ISSC member, two Participant representatives), the single-Fund membership rule with limited two-Fund exceptions, appointment of an independent chairman, CBUAE prior approval for dismissal, notification and replacement timelines on resignation (7 business days / 30 days), minimum three-year terms, at least two meetings per financial year, and Fund-borne remuneration and meeting costs. It binds the Company and its Board in constituting and maintaining the Board of Trustees.

This node concerns the duties of the Board of Trustees in protecting the interests of the Takaful Insurance Fund and its Participants, read together with the composition, tenure, meeting and remuneration rules for that Board. The supplied context largely reproduces the Article 6 provisions on constitution, dismissal, resignation replacement, term length and meeting frequency, so the substantive duty list should be verified in the source. It binds the Board of Trustees members and the Company that appoints and supports them.
lookup_terms: Board of Trustees term and meetings

data.summary: Article 8 of the CBUAE Standard on controls and procedures for establishing a Takaful Insurance Fund, dealing with who represents the Fund externally. It makes the Takaful Company the Fund's exclusive legal representative before third parties and judicial authorities, and channels all lawsuits or claims arising from Takaful Insurance Policies against the Company, subject to a judicial carve-out where a conflict of interest exists. It binds licensed Takaful Insurance Companies (including insurers operating Takaful Windows) managing a Fund that has separate legal personality.
lookup_terms: claims against the Company Takaful policy
conflict of interest Fund and Company

data.summary: Article 9 (read with the Fund Charter requirements in Article 5) of the CBUAE Standard on establishing a Takaful Insurance Fund, governing the terms and conditions under which the Fund operates and contracts with the Company. It requires the Fund to act per its Charter, fixes the Charter as the basis of the Fund–Company contractual relationship, and underpins Charter content on participation terms, Beneficiaries, asset/liability separation, liquidation distribution, the 100-year renewable term, and the Company's entitlement limited to the Wakala Fee. Binds Takaful Insurance Companies establishing or managing a Fund.
lookup_terms: independent financial position of the Fund

data.summary: Article 10 of the CBUAE Standard on establishing a Takaful Insurance Fund, covering transfer of Fund management or of specific Fund accounts (assets, liabilities and Beneficiaries) to another Company or Fund. It requires the Fund Charter to permit such assignment, makes prior approval of the Central Bank and the Higher Shari'ah Authority mandatory, prohibits assignments contrary to Beneficiaries' interests, preserves a Beneficiary right to object, and requires protection of Participants' Investment Account rights. Binds the Company managing the Fund and any transferee Company or Fund.
lookup_terms: prior approval Central Bank and HSA

data.summary: CBUAE Standard setting minimum requirements for the operational model of Takaful Insurance business and the efficient conduct of operations of both the Company and the Takaful Insurance Fund, reflecting the Central Bank's and HSA's Shari'ah and supervisory expectations. It covers establishment of the Fund, the mandatory Wakala-based operational model, contractual relationships, Wakala Fee and expenses, Qard Hasan for deficits, and Re-takaful policy, and defines terms such as Company, Takaful Insurance Fund, Wakala Contract and Insurance Surplus. It applies to all UAE-incorporated and licensed foreign Takaful Insurance Companies, including insurers housing Takaful Windows, for their Takaful activities.

Article 6 of the CBUAE Takaful Operational Model Standard, a bridging obligation requiring the Company to establish the Takaful Insurance Fund in line with the separate Central Bank Standard on controls and procedures for establishing a Takaful Insurance Fund. The surrounding definitions confirm the Fund's independent legal personality and financial liability, its ownership of donated Contributions, and the Wakala Contract structures between Fund/Participant (principal) and Company (agent). Binds licensed Takaful Insurance Companies, Re-takaful companies and insurers with Takaful Windows.

Article 7 of the CBUAE Takaful Operational Model Standard requires any company applying to conduct Takaful business to set an operational model based on the Wakala model, covering property and liability insurance as well as insurance of persons and fund accumulation. The model must be approved in full by the Company's Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee before submission to the Central Bank and HSA, be known to relevant staff, be published on the Company's website, and set out contracting parties, contractual relationships and financial flows between Fund, Company, Participant and Beneficiary (feeding into Article 8). It binds Takaful licence applicants and licensed Takaful Insurance Companies.
lookup_terms: disclosure of operational model on website

data.summary: Article 23 of the CBUAE Takaful Insurance Regulation is a permissive-but-conditional provision on the Zakat fund account: a Takaful Insurance Company may establish one only if its articles of association allow it, and once established it must be kept segregated from the Company's other accounts and from the Takaful Insurance Fund. The management method requires Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee (ISSC) approval, disbursements require a Board decision consistent with ISSC-approved Shari'ah rulings, the Board must adopt a governing policy, and those appointed to manage or supervise the fund may not be remunerated. In all cases the Company must compute Zakat due on shareholders and disclose it, after ISSC approval, in the annual financial statements.

Article 24 requires Takaful Insurance Companies to meet the solvency requirements of the applicable Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies, with regulatory solvency assessed at company level on a consolidated basis covering both the Shareholders' Account and the Takaful Insurance Fund. Consolidation does not dilute the separate financial position of the Fund (distinct assets and liabilities), which must be disclosed in the financial statements. Where the Fund is in recurring deficit or dependent on Qard Hasan, the Central Bank may require the Fund's solvency to be assessed on a standalone basis to protect Participants and Beneficiaries.
lookup_terms: Takaful Insurance Fund separate financial position
Financial Regulations for Takaful Insurance Companies

data.summary: Node for Article 25 (Disclosure Requirements) of the CBUAE Takaful Insurance Regulation, which sits immediately after the solvency article and governs what Takaful Insurance Companies must disclose. The retrieved context contains only the table of contents entry and the article heading, not the operative text, so the substantive obligations must be read in the source document. It binds companies licensed to conduct Takaful Insurance business, including those operating through a Takaful Insurance Window.

Node for Article 26 of the CBUAE Takaful Insurance Regulation; note the label here refers to transfer of the Fund and investment account, while the Regulation's table of contents titles Article 26 "Participant's Investment Account" — confirm the correct heading in the source. The retrieved context does not contain the operative Article 26 text; it instead carries Article 18, which sets the Wakala operating model and requires companies licensed for insurance of persons and fund accumulation to establish both a Participants' Investment Account (managed under Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar with the Participant) and a Takaful Insurance Fund (managed under Wakala with the Company), with revenues and expenses separately determined for the Fund, the Participants' Investment Account and the Shareholders' Account.
lookup_terms: insurance of persons and fund accumulation

data.summary: Article 28 is the repeal and continuity clause: this Regulation cancels and supersedes the 2022 CBUAE Regulation Regarding Takaful Insurance, and confirms that Takaful Insurance Companies remain subject to all CBUAE prudential regulations, standards and instructions for insurance business unless the Central Bank states that particular provisions do not apply to them. The same passage carries Article 29 (violations may attract supervisory action and sanctions, including withdrawing or restricting Senior Management or Board powers, appointing interim management, or barring individuals from the UAE insurance sector) and Article 30 (the Regulatory Development Department is the reference for interpretation).

Concept node for the CBUAE Regulation Regarding Takaful Insurance issued in 2022, the predecessor instrument expressly cancelled and superseded by the current Takaful Insurance Regulation under Article 28. It is relevant mainly for historical/transitional analysis — e.g. assessing obligations arising before the new Regulation's application date, or comparing prior treatment of Takaful Insurance Windows, Shari'ah governance, the ISSC and the Higher Shari'ah Authority with the current requirements. It no longer binds Takaful Insurance Companies prospectively.

Article 8 of the CBUAE Takaful Insurance Standard sets the required contractual architecture between the Takaful Company, the Takaful Insurance Fund, the Participant and the Beneficiary, and requires that architecture to be stated plainly in the operational model, Fund Charter, Participation Membership Policy and Takaful Insurance Policy. It mandates the Wakala model for property and liability takaful (Company as agent of the Fund) and for persons/fund-accumulation business, with the Participant–Fund relationship built on Tabaru (donation) and the Participants' Investment Account governed by a Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar contract. It binds licensed Takaful companies (including takaful windows) and determines how the Beneficiary of the Fund is identified.

Article 9 requires the Takaful Company, acting as agent for the Fund, to prepare and sign with the Participant a Participation Membership Policy regulating the Participant–Fund relationship, drafted in Arabic (or with accurate Arabic translation) and matched to the takaful type and class. It prescribes minimum disclosure content in clear, non-misleading language, including definitions of the Fund and its Charter, membership term, contribution allocation, surplus distribution and deficit-handling policies. Templates must be approved by the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee and Board of Trustees, cleared by the Central Bank and HSA via non-objection, and published on the Company's website and branches.

Article 10 governs the Contribution: each Participant must pay it to the Takaful Insurance Fund on a Tabaru basis upon participation, in a lump sum or instalments depending on the product. The Company must set Contributions on technical and actuarial bases consistent with the nature, scope and duration of the risk, and for fund-accumulation products must split the Contribution transparently between the Fund and the Participants' Investment Account, with material investment information disclosed. Invested amounts in fund-accumulation products are owned by the Participant and subject to ownership rules including inheritance.
lookup_terms: ownership and inheritance of invested amounts

data.summary: Article 11 regulates the Wakala Fee payable from the Takaful Insurance Fund to the Company for managing the Fund. The fee must be pre-determined under Central Bank rules, clearly disclosed, calculated by a known mechanism based on a technical study (lump sum or percentage of Contribution), stipulated in the Participation Membership Policy, balanced across the interests of the Company, Fund, Participants and Beneficiaries, approved annually by the ISSC, and capped at any maximum set by the Central Bank. It also addresses deduction of Wakala Fees for insurance and investment operations and related charges borne by the Fund and the Participants' Investment Account.

Article 15 requires the Takaful Insurance Fund to have an approved Re-takaful policy, prepared by the Company as agent of the Fund and approved by the Board and the ISSC, consistent with the business of the Company and Fund. Where risks are ceded to Re-takaful companies, the Fund must be the contracting party; use of conventional reinsurers is permitted only under specified controls, including prioritising Re-takaful capacity and demonstrating that takaful/re-takaful capacity is unavailable or insufficient. It binds Takaful companies, re-takaful companies and insurers/reinsurers operating takaful windows.

Article 17 requires the Takaful Insurance Fund to maintain an approved Insurance Surplus policy covering how surplus from insurance business is determined, the criteria for entitlement, and the basis and method of distribution. Surplus is defined as amounts remaining in the Fund at financial year end from total Contributions, investment return and other income after obligations. The surrounding provisions also cover co-insurance participation on behalf of the Fund, permitted only with Shari'ah-compliant risks and terms and with prior ISSC approval.

Article 18 of the CBUAE Takaful Insurance standard sets the regime for Qard Hasan: the Takaful Insurance Company must adopt a Board-approved, ISSC-endorsed deficit-management policy and must fund a Shari'ah-compliant interest-free loan from the Shareholders' Account to the Takaful Insurance Fund when the Fund cannot meet its obligations. It frames this as a regulatory (not contractual) obligation, excludes it from Wakala Fee pricing, permits recovery only out of future Surplus subject to solvency limits, requires annual assessment and full write-off three years after maturity, and bars granting Qard Hasan to ineligible persons. It binds licensed Takaful insurers, their Boards and Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committees.

This node covers Articles 6–8 of the CBUAE Takaful standard on establishing the Takaful Insurance Fund and setting the operational model, which must be a Wakala model for both property/liability takaful and insurance of persons and fund accumulation. It requires ISSC approval before submission to the Central Bank and HSA, public disclosure on the company website, and clear articulation of contracting parties, financial flows and the contractual relationships between Participant/Beneficiary, Fund and Company in the Fund Charter, membership and takaful policies. It binds companies applying for or holding a Takaful Insurance licence.

Article 14 (with related definitions) defines the Shareholders' Account as the account representing the Company's own assets and liabilities and lists the revenue streams it may receive from takaful business: Wakala Fee from the Fund, Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar fee from the Participants' Investment Account, investment returns on shareholder funds, the performance incentive for generating Surplus, and repayment of Qard Hasan. It also confirms the Fund may grant up to 10% of Surplus to the Company and that the Shareholders' Account must meet its own obligations and expenses. It binds Takaful Insurance Companies in segregating shareholder and Fund monies.

This node covers the Participants' Investment Account under the CBUAE Takaful standard: the account holding the investment portion of Contributions for insurance of persons and fund accumulation, managed under a Wakala Bi Al-Istithmar contract between Company and Participant. It sets how Contributions are split (or allocated then partly donated) between the Takaful Insurance Fund and the investment account, requires transparency and material disclosure to Participants, confirms invested amounts are owned by the Participant (including inheritance rules), and identifies income sources and the Company's duty to ensure the account meets its obligations. It binds licensed Takaful insurers writing fund-accumulation products.

The CBUAE Operational Risk Management Regulation sets governance and control requirements for operational risk and operational resilience across Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs). It allocates responsibility to the Board (ultimate authority, risk reporting requirements, mandatory Board operational risk committee for systemically important LFIs), to Senior Management (implementing the framework, monitoring the risk profile, training, risk culture), and to an independent Operational Risk management function under the Chief Risk Officer. It binds all LFIs supervised by the CBUAE, with escalating expectations by size, complexity and systemic importance.

This node points to the operational risk management framework requirement within the CBUAE Operational Risk regulation, read alongside the Board, Senior Management and risk-function articles that give it effect. The framework (including the operational resilience strategy) must be Board-approved and translated by Senior Management into implemented policies, processes, controls and systems, with an independent operational risk function that challenges business units, maintains measurement policies and reports on material risks. It binds Licensed Financial Institutions, their Boards and Senior Management.

Article 3 of the CBUAE Operational Risk / Operational Resilience regulation sets the resilience requirements that sit inside the wider operational risk framework, including the planning instruments a Licensed Financial Institution must maintain for Critical Operations (business continuity and disaster recovery planning for prolonged or permanent unavailability of assets). It frames tolerance for disruption and the expectation that resilience is managed on an ongoing, tested basis rather than as a static plan. It binds LFIs licensed by the CBUAE, with responsibility escalating to the Board and Senior Management under the following articles.

Article 4 allocates ultimate, non-delegable responsibility to Board members for ensuring the LFI has an adequate operational risk management framework integrated into its broader risk management framework and covering Operational Resilience. It reserves to the full Board (not a committee) annual approval and review of key operational risk and resilience strategies, the Risk Appetite and Tolerance statement with Risk Limits, and the tolerance for disruption including where capabilities fall short. It also requires a Board operational risk (or equivalent) committee for LFIs designated systemically important, and allows the Central Bank to impose that on other LFIs based on size and complexity.
lookup_terms: Role of the Board of Directors

data.summary: Article 5 makes Senior Management accountable for translating the Board-approved operational risk framework and Operational Resilience strategy into effective policies, processes, controls and systems across the LFI, and for monitoring the operational risk profile and material exposures. It requires timely, direct reporting to the Board (not a committee) of actual or expected breaches of Risk Appetite and Tolerance, thresholds and Risk Limits, maintenance of an internal control system with clear authority and accountability, periodic (at least annual for Banks and (Re)Insurance Companies) internal control assessment reported to the Board and the Central Bank, evaluation of ICT and cybersecurity risk management, adequate staffing, training and risk culture.
lookup_terms: breach of Risk Appetite and Tolerance

data.summary: Article 6 requires each LFI to maintain, within its risk management function, a dedicated Operational Risk management function that is adequately resourced, sufficiently independent, and for which the Chief Risk Officer is responsible and accountable. It sets the function's minimum mandate: forming an independent view of business units' material operational risks, controls and Risk Tolerance; challenging business-unit use of operational risk tools, measurement and reporting; owning operational risk policies and standards; monitoring and reporting the risk profile; identifying internal and external threats; assessing vulnerabilities of Critical Operations; and delivering training and awareness. The function must report its findings and recommendations to the Board regularly.

Article 7 requires the operational risk framework to be underpinned by a strong control environment and an effective internal control system covering risk assessment, control activities, monitoring activities, and information and communication. The system must extend to all LFI activities, including those performed wholly or partly by Third-Party Service Providers, and consists of policies, processes, systems and control measures that mitigate, reduce likelihood of, or limit the impact of risks. The article also prescribes the content and quality of operational risk reporting, including risk profile indicators, Risk Limits and thresholds, residual risks and control deficiencies, non-compliance with tolerances, key and emerging risks, loss events with root cause analysis, external and regulatory developments, and audit/second-line recommendations.

Article 8 sets ICT and cybersecurity risk management obligations for LFIs, requiring the Risk Appetite and Tolerance to expressly address ICT and cyber risk and resilience, and requiring infrastructure that supports business needs in normal and stressed conditions while preserving data and system integrity, confidentiality and availability. It mandates protection, detection, response and recovery programmes that are regularly tested, regular Board and Senior Management information on ICT and cyber exposures, incidents and identified weaknesses, and a policy covering governance, risk ownership and compliance, security controls (access, identity, Critical Information Asset protection, network and vendor security, vulnerability testing, information classification), data management, ICT operations and change/patch management, incident response and recovery, business continuity and disaster recovery plans, project management and systems development/acquisition. Processes must be reviewed and tested regularly against evolving threats and Risk Tolerance.

Article 5 of the CBUAE Insurance Company Licensing Regulation sets the Register entry requirements for licensed insurance Companies: application on the Central Bank's prescribed form with proof of fee payment, a one-year registration term, and annual renewal at least one month before expiry. It also obliges the Company to notify changes to registration data or attached documents via an endorsement application within fifteen business days, and to display its name, registration number and registration date on all publications, contracts, correspondence, notices, certificates and Insurance Policies. It binds all licensed Companies, including branches of Foreign Insurance Companies.

Article 6 requires a registered insurance Company to begin insurance activities within sixty business days of Register entry, with the commencement date fixed as the date the first Insurance Policy is concluded; the Central Bank may grant one equivalent extension in duly justified circumstances. Failure to commence triggers a duty to inform the Central Bank and exposes the Company to suspension of registration or removal from the Register, with a defined route to re-registration. The surrounding context also sets out the classification of property and liability insurance classes and the licence application requirements (Article 3).
lookup_terms: classes of property and liability insurance

data.summary: Article 7 governs a State-established insurance Company opening a Branch outside the State or in a Financial Free Zone, or a subsidiary inside or outside the State: an application on the Central Bank's prescribed form must be filed with supporting documents including a Board resolution and a business plan. The Central Bank may approve, approve with conditions or limitations, or reject with written reasons, and prior Central Bank approval plus evidence of the host supervisor's consent is required before relocating or closing such a Branch. It binds Companies established in the UAE pursuing cross-border or free-zone expansion.

Article 8 sets the approval process for an insurance Company opening a Branch within the UAE: an application on the Central Bank's prescribed form supported by a Board resolution (or a decision of the Authorized Manager for a branch of a Foreign Insurance Company), an economic feasibility study and work plan, the Branch organizational structure, and the names of the Branch manager and senior officers. It binds both Companies established in the State and UAE branches of Foreign Insurance Companies, and sits alongside the Article 7 regime for branches outside the State.
lookup_terms: opening a Branch in the State

data.summary: Annex 1 lists the documents and statements that must accompany a licence application under Article 3, and is referenced together with the Central Bank's power to request further material when assessing an application. The related Article 3 and 4 context sets the assessment criteria (introducing new or high-demand products, increasing Premium retention in the State), possible liaison with a Foreign Insurance Company's home supervisor, and the sixty-business-day cure period after which an incomplete application lapses. Relevant to founders' committees and Foreign Insurance Companies applying for a UAE insurance Licence.

This node captures the Central Bank Law as defined for these instruments: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 on the Central Bank, Regulation of Financial Institutions and Activities, and Insurance Business, which is the enabling statute for the Insurance Company Licensing Regulation (Circular No. 4/2026). It also carries the regulation's definitional context, including Authorized Manager, Beneficiary, Board, Branch, Company, Control Function and Corporate Governance, and the companion instruments the regulation must be read with (Commercial Companies Law, Financial Free Zones Law, minimum capital and financial regulations decisions). It binds all insurance Companies, including Takaful insurers and branches of Foreign Insurance Companies.

Article 9 of the CBUAE Operational Risk and Operational Resilience Regulation sets the incident management obligations of Licensed Financial Institutions (LFIs), requiring response and recovery plans that are regularly reviewed, tested and updated, with root-cause remediation of material incidents. It prescribes coverage of the full incident life cycle: severity classification against predefined criteria, response and recovery procedures linked to the Business Continuity Plan, allocation of roles for staff and external parties, and communication/escalation plans including reporting to the Central Bank and other authorities. It binds all LFIs supervised by the CBUAE, with accountability sitting with the Board and Senior Management through the operational risk framework.
lookup_terms: escalation and notification to Central Bank

data.summary: Article 11 of the CBUAE Operational Risk and Operational Resilience Regulation requires LFIs to maintain Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plans for their Critical Operations, integrated with the operational risk and resilience framework and built on the mapping of critical operations and assets. It mandates disruption scenario analysis with quantitative and qualitative business impact assessment, clear activation triggers, Board-approved recovery time and recovery point objectives, stakeholder communication arrangements, and at least annual review and testing for Critical Operations (including key Third-Party Service Providers), with results reported to the Board and Senior Management. Second and third lines of defence must review the plans; the obligation binds all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Article 13 of the CBUAE Operational Risk and Operational Resilience Regulation governs LFIs' management of risk arising from Third-Party Service Providers, including ongoing monitoring of provider financial condition and of dependencies supporting Critical Operations. It requires reliance on third parties to be reflected in the operational risk and resilience framework, the Business Continuity Plan and the mapping of critical assets, and requires viable contingency and exit plans plus an assessment of substitutability where timely replacement would be costly, high-risk or impossible. The Central Bank retains discretion to require discontinuation of a third-party arrangement or of an over-dependent Critical Operation, so the article binds LFIs and constrains outsourcing decisions.

Article 14 of the CBUAE Operational Risk and Operational Resilience Regulation addresses Shari'ah Non-Compliance Risk (SNCR), defined as the risk of financial loss or reputational harm from failure to comply with Shari'ah, and applies to Islamic Finance Institutions (including Islamic windows within its scope). It requires a Shari'ah governance framework aligned with Higher Shari'ah Authority resolutions, product and contract approval policies, dedicated systems, controls and limits for SNCR across the contract life cycle, proactive identification by the risk management function, and formal recording and reporting of non-recognised income to the internal Shari'ah supervision committee. The internal Shari'ah supervision committee holds the determinative authority on Shari'ah matters, and control frameworks must be reviewed and improved where SNCR materialises.

Article 19 is the repeal provision of the CBUAE Operational Risk and Operational Resilience Regulation, cancelling and replacing Circular No. 163/2018 (the Operational Risk Regulation and Operational Risk Standards of 29 August 2018). It sits alongside Article 18 (the Regulatory Development Department as interpretive authority) and Article 20 (publication in the Official Gazette in Arabic and English, effective one month after publication). Relevant to anyone checking which instrument governs an LFI's operational risk obligations for a given date.

This node concerns Circular No. 163/2018 (the earlier CBUAE Operational Risk Regulation and Operational Risk Standards, issued 29 August 2018), which has been cancelled and replaced by the current Operational Risk and Operational Resilience Regulation. The surrounding material shows the successor regime's content: Article 7 requirements on operational risk reporting (risk profile, limits and tolerances, residual risks and control deficiencies, loss events with root-cause analysis, emerging risks, audit recommendations) and Annex 1 examples of risk identification and assessment tools such as event management and internal/external loss data collection. Useful mainly for historical/transition analysis of obligations applying to LFIs before the current regulation took effect.

Concept node capturing the Islamic-finance-specific provisions (Article 14) of the CBUAE operational risk instrument, dealing with Shari'ah Non-Compliance Risk as a category of operational risk. It requires an Islamic Financial Institution to maintain a Shari'ah governance and risk framework, test interlinkages of Shari'ah non-compliance with other risks across the contract life cycle, record and report non-recognised (purified) income, keep separate accounts for restricted/unrestricted investment accounts and Takaful funds, and refrain from circumventing contractually assumed risk. It binds licensed financial institutions conducting Islamic finance business, with determinative authority vested in the internal Shari'ah supervision committee and the Higher Shari'ah Authority's resolutions.

Annex to the CBUAE operational risk instrument listing illustrative tools for identifying and assessing Operational Risk, including event management processes, internal loss/event data collection and analysis (including near misses), and external loss data analysis. It is explanatory rather than prescriptive, supporting the substantive reporting duties (risk profile, limits, residual risks, control deficiencies, root cause analysis, emerging risks). Relevant to licensed financial institutions designing and evidencing their operational risk identification and assessment practices.

CBUAE Insurance Company Licensing Regulation (Circular 4/2026, addressed to all insurance companies), setting the framework for licensing insurance companies incorporated in the UAE and branches of Foreign Insurance Companies, and for opening branches and subsidiaries inside and outside the State. It covers classification of insurance business, licence application and process, registration, commencement of activities, cancellation of prior regulatory instruments, enforcement and sanctions, with an annex of required application documents. It binds founders/applicants and licensed insurance companies, and must be read with the Central Bank Law and related company, free-zone and minimum-capital instruments.

Article 2 of the CBUAE Insurance Company Licensing Regulation, which classifies insurance business into categories and enumerates the classes of property and liability insurance (fire, transport, marine and aviation hull, satellites, railways, land vehicles, engineering, oil, health, and miscellaneous accident lines such as personal accident, fidelity guarantee, cash/securities, theft, glass, professional indemnity, workers' accidents and employer liability, agriculture and livestock). It determines the scope of activity a licence may authorise and therefore what an applicant or licensee may write.

Article 3 of the CBUAE Insurance Company Licensing Regulation, governing who submits a licence application and in what form: the founders' committee for a company to be established in the State, or the Foreign Insurance Company itself for a branch. It requires the documents and statements in Annex 1 plus anything further the Central Bank requests, and sets assessment considerations including whether the company will introduce new or strongly demanded products and increase premium retention in the State; the Central Bank may liaise with the foreign home supervisor.

Article 4 of the CBUAE Insurance Company Licensing Regulation, setting the procedural mechanics of the licensing decision: an application is formally received only when complete with all required documents, and deficiencies or clarification requests must be remedied by the applicant within sixty business days of notification, failing which the application lapses as null and void. It binds applicants (domestic companies and foreign insurers seeking branch licences) and frames the Central Bank's handling of incomplete files ahead of registration and commencement of insurance activities.

CBUAE Regulation No. 1/2026 issued under Article 471 of Federal Decree-Law No. 50/2022 (Commercial Transactions Law), approved by the Higher Shari'ah Authority and the CBUAE Board, setting the controls and rules for the commercial transactions of Islamic financial institutions and takaful insurance companies. It is organised in six chapters covering definitions and scope, Shari'ah compliance and interpretation, general contract and obligation rules, promise (wa'd) and revocation of a binding promise, Islamic deposits and investment accounts, Islamic banking financing contracts (instalment sale, murabaha, istisna'a, salam, ijarah, mudaraba, investment wakala, musharaka, financing security, documentary credit), takaful insurance, and compliance with the regulation. It binds CBUAE-licensed Islamic financial institutions, takaful and retakaful companies, and is the reference framework for their contracts with customers.

Chapter Five (Article 32) of CBUAE Regulation 1/2026 is the takaful insurance provision, the sole article dedicated to takaful within a regulation otherwise focused on Islamic banking contracts. It sits alongside the Article 1 definitions of 'takaful insurance company' (licensed to conduct takaful activities per Shari'ah principles) and 'retakaful company' (a legal person licensed under the Central Bank Law and its implementing regulations). It binds licensed takaful and retakaful undertakings in the conduct of their commercial transactions.

Federal Decree-Law No. 50/2022 issuing the Commercial Transactions Law is the parent statute; Article 471 (Book Three, Chapter Six) is the express enabling provision under which CBUAE issued Regulation 1/2026. The Regulation defines 'Commercial Transactions Law' as this Decree-Law and derives its authority from it together with Higher Shari'ah Authority approval and a CBUAE Board decision. Relevant for tracing the legal basis and hierarchy of the Islamic commercial transactions rules, and their interaction with Federal Decree-Law No. 6/2025 on the Central Bank and the regulation of financial institutions, activities and insurance business.

Article 21 of CBUAE Regulation 1/2026 governs the murabaha contract, placed in Chapter Four on Islamic banking financing alongside instalment sale (Art. 20), istisna'a (Art. 22), salam (Art. 23) and ijarah (Art. 24). It should be read with the general contract rules of Chapter One and the promise/wa'd provisions of Articles 7-9, which matter for purchase-order murabaha structures. It binds Islamic financial institutions offering murabaha-based financing in the UAE.

Mudaraba appears twice in CBUAE Regulation 1/2026: Article 12, on applying mudaraba or investment wakala rules to investment deposits and investment accounts (Chapter Three), and Article 26, on banking mudaraba as a financing form (Chapter Four). Related deposit-side articles address commingling of investment deposit funds with institution funds, allocation of expenses, account statements and investment deposit assets. It binds Islamic financial institutions in structuring investment accounts and mudaraba-based financing, and is central to profit-sharing and loss-allocation questions (read with the defined terms for infringement/ta'addi and negligence/taqsir).

Article 24 of CBUAE Regulation 1/2026 governs the ijarah contract, the longest of the financing-contract articles in Chapter Four on Islamic banking financing. It applies to Islamic financial institutions providing lease-based financing and should be read with the general contract provisions, the financing security article (Art. 30) and the undertaking to purchase assets (Art. 29). Relevant to allocation of ownership risk, maintenance and rental obligations in lease structures.

CBUAE guidance addressing money laundering and terrorist/illegal-organisation financing risks arising from cash-intensive business customers, including illustrative sectors (e.g. travel agencies, car dealers) and related instruments such as open- and closed-loop prepaid cards. It expects licensed financial institutions to define cash-intensive business using a documented, senior-management-approved methodology, understand expected activity, and apply risk-based CDD and ongoing monitoring against peer and profile baselines. Binding on CBUAE-licensed financial institutions (LFIs); note this is UAE, not SAMA, material and does not itself apply in KSA.
lookup_terms: money service / high cash turnover customers

data.summary: Node capturing the UAE AML-CFT legal anchor (Federal Decree-Law 20/2018 and its implementing Cabinet Decision) as referenced in the cash-intensive business guidance, principally the obligation to report suspicious transactions or activity to the UAE FIU whenever there are reasonable grounds to suspect a link to criminal proceeds or a crime, regardless of amount or whether the transaction was completed. It also frames the duty to maintain policies, procedures and controls to identify, assess and mitigate risk in higher-risk relationships. Binds LFIs and other regulated entities under UAE law.

CBUAE guidance setting supervisory expectations for two linked control pillars: transaction monitoring for ML/TF/PF detection and sanctions screening for targeted financial sanctions compliance. It covers risk assessment, risk-based deployment of manual versus automated controls, data quality and integrity, pre-implementation testing, governance and board/senior-management oversight. Applies to CBUAE-licensed financial institutions; a UAE instrument, useful comparatively rather than as KSA authority.

Concept node on the transaction monitoring programme: the control by which an institution detects, investigates and reports suspicious transactions and keeps customers and activity within risk appetite. It ties TM effectiveness to CDD/KYC quality and expected-activity baselines, requires risk assessment updates at least annually and on trigger events, and calibrates manual versus automated monitoring to institutional size, nature and complexity, with larger institutions expected to automate. Directed at LFIs' compliance function and senior management.

Concept node on the sanctions screening programme, treating screening of all customer relationships and transactions as a minimum legal requirement that the risk-based approach may enhance but never displace. It sets expectations on sanctions risk assessment, automated updating of sanctions lists, training where manual processes are used, quality assurance, and active board and senior-management oversight including timely escalation of calibration or system failures. Binds LFIs and their governing bodies.
lookup_terms: risk appetite / tone from the top

data.summary: Concept node distinguishing transaction screening — screening a movement of value (funds, goods or assets) into, out of or through the institution between parties or accounts — from name screening of customer, employee, vendor and related-party reference data. It addresses which data elements are relevant to sanctions risk, data capture and reconciliation between core systems and screening systems, detection controls such as exception reporting and trend analysis, and root-cause escalation of data quality failures. Relevant to LFI compliance and operations functions.

A concept node within CBUAE guidance on transaction monitoring and sanctions screening that covers how licensed financial institutions should govern the sanctions lists they screen against — list selection and scope, internal versus vendor sourcing, maintenance and update controls, enrichment of list entries, and the controlled use of whitelists to manage false positives. It also addresses when screening must occur in the transaction lifecycle and the treatment of paper-based versus electronic transaction flows. It binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions (LFIs); screening against UNSC and UAE Cabinet lists is mandatory, while other lists may be applied on a risk basis.

Reference node identifying UAE Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020 as one of the legal bases of the CBUAE transaction monitoring and sanctions screening guidance, alongside the AML-CFT Law (Federal Decree-Law 20/2018) and the AML-CFT Decision (Cabinet Decision 10/2019). It establishes the terrorism lists regime and implementation of UNSC resolutions on terrorism, terrorist financing and proliferation financing, with Article 21.2 cited as the source of LFI screening obligations. It binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions; the guidance itself sets supervisory expectations rather than new law.

Concept node drawing on two CBUAE guidance documents, covering the institution-level risk assessment as the basis for a risk-based approach to sanctions compliance and transaction monitoring, together with supporting expectations on board and senior management oversight, staff training, quality assurance and integration into the wider AML/CFT programme. It makes clear that the risk-based approach cannot justify omitting sanctions screening of any customer relationship or transaction, which is a minimum legal requirement; risk sensitivity only justifies additional or more rigorous controls. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions and their boards.
lookup_terms: risk appetite tone from the top

data.summary: The CBUAE guidance document on implementation of Targeted Financial Sanctions, issued under Article 44.11 of Cabinet Decision 10/2019, setting out supervisory expectations for how licensed financial institutions demonstrate compliance with UAE TFS obligations. It is to be read with the CBUAE AML/CFT Procedures (Notice 74/2019) and the Executive Office's TFS Guidance for FIs and DNFBPs, and expressly does not create new law — the underlying legal framework prevails in any conflict. It is directed at CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.
lookup_terms: UN Consolidated List and Local Terrorist List

data.summary: Reference node for UAE Federal Decree-Law No. 20 of 2018 on Anti-Money Laundering, Combating the Financing of Terrorism and Illegal Organizations, cited as the primary statutory basis of the CBUAE TFS guidance. Together with its implementing regulation it requires financial institutions to promptly apply directives of UAE competent authorities implementing UNSC Chapter VII decisions. It binds financial institutions and DNFBPs subject to the UAE AML/CFT framework.

Reference node for UAE Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020 as the legislative framework for Targeted Financial Sanctions, establishing the Local Terrorist List and the mechanism for giving effect to the UN Consolidated List, and allocating the Executive Office's coordination and grievance-handling role. This node also carries the key defined terms used across the TFS regime, including Funds, Listed Person, Listing, and direct versus indirect relationship. It binds financial institutions and DNFBPs subject to UAE TFS obligations.

Umbrella section of the CBUAE targeted financial sanctions guidance setting out how Licensed Financial Institutions must operationalise screening against the UN Consolidated List and the UAE Local Terrorist List, both on a regular basis and immediately upon notification of list changes. It covers the required scope of searches (customer databases, prospective customers, parties to transactions, beneficial owners, and persons with direct or indirect relationships) and the sub-topics of evasion detection, list maintenance, customer and name screening, and match adjudication. It binds LFIs supervised by CBUAE under Cabinet Decision 74.

Guidance expectation that LFIs detect and block attempts to evade, avoid or circumvent sanctions, not merely direct list matches. It flags typical evasion tactics (renaming, intermediaries, front companies, alternative financial networks) and positions CDD/EDD alongside screening as the mechanism for identifying complex evasion; it also sits next to the sanctions risk appetite and internal controls expectations (applicable regimes, 50% ownership/control treatment, unilateral and secondary sanctions exposure). Applies to all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Sets the expectation that screening occurs across the whole customer lifecycle rather than at onboarding only, distinguishing periodic name screening (triggered by changes to customer data or to the UN/Local lists), ad hoc screening (business need, competent authority request, or downstream institution feedback) and re-screening (e.g. high-risk jurisdiction identified in updated customer data). Adjacent guidance makes LFIs responsible for due diligence on external list vendors and for registering with the Executive Office for listing/de-listing notifications. Binds LFIs.

Addresses adjudication of screening alerts: LFIs must compare potential matches against the UN Consolidated List and Local Terrorist List to determine whether a hit is a true match or a false positive. Where a false positive is established, freezing and other sanctions measures are not required and the transaction or relationship may proceed; the surrounding material includes the control criteria used to judge whether an entity is controlled by a Listed Person. Applies to LFIs.

Component of the CBUAE screening guidance dealing with sanctions screening applied to payments and transactions, complementing customer-level name screening; the surrounding obligations require searching names of parties to any transaction and screening before conducting any transaction or entering a business relationship. It also ties to list maintenance from the UNSC and Executive Office sources and to name-screening controls such as ownership/control, fuzzy matching and weak aliases. Binds LFIs.

Deals with the treatment of a screening hit confirmed as a true match against the UN Consolidated List or Local Terrorist List, as distinct from a false positive that requires no freezing action. It is read together with the ownership/control criteria for determining when a person, entity or arrangement is controlled by a Listed Person and therefore in scope of freezing and reporting obligations. Applies to CBUAE-licensed financial institutions.

Operative notification duty within the CBUAE sanctions compliance guidance: it sets out when a Licensed Financial Institution must immediately inform the Central Bank and, separately, the Executive Office, anchored in Cabinet Decision 74 (Art. 21(5) and Art. 15(2)). Triggering events include freezing action taken under relevant UNSCRs or the Local Terrorist List, confirmed matches with Listed Persons, discovery that a current, previous or occasional customer is listed, suspicion of a direct or indirect relationship with a Listed Person, unresolvable potential matches where no action could be taken for lack of identifying data, and unfreezing of funds with related particulars. Attempted transactions are reportable alongside executed ones; the duty binds all LFIs supervised by CBUAE.

Defines the UN Consolidated List as the UNSC-issued designation list that LFIs must source from the official UN website and keep current, including mandatory registration with the Executive Office for automated listing/de-listing alerts under Cabinet Decision 74 Art. 21. It underpins customer and transaction screening across the customer lifecycle, and where third-party vendor lists are used the LFI retains responsibility for vendor due diligence and completeness of the list. Also frames false-positive dispositioning and the controlled use of cleared-name (white) lists.

Covers the UAE Cabinet-issued Local Terrorist List, published by the Executive Office, which LFIs must obtain from the official source and register to receive listing/de-listing notifications. It operates in parallel with the UN Consolidated List for screening, freezing and reporting, and feeds the definition of Listed Person together with related concepts such as Funds, control, and direct/indirect relationship. Binds all CBUAE-supervised LFIs, including those relying on external vendor list feeds.

Concept node on the ownership and control test applied in sanctions screening: LFIs are expected to set policy on interests, assets or entities owned or controlled 50% or more by a Listed Person, and to assess control through criteria such as board appointment rights, dominant influence, voting-rights agreements, use of assets, unified management or joint liability. It sits within the sanctions risk appetite and name-screening expectations and determines whether non-listed entities are treated as within scope of a freeze.

Addresses fuzzy matching as a required element of LFI name-screening procedures, alongside the ownership/control rule and handling of weak or low-quality aliases, to prevent and detect sanctions breaches. It concerns the tolerance for approximate name matches against the UN Consolidated List and Local Terrorist List and the subsequent true-match versus false-positive disposition. Guidance-level expectation on CBUAE-supervised LFIs, not a system-specification.

Annex-style red-flag material in the CBUAE sanctions guidance covering terrorist financing, proliferation financing (drawn from FATF typologies) and sanctions circumvention indicators published by the Executive Office. Indicators span trade and shipping anomalies, shell and intermediary companies, linked counterparties, cash or precious metals use, and falsified documentation. Non-exhaustive detection aids for LFIs feeding monitoring, escalation and reporting obligations rather than standalone prohibitions.

Orientation node for the CBUAE-issued guidance on targeted financial sanctions, which sits on top of the Executive Office's TFS guidance for FIs and DNFBPs and rests on UAE Decree Federal Law No. 20 of 2018, Cabinet Decision 10 of 2019 and Cabinet Decision 74 of 2020. It explains the institutional architecture (Executive Office as national TFS coordinator, UN Consolidated List and Local Terrorist List sourcing and registration for notifications) and expectations on customer/name screening, false-positive handling and detection of sanctions evasion. It binds all CBUAE-licensed financial institutions (LFIs), including banks, exchange houses, finance companies, payment service providers, registered hawala providers and insurers; note this is a UAE instrument, not SAMA, and is relevant only comparatively for KSA work.

Concept node for the Sanctions Compliance Program (SCP) that CBUAE expects LFIs to develop, implement and keep updated to meet Cabinet Decision 74 obligations and directives of competent and supervisory authorities. It sets the proportionality principle (scope tailored to risk profile, nature, scale, complexity, products, customer base and geographies) and frames the SCP pillars: senior management commitment, risk assessment, risk appetite, internal controls, training, and independent audit. Applies to all CBUAE-licensed/supervised FIs, including payment service providers, finance companies, exchange houses, hawala providers and insurance entities.
