Sub-element of the SCP addressing governance accountability: senior management must review and approve the SCP, formally designate the persons responsible for its implementation, and ensure it is embedded in daily operations with adequate resources. It converts sanctions compliance from a control function matter into a board/executive responsibility within CBUAE-licensed institutions.

Concept node requiring LFIs to maintain a written, senior-management-approved sanctions risk appetite embedded in policies, procedures and screening parameters. It must state which sanctions regimes apply (UNSCR, OFAC, EU, UK), the treatment of interests owned or controlled 50% or more by a Listed Person, the approach to unilateral and extra-territorial/secondary sanctions exposure, and the handling of alias, vessel and paper-instrument names; deviations must be documented and approved. Binds CBUAE-licensed financial institutions and shades into the internal controls requirement under Cabinet Decision 74.

Sub-element of the SCP setting expectations for senior-management-approved sanctions policies and procedures: identification, escalation and reporting of suspicious activity, tipping-off prohibition regarding freezing or Other Measures, enhanced due diligence for customers and transactions assessed as high-risk for TF and PF, and detailed record-keeping. Requires consistent implementation across branches, subsidiaries and majority-held entities, communication to staff and outsourced providers, timely updates for emerging risks, at least annual formal review, and documented approval of any deviations.

Sub-element of the SCP on independent audit and risk-based testing: regular assessment of sanctions policies, procedures, systems and controls by internal audit and/or a competent external auditor, resourced with skilled staff and scaled to the sophistication of the program. The audit function must be independent of audited activities with sufficient authority and resources; negative findings require immediate action and compensating controls pending root-cause remediation. Separately requires independent risk-based testing that screening produces expected alerts and that thresholds and rules align with the stated risk appetite.

An annex section of the CBUAE targeted financial sanctions guidance listing red-flag situations, drawn from the Executive Office's typologies on circumvention of targeted sanctions against terrorism and WMD proliferation, that may signal attempts by customers or counterparties to evade listings. It is an indicator set rather than a standalone obligation, feeding the suspicion-assessment, monitoring and screening duties that licensed financial institutions (and DNFBPs, by analogy) owe under the UAE AML-CFT framework and Cabinet Decision 74. Relevant to LFIs designing sanctions evasion detection and to escalation/reporting decisions.

A cited external source (the US FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual) reproduced in Annex 1 of the CBUAE guidance as a catalogue of potentially suspicious activity indicative of terrorist financing, organised by themes such as activity inconsistent with the customer's business and funds transfers. It has no legal force in the UAE; it is illustrative material supporting LFIs' TF risk identification under the AML-CFT Law, AML-CFT Decision and Cabinet Decision 74. Useful when calibrating TF typologies and suspicion thresholds.

A cited external source (terrorist financing indicators published by Canada's FIU, FINTRAC) reproduced in the CBUAE guidance annex, covering high-risk conflict jurisdictions, NPO/charity misuse, unofficial donation collection and travel-related indicators. Persuasive typology material, not a UAE legal requirement, used to support LFIs' TF detection and suspicious transaction assessment alongside sanctions screening duties. Relevant for NPO-sector and conflict-zone risk analysis.

A cited external source (Annex 1 to the 2008 FATF Typologies Report on Proliferation Financing) reproduced in the CBUAE guidance as an enumerated list of PF indicators, including countries of proliferation or diversion concern, shell companies, circuitous shipping and payment routes, denied-party name similarity, end-user mismatch and misleading trade documentation. It is illustrative guidance rather than binding text, supporting LFIs' PF risk identification, trade-finance due diligence and reporting under the UAE TFS framework. Open it for a ready-made PF red-flag taxonomy.

A referenced industry standard (Wolfsberg guidance on sanctions screening) cited in the CBUAE guidance's treatment of name and customer screening, screening operations, list maintenance and evasion detection. It informs expectations on the ownership/control (50%) rule, fuzzy matching, weak aliases and false-positive resolution, but the binding obligations on LFIs come from Cabinet Decision 74 and the AML-CFT framework, not the industry paper. Useful for benchmarking screening programme design expectations at policy level.

A reference to CBUAE supervisory work on sanctions screening testing, feeding the guidance's summary expectations and the annexed lessons learned from CBUAE supervision on screening effectiveness, list maintenance, risk appetite and evasion monitoring. It signals supervisory findings and examination focus areas for LFIs rather than creating new rules, and is read together with the binding TFS obligations under Cabinet Decision 74. Consult it to understand how the regulator assesses screening adequacy.

data.theme: Prudential risk-management obligations for SAMA-supervised institutions: board-level risk governance, an independent risk function, risk appetite, stress testing of material risks and their feed into capital adequacy assessment.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the Central Bank Law supplies supervisory authority; the Risk Management Regulation sets the binding obligations; the accompanying Standards elaborate them article-by-article in mirrored numbering (e.g. Article 5 stress testing in both instruments).
Obligation chain runs board → risk governance framework → risk appetite statement → risk management function → stress testing outputs used in the ICAAP.
Corporate governance rules cross-reference the Regulation, so risk-management duties are enforceable both as a prudential requirement and as a board governance duty.
Defined constructs (material risk, risk appetite, ICAAP) are shared across Regulation and Standards and should be read consistently.

data.theme: Institutional governance and accountability: board and senior management responsibilities, board committees, conflicts and related-party controls, Shari'ah governance, SAMA examinations, and the consumer-facing complaint handling function.
how_members_connect: Governance hierarchy: board of directors delegates to senior management and mandates committees (audit, risk, compensation), each with its own defined remit under the corporate governance framework article.
Integrity controls are linked definitionally — conflict of interest policy and related-party transaction rules address the same independence risk from different angles.

Consumer-protection strand attaches to governance: the complaint management function and its article are anchored in the fair treatment of consumers principle, making complaint outcomes a board-oversight matter.
Supervisory strand: the examinations chapter and transmittal letter route findings to the manager in charge and the board, closing the loop between governance duties and SAMA enforcement.
Shari'ah governance (external Shari'ah audit, compliance with Islamic Shari'ah provisions) is a parallel assurance line reporting into the same senior management/board structure.

data.theme: Requirements on how institutions measure risk and govern the use of internal models, including validation and the limits of model reliance.
how_members_connect: Two-tier pairing: the Regulation article states the obligation; the identically numbered Standards article supplies the detailed expectations and is read as its implementing text.
Model-measurement duties are the input layer to risk appetite monitoring and stress testing in the wider risk-management regime.
start_here: Article 4: Risk Measurement & Use of Models (Regulation)

data.theme: Obligations on risk-related information systems, data quality and internal reporting lines that supply the board and senior management with timely, accurate risk information.
how_members_connect: Same Regulation-to-Standards pairing: the Standards article elaborates the corresponding Regulation article at matching numbering.
Reporting duties are the delivery mechanism for other risk obligations — measurement outputs and stress-test results must reach the governing body through these systems.
start_here: Article 6: Information Systems and Internal Reporting (Regulation)

data.theme: Books-and-records obligations and the control functions that assure their integrity — who must keep accounting records, and the internal audit, audit committee and external auditor roles that verify them.
how_members_connect: A single records provision anchors the cluster and points outward to each assurance actor, making record-keeping the obligation and audit the verification chain.
Internal audit and the audit committee are linked as a reporting/oversight pair (function reports, committee oversees), sitting under board-level governance.
External auditor duties sit at the top of the chain: independent attestation over the same accounting books the entity is required to maintain.
Governance-regime cluster; note its interaction with AML/CTF and payments record-retention duties, which impose separate retention periods on the same underlying records.

data.theme: Administrative sanctions in the insurance regime — the fines schedule and the licensing, conduct and electronic-insurance rules whose breach triggers it.
how_members_connect: A Cabinet-level resolution sets the penalty regime and its annexed schedule enumerates specific breaches and amounts — law-to-schedule hierarchy.
The licensing resolution for insurance producers is the main citing node, pulling in the companies law, the electronic insurance rules and the code of conduct as the substantive duties it enforces.
The fines schedule cross-refers to the financial regulations for insurers, tying prudential/financial breaches to monetary penalties.
Non-SAMA (UAE/IA) material: useful comparatively, but do not transpose fine amounts or article numbers into KSA insurance analysis.
start_here: IA Board Resolution No. 27 of 2020 - Licensing Insurance Producers

data.theme: Bank liquidity regulation: the qualitative governance requirements and the quantitative ratios (ELAR/ASRR, LCR/NSFR) banks must meet, with Basel III as the underlying standard.
how_members_connect: Clear hierarchy: central bank law → liquidity regulation (qualitative vs quantitative articles) → guidance manual/circulars, with an earlier circular expressly superseded.
The quantitative article is the hub referencing each ratio; the ratios in turn depend on the shared defined term High Quality Liquid Assets and cite Basel III/BCBS as source.
Qualitative requirements chain into governance artefacts — liquidity risk framework, contingency funding plan and stress testing — which condition how the ratios are managed, not just calculated.
An Islamic-banking standard sits alongside as a scope variant, signalling that the same ratios apply with Shariah-specific treatment of liquid assets and funding.

data.theme: Enterprise risk governance applied to specific risk types — country and transfer risk, IRRBB and solvency self-assessment — anchored in board responsibility and a documented risk governance framework.
how_members_connect: Board responsibilities article is the source obligation; the risk governance framework and an independent risk management function are the required delivery mechanisms.
Two parallel regulations (country/transfer risk; IRRBB) reuse the same governance architecture, so the framework and function definitions carry across risk types.
Stress testing is the common analytical obligation linking country risk ratings, IRRBB and the insurance-side ORSA.

A regulation-plus-standards pairing (circular and accompanying standards) shows the detailed-requirements layer beneath the headline rule; country risk rating systems are the operative classification tool.

data.theme: Governance architecture for internal control: the mandated control functions (compliance, internal audit, risk, actuarial), their independence and reporting lines, and board/senior-management accountability for an effective internal control framework across banks, finance companies and insurers.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Regulation and the Risk Management and Internal Controls Regulation sit above the defined 'Control Functions', which are then broken out into compliance, internal audit and actuarial roles.
Shared organising concept: the Three Lines of Defense model links control functions to internal policies, controls and procedures, allocating ownership between business, oversight and assurance.

Obligation chain upward: board (bank/insurer/finance company) and senior management carry non-delegable responsibility for approving, resourcing and reviewing the framework; control functions report into them.

External standards incorporated by reference: internal audit obligations are benchmarked to IIA international standards; insurance-specific fraud-countering duties attach the same governance machinery to a sector control objective.
start_here: Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Regulation 161/2018

data.theme: Prudential treatment of market risk: trading book scope, valuation discipline, capital requirements and the systems, validation and reporting controls supervisors expect around internal market-risk models, including Islamic banking variants.
how_members_connect: Rule-to-detail chain: the Market Risk Regulation sets capital, reporting and systems-and-controls obligations; the Market Risk Standards elaborate valuation, controls and Islamic banking treatment.
Definitional dependency: valuation obligations only bite on positions falling inside the defined Trading Book, so boundary classification drives the capital outcome.
Model-governance loop: internal validation and back-testing are the evidentiary conditions for relying on internal approaches, sitting under the systems and controls requirement.
Legal basis: the regulation traces its authority to the central bank establishing law, with Islamic banking provisions as a parallel scope carve-out rather than an exemption.

data.theme: Licensing and ownership gatekeeping in payments and banking: authorisation of retail payment systems and stored-value facilities, settlement finality and netting protection, and regulatory control over significant or national shareholdings and minimum capital by licence type.
how_members_connect: Common legal anchor: the payment-system, stored-value, shareholding and restricted-licence instruments all cite the central bank law as their enabling authority.
Designation as a gate: retail payment system designation triggers the regime under which settlement finality and netting protections operate.
Ownership control chain: national shareholding rules cross-refer to the transfer of significant shareholding regime, so changes in control require prior regulatory clearance.

Licence-scope calibration: restricted-licence banking sits against minimum capital and wholesale banking rules and is bounded by the high-net-worth customer definition, which limits permissible clientele.

data.theme: Oversight of systemically important payment infrastructure: designation of large-value payment systems, the duties of system operators and settlement institutions, and alignment with international CPMI-IOSCO standards.
how_members_connect: Definitional core: the Large Value Payment Systems Regulation defines the LVPS and distinguishes it from a retail payment system, with obligations attaching to the defined System Operator and Settlement Institution roles.
Designation as the trigger: being designated systemically important is the event that pulls a system into the heightened oversight regime.
International standards incorporated: the PFMI, issued by CPMI and IOSCO, function as the substantive benchmark against which operators are assessed.
Adjacent supervisory expectation: the CPMI wholesale payments fraud strategy extends operator responsibilities to endpoint security and fraud resilience within the LVPS.

data.theme: Allocation of decision-making authority over strategic and operational matters — i.e. which decisions must be taken (or ratified) by the regulated entity's own governing body in the Kingdom rather than elsewhere in a group. The paired Regulation and Standards set the obligation and then its operative detail.
how_members_connect: Two-tier instrument pair on the same numbered article: the Regulation states the binding requirement, the Standards article expands it into supervisory expectations for the same subject matter.
The Standards article expressly cross-refers back to the Regulation article, so the Standards cannot be read as a free-standing obligation — it takes scope and defined terms from the Regulation.

Sits alongside the group risk management article (community 159): both govern the local entity/group boundary, so decision-authority and risk-control duties must be read together to avoid conflicting escalation lines.

data.theme: Group-level risk management duties — how risks arising from, or shared with, affiliated entities are identified, controlled and reported, and the extent to which group frameworks may be relied on locally.
how_members_connect: Same Regulation/Standards hierarchy as community 158: the Regulation article imposes the duty, the Standards article specifies how compliance is demonstrated.
The Standards article references the Regulation article, inheriting its scope and defined terms (group, affiliate, risk framework) rather than creating new ones.
Obligation chain runs into the decision-authority article (Article 7): reliance on group risk functions is constrained by which decisions must remain with the local governing body.
Group risk outputs feed the disclosure obligation (community 189), linking internal risk reporting to external reporting duties.

data.theme: Disclosure obligations under the Regulation — what the regulated entity must publish or report, to whom, and on what cadence, as a transparency counterpart to the governance and risk articles.
how_members_connect: Single Regulation-level node with no paired Standards article in the graph, so the requirement is read directly from the Regulation text without elaborating guidance in this cluster.
Content of the disclosure is functionally supplied by the governance and group risk articles (Articles 7-8), which determine what information exists to be disclosed.
Sequentially and thematically adjacent to Article 10, so scope carve-outs or additions for Islamic banking activity may qualify what must be disclosed.

data.theme: Islamic banking treatment within the Regulation — how the general requirements apply to, or are modified for, Shariah-compliant activity and its governance.
how_members_connect: Stand-alone Regulation article acting as a scope/qualification provision: it conditions how the preceding general articles apply rather than creating a separate regime.
No paired Standards article in this cluster, so supervisory detail must be sought outside the community; do not assume elaboration exists.
Interacts with the governance, group risk and disclosure articles because Shariah governance arrangements affect decision authority and what is reported.

data.theme: Shari'ah governance architecture for Islamic financial institutions and takaful insurers: who certifies Shari'ah compliance, how it is controlled internally, and how it is independently audited and reported.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy runs from the governing Shari'ah governance standard (and the takaful-specific Shari'ah governance standard / Insurance Authority Decision No. 50 of 2019) down to institution-level framework, divisions and audit obligations.

The ISSC is the hub definition: the internal Shari'ah control and internal Shari'ah audit divisions report to or support it, and the external Shari'ah auditor's report is addressed to/interacts with it.
Three Lines of Defense allocates the obligation chain — business first line, Shari'ah control second, Shari'ah audit third, with external audit as an outside assurance layer.

Takaful-specific substantive rules (insurance surplus, qard hasan from the shareholders' account) are the transactions the ISSC and Shari'ah auditors must opine on; AAOIFI standards supply the substantive compliance benchmark.
start_here: Shari'ah Governance Standard for Takaful Insurance Companies

data.theme: Supervisory-level Shari'ah oversight: the central-authority/ISSC relationship, the operating Shari'ah compliance function, and the special regime for conventional institutions running an Islamic window.
how_members_connect: Statutory base (Central Bank Law) → Shari'ah Governance Standard → guidance notes on the ISSC charter and on the Shari'ah compliance function, i.e. a clean law→regulation→guidance chain.
The Higher Shari'ah Authority sits above institution-level ISSCs; its rulings bind the ISSC and, through it, the compliance function.

The Shari'ah compliance function's duties are elaborated operationally through review-process stages, annual plan, prioritisation parameters, sampling methodology, product checklist and field review — all directed at controlling Shari'ah non-compliance risk.
The Islamic window standard extends the same governance and ALM requirements to institutions that are not wholly Islamic, marking a scope boundary.
start_here: Guidance Note Re Shari'ah Compliance Function
Standard re. Regulatory Requirements for Financial Institutions Housing an Islamic Window

data.theme: Prudential corporate governance and remuneration obligations for banks (and insurers/takaful): board and senior management accountability, control-function independence, and pay structures that must not incentivise excessive risk.
how_members_connect: Central Bank Law is the enabling statute; the Corporate Governance Regulation (Circular 83/2019) and the Remuneration Regulation for banks and insurance companies are the implementing instruments, with accompanying standards elaborating them.
Remuneration obligations chain from the board → remuneration committee → remuneration policy/framework → variable remuneration, material risk takers, and malus/clawback.
Control-function independence is a shared thread: independent audit function, risk committee responsibilities, and separate pay rules for control-function staff protect against conflicts.

Cross-regime touchpoint: senior management governance duties pull in sanctions/TFS obligations (international financial sanctions, terrorism lists decision); proportionality is addressed for small organisations.
start_here: Remuneration Regulation for Banks and Insurance Companies

data.theme: Financial reporting, external audit and market disclosure obligations for banks — the assurance and transparency layer sitting on top of corporate governance.
how_members_connect: The Financial Reporting and External Audit Regulation is the anchoring instrument; it expressly links to the Corporate Governance Regulation, so audit duties and board duties are read together.
External audit obligations are benchmarked to international auditing standards, and audit scope reaches into Pillar 3 disclosure content.
Board responsibilities and the compensation system are governance inputs that must be disclosed/reported, closing the loop between governance and transparency.
start_here: Financial Reporting and External Audit Regulation 162/2018

data.theme: Conduct and operational rules for selling insurance through electronic channels, including insurer websites, apps and price comparison platforms, and the identity-verification duties that attach when the contract is concluded remotely.
how_members_connect: The electronic insurance resolution is the hub instrument: it sets the permitted scope of electronic insurance operations and delegates detailed conduct duties to website management and price-comparison requirements.

Remote onboarding creates a cross-regime link into AML/KYC customer identification — the 'Customer' being identified electronically is the same person as the insurance policyholder, so CDD standards ride on top of the insurance conduct rules.
The e-commerce law supplies the enabling legal basis for electronic contracting, signatures and records that the insurance regulation presupposes.
Price comparison websites and electronic insurance operations are conceptually parallel channels, both constrained by disclosure, data accuracy and intermediary-licensing limits.

data.theme: Prudential entry requirements for insurers — minimum paid-up capital, its amendment over time, and related licensing conditions for investment limits and points of sale.
how_members_connect: The insurance law is the parent statute; the Cabinet Resolution on minimum capital is the implementing instrument, and board decisions sit below as supervisory detail — a clean law → resolution → decision hierarchy.
Version control matters: the original 2009 resolution, the 2017 amendment and the consolidated text must be read together to identify the currently operative capital threshold.
The commercial companies law is cited as the general corporate-form baseline that the insurance-specific capital floor overrides or supplements.

Investment-limit and point-of-sale decisions attach continuing conditions to the entity whose capital adequacy the resolutions establish, linking entry capital to ongoing asset and distribution constraints.

data.theme: Licensing and ongoing conduct regime for health insurance third-party administrators, covering entry conditions, financial security, and the contractual chain between TPA, insurer and medical service providers.
how_members_connect: The TPA licensing instructions define the regulated person ('Third Party Administrator') and impose the licensing conditions; the consolidated version is the operative text and supersedes the original where amended.

The TPA–insurance company agreement is the mandated contractual instrument through which delegated claims/administration functions are performed — outsourcing responsibility remains with the licensed insurer.
Medical service providers sit at the end of the obligation chain: TPA duties on network contracting and claims handling run through to them.
The bank guaranty requirement is the financial-security condition tied to licence grant and renewal.

data.theme: The core prudential and financial-reporting rulebook for insurers and takaful operators: technical provisions, solvency and own funds, admissible assets and investment limits, actuarial and audit functions, and the governance wrappers (outsourcing, fraud, internal audit) around them. It also carries the actuary licensing regime and an insurance FinTech sandbox pathway.
how_members_connect: A single statutory root (the insurance law) supports the conventional and takaful financial regulations, which in turn define the calculation chain: technical provisions (UPR, URR, OSLR, IBNR, ALAE/ULAE, mathematical reserve) feed solvency margin, solvency capital requirement, own funds and the minimum guarantee fund.

Asset-side rules link together: policyholders' rights investment basis, admissible assets, allocation limits and the investment committee are cumulative constraints on the same balance sheet, with AAOIFI standards substituting for takaful entities.

Assurance and gatekeeping obligations interlock: the actuary (and its separate licensing regulation and professional indemnity condition), the external auditor with its duty to report to the Central Bank, and internal audit all validate the same prudential figures reported under IFRS on the prescribed financial statement forms.

The chapter-level continuing obligations — licensing, accounts and audit, outsourcing, fraud management — and the sandbox decision operate as the governance and entry perimeter within which the financial regulations bite.

Shared defined terms in the glossary are what make the conventional and takaful regimes comparable; differences are mainly in fund segregation and Shariah-compliant asset treatment, not in the solvency architecture.
start_here: Solvency Margin and Minimum Guarantee Fund

data.theme: Prudential, governance and conduct regime for Stored Value Facilities (SVFs) as a licensed payment activity: what an SVF is, how customer float must be held and safeguarded, and the risk-management, technology, conduct and enforcement duties attaching to the licensee.
how_members_connect: Definitional spine: the SVF Regulation defines Stored Value Facility by reference to 'money's worth', which scopes every downstream obligation including clearing and settlement arrangements.

Obligation chain within one instrument: the Regulation's articles cascade from general risk management and internal control, through information and accounting systems, float management and safekeeping, to technology and specific risk management.

The technology risk article acts as a parent for the specific sub-disciplines — cyber resilience, payment security, business continuity and reputation risk — so each is read as a component duty, not a standalone rule.

Cross-regime hooks: the Regulation pulls in AML/CFT procedures (customer due diligence and monitoring applied to SVF holders) and consumer-protection/business-conduct duties, with Article 15 supplying the supervisory enforcement and sanctions consequence for breach of any of the above.
start_here: Management and Safekeeping of the Float (Article 11)

data.theme: Minimum aggregate capital funds a licensee must hold and maintain on an ongoing basis — a prudential entry and continuing-authorisation condition rather than a conduct rule.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster: no internal cross-references captured; it functions as a standalone prudential threshold.
Practically it should be read against the licensing and enforcement provisions of whichever regime imposes it, since capital shortfall is typically a supervisory trigger.
Check the source instrument before applying — the applicable figure and calculation basis are regime-specific (payments/SVF vs finance companies).

data.theme: Conditions under which a regulated entity may outsource functions to a third party while retaining full regulatory responsibility for the outsourced activity.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster with no captured internal linkage; it is a horizontal obligation that attaches to multiple regimes.
Legally relevant as a non-delegation principle: outsourcing does not transfer accountability for AML/CFT, risk management, data protection or customer-protection duties.
Should be cross-read with governance, technology-risk and third-party reliance provisions in the operative regime (e.g. reliance on third parties for CDD).

data.theme: AML/CFT obligations applied to licensed exchange houses / money-changing businesses, including the statutory basis, supervisory standards and sector-specific guidance.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy is visible: primary AML/CFT statute → sectoral standards chapter for exchange business → supervisory guidance for licensed exchange houses, with an article-level AML/CFT procedures provision operationalising them.
All members anchor to the FATF Standards as the interpretive benchmark, so guidance is read as elaborating, not extending, the statutory duties.
Duplicate labelling of the same decree (cited two ways) means the statute is the single common authority behind both the guidance and the general AML/CFT requirements.

Scope caution: the cited Federal Decree Law is a UAE instrument, not KSA legislation — before relying on this cluster for a SAMA question, confirm the equivalent Saudi AML Law and its Implementing Regulation apply instead.
start_here: AML/CFT Guidance for Licensed Exchange Houses

data.theme: Constitutional and institutional layer of central banking: the central bank's legal mandate, the Governor's powers, licensing of financial activities/institutions, resolution powers over licensees, oversight of financial market infrastructures, currency issuance, and the administrative/financial sanctioning regime with its appeal route.
how_members_connect: All nodes hang off the central bank as the source of authority; licensing, resolution, FMI designation and currency are separate heads of the same statutory mandate.
Definitional chain: 'Licensed Financial Activities' determines who qualifies as a 'Licensed Financial Institution', which in turn fixes the perimeter of resolution and sanctioning powers.
'Designated Infrastructure' is a sub-set of 'Financial Market Infrastructure', triggering heightened oversight obligations.
Enforcement chain: sanctions imposed by the authority are reviewable by the Grievances & Appeals Committee — the due-process counterweight to the sanctioning power.

data.theme: Market-conduct and ethics regime for insurance companies and their intermediaries — pricing, policy documentation, and claims handling — as successively restated by regulator resolutions.
how_members_connect: Vertical consolidation chain: earlier ministerial resolution → the 2010 Code of Conduct → the 2019 consolidated Code adopted by IA Board Decision No. 40 of 2019; the later instrument supersedes/restates the earlier for currency purposes.
The article-level nodes (pricing, the policy, claim procedures) are the substantive obligation set sitting inside the Code.
Conduct duties here mirror general consumer-protection themes (disclosure, fair pricing, timely claim settlement) but are insurance-sector specific in scope.
start_here: Code of Conduct and Ethics for Insurance Companies (Res 3/2010)

data.theme: Authorisation and ongoing supervision of loan-based crowdfunding platforms: licensing gate, prudential floor, governance/risk/internal-control requirements, conduct of business toward lenders and borrowers, client money segregation, and reporting/record-keeping.
how_members_connect: Single parent regulation branches into article-level obligations; each article is a distinct, independently enforceable duty on the licensed platform.

Obligation chain: licensing (Art. 3) is the precondition; prudential (Art. 4), governance (Art. 5–6) and internal controls (Art. 7) are continuing licence conditions; Art. 9 is the supervisory evidence layer.
Conduct of business (Art. 8) carries the customer-facing duties and pulls in credit-bureau reporting/enquiry and client-money protection — money held for participants is not platform property.
Cross-reference to Central Bank Regulation No. 29/2011 links crowdfunding lending to the pre-existing retail bank-lending conduct rules.

data.theme: Retail consumer protection framework and its Shari'ah-governance overlay: responsible business and market conduct, responsible financing, disclosure of rates and fee caps, complaint handling, consumer data/asset protection, financial inclusion and accessibility, plus Shari'ah compliance duties for Islamic financial institutions.
how_members_connect: Law-to-regulation hierarchy: the central bank decretal law is the enabling statute cited by the Consumer Protection Regulation and by each of its standards/articles.

The Regulation acts as a hub: each principle (responsible conduct, financing, complaints, data protection, education, inclusion, oversight) is a separate standard with its own obligations; the fee-and-commission annexure and interest/profit-rate provisions are the hard quantitative limits.

Shari'ah layer: the Shari'ah governance standard and annual Shari'ah report guidance impose parallel compliance and board-reporting duties on Islamic financial institutions, so Islamic products must satisfy both conduct and Shari'ah requirements.

Accessibility obligations import the People of Determination law into the inclusion standard; payment-data protection provisions interlock with general consumer data duties — flag overlap where a payments regime also regulates the same data.
start_here: Standard Re Shari'ah Governance for IFIs

data.theme: Crowdfunding intermediation: the licensed platform's contractual and disclosure duties toward the two counterparty classes it brings together, lenders and borrowers.
how_members_connect: The Crowdfunding Platform is the regulated actor at the centre; all other members are either its counterparties or its obligations.
The Client Agreement is the instrument through which the platform's duties bite, defining rights and terms for both Lender and Borrower as defined client categories.
Required Crowdfunding Company Disclosures attach to the platform as an ongoing transparency obligation running alongside the contractual layer.
Definitional linkage matters: whether a participant is a Lender or Borrower determines which disclosure and agreement terms apply.

data.theme: Licensing and conduct of payment service providers and card schemes, and the AML/CFT overlay that applies to payment and stored-value products.
how_members_connect: The Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation is the hub: it defines Payment Service Provider, Retail Payment Service and Retail Payment Service User, and carries its Annexes as binding scope and control detail.
Annex I fixes the taxonomy of services (and therefore licence category); Annex II imposes the technology risk and information security expectations on the same licensees.
Cross-regime link: the payments regulation cites the AML/CTF law, so a PSP carries both prudential/conduct duties and customer due diligence, screening and reporting duties.

The AML/CFT payments guidance sits below the law as interpretive material and pulls in the terrorism-list decision and the Stored Value Facilities Regulation, extending sanctions/TFS screening expectations across payment and e-money products.
start_here: Retail Payment Services and Card Schemes Regulation

data.theme: Prudential credit risk containment for banks: concentration limits on single and connected exposures, plus the classification, provisioning and write-off framework for credit portfolios.
how_members_connect: Clear hierarchy: the Central Bank Law is the enabling statute; the Large Exposures Regulation and Credit Risk Management Regulation are made under it; standards, circulars and notices sit beneath as implementing detail.
The Credit Risk Management Regulation cross-refers to the Large Exposures Regulation, so concentration limits are read as one component of the wider credit risk governance duty.
Transitional layer: the Grandfathering Scheme and the large exposure monitoring circular determine how legacy exposures are treated against current limits — decisive for breach assessment.
Accounting-facing instruments (loan classification, write-off, IFRS 9 guidance) feed the provisioning inputs that the credit risk regulation assumes.
Peripheral statutory links (Higher Shari'ah Authority, Insurance Law) reflect the enabling law's broader scope rather than credit-specific obligations.
start_here: Circular No. 32 of 2013 (Monitoring of Large Exposure Limits)

data.theme: Card scheme operator obligations: periodic regulatory reporting and adherence to recognised payment card and national information security standards.
how_members_connect: Card Scheme is the defined regulated entity; the other members are the duties attached to that status.
Annex III sets the reporting content and cadence owed to the regulator by the scheme.
PCI DSS and the national information assurance standards are incorporated by reference, converting external technical standards into supervisory expectations.
Reads as the card-scheme branch of the retail payments regime, so it should be interpreted with the parent payments regulation and its security annex.

data.theme: Capital treatment of counterparty credit risk arising from derivatives and securities financing, including exposures to central counterparties, the CVA add-on, and the look-through regime for banks' equity investments in funds. The problem-space is how much regulatory capital a bank must hold for risks it takes through counterparties, clearing arrangements and fund structures.
how_members_connect: The Counterparty Credit Risk Standard is the anchor obligation; the CVA Standard and the Equity Investments in Funds Standard both route back to it for exposure measurement, so a change in CCR measurement propagates into CVA and fund capital.
QCCP is a qualified sub-set of the defined term CCP, and qualification status drives the concessionary treatment of trade exposures and default fund contributions.

The EIF hierarchy (LTA, then MBA, then FBA) is a mandatory cascade: the bank must use the most granular approach for which it has sufficient information, with the leverage adjustment applied to the resulting risk weight.
CVA Hedges and CVA Capital Calculation are sub-components specified within the CVA Standard rather than free-standing rules.

data.theme: The standardised approach for measuring counterparty credit exposure (SA-CCR): how a bank determines exposure at default for derivative transactions at netting-set level.
how_members_connect: EAD is the output obligation; it is defined as a function of Replacement Cost and Potential Future Exposure, so each input definition is legally load-bearing for the capital number.
The Netting Set is the unit of account — recognition of netting determines whether exposures may be offset, and the PFE Multiplier and RC are both computed per netting set.
Supervisory Duration and the PFE Multiplier are supervisor-prescribed parameters, leaving limited firm discretion; deviation requires SAMA acceptance rather than internal judgement.
Duplicate-looking terms (Netting Set/Netting Sets, PFE/Potential Future Exposure) reflect parallel drafting across the standard and should be read as the same defined concept.

data.theme: The asset-class add-on mechanics that feed the potential future exposure component of SA-CCR, covering interest rate, FX, credit, equity and commodity derivatives.
how_members_connect: The Hedging Set is the common organising unit: each asset-class add-on is calculated within hedging sets, and hedging-set definition determines permitted offsetting.

Each add-on is built from the same chain of prescribed inputs — Adjusted Notional Amount, Supervisory Delta Adjustment, Maturity Factor — so the inputs are shared obligations, not asset-class specific ones.
Supervisory Factors and Correlations (Table 2) is the prescribed parameter table; the values are set by the supervisor and are not open to internal calibration.
This cluster is the computational layer beneath the SA-CCR exposure cluster and should be read alongside it rather than in isolation.

data.theme: Calculation of the credit valuation adjustment capital charge and the recognition of hedges against it, and how the resulting charge enters risk-weighted assets and the wider capital adequacy assessment.
how_members_connect: The CVA Capital Formula is the operative calculation; Single-Name Exposure and the Supervisory Discount Factor are its defined inputs.
Hedge recognition is conditional: only Eligible CVA Hedges (including qualifying Index CDS Hedges) may reduce the charge, so eligibility criteria are the decisive legal test.
Prescribed Risk Weights convert exposures into the charge, which then aggregates into Risk-Weighted Assets.
Pillar 2 Capital sits at a different level — a supervisory assessment overlay on top of the Pillar 1 RWA outcome, not an input to the formula.

data.theme: Prudential capital adequacy for banks under the Basel III construct: what qualifies as regulatory capital, the deductions and adjustments applied to it, the buffers layered on minimum ratios, and the distribution and exposure-concentration consequences of falling short.
how_members_connect: Anchored on a shared defined-term hierarchy of capital tiers (CET1, AT1, T2 feeding Tier 1 and total capital supply), with regulatory adjustments, threshold deductions, DTA and minority-interest treatment operating as corrections to the same base definitions.

Obligation chain runs from the Basel III framework into the domestic capital adequacy regulation and its implementing circular (Circular 52/2017), then into specialist standards such as the leverage ratio standard, which cites the regulation and reuses its capital definitions.

Buffer and distribution mechanics are interlocking: conservation and countercyclical buffers are met in CET1, and buffer shortfalls bite through the Maximum Distributable Amount; D-SIB designation and PONV/loss-absorption terms add systemic and instrument-level conditions.

Exposure-side members (large exposure definition, group of connected counterparties, sovereign/PSE and related-party exposures) are calibrated as percentages of the capital base, so they inherit the capital definitions; transitional grandfathering and amortisation govern legacy instruments.

data.theme: Risk-weighting of banking-book credit exposures under the standardised approach: how exposures are bucketed by counterparty class and how external ratings and conversion factors drive the applicable risk weight.
how_members_connect: A single parent rule (the standardised approach) enumerates the exposure classes — sovereigns, PSEs, banks, corporates, regulatory retail, residential property-secured claims — each a defined term with its own eligibility conditions.
Off-balance-sheet items enter the same calculation via credit conversion factors, linking the exposure classes to a common exposure-at-default measure.
Rating inputs depend on recognised ECAIs, whose eligibility is tied to international standards (IOSCO CRA conduct code) and whose grades are mapped through rating scale correspondence tables.
Preferential treatment of PSE claims is conditioned on inclusion in the published government-related entities list, a cross-reference that determines whether sovereign-equivalent weights apply.

data.theme: Recognition of collateral, guarantees and credit derivatives as credit risk mitigants, and the conditions and haircuts that limit how much capital relief a bank may claim.
how_members_connect: One parent CRM rule sets the eligibility gateway and then branches into two mutually exclusive computational routes — the simple and comprehensive approaches to collateral.
Unfunded protection (guarantees, credit derivatives) shares the same recognition preconditions as funded collateral: legal certainty, eligible protection providers and defined credit events.
Haircut and adjustment members (currency mismatch, maturity mismatch) act as mandatory reductions applied across both funded and unfunded protection.
Basket products (first- and second-to-default derivatives) are carve-outs from the general credit derivative recognition rule with their own attribution logic.

data.theme: Technical field-level specification for payment messages in a central bank payment system — the mandatory content and formatting of instruction data that supports downstream traceability and settlement.
how_members_connect: Isolated node in the graph: no internal cross-references, so it should be read as a standalone operational annex rather than part of an obligation chain.

Its regulatory significance is indirect — message field content underpins originator/beneficiary information duties in the payments and AML/CTF wire-transfer regimes, so interpret it alongside those rules rather than on its own.
Note jurisdictional scope: this is a UAE central bank artefact and is not itself a SAMA obligation; treat it as comparative material unless a SAMA instrument adopts equivalent requirements.

data.theme: Definitional perimeter for payment tokens and related crypto-asset activity: what counts as a payment token versus a broader crypto-asset, what backing must sit behind it, and what must be disclosed before it is offered.
how_members_connect: Anchored on the defined term 'Payment Token', which sets the scope boundary against the wider 'Crypto-Asset' category and thereby determines which licensing regime applies.
'Reserve of Assets' is the backing obligation attached to the token, i.e. an ongoing prudential/segregation duty rather than a one-off condition.
'White Paper' operates as the mandatory disclosure instrument, cross-referencing both the token's characteristics and its reserve arrangements.
'Payment Token Services' extends the perimeter from issuance to service provision, pulling intermediaries into the licensed activity list.

data.theme: The AML/CFT obligation stack for financial institutions — primary law, implementing decision, supervisory guidance — plus the international standard-setting bodies and typology material (notably trade-based money laundering) that inform risk assessment.
how_members_connect: Clear hierarchy: the AML/CFT primary law sits above the implementing Cabinet Decision, which is in turn operationalised by the supervisory Guidelines for Financial Institutions.
FATF (with MENAFATF and the Egmont Group) is the common upstream reference used to interpret standards; guidance cites them rather than creating independent obligations.
Institution-level duties — staff screening and training, group-wide oversight of branches and subsidiaries — trace directly back to specific articles of the Decision and Law.
Typology annexes (TBML red flags, vulnerable economic sectors) feed the risk-based approach: they shape risk ratings and suspicious-transaction judgement but are indicative, not prescriptive lists.
The Glossary ties the whole cluster together by fixing defined terms used across law, decision and guidance.

data.theme: Licensing and prudential entry conditions for exchange houses: permitted scope of exchange business by licence category, legal form, minimum capital and bank guarantee, with adjacent trade-finance and wage-remittance activities.
how_members_connect: Regulation-to-standards chain: the 2014 licensing and monitoring regulations are the legal base, with the Standards document elaborating requirements chapter by chapter.
Chapter 1 fixes the activity perimeter (what 'exchange business' covers and what each licence permits); Chapter 2 attaches the entry conditions to that perimeter.
Licence category determines permitted activities — e.g. WPS salary disbursement is tied to a specific category rather than available to all licensees.
Bank guarantee functions as a continuing prudential condition of licence, distinct from its commercial use in documentary trade finance and letters of credit.
start_here: Regulations regarding Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business 2014
Chapter 1: Scope of License and Exchange Business
Chapter 2: Legal Forms, Capital and Bank Guarantee

data.theme: Conduct and prudential obligations on licensed payment token issuers, covering disclosure, finality of transfers on distributed ledgers, and the risk-management and technology-security framework expected of the issuer.
how_members_connect: 'Payment Token Issuer' is the obligated person; the licence requirement and the dirham-denominated token definition set who is in scope and for what.
The white paper article is the disclosure gateway, and the transfer-finality article cross-refers to it — settlement certainty representations must match what was disclosed.
General risk management and internal controls is the parent obligation; technology risk and information security is its specialised limb, applied to the underlying DLT arrangements.
The 'Virtual Asset' reference marks a scope boundary — tokens meeting the payment token definition are carved out of, or distinguished from, the virtual asset regime.
start_here: Article 34: General Risk Management & Internal Control Systems

data.theme: Prudential capital treatment of securitisation and resecuritisation exposures under SAMA's adoption of the Basel securitisation framework, including hierarchy of calculation approaches and the qualifying conditions for preferential treatment.
how_members_connect: The Securitisation Standard sits at the top of the hierarchy and points down to each calculation method (SEC-ERBA, SEC-SA) and to the qualifying regime for STC transactions.

Both approaches share the same defined risk-parameter vocabulary — attachment/detachment points, tranche thickness and tranche maturity — so a definitional change propagates across all risk-weight outcomes.

Scope and integrity conditions (resecuritisation exclusions, ABCP conduit treatment, clean-up call limits, prohibition on implicit support) act as gating conditions: failing them removes recognition of risk transfer or preferential STC weights.
Clean-up calls and implicit support are conceptually linked as forms of non-contractual or residual sponsor exposure that can force re-consolidation of transferred risk.

data.theme: Capital requirements for trading-book and market-risk exposures: equity, FX, commodities and options, plus the valuation standards that underpin the positions being measured.
how_members_connect: The Market Risk Standard is the parent instrument; each risk category (equity, FX, commodity) is a subordinate charge computed under it.

Duplicate-labelled nodes (Market Risk / Market Risk Standard; Equity Position Risk / Equity Risk) reflect the same obligations expressed in different source instruments — treat as one obligation set when citing.
Options treatment branches into alternative methods (simplified vs delta-plus), with eligibility to use the simpler method being a scope limit on the institution, not a free choice.
Prudent Valuation Guidance conditions the inputs to every charge, so valuation adequacy is a precondition to a compliant market-risk calculation.

data.theme: Non-market prudential risk regimes — operational risk, leverage, counterparty credit and the Pillar 2 supervisory review — covering how banks self-assess capital adequacy beyond minimum Pillar 1 charges.
how_members_connect: Pillar 2 / ICAAP is the integrating obligation: it pulls in risks not fully captured in Pillar 1 (concentration, IRRBB, liquidity, reputational/implicit support, securitisation supervisory review).
Operational risk is a tiered approach hierarchy (basic indicator → standardised → alternative standardised), with supervisory permission and qualifying criteria governing movement up the tiers.
The leverage standard chains from the exposure measure definition through derivative exposures into counterparty credit risk methodology — a shared measurement basis across two regimes.
Multiple members cite the Basel Committee as the source framework, which is relevant to interpretation where SAMA text is silent or adopts Basel by reference.
Reputational risk and implicit support cross-link this cluster to the securitisation framework.

data.theme: Pillar 3 public disclosure obligations — the market-discipline leg of the Basel framework, requiring banks to publish prescribed quantitative and qualitative information on capital, risk exposures and risk assessment processes.
how_members_connect: Single-member community; its legal significance is derivative — it imposes disclosure duties over the computations produced under the Pillar 1 standards (credit, market, operational, securitisation, leverage) and the Pillar 2 process.
Read alongside the Basel Risk Approaches and Securitisation clusters, since disclosure templates and frequency are keyed to the approach the bank actually applies.

data.theme: Supervisory expectations for financial institutions deploying big data analytics and artificial intelligence, covering the governance, ethical and model-lifecycle controls that must sit around such use before and during deployment.
how_members_connect: A single overarching big data/AI subject node anchors the cluster, with the governance framework, ethics/fairness and model validation items operating as its mandatory control components.
The governance framework supplies the institutional layer (ownership, approval, oversight) that the fairness and validation obligations are executed under.
Model validation and versioning is the operational evidence trail that supports ethics/fairness claims, so the two are read together rather than independently.
Cross-regime relevance: AI-driven decisioning touches consumer protection (fair treatment, explainability) and data/credit information rules where personal data feeds the models.
start_here: Big Data and AI Governance Framework

data.theme: Regulatory treatment of distributed ledger technology in the KSA financial sector, focusing on governance accountability, permissible design choices, and the control risks of permissionless/anonymous ledgers.
how_members_connect: The DLT concept node is the definitional hub; governance framework, design principles and the permissionless/anonymity item are its scoping and conditioning limbs.
Design principles flow directly into cryptographic key management, making key custody and lifecycle a technical precondition for an acceptable DLT design.
The permissionless/anonymity item functions as a scope limit or heightened-scrutiny trigger, since anonymity cuts against CDD, traceability and wire-transfer originator/beneficiary obligations.
Hierarchy runs from the governance framework (who is accountable) down to design and key-management expectations (how the arrangement must be built and controlled).

data.theme: Controls governing application programming interfaces and the authentication of users and identities, including where API activity is outsourced and where customer data is exposed through interfaces.
how_members_connect: The API governance framework is the parent obligation; design principles and management/monitoring are its build-stage and run-stage counterparts.
API governance cross-references data protection and the Outsourcing Service Provider definition, pulling third-party and confidentiality regimes into the API perimeter.

Authentication forms a nested chain: identity lifecycle management sets enrolment/change/revocation duties, multifactor authentication is the required strength, and biometric authentication is a specific factor type subject to its own conditions.
API design principles reference multifactor authentication, linking interface design obligations to access-control requirements rather than treating them as separate regimes.

data.theme: AML/CTF obligations attaching to cross-border correspondent banking and wire transfers, including the prohibition on dealing with shell banks, nesting/downstream relationship risk, and group-wide and supervisory oversight.
how_members_connect: Shared AML defined terms drive the obligations: Financial Institutions is the obligated-person definition, and Correspondent Banking Relationship, Wire Transfers, Shell Bank, Nesting and Intermediation set the scope of enhanced due diligence.
Nesting and intermediation describe the indirect-access risk that makes respondent-side CDD and the shell bank prohibition operative in practice.
Financial Group extends obligations beyond the single institution to group-wide programmes, branches and majority-owned subsidiaries.
Supervisory Authority is the enforcement and reporting counterpart, confirming who supervises the obligated institutions and receives the relevant filings.

data.theme: Market-risk capital treatment of interest rate exposures in the trading book, splitting the charge into issuer-specific risk and general market risk and prescribing the permitted measurement methodologies.
how_members_connect: Hierarchical decomposition: the trading book interest rate risk charge is defined as the sum of a specific risk component and a general market risk component.

General market risk is operationalised through two alternative prescribed measurement approaches (maturity-band and duration-based), so the choice of method is an exercise of a permitted option, not a deviation.
The generic interest rate risk node links the trading-book treatment to the wider rate-risk concept, marking the scope boundary between trading book capital charges and banking book rate risk.
All members share the same defined terms used for capital adequacy reporting, so definitional drift between them changes the capital number.

data.theme: Retail and consumer credit conduct rules for banks — product perimeter (personal loans, car loans, credit cards), pricing/interest calculation method, and affordability limits on instalment deductions.
how_members_connect: A single regulation acts as the parent instrument and defines each credit product type, the interest computation method, and the deduction cap; the products are obligations-bearing sub-nodes rather than independent rules.
Version lineage matters: the consolidated version supersedes/amends the earlier version, so the operative text for any obligation must be taken from the consolidated instrument.
The instalment cap is an affordability constraint attached primarily to personal lending and interacts with the interest computation formula in determining a compliant offer.
Older labour/salary legislation is cited as the source of the salary concept underpinning the deduction cap, an external cross-reference outside the banking regime.
start_here: Bank Loans & Other Services Regulation (Consolidated VER2)

data.theme: A mixed licensing-and-conduct cluster anchored on the central bank law: the prudential perimeter for low-risk specialised banks, recovery planning duties, the regulatory sandbox route for innovators, and telemarketing/consumer-consent restrictions.
how_members_connect: Common statutory parent: the specialised banks regulation, sandbox conditions and recovery-planning articles all derive authority from the central bank law, giving a law → regulation → circular hierarchy.
Specialised bank licensing is defined by a triangle of permitted activities, minimum capital, and credit exposure restrictions, with credit-bureau reporting as an underwriting input.

Recovery planning is an internally sequenced obligation chain: plan requirement → indicators → options → scenario testing → recovery capacity, with central bank liquidity facilities excluded/limited as a recovery option, plus continuity and communication annexes.

The sandbox and telemarketing/DNCR consent rules sit here through the consumer protection regulation, which is the conduct bridge between innovation-stage firms and customer-contact restrictions — a different regime from prudential licensing and should not be read as one.
start_here: Specialized Banks with Low Risk Regulation

data.theme: Core AML/CFT obligations imposed on financial institutions: the statutory offence and duty framework, its implementing executive regulation, and the supervisory procedures that operationalise CDD, reporting and controls.
how_members_connect: Clean instrument hierarchy: AML decree-law → cabinet-level executive regulation → board-level supervisory AML/CFT procedures, each narrowing the preceding layer.
The supervisory procedures cite both the law and the executive regulation as their legal basis, so obligations must be read cumulatively rather than substituted.
The earlier AML circular is carried forward by reference, raising a supersession question about which text governs where the older guidance conflicts.

'Financial Institution' is the defined scope term that determines who bears the obligations; its perimeter differs from customer/consumer definitions used in conduct regimes and should be checked before applying duties cross-regime.

data.theme: Takaful fund mechanics: the participants' risk fund as a segregated pool and the interest-free loan mechanism used to cover its deficits.
how_members_connect: Qard Hasan is defined by reference to the Participants' Risk Fund — it is the remedy triggered when that fund is in deficit, creating a conditional funding obligation on the operator/shareholders' account.
Both terms are definitional anchors that other takaful instruments (fund segregation, solvency, operator fee rules) rely on rather than standalone obligations.

Linkage is hierarchical in practice: fund segregation rules create the deficit risk; the Qard Hasan obligation is the prescribed consequence, including repayment/recovery conditions from future surpluses.

data.theme: Insurance and takaful sector regulation covering licensing and conduct of intermediaries, composite-company separation, solvency and financial regulations, motor unified policies, life/family takaful pricing and distribution, surveyors/loss adjusters, plus the AML/CTF and targeted-financial-sanctions overlay applicable to insurers. Note that a substantial portion of these instruments are UAE Insurance Authority / federal instruments, so jurisdictional scope must be checked before applying them to a KSA question.
how_members_connect: Clear law → regulation → decision hierarchy: the establishing insurance law is the cited authority for nearly every Board/Administrative Decision in the cluster, and the Financial Regulations for Insurance/Takaful Companies is the shared prudential reference for solvency, composite separation and reinsurance decisions.

Shared defined terms bind sub-groups: separation of persons/fund versus property/liability insurance links composite-company, reinsurance and takaful rules; Wakala and Mudaraba fees link the Shari'a committee, takaful regulations and life/family takaful instructions.

Product-level chains: the unified motor vehicle policy decisions, their consolidated versions, the TPL and loss-and-damage policy documents, depreciation schedules and surveyor/loss-adjuster appointment for disputes form one continuous obligation chain from policy wording to claims settlement.

AML/CTF sub-chain runs law → executive regulations → terrorist-lists regulations, and attaches to firm-level duties (compliance officer, risk assessment framework, reporting) and to the data/reporting guidance manuals used for supervisory submissions.

Distribution and conduct cross-links: marketing insurance through banks, designated officer conditions, insurance consultant licensing, commission limits, free-look period and the code of conduct all govern the intermediary-to-policyholder relationship.
start_here: Federal Law 6/2007 - Establishment of Insurance Authority

data.theme: Adjudication of insurance disputes in KSA: the constitution, jurisdiction and procedure of the committees that settle disputes and violations arising under insurance contracts and supervision, including hearings conducted by remote means.
how_members_connect: The two versions of the Regulation of Insurance Dispute Committees sit in a version hierarchy — the consolidated text supersedes/amends VER1, so effective-date and transitional questions turn on which version governs a filed claim.
Both versions constitute and empower the Committee for Settlement of Insurance Disputes, which is the operative defined body for jurisdiction, quorum and appeal routes.
Remote Communication Technology appears as a procedural permission within the Regulation (service, hearings, pleadings), not as a standalone instrument.
Dispute Settlement & Resolution is the umbrella concept linking committee procedure to broader consumer-protection and complaint-handling channels.
start_here: Regulation of Insurance Dispute Committees (Consolidated VER2)
Committee for Settlement of Insurance Disputes

data.theme: Supervisory expectations for financial institutions adopting enabling technologies (APIs, biometrics, digital identity), including where such adoption is treated as outsourcing and therefore pulls in third-party risk obligations.
how_members_connect: The enabling-technology guidelines are the parent instrument; the defined term Enabling Technology scopes which technologies and use cases the expectations bite on.
The guidelines expressly route technology arrangements into the outsourcing/OSP regime, meaning accountability remains with the institution and outsourcing controls and notification duties apply.
Biometrics sits inside a digital-identity chain — credential service provider and identity lifecycle management — which is the point of contact with CDD/identification obligations in the AML regime.
APIs are treated as a delivery mode of enabling technology, linking this cluster to data-sharing and third-party access controls.
start_here: Guidelines for Financial Institutions adopting Enabling Technologies

data.theme: The preventive AML/CTF core: risk assessment, customer due diligence and record keeping obligations that a financial institution must build into its AML/CFT programme on a risk-sensitive basis.
how_members_connect: Obligation chain runs law/Cabinet Decision → Implementing Regulation → supervisory guidelines, with the July 2023 AML/CFT Guidelines citing the implementing regulation as its legal base (note this strand is UAE-sourced material; confirm jurisdictional fit before relying on it for KSA obligations).
CDD is the hub definition: it drives customer risk profiling, ongoing monitoring, and the identification of Legal Persons and Legal Arrangements (beneficial ownership and control).

The Risk-Based Approach conditions intensity of measures — Simplified Due Diligence and variants such as Customer Identification Diligence and Agent Due Diligence are calibrations of, not exceptions to, the CDD duty.
Record Keeping and Required Record Types are the evidentiary back-end of CDD and monitoring, fixing what must be retained and made available to supervisors.

data.theme: Governance of cloud outsourcing: classifying cloud arrangements by materiality and ensuring the institution can continue operating or withdraw from a provider without disrupting regulated services.
how_members_connect: Cloud computing is the parent concept; materiality assessment is the gating step that determines the intensity of supervisory requirements (approval/notification, contractual terms, controls).
Exit and resolution planning is a downstream obligation conditional on the materiality classification — material workloads require a documented, testable exit path.

Business continuity planning is the overlapping general obligation: cloud dependencies must be reflected in continuity and recovery arrangements, so the two duties are read together rather than in isolation.
Effectively a sub-regime of third-party/outsourcing risk, so concentration risk and non-delegable accountability of the institution carry across.

data.theme: The detection-to-reporting leg of AML/CTF: transaction monitoring, internal escalation, and mandatory suspicious transaction/activity reporting to the FIU, plus the governance, training and confidentiality duties that support it.
how_members_connect: Monitoring and red-flag indicators feed a reporting obligation: suspicion triggers an STR/SAR filed with the Financial Intelligence Unit through the goAML channel, with the Compliance Officer/MLRO as the accountable filer.
Tipping Off is the confidentiality constraint attaching to the same reporting event — it limits customer communication and account-handling decisions after suspicion arises.

Three-lines-of-defence roles allocate the obligation: business-line detection, compliance escalation and filing, and independent audit assurance, each mapped to role-based training and training needs assessment.

Board and senior management carry ultimate responsibility for the reporting framework; counterfeit currency reporting is a parallel, separately triggered notification duty routed to the same authority.
Terminology and platform names differ across source instruments (STR vs SAR; goAML variants; UAE FIU references) — align the label to the instrument and jurisdiction actually being applied.

data.theme: Prudential capital adequacy for banks: the minimum capital floor for licensing and ongoing operation, and how it sits within the Basel three-pillar architecture.
how_members_connect: The Minimum Capital for Banks Regulation is the binding instrument; it fixes the Minimum Capital Requirement as a licensing and continuing condition, distinct from risk-weighted ratio requirements.
The Basel Framework is the adopted reference standard from which the Pillar 1 / Pillar 2 / Pillar 3 structure and the leverage ratio derive.

Pillar 1 methodologies (Foundation IRB, standardised counterparty credit risk) determine risk-weighted exposures; Pillar 2 captures risks not fully covered in Pillar 1; Pillar 3 imposes the corresponding public disclosure duty.
The leverage ratio operates as a non-risk-based backstop cross-referencing Pillar 1 exposure measurement, including counterparty credit exposures.

data.theme: Market-conduct obligations owed to SME customers by licensed financial institutions, covering pre-contract disclosure, fair dealing in credit provision, complaint handling and Shari'ah-compliant product conduct.
how_members_connect: A single parent regulation acts as the hierarchy root; each article is an obligation branch (disclosure, responsible conduct, complaints, Shari'ah compliance) that inherits its scope and 'SME customer' definition from the parent.

Responsible conduct links outward to the credit information agency, creating an affordability/creditworthiness assessment chain that ties conduct duties to credit-reporting inputs and permissible-purpose limits.
Complaint management sits downstream of the disclosure and conduct duties: breaches of the earlier articles are what the complaints article must capture, escalate and remediate.
Shari'ah compliance overlays the other articles for Islamic windows/products, so the same conduct duty can attract a second compliance test.

data.theme: Prudential and conduct conditions under which banks may outsource functions to third parties, including board accountability, record-keeping of arrangements, protection of confidential customer data and cross-border outsourcing limits.
how_members_connect: Two-tier hierarchy: the outsourcing regulation sets the binding rule and the accompanying standards elaborate expected implementation; the articles are the individual obligation heads beneath the regulation.
The governance article cross-refers to the general risk management regulation/standards, so outsourcing risk is a sub-set of the bank's enterprise risk framework rather than a standalone regime.

Defined terms carry the substance: 'Confidential Data' fixes the scope of the data-protection duty and 'Master System of Record' conditions when cross-border outsourcing is permissible (data must remain retrievable/onshore-anchored).

The outsourcing register and outsourcing agreements articles form a documentation chain evidencing that the governance, data and cross-border conditions were met — the usual supervisory inspection path.

data.theme: Quantitative risk regimes for the banking book — interest rate and rate of return risk, related market/credit risk categories for Islamic banks, and the model governance framework that validates the measurement models used for those risks.
how_members_connect: Regulation-then-standard hierarchy: circular-level regulations (risk management, market risk, IRRBB) are the binding layer; the IRRBB standards, Islamic-bank risk standards and model management standards/guidance elaborate them.

Rate of return risk and displaced commercial risk are the Islamic-banking analogues of IRRBB, so the same measurement duty (EVE, NII, stress testing, option risk) is mapped onto Shari'ah-compliant balance sheets with an added Shari'ah non-compliance risk head.

Model management standards and guidance supply the control chain over the measurement layer: model life-cycle, independent validation, performance monitoring and board/model oversight committee accountability, applied to rating, PD, LGD, macroeconomic, IRRBB and NPV models.

Methodological nodes (PIT/TTC estimation, transition matrices, Vasicek, credit index, ECL, scenario forecasting) are not independent obligations but the techniques whose use must be justified and validated under the model standards and numerical thresholds.
Basel IRRBB standards sit upstream as the international baseline that the national IRRBB standards transpose.
start_here: Interest Rate and Rate of Return Risk in the Banking Book Standards

data.theme: Internal governance architecture requiring banks to maintain an independent compliance function and an independent internal audit function within a defined internal control system.
how_members_connect: Regulation sets the binding requirement; the accompanying standards specify mandate, independence, reporting lines and board/audit-committee access for each function.
The three lines of defence model is the organising concept that allocates the compliance article (second line) and internal audit article (third line) and prevents overlap of assurance duties.
'Internal Control' is the defined umbrella term that fixes the scope both functions must cover, so a gap in the control system is simultaneously a compliance and an audit finding.
This cluster is the accountability layer other regimes (outsourcing, risk, conduct) rely on for evidence of ongoing supervision and independent challenge.
start_here: Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Regulation
Internal Controls, Compliance and Internal Audit Standards

data.theme: Basel-derived credit risk capital treatment, covering risk weighting of exposures to multilateral development banks and the capital charge for credit valuation adjustment risk on derivative counterparty exposures.
how_members_connect: Members share a common source hierarchy: SAMA's capital adequacy framework transposes BCBS standards, so both MDB claims and CVA rules trace back to the same Basel text.
The CVA charge is the parent obligation; the simple alternative approach is a permitted computational election within it, so scope and eligibility conditions must be read together.
Weighted average maturity is an input parameter feeding the CVA calculation, making it a definitional dependency rather than a standalone obligation.
MDB claims sit alongside CVA as exposure-classification rules determining the risk weight applied in the same capital ratio.

data.theme: Calculation of the regulatory capital requirement for operational risk, and the menu of permitted measurement approaches a bank may use subject to supervisory eligibility conditions.
how_members_connect: Operational Risk is the head obligation; BIA, SA and ASA are alternative calculation methods ranked by sophistication, with movement between them typically requiring SAMA consent.
BIA, SA and ASA all rely on the same defined financial indicator (gross income), so the definition and its exclusions drive the outcome under every approach.
ASA is drafted as a variant of SA for specified business lines, meaning SA's conditions are read into it by reference.
Approach selection is a supervisory permission question, not a free accounting choice — relevant to any capital adequacy filing.

data.theme: The bank's internal capital adequacy assessment and its supervisory counterpart, covering how institutions must self-assess all material risks, plan capital, stress test, and how SAMA evaluates the result.
how_members_connect: ICAAP Guidance is the hub document; the individual risk headings (concentration, liquidity and funding cost, business model/strategic, climate-related financial risk) are mandated content chapters within it.
The ICAAP output feeds SREP — the supervisory review determines whether additional capital is imposed, so ICAAP quality carries direct prudential consequence.
