Governance and the use test are cross-cutting conditions: the assessment must be board-owned and genuinely used in decision-making, not a compliance artefact.

Stress testing and reverse stress testing are methodological obligations supporting capital planning; HHI is a prescribed measurement technique for concentration; ILAAP is the liquidity-side parallel process.

data.theme: Governance of models used for regulatory and risk measurement purposes, covering identification of model risk, independent validation, escalation of findings and remediation accountability.
how_members_connect: SAMA's model management standards are the governing instrument; model risk is the defined risk category the standards exist to control.
The CRO is the named accountable function, creating a personal/functional ownership link between governance roles and model risk outcomes.
Validation findings trigger a defined remediation chain — reporting, tracking and closure — making the two members sequential steps in one obligation.
IRRBB is included as a substantive risk area whose measurement models fall expressly within the model management standards, showing cross-regime application.
start_here: Central Bank Model Management Standards and Guidance

data.theme: Saudi consumer protection and market-conduct regime for financial institutions: pre-contractual disclosure, product-level conduct rules, advertising, and institutional accountability for how products are designed, sold and serviced to Consumers.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the Consumer Protection Regulation (Circular 8-2020) sits above the Consumer Protection Standards, which are then broken into article-level obligations (Disclosure and Transparency, Institutional Oversight, Market Conduct, Business Conduct) and product-specific sections.

Shared defined terms carry the obligation chain: the Key Facts Statement, APR/profit-rate disclosure and Base Lending/Financing Rate recur across the general, deposit, credit/financing, investment and remittance provisions, so a disclosure breach is usually a breach at several levels at once.

Institutional Oversight links conduct outcomes back to governance artefacts - Conduct Risk Management Framework, Product Approval Framework, the annual consumer protection/conduct risk report and the No Objection Letter gate - making the board and senior management the accountable parties.

Business Conduct aggregates consumer-remedy rules (cooling-off, consumer mobility, unauthorized transaction handling, responsibility for authorized agents) and interacts with the Shari'ah governance standard for Islamic financial institutions offering the same products.

data.theme: Prior-approval regime for changes in ownership and large corporate acquisitions by licensed institutions - i.e. when a transaction triggers supervisory consent rather than mere notification. Note this cluster is UAE (CBUAE) material, not SAMA, and should not be cited as KSA authority.
how_members_connect: Two parallel instruments address the same control question from different angles: Major Acquisitions (the institution acquiring) and Transfer of Significant Shareholding (the institution being acquired into).

Thresholds are definition-driven: whether a deal is a Major Acquisition turns on its size relative to Total Regulatory Capital; whether a holder is caught turns on the Significant Shareholder / Controlling Shareholder definitions.

Obligation chain runs definition to trigger to consent: meeting a threshold produces a Requirement for Approval, with the board carrying non-delegable responsibility and the shareholder register serving as the evidentiary record.

data.theme: Prudential and transparency rules for mortgage and real-estate lending to individuals, including lending limits and disclosure of borrowing cost. This cluster is UAE Central Bank material and is only persuasive, not binding, in a KSA analysis.
how_members_connect: Vertical hierarchy from enabling statute (Union Law No. 10 of 1980) down through regulations, board resolutions and a notice, so the amending resolutions determine the currently operative text.
Version control matters: the consolidated VER2 supersedes/incorporates VER1 as amended by the 2019 and 2020 board resolutions - answers should cite the consolidated text.

Cross-regime overlap with retail conduct: the mortgage rules sit alongside the regulations on bank loans and other services to individual customers and the real-estate lending transparency regulations, so one facility can be subject to both prudential caps and disclosure duties.
start_here: Regulations Regarding Bank Loans and Other Services to Individual Customers

data.theme: Licensing, conduct and fee framework for insurance intermediaries and administrators under the former UAE Insurance Authority. Relevant as comparative material only; in KSA, insurance supervision sits outside this instrument set.
how_members_connect: Clear law-to-regulation hierarchy: Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 establishes the Authority and confers rule-making power, which the IA board resolutions and implementing regulations exercise.
The insurance agents resolution derives its licensing and conduct obligations from both the establishing law and the 2009 implementing regulations, so agent duties must be read cumulatively.
Cabinet resolutions form a separate fee layer, with the 2013 third-party health insurance administrator fees building on the earlier 2009 insurance fee schedule.
start_here: Federal Law No. 6 of 2007 (Establishment of Insurance Authority)
IA Board Resolution No. 2 of 2009 (Implementing Regulations)

data.theme: Time-limitation (lapse/expiry) of disciplinary sanctions imposed on supervised insurance-sector persons, i.e. when a recorded penalty ceases to carry forward legal effect for fit-and-proper, licensing or repeat-offence purposes.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a standalone Insurance Authority board resolution operating as subordinate instrument under the insurance supervisory law and its implementing regulation.
Links outward rather than internally — the lapse rule qualifies the disciplinary/penalty powers exercised elsewhere in the insurance enforcement regime.
Relevant to governance and fit-and-proper assessments, where past sanctions are an input; the lapse period determines how long that input remains live.
start_here: IA Board Resolution No. 12 of 2016 Elapse of Disciplinary Sanctions

data.theme: Shareholding and ownership thresholds in licensed insurance companies — controlling/significant ownership limits and the supervisory approval consequences that attach to crossing them.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: an Insurance Authority board decision setting ownership ratio parameters for insurance licensees.
Connects legally to licensing and change-of-control obligations: ownership ratios are the trigger condition for prior non-objection and for ongoing shareholder suitability.
Cross-regime relevance to governance/risk: ownership concentration feeds beneficial-ownership identification and control-person assessment.
start_here: IA Board Decision No. 15 of 2019 Ownership Ratios in Insurance Companies

data.theme: Adjustment of the reporting periods for submission of financial data by insurance-sector entities — a timing relief/extension measure against standing periodic reporting duties.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a board resolution that varies deadlines rather than creating a new substantive obligation.
Legal effect is parasitic on the underlying periodic financial-reporting requirements in the insurance regulation; it must be read together with them to determine the operative due date.
Time-bound instrument: compliance teams must confirm whether the extension remains in force or has reverted to the baseline reporting cycle.
start_here: IA Board Resolution No. 20 of 2020 Extension of Financial Data Periods

data.theme: Procedural route for supervised persons to contest or appeal financial penalties imposed by the Insurance Authority — grievance filing, handling and determination.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a procedural instrument sitting downstream of the substantive fining powers in the insurance supervisory framework.
Forms an obligation chain with the enforcement/penalty provisions: violation → fine decision → grievance and review procedure → finality.
Complements the sanctions-lapse rule in the same enforcement space, since both govern the lifecycle and lasting effect of a penalty decision.
start_here: IA Board Resolution No. 25 of 2020 Grievance Procedures for Fines

data.theme: Internal control and governance architecture for an AML/CFT-regulated institution: appointment and role of the Compliance Officer (and alternate), periodic compliance reporting to the supervisor, and the suspicious-transaction reporting chain into the FIU, sitting alongside risk, security and information-security chapters of the same rulebook.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the AML/CFT Law is the primary source; the rulebook chapter on AML/CFT compliance operationalises it into named functions (Compliance Officer, Alternate) and deliverables (bi-annual report).

Obligation chain: Compliance Officer is the designated recipient of internal escalations, the filer of STRs to the FIU, and the signatory of periodic compliance reporting; the Alternate inherits the same duties in absence.
FIU reporting links to provisional measures and freezing — i.e. the report is not the end of the obligation; downstream restraint/no-tipping-off consequences follow.

Risk management, general security and information security chapters cross-reference the compliance chapter, making AML controls part of the institution-wide control framework rather than a standalone silo.

data.theme: Business continuity and operational resilience obligations — maintaining critical financial services through disruption, with continuity planning and testing as a supervisory expectation.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a standalone rulebook chapter that sets the continuity obligation without dense internal cross-referencing in this graph.

Reads naturally against the adjacent risk management, general security and information security chapters (community 22), which supply the risk-assessment and incident foundations continuity planning depends on.

data.theme: Targeted financial sanctions, terrorist financing and proliferation financing: the legal duty to screen, freeze and report without delay, plus the typology/red-flag material used to detect TF and sanctions-evasion behaviour, including risks arising from new payment products and services.
how_members_connect: Law-to-guidance chain: the AML/CTF law and its implementing Cabinet Decision set the freezing and reporting duties; central-bank guidance and the Executive Office guidance translate them into supervisory expectations for FIs and DNFBPs.

Red-flag sets for TF and for sanctions circumvention are derivative indicators — they inform suspicion and escalation, but the enforceable obligation remains in the law/decision, not in the indicator lists.
International sources (FATF standards and typologies, FFIEC manual, FINTRAC indicators) are cited as persuasive benchmarks; they shape risk assessment but are not themselves binding instruments.
New payment products and services connect the sanctions regime to the payments/PSP regime, where anonymity, speed and cross-border reach change the screening and CDD risk profile.
start_here: CBUAE Guidance on Implementation of Targeted Financial Sanctions
Red Flag Indicators for Sanctions Circumvention

data.theme: Prudential and AML/CFT conduct standards for exchange houses and money remitters: licensing and appointment approvals, the CID/KYC/CDD sequence, wire transfer originator/beneficiary information, third-party transactions, screening, record retention, training, unclaimed funds and complaints handling.
how_members_connect: The exchange business standards act as the umbrella instrument, cross-referencing each operational obligation and citing the AML/CTF law as its statutory anchor.

Definitional layering: customer identification is the narrower verification step inside KYC, which in turn sits inside the broader risk-based CDD obligation — conflating them misstates the required depth of enquiry.

Third-party transactions link back to KYC and to sanctions screening: acting for a non-customer triggers additional identification and screening duties rather than reliance on the presenting party alone.
Licensing/appointment forms (licensed person, authorised person appointment, foreign account) form a fit-and-proper approval chain that gates who may operate or be appointed.
Wire transfer information, record retention and training are the standing controls that make CDD outputs usable for later investigation and supervisory review.
start_here: Standards for Exchange Business in the UAE

data.theme: Enhanced due diligence triggered by customer status rather than transaction type: identifying politically exposed persons, their beneficial owners and related/associated customers, and establishing source of funds and wealth before and during the relationship.
how_members_connect: All members hang off the PEP definition; classification as a PEP (or a PEP's beneficial owner, family member or close associate) is the trigger that upgrades standard CDD into the EDD obligation chain.
Screening is the detection step, EDD is the consequence: screening results feed senior-management approval, source of funds/wealth establishment and ongoing enhanced monitoring.
The 'Related Customer' and 'Beneficial Owner' nodes extend PEP treatment through ownership and control layers, so EDD cannot be scoped to the named account holder alone.
Sector variants (insurance EDD, DNFBP-facing EDD) show the same obligation applied under different supervisory regimes, so applicability depends on which entity type is in scope.

data.theme: AML/CFT risk arising where financial institutions bank or service non-financial sectors — real estate and dealers in precious metals and stones — which are themselves designated obliged entities. Note: these members are UAE federal instruments and FATF material, not SAMA rules, and are relevant only as comparative or cross-border reference.
how_members_connect: Clear hierarchy: the federal AML/CFT decree-law sets the primary obligations, the Cabinet implementing regulation defines DNFBP scope and detail, and the supervisory guidance operationalises both for institutions servicing these sectors.
DPMS is a sub-category of the DNFBP definition, so the definitional node controls which businesses fall inside the regime.
Real estate sector risk and DPMS risk are the typology inputs that justify the guidance's expectations on risk-based CDD, source of funds and monitoring of sector clients.
The FATF mutual evaluation is cited as the evidentiary basis for the identified sector vulnerabilities and the resulting supervisory expectations.
start_here: AML/CFT Guidance for LFIs Servicing Real Estate and Precious Metals Sectors
Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2019 Implementing Regulation

data.theme: Prudential/credit restriction on bank lending extended to finance the purchase of company shares, addressing leverage-driven equity speculation and concentration risk.
how_members_connect: Two versions of the same instrument: the original circular and its later consolidated text, so the consolidated version governs the currently applicable wording.
Version linkage matters for compliance dating — any conclusion on the permitted scope of share-purchase lending must cite the consolidated text rather than the superseded original.

data.theme: Insurance supervisory intervention in product pricing — revision of the pricing policy applied by insurers, sitting at the intersection of prudential adequacy of premiums and consumer/market-conduct fairness.
how_members_connect: Isolated node with no mapped cross-references in this graph; it should be read as a standalone regulator resolution and checked for later amendment or supersession by SAMA insurance instruments.
Its practical effect is on pricing approval and actuarial justification obligations for insurers rather than on any AML or credit regime in the wider graph.
start_here: IA Board Resolution No. 11 of 2016 Pricing Policy Revision

data.theme: Bancassurance-style distribution: the conditions under which insurance policies may be marketed and sold through banks, and the statutory bases (central bank, banking and electronic transactions legislation) that authorise and constrain that channel.
how_members_connect: The core Board Decision is the operative instrument; it draws authority from the central bank law and the banks/financial institutions law, and relies on the electronic transactions law to validate remote/e-signed sales.
A later amending decision modifies the core decision, and a consolidated version merges original plus amendment - the consolidated text is the one to cite for current obligations.
Hierarchy runs primary law -> regulator board decision -> amendment -> consolidation; the amendment has no standalone meaning outside the parent decision.
Scope caution: these are Insurance Authority / federal-law instruments, not SAMA rules; use only for comparative analysis unless the KSA equivalent is separately identified.
start_here: IA Board Decision No. 13 of 2018 - Marketing Insurance Policies through Banks

data.theme: Standardised motor insurance contract terms - the unified own-damage/loss policy wording and the regulatory decisions that mandate, amend and consolidate it.
how_members_connect: The unified policy is the mandated contract wording; the regulating Board Decision is its enabling instrument and defines when insurers must use it.
Two later amending decisions alter specific policy terms; the consolidated version (VER2) reflects the amended wording and is the operative text for policies issued after its effective date.
Legal effect is temporal: which version governs a claim depends on policy inception date relative to each amendment.
Scope caution: Insurance Authority instruments, not SAMA-issued; treat as comparative material for KSA questions.
start_here: Unified Motor Vehicle Insurance Policy (Consolidated VER2)
IA Board Decision No. 25 of 2016 (Regulation of Unified Motor Policies)

data.theme: The AML/CFT customer due diligence regime as applied in the insurance sector: identifying and verifying customers and beneficial owners, calibrating measures by risk, monitoring the relationship, and escalating to suspicious transaction reporting.
how_members_connect: All members hang off the statutory CDD duty in the AML/CFT law; the generic CDD node is the hub, with SDD, EDD, beneficial owner identification and ongoing monitoring as branches of the same obligation.

The risk-based approach is the switch that determines which branch applies: risk profiling at onboarding sets the tier (simplified vs enhanced), and source of funds/wealth enquiry is the principal EDD add-on.

Insurance-specific nodes (general CDD measures, simplified DD for insurance) are sectoral applications of the general standards - read them as overlays, not replacements; note the policyholder/beneficiary distinction, since the insurance 'customer' is not always the payer or the beneficial owner.
Ongoing monitoring feeds the risk profile and red-flag indicators, which in turn trigger the STR duty - a closed obligation chain from onboarding to reporting.
Cross-regime flag: the cash-intensive business guidance imports merchant/commercial-customer risk typologies into the insurance CDD analysis.

data.theme: Human resources and staffing requirements within an institution's governance framework - fit and proper staffing, training and internal accountability as a control function input.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster with no internal cross-references; it is an isolated chapter node rather than a linked obligation chain.
Its regulatory weight derives from the parent manual or rulebook it sits in, so establish that parent before relying on it.
Practically it interacts with AML/CFT training and compliance-officer competence duties and with governance/fit-and-proper regimes, though those links are not captured in this graph.

data.theme: Identification, recording and registry-filing of beneficial owners of legal persons and legal arrangements as an AML/CFT control, and the parallel duties of registrars and of financial institutions doing CDD on corporate customers. Note the instruments here are UAE federal texts, so they are comparative/cross-border reference points rather than SAMA rules.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy runs from the primary AML/CFT decree-law down to Cabinet-level beneficial owner procedures and then to supervisory guidance for financial institutions serving legal persons and arrangements.
All members turn on the same defined term, Beneficial Owner, plus the scoping terms Legal Arrangements and Registrar, which fix who must disclose and who must maintain the register.
The later Cabinet decision on beneficial owner procedures supersedes/updates the earlier one while continuing to cite the AML/CFT decree-law as its enabling authority.
Two obligation chains intersect: the entity/registrar disclosure-and-filing duty, and the institution's CDD duty to verify ownership and control - registry data supports but does not discharge CDD.
start_here: Cabinet Decision No. 109 of 2023 on Beneficial Owner Procedures
AML/CFT Guidance for LFIs Serving Legal Persons and Arrangements

data.theme: The United Nations as the source of international sanctions and targeted financial sanctions listings and of AML/CFT standards that domestic regimes implement.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster: functions as the external authority referenced by sanctions/TFS and AML obligations elsewhere in the graph.
Relevant as the origin of consolidated list obligations (freeze without delay, no funds made available) that local rules transpose.

data.theme: The conceptual core of the AML/CTF regime: what money laundering is, the predicate offences that generate criminal proceeds, the stages by which proceeds are laundered, and the adjacent offences of terrorist financing and proliferation financing.
how_members_connect: Definitional dependency: money laundering is defined by reference to proceeds of a predicate offence, so the predicate catalogue sets the perimeter of the offence and of reporting duties.
The placement/layering/integration typology is the analytical frame used to characterise suspicion and to calibrate risk-based controls.
Terrorist financing and proliferation financing sit alongside laundering as separate offences with overlapping detection and reporting obligations but different (often sanctions-driven) triggers.
Falsely described goods and services links in as a trade-based red flag typology, principally for proliferation and sanctions evasion.

data.theme: Financing of terrorism as a distinct predicate/standalone offence driving suspicious transaction reporting, targeted financial sanctions screening and freezing duties.
how_members_connect: Isolated definitional node that supplies the trigger term for TF-specific reporting and freeze obligations referenced across the AML/CTF and sanctions clusters.
Should be read against the money laundering cluster, since TF may involve lawfully sourced funds and therefore does not follow the proceeds-of-crime logic.

data.theme: Historic SAMA circulars governing banks' involvement in public subscriptions to company share capital, including subscriptions to the capital of foreign companies. The problem-space is control over the marketing and receipt of subscription monies through the banking channel.
how_members_connect: Both are SAMA circulars from the same period addressing the same activity — banks acting as a channel for public subscription to company capital.
The foreign-company circular narrows or qualifies the general subscription position by reference to the issuer's jurisdiction, so the two are read as a general rule plus a scope-specific overlay.
Linkage is conceptual/subject-matter rather than an express cross-reference; neither should be assumed to amend the other absent explicit wording.
Note temporal scope: pre-Capital Market Authority instruments, so applicability must be checked against later securities-offering regimes and supervisory perimeter.
start_here: Circular 444/1987 Public Subscription to Company Capital

data.theme: Consumer/retail credit conduct for personal lending by supervised institutions — eligibility, disclosure, deduction limits and contract terms for individual borrowers.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: the manual is a standalone consolidated conduct instrument for personal loans rather than part of an internal cross-reference chain.

Its obligations sit downstream of the Finance Companies Control Law / Banking Control Law framework and interact with consumer-protection and responsible-lending rules elsewhere in the knowledge base.
Relevant cross-regime check: the borrower here is a consumer, distinct from the AML notion of customer, so CDD obligations arise from separate instruments.

data.theme: Prudential and accounting treatment of expected credit loss provisioning under IFRS 9, and the transitional capital relief and pandemic-era support measures that modify how provisions feed into regulatory capital.
how_members_connect: The transitional arrangements regulation is the operative instrument; it expressly builds on IFRS 9 ECL provisioning outcomes to determine add-backs to regulatory capital over a phase-in period.
The same regulation references the support scheme, linking deferred/restructured exposures under that scheme to staging, significant-increase-in-credit-risk judgements and provisioning consequences.
Hierarchy runs accounting standard (IFRS 9) → SAMA prudential regulation → scheme-specific supervisory expectations, so the standard defines measurement while SAMA controls capital effect.
Time-bound scope: transitional relief and the support scheme are period-limited, so any answer must fix the reporting date before stating the applicable treatment.
start_here: Regulation on Accounting Provisions and Capital Requirements Transitional Arrangements

data.theme: The national and institutional risk-assessment architecture for AML/CTF: how the country-level risk picture and national strategy drive each institution's business risk assessment, risk factors, and the enhanced measures applied to higher-risk customers, products, channels and jurisdictions.
how_members_connect: Top-down obligation chain: the national committee sets the strategy, the strategy rests on the national risk assessment, and institutions must take that assessment into account when producing their own ML/TF business risk assessment.
Risk factors and typologies feed the risk assessment, which in turn determines where a risk-based approach requires enhanced due diligence rather than standard CDD.

EDD acts as the hub obligation, attaching to specified higher-risk categories — correspondent relationships, high-risk jurisdictions designated through the national process, money or value transfer services and non-profit exposures.

Payment-channel and sectoral rules sit alongside: wire transfer originator/beneficiary information requirements extend to virtual asset transfers, while international industry material (Wolfsberg) is persuasive guidance only, not an enforceable SAMA source.

data.theme: Sector-specific AML/CFT supervisory guidance sitting on top of the federal AML/CFT statutory framework, covering CDD/EDD, suspicious transaction reporting, sanctions screening and typologies such as shell/front company misuse and trade-based money laundering.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the AML-CFT Law and its implementing Cabinet Decision supply the enforceable obligations; the payment-sector, insurance and PEP guidance documents interpret them for defined licensee populations without creating new duties.

Shared defined terms drive the linkage - 'Customer', beneficial owner, PEP, suspicious transaction - so a single CDD/EDD standard is applied with sector-specific risk overlays (correspondent relationships, enterprise risk assessment, payment flows).

Obligation chain around reporting: transaction monitoring feeds STR filing, which triggers the statutory tipping-off prohibition; sanctions obligations run in parallel and are not discharged by STR filing.

Typology entries (shell/front/shelf companies, TBML) are conceptually paired with the CDD/EDD entries as red-flag material informing risk rating rather than standalone obligations; FATF Recommendations are the external benchmark cited throughout.

data.theme: Institutional-level AML/CFT/CPF programme foundations: the risk-based approach, enterprise-wide risk assessment, proliferation financing risk analysis, and role-differentiated staff training.
how_members_connect: Both best-practice notes derive from the same statutory base (AML-CFT Law plus Cabinet Decision) and elaborate programme-level duties rather than transaction-level ones.

Logical chain: institutional risk assessment determines risk appetite and controls, which in turn determines what each role must be trained on - training adequacy is judged against the assessed risk profile.
PF risk (threat/vulnerability/consequence) extends the same methodology from ML/TF to proliferation financing, aligning with the FATF standard cited by all members.
FATF materials function as the interpretive benchmark; they are persuasive, not directly enforceable, and should be distinguished from the binding local instruments.
start_here: Best Practices for RBA and Institutional Risk Assessment
Federal Decree Law No.20 of 2018 (AML-CFT Law)

data.theme: Strict-liability administrative sanctions for breaches of specified prudential, operational and regulatory reporting duties - counterfeit currency handling, court-case data, cross-border and card transaction reporting, certificate issuance deadlines and periodic returns.
how_members_connect: Single parent instrument: the strict-liability sanctions regulation enumerates the listed articles as sanctionable violations, so each article is both an obligation and a penalty trigger.
Liability is strict - no intent or harm element - so the analysis turns on whether the specified act or reporting deadline was met, not on culpability.
Reporting articles converge on the Integrated Regulatory Reporting System as the prescribed channel, making timeliness and completeness of submission the operative test.
Cross-reference to the bank loans and services regulation supplies the substantive customer-facing duty (certificate issuance within a fixed period) that the sanctions regime enforces.
start_here: Regulation to Impose Financial Sanctions for Strict Liability Violations

data.theme: An isolated transparency provision, concerning disclosure of terms, pricing or information to counterparties or customers.
how_members_connect: Single-member community with no captured cross-references; its regulatory weight depends on the parent instrument in which it sits.
Should be read against the consumer protection and disclosure regimes before being treated as a standalone obligation.
Flagged for enrichment - the governing law/regulation and scope of application are not evidenced in the current graph.

data.theme: Customer due diligence architecture under the AML/CTF regime: the baseline CDD obligation, when it escalates to enhanced measures (notably for politically exposed persons), which non-bank sectors are pulled into scope, and the conditions for relying on a third party to perform elements of CDD.
how_members_connect: All members hang off the core CDD obligation as the parent duty; EDD is a risk-triggered intensification of it rather than a separate regime.
PEP status is the classic trigger condition that converts baseline CDD into enhanced measures, including source-of-funds/wealth and senior-management approval style controls.
DNFBPs and VASPs are scope-extension nodes: they import the same CDD/EDD duties into non-bank sectors, which matters for who can be a 'third party' at all.

Reliance on a third party is conditional and does not transfer accountability - the relying institution retains ultimate responsibility, so the reliance rule must be read against the CDD article it cross-references.

data.theme: Automatic exchange of financial account information under the OECD Common Reporting Standard: which institutions report, what account-level due diligence they must run, and which accounts and controlling persons become reportable to the competent authority.
how_members_connect: The CRS Regulations are the domestic implementing instrument for the OECD standard, so the defined terms (Reporting Financial Institution, Reportable Account, Passive NFE) are standard-derived and should not be read against ordinary AML definitions.

Obligation chain: entity classification as a Reporting Financial Institution triggers CRS due diligence procedures, which in turn determine Reportable Account status and the reporting flow to the competent authority.

CRS due diligence expressly leans on existing AML/KYC records - a cross-regime interaction where AML customer identification and beneficial-ownership work is reused for tax-transparency purposes, but with different scope and thresholds.
Passive NFE treatment is the look-through mechanism connecting entity accounts to controlling persons, mirroring but not identical to AML beneficial ownership.
Note the competent-authority node is UAE-facing; confirm jurisdictional applicability before relying on it for a KSA question.

data.theme: Prudential liquidity/funding constraint expressed as a ceiling on lending relative to deposit funding, issued by circular rather than as a standalone regulation.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: a circular-level instrument, so it sits below primary regulation in the hierarchy and should be read as a supervisory limit or reporting requirement layered onto existing banking rules.
Isolation in the graph means the operative definitions of 'advances' and 'deposits' must be sourced from the parent banking framework rather than from within the cluster.
Confirm issuing authority and jurisdiction before citing, as the label does not itself establish which central bank issued it.

data.theme: Minimum and ongoing capital requirements for restricted-licence banks: what counts as eligible capital, what happens on breach, how the wider bank prudential rules apply, and the supervisory consequences of non-compliance.
how_members_connect: Classic parent-regulation-to-article hierarchy: a single capital regulation is the anchor and every other member is one of its operative articles.
Obligation chain runs from quality-of-capital criteria, through the breach provisions that set notification and remediation duties, to enforcement and sanctions as the consequence limb.
The application article determines how far the general bank regulations are imported into the restricted-licence context - the key scope-limiting provision.
The cancellation article performs the repeal function, so prior resolutions and circulars on this subject are superseded and should not be cited as live obligations.
Jurisdictional flag: this is CBUAE material, not SAMA; do not transpose the capital thresholds into a KSA analysis.
start_here: CBUAE Restricted Licence Bank Capital Regulation
Article 6: Quality of Capital to be Held
Article 8: Breaches of Minimum Capital Requirement

data.theme: Consumer data protection duties owed by supervised entities: safeguarding consumer data and assets, obtaining express consent before use or disclosure, and the narrow gateway for sharing with authorized agents.
how_members_connect: A single principal obligation (Article 6 on protection of consumer data and assets) anchors the cluster; the other members are its operative components.
Consent is the legal precondition that conditions downstream disclosure — sharing with authorized agents is only lawful within the scope of the consumer's expressed consent.
The data management and protection function is the governance/accountability leg: an internal control obligation that implements the Article 6 standard rather than a separate right.
Cross-regime note: consent here is a consumer-protection concept and does not substitute for AML/CDD data-handling or credit-information disclosure permissions.
start_here: Article 6: Protection of Consumer Data and Assets

data.theme: Shari'ah compliance obligations for financial services offered to consumers, and their concrete effect on early settlement (early repayment) treatment in financing contracts.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: a general Shari'ah-compliance requirement in the regulatory article is given specific content by a Shari'ah Higher Authority resolution on early settlement.
Direct citation chain — the article invokes the HSA resolution, making the resolution binding on how early settlement amounts are calculated and charged.
Practical consequence: pricing and early-termination terms in Islamic financing products must satisfy both the SAMA consumer/finance regime and the cited Shari'ah determination.
start_here: Article 11: Shari'ah Compliance for Financial Services
HSA Resolution No. 76/3/2019 on Early Settlement

data.theme: Mandatory motor insurance pricing: the regulatory framework setting permitted tariffs for compulsory third-party liability and optional loss-and-damage cover, tied to the unified motor policy wordings.
how_members_connect: The tariffs regulation is the parent instrument; the two tariff tables are annexed schedules it incorporates by reference and are enforceable as part of it.
The regulation cross-refers to the resolution approving the unified motor policies, linking permitted pricing to the standard coverage terms being priced.
Split by product line: one table governs compulsory third-party liability rating, the other governs own-damage (comprehensive) rating, so the applicable table depends on the policy type issued.
start_here: Regulation for Motor Vehicle Insurance Tariffs
Resolution No. 25 of 2016 Unified Motor Policies

data.theme: Use of digital identity systems to perform AML/CTF customer due diligence: when a digital ID is fit for identification and verification, how its assurance is assessed, and the rules for relying on third parties or outsourced providers.
how_members_connect: The digital ID CDD guidance is the hub; appropriateness assessment and assurance level assessment are its two decision tests for accepting a digital ID for identification/verification.
Standards chain: the guidance cites external sources (FATF digital identity guidance and the NIST 800-63 identity assurance levels) which supply the benchmarks used in the assurance assessment.

Third-party reliance appears twice — in the digital ID context and in the insurance outsourcing context — reflecting the same legal principle that reliance does not transfer ultimate CDD responsibility from the regulated entity.
Scope caution: the external standards are referenced as guidance for calibrating assurance, not as independent SAMA obligations.
start_here: Digital ID Systems Guidance for CDD

data.theme: Fraud risk at the consumer-facing channel level: safeguarding customer funds and card/account assets used through ATM and point-of-sale infrastructure, and the institution's duty to detect, investigate and remediate fraudulent transactions.
how_members_connect: The ATM/POS channel provisions set the operational service conditions that the anti-fraud asset-protection duty presupposes — the channel rules define where the exposure arises.
The fraud detection and investigation obligation cross-references the consumer asset protection duty, creating an obligation chain: prevent, then detect, then investigate and make the consumer whole.
All three sit in the consumer protection regime but interact with payments/PSP supervision, so liability allocation between issuer, acquirer and merchant should be read across both.
Shared subject matter is the consumer's account/instrument, so the defined scope of 'consumer' (as opposed to AML 'customer') limits who can claim these protections.
start_here: Protection of Consumer Assets against Fraud

data.theme: Responsible lending to retail consumers: the pre-contractual assessment duties (affordability, suitability) and quantitative leverage limits that condition whether and on what terms credit may be extended.
how_members_connect: The general credit product provisions and the responsible financing article form the umbrella obligation; the suitability and affordability assessments are the operative duties that discharge it.

The Debt Burden Ratio is the shared quantitative test referenced by the responsible financing article, the affordability assessment and the financing terms — it is the common binding constraint across the cluster.
Suitability and affordability are distinct but paired tests (is the product right for this consumer vs. can this consumer repay); both must be satisfied before terms are set.
Relevant to finance companies and BNPL providers, where the 'Consumer' definition and any exemptions from full affordability testing determine which of these duties actually bite.

data.theme: Cross-border and domestic money transfer and foreign exchange activity, including the conduct and consumer-disclosure conditions attaching to remittance services.
how_members_connect: Standalone node in this graph: it links outward rather than internally, principally to AML/CTF wire-transfer and originator-information duties and to sanctions/TFS screening obligations.
Also intersects with consumer protection disclosure duties (fees, exchange rate, execution time) and with licensing scope for money transfer businesses.

data.theme: Treatment of consumers in financial difficulty and the information consequences that follow: forbearance and fair treatment of distressed borrowers, permissible debt collection conduct, credit bureau reporting, and record retention.
how_members_connect: The financial inclusion article anchors the cluster and cross-references the fair-treatment duty for distressed consumers, framing forbearance as an access/inclusion obligation, not a discretionary concession.
Fair treatment and debt collection are two faces of the same arrears lifecycle: what the institution must offer, and what conduct is prohibited in pursuing the debt.

Debt collection practice references credit information sharing, tying recovery conduct to the accuracy and lawfulness of data reported to licensed credit bureaus — a credit information regime overlay on a consumer protection duty.
Record retention standards underpin both, since evidentiary retention periods determine the institution's ability to substantiate assessments, reporting and collection contacts.
start_here: Fair Treatment of Financially Distressed Consumers
Sharing with Authorized Credit Information Agencies

data.theme: Licensing and Shari'ah-compliant structuring of takaful insurance business: how an insurance company is authorised, and how a separate takaful insurance fund is constituted, governed and contractually linked to the operator.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy runs from the Central Bank Law and the Islamic commercial transactions regulation down to the takaful regulation and the insurance company licensing regulation, with the Higher Shari'ah Authority as the common Shari'ah oversight anchor cited across them.

An obligation chain governs the takaful fund lifecycle: establishment, fund charter, board of trustees and its duties, legal representation, terms and conditions, and assignment of accounts — each article cross-referencing the charter or the wakala contract.

Licensing articles form a sequential procedural chain (classification of business, application and annexed attachments, licensing decision, registration, commencement, branch openings inside and outside the State).

Shared defined terms (Licensee, Insurance Company, Takaful Insurance Fund, Wakala Contract) tie the prudential/licensing regime to nominate Islamic contract forms (murabaha, mudaraba, ijarah) and to consumer-facing bodies such as the customer protection unit.

data.theme: Prudential expectation that an insurer operate an integrated enterprise risk management framework linked to its solvency position, including forward-looking self-assessment and recovery planning.
how_members_connect: The ERM for solvency purposes standards is the parent instrument; enterprise risk management is the defined framework it imposes and from which the other obligations hang.
ERM branches into substantive components — risk appetite and risk limits, asset-liability management, and capital adequacy — each a required element rather than a separate regime.

The own risk and solvency assessment is the forward-looking output of the ERM framework and feeds recovery planning, creating a data and escalation link between routine assessment and stress response.
A residual cross-reference to other relevant regulations means the standards are not self-contained and must be read with the wider prudential rulebook.

data.theme: Individual authorisation regime: which roles are controlled functions, the suitability test applied to the persons holding them, and the ongoing competence obligation once authorised.
how_members_connect: The fit and proper process is the procedural hub, linking the substantive fit and proper criteria to the scope of roles caught by the regime.
Scope is fixed by the defined term designated functions, which is populated by the attached list rather than by open-ended interpretation.

The authorized individual is the obligated person: subject to the fit and proper process at entry and to continuing professional development thereafter, making suitability an ongoing rather than one-off condition.

data.theme: Governance interface between conventional risk management and Shari'ah governance in Islamic financial activity.
how_members_connect: The governance article is the source obligation and cross-references both the enterprise risk management framework and the internal Shari'ah supervisory committee.
The linkage makes Shari'ah compliance a governance input to risk management, not a parallel silo — the same governing body must accommodate both.
Small bridging cluster: it connects the general ERM/solvency expectations to the Islamic-finance instruments governed elsewhere in the framework.

data.theme: Insurance-sector authorisation and prudential regulation (broker/representation-office licensing, fit-and-proper, group supervision) together with the climate-related financial risk regime applied to licensed financial firms. The problem-space is who may be licensed, how a group is supervised, and how climate risk must be governed, capitalised and disclosed.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the central bank law and the insurance activities decree-law are the enabling statutes cited by the subordinate regulations (brokers, representation offices, group supervision, climate risk), with the 2025 central bank decree-law superseding/referencing the 2018 instrument.

Obligation chain on entry and exit: licensing conditions feed the fit-and-proper test and the powers of revocation, suspension, restriction and variation; representation-office rules import the same licensing and fitness gates plus director responsibilities.

Group supervision links parent responsibilities, holding-company identification, supervisory colleges and mandatory reporting of risk concentration and intragroup transactions into a single consolidated-oversight obligation set.

Climate strand shares defined terms (physical, transition and liability risk; scenario analysis) and runs from international soft law (Paris Agreement, NGFS, BCBS-aligned principles, national sustainable finance working group outputs) into binding governance, strategy, risk-management and capital articles.
start_here: Decretal Federal Law No. 48 of 2023 Regulating Insurance Activities

data.theme: Board- and management-level allocation of accountability for climate risk and its embedding into the firm's existing enterprise risk management framework, gated by materiality.
how_members_connect: Assignment of responsibilities is the precondition for the integration obligation: named accountable functions must then carry climate risk into the ERM framework.
Materiality assessment operates as the scoping device determining the depth of integration required.
Both principles are anchored to the Basel Committee's climate principles as the international benchmark they implement.
start_here: Principle 4 - Incorporation into Risk Management Framework

data.theme: Ongoing supervisory and internal monitoring of climate risk exposures and the associated reporting obligations to the board and the regulator.
how_members_connect: Stands as a single obligation node on data collection, metrics and escalation, downstream of the responsibility-allocation and risk-integration principles.
Its outputs feed capital adequacy assessment and external disclosure duties in adjacent clusters.

data.theme: Whether and how climate-related financial risks must be reflected in internal capital and liquidity adequacy, and the use of scenario analysis as the evidentiary basis for that assessment.
how_members_connect: Scenario analysis is the input obligation; the capital and liquidity adequacy principle is the output decision that must take those results into account.
Both attach to the firm's existing ICAAP/ILAAP/ORSA processes rather than creating a separate capital regime.
Reference climate scenarios are cited as the recognised methodological baseline for the analysis.

data.theme: Prudential credit-risk measurement: how exposure values are determined and how eligible collateral, guarantees and netting reduce them, including the ring-fenced cover pool logic of covered bonds.
how_members_connect: Exposure measurement is the base obligation; credit risk mitigation operates as a recognised adjustment to that measured value, so the two are read in sequence.
Eligibility, valuation and legal-certainty conditions for mitigants are shared definitions across both items.
Covered bonds sit alongside as a structural form of collateralisation (cover pool/dual recourse), conceptually drawing on the same exposure and collateral-valuation concepts.

data.theme: Shari'ah governance and external Shari'ah audit obligations for takaful insurers and Islamic financial institutions, sitting under the insurance and commercial transactions statutory framework.
how_members_connect: Law-to-standard hierarchy: the Insurance Law and Commercial Transactions Law are the statutory anchors cited by the Shari'ah audit standards.
The Takaful Regulation is the operative regime the governance and external audit standards elaborate; both standards cross-refer to it.
The takaful external Shari'ah audit standard parallels the generic Islamic financial institution standard, so scope-of-entity distinctions drive which applies.
Governance standard (internal control, ISSC) and audit standard (independent external assurance) form a two-layer assurance chain.
start_here: Standard re External Shari'ah Audit for Takaful Insurance Companies

data.theme: Internal Shari'ah governance architecture for Islamic financial institutions and takaful operators: constitution of the Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee, its charter, annual Shari'ah reporting, and management of Shari'ah non-compliance risk.
how_members_connect: Defined-term chain: Islamic Finance Institution -> Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee -> its Charter, each standard giving content to the next.
The Annual Shari'ah Report standard is the output/disclosure obligation of the ISSC, cross-referencing both the governance standard and the charter standard.
Shari'ah non-compliance risk provisions allocate identification, escalation and remediation duties to the ISSC, closing the loop back into the annual report.
Hierarchy runs from the takaful/Islamic governance standard down to charter and reporting standards as implementing instruments.
start_here: Standard Re Shari'ah Governance for Takaful

data.theme: Licensing and conduct regime for finance companies, including restricted-licence and short-term credit models, use of agents, Islamic finance company requirements and credit-information obligations.
how_members_connect: The Finance Companies Regulation is the parent instrument defining Finance Company and Restricted Licence Finance Company, with a circular operationalising it.
Corporate-form requirements are imported from the Commercial Companies Law, creating a statute-to-regulation hierarchy.
Product/scope limits link Restricted Licence Finance Company and Agent to Short-Term Credit, which constrains permitted activity and outsourced distribution.
Islamic Finance Company adds a Shari'ah layer: Sharia'a Supervision Committee reporting into the Higher Sharia'a Authority.
Credit Information Agency linkage creates data-reporting and enquiry duties relevant to affordability and credit-information rules.

data.theme: Recovery planning at group level for financial institutions, addressing how a group-wide recovery plan must be prepared, scoped and maintained as a condition of prudential/resilience supervision.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster: the group recovery plan obligation sits as an article-level requirement whose scope term ('group') determines which entities and subsidiaries the plan must cover.
Links outward rather than internally — it presupposes the entity-level recovery planning and governance regime (board approval, triggers, escalation) sitting above it in the hierarchy.
Read as an enforceable planning duty with supervisory submission/approval consequences, not as guidance.

data.theme: Control environment obligations: the protective measures a regulated entity must have in place and the paired duty to test those measures and report outcomes to the supervisor or governing body.
how_members_connect: Direct obligation chain: safeguards create the control duty; testing and reporting create the assurance duty that evidences the first is effective.
Cross-reference means a safeguard failure and a testing/reporting failure are separate breaches — remediation of one does not cure the other.
Reporting element drives the notification trigger and timing that a compliance function must diarise.

data.theme: The payment token / stablecoin regime: licensing and permitted activities for token issuance, conversion, custody and transfer, with prudential capital, non-objection gating and outsourcing controls layered on top.
how_members_connect: The Payment Token Services Regulation is the parent instrument; conversion, custody/transfer and capital requirements are its dependent obligation sets, and algorithmic stablecoins are addressed as a defined (and scope-limited) category.
Non-objection registration acts as a supervisory gate that conditions whether conversion activity may be performed — a prior-approval chain rather than a notification.
Cross-reference to the Outsourcing Regulation imports the general third-party risk regime, so token service providers remain accountable for outsourced functions.
Reference to a foreign regulator (UAE SCA) signals cross-border recognition/registration interaction and a jurisdictional scope limit that must be checked before relying on foreign authorisation.

data.theme: Treatment of payment tokens issued outside the jurisdiction and the registration pathway their issuers must follow before the token can be offered or used locally.
how_members_connect: The defined term 'Foreign Payment Token' sets the scope trigger; the registration obligation attaches only once a token falls within that definition.
Sequencing matters: registration of the foreign issuer is the gating condition, so local distribution or service provision on an unregistered foreign token is a scope breach.
Sits beneath the broader payment token services regime and inherits its licensing, capital and conduct expectations for domestic intermediaries.

data.theme: Institutional architecture for resolving insurance complaints outside the courts — the Ombudsman Unit, its funding and its appeal/escalation path — with an adjacent banking prudential item on own-share acquisition limits.
how_members_connect: The Establishment Regulation is the constituting instrument; the Ombudsman Unit is the obligated body, and Complaint/Determination are its defined inputs and outputs.

Obligation chain: a Complaint is decided by a Determination, which is reviewable by the Appeals Committee, with the Insurance Dispute Resolution Committee as the parallel/alternative statutory forum — scope boundaries between these fora matter for a decision.
Funding is tied to the Unit by the Annual Levy and Case Fee, making participating insurers cost-bearing as well as subject to outcomes.

The Banks' Acquisition of Own Shares Regulation and its 10% ceiling sit here only via the drafting/issuing Regulatory Development Division, not by subject matter — treat as a separate prudential regime.

data.theme: Two regimes clustered together: governance and process of an insurance ombudsman body, and the non-KSA (UAE/CBUAE) AML-CTF and targeted financial sanctions framework applicable to hawala providers and licensed financial institutions.
how_members_connect: Governance chain: the Board of the Ombudsman Unit and Chief Ombudsman own the Complaint Resolution Process, which binds the insurance company and confers rights on the consumer/complainant.

AML hierarchy: the AML-CTF Decree-Law sits above the implementing Cabinet Decision, with Cabinet Decision (74) of 2020 carrying TFS duties and Circular 24/2019 licensing/regulating hawala providers; the CBUAE Guidance interprets all of them.
Obligation chain: transaction monitoring generates STR/SAR duties discharged through the goAML platform; freezing and reporting under TFS run to the same channel.

Cross-regime link: LFIs and registered hawala providers are conceptually related because LFIs bank RHPs and must apply CDD/KYB to them — note the jurisdictional caveat that these are UAE instruments, not SAMA rules.
start_here: CBUAE Guidance for Registered Hawala Providers and LFIs
Decree Federal Law No. (20) of 2018 (AML-CFT Law)

data.theme: Prudential and conduct treatment of profit smoothing in Islamic banking: how reserves are built and used to manage displaced commercial risk borne in respect of unrestricted investment account holders.
how_members_connect: The Profit Equalization Standard is the operative instrument and cross-refers to the broader Islamic bank risk management standards, creating a specific-within-general hierarchy.
Shared defined terms drive the obligations: PER (smoothing returns to IAHs and shareholders) and IRR (absorbing future investment losses of IAHs) are the two regulated reserve mechanisms.
DCR is the risk concept that justifies both reserves; its incidence falls on IAHs, linking prudential capital treatment to fair-treatment/disclosure duties toward account holders.
Consequence for decisions: reserve usage, disclosure and governance approvals must be traceable to the standard's conditions, not to management discretion.
start_here: Standard Regarding Profit Equalization for Islamic Banks

data.theme: Board-level governance over Islamic bank profit-smoothing reserves — allocation of decision rights between the board and a dedicated independent committee.
how_members_connect: The Board of an Islamic bank is the accountable governing body and delegates or oversees reserve decisions through the Independent Committee for Reserves.
This pairing is the governance layer that operationalises the PER/IRR and DCR requirements in the profit equalization standard cluster.
Practical consequence: reserve transfers and drawdowns require the committee's independent determination, limiting unilateral management action.

data.theme: Remote customer identification and verification (e-KYC) using national digital identity infrastructure, and the data-protection constraints that attach to relying on government identity attributes for CDD purposes.
how_members_connect: Shared defined activity: identity proofing/enrollment as the operative step that satisfies the CDD duty to identify and verify a customer before or during onboarding.

Obligation chain: e-KYC guidance points to authoritative identity sources (national ID credential, digital ID app, government validation gateway) as acceptable verification evidence, making source reliability a compliance condition rather than a technical choice.
Cross-regime interaction: use of identity attributes triggers data protection and privacy obligations (consent, purpose limitation, retention) alongside AML/CTF record-keeping.
Comparative note for KSA users: members are UAE-jurisdiction instruments; they are persuasive analogues, not SAMA obligations, and cannot be cited as authority for Saudi e-KYC acceptance.
start_here: UAE Data Protection and Privacy Framework

data.theme: Targeted financial sanctions and terrorism listing: how persons get on UN and domestic lists, who decides, and the freezing and reporting duties that bite on financial institutions and DNFBPs without delay.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: UNSCR 1373 and the UN Sanctions Committee feed the international list; the Cabinet Decision operationalises listing domestically, with the national security council as designating authority and the Executive Office as the implementing/communicating body.
Obligation chain: listing (UN or local) → notification via the Executive Office → immediate freezing and prohibition on making funds available → reporting to the competent authority.
Shared defined terms: 'Local Lists' versus 'UN Sanctions List' determine the legal basis and the delisting route (Ombudsperson/Focal Point versus domestic petition).
Cross-regime link: sanctions screening duties sit on top of, and are distinct from, risk-based CDD under the AML/CTF law; a sanctions hit is a strict prohibition, not a risk factor.
start_here: Cabinet Decision No 74 - Terrorism Lists Regulation

data.theme: Licensing and supervision of money-transfer intermediaries operating outside the banking channel, bringing hawala activity inside the AML/CTF perimeter through registration and transaction reporting.
how_members_connect: Status chain: the regulation creates the 'Registered Hawala Provider' status, evidenced by a certificate, which is the condition for lawfully conducting the activity.
Registered status pulls the provider into the AML/CTF law as a reporting entity, with CDD, record-keeping and STR duties equivalent in substance to other transfer providers.
Reporting obligation: periodic submission of remittance data to the supervisory reporting system is the ongoing supervisory hook attached to registration.
Standards anchor: FATF recommendations on money or value transfer services supply the policy rationale and the benchmark against which the registration regime is assessed.
start_here: Decretal Federal Law No. 20 of 2018 AML/CFT

data.theme: Governance, risk management and internal control requirements applicable to insurance undertakings, including board and control-function duties, outsourcing accountability and fraud countermeasures.
how_members_connect: Clear instrument hierarchy: primary insurance law → corporate governance and risk/internal-control regulations issued by circular → detailed standards elaborating each regulation's articles.

Paired structure: the governance standards and the risk management/internal controls standards are complementary, with control functions, the three-lines concept and board oversight defined once and relied on across both.

Cross-references outward: the corporate governance regulation cites the financial (prudential) regulations and the securities-regulator governance rules for listed insurers, so a listed insurance company faces cumulative obligations.

Scope-sensitive topics: outsourcing and insurance fraud are treated as governance responsibilities that cannot be delegated away, keeping accountability with the licensed entity's board and senior management.
start_here: Corporate Governance Regulation for Insurance Companies
Corporate Governance Standards for Insurance Companies
Risk Management and Internal Controls Standards for Insurance Companies

data.theme: Accounting and audit obligations on a licensed entity — maintaining proper books and records and submitting to independent audit as a supervisory assurance mechanism for SAMA.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster: the accounting/audit duty sits upstream of the reporting obligations in the neighbouring clusters, since audited records are the basis of what is reported to SAMA.
Linked by shared addressee (the licensee) and by SAMA's supervisory power to inspect records and rely on external auditors.

data.theme: Conduct-of-business requirements governing how a licensed entity deals with customers and the market — fair dealing, disclosure and the consumer-protection interface with prudential licensing conditions.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster; connects outward to consumer protection principles and to the defined 'Customer'/'Consumer' population used elsewhere in the same instrument.
Breach of conduct rules typically feeds the supervisory/enforcement chain rather than the reporting chain, so read alongside SAMA's general supervisory powers.

data.theme: Periodic financial reporting to SAMA — the form, content and timing of financial statements a licensee must produce.
how_members_connect: Depends on the accounting and audit obligation (Art. 11) for the underlying records and audit sign-off.
Overlaps in scope with the broader reporting duties (Art. 14); read the two together to distinguish financial statements from other regulatory returns and notifications.

data.theme: General regulatory reporting and notification duties owed to SAMA, beyond periodic financial statements — the ongoing information flow that sustains supervision.
how_members_connect: Sits at the end of the obligation chain: records (Art. 11) → financial statements (Art. 13) → returns and notifications to SAMA (Art. 14).
Shares addressee and enforcement route with the conduct-of-business duties; failure to report is independently actionable.

data.theme: Application of the FATF-style travel rule to virtual asset transfers: which participant (originating VASP, intermediary, beneficiary VASP) must collect, transmit, retain and screen originator/beneficiary identification data, and how anonymity-enhancing features such as privacy tokens constrain compliance.
how_members_connect: Shared defined terms chain the obligation: a Virtual Asset Transfer is framed by the Originator/Beneficiary pair, with the VASP as the obliged entity and the Intermediary Provider carrying forward the same data set along the payment chain.

Hierarchy runs from the Cabinet Decision down to the UAE Virtual Assets Travel Rule instrument, which is the operative source of the data-transmission and record-keeping duties cited here (note: a non-KSA comparator, relevant only for cross-border/benchmarking analysis).

Privacy Token links in as a scope/risk limitation - transfer mechanics that obscure originator or beneficiary data bear on whether the transmission obligation can be met and on the AML/CTF risk assessment.

Cross-regime interaction with core AML/CTF CDD: travel-rule data is an overlay on customer identification, not a substitute for it, and intermediary reliance raises third-party CDD reliance questions.

data.theme: Contractual and disclosure duties owed by a Payment Token Service Provider to its customers - what must be agreed in writing, what must be disclosed before contracting, and what transaction-level information must be provided afterwards.
how_members_connect: Sequential obligation chain within one instrument: the requirement to have a customer agreement, then the mandated content and pre-contractual disclosure, then ongoing transactional information duties.
All three provisions attach to the same obliged entity, the Payment Token Service Provider, so scope turns on that definition.
Consumer-protection style transparency obligations sitting inside a payments/token licensing regime - read alongside general SAMA consumer protection principles for overlap.
start_here: Article 28: Required Terms and Pre-Contractual Information

data.theme: Allocation of loss between provider and customer for unauthorised or incorrectly executed transfers, and the corresponding refund/remediation entitlement.
how_members_connect: Standalone provision in this graph; its practical effect depends on the customer agreement and disclosure provisions that define authorisation and notification duties.
Determines burden of proof and timing consequences for a dispute decision - i.e. when the provider must refund and when customer conduct shifts liability.
start_here: Article 31: Liability for Unauthorized Transfers and Refunds

data.theme: Governance requirements imposed on the licensed entity - board and senior management responsibility, internal control and accountability arrangements as a licensing/ongoing condition.
how_members_connect: Isolated node in this graph; operates as the governance overlay on the conduct and contractual obligations elsewhere in the same instrument.
Relevant cross-regime read-across to SAMA's general governance and risk-management frameworks for supervised institutions.

data.theme: Sustainable finance disclosure expectations for reporting entities, drawing on international sustainability reporting standards and a governance/strategy/risk-metrics disclosure principle. Note the scope limit: this material originates from a UAE working group, so it is comparative or guidance-level context rather than a SAMA enforceable obligation.
how_members_connect: The working group is the issuing body; the reporting-entity concept defines the addressee of the disclosure expectations, creating the who-must-disclose link.
Principle 3 attaches substantive disclosure content (governance arrangements, strategy, risk management and metrics) to those same reporting entities.
The ISSB reference operates as an external standard-setting anchor, i.e. the principles are framed as convergence with an international baseline rather than as free-standing rules.
Hierarchy runs standard-setter (ISSB) -> national/regional working-group guidance -> principle-level disclosure expectations on entities.

data.theme: The factors that determine what environmental, social and governance information must be disclosed, i.e. the qualitative gate between a general disclosure duty and specific ESG content.
how_members_connect: Principle 2 supplies the criteria (disclosure factors) that scope and shape the ESG-related disclosure category.
The ESG-Related Disclosures term is the defined output the principle governs, so the two are definition-to-obligation linked.
Sits alongside the entity-level (Principle 3) and product-level (Principle 4) disclosure principles in the same framework.

data.theme: Disclosure obligations at the level of individual financial products rather than the entity, covering how a product's sustainability characteristics must be presented.
how_members_connect: Isolated node in this graph; its legal meaning derives from the wider principles set, where entity-level disclosure is addressed separately.
Read together with the disclosure-factor criteria, which determine what product information is disclosure-relevant.
Distinguish the addressee: product-level duties bite on offering/marketing of a product, engaging consumer-protection style mis-selling concerns, not only periodic reporting.

data.theme: Definitional scope for insurance brokerage, establishing who counts as an insurance broker and therefore who falls within the licensing and conduct obligations of the instrument.
how_members_connect: The definitions article is the gateway provision: the broker term takes its legal content from it, and all downstream duties in the instrument key off that status.
Classification matters cross-regime, since broker status can trigger separate AML/CTF customer due diligence and consumer-protection conduct duties.
Typical hierarchy: enabling insurance law -> implementing regulation whose Article 1 fixes the defined terms used throughout.

data.theme: Operational resilience obligation requiring a supervised entity to maintain continuity of critical services and recover from disruption without harming customers or the payment ecosystem.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster: the business continuity duty sits within the entity's ongoing governance and risk-management licensing conditions rather than as a standalone regime.
Practically chained to supervisory oversight — failure to maintain continuity is the kind of breach that feeds the enforcement and information-gathering articles elsewhere in the instrument.
Read alongside broader SAMA governance/BCM expectations, which sit hierarchically above this article as general framework requirements.

data.theme: Supervisory consequence layer: SAMA's power to act against a regulated entity for non-compliance with the instrument's obligations.
how_members_connect: Terminal node in the obligation chain — every substantive duty in the instrument is enforceable through this article.
Draws its ultimate authority from the enabling statute (banking/payments law) that empowers SAMA to impose measures; the article is the instrument-level expression of that power.
Operationally paired with the information-gathering power, which supplies the evidentiary basis for enforcement action.

data.theme: Supervisory access rights allowing SAMA to require information beyond routine reporting, supporting ongoing monitoring and investigation.
how_members_connect: Feeds the enforcement article: information obtained under this power underpins any subsequent supervisory measure.
Complements periodic reporting duties elsewhere in the instrument by adding an ad hoc, on-demand layer.
Scope note: the power is exercisable against the licensed/registered entity, so outsourcing and third-party arrangements must be structured so the entity can still produce the information.

data.theme: Interface with the existing retail payments/stored-value framework: the instrument amends the Retail Payment and SVF Regulation and sets the timeline for incumbents to come into compliance.
how_members_connect: Direct hierarchical linkage — the amendment article modifies a prior SAMA regulation, so the two texts must be read as a consolidated regime rather than in isolation.
The transition article conditions the amendment: it fixes when amended obligations bite and what status existing licensees hold in the interim.
Together they determine grandfathering scope — which entities may continue operating under prior terms and for how long, a threshold question before any enforcement analysis.
Cross-regime consequence: amended SVF/retail payment scope can change whether an activity is licensable, which in turn changes AML/CTF and consumer-protection obligations attaching to that activity.
start_here: Article 39: Amendment to Retail Payment & SVF Regulation

data.theme: Continuing licence conditions — the obligations a licensed entity must satisfy on an ongoing basis after authorisation, as distinct from entry/licensing criteria.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster acting as the hinge between initial authorisation and the substantive conduct, solvency and governance duties elsewhere in the same regime.

Functions as a chapeau obligation: breach of downstream requirements (financial soundness, governance, conduct) typically crystallises as a failure of on-going requirements and a supervisory/licensing consequence.

data.theme: Conduct and contractual duties in insurance intermediation: the required content and status of brokerage agreements, and the handling of client money flowing through the broker (premiums, claim settlements, refunds).
how_members_connect: The premium/claims/refund duties operate on amounts arising under the brokerage agreement, so the money-handling article is read against the contractual scope set by the agreement article.

Explicit cross-reference between the two members creates an obligation chain: agreement terms define the mandate; the money article constrains collection, remittance and repayment within that mandate.
Both are conduct-of-business obligations owed toward insureds and insurers, with fiduciary-style implications for segregation and timeliness of transfers.

data.theme: Prudential standing of the licensed entity — the requirement to maintain financial soundness on a continuing basis as a condition of operating.
how_members_connect: Stands alone as the prudential limb of the licence, but is functionally dependent on the on-going requirements article and on the governance/internal control cluster that must monitor and evidence it.
Supervisory consequence: deterioration in financial soundness is a trigger point for SAMA intervention and for reassessment of continued authorisation.

data.theme: Governance, risk and control architecture of the licensed entity, including accountability for functions and activities transferred to third parties through outsourcing.
how_members_connect: Hierarchical linkage: the corporate governance article sets board and senior management accountability, which the risk governance/internal controls article operationalises as a framework requirement.
The outsourcing article references the risk framework — outsourced activity is treated as in-scope risk, so the entity retains regulatory responsibility and control duties over the service provider.
Together these articles supply the control environment that evidences compliance with the ongoing licence conditions and prudential soundness obligations in adjacent clusters.
Cross-regime relevance: the same governance and outsourcing chain typically governs reliance on third parties for customer-facing and compliance functions, so delegation does not transfer liability.
start_here: Article 10: Risk Governance Framework and Internal Controls

data.theme: Record-keeping obligations: what documentation a supervised entity must retain, in what form, and for how long, so that transactions, customer files and compliance decisions remain reconstructable for supervisory review.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster; its legal force comes from being an obligation owed to the supervisor rather than to the customer, and it underpins evidentiary proof of compliance with all other articles.

Interacts across regimes: AML/CTF retention duties (CDD records, transaction records, STR files) typically set the floor, while sector rules (payments, finance/BNPL, consumer protection) add product- and complaint-specific retention.
Feeds directly into the supervisor's inspection and information-request powers - inability to produce records is itself a compliance failure.

data.theme: Protection of personal data and cyber security: the duty to safeguard customer information and maintain information-security controls, sitting at the intersection of KSA data-protection law and SAMA prudential/operational-risk expectations.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster; it qualifies how record-keeping and customer-onboarding data may be stored, used, shared and disclosed.

Cross-regime linkage: personal-data duties constrain data sharing with credit bureaus, outsourcing providers and third parties relied on for CDD, and interact with consumer-protection consent requirements.
