Breach and incident consequences typically escalate to the supervisor, connecting this article to supervisory powers and enforcement.
start_here: Article 16: Protection of Personal Data and Cyber Security

data.theme: Powers of the Central Bank: the supervisory and enforcement authority reserved to SAMA over licensed/registered entities - inspection, information demands, directions, and corrective or sanctioning measures.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster that operates as the enforcement backbone for every substantive obligation elsewhere in the instrument.
Legal consequence chain: substantive duty (e.g. record-keeping, data protection) -> supervisory request or inspection -> direction or sanction under this article.
Also the gateway for approvals and no-objection requirements that condition corporate events such as mergers and wind-downs.
start_here: Article 18: Powers of the Central Bank

data.theme: Mergers, liquidations and bankruptcies: how corporate restructuring, exit or insolvency of a supervised entity is regulated, including supervisory notification/approval and continuity of obligations toward customers and creditors.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster; it presupposes the supervisor's approval and intervention authority, so it reads together with the Central Bank powers article.
Continuity linkage: customer records, personal data and outstanding consumer/finance obligations must survive the corporate event, tying back to record-keeping and data-protection duties.
Sits above general company/insolvency law as a sector-specific overlay - the supervisory consent step is additional, not a substitute.

data.theme: Governance-level risk management obligation: the licensed entity must maintain an internal risk management function/framework proportionate to its activities, sitting within the prudential and governance regime rather than a single risk type.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster; the article operates as the umbrella risk obligation that more specific control articles (fraud, continuity, outsourcing) implement in practice.
Legal linkage is hierarchical: framework-level duty set in the regulation, with board/senior management accountability for adequacy and review.
Isolated in the graph, so cross-references must be traced outward to the specific-control articles rather than within the cluster.

data.theme: Fraud prevention and detection duty: the entity must establish and maintain an anti-fraud framework covering identification, monitoring, reporting and mitigation of fraud affecting its services and customers.
how_members_connect: Standalone article; legally it is a specific-control obligation nested under the broader risk management duty.
Interacts across regimes — fraud typologies overlap with AML/CTF suspicion reporting and with consumer protection remedies for unauthorised transactions.
No internal edges: linkage is through shared defined terms (customer, payment transaction) rather than express cross-reference in this cluster.

data.theme: Operational resilience: the obligation to maintain business continuity arrangements so that payment/financial services and customer access are preserved and restored after disruption.
how_members_connect: Standalone article functioning as a specific-control obligation under the general risk management framework.
Consequence chain: continuity failures engage both prudential supervision and consumer-facing service obligations (access to funds, service availability).
Stay at obligation level — the article sets what must exist and be tested, not how systems are built.

data.theme: Segregation, accounting and assurance over customer/remittance funds: how the entity must hold and account for funds in dedicated accounts and subject its financial statements to external audit.
how_members_connect: The remittances intermediate account provision expressly references the accounts and external audit article, creating a direct obligation chain from fund segregation to independent verification.
Shared subject matter: customer funds held on an intermediate basis are within the scope of the accounting records and audit duty.
Hierarchical reading — general accounts/audit duty first, then the specific treatment for remittance intermediate balances as a carve-out or specification.
Cross-regime relevance: segregated remittance flows also matter for AML/CTF traceability of transfers and for consumer claims on held funds.

data.theme: Transitional and repeal mechanics for insurance-sector instruments: how a new Insurance Authority instrument extinguishes the legal force of earlier resolutions and what continues to apply in the interim.
how_members_connect: The cancellation article operates directly on the earlier resolution, so the two must be read as repealing instrument and repealed instrument.
Linkage is hierarchical/temporal rather than substantive: the later instrument determines the effective date from which obligations under the 2013 resolution cease.
Relevant to any compliance position that still cites the superseded resolution as its legal basis; grandfathering and saved provisions, if any, must be confirmed in the repealing text itself.
start_here: Article 20: Cancellation of Previous Legal Instruments

data.theme: Prudential credit risk classification: when an exposure is in default, when credit risk has increased significantly, and the resulting staging, provisioning and capital consequences. Note the standards and cross-references here are Central Bank of the UAE instruments, so they are persuasive comparators rather than SAMA obligations.
how_members_connect: A definitional chain: the default definition anchors the SICR test, which in turn drives stage allocation and the provisioning obligation.
Article-to-standards pairing — each substantive article has a corresponding Standards article that elaborates the supervisory expectation, a classic rule-to-implementing-standard hierarchy.

Provisioning is the convergence point: restructuring treatment, credit risk mitigation recognition, capital adequacy and model governance all feed into or draw from the classification and provisioning obligation.
The three-stage classification concept is the shared taxonomy that makes the default and SICR definitions operationally binding.
start_here: Article 7: Significant Increase in Credit Risk

data.theme: Treatment of restructured and forborne exposures and the provisioning/classification consequences that follow, including whether restructuring permits stage or classification improvement.
how_members_connect: The restructuring article expressly feeds the classification and provisioning article: restructuring is a trigger event, not a reset.
Both articles share the default/SICR definitions used elsewhere in the credit risk framework, so they cannot be applied in isolation.
Practical consequence: cure periods and upgrade conditions sit in the restructuring rule, while the resulting provision level is set by the classification rule.

data.theme: Recognition and valuation of collateral, guarantees and other credit risk mitigants, and the limits on using them to reduce measured credit risk or provisions.
how_members_connect: Stands as the eligibility gate feeding the classification and provisioning framework — mitigants only reduce provisioning if they satisfy this article's recognition conditions.
Isolated in the graph but substantively dependent on the default and staging definitions; read alongside the provisioning article rather than alone.
Watch the interaction with capital adequacy treatment: the same mitigant may be recognised differently for provisioning and for capital.

data.theme: Prudential treatment of credit risk models — the governance, validation and use-test expectations attaching to models that drive credit risk measurement and capital or provisioning outcomes.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster: the obligation sits on the licensee's board/senior management to own model design, approval and periodic validation rather than on any external body.
Functions as a downstream detail of a broader risk-management/governance regulation, so it should be read together with internal audit and independent review duties found in adjacent clusters.
Isolated node — no internal cross-references captured, so scope limits must be taken from the parent instrument, not inferred.

data.theme: Authorisation-stage and ongoing fitness and propriety of controllers, directors and senior/controlled-function holders across exchange business, open finance and insurance activities, including supervisory consent gateways for outsourcing and material changes.
how_members_connect: Clear hierarchy: the Fitness and Propriety Regulation is issued by circular (4/2024) and operationalised by the Fitness and Propriety Standards, which sit beneath it as detailed criteria.

Sector regulations (Exchange Business, Open Finance, Licensing and Monitoring of Exchange Business) each cross-refer to the fit-and-proper regime, making it a common gateway condition rather than a standalone regime.
The Letter of No Objection is the shared consent instrument linking appointment/outsourcing decisions (Article 15) to the licensing framework — no LNO, no lawful change.
AML/CTF law and the Insurance Law enter as integrity inputs: adverse AML findings or insurance-sector conduct feed the propriety assessment, creating a cross-regime interaction.
Older and newer instruments coexist (Notice 1/2014 vs. current regulations), so supersession and transitional scope must be checked before relying on a provision.

data.theme: Entry and continuing prudential conditions for exchange business, including who qualifies as a Licensed Person, the activities in scope, and the capital and guarantee floors that condition the licence.
how_members_connect: 'Licensed Person' is the anchor defined term; every other member is either an activity it may conduct (Exchange Business, IMTS Provider) or a condition it must continuously satisfy.
Minimum Paid-up Capital and Minimum Bank Guarantee operate as licence conditions — breach is a prudential failure, not merely a reporting matter.
IMTS provision pulls the licensee into the AML/CTF regime, so money transfer activity triggers customer due diligence and reporting duties in addition to prudential floors.
Scope note: obligations attach to the licensed entity; activity-specific thresholds may differ by category of licence.

data.theme: The assurance layer over AML/CTF compliance — independent internal audit testing of the AML/CTF programme, distinct from the compliance function's own first- and second-line duties.
how_members_connect: The internal audit provision expressly reaches the AML/CTF compliance article, creating an obligation chain: compliance function designs and runs controls, internal audit independently tests their adequacy and effectiveness.
Three-lines separation matters legally: audit independence and reporting lines to the board/audit committee are conditions of a compliant programme, not good practice.
Findings from audit feed back into the AML/CTF programme's required periodic review and into supervisory reporting expectations.

data.theme: Institution-level AML/CTF risk assessment methodology: how a supervised entity measures inherent ML/TF risk, evaluates the quality of its control environment, and derives residual risk to drive a risk-based approach.
how_members_connect: Shared calculation chain: inherent risk minus assessed control effectiveness yields residual risk, which in turn calibrates the risk-based approach.
The control-environment assessment is the hub node, decomposing into the mandated control pillars — CDD/KYC, training, independent testing, governance and internal controls.
The MLRO is the accountable function linking the institutional risk assessment to governance and reporting obligations.
External soft-law (Wolfsberg sanctions screening guidance) is cited to benchmark internal control adequacy, not as a binding SAMA obligation.

data.theme: Cross-border payment execution and messaging, covering correspondent banking channels, SWIFT message content and relationship-management arrangements, and migration to the ISO 20022 data standard.
how_members_connect: Correspondent banking guidance frames cross-border payments as the operating context in which messaging obligations bite.
Payment message integrity (originator/beneficiary data) is the shared obligation linking cross-border payments to SWIFT message rules.
RMA relationships with non-customers are treated as a distinct exposure within the same messaging infrastructure.
ISO 20022 is conceptually linked as the evolving data standard affecting the content and quality of payment messages.

data.theme: Due diligence regime for correspondent banking relationships: identifying risk factors, applying standard, specific and enhanced due diligence, and sustaining monitoring, governance and record-keeping.
how_members_connect: Risk mitigation is the obligation hub, chaining standard CDD, correspondent-specific due diligence, EDD for high-risk relationships, ongoing monitoring, independent audit and record-keeping.
Risk factors (nesting, payable-through accounts, geography, ownership/management structure) are the trigger set that escalates a relationship to enhanced due diligence.
FATF Recommendation 13 is the international source obligation; the Wolfsberg CBDDQ is the market-standard information-gathering instrument referenced to satisfy it.
Standard CDD and record-keeping cross-refer to the general CDD/KYC and record-keeping guidance, showing hierarchy from general AML rules to the correspondent-banking overlay.
start_here: Specific Due Diligence for Correspondent Banking

data.theme: Indicators of suspicion arising in correspondent banking relationships, used to trigger enhanced scrutiny and suspicious transaction reporting.
how_members_connect: Isolated node in the graph: no internal edges, so its legal effect is understood only by reading it against the correspondent banking due diligence and monitoring cluster.
Functions as a supervisory expectation feeding ongoing monitoring and escalation, rather than a standalone obligation.

data.theme: Obligation on the service provider to ensure that communications and credentials exchanged with the customer are conducted through secure channels, protecting authentication data from interception or misuse.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster: the secure communication duty stands alone in the graph but sits in the payment/electronic services obligation chain alongside authentication and customer notification duties.
Functionally linked to liability allocation rules, since failure to provide a secure channel bears on who carries the loss from a disputed transaction.
Operates as a conduct/consumer-protection requirement rather than a prudential one, so breach is assessed against the provider, not the user.

data.theme: Allocation of loss between provider and customer for transactions the customer did not authorise, including the thresholds and conduct (gross negligence, fraud, late notification) that shift liability.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster; its operative effect depends on the definitions of 'authorisation' and 'customer' used elsewhere in the same instrument.
Chains to security and notification obligations: the provider's compliance with secure communication and strong authentication duties is the pivot for rebutting liability.
Consumer-protection regime rule — outcomes are decided on burden of proof and evidence of the provider's controls, not on the customer's assertion alone.

data.theme: The primary AML/CFT/PF statutory framework: the criminalisation of money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing, and the national governance bodies that set policy and assess risk.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy is explicit: the 2025 Decree Law is the parent instrument, repealing and replacing the 2018 Decree Law, and all offence articles and committees derive their authority from it.
Definitional chain: the money laundering, TF and PF offence articles supply the predicate concepts that downstream CDD, reporting and sanctions obligations depend on.

Institutional chain: the Supreme Committee and National Committee are creatures of the Law, with the National Committee owning the National Risk Assessment that drives the risk-based approach for supervised entities.
Transitional issue: references in older guidance to the repealed 2018 Law must be read against the 2025 text before being relied on.
start_here: Federal Decree Law No.10 of 2025 AML/CFT/PF

data.theme: Targeted financial sanctions, particularly the proliferation-financing limb: the UN-to-national transmission of listings, the domestic competent authority, and the resulting freezing and screening duties, including in a trade-finance context.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy runs from UNSC resolutions (including UNSCR 1540) down through the Cabinet Decision on TFS and the 2025 Executive Regulations, with the Executive Office as the designated implementing authority.

Shared defined term: 'Targeted Financial Sanctions' links the general regime node to its trade-based money laundering application, so the same freezing/no-dealing obligation applies across product lines.
FATF Recommendation 7 supplies the international standard the national instruments implement, which matters when interpreting scope and timeliness of freezing.
Sanctions screening of trade transactions is the operational consequence of the listing obligations — an obligation to screen counterparties, goods and routes, not a discretionary control.

data.theme: Treatment of dormant accounts, unclaimed balances and their eventual transfer to the central bank, sitting at the intersection of consumer protection (preserving the customer's claim) and AML/CTF customer due diligence obligations that persist over inactive relationships.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy runs from the dormancy article on unclaimed funds up to the Dormant Accounts and Unclaimed Funds Regulation, which supplies the operative defined terms (Dormant Customer, Unclaimed Balances and Funds) and the transfer/reclaim obligation chain.
Transfer of funds to the central bank and reclaim procedures are two halves of one obligation: extinguishing the institution's holding duty without extinguishing the beneficial owner's entitlement.

AML linkage: dormancy does not suspend CDD — identification and verification standards (and the limits on third-party reliance) under the AML/CFT decision govern reactivation and any payout, so an unclaimed-funds reclaim is also a KYC event.

Consumer protection duties (notification, fee limits, access to remedy) overlay the dormancy regime; note the cluster mixes a non-KSA (UAE) AML framework reference, so confirm jurisdictional applicability before relying on it for SAMA questions.
start_here: Dormant Accounts and Unclaimed Funds Regulation

data.theme: The standalone statutory duty to report specified matters to the central bank — a supervisory notification obligation distinct from AML suspicious transaction reporting to the FIU.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: the article stands alone in the graph, with no internal cross-references extracted.

Its practical significance is as a destination for obligation chains elsewhere (breach, incident, governance and dormancy events that must be escalated to the regulator rather than only recorded internally).
When applying it, keep the recipient and trigger distinct from AML/CTF reporting duties, which run to the financial intelligence unit and carry tipping-off restrictions.
start_here: Article 26: Duty to Report to the Central Bank

data.theme: The architectural and governance layer of the Open Finance regime: the central framework instrument and the shared infrastructure (API hub, trust framework, common services) through which regulated open finance participation is delivered.
how_members_connect: The Open Finance Framework is the parent instrument; the API Hub, Trust Framework and Common Infrastructural Services are its mandated components, so obligations flow downward from the framework to each infrastructural element.
Use of the central API hub engages the outsourcing regulation circular, meaning reliance on shared infrastructure does not displace the participant's own accountability for outsourced functions.
The infrastructure is benchmarked against international financial market infrastructure principles, which supplies the resilience, governance and access-criteria expectations.
This cluster is the institutional counterpart to the participant-role cluster on data sharing and service initiation.

data.theme: The role taxonomy and customer-facing obligations of Open Finance: who is a data holder, data sharing provider, service initiation provider or service owner, and the consent, privacy and authentication duties attaching to each.
how_members_connect: Everything turns on defined roles: the Open Finance Provider is the umbrella term, split into data sharing and service initiation activities, each with a counterparty role (data holder, service owner) that bears reciprocal duties.
Consent and data privacy requirements are the common gate for both activity types — no data sharing or service initiation is lawful without a valid, scoped customer consent.
Authentication obligations bind the data holder and service owner side, allocating responsibility for verifying the customer at the point of access or initiation.

The 'person deemed licensed' concept is the licensing bridge: it determines which entities may act as providers without a separate authorisation, and should be read against the framework and infrastructure cluster.

data.theme: Sets the purpose and the measurement discipline of a climate transition plan: why a supervised institution prepares one and how progress against it is evidenced over time.
how_members_connect: Both sit in the same principles-based instrument on climate transition planning, so they share its scope, defined terms and addressee institutions.

Obligation chain: the stated transition objectives determine which metrics and targets are relevant, and the metrics/targets provision is the accountability mechanism that makes the objectives supervisable.
Conceptually paired - objectives without calibrated targets are unenforceable in practice, and targets are only assessable against declared objectives.
start_here: Principle 1 - Objectives of Climate Transition Planning

data.theme: Allocation of board and senior management responsibility for climate transition planning - who owns approval, oversight and internal accountability.
how_members_connect: Standalone governance principle within the climate transition planning framework; it names the accountable bodies that the other principles' obligations attach to.

Interacts with the broader SAMA governance/risk regime (board oversight, risk appetite, internal control), so it should be read alongside general corporate governance requirements rather than in isolation.

data.theme: Requirement to embed the climate transition plan into the institution's business strategy, rather than maintaining it as a parallel disclosure exercise.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster; it is the bridge principle linking governance ownership to operational execution of the transition objectives.
Cross-regime relevance: strategy integration touches risk management, capital and business planning obligations, so consequences extend beyond the climate instrument itself.

data.theme: Expectations on data underpinning the transition plan and on engagement with customers/counterparties whose activities drive the institution's climate exposure.
how_members_connect: Standalone principle; supplies the informational basis that metrics, targets and strategy integration depend on.

Potential interaction with consumer protection and data/credit information regimes where customer engagement involves collecting or using client-level data - scope limits of those regimes should be checked before acting.

data.theme: Screening obligations at the intersection of CDD and targeted financial sanctions: identifying the customer and the beneficial owner, then testing those identities and their transactions against sanctions and watchlists.
how_members_connect: Shared definitional spine: the customer/beneficial owner identified under CDD is the same subject fed into name screening, so the ownership/control test determines screening scope.

Obligation chain: identify and verify -> screen names at onboarding and on list updates -> screen transactions -> resolve matches; list management is the upstream control that makes each step effective.
Ownership/control rule creates derivative exposure - an unlisted entity can be in scope through a listed owner or controller - linking sanctions screening back to beneficial ownership findings.
Fuzzy matching is a calibration parameter of the name screening duty, not a separate obligation; it bears on whether the screening obligation is adequately discharged.

data.theme: Treatment of virtual asset transfers involving wallets not controlled by a regulated intermediary, where counterparty information is absent and standard transfer-rule data cannot be obtained.
how_members_connect: A single definitional dependency: the enhanced due diligence duty applies only once a transfer is characterised as involving an unhosted wallet.
The EDD requirement operates as a risk-mitigation substitute for counterparty identification that the travel-rule/transfer regime cannot supply.

data.theme: UAE labour-nationalisation (Emiratization) compliance for licensed financial institutions, including penalties for non-compliance and for artificial or fictitious hiring arrangements.
how_members_connect: Regulation-to-definition hierarchy: the penalties regulation supplies the operative sanctions and defines the regulated population (licensed institutions) and the prohibited conduct (fictitious Emiratization).
NAFIS and the Tawteen system are the registration/reporting channels through which compliance is evidenced and breaches detected.
Cross-jurisdiction flag: this is a UAE/CBUAE regime, not a SAMA obligation - use only for comparative purposes, not as KSA authority.

data.theme: Proliferation financing and trade-based money laundering risk in trade finance, including export-control evasion, dual-use goods and transshipment abuse.
how_members_connect: Two supervisory guidance documents anchor the cluster and are mutually reinforcing: PF risk guidance and TBML/transshipment guidance share typologies and red-flag logic.
Substantive linkage runs from trade finance vulnerability to dual-use/controlled goods and export-control circumvention, with transshipment as the concealment mechanism.
The competent authority (EOCN) is the referenced control and reporting counterpart for export-control and non-proliferation matters.
Industry standards (Wolfsberg/ICC/BAFT) are cited as persuasive benchmarks, not binding rules - treat as expectation-setting, not enforceable text.
Cross-jurisdiction flag: CBUAE material; PF obligations in KSA rest on the separate SAMA/TFS framework.
start_here: CBUAE Guidance on Proliferation Finance Risks
CBUAE Guidance on TBML and Transshipment

data.theme: Risk-based customer due diligence applied to trade finance and cross-border goods flows, where the underlying typology is diversion, transshipment and dual-use/sanctions-evasion risk rather than conventional payment risk.
how_members_connect: Obligation chain: institution-level (enterprise-wide) risk assessment identifies trade/transshipment exposure, which in turn calibrates whether baseline CDD suffices or EDD is triggered.
Shared risk factor: illicit transshipment indicators are the common reference point cited by both the enterprise-wide assessment and the heightened-risk EDD measures.
Hierarchy of measures: CDD is the standing baseline; EDD is the escalated, case-specific overlay for trade relationships assessed as higher risk.
Cross-regime interaction: trade due diligence sits at the AML/CTF and sanctions/TFS boundary, since goods-level red flags drive both suspicious-activity and sanctions-evasion analysis.
start_here: EDD Measures for Heightened Trade Risks

data.theme: The design and governance of a sanctions compliance programme and its supporting transaction monitoring function - what a supervised institution must have in place to detect listed persons and suspicious activity, and how that framework is tested and supervised.
how_members_connect: Programme hierarchy: the Sanctions Compliance Program is the umbrella obligation, with senior management commitment, risk assessment, risk appetite, policies and procedures, training and independent audit/testing as its mandated components.

Guidance layer: the AML/CFT transaction monitoring and sanctions screening guidance interprets the underlying obligations and pulls the risk assessment and monitoring programme elements into a single expected standard.
Legal anchor: the terrorism-list decision supplies the designation source that screening must operate against, converting programme design into a concrete listing obligation.
Supervisory feedback loop: thematic review findings on screening testing inform risk appetite calibration and the adequacy of independent testing.
Note the regime distinction - sanctions/TFS obligations are strict and list-driven, whereas AML/CTF monitoring is risk-based; a single system supports both but the legal triggers differ.
start_here: AML/CFT Guidance on Transaction Monitoring and Sanctions Screening

data.theme: Cross-border mutual legal assistance and the recovery, freezing and repatriation of criminal proceeds - the outward-facing arm of the AML/CTF regime.
how_members_connect: Single-member cluster: functions as the anchor node for requests for assistance, information exchange and confiscation/asset-return mechanisms.
Connects outward to predicate-offence, confiscation and financial-intelligence provisions rather than internally.
Relevant to institutions chiefly as the legal basis for responding to foreign-origin freezing or information requests channelled through the competent authority.

data.theme: International cooperation specifically for virtual asset-related offences, addressing the jurisdictional gap created by borderless VA transfers.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster acting as the VA-specific counterpart to the general international cooperation and asset recovery provisions.
Its operative effect depends on how virtual asset and VASP are defined elsewhere in the regime, so the scope limit must be read against those definitions.
Practical consequence is at authority level (assistance, tracing, evidence-sharing) rather than a direct institutional compliance duty.
start_here: Article 64 - International Cooperation on VA Crimes

data.theme: Cross-border and inter-agency exchange of law enforcement information in the AML/CTF cooperation chapter, i.e. the legal gateway allowing competent authorities to share intelligence and case information with counterparts.
how_members_connect: Single-article community sitting in the international cooperation block that runs alongside judicial cooperation and foreign-judgment provisions.
Operates at the authority-to-authority level (law enforcement/competent authority), distinct from formal judicial channels and from FI reporting duties.
Relevant to supervised entities only indirectly: information they report can lawfully travel abroad through this gateway.

data.theme: Formal judicial cooperation with foreign states (mutual legal assistance, letters rogatory, evidence and procedural requests) in money laundering / terrorist financing matters.
how_members_connect: Complements the law enforcement exchange gateway: same cooperation chapter, but through judicial rather than administrative channels.
Feeds the recognition-and-enforcement provisions, since assistance requests often precede or accompany foreign judgment execution.
Conditioned by reciprocity and domestic procedural safeguards typical of this chapter.

data.theme: Recognition and execution in KSA of foreign judgments, including confiscation and asset-related orders, and the substantive conditions that must be satisfied before execution is granted.
how_members_connect: Article 68 expressly qualifies Article 67: the enabling power to execute is subject to the enumerated conditions - a classic rule/proviso pair.
Both sit downstream of the judicial cooperation gateway; a foreign judgment typically arrives through those channels.
Consequence for practice: assets frozen or seized on foreign request cannot be finally disposed of unless the Article 68 conditions are met.

data.theme: Transitional/repeal provision terminating the prior Cabinet Resolution instrument and establishing which text governs going forward.
how_members_connect: Final-provisions article: no substantive obligations of its own, but it determines the temporal validity of the whole instrument's obligations.
Critical for citation hygiene - references to the repealed resolution in older policies, circulars or contracts must be re-mapped to the current text.
Interacts with every other community by fixing the effective legal basis for their obligations.

data.theme: Cross-border correspondent banking as a distinct higher-risk category under AML/CTF rules, where a Saudi institution provides account and payment services to a respondent foreign institution and inherits exposure to that respondent's own customer base.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster: the concept anchors the enhanced due diligence regime applicable to correspondent relationships (respondent institution assessment, senior management approval, understanding of respective AML/CTF responsibilities).
Legally dependent on the AML Law and Implementing Regulation's EDD obligations rather than standing alone; read as a scope-triggered add-on to ordinary CDD.
Interacts with the payable-through account and shell-bank prohibitions, and with sanctions/TFS screening of respondent traffic.
Links outward to remittance and trade-finance clusters, which are common channels through which respondent risk materialises.

data.theme: Governance-style principle requiring a supervised entity to translate an adopted policy/framework into a concrete implementation strategy with assigned actions, owners and timelines. The compliance question is whether a board-approved policy alone satisfies the rule, or whether documented execution steps are separately enforceable.
how_members_connect: Singleton node: the principle stands alone in the graph but is structurally part of a numbered principles sequence, so it inherits the scope and definitions of its parent framework.
Operates downstream of the earlier principles (policy adoption/approval) and upstream of the review principle, forming an obligation chain: set policy -> implement -> review.
Typical hierarchy linkage: enabling law or SAMA regulation sets the duty; the principle text supplies the implementation expectation used in supervisory assessment.

data.theme: Money or value transfer services outside conventional banking channels (hawala and similar alternative remittance arrangements) and their treatment under Saudi AML/CTF licensing and supervision requirements.
how_members_connect: Single-node cluster functioning as a definitional hook for MVTS/money remittance activity, which triggers licensing, registration and full CDD/recordkeeping duties.
Obligation chain runs from the AML Law and its Implementing Regulation into the customer identification, wire-transfer information and STR-filing requirements.
Cross-references the trade-based money laundering cluster, where registered and unregistered hawala providers appear as settlement mechanisms.
Also intersects the payments/PSP regime where value transfer is conducted by non-bank operators.

data.theme: Principle imposing a periodic (and event-driven) review and update duty over the adopted framework or policy, keeping it current with regulatory change and the entity's risk profile.
how_members_connect: Singleton node; its legal force derives from the parent principles instrument rather than from cross-references to other nodes.
Closes the loop with the implementation principle: what is implemented must be reassessed, with governance sign-off on updates.
Commonly the hook supervisors use to test staleness of policies during inspections, so it interacts with board/senior-management responsibility provisions in the same instrument.

data.theme: Trade-based money laundering: the use of commercial trade transactions, documentation and settlement to disguise illicit proceeds or move value across borders, and the typologies institutions are expected to detect during transaction monitoring and trade-finance review.
how_members_connect: Hub-and-spoke structure: the TBML concept is the parent node and each typology (invoicing and shipment manipulation, multiple invoicing, fictitious documents, back-to-back letters of credit, pass-through accounts) is a referenced red-flag category feeding the same suspicion-reporting duty.
Shared legal consequence: identification of any typology engages CDD/EDD, source-of-funds enquiry, and the obligation to file a suspicious transaction report.

Actor-based spokes (third-party intermediaries, surrogate shopping networks, registered hawala providers) link this cluster to beneficial ownership and MVTS obligations; jurisdictional spokes (free trade zones) link to country-risk and higher-risk geography assessment.
Duplicate free-trade-zone nodes and the services-based variant show the same typology framing extended from goods to services, indicating the concept is applied by substance, not by documentary form.

data.theme: Article-level requirement governing re-takaful arrangements, i.e. the cession of takaful risk to re-takaful (or, where permitted, reinsurance) providers and the conditions attaching to such arrangements.
how_members_connect: Singleton article node within a takaful/insurance instrument; it depends on that instrument's defined terms (takaful operator, participants, surplus) rather than on other clustered nodes.
Interacts with solvency, risk-retention and outsourcing-type controls elsewhere in the same regime, and with SAMA approval or notification requirements for counterparties.
Sits at the regulation/rules tier beneath the insurance law, with supervisory circulars typically refining acceptable counterparty criteria.

data.theme: Trade finance product structures - particularly non-documentary and open-account arrangements - where the financing institution has limited sight of underlying goods, creating heightened AML/CTF and credit-risk scrutiny expectations.
how_members_connect: Non-documentary trade finance is the organising node; factoring, forfaiting and structured trade finance are referenced as its product sub-types sharing the same reduced-documentation risk profile.
Open account trade is treated as conceptually equivalent in risk terms, because settlement occurs without bank-intermediated documentary control.
The absence of documentary evidence shifts the compliance burden onto customer-level CDD, beneficial ownership and transaction monitoring rather than document examination.
Directly adjacent to the trade-based money laundering cluster: these products are the channels in which those typologies are expected to be detected.

data.theme: Article-level requirement concerning the zakat fund account within a takaful/insurance structure - its establishment, funding and the segregation of amounts held for zakat purposes from other accounts.
how_members_connect: Singleton article node; its meaning is fixed by the fund-segregation and surplus-distribution definitions of the same instrument.
Links conceptually to the separation of participants' and shareholders' accounts, so it constrains how surplus and contributions may be applied.
Cross-regime touchpoint: accounting and Shariah-governance expectations sit outside SAMA's article but shape how the account is operated and reported.

data.theme: Solvency adequacy for takaful operators — the prudential requirement to hold and maintain capital/technical resources sufficient to meet obligations to participants and creditors.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster: a standalone prudential obligation within the takaful regulatory framework, addressed to the licensed insurer/operator rather than to consumers.
Operates alongside the wider takaful regulation as an ongoing licensing condition, with supervisory consequences where the solvency margin is breached.
Interacts with governance/risk expectations and with the separation of participants' funds from shareholders' funds, which determines what resources count toward solvency.

data.theme: Transparency obligations of takaful operators — what must be disclosed, to whom (participants, SAMA, the market) and on what cycle.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster imposing reporting/disclosure duties that make the prudential and fund-segregation rules verifiable.
Functionally paired with the solvency and participants'-fund provisions: disclosure is the mechanism by which compliance with those substantive rules is evidenced.
Overlaps the consumer-protection regime where the disclosure runs to participants (clarity, timeliness, no misleading content).

data.theme: Movement of monies between the participants' (takaful) fund and the shareholders'/investment account — when transfers are permitted and on what conditions.
how_members_connect: Single-article cluster governing fund segregation, the structural principle underlying the takaful model.
Directly constrains the solvency and surplus-distribution analysis: transfers change the assets available to each fund.
Any permitted transfer is expected to be visible through the disclosure obligations, linking this article to the reporting cluster.
start_here: Transfer of Fund and Investment Account (Article 26)

data.theme: The 2022 takaful insurance regulation as the governing instrument, including its repeal of the prior regulation and the resulting transition in applicable rules.
how_members_connect: Hierarchy: the 2022 regulation is the parent instrument from which the operative articles (solvency, disclosure, fund transfer) derive their authority.
The cancellation article expressly displaces the earlier regulation, so effective-date and grandfathering questions turn on this cross-reference.
Defined terms used across the other clusters (participant, takaful fund, operator) are anchored in this instrument; scope limits should be read here first.

data.theme: Licensing-level architecture for takaful insurance: the statutory basis for establishing and operating a takaful insurance fund, the standards that give it operational content, and the operational risk regime applied to the takaful operator.
how_members_connect: All instruments in the cluster derive authority from the same primary statute (the Central Bank Law), giving a law → standard → article hierarchy.
The fund-establishment article operates as the trigger provision; the controls-and-procedures standard supplies the conditions a takaful operator must satisfy to comply with it.

The operational-model standard and the operational risk regulation attach parallel conduct and governance duties to the same licensed takaful operator, so a fund cannot be assessed for compliance on segregation rules alone.
Cross-regime point: takaful fund segregation obligations sit alongside generic prudential/operational-risk obligations; the two must be read cumulatively, not as alternatives.
start_here: Federal Decree-Law No. (6) of 2025 (Central Bank Law)
Standard re Controls and Procedures for Establishing Takaful Insurance Fund

data.theme: The Wakala operational model for takaful: how the operator's agency relationship with participants is constituted, documented, priced and accounted for, including contributions, wakala fees and participants' investment balances.
how_members_connect: The provisions form a single obligation chain: choosing and setting the operational model, then documenting the contractual relationship, then the membership policy, then the cash flows (contribution, fee).
They share defined terms — Wakala Operational Model, Participants' Investment Account — so an interpretation of one article constrains the others.
Fee and contribution articles both resolve into the Participants' Investment Account, making fund-separation and fee-entitlement questions interdependent.
The membership policy is the disclosure vehicle through which fee terms must be made transparent to participants, linking conduct/consumer-facing duties to the structural model.

data.theme: Treatment of re-takaful arrangements — the conditions under which a takaful fund may cede risk and the constraints applying to that cession.
how_members_connect: A standalone provision within the takaful operational-model regime; it should be read against the fund-establishment and Wakala-model articles because cession affects the participants' fund.
Its obligations bind the same licensed takaful operator addressed by the broader takaful standards.

data.theme: The operational risk and operational resilience regime for licensed entities: the required risk management framework, its governance and control infrastructure, and the specific domains (ICT/cyber, incidents, continuity, third parties) it must cover.
how_members_connect: The operational risk management framework article is the hub; nearly every other provision is expressed as a requirement feeding into or implementing that framework.
A second sub-chain runs from operational resilience into incident management and business continuity planning, i.e. resilience is the outcome obligation and those articles are its components.
Governance layering: the dedicated risk function plus the internal control system are the accountability structures through which the framework must be discharged.

Third-party risk management extends the framework to outsourced and vendor arrangements, so responsibility is not transferred with the activity; the annex of risk tools supplies the methodology the framework is expected to apply.

data.theme: Allocation of governance accountability between the board and senior management within a risk/compliance framework — who sets and approves strategy, policy and risk appetite versus who implements, monitors and reports.
how_members_connect: Both articles sit in the same governance chapter and form a single delegation chain: board approval and oversight above, senior management execution and escalation below.
Article 5 is drafted by reference to Article 4, so management duties are defined as the operational counterpart of board-reserved matters.
Shared defined terms (board, senior management, policies, reporting lines) mean a compliance gap at one level is usually a breach attributable at the other.
Typical supervisory consequence: failure of implementation is assessed against board oversight adequacy, not treated as management-only.

data.theme: Transitional and instrument-hierarchy effects of the operational risk regime — how a circular issues the rules and what earlier supervisory notices it displaces.
how_members_connect: The circular is the issuing instrument; the cancellation article is the repeal clause inside the rules it issues, so they must be read together to fix the applicable text.
The linkage answers a dating question: which obligations were superseded and from when, relevant to legacy policies and supervisory findings.
Illustrates the law → regulation → circular hierarchy: prior notices remain relevant only for conduct before the cancellation takes effect.

data.theme: Targeted financial sanctions arising from terrorism listing decisions: identifying a confirmed match against listed persons and the mandatory notification duty to the supervisor and the competent listing office. Note this cluster reflects a UAE instrument, so scope must be checked before analogising to the KSA/SAMA regime.
how_members_connect: The Cabinet Decision is the parent instrument; both the match-determination concept and the notification duty derive their definitions and triggers from it.
Obligation chain: screening produces a potential hit → confirmation of the match → immediate freezing and reporting obligations crystallise, with strict timing.
'Confirmed match' is the defined trigger term — the notification duty is conditional on it, so its threshold governs whether a reporting breach exists.
start_here: Cabinet Decision No. 74 of 2020 (Terrorism Lists Regulation)

data.theme: Sanctions and TFS screening obligations across the customer lifecycle and the payment message, including the lists to be screened against, disposition of false positives, and detection of evasion typologies.
how_members_connect: 'Screening Operations' is the umbrella obligation; customer screening, payments screening, false-positive verification and evasion detection are its component duties.
List sources (UN Consolidated List, local terrorist list) define the screening universe — the scope of the lists determines the scope of the obligation, and omission of a list is itself a breach.

Customer screening sits at the CDD/onboarding and ongoing-monitoring interface, while payments screening attaches to transaction execution; the same name-match logic produces different consequences (refuse relationship vs reject/hold transfer).
False-positive verification is the control that makes discounting an alert defensible; evasion typologies extend the duty beyond literal name matching.

data.why: Treat these two nodes as references to the same primary statute — the federal law establishing the insurance authority and organising its operations — rather than as two independent legal bases. One node surfaces the law in its enabling/fee-setting context and the other in its definitional context (e.g. the meaning of insurance broker), so definitions and scope drawn from one should be read as applying to the other unless an amendment says otherwise. For a decision, cite the parent law once and confirm which consolidated version and amendments apply; because the linkage is inferred from overlapping labels, verify the primary text before relying on the definitional wording.

When assessing whether an institution's risk appetite statement is adequate, it cannot be judged in isolation: the governance framework is the instrument that defines how the board sets, articulates and monitors adherence to appetite and limits. The appetite statement supplies the substantive risk coverage (concentration, IRRBB, liquidity, currency, reputation and compliance, contagion, country/transfer, legal, strategic), while the framework supplies the ownership, escalation and monitoring obligations. Practically, a gap in either instrument undermines the other, so a compliance finding on appetite coverage should be paired with a review of board-level monitoring duties. The link is inferred from conceptual overlap, so confirm the operative articles in the primary text.

Read the governance framework as the board-level layer and the risk management and internal controls regulation as the operational layer imposing enforceable system requirements, including a feedback loop that converts changes in risk into changes in policy, limits and mitigation. A decision on whether a firm meets its risk management obligations should therefore test both the board's articulation and monitoring of appetite and the existence of the dynamic control process required by the regulation. Compliance with one does not evidence compliance with the other. As the link is inferred, verify how the regulation's scope and definitions map to the governance instrument.

The risk management function is one of the named control functions (alongside compliance and internal audit), so obligations attaching to control functions generally — independence from management, objective assessment, reporting and assurance — apply to it directly. Its firm-wide or group-wide strategy-setting, independent challenge of business lines and monitoring duties feed the reporting lines that the control-function regime presumes. For a decision, do not assess the risk function's mandate without also applying the independence and reporting requirements of the control-function definition; this inferred linkage should be confirmed against the defined term in the primary text.

For an Islamic bank, risk appetite is a layered obligation: the baseline risk management standard applies, and the Islamic-specific standard adds mandatory coverage of Shari'ah non-compliance risk, displaced commercial risk, rate of return risk and equity investment risk, with the Higher Shari'ah Authority setting the rules, principles and standards against which Shari'ah compliance is assessed. This means Shari'ah non-compliance is treated as a supervised risk category, not solely an internal religious governance matter, and the internal Shari'ah committee's determinations must sit within HSA parameters. In practice, an appetite statement that meets only the conventional minimum is deficient for an Islamic bank; verify the operative provisions of both standards before concluding.

When deciding whether an Islamic financial institution's product or activity is properly Shari'ah-compliant, treat the HSA framework as the benchmark against which the compliance test is measured, not as a separate parallel standard. The link is conceptual: the definition of Shari'ah compliance for an IFI is expressed by reference to the rules, principles, resolutions and standards set by the Higher Shari'ah Authority, so the internal Shari'ah supervision arrangements operate within that ceiling. Practically, an internal Shari'ah committee determination that conflicts with an HSA position cannot cure non-compliance. This linkage is inferred from the overlapping definitional language, so verify the operative definitions and the HSA's binding effect in the primary texts before relying on it.

For a governance assessment, read the board obligations and the control-function requirements as two halves of the same accountability chain: the board owns oversight, and the control functions (risk, compliance, internal audit) are the mechanism through which that oversight is exercised and evidenced. The connection is inferred from a shared corporate-governance regime rather than an explicit cross-reference, and note the scope difference — one addresses a locally incorporated company's board, the other addresses branches whose control functions report locally but are accountable to group heads. That distinction matters: for a branch there is no local board, so supervisory expectations must be mapped onto local management plus group reporting lines. Confirm which entity type your subject is before applying either set of requirements.

Treat these as the same enabling statute referred to under different labels rather than as two distinct instruments, so obligations sourced to either should be traced to one parent law. The similarity is inferred from the shared citation to the Decretal Federal Law of 2018 concerning the Central Bank and the organisation of financial institutions and activities, which supplies the licensing and rule-making powers underpinning the subordinate regulations. The consequence is that a single amendment or repeal of that statute cascades to both references. Because the naming is inconsistent across documents and one excerpt also cites a different 2018 decretal law on public debt, verify the exact law number and year in the primary text before treating them as identical.

If you are advising a loan-based crowdfunding applicant, read the regulation's grant of licensing and supervisory authority to the Central Bank together with the substantive licensing conditions imposed on the licensee, including governance and residency-style requirements for the chairman, board majority, mandatory positions and heads of functions. The link is an obligation chain: the regulation vests the regulator with authority, and the conditions it enforces define what an applicant must satisfy. Practically, the entity's board composition and local presence are gating items for authorisation, not post-licensing matters. The cross-reference is inferred, so confirm in the primary text that the residency and nationality conditions apply to the crowdfunding regime and not only to another licensed category.

For any question about the legal force of a Central Bank regulation, this link identifies the hierarchy: the regulation is subordinate legislation issued under powers vested in the Central Bank by the Federal Decree-Law establishing it, so its requirements are enforceable as regulator-issued obligations rather than guidance. That matters when assessing whether a notification or filing to the regulator — such as a regulatory capital instrument notification — is mandatory and what sanction follows non-compliance. Note also the dating issue: one reference points to a later decree-law, which may have superseded the earlier enabling statute. Because the relationship is inferred, verify which version of the Central Bank Law is in force and whether transitional provisions preserve regulations issued under the predecessor.

Treat these as related but not interchangeable when deciding which onboarding standard governs a file: the CDD instrument sets the AML/CTF obligation to identify and verify, apply enhanced or simplified measures, keep records current and control reliance on third parties, while the AML/KYC procedures text uses that same terminology inside an account-reporting/due diligence regime that permits satisfying account-level checks by relying on procedures already performed on a pre-existing account. The overlap is the defined concept of KYC/CDD, not the obligation owner or trigger, so a reliance permitted for reporting purposes does not automatically discharge the AML/CTF CDD duty. Because this link is inferred, confirm in the primary texts which regime each requirement sits under before using one to evidence compliance with the other.
data.label: AML/KYC Procedures

data.why: When deciding the depth of diligence on a respondent institution, read the correspondent banking provisions as a specific overlay on the general CDD duty rather than a separate track. The correspondent relationship is a defined term covering accounts and related services, including securities-related arrangements, and such relationships are conventionally treated as higher risk, which engages the enhanced due diligence branch of the CDD framework. Practically, baseline CDD on the respondent is the floor and the correspondent-specific requirements determine the additional checks; verify the primary text for the exact enhanced measures, as this connection is inferred.
data.label: Correspondent Banking Relationship

data.why: For a decision on whether monitoring arrangements are adequate, these two instruments should be read together as statements of the same obligation at different levels: one frames the purpose of ongoing, retrospective review of customer activity against expected behaviour, the other frames the programme-level expectation to detect, investigate and report suspicious transactions and keep activity within risk appetite. They share the same suspicious-transaction reporting chain, so a gap in detection logic is simultaneously a gap in the reporting obligation. Use the programme-level text to judge governance and coverage and the purpose-level text to judge whether alerts are calibrated to anomaly detection; as the link is inferred, check the primary texts for any differing scope or institution type.
data.label: Transaction Monitoring Program

data.why: If the question is what "Shari'ah compliance" requires of an Islamic financial institution, the compliance definition should not be applied in isolation: it points to the governance standard that specifies the framework, organs and oversight through which that compliance is achieved. The relationship is definitional-to-operative, so the governance standard supplies the enforceable structure behind the compliance concept, including for institutions conducting only part of their activities on Shari'ah terms. Read the definition to establish scope and the governance standard to establish the actual duties; the cross-reference is inferred, so confirm the citation in the primary text before relying on it.
data.label: Standard re Shari'ah Governance for IFIs (CBUAE 2825)

data.why: These address the same obligation from two directions and should be used together when assessing residual risk: one treats CDD/KYC as a mitigating control sitting alongside governance, oversight and suspicious-transaction controls, while the other states the underlying duty to perform KYC, CDD and enhanced due diligence as set out in the AML executive regulations. The control-based text presupposes the statutory duty, so weakness in the substantive CDD obligation cannot be offset by describing it as a control that is in place. In practice, credit for mitigation in a risk assessment is only defensible where the underlying regulatory CDD requirements are actually met; verify the specific provisions cited, as this link is inferred.
data.label: Customer Due Diligence

data.why: Treat these as two guidance treatments of the same typology rather than two separate obligations, so a trade-finance control decision should be tested against both rather than one in isolation. Both describe trade-based money laundering as the manipulation of trade transactions to disguise underlying value, counterparties or the true nature of the activity, and both sit in the same AML/CTF guidance family drawing on FATF's TBML work — one framing it alongside proliferation-financing exposure, the other in the general LFI trade-finance context. Practically, red-flag sets and CDD expectations in one should be read as reinforcing the other, and the PF-context framing may add sanctions/TFS screening consequences that the general text does not spell out. The link is inferred from overlapping subject matter, so confirm the specific obligations and scope wording in each primary document before relying on one as a substitute for the other.

When assessing whether an insurer meets capital adequacy, the solvency margin rules cannot be applied without the financial regulations that define who is in scope and on what accounting basis the figures are struck. The solvency text sets the quantitative test — Own Funds, being Basic Own Funds plus a capped portion of Ancillary Own Funds, must cover the Solvency Capital Requirement and Minimum Guarantee Fund — while the financial regulations supply the defined term "Company", which expressly reaches locally incorporated insurers, licensed foreign insurers operating through a branch or agent, and Takaful companies. The consequence is that a foreign branch or a Takaful operator cannot be assumed outside the solvency test on entity-form grounds. The relationship is inferred from shared definitional and prudential subject matter; verify the scope and commencement provisions in the primary instruments.

If you are deciding whether an institution's stress-testing programme is adequate, read it as an output of the risk management system rather than a standalone exercise. The risk management standard enumerates the risk domains that must be covered — underwriting and reserving, asset–liability management, investment including derivatives, liquidity and concentration, and operational risk — while the stress-testing standard frames the risk governance framework through which the board sets strategy, articulates risk appetite and monitors adherence. In practice, a stress-testing scope that omits a domain the risk management system requires to be covered is a defensible finding, and board-level risk appetite is the common anchor for both. Note the two sit in different prudential regimes (insurance-oriented risk management versus bank-oriented stress testing), so check sectoral applicability in the primary text before transposing requirements.

For a record-keeping or books-and-records question, identify the obliged entity from the financial regulations first, then apply the accounting-records requirements. Section 6 governs the principles for organising accounting books and records and the data to be maintained by companies, agents and brokers, while the financial regulations define "Company" to include locally incorporated insurers, licensed foreign insurers operating through a branch or agent, and Takaful companies. The consequence is that intermediaries and foreign-insurer branch structures fall within the record-keeping duty, and the records so maintained are the evidential base for prudential and solvency reporting. The connection is inferred from shared definitions and subject matter; confirm the exact scope and retention terms in the primary instruments.

When testing liquidity risk governance, treat the general risk management standards as the umbrella and the liquidity qualitative requirements as the specific application, so a gap in one is usually a gap in both. The risk management standards place board oversight at the centre — review of risk management policies, approval of the risk appetite statement, and regular and ad hoc reporting from senior management, the risk function and compliance — while the liquidity article allocates to senior management the execution of the board-approved strategy, development of liquidity risk policies and a holistic view of liquidity sources and linkages. The practical consequence is a two-tier accountability chain: board approval of appetite and strategy, senior-management implementation and escalation, with the liquidity-specific rule prevailing where it is more detailed. The link is inferred from a common governance architecture; verify the applicability and any lex specialis wording in the primary text.

For a decision, treat this as a weak institutional association rather than an operative cross-reference: the common factor is the Central Bank itself, which both issues prudential process forms (here, notification in respect of a regulatory capital instrument) and participates in the national sustainable finance coordination body. Nothing in the linked material indicates that sustainable finance workstreams alter the content or timing of a capital instrument notification, which sits in the prudential/governance regime. Practically, do not import sustainability expectations into a regulatory capital filing decision on the strength of this link; because the connection is inferred, confirm against the primary texts before relying on it either way.

These two nodes are best read as two labels for the same enabling statute, so a compliance analysis should not treat them as separate sources of authority or double-count obligations. Both are cited as the power under which subordinate regulation is issued, which places them at the top of the hierarchy: every implementing regulation, standard or circular beneath them must be read consistently with this parent law. The consequence is that a citation to either label anchors the same legal basis; the reader should still verify which consolidated or amended version applies, since amendments to the parent law flow down to all instruments made under it.

The practical question is whether a specialized bank with a low-risk designation is governed by its own tailored circular alone or also by the general capital adequacy regime; the link indicates the former is layered on the latter, not a substitute for it. Both instruments are issued under the same Central Bank authority, and a specialized-bank regime typically operates by modifying or calibrating the baseline capital adequacy requirements rather than displacing them. For a decision, apply the general capital adequacy rules unless the specialized-bank instrument expressly disapplies or varies a specific requirement; as the link is inferred, verify the exact scope and any express carve-outs in the primary texts.

When assessing whether onboarding obligations have been discharged, remember that CDD is one component of a wider KYC obligation chain that also includes customer identification and, where risk warrants, enhanced due diligence. The two nodes share the same AML/CTF defined-term framework, so CDD language in one instrument carries the same meaning within the KYC structure of the other. The consequence is that completing CDD alone does not evidence full KYC compliance, and any gap in identification or in triggering EDD remains a separate breach; confirm the precise definitional boundaries in the primary text before concluding.

This link matters where an insurance sector operator asks which CDD standard governs: the sector-specific measures are an application of the same AML/CTF defined obligation to entities identified by the Insurance Law, not an independent or lighter regime. The general CDD provisions set the baseline (including EDD and simplified due diligence, review and updating, and reliance on third parties), while the insurance material calibrates it to insurance products, intermediaries and policyholder relationships. For a decision, apply the general CDD standard and then layer the sector-specific expectations on top; because the alignment is inferred, verify in the primary texts whether any insurance provision is intended to displace rather than supplement the general rule.

When testing whether a bank's board has discharged its governance duties, treat the Pillar 3 disclosure package as one of the outputs the board is accountable for approving and overseeing, not a purely technical reporting exercise. Both provisions sit in the same instrument, so the board-responsibility article supplies the accountable organ while the Pillar 3 definition imports the Basel Committee's consolidated disclosure framework and its later revisions as the content standard. Practically, a gap in disclosure quality or accuracy can be escalated as a board-level governance failing, and the applicable Basel revision must be identified before judging adequacy. The link is inferred rather than stated, so confirm in the primary text whether the board article expressly names disclosure sign-off.

For a product that holds prefunded value for customers, the first decision is which licensing perimeter it falls into: the stored value facility regime or the payment token regime, since each carries its own authorisation, safeguarding and conduct obligations. Both defined terms capture value held or transferred on behalf of users, with SVF split by device-based and non-device-based delivery and payment token services broken into issuing, buying, selling and exchange activities, so a single business model can appear to touch both. The consequence is that classification must be driven by the defined terms and any express carve-out between the two instruments, because dual or mistaken categorisation changes capital, reserve and reporting duties. This relationship is inferred; verify the scope and exclusion provisions in each regulation before concluding.

A licensee serving retail users must satisfy two distinct obligation sets at the same customer touchpoint: financial crime controls and market conduct duties, and compliance with one does not discharge the other. The AML/CFT provision requires policies and procedures aligned to the AML law and its regulations, while the conduct provision operates within a different regime whose defined persons (such as the lender for whom regulated activities are performed) do not necessarily map onto the AML concept of customer. The practical consequence is a scoping exercise: identify which regime's defined term captures each counterparty before designing onboarding or disclosure controls, since the same relationship may be in scope for one regime and out of scope for the other. The connection is inferred from subject-matter overlap, so verify the applicability clauses of both instruments.

Treat backing assets and regulatory capital as separate pools when assessing a licensee's financial resource adequacy. The reserve of assets exists to back outstanding token liabilities and is also used as a sizing threshold for certain relief, whereas the regulatory capital article sets an own-funds floor and expressly refuses credit for capital held under another authority's requirements, signalling a general anti-double-counting stance. The consequence is that a firm cannot present reserve assets as evidence of capital adequacy, and any assessment must confirm both tests are independently met. The cross-instrument link is inferred; confirm the precise wording of the capital article before relying on the no-double-counting reading.

When assessing exposure to supervisory action on sanctions matters, the relevant question is which authority holds supervisory competence over the entity, because targeted financial sanctions compliance is examined through that supervisory relationship. The AML law provision expands supervisory authority competences over financial institutions, DNFBPs and virtual asset service providers, while the sanctions material sets out the substantive obligations, including UN Security Council regimes that combine targeted financial, activity-based and sectoral measures. The consequence is that TFS failures are supervisable and enforceable through the AML supervisory channel, not only through the sanctions instrument itself. The reference is inferred, so verify that the supervisory competence article expressly extends to sanctions obligations in the primary text.

If you are assessing whether a distribution channel is properly authorised and whether advice duties are met, read the agents regulation and the bank-marketing decision together: both regulate intermediated placement of insurance and Takaful products on behalf of an insurer, but they attach different conditions to different distributors. The agents instrument fixes the agent's mandate limits and duty to advise the applicant on suitable programmes, while the bank decision restricts which product types and classes may be marketed through banks at all. The link is inferred rather than an express cross-reference, so the practical consequence is that a bank channel cannot be treated as equivalent to an appointed agent: check the product-class permission under the banks decision and the conduct/advice obligations separately, and verify the primary text before relying on either as authority for the other.

When classifying an intermediary, you need to decide which licensing and conduct regime applies — insurance agent or insurance producer — and these two instruments define the two adjacent categories within the same insurance intermediation framework. The producers resolution sits in the same series of Insurance Authority board resolutions on insurance-related professions and its recitals chain back to earlier registration and intermediation resolutions, so the definitions and licence conditions are meant to be read as a set rather than in isolation. Consequently, do not apply agent-level authority limits or advice duties to a producer without confirming the producer resolution's own scope; the relationship is inferred, so verify the defining articles in the primary texts.

For a licensing or capital-adequacy decision, treat the transmittal letter as the trigger that fixes the deadline and the bank guarantee as the instrument that must satisfy it. Both sit within the same licensing provision: the letter communicates the Central Bank's requirement for an additional guarantee, and the guarantee itself must be in the format prescribed by the Licensing Division and lodged before the stated date. The consequence is that timing and form are cumulative conditions — a guarantee in the correct format filed after the letter's deadline, or a timely guarantee in a non-prescribed form, is non-compliant.

If you are testing an Islamic financial institution's Shari'ah governance, read the statutory article as the source of the obligation and the standard as the operating detail. The article establishes the Higher Shari'ah Authority and requires institutions conducting Shari'ah-compliant business to submit an annual Internal Shari'ah Supervision Committee report, while the standard elaborates the governance and disclosure expectations flowing from that committee's approval of products and services. The practical consequence is a hierarchy: compliance with the standard's disclosure and governance requirements is how the institution discharges the statutory duty, so a gap in the standard's requirements is evidence of a breach at the higher level, though the precise linkage should be confirmed in the primary text.

When deciding the correct supervisory perimeter for a transaction, note that the same insurance entity can be regulated both at solo level and as part of a group. The first provision governs solo-entity conduct — transfer of a portfolio of policies with its attaching rights and obligations to another insurance company — while the second determines at which level in an ownership chain (company or holding company) group supervision is applied. The consequence is that a portfolio transfer within a group may satisfy the solo transfer conditions yet still engage group-level supervisory requirements or Central Bank discretion over the level of consolidation; this connection is inferred, so confirm both articles before scoping a filing.

When deciding whether a person or entity may act as an insurance producer, agent or broker, read the licensing resolution as the operating rules sitting under the insurance law's definitional and authorising framework rather than as a standalone regime. The law supplies the defined terms (including the status of the insurer and of intermediaries) and the legal basis for licensing, while the Board resolution sets the eligibility, conduct and registration conditions that give those terms practical effect. Consequently, a licensing assessment must satisfy both the statutory definition of the role and the resolution's conditions, and any conflict is resolved in favour of the primary law.

For pricing and policy-documentation decisions in motor insurance, the tariff regulation should be treated as subordinate detail issued under the insurance law's supervisory powers over licensed companies. The law defines who is a company and an intermediary and authorises the regulator to set pricing and disclosure requirements; the tariff regulation then imposes the specific obligations on premium/contribution disclosure in the policy and certificate. In practice, a breach of the tariff rules is also a supervisory breach under the parent law, so enforcement exposure is not limited to the regulation itself.

When allocating responsibility for external audit engagement, independence and oversight, the audit committee rules cannot be applied without the board governance instrument, because the committee derives its mandate, composition and reporting line from the board. The board instrument sets the overarching duties, conflict-of-interest prohibitions and delegation architecture; the audit committee instrument specifies the delegated oversight tasks. The consequence is that delegation to the committee does not discharge the board's residual accountability, and any committee arrangement must be tested for consistency with the board-level conflict and independence requirements.
