These are parallel stress-testing obligations in different prudential instruments, so a bank should not assume one exercise discharges both: the liquidity standard drives sizing and composition of the liquid asset buffer and payment/settlement resilience, while the broader material-risks standard requires stress testing across risk types with contingency and business continuity arrangements. They share a common supervisory expectation of forward-looking scenario analysis but differ in scope and in what the outputs must feed. Read them as cumulative requirements with overlapping methodology; confirm in the primary texts whether the regulator permits an integrated programme to satisfy both.

Back-testing should be assessed as one input into the model validation framework, not as a standalone compliance item: the validation requirements place initial and ongoing model assessment under Board-approved policies with independent review, and back-testing results are among the evidence that ongoing validation relies on. Both provisions sit in the same market risk instrument, which makes the governance chain run from Board policy, through validation, to the testing programme. In practice, deficient or too-short back-testing exposes the firm on the validation obligation as well; the linkage is inferred, so check the primary text for how explicitly back-testing is tied to validation.

A bank seeking trading book treatment must satisfy both limbs together: the trading book provision conditions the book's establishment on a Central Bank-reviewed policy statement identifying eligible activities, and the systems and controls provision imposes frequent revaluation of mark-to-market positions in both banking and trading books. The controls requirement presupposes the trading book boundary set by the policy statement, so the two operate as a single approval-plus-ongoing-obligation chain. The consequence is that trading book designation is not complete at approval; valuation controls must be demonstrable on an ongoing basis. The cross-reference is inferred, so verify the article text.

When assessing risk in a clearing arrangement, do not treat netting as risk reduction unless the resulting net positions settle with legal finality. Netting is defined as a step within clearing that establishes final positions for settlement, while the settlement finality principle governs when and how those positions become irrevocable, including conditioning final settlement of one leg on the other in exchange-of-value systems. Both sit within the same systemically important payment system framework, so the reader should evaluate the netting and finality arrangements together rather than in isolation; the link is inferred from the definitional chain, so verify the governing provisions.

For an SVF issuer, decide which obligations attach to the payment obligations it generates and which attach to the facility itself. The clearing and settlement system definition captures the infrastructure through which SVF payment obligations are cleared or settled, whereas the SVF material addresses product-level risk factors such as maximum stored value and transaction size for money laundering and terrorist financing purposes. Practically, an SVF assessment must cover both the prudential/settlement dimension and the AML/CTF risk rating of the product; this connection is inferred, so confirm the definitions and scope in the primary instruments.

Apply the consolidated version, not the original 2010 text, when advising on conduct obligations. The consolidated instrument is the same Resolution No. 3 of 2010 as amended, and its title shows the scope was widened from insurance companies to insurance companies and insurance-related professions. The consequence is both a currency point and a scope point: entities that were outside the original addressee class may now be captured, so check the amending decision and effective dates in the primary text.

A licence under the retail payment services framework does not exhaust the applicant's obligations: the AML/CFT statute applies in parallel to the licensed activity. The payment services regulation covers the nine categories of digital retail payment services and sits under the central bank's licensing powers, while the AML/CFT law is the primary legislation imposing customer due diligence, reporting and related duties on financial institutions including payment service providers. For a decision, treat authorisation conditions and AML/CFT statutory duties as cumulative; this cross-reference is inferred, so verify how the regulation expressly invokes the law.

Both provisions bear on how a bank may recognise offsetting when calculating capital for derivative exposures, so they should be read together before concluding a given exposure is reduced. The clearing member provision governs when a client bank's exposure may receive favourable counterparty treatment where a clearing member faces a qualifying central counterparty, while the written credit derivatives provision limits when purchased protection may be offset against protection sold on a pool. The practical consequence is that recognition of offsets is conditional in each case and the conditions are not interchangeable; the relationship is inferred from their shared capital-treatment context, so verify the specific paragraphs.

data.summary: An excerpt of CBUAE guidance drawing on the FATF Guidance on Digital Identity, explaining how licensed financial institutions should assess whether a digital ID system is sufficiently reliable and independent for CDD purposes. It sets out assurance-level concepts for the identity proofing and enrollment stage (presence, resolution, evidence, validation, verification, illustrated by NIST-derived tiers) without mandating any particular level, and describes enrollment-stage threats such as impersonation, counterfeit or stolen identity evidence, synthetic identities and IDSP compromise. It addresses institutions subject to CBUAE AML/CTF supervision (UAE regime, not SAMA), and is guidance-level expectation rather than a prescriptive rule.

data.why: When setting or reviewing a remuneration package, the first question is whether the individual sits within a Control Function, because that classification changes the permitted pay mix rather than merely the amount. The compensation rule expressly keys off the Control Functions definition, and the control-functions provisions set out how those functions must be structured in a branch — locally reporting but accountable to group function heads. Practically, staff identified under that definition must receive a pay structure weighted toward fixed rather than variable compensation, so misclassifying a risk, compliance or audit role creates a remuneration breach as well as an independence weakness.

For an Islamic financial institution or Takaful company, the annual reporting package is not only financial: the statutory financial year that frames accounts also frames the annual Shari'ah compliance reporting cycle. The financial-accounts provisions fix the reporting period for licensed financial institutions, while the Shari'ah governance requirements add an annual report on compliance with Shari'ah rules and Higher Shari'ah Authority resolutions, plus any further disclosures the Authority requires. The consequence is that Shari'ah compliance reporting must be planned to the same annual timetable as the financial statements, and HSA resolutions issued during the year form part of the compliance benchmark being reported against.

If a customer, or the beneficial owner of a legal person or arrangement, is identified as a PEP, the due diligence decision is already made: enhanced due diligence applies, and neither transaction size nor apparent low risk permits standard or simplified measures. The PEP provisions operate as a mandatory trigger into the EDD requirements within the wider CDD framework, which also governs review, updating and reliance on third parties. In practice, PEP screening must reach through to beneficial owners, and any third-party reliance arrangement must still deliver EDD-grade information for that relationship.

Before a bank can risk-weight a securitisation exposure under the external ratings-based approach, it must confirm that the rating comes from an external credit assessment institution the Central Bank has recognised as eligible for capital purposes. The ECAI eligibility criteria that govern the standardised approach carry through to SEC-ERBA, which is one of only two permitted securitisation approaches alongside SEC-SA. The consequence is binary: an unrecognised or ineligible rating source removes SEC-ERBA as an option and pushes the exposure to the standardised securitisation treatment, typically with a different capital outcome.

The link appears to be the risk-based approach: the ML/FT risk assessment identifies the factors — customer, product, channel, technology, geography, counterparty — that should determine how intensively CDD is applied, including whether enhanced or simplified measures are justified. On that reading, a firm cannot defend an SDD decision without a documented risk assessment supporting it, and changes in the risk assessment should feed through to the review and updating of existing CDD files. This connection is inferred rather than stated as a direct cross-reference, so the reader should verify the primary text of both instruments before relying on it to justify a calibration decision.

When deciding how far to go on CDD and beneficial-ownership work for corporate and trust-type customers, treat the CBUAE guidance on legal persons and arrangements as the operative expectation and the FATF material it invokes as the interpretive benchmark behind it. The citation signals that the guidance is drafted to align the local AML/CFT obligation set with the international standard-setter's risk-based approach, so FATF language on legal persons/arrangements informs meaning but does not itself create an enforceable duty — enforceability sits in the national AML framework and the CBUAE instrument. Practically, a supervisor is likely to read a control gap against both the guidance and the FATF concept it reflects, so justify risk decisions in those terms. Note this is a CBUAE (UAE) chain, not a SAMA one, and should not be transposed to KSA obligations without separate authority.

For payment-product risk assessments, this link tells you the CBUAE payment-risk guidance is built on specific FATF risk-based-approach papers rather than on general principles, so the reasoning imported is product-scoped — prepaid cards, mobile and internet-based payment services, and correspondent banking. That matters for scope: arguments drawn from the cited FATF material carry weight for those payment channels, but extending them to unrelated products is an analytical stretch you would need to justify separately. Use the citation to evidence that your risk-rating methodology for payment channels is standard-aligned, while recognising the binding obligation still flows from the national AML/CFT framework. Verify the cited FATF versions remain current, as these are dated 2013/2016 publications.

If you are allocating responsibility for a model failure, this link fixes the escalation path: the Model Oversight Committee performs the oversight role but answers upward, with Senior Management and the Board carrying the duty to ensure model risk is actually managed to the required standard. Establishing the committee is therefore delegation of function, not of accountability — a defect in model governance remains attributable to the Board and Senior Management. The consequence is that committee terms of reference, membership and reporting lines should be demonstrably approved and monitored at Board/Senior Management level, since that is where a supervisory finding will land.
